by Allene Symons 


LOS ANGELES — 
Leonard Green & Partners, 
the investment firm behind 
Los Angeles-based Thrifty 
Drug Stores, reportedly has 
moved ahead of other bid- 
ders with an estimated $1 
billion dollar offer and letter 
of intent to acquire PayLess 
Drug Stores from parent 
Kmart Corp. 

If successful in _ its 
takeover bid, the invest- 
ment house will become the 
dominant drug store power 
in the West. Thrifty cur- 
rently has 497 stores in Cal- 
ifornia and PayLess has 565 
stores in 12 Western states, 
including some 200 in Cali- 
fornia. In 1992, sales for pri- 
vately-held Thrifty were 
roughly $2 billion; PayLess 
sales totaled approximately 
$2.3 billion. 

The deal would also re- 
turn Thrifty to states it de- 
parted in recent years—in- 
cluding Idaho and Hawaii. 
Thrifty left those states 


when its Pay ‘n Save sub- 
sidiary was acquired by 
PayLess a year ago. 
Executives at PayLess, 
Kmart and Thrifty would 
not acknowledge that a let- 
ter of intent has been 


signed. Such a document 
would enable Leonard 
Green & Partners to review 
PayLess’ financial records. 
Kmart spokesman Orren 
Knauer told Drug Store 
News that he would “nei- 


ther confirm nor deny” the 
reported negotiations with 
Leonard Green & Partners. 
Kmart announced its in- 
tention to sell PayLess 
roughly two months ago. 
The Los Angeles Times 


Chain drug operators 
may want to keep a closer 
eye on Sam’s Club now 
that the 385-unit division 
of Wal-Mart Stores has 
agreed to acquire the bulk 
of Kmart Corp.’s PACE 
Membership Warehouse 
subsidiary. 

In a deal valued at 
roughly $300 million, 
Sam’s will purchase the 
assets and leases of 91 of 
Kmart’s 113 PACE ware- 
house club units. Sam’s is 
already the largest of the 
club store operators, and 
the acquisition will pre- 
sent Wal-Mart with even 


Kmart’s PACE division to go to Wal-Mart 


greater volume buying op- 
portunities and opera- 
tional efficiencies. Sam’s 
derives most of its sales 
from food and hard lines, 
but a shift in product mix 
toward increased HBA of- 
ferings could siphon off 
some drug store shoppers. 


Analysts wondering 


The deal is expected to 
be complete in January 
1994 and must clear feder- 
al antitrust provisions. It 
has produced a bit of head 
scratching among retail 
wags, given the recent 
weakening of the funda- 


mentals of the club store 
business. Some analysts 
are wondering why Wal- 
Mart would sink resources 
into PACE, which had $63 
million in operating losses 
during the first six 
months of the year. 

Kmart will suffer addi- 
tional losses as well. The 
2,430-store discounter will 
take a $450 million charge 
against fourth-quarter 
earnings associated with 
closing 41 PACE units 
that weren’t sold to Sam’s. 
Nineteen of those 41 units 
are under contract but 
haven’t been opened.

Sr. vp Moore resigns from Hook-SupeRx 


CINCINNATI, Ohio — 
Michael Moore, who as se- 
nior vice president and chief 
operating officer served as 
the No. 2 executive at Hook- 
SupeRx, Inc., has abruptly 
resigned “to pursue other 
business interests,” accord- 
ing to a statement by HSI 
chairman and chief execu- 
tive Phil Beekman. 

No other explanation was 
given for Moore’s resigna- 
tion, which was effective 
Oct. 20. According to Chris 
Beseler, HSI vice president 
of advertising and sales 


promotion, no replacement 
for Moore is planned “in the 
foreseeable future.” 

The executives overseen 
by Moore under HSI’s re- 
cently consolidated man- 
agement structure—includ- 
ing corporate vice president 
of store operations Tom 
Stilgenbauer, vice president 
of marketing Bill Welsh and 
vice president of pharmacy 
services Richard Powis— 
will now report directly to 
Beekman, Beseler told 
Drug Store News. 

Moore’s is the second re- 


cent high-level departure at 
HSI, following that of for- 
mer vice president of mar- 
keting Margaret Urquhart. 
It comes in the midst of an 
ongoing consolidation in 
which Stilgenbauer rose to 
become head of company- 
wide store operations for 
HSI’s Hook, SupeRx and 
Brooks Drug divisions. 

Recently, Stilgenbauer 
completed the realignment 
of HSI into five new operat- 
ing regions which split the 
three divisions along geo- 
graphic lines. 


Wilber to sever ties at Drug Emporium 


by James Frederick 


COLUMBUS, Ohio — Cit- 
ing poor health, Drug Em- 
porium vice chairman and 
former chief executive Gary 
Wilber said he will leave the 
deep discount chain founded 
by his father 16 years ago. 

Wilber, who is battling 
cancer, said his decision to 
step down was strictly per- 
sonal and health related, 
and “reflects in no way on 


the company. 

“In fact,” he said, “I have 
the greatest confidence in 
the current direction of Drug 
Emporium, its long-term 
prospects, its management 
and its board of directors.” 

Wilber told Drug Empori- 
um’s board in mid-October 
that he would step down as 
vice chairman effective 
April 29, 1994. He also an- 
nounced ke would not 
stand for re-election to the 
board when his term ex- 


pires in June. 

Wilber has been an officer 
and director of Drug Empo- 
rium since its founding in 
1977, and served as its chief 
executive from January 
1990 to December 1992. Be- 
ginning with a single off- 
price store, the father-son 
team of Phil and Gary 
Wilber guided Drug Empo- 
rium into national promi- 
nence through corporate 
and franchise expansion in

NEWS IN BRIEF 


Revco acquires 7 Cleveland sites 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco D.S. has acquired sev- 
en units from eight-unit Fox Drug Stores in the 
greater Cleveland area. The addition of the stores 
brings Revco’s store count in the greater Cleveland 
area to 111 units. 

The Fox family will continue to operate one unit as 
an independent. 


Kmart adds execs, Super Center div. 


TROY, Mich. — Kmart Corp. has announced a se- 
ries of executive moves in conjunction with the cre- 
ation of a distinct division for its Super Kmart Center 
operations. 

Joseph Thomas, formerly executive vice president of 
international and administration, will become execu- 
tive vice president of U.S. Kmart Stores. Richard 
Miller, formerly executive vice president of U.S. 
Kmart stores, has been named executive vice presi- 
dent of Super Kmart Stores. 

Chairman and chief executive officer Joe Antonini 
said the creation of a separate division reporting to 
Miller will sharpen Kmart’s focus on the growth and 
development of Super Kmart Centers, which include 
pharmacies and full grocery departments. Kmart will 
operate 17 Super Centers by the end of 1993; 60 to 75 
more sites are planned for 1994. 


Revco names new Rx director 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco D.S. has named for- 
mer pharmacy supervisor Melenie Petropoulos to re- 
place Jim Ayres as director of pharmacy operations. 


Ayres hag Se Oct. 22 to take a post with Blue 
Cross/Blue Shield of Ohio. 


NAGMR honors Hirschfield 


CHICAGO — The National Association General 
Merchandise Representatives (NAGMR) honored 
Allen Hirschfield, president of Pankow Associates, 
with its Award of Excellence at its 45th annual con- 
vention in Orlando, Fla., last month. | 

The award is given to members who have con- 
tributed their talents to the sales rep profession, the 
association and the community. 


AHBAI elects several officers 


CHICAGO — Frank Davie, president of W.O.C. 
Products Inc., has been named chairman of the Amer- 
ican Health and Beauty Aids Institute (AHBAI). He 
replaces outgoing chairman Nathaniel Bronner Jr., 
vice president of manufacturing for Bronner Brothers. 

Other newly elected officers include: Joe Dudley 
Sr., president of Dudley Products Inc.; Ernest 
Joshua, chairman of J.S. Products Inc.; Chapman 
Cannon Jr., chairman and president of American 
Beauty Products Company; Al Washington, presi- 
dent of AFAM Concepts Inc.; Jerry White, president 
of Kizure Professional Products; and A.W. Curtis of 
A.W. Curtis Laboratories. 


Solganik receives Revco award 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Marvin Solganik, formerly 
Revco's senior vice president of real estate and corpo- 
rate development, was this year's recipient of Revco's 
Governor's Award, which is presented annually to an 
individual whose performance is deemed outstanding. 

Solganik, who retired this spring and continues to 
work with Revco as a consultant, was recognized for 
his pivitol role in the growth of the company. During 
his 25 years at the chain, he was responsible for real 
estate acquisitions totalling over 14 million square 
feet and leasing 3,000 stores.

Drug Store News, November 15, 1993 


by Mike Troy 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
Crown Drugs, a 19-unit 
chain based in Winston- 
Salem, N.C., has agreed to a 
takeover by Eckerd Corp. in 
a deal expected to be com- 
pleted by late November. 

The purchase will push 
Eckerd’s North Carolina 
store count to almost 200, 
and is in line with the chain’s 
strategy of strengthening its 
position in existing markets 
through acquisitions. The re- 
tailer already has 178 stores 
in that state, compared to its 
two largest markets, Florida 
with 543 stores and Texas 
with 476 stores. 


Eckerd plans to acquire 
N.C.-based Crown Drugs 


“The acquisition of Crown 
Drugs is an excellent addi- 
tion to our company and a 
solid merger with our exist- 
ing operation in the Win- 
ston-Salem area,” said 
chairman and chief execu- 
tive Stewart Turley. 

Crown president Ray 
Gentry, who began his ca- 
reer behind the soda foun- 
tain in 1954 when Crown 
only had one store, told 
Drug Store News he is 
pleased with the deal. 

“We have been courted by 
a whole lot of people in the 
last year, but Eckerd came 
in with what we felt was a 
very good marriage,” Gentry 
said. “They have a really 
good name here.” 


Once conversion of the 
Crown units is complete, 
Eckerd should be able to 
overtake Revco D.S. as the 
Winston-Salem market 
leader. Elsewhere in the 
state, Eckerd leads Revco in 
the Charlotte/Gastonia mar- 
ket, but trails Kerr Drug in 
the Raleigh/ Durham/Chapel 
Hill market, where Kerr has 
the bulk of its 96 stores. 

“lm not a bit surprised 
that Eckerd has bought 
[Crown],” said Johnny Kerr, 
president of Kerr Drug. 
“We'd have loved to have 
bought [it]. [It has] some 
good stores and it would 
have given us a new market.” 

The buyout will push Eck- 
erd’s store count above 1,700.

NEW YORK— Marie Grif- 
fin has joined Drug Store 
News and Drug Store News 
For the Pharmacist as editor- 


in-chief. Reporting to Jay 4 


Forbes, vice president/pub- Re 
lisher, Griffin will oversee all 


editorial functions of the two 
publications. 

Griffin comes to Lebhar- 
Friedman from Jobson Pub- 
lishing, where she was editor 
of 20/20, the leading monthly 


Griffin 


publication in the eyewear 


field. Prior to that, she spent four years with 
Fairchild Publications, where she was editor 
of three different retailing publications: 
High Points, a tabloid for furniture retail- 
ers; HF'D’s Housewares & Tabletop Report, a 
weekly section on product news and mer- 
chandising, and Entree, a monthly magazine 
for retailers of upscale housewares products. 


Earlier in her 12-year ca- 
reer in business journalism, 
Griffin held editorial posi- 
tions on Kitchen & Bath De- 


| sign News and Successful 


Meetings, a monthly maga- 
zine for corporate and associ- 
ation meeting planners. 
“Drug Store News is the 
leading publication in its field, 
and we're proud of that fact,” 
said Griffin. “But the competi- 
tive and constantly changing 


business environment today de- 
mands more from everyone—drug chains, 
suppliers and, of course, publications. With 
the talented team of people we have in place, 
we will be working to bring even more valu- 
able information to all our readers, whether 
that is in the form of news stories, special 
sections, research projects, conferences and 
roundtables or other vehicles.” 


Walgreens to build $60M western DC 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Un- 
derscoring its determined 
assault on Northern Califor- 
nia, Walgreen Co. said it 
will build a $60-million, 
300,000-square-foot 
distribution center in Wood- 
land, Calif. Construction is 
set to begin in the spring, 
with a scheduled opening 


date of June 1, 1995. 

The center—which wil] 
feature electronic sortation 
systems and be expandable 
to 500,000 square feet—will 
initially serve some 125 
Walgreens stores in Califor- 
nia. The chain now has 96 
units open in the state, with 
20 new stores due in the 


next 12 months. 

“We've targeted Northern 
California and the Central 
Valley as one of our top ex- 
pansion areas,” says Bill 
Shiel, senior vp of facilities 
development. “That brings 
with it the need for a full-line 
[DC] in California that will 
take us into the year 2000.”

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


In Harrisburg, Pa., a U.S. district 
court is poring over charges filed by 
Revco, Rite Aid, Thrifty and other 
leading drug chains that major phar- 
maceutical manufacturers systemati- 
cally engage in price fixing conspira- 
cies, as well as illegal price 
discrimination, in favor of HMOs and 
mail-order pharmacy operators. 

In San Francisco, independent Fred 
Mayer is spearheading a series of class 
action antitrust suits to curb discrimi- 
natory pricing by drug wholesalers, as 


while, federal an- 
titrusters are 
awakening, after 
over a decade of 
inaction, to discover that the nation’s 
drug stores are in the center of a series 
of serious competitive problems. 

The Federal Trade Commission has 
filed antitrust charges against both the 
Baltimore and Maryland Pharmacists 
Associations for allegedly orchestrating 
a boycott of the third-party pre- 
scription drug plan for city employees. 

Across the street at the Justice De- 
partment, Anne Bingaman, antitrust 
division director, turned down plans 
by major pharmaceutical manufactur- 


ourts carve out drug industry's future 


ers to jointly limit future price increas- 
es, calling the scheme a “clearly ille- 
gal” effort to fix prescription prices. 

At the same time, federal an- 
titrusters are continuing to delay final 
approval of the Merck/Medco merger 
pending further information from 
tight-lipped officials at the drug firm. 

In addition to sifting through widely 
publicized charges that the merger 
would have anticompetitive effects 
throughout the drug delivery system, 
FTC antitrusters have fresh meat to 
chew on—suggestions that the APhA’s 
involvement in designing new pharma- 
cy compensation plans for Medco may 
create still more antitrust concerns. 

All this has taken place within the 
past 90 days or so. And the indications 
are it’s just the beginning. 

Pharmacy groups in Oklahoma, Cal- 
ifornia and more than a dozen other 
states with anti-loss-leader statutes 
have been encouraged by Arkansas’ 
predatory pricing decision to bring 
similar damage suits against Wal- 
Mart and other chains. 

The litigation alleging price discrim- 
ination by manufacturers and whole- 
salers is certain to generate additional 
courtroom fireworks over the next 12 
months. 

Provisions of the Clinton Adminis- 
tration’s health reform plan to elimi- 
nate “class of trade” discounts by 
suppliers of pharmaceutical products 
could keep the antitrust pot boiling 
for years. 

By then, we may all be ready to take 
the bar exam. 


by Barbara White 


NEW YORK — In a long- 
awaited move, Genovese 
Drug Stores has finally 
weighed into the Manhattan 
market with a glitzy, 7,500- 
square-foot store on the 
city’s Upper East Side. The 
chain’s entry was a splashy 
one, with top company brass 
mingling with hundreds of 
customers who packed the 
store throughout opening 
day Nov. 2. 

Genovese will operate 
both front-end and pharma- 
cy here 24 hours a day, mak- 
ing it one of only two round- 
the-clock pharmacies in 
Manhattan. (The other is

with the opening-day crowd at Genovese’s first Manhattan site.

THE VITAMIN CONSUMER: AN EXCLUSIVE REPORT 


by Mike Troy 
OTC Specialist 


itamins and nutri- 
tional supplements 
have been a strong 


drug store staple for genera- 
tions, and factors like an ag- 
ing population and a more 
health-conscious consumer 
are injecting new growth po- 
tential into the category. 
What’s more, a new, exclu- 
Sive consumer survey con- 
ducted by Leo J. Shapiro & 
Associates and sponsored by 
Drug Store News indicates 
that the sales potential for 
vitamins and other supple- 
ments has yet to be fully 
tapped. 

Sales of vitamins and nu- 
tritionals are up 10 percent 
through June of this year, 
and they show no sign of 
slowing. One reason: The 
benefits of antioxidant 
nutrients continue to get 
wide play in the consumer 
press. Growing numbers of 
consumers managing their 
health through diet, exer- 
cise and nutritional supple- 
mentation want the vitamin 
products drug stores sell, 
and the Shapiro study indi- 
cates the market is far from 
saturated. 


Survey statistics 


Four out of 10 Americans 
supplement their diets with 
vitamins and mineral prod- 
ucts, study results indicate. 
Consumption is greater 
among those under 17, with 
half of those in the adoles- 


Pharmacist input in vitamin sales remains minimal 


Vitamins frequently have 
a shelf position that is one 
of the closest to the pharma- 
cy. Yet the role of the phar- 
macist in the category is 
minimal, according to the 
Drug Store News/Leo J. 
Shapiro study of consumer 
attitudes on vitamins. 

Only 2 percent of survey 
respondents said the vita- 
mins they bought were rec- 
ommended by a pharmacist. 
A physician is the most fre- 
quent source of advice on 
the category, with 26 per- 
cent of those surveyed indi- 
cating they follow their doc- 
tor’s suggestions.

Educating the consumer 


“IT can say retailers had 
better educate themselves 
and learn about these prod- 
ucts so they can educate 
their customers and make 
recommendations,” said Jef-

of the Antioxidant Research 
Laboratory with’ the 
U.S.D.A. Human Nutrition 
Research Center on Aging 


at Tufts University. “People 
want information, and the 
pharmacists that can pro- 
vide it will be offering an 
important service to their 
customers.” 

Blumberg, one of the 
foremost authorities on 
antioxidants, the hottest 
segment of the vitamin cat- 
egory, is well regarded for 
his work on the different 
nutritional needs of the el- 
derly. He noted that al- 
ready products targeted to 
specific age groups line 
sture shelves.

@ About 30 percent of sur-

last bought their nutritional

Health food stores were only 
one percentage point behind 
at 16 percent. 

@ Vitamins are a valuable 
trip generator for drug 
stores. Respondents said 
they buy supplements about 
once a month and spend an 
average of $80 a year. 
Among heavy users—those 
who spend more than a 
$100 annually—discount

the location of their most re- 
cent purchase. Health food 
and drug stores account for 
24 percent each among 
heavy users, followed by 
food stores with 10 percent.

One change Blumberg 
would like to see is a move 
by the Food and Drug Ad- 
ministration to allow manu- 
facturers of vitamins to 
make health-related claims 
for products. Such a move, 
he said, would likely boost 
vitamin sales further. 

“(The] FDA’s position has 
been any health claim for 
any compound turns that 
compound into a drug, and 
then you get into clinical 
trials, toxicity tests and all 
sorts of other things. For 
obvious reasons, no one is 
going to do that for a nutri- 
ent because they are not 
patentable,” Blumberg said. 

“They ought to be able to 
make health claims for 
these things. Valid and 
truthful claims on labels 
will make it easier for con- 
Sumers to understand 
which product is right for 
them,” he added.

The power of nutrition, as

to benefit the vitamin cate- 
gory as new _ research 
strengthens the health pro- 
moting and disease fighting

minerals. 

“Clearly, one way to get 
this information to people is 
through labels,” Blumberg 
said. 


The Clinton Administra- 
tion’s health care reform 
proposals are weighing 
heavily on the minds of 
chain drug executives, but 
reform of another kind is 
looming over one aspect of 
their business. 

Congress and the Food 
and Drug Administration 
are wrestling with how to 
rein in a rapidly growing 
nutritional supplement in- 
dustry. Vitamins and min- 
erals are regulated as 
foods and are not required 
to undergo the same rigor- 
ous standards as other 
OTC products which carry 
an indication and must 
prove their safety and ef- 
fectiveness. 

The FDA contends that 
some manufacturers take 
advantage of this situation 
and make unsubstantiated 
health claims for their 
products. Recent months 
have seen this issue debat- 
ed in congressional hear- 
ings. 

During an October hear- 
ing of the Senate Labor 
and Human Resources 
Committee, chairman Sen. 
Edward Kennedy (D- 
Mass.) said he believes the 
FDA should have a sepa- 
rate category for the regu- 
lation of dietary supple- 
ments. FDA commissioner 
David Kessler, speaking 
before the committee, 


Federal regulation 
appears likely 


‘based on an FDA report 


agreed with the concept of 
a separate category. Previ- 
ously, Kessler had said the 
dietary supplement indus- 
try is essentially unregu- 
lated. 

“For every dietary sup- 
plement on the market 
that has some value, un- 
fortunately, there are 100 
or even more out there 
that are worthless,” 
Kessler said. 

Kessler’s comments were 


called “Unsubstantiated 
Claims and Documented 
Health Hazards in the Di- 
etary Supplement Market- 
place.” 

While involvement by 
federal regulatory agencies 
is generally regarded as a 
bad sign, it could actually 
fuel product sales. If the 
FDA allows manufacturers 
to make health claims 
based on a standard of sig- 
nificant scientific agree- 
ment for certain vitamins 
and minerals, it would in- 
crease consumer under- 
standing of what the prod- 
ucts can and cannot do. 

Many retailers have no- 
ticed sales increases in the 
category whenever there is 
increased publicity in the 
consumer press about the 
benefits of nutritional sup- 


plements. Health claims 
on labels could produce a 
similar result. 


product quality.

A familiar name with 
consumers will get a new 
look in early 1994 when 
Miles Inc. repositions its 
53-year-old line of One-A- 
Day vitamins. 

The relaunch will in- 
clude new _ products, 
reformulations, repackag- 
ing and a new retail shelf- 
stocking system that at- 
tempts to make vitamin 
shopping and selling easi- 
er, according to the manu- 
facturer. 

“Many consumers have 
responded that buying 
vitamins today is especial- 
ly confusing, considering 
the proliferation of prod- 
ucts and lack of informa- 
tion available to make 


Miles plans One-A-Day relaunch 


wise selections,” said One- 
A-Day product manager 
Steve Levy. “We aim to 
take the confusion out of 
the vitamin buying process 
by providing vitamins for- 
mulated for who you are 
and how you live.” 

The new One-A-Day line 
comes in five formulations, 
including individual prod- 
ucts for men and women 
as well as a maximum 
strength formula with 12 
essential vitamins and 13 
minerals; an “essential” 
formula which provides 
100 percent of the U.S. 
RDA for 11 essential vi- 
tamins; and 55 Plus, a for- 
mula targeted to mature 
adults.

Wall Street hungry 
for Eckerd debt 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
Eckerd Corp. has achieved 
further reductions in annual 
interest expenses with a re- 
cent $200 million bond offer- 
ing. Originally planned as a 
$100 million offering, Eckerd 
spokesman Gerry Hoeppner 
said strong investor interest 
and favorable rates allowed 
the issue size to be doubled. 

The issue was priced at 
par to yield 9.25 percent. 
The original range was 
9.375 percent to 9.5 percent. 

“We are pleased with the 
reaction in the financial com- 
munity, and believe it shows 
confidence in our manage- 
ment and in our company’s 
direction,” Hoeppner said. 

Proceeds were used to re- 
deem higher yielding bonds 
and will save about $5.5 
million annually in interest 
expenses. That will add to 
an estimated $40 million in 
annual interest savings 
associated with a $950 mil- 


lion bank refinancing and 
stock offering completed 
earlier this year. 

Debt reduction is crucial 
to Eckerd’s success. The 
company has seen earnings 
in recent years eroded by 
debt payments related to its 
1986 leveraged buyout. 

Standard & Poor’s (S&P) 
and Moody’s Investors Ser- 
vice still give the retailer be- 
low-investment-grade debt 
ratings, but reports from 
both agencies reflect aware- 
ness of continuing improve- 
ments. S&P recently re- 
moved Eckerd from its 
CreditWatch and rated its 
senior debt BB-. The recent 
offering, which is subordi- 
nated debt, is rated B by 
S&P and B-2 by Moody’s. 

“We like drug retailing 
and think Eckerd is a fairly 
good business,” said S&P as- 
sociate director Alison Lew. 
“It’s just that [its] balance 
sheet needs to be shored up.” 


Arbor settles dispute, 
takes loss in final quarter 


TROY, Mich. — Putting a 
major headache behind it, 
Arbor Drugs announced the 
$15 million settlement of a 
reimbursement claim with 
Blue Cross of Michigan 
which significantly cut into 
earnings for its fiscal year 
ended July 31. 

The dispute with Blue 
Cross stemmed from dis- 
agreement over prescription 
charges billed to the giant 
third-party carrier. 

Said Arbor chief executive 
Eugene Applebaum, “Al- 
though we believe that our 
charges to Blue Cross were 
consistent with the terms of 
Our agreements, we feel 
that the settlement of the 
dispute is in the company’s 
best overall interests. I am 
pleased to add that Arbor 
will be participating in Blue 


Cross’ pharmacy plans, con- 
tinuing a working relation- 
ship that extends back over 
25 years.” 

The one-time charges— 
and disposition of an earlier 
lease dispute—led to a 
fourth-quarter loss of $6.0 
million and cut fiscal 1993 
earnings to $6.9 million. Ex- 
cluding the charges, net in- 
come for the year would 
have been up 14 percent to 
$18.0 million. 

Net sales for the year rose 
12.2 percent, to $535.0 mil- 
lion, cracking the half-bil- 
lion-dollar milestone for the 
first time. Same-store sales 
for the year were up a 
healthy 7.0 percent. 

The 141-store chain 
opened 15 new stores in fis- 
cal 93, with 20 openings set 
for 1994.

NEWS IN BRIEF | . 


Former Phar-Mor CFO sentenced 


CLEVELAND — Patrick Finn, former chief finan- 
cial officer of Phar-Mor, has been sentenced to 33 
months in prison for participating in a $1 billion fraud 
and embezzlement scheme that staggered the off-price 
drug chain last year and led to Chapter 11 filing. 

Finn, who pleaded guilty last spring to fraud and 
money laundering charges, was also ordered by U.S. 
District Judge George White to pay $7,700 in fines. At 
press time, Finn remained free on bond but was due 
to surrender voluntarily to begin serving his sen- 
tence—probably at the McKean Correctional Facility 
in Bradford, Pa. 

In a plea-bargain, Finn has also agreed to testify 
against his former boss at Phar-Mor, Michael “Mick- 
ey” Monus. Monus, a Phar-Mor founder and former 
president who is accused of masterminding the 
scheme and embezzling more than $10 million from 
the chain largely to finance the now-defunct World 
Basketball League, is due to stand trial beginning 
Feb. 14, 1994 in White’s courtroom here. 

Monus, Finn and Jeffrey Walley, a former vice 
president, were accused of a massive scheme to de- 
fraud Phar-Mor and its investors by overstating in- 


ventory values and misrepresenting the company’s © 


level of profitability. The bookkeeping scandal, which 
came to light in mid-1992, led Phar-Mor to take $499 
million in charges against earnings, to file for Chapter 
11 bankruptcy protection and to sell or shutter nearly 
half its 310 deep discount stores. 

Walley was sentenced in May to six months of home 
detention. 


Contracts go to Bergen Brunswig 


ORANGE, Calif. — Bergen Brunswig Corp. has 
been awarded two renewable one-year contracts by 
the Department of Defense to supply the majority of 
the DOD’s pharmaceutical purchases for 18 military 
hospitals in the Department’s Philadelphia and Tide- 
water, Va. regions. 


Walker Drug expands its reach 


MACON, Ga. — Georgia drug wholesaler Coleman, 
Meadows and Pate has been acquired by Walker Drug 
Company of Birmingham, Ala. The acquisition will 
strengthen Walker’s position, particularly in Georgia, 
where most of the clients served by Coleman, Mead- 
ows and Pate (CMP) are located. Walker currently 
serves about 1,000 retail and institutional customers 
throughout the southeast. 

Walker will continue to operate CMP in its current 
location in Macon with its current management, sales 
and work force intact, according to Bill Walker III, 
chief executive officer of Walker. 

Walker is one of the nation’s top 15 drug wholesalers. 


Pathmark recapitalization finished 


WOODBRIDGE, N.J. — Pathmark Stores Inc. has 
completed a recapitalization plan that is designed to re- 
duce its interest expense and allow it to devote its capi- 
tal to its core supermarket and drug store businesses. 

Under the plan, a new holding company subsidiary, 
Newco, has been created, and all capital stock has 
been transferred to that new subsidiary. Pathmark 
has also spun off to Newco its Rickel home center 
business, along with other inventory and assets, in- 
cluding the warehouse and transportation facilities 
that service Pathmark food and drug stwres. 

Under the recapitalization, the compariy has secured a 
bank credit ment, which includes $575 million in 
loans and working capital agreements. It has also issued 
$560 million in senior and junior subordinated notes, or 
junk bonds, due in 2003. The recapitalization involves 
the issue of new subordinated notes and debentures in 
exchange for nearly $300 million in existing debt. 

Pathmark’s earnings have sunk to $23.9 million for 
the second quarter ended July 31, compared to the $44.5 
million reported in the same period the previous year.

® Retailers will need to

& Co. known for his bullish

the minor to the major 
leagues. Understand that

employees by $15.5 billion in the first 
year alone. 

Meanwhile, small business groups, 
which have sided with independent 
druggists on other issues, are even 
more strident in their opposition to the 
Clinton health reform prescription. 
The National Federation of Indepen- 
dent Business is warning that the 
plan will force thousands of small em- 


ployers to close shop altogether and 
eliminate hundreds of thousands of 
jobs for American workers. 

Within the drug industry, wholesale 
druggists have raised concerns over 
the Administration’s failure to guaran- 
tee all patients the freedom to choose 
their own pharmacy provider, while 
pharmaceutical manufacturers are 
outraged by provisions they say would 
regulate drug prices like a “public util- 
ity.” 

Even within the pharmacy family, 
support for the Clinton reforms is far 
from unqualified. Unlike the 
NARD/NACDS coalition, the APhA’s 
rival alliance of non-retail pharmacy 
organizations appears to be with- 
holding its unequivocal endorsement 
of the plan pending additional legisla- 
tive concessions. 

And mail-order pharmacy leaders 
are pushing an agenda of their own 
that differs materially from that of the 
drug store industry. These conflicting 
positions and interests will place retail 
pharmacy in a delicate position as the 
debate over health care reform 
intensifies. 

On one hand, NARD and NACDS 
must make sure that their own mem- 
bers aren’t overly influenced by critics 
of the White House package. 

On the other, they must guard 
against the possibility that the Clinton 
Administration may seek to win sup- 
port from other groups by back- 
tracking on the provisions that at- 
tracted retail pharmacy’s endorsement 
in the first place.

Both appointments signal 
Perry’s growing recognition 
that the marketplace of the 
90s will demand new think- 
ing and new solutions. In an 
exclusive interview with 
Drug Store News, Giancamil- 


li said the chain must focus 
on its image as a customer- 
friendly, conveniently locat- 
ed basic drug store. “The 
days of going toe-to-toe (on 
price) with the Wal-Marts 
and Pace Clubs of the world 
are over,” he said 

Instead, Giancamilli said, 
Perry will attack its costs 
through technology and

cultivates its health care 
and convenience image and 
positions itself for the era of 
health care reform. That 
means the 212-store chain 
“will continue to make big 
strides in tecnnology,” he 
said, in a quest for ever- 
smarter merchandising, 
faster turns and quicker re- 
sponse to consumer demand. 

The next step in that pro- 
cess: rollout of a direct store 
delivery system, by which 
all inventory coming into 
the back room of the store is 
scanned into the inventory 
control system. Perry is al- 
ready chainwide with point 
of sale scanners, so the 
back-end receiving system 
will forge another big link 
in its efforts to buy, move 
and track its products from 
supplier to checkout. 

“Having a computer in the

back room of every store will

Stand-up tubes, baking soda, 
promotion propel toothpaste 


by Barbara White 


ew introductions and 
| N packaging changes are 
driving the $1.3-billion 

U.S. toothpaste market. 

The national rollout of 
Chesebrough-Pond’s Men- 
tadent, the first product to 
combine baking soda, per- 
oxide and fluoride in one 
formulation, began in Sep- 
tember. 

Regional tests showed a 
strong market for the prod- 
uct, which retails for a hefty 
$3.49. And retailers are 
making a nice margin— 
about 25 percent—on the 
product in this competitive 
category made up largely of 
loss leaders. 

Said one retailer: “This is 
the first innovative product 
to come along in a while. It 
gives us a niche and a nice 
ring. I just hope that every- 
one doesn’t discount it right 
away. We’re our own worst 
enemies where that’s con- 
cerned.” 


The baking soda craze 


Baking soda is certainly 
the most popular ingredient 
in toothpastes. First incor- 
porated in product years 
ago by Arm & Hammer and 
regional supplier Tom’s of 
Maine, baking soda is now 
found in a number of premi- 
um price niche products. 

Among the newest are 
Colgate’s two baking soda 
products, sold under the Col- 
gate and Ultra Brite names. 
Colgate is also testing its 
Total product abroad while 
it awaits a green light from 
the Food & Drug Adminis- 
tration to market it here. 
The product contains a bac- 
teria-fighting ingredient not 
yet approved by the FDA. 

Thanks in part to the 
graying of America—and re- 
ceding gums—sales of sen- 
sitive formulas have spurt- 
ed. That segment alone 
grew 20 percent last year, 
according to one manufac- 
turer’s estimate. 

Oral-B will enter the 
toothpaste market this 
month with two formula- 
tions—sensitive and tooth 
and gum care. The products 
will be premium priced, at 
$1.99 to $2.99. 

SmithKline has a sensi- 
tive formula version of Aqua 
Fresh, and P&G will be in- 
troducing a sensitive Crest 
line extension this year. 


Stand-ups are in 


But niche products aren’t 
the only news in toothpaste.

Toothbrushes have gone 
high-tech. Consumers, more 
concerned than ever about 
the health of their teeth and 
gums, are paying more for 
toothbrushes that promise a 
Superior performance. 

“The increased media at- 
tention to oral hygiene and 
heightened promotions have 
really grown the category,” 
says Nigel Burton, general 
manager of U.S. oral care 
for Colgate-Palmolive. “In- 
dustry-wide, growth in the 
category has been about 7 
percent so far for 1993 
across all outlets.” 

Everyone is getting into 
the game. 

Procter & Gamble, which 
didn’t have a toothbrush on

the market two years ago, 
added its high-tech Crest 
Complete last year. 

Says Colgate’s Burton, as 
manufacturers add features 
that give brushes a value- 
added aspect, consumers 
have been willing to trade 
up to brushes that retail 
above $2. 

Added value can mean 
color-streaked bristles that 
“tell” the consumer that a 
brush should be replaced, as 
in Oral-B’s Indicator; triple- 
action bristles to help fight 
gum disease, as in Colgate’s 
Precision; or a tapered head 
that makes brushing rear 
teeth easier, as in Oral-B’s 
new Advantage line. 

Suppliers are also spend- 


New, improved toothbrushes are crowding shelves, and con- 
sumers are willing to trade up to brushes that retail over $2. 


More Americans, motivat- 
ed by increased media atten- 
tion on gum disease, are fo- 
cusing more intently on 
tooth and gum care. 

Not only is that trend ex- 
pressed in the array of high- 
er-performance toothbrush- 
es and toothpastes currently 
crowding drug store shelves 
(see “Stand-up tubes, baking 
soda and promotion drive 
toothpaste” and “Consumers 
continue toothbrush trade- 
up” for more details), it’s 
also evident in the boom in 
dental implements and den- 
tal systems now available to 
consumers. 

Here’s what some retail- 
ers are saying about those 
segments: 

Lower-priced oral care 
implements are proving to 
be good impulse products, 
producing swift turns and 
steady margins at many 
chains. According to John 
Cunningham of May’s Drug 
Stores, the implements he 
carries in his permanent set 
carry margins of 30 percent 
to 40 percent. 

According to buyer Ben 
Barnett, Genovese has had 
good sales on Butler’s Prox- 
abrush system of interden- 
tal brushes, travel brushes 


and refills. 

Gum stimulators, picks 
and dental mirrors from 
Dental Concepts are also 
selling well, said Barnett. 
He originally merchandised 
the items on power wings, 
but has planogrammed 
them now into his perma- 
nent set. 

In another planogram 
change, he is merchandis- 
ing oral irrigators and gin- 
givitis-fighting appliances 
in the small appliance sec- 
tion rather than in the oral 
care set. 

Some retailers are seek- 
ing to spark impulse pur- 
chases by cross-merchandis- 
ing Orapik’s key chain/ 
dental stimulator and sword 
flosses at the checkout 
stand. 

At Kerr Drug, dental ac- 
cessories are brought in on 
an in-and-out basis. The 
chain has added U.S. Den- 
tek’s Gingibrush to its mix 
this fall. The system brings 
professional-quality gum 
therapy to the home for be- 
tween $19.99 and $24.99 
retail.

Drug Store News, November 29,1993 13 


Salon nail care 


comes 


t's been one of the best-kept se- 
crets in cosmetics, but now the 
word is out: the artificial nail 
and manicure segments of nail 
care have become the two biggest 
growth segments within cosmetics. 
and the attention they are drawing 
seems to be helping sales of nail 
color, nail implements and nail 
treatment products as well. 

There are several reasons, cos- 
metic buyers say, why nail care 
has become such a bright Spot. 
Buyers point out that the category 
is “affordable,” “fashion driven” 
and, thanks to the growth in nail 
salons, “more visible and accessi- 
ble” than ever before. 

According to Nails magazine. a 


Le 


nome 


salon trade publication, nail salons 
in this country are projected to 
bring in $4.6 billion in revenues in 
1993, with the number of salons 
increasing 14 percent, to 32.674. 
by the end of 1993. Sales of retail 
products in salons are not counted 
in the $4.6 billion figure. Products 
in hair care, skin care and makeup 
as well as professional nail polish- 
es, top coats, treatments, quick 
dries, glues and adhesives, files 
and buffers will represent an addi- 
tional $25.5 million to nail salons 
by the end of the year, for an in- 
crease of 48 percent over 1992, ac- 
cording to Nails magazine. 
Growing sales of nail products 
in salons, however, do not seem to 


be coming at the expense of drug 
chains. Without exception, chain 
drug cosmetic buyers say nail sa- 
lons are in fact “driving” the sales 
of their own manicure products. 

Sales of nail care products in 
drug chains for the 12 months end- 
ed Aug. 31, 1993, were $290 mil- 
lion, according to research firm 
Towne-Oller, for an increase of 6 
percent. 

According to Towne-Oller, for 
the 12 months ended Aug. 31, sales 
of false nails—which account for 20 
percent of the total category —were 
up 11 percent, to $58 million. 
while sales of conditioning and 
treatment products — representing 
12 percent of the category — were 


up 7 percent, to $34 million. 

Nail polish, which accounts for 
45 percent of all nail care sales, in- 
creased 9 percent to $134 million. 

The strongest growth in nail im- 
plements came from nail files and 
scissors, up 11 percent and 10 per- 
cent, respectively, and from nail 
buffers and emery boards, both up 
by 9 percent for the period. Nail 
clippers were up 5 percent. The 
implement category in total was 
up 7 percent, to $72 million.

cosmetic buyer Donna McManus 


points out that women are buying

SPECIAL REPORT: NAIL CARE 


Trends in false nails help to 
shape entire category 


buyers called the false 

nail category “the hottest 
segment” in color cosmetics. 
Then, as consumers seemed 
to grow disenchanted with 
the category, sales plum- 
meted. Today, however, the 
category’s back in the news 
again, as hot or even hotter 
than before. 

In the 12 months ended 
last August, sales in the cat- 
egory shot up 11 percent, 
Towne-Oller and Associates 
reports. And, say many 
chain store cosmetic buyers, 
the category’s growth is 
even more dramatic than 
the numbers suggest. 

“My false nail sales are ex- 
ploding,” says Judy Wray, se- 
nior cosmetic buyer for 
Twinsburg, Ohio-based 
Revco. “Sales for Cosmar are 
up dramatically; sales for 
Fing’rs are up dramatically; 
IBD’s Five Second Nail Glue 
is doing fabulous. I am get- 
ting tremendous increases on 
Melvco’s Nail Magic, and 
Cosmar’s new PRO10 line is 
doing just great.” 

“Professional-type nail 
products and treatment 
products are our biggest 
growth areas,” adds Gerry 
Hoeppner, spokesnerson for 
Clearwater, Fla.-based Eck- 
erd Drug. 

Eckerd regularly sched- 
ules training schools for its 
cosmeticians to help them 
answer the kinds of sophisti- 
cated questions that con- 
sumers usually ask. Hoepp- 
ner believes drug stores can 
persuade consumers to shop 
drug chains for manicure 
items if they provide the ser- 


[: the mid-80s, cosmetic 


vice, variety and prices that 
consumers want. 

A source for one of the in- 
dustry’s biggest chains re- 
ported that sales of manicure 
products were outstanding. 
Jonel and Kiss were particu- 
larly strong. 


Professional or retail? 


Most chain drug cosmetic 
buyers make a distinction 
between professional and re- 
tail brands of false nails and 
other products. They classify 
brands like IBD, SuperNail 
or Perfect Nail—bought 
through distributors—as 
professional or salon lines. 
Brands bought direct—like 
Cosmar, Jonel, Fing’rs, Nai- 
lene and Lee—are retail 
lines. The distinction can be 
confusing, however, because 
before going direct, some of 
these popular retail brands 
were originally salon brands. 

Revco’s Wray notes that 
the distinction can be tricky. 
“PRO10, in the true sense of 
the word, is not a salon 
brand, but it is a top-quality 
professional product in a sa- 
lon-type package made for 
the retail market. It’s doing 
beautifully, so I think that, 
to some extent, professional 
is what the consumer per- 
ceives as professional.” 

“Other companies, like 
Cosmar and Del Labs, are 
creating professional-style 
lines just for retail, and that 
kind of visibility also helps 
the category grow,” Says one 
buyer. “The more that Cos- 
mar and Del do to broaden 
the market, the better for 
us, as long as we don't start 
to see a lot of price discount- 


ing, because that would kill 
the category’s profitability.” 
Wray feels consumers 
may not even remember 
brands from a salon. “They 
remember packages,” she 
says, “so if they see a profes- 
sional style package, they 
react as if itis a profession- 
al brand in many cases. 
Many buyers also point 
out that several brands are 
getting more sophisticated 
about their packaging, 
adding directions that make 
it easier than ever for 
women to apply false nails. 
“Cosmar does very well for 
us,” said Penny Wade, of 
Tuscaloosa, Ala.-based Harco 
Drug, “and it may be because 
[its] packages are so user- 
friendly. [It] give[s] very clear

McKesson profit up 6%, 
boosted by health division 


SAN FRANCISCO 
McKesson Corp. reported 
revenues up 6 percent to 
$3.03 billion from $2.87 bil- 
lion for its three business 
segments, with net income 
of $29.7 million up from 
$25.6 million for the second 
quarter ended Sept. 30. 

For the first six months of 
the fiscal year, income from 
continuing operations before 
special items for all McKes- 
son business segments in- 
creased to $60.5 million 
from $53.1 million. Rev- 
enues rose 5 percent to $6 
billion from $5.71 billion. 

In the health care seg- 
ment— which includes McKes- 
son Drug Co. and PCS Health 
Systems and accounts for 97 
percent of revenues and 75 
percent of operating profit — 
revenues were up 6 percent 
for the quarter to $2.93 billion. 
In the first six months, health 
care revenues increased 5 per- 
cent to $5.97 billion. 

“The increased profit of the 
segment is due in large mea- 
sure to the rapid expansion of 
PCS’s managed prescription 
benefit programs, offsetting 
pressure on McKesson Drug 


Co.,” said Alan Seelenfreund, 
chairman and chief executive. 
Revenues of PCS were up 
56 percent in the quarter to 
$39.5 million and 49 percent 
in the half to $77.2 million. 
PCS provides managed pre- 
scription care services for 42 
million people, about double 
the enrollment of a year ago. 
Seelenfreund noted that 
the impact of managed care 
is having a short-term nega- 
tive impact on McKesson 
Drug, but he predicted long- 
term opportunities in the 
managed care marketplace. 
Due to depressed margins 
and operating profits in 
McKesson Drug, the com- 
pany has reduced its work 
force around 5 percent this 
year and refocused its gener- 
ic drug line, which doubled 
in sales last year. It is also 
expanding its Valu-Rite vol- 
untary drug store group to 
include bidding on managed 
prescription plans. 
McKesson Corp.’s other 
two business segments, Ar- 
mor All Automotive Prod- 
ucts and McKesson Water 
Products, also recorded 
gains for the quarter.

No margin for error 


Faced with steadily shrinking margins, stiff- 
ening competition, and the uncertainties of 
health care reform, the nation’s wholesale 
druggists are under the gun again this year. 
The industry’s two-track prescription for sur- 
vival: boost productivity through technology, 
like McKesson’s Econolink system pictured 
above, and break into new markets.

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, November 15, 1993 


Minocycline Hydrochloride Capsules 
Brief Summary. For full prescribing information, see package insert. 


CONTRAINDICATIONS: This drug is contraindicated in persons wtio have shown hypersensitivity to any of the tetracyclines 

WARNINGS: MINOCYCLINE, LIKE OTHER TETRACYCLINE-CLASS ANTIBIOTICS, CAN CAUSE FETAL HARM WHEN ADMINISTERED TO A 
PREGNANT WOMAN. IF ANY TETRACYCLINE IS USED DURING PREGNANCY OR IF THE PATIENT BECOMES PREGNANT WHILE TAKING 
THESE DRUGS, THE PATIENT SHOULD BE APPRISED OF THE POTENTIAL HAZARD TO THE FETUS. THE USE OF DRUGS OF THE 
TETRACYCLINE CLASS DURING TOOTH DEVELOPMENT (LAST HALF OF PREGNANCY, INFANCY, AND CHILDHOOD TO THE AGE OF 8 
YEARS) MAY CAUSE PERMANENT DISCOLORATION OF THE TEETH (YELLOW-GRAY-BROWN). 

This adverse reaction is more common during long-term use of the drug but has been observed following repeated short-term courses 
Enamel hypoplasia has also been reported. TETRACYCLINE DRUGS, THEREFORE, SHOULD NOT BE USED DURING TOOTH DEVELOPMENT 
UNLESS OTHER DRUGS ARE NOT LIKELY TO BE EFFECTIVE OR ARE CONTRAINDICATED 

All tetracyclines form a stable calcium complex in any bone-forming tissue. A decrease in fibula growth rate has been observed in young ant 
mals (rats and rabbits) given oral tetracycline in doses of 25 mg/kg every six hours. This reaction was shown to be reversible when the drug 
was discontinued. 

Results of animal studies indicate that tetracyclines cross the placenta, are found in fetal tissues, and can have toxic effects on the developing 
fetus (often related to retardation of skeletal development). Evidence of embryotoxicity has been noted in animals treated early in pregnancy 

The anti-anabolic action of the tetracyclines may cause an increase in BUN. While this is not a problem in those with normal renal function, in 
patients with significantly impaired function. higher serum levels of tetracycline may lead to azotemia, hyperphosphatemia, and acidosis. If 
renal impairment exists, even usual oral or parenteral doses may lead to excessive systemic accumulations of the drug and possible liver toxic 
ity. Under such conditions, lower than usual total doses are indicated, and if therapy is prolonged, serum level determinations of the drug may 
be advisable. 

Photosensitivity manifested by an exaggerated sunburn reaction has been observed in some individuals taking tetracyclines. This has been 
reported rarely with minocycline. 

Central nervous system side effects including lightheadedness. dizziness, or vertigo have been reported with minocycline therapy 
Patients who experience these symptoms should be cautioned about driving vehicles or using hazardous machinery while on minocycline ther 
apy. 

These symptoms may disappear during therapy and usually disappear rapidly when the drug is discontinued. 
PRECAUTIONS: General: As with other antibiotic preparations, use of this drug may result in overgrowth of nonsusceptible organisms, includ 
ing fungi. If superinfection occurs, the antibiotic should be discontinued and appropriate therapy instituted. 

Pseudotumor cerebri (benign intracranial hypertension) in adults has been associated with the use of tetracyclines. The usual clinical mani 
festations are headache and blurred vision. Bulging fontanels have been associated with the use of tetracyclines in infants. While both of these 
conditions and related symptoms usually resolve after discontinuation of tetracycline, the possibility for permanent sequelae exists. 

Incision and drainage or other surgical procedures should be performed in conjunction with antibiotic therapy when indicated. 

Information for Patients: Photosensitivity manifested by an exaggerated sunburn reaction has been observed in some individuals taking tetra- 
cyClines. Patients apt to be exposed to direct sunlight or ultraviolet light should be advised that this reaction can occur with tetracycline drugs, 
and treatment should be discontinued at the first evidence of skin erythema. This reaction has been reported rarely with use of minocycline. 

Patients who experience central nervous system symptoms (see WARNINGS) siiould be cautioned about driving vehicles or using hazardous 
machinery while on minocycline therapy. 

Concurrent use of tetracycline may render oral contraceptives less effective (see Drug Interactions). 

Laboratory Tests: In venereal disease when coexistent syphilis is suspected, a dark-field examination should be done before treatment is start 
ed and the blood serology repeated monthly for at least four months. 

in long-term therapy, periodic laboratory evaluations of organ systems, including hematopoietic, renal, and hepatic studies should be per 
formed. 

Drug Interactions: Because tetracyclines have been shown to depress plasma prothrombin activity, patients who are on anticoagulant therapy 
may require downward adjustment of their anticoagulant dosage. Since bacteriostatic drugs may interfere with the bactericidal action of pen 
Cillin, it is advisable to avoid giving tetracycline-class drugs in conjunction with penicillin. Absorption of tetracyclines is impaired by antacids 
containing aluminum, calcium or magnesium, and iron- containing preparations. The concurrent use of tetracycline and methoxyflurane has 
been reported to result in fatal renal toxicity. Concurrent use of tetracyclines may render oral contraceptives less effective. Breakthrough bleed 
ing has been reported. 

Drug/Laboratory Test Interactions: False elevations of urinary catecholamine levels may occur dus to interference with the fluorescence test 
Carcinogenesis, Mutagenesis, Impairment of Fertility: Dietary administration of minocycline in long-term tumorigenicity studies in rats 
resulted in evidence of thyroid tumor production. Minocycline has also been found to produce thyroid hyperplasia in rats and dogs. In addition, 
there has been evidence of oncogenic activity in rats in studies with a related antibiotic, oxytetracycline (i.e., adrenal and pituitary tumors) 
Likewise, although mutagenicity studies of minocycline have not been conducted, positive results in in vitro mammalian cell assays (i.e., 
mouse lymphoma and Chinese hamster lung cells) have been reported for related antibiotics (tetracycline hydrochloride and oxytetracycline) 
Segment | (fertility and generat reproduction) studies have provided evidence that minocycline impairs fertility in male rats 

Teratogenic Effects: Pregnancy. P 

(See WARNINGS). 

Labor and Delivery: The effect of tetracyclines on labor and delivery is unknown 

Nursing Mothers: Tetracyclines are excreted in human milk. Because of the potential for serious adverse reactions in nursing infants from the 
tetracyclines, a decision should be made whether to discontinue nursing or discontinue the drug, taking into account the importance of the 
drug to the mother (see WARNINGS). 

Pediatric Use: (See WARNINGS). 

ADVERSE REACTIONS: Due to oral minocycline's virtually complete absorption, side effects to the ower bowel, particularly diarrhea, have 
been infrequent. The following adverse reactions have been observed in patients receiving tetracyclines. Gastrointestinal: Anorexia, nausea, 
vomiting, diarrhea, glossitis, dysphagia, enterocolitis, and inflammatory lesions (with monilial overgrowth) in the anogenital region, increases 
in liver enzymes, and rarely hepatitis have been reported. Rare instances of esophagitis and esophageal ulcerations have been reported in 
patients taking the tetracycline-class antibiotics in capsule and tablet form. Most of these patients took the medication immediately before 
going to bed (see DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION). 

Skin: Maculopapular and erythematous rashes. Exfoliative dermatitis has been reported but is uncommon. Erythema multiforme and rarely 
Stevens-Johnson syndrome have been reported. Photosensitivity is discussed above (see WARNINGS). Pigmentation of the skin and mucous 
membranes has been reported. 

Renal toxicity: Elevations in BUN have been reported and are apparently dose related (See WARNINGS) 

Hypersensitivity reactions: Urticaria, angioneurotic edema, anaphylaxis, anaphylactoid purpura, pericarditis, exacerbation of systemic lupus 
erythematosus and rarely pulmonary infiltrates with eosinophilia have been reported. 

Blood: Hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, neutropenia, and eosinophilia have been reported. 

Central nervous system: Bulging fontanels in infants and benign intracranial hypertension (Pseudotumor cerebri) in adults (see PRECAU- 
TIONS-General) have been reported. 

Other: When given over prolonged periods, tetracyclines have been reported to produce brown-black microscopic discoloration of the thyroid 
glands. No abnormalities of thyroid function are known to occur in man 

Tooth discoloration in children less than 8 vears of age (see WARNINGS) and also, rarely, in adults have been reported. 

OVERDOSAGE: In case of overdosage, discontinue medication, treat symptomatically and institute supportive measures 

DOSAGE AND ADMINISTRATION: THE USUAL DOSAGE AND FREQUENCY OF ADMINISTRATION OF MINOCYCLINE DIFFERS FROM THAT OF 
THE OTHER TETRACYCLINES. EXCEEDING THE RECOMMENDED DOSAGE MAY RESULT IN AN INCREASED INCIDENCE OF SIDE EFFECTS. 
Minocycline hydrochloride capsules may be taken with o: without food. 

Adults: The usual dosage of minocycline hydrochloride is 200 mg initially followed by 100 mg every 12 hours. Alternatively, if more frequent 
doses are preferred, two or four 50 mg capsules may be given initially followed by one 50 mg capsule four times daily. 

For children above 8 years of age: The usual dosage of minocycline hydrochloride is 4 mg/kg initially followed by 2 mg/kg every 12 hours. 
Uncomplicated gonococcal infections other than urethritis and anorectal infections in men: 200 mg initially, followed by 100 mg every 12 
hours for a minimum of four days, with post-therapy cultures within 2 to 3 days. In the treatment of uncomplicated gonococcal urethritis in 
men, 100 mg every 12 hours for five days is recommended. For the treatment of syphilis, the usual dosage of minocycline should be adminis 
tered over a period of 10 to 15 days. Close follow-up, including laboratory tests, is recommended. In the treatment of meningococcal carrier 
State, the recommended dosage is 100 mg every 12 hours ior five days 

Mycobacterium marinum infections: Although optimal doses have not been established, 100 mg every 12 hours for 6 to 8 weeks have been 
used successfully in a limited number of cases. 

Uncomplicated nongonococcal urethral infection in adults caused by Chlamydia trachomatis or Ureaplasma urealyticum 100 mg orally, every 
12 hours for at least seven days. 

Ingestion of adequate amounts of fluids along with capsule forms of drugs in the tetracycline-class is recommended to reduce the risk of 
esophageal irritation and ulceration. 

In patients with renal impairment (see WARNINGS), the total dosage should be decreased by either reducing the recommended individual 
doses and/or by extending the time intervals between doses. 

HOW SUPPLIED: Minocycline Hydrochloride Capsules, USP, equivalent to 50 mg minocycline are opaque yellow/opaque yellow capsules sup- 
plied in bottles of 50, 100 and 500. Minocycline Hydrochloride Capsules, USP, equivalent to 100 mg minocycline are opaque dark gray/opaque 
yellow capsules supplied in bottles of 50, 100 and 500.

YOCON 


YOHIMBINE HCI 


I 


Description: Yohimbine is a 3a-15a-20B-17a-hydroxy Yohimbine-t6a-car- 
boxylic acid methyl ester. The alkaloid is found in Rubaceae and related trees. 
Also in Rauwolfia Serpentina (L) Benth. Yohimbine is an indolaikylamine 
alkaloid with chemical similarity to reserpine. It is a crystalline powder, 
odorless. Each compressed tablet contains (1/12 gr.) 5.4 mg of Yohimbine 
Action: Yohimbine blocks presynaptic alpha-2 adrenergic receptors. Its 
action on peripheral blood vessels resembies that of reserpine, though it is 
weaker and of short duration. Yohimbine's peripheral autonomic nervous 
system effect is to increase parasympathetic (cholinergic) and decrease 
sympathetic (adrenergic) activity. {t is to be noted that in male sexual 
performance, erection is linked to cholinergic activity and to alpha-2 ad- 
renergic blockade which may theoretically result in increased penile inflow, 
decreased penile outflow or both. 

Yohimbine exerts a stimulating action on the mood and may increase 
anxiety. Such actions have not been adequately studied or related to dosage 
although they appear to require high doses of the drug. Yohimbine has a mild 
anti-diuretic action, probably via stimulation of hypothalmic centers and 
release of posterior pituitary hormone. 

Reportedly, Yohimbine exerts no significant influence on cardia¢ stimula- 
tion and other effects mediated by B-adrenergic receptors, its effect on blood 
pressure, if any, would be to lower it; however no adequate studies are at hand 
to quantitate this effect in terms of Yohimbine dosage. 
indications: Yocon® is indicated as a sympathicolytic and mydriatrie. it may 
have activity as an aphrodisiac. 

Contraindications: Renal diseases, and patient's sensitive to the drug. in 
view of the limited and inadequate information at hand, no precise tabulation 
can be offered of additional contraindications.

Private label pervasive 


“OTCs have evolved into 
a huge market with huge 
potential, and private label 
products have become 
pervasive in OTCs,” ac-

the market research firm 
Towne-Oller, a division of 
Information Resources

dozen speakers at a recent 
two-day OTC conference 
sponsored by the Institute 
for International Research. 
Powerful OTC Positioning 
Strategies, as the event 
was billed, turned into a 
two-day survival course 
for branded manufactur- 
ers. Nearly every speaker 
mentioned the market 
share gains made by pri- 
vate label products and 
the expectation that future 
gains are inevitable. 

“There is a shift in con- 
Sumer buying behavior to- 


by Mike Troy 


ward value,” said Gabe 
Lowy, a private label

can compare branded 
products with a new breed 
of private label competitor 
and get the same perfor- 
mance at half the price.” 

Lowy goes out on a limb 
and predicts private label 
products will account for 
at least 40 percent of all 
OTC sales within five

three years many manu- 
facturers of OTC brands 
will also service retailers’ 
private label needs. 


Faced with the specter

predictable strategies for 
growing or at least main-

Leveraging brand equity

and new product forms 
and delivery methods is 
one frequently cited ap- 
proach that works if the 
brand is extremely strong,

but fails when it’s over- 
done, as in the case of the 
five Bayer Select pain 
products and the new 
Bayer Select cough/cold 
line. Segmenting a prod- 
uct’s market by age 
groups also works some- 
times as it did with vita- 
mins and the Centrum Sil- 
ver line extension. 
Rx-to-OTC switches hold 
the most promise for man- 
ufacturers, and a handful 
of companies may be in for 
a windfall if they are fortu- 
nate enough to get their 
applications through the 
regulatory process. For the 
most part, product man-

Outlooks optimistic as chains gear up for 1994 


Mood is upbeat as drug 
chains face an extremely 
competitive 1994 

Total dollar sales of 49 of 
drug chains’ core categories 
climbed to some $39.7 bil- 
lion in the mass market for 
the year ended Sept. 12, 
1993, according to Informa- 
tion Resources Inc. Drug 
chains’ piece of that pie rose 
some 1.4 percent from year 


ago figures, as drug stores 
commanded 40.3 percent of 
the U.S. mass market. In 
comparison, food outlets ac- 
counted for some $14 bil- 
lion, for a 35.6 percent mar- 
ket share, up 1.5 percent 
from a year ago, and mass 
merchandisers captured 
$9.6 billion in sales, for a 
24.1 percent market share, 
according to IRI. 


That’s the good news. At 
closer examination, howev- 
er, it’s apparent that drug 
chains are locked in a battle 
for consumers’ dollars and 
share of mind. For details 
about this battle, you can 
turn to Drug Store News’ 
annual year-end review on 
chain drug stores, begin- 
ning on p. 17 of this issue.

Genovese eyes more NYC sites 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — Flush with the initial success 
of its first Manhattan store, Genovese Drug Stores is 
actively scouting additional sites in the Big Apple. 
“The store is far exceeding expectations and has al- 
ready set records for the chain,” said vice president of 
marketing Don Gross. “It is already one of our top-vol- 
ume stores, and in one year, it will probably become 
the top-volume store in the chain.” 

The chain’s initial foray into Manhattan was greeted 
with mobs of shoppers during the Nov. 2 grand open- 
ing. Traffic has remained heavy in the weeks that fol- 
lowed—so heavy, in fact, that Genovese had to contend 
briefly with out-of-stock problems. “We are now deliv- 
ering to the store every day,” said Gross. “Since open- 
ing, we’ve learned some lessons.” He said store person- 
nel have been brought up to speed, a process that had 
to be accomplished in record time because of the store’s 
heavy traffic. “Thankfully, we have very good store- 
level people in place,” he added. The chain is now con- 
sidering additional Manhattan locations, including a 
few sites on the city’s Upper West Side. “We will prob- 
ably open only one location on the West Side at first,” 
said Gross. The chain is also interested in another 
East Side location further uptown from its initial site. 


McK: Home health care program 


SAN FRANCISCO — The McKesson Home Health 
Care division of McKesson Drug Co. has introduced a

market home medical equipment products and ser-

HMOs/PPOs, home care agencies, hospices, hospital 
discharge planners and nursing homes. 


Charities No. 1 in Revco outing 


CLEVELAND — Revco D.S. presented more than 
$450,000 last month to 12 local charities, representing 
the proceeds from this year’s Nike Cleveland Open. 

Proceeds of the Open, which is co-sponsored by the 
drug chain, fund the tax-exempt Revco Golf Charities 
Foundation, which supports local charities serving the 
needs of children in northeast Ohio. In its three years 
of existence, the foundation has distributed more than 


$1.3 million. Recipients included Boys & Girls Club of 


Cleveland, which was awarded $150,000; Ronald Mc- 
Donald Children’s Charities of Northeastern Ohio, 
which received $75,000; and the Urban Community 
School, which received $35,000. 

Revco has also launched its annual holiday fundrais- 
er to benefit 33 Ronald McDonald Houses nationally. 
The promotion, expected to raise more than $250,000 
for the cause, is based on donations from the sale of 
wooden nutcrackers sold at Christmas in Revco stores.

Drug Store News, December 13, 1993 


TORONTO — The leaders 
of Shoppers Drug Mart have 
reacted angrily to proposed 
legislation that would ban 
the sale of all tobacco prod- 
ucts in Ontario’s drug 
stores, calling it “irresponsi- 
ble” and potentially damag- 
ing to retail pharmacy. 

The sweeping Tobacco 
Control Act, introduced in 
November by Ontario’s Min- 
istry of Health, would pro- 
hibit the sale of tobacco “in 
pharmacies and _ other 
health facilities,” as well as 
in vending machines. It 
would also boost the legal 
age to buy tobacco to 19, 


Proposed tobacco ban in Ontario 
elicits sharp response from Shoppers 


ban smoking in most public 
places and require health 
warnings in retail outlets 
allowed to sell tobacco. 
Ontario Health Minister 
Ruth Grier called the pro- 
posal a “giant step toward 
reducing the province's 
leading cause of preventable 
death.” But Shoppers, which 
has led a campaign against 
the ban since it was first 
proposed by Ontario’s Col- 
lege of Pharmacy in 1990, 
called the effort “misguided” 
with regard to the removal 
of tobacco from pharmacies. 
The ban’s only meaning- 
ful effect, Arthur Konviser, 


senior vice president of pub- 
lic affairs, argued, would be 
to hurt retail pharmacists. 
“Evidence was presented (in 
earlier hearings) that clear- 
ly indicated many pharma- 
cies would be forced to close 
and jobs would be lost.” 
However, not all Ontario 
pharmacy retailers shared 
that view. Said Norm Puhl, 
president of 117-store Big V 
Pharmacies, “We’ve always 
shared the objective...to 
make society smoke-free, 
and we’ve always de-empha- 
sized tobacco. Because of 
this, we’re able to deal more 
easily with the legislation.” 


SAS/ previews its new system; 
Rite Aid to test next year 


BRISTOL, Pa. — Stores 
Automated Systems Inc. 
(SASI), the company that 
pioneered integrated point- 
of-sale systems using per- 
sonal computer technology, 
opened a new facility here 
and is currently working on 
a new advanced system. 

The new system, called the 
“flapjack” in its demo stage 
because of its flat, space-sav- 
ing design, will feature color 
and sound. The use of sound, 
combined with the system’s 
help feature, enables the sys- 
tem to “talk” to cashiers 
through transactions. SASI’s 
new system will be tested at 
retail in the first quarter of 
1994 and will be available 
to other retailers the follow- 
ing quarter. 

Martin Grass, president 
of Rite Aid, which owns an 
interest in SASI, said the 
chain will test the system 
some time next year. “The 
flapjack system gives us a 
lot of horsepower, but takes 
up a lot less space,” said 
Rite Aid director of retail 
support Aaron Crosson. 

Crosson said the system 
will allow Rite Aid to scan 


coupons, a process that is 
currently recorded manual- 
ly by Rite Aid cashiers. 

The system will allow the 
chain to integrate other 
functions with its software 
system. For example, this 
December, it will begin test- 
ing transactions completed 
with debit cards. The chain 


will also move to processing 
money orders by computer. 
Integrating such services 
into the computer system 
will help the chain generate 
more thorough data on its 
Rite Express counters, which 
offer a number of customer 
services, including money or- 
ders, faxing and key making.

Eckerd earnings outlook improves 


by Mike Troy 


As expected, Eckerd Corp. reported 
a net loss for its first fiscal period 
since returning to public ownership 
via an August stock offering. But 
steadily improving operating profits, 
declining interest charges and healthy 
sales gains point to a brighter future 
for the 1,710-store drug chain. 

Due in large part to one-time charges 
and heavy interest expenses, Eckerd 
lost $11.5 million in the third quarter 
ended Oct. 31—its first since its early 
August initial public offering (IPO). 
That marks an improvement from the 
Same period a year earlier, when the 
chain’s losses totaled $23.8 million. 

Eckerd also showed a healthy im- 
provement in same-store sales—up 
0.0 percent for the quarter. That 
helped boost third-quarter sales to 


slightly more than $972 million, up 
from $907 million for the same period 
last year. In another bright spot in 
the quarterly report, operating profit 
increased 14.7 percent over the previ- 
ous year to $15.5 million. 


Eckerd showed a healthy 
improvement in same-store 
quarterly sales—up 5.5 percent. 


“We are pleased with our sustained 
increase in sales for the third quarter 
and year-to-date period,” said Stewart 
Turley, Eckerd chairman and chief ex- 
ecutive. “Our pharmacy operation—es- 
pecially third-party plans—[as well as] 
health-related products, skin care, 
greeting cards and convenience food 
categories continue to post notabie 
gains, in spite of continued deflation in 


certain categories and last year’s sales 
bulge due to Hurricane Andrew.” 

The sales gains and a major refinanc- 
ing package completed this year are 
also helping Eckerd’s return to prof- 
itability. The refinancing—which in- 
cluded the IPO and major debt swaps— 
cut third-quarter interest expenses to 
$25.1 million from $34 million during 
the previous year’s third quarter. 

Declining interest costs and Eckerd’s 
sales results are creating optimism. St. 
Petersburg, Fla.-based Raymond 
James & Associates, one of the broker- 
age houses involved in Eckerd’s Aug. 5 
IPO and one of Wall Street’s top stock 
pickers, issued Eckerd its strongest 
buy rating on Nov. 3. The investment 
firm characterized Eckerd as a “ground 
floor opportunity” and encouraged “ag- 
gressive accumulation of the stock.” 
Other brokerage firms had not issued 
opinions on Eckerd at press time. 


Flaschen replaces 


by James Frederick 


NORTHBROOK, Ill. — 
Moving quickly to restore 
its momentum and competi- 
tive posture, A.C. Nielsen 
has named David Flaschen, 
37, president and chief oper- 
ating officer of Nielsen Mar- 
keting Research. Flaschen 
replaces 40-year-old George 
Garrick, whose abrupt res- 
ignation and return to arch- 
rival Information Resources 
Inc. after just four months 
on the job shook Nielsen 
and ratcheted up the al- 
ready intense competition 
between the two market in- 
formation powerhouses. 

Newly appointed Fla- 
schen was last based in 
London as head of software 
development and production 
for IMS, which, along with 
Nielsen, is a division of Dun 
& Bradstreet. At Nielsen, 
he faces a major challenge: 
to try to recapture market 
share lost to IRI’s aggres- 
sive, solutions-oriented com- 
petitive assaults over the 
past decade. 

To keep pace with newer 
competitors in a time of dra- 
matic changes in market re- 
search and retail systems, 
Nielsen developed informa- 
tion systems like ScanTrack 
and Procision that blend 
scan data with its audit 
data, but its own executives 
acknowledge the company 
was Slow to react in the ’80s. 

Nielsen is working to 
complete a comprehensive, 
rapid-response package of 
information solutions to 
help suppliers and retailers 
target specific consumer de- 
mand patterns, speed turns 
and eliminate dead shelf 
space under the aegis of effi- 
cient consumer response, or 
ECR. “Fast turnaround of 


decision-support informa- 
tion is a strategic edge our 
customers are demanding,” 
said Serge Okun, president 
and chief executive of A.C. 
Nielsen and IMS. “David 
Flaschen consistently pro- 
duces innovative, technical- 
ly superior products—usual- 
ly ahead of schedule.” 

In his short tenure at 
Nielsen, Garrick was cred- 
ited with initiating some 
positive steps to make 
Nielsen more responsive to 
its market. One example: he 
named former Frito-Lay ex- 
ecutive Douglas Adams to 
head a new division on ECR. 

In other news, the compa- 
ny also named Richard 
Derr, 36-year-old former 
head of Nielsen Information 
Services, to the post of se- 
nior vice president of soft- 
ware development for both 
A.C. Nielsen and IMS 
International.

Big B source tagging under fire 


The use of electronic secu- 
rity tags on African-Ameri- 
can hair care products has 
put Southeastern drug re- 
tailer Big B’s loss preven- 
tion program in the national 
spotlight. 

consumer complaint 
about Big B’s use of elec- 
tronic article surveillance 
tags on African-American 
hair care products led to a 
recent front page article in 
the Atlanta Constitution. 
The story went nationwide 
when it was picked up by 
Atlanta-based Cable News 
Network. 

Controversy about the 
complaint escalated when 
TV talk show host Arsenio 
Hall quipped that the re- 
tailer’s motto is “the cus- 


tomer is always white.” And 
archconservative commen- 
tator Rush Limbaugh 
weighed in with support of 
Big B for its shoplifter ap- 
prehension efforts. 

According to Bobby Little, 
Big B’s vice president of 
store operations, the 
woman’s complaint centered 
on the fact that African- 
American hair care products 
had tags and white hair 
care products did not. Little 
doesn’t dispute the woman’s 
claim, but disagrees the 
chain exclusively targets 
African-American-oriented 
products for tagging. 

“We tag products that we 
have experienced problems 
with,” Little said. “We are 
against shoplifters whether 


that person is [African- 
American] or white and we 
are not singling out any one 
group. We are just tagging 
items we are losing.” 

Big B has Sensormatic 
security alarm equipment 
in 50 of its 352 stores. Of 
the roughly 25,000 SKUs 
carried in each store, about 
15 percent are tagged, ac- 
cording to Little. Of that 15 
percent, about 10 percent 
could be characterized as 
African-American-oriented 
products. 

“Our plan is similar to the 
plan that everyone is using,” 
Little said. “You find out 
what you are losing and tag 
it. If you stop losing the 
item, you'll take the tag off 
because they are expensive.”

Drug stores, on the other 
hand, have the dominant

categories.

and sometimes as much as a 
40 percent share—in the 20 
highest dollar-volume seg- 
ments, but even more im- 
pressive are the gains they 
are showing in these cate- 
gories, consistent double- 
digit increments in all major 
segments. 


The only two 
major categories 
where drug stores 
have stronger 
gains than food 
stores are first aid 
accessories, up 13 
percent in dollars 
in drug compared 
to 5 percent in 
food, and suntan 
products, up 9 
percent vs. 7 
percent in food. 


Meanwhile, drug stores 
are generally lagging be- 
hind the competition in all 
the major segments. Not 
only are their dollar sales 
flat or down in 27 seg- 
ments while their unit 
sales are flat or down in 40 
of the 49 seginents tracked 
in this study by IRI, but 
also their gains in dollars 
and units are usually in 
low single increments. 


Drug store gains 


The only two major cate- 
gories where drug stores 
have stronger gains than 
food stores are first aid ac- 
cessories, up 13 percent in 
dollars in drug compared to 
5 percent in food, and sun- 
tan products, up 9 percent 
in dellars in drug and 7 per- 
cent in food. There are no 
HBA categories where drug 


stores do better than mass 
merchandisers. 

The competitive envi- 
ronment, without doubt, is 
intense. The good news, 
however, is that many chain 
drug executives are aware 
of the danger and are taking 
strategic steps to improve 
their position. 

As Drug Store News has 
reported throughout the 
year, many drug chains are 


using technology to develop 
more sophisticated inventory 
management and replenish- 
ment programs. Many are 
upgrading their stores to 
give them more of a fashion 
image; some are investing in 
more sales help for core 
destination departments like 
cosmetics and photo process-

possible destination shop 
categories like bath care and

more are developing adver-

their stores as attractive 
destination shops.

mass merchandisers are 
also pursuing similar 
strategies, so there is no 
guarantee that drug stores 
will win their battle for the

But at least, the battle 
lines have been drawn, and 
drug chains are doing their 
best to fight back.

1993 REVIEW: SALES TRENDS 


he rapid growth of 
food/drug combination 
chains has precipitated 
the food store industry into 
a new role: that of major 
player in the HBA category. 
Over the past decade, the 
food industry has evolved 
from merely promoting 
high-consumption HBA, GM 
and OTC products at low 
cost as traffic generators to 
developing their own unique 


degree of specialization in 
the category. 

These combos and the 
high-volume supermarkets 
with extensive HBA depart- 
ments and pharmacies now 
offer a broad selection of 
HBA. They feature the same 
brand names that drug stores 
carry, offer the additional 
convenience of one-stop shop- 
ping and compete aggressive- 
ly on price. Today, many have 


extensive boutiqued cosmetic 
departments, enhanced with 
a wide selection of better 
name brands and given extra 
consumer value, in many cas- 
es, by the presence of trained 
service cosmeticians. 
Research provided by 
Towne-Oller and Associates, 
a division of IRI, offers a look 
at the impact of food stores, 
including the combo stores, 
on the market. Nationwide, 


Food/drug combos aggressively convert HBA shoppers 


drug stores’ share of dollar 
sales in key HBA segments is 
48 percent; food and 
food/combo stores is 52 per- 
cent. Figures are based on 
dollar sales for the 12 months 
through June 1993 and deter- 
mined by product movement 
from distribution centers 
among Towne-Oller reporting 
retailers and distributors. 
Regionally, the story 
varies significantly. Drug
