Drug Store News, December 13, 1993 


stores dominate in such cities 
as Miami, where they cap- 
ture 58 percent of the market 
vs. the nation’s 48 percent; 
Baltimore/Washington, D.C., 
65 percent; Cleveland, 67 
percent; Boston, 60 percent; 
New York, 59 percent; and 
Chicago, 58 percent. 

In other cities, the race 
gets tighter: The battle for 
dollars is virtually a dead 
heat in Los Angeles, with 
drug stores claiming 51 per- 
cent of dollar sales; Rich- 
mond (51 percent); and Al- 
bany, N.Y. and Pittsburgh 
(53 percent). In yet other 
cities, drug stores lag far be- 
hind: 15 percent of dollar 
sales in Salt Lake City and 
21 percent in Portland, Ore. 


From soup to...notions 


Food chains were origi- 
nally attracted to HBA and 
cosmetics by the profit 
potential of their higher 
margins. Management in 
the food store industry 
looked at the 40 percent to 
50 percent margins that 
drug stores were averaging 
on HBA and realized this 
was a category they could 
use to offset the lower mar- 
gins they were taking on 
groceries and beverages. 

As the years have passed, 
their concentration on the 
HBA category has been pay- 
ing off. For the most recent 
52-week period ended Sept. 
12, 1993, the food store indus- 
try, led by such combo giants 
as Jewel/Osco, Skaggs/Alpha 
Beta, Tom Thumb/Page, 
Pathmark, Smith’s, Vons, 
H.E. Butt, Randall’s, Do- 
minick’s/Omni and Buttrey, 
virtually drew abreast of drug 
stores as HBA retailers. They 
now sell as many units of 
HBA as drug stores do. 

According to the IRI scan- 
ning service InfoScan, food 
stores for the 52 weeks ended 
Sept. 12, 1993 generated a 37 
percent share of all HBA 
units sold in mass markets 
this year. Drug stores, which 
once dominated the HBA 
category, trailed by a point, 
generating a 36 percent 
share of unit sales. Mass 
merchandisers, who are also 
growing their share of the 
HBA pie dramatically, con- 
sumed a threatening 27 per- 
cent share of HBA unit sales.

Drug Store News, December 13, 1993 


How drug 
stores are 
reacting 


rug stores are fighting back. 
Although food and mass 
merchandise stores have 
been steadily biting off bigger and 
bigger chunks of the pie, drug 
stores, particularly chains, have 
not given up on reclaiming their 
dominance in several categories. 
Today many chains are upscaling 
and modernizing their stores, hop- 
ing to attract more consumers with 
an enhanced ambiance and warm, 
friendly surroundings. 


Adding service 


Drug chains are also trying to 
add more service to their stores, 
expanding the hours they allocate 
to service cosmeticians and train- 
ing their pharmacists to be expert 
patient counselors as well as dis- 
pensers of medications. 

Lately, some chains have begun 
experimenting with marketing pro- 
erams that stress their fashion im- 
age or their courteous service. 
There is less industry dependence 
in the traditional drug store 
strengths of convenience and pro- 
motional pricing. 

It’s too soon to say whether these 
experiments will be successful, but 
clearly they are a step in the right 
direction. 


Selling the store 


Many chain executives say they 
realize they have to find what they 
call a “point of difference” to trans- 
form their stores into “destination 
shops” for consumers. 

It is a marketing challenge. 
Meeting that challenge, one drug 
store executive told Drug Store 
News, will mean developing an en- 
tirely new marketing strategy for 
the chain drug industry. 

“A drug chain will have to sell 
its stores,” this source said, “exact- 
ly the way a manufacturer sells 
products, as something that has 
been designed to satisfy the key 
needs of its specific target market 
customers.”

Shoppers continue to turn to 
drug stores for their school 
and home office stationery 
supplies, despite encroach- 
ment into the category by 
wholesale clubs and specialty 
discounters. 


GENERAL MERCHANDISE / STATIONERY 


I 
: 


~ 


~~ 


hoost stationery sales at chains 


n homes around the 
country, desks bristle 
with tasks: a list to 
compile, paperwork to 
file, homework to finish or a 
checkbook to balance. 

Fueled by consumers’ busy 
lives, stationery continues to 
grow in most drug chains. 
“The office discounters and 
mass merchandisers are get- 
ting the larger [commercial] 
office supply business. Drug 
retailers can offer opportuni- 
ties for home office and per- 
sonal needs,” says Gerry 
Hoeppner, spokesperson for 
Eckerd Drug. 

Drug chains generate ap- 
proximately $2.25 billion in 
annual stationery sales and 
lead other mass retail chan- 
nels—including second- 
place wholesale clubs with 
$2.12 billion—in the nearly 
$10 billion mass market sta- 
tionery marketplace, accord- 
ing to a preliminary study 
by the School and Home Of- 
fice Products Association 
(SHOPA). 

Drug chain customers are 
shopping for value and con- 
venience. Plus, they want 


more control over daily de- 
mands, and this means a 
brisk business for one of 
this year’s growth prod- 
ucts—day planners and or- 
ganizers. 

At Snyder Drug, buyer 
Ron Riviere reports that 
the entire stationery cate- 
gory is up, but the driver is 
day planners: “It’s far and 
away the largest growth 
category we have in sta- 
tionery,” he says. 

Buyer Paul Lofgren at 
Bartell Drug in Seattle re- 
ports that home office is 
growing and the chain is ag- 
gressively promoting the 
category, opening new stores 
with expanded stationery 
sets. Lofgren concurs that 
the personal organizer cate- 

ory is hot, especially in the 

30 price range. 

Day planners garner 
healthy margins in the mid- 
40 percentage range, mak- 
ing up for margin lost on 
commodity stationery items 
like filler paper. Buyers also 
look for sleepers. Cynthia 
Stahley-Zuniga, merchan- 
dise manager of Genovese, 


says paper clips produce 
around a 48 percent margin. 
Marble composition books 
offer good margins for a 
commodity item, she adds, 
and notes that this is her 
department’s No. 1 item. 

Greeting cards make a 
solid 50 percent margin con- 
tribution, and since this is a 
growth category, it helps 
offset office supply business 
lost to category killers. 
Cards also encourage relat- 
ed stationery sales, from ad- 
dress books and organizers 
to pens, clips and social sta- 
tionery. 


Trading up 


Drug chains continue to 
feel the bite from specialty 
discounters like Office Max 
and Staples. Michael Polzin, 
spokesperson for Wal- 
greens, says the chain did 
well with back to school this 
year but adds: “We didn’t 
see a similar growth in of- 
fice supplies. Customers 
looked to the specialty 
stores for those items.” 

In both school supplies 
and home office, many drug

chains are finding their 
niche by offering a selective 
assortment that often in- 
cludes more upscale lines. 

Eckerd’s growing sta- 
tionery categories include 
art supplies, mailing prod- 
ucts, upgraded notebooks 
for older students and fash- 
ion writing instruments like 
Yikes pencils and markers. 
As parents get proactive 
about their child’s early de- 
velopment, children’s arts/ 
crafts kits contribute to cat- 
egory growth at Eckerd and 
other chains. 

Walgreens is also seeing a 
trend toward high-quality, 
upscale items. Says Polzin: 
“Customers are looking for a 
good product at a fair price. 
Quality is important to 
them.” Snyder’s Riviere and 
Genovese’s Stahley-Zuniga 
see a similar trend, both not- 
ing an increase in sales of 
upscale school supplies like 
Mead’s 5-Star First Gear. 

Upscale in 1993 isn’t the 
same as in the conspicuous- 
ly consumptive 1980s, but 
shoppers still want good de-

HOW SERVICE & EXPERIENCE 
TRANSLATES 
TO THE BOTTOM LINE 


he NCRS cus- 
tomer service 
staff is ready to 
meet your 
needs. Its expe- 
rienced representatives, av- 
eraging eight years of ser- 
vice with NCRS, know who 
to call to get to the bottom 
of payment denial prob- 
lems. The customer reps 
know your account and take 
the extra steps necessary to 
resolve issues for their re- 
tail clients. We can’t 
promise 100% success, but 
we guarantee 100%-plus ef- 
fort. 

NCRS executives repre- 
sent years of experience in 
all facets of the drug and 
grocery industry: Along 
with founder Leo Paul Kou- 
los, the team includes Wal- 
ter Kreuter, a three-decade 
veteran of service-oriented 
Bergen Brunswig who 
works on National Account 
Sales; Harvey Slate, who 
brings years of manufac- 
turer experience in the food 
industry as Vice President 
of Corporate Marketing, 
Ann Bertiglia who serves as 
Vice President of Adminis- 
tration and MIS and Nick 
Misthos, Sr. Vice President 
of Retailer Services. 

Each member of the exec- 
utive group is authorized to 


make a decision. No bu- 
reaucratic layers. No com- 
mittee delays. Usually 
you'll get a same-day re- 
sponse, or in more complex 
cases a 24 to 48 hour re- 
sponse. With offices and 
agents in San Francisco, 
metro New York, the Mid- 
west, Texas, Southern Cali- 
fornia and Hawaii, plus 
their own processing plants, 
NCRS is primed to respond. 

“Volume driven price 
wars are not our style,” says 
Koulos. “Well managed 
growth, partnering with se- 
lective clients and working 
hard to improve the retail- 
er’s coupon profile is the 
NCRS way of doing busi- 
ness.” 

At times NCRS has car- 
ried the manufacturers’ re- 
ceivables an extra period of 
time while working through 
a snag for one of their re- 
tailers. NCRS’s attention to 
detail comes out of their 
pocket, but it’s the cost of 
doing a service business 
right. 

When a price raise is the 
issue, they meet with retail- 
ers individually. Your bud- 
get is their concern; they 
are partners in your suc- 
cess.

sign. Today, buyers say, this 
means a quality look and 
added features and bene- 
fits—in other words, value- 
added packaging. 

“We’re always looking for 
value added,” says Stahley- 
Zuniga. “Customers under- 
stand bonus sizes like 20 
more pages free or 20 per- 
cent more glue or two 
crayons free. When the dol- 
lar gets tight, that’s the 
thing to look for.” 

This season for back to 
school, Genovese tried a buy- 
one-get-one-free Papermate 
Liquid Paper promotion. It 
was so successful that the 
chain will repeat the promo- 
tion in January and use the 
same bonus strategy with 
Flair pens. 


Planner boom 


Day planners are doing so 
well at Bartell that, accord- 
ing to buyer Lofgren, sales 
in the home office category 
are increasing even without 
promotional activity. At 
Snyder, Mead Cambridge 
day planner sales continue 
to grow. “Even at the high- 
er retail, it seems like 
there’s a real acceptance, 
which, in a drug store, has 
not traditionally been the 
case,” says Riviere. 

At Snyder, midsized plan- 
ners outsell small and large 
styles. Line extensions still 
have legs, Riviere notes. 
“When they add a feature— 
a snap to a zipper or a 
change of fabric—this seems 
to stimulate further sales,” 
he says. 

Men, women and children 
turn to drug chains just be- 
fore and after school starts. 
Says Bartell’s Lofgren: 
“We’re the convenience 
store. When school starts 
and students get a list, they 
bring it in.” Lofgren looks 
for niches in B-T-S promo- 
tions, advertises full size 
notebooks at two-for-a-dol- 
lar (instead of the 70-count 
“cheater size” notebooks) 
and says, “These keep us 
out of the price wars” 
against competitors like 
Kmart and Fred Meyer. 

Snyder’s Riviere reports 
that mass merchants are 
hitting hard in his market 


' but with fewer items and 


that they advertise early. 
“Our business in back to 
school tends to come closer 
to school openings and in 
the two weeks immediately 
following,” he says. 

His pricing reflects mass 
merchant competition with 
sharp prices on 70-count 
theme books, two-pocket 
portfolios, three-subject 
notebooks, 24-count cray- 
ons, and 12- or 24-pack 
pencils. Some key markets 

“are very, very price sensi- 
tive and we price right,” 
Riviere adds. 


strong BTS boost sales 


For back to school, Gen- 
ovese had an “excellent, 
clean sell-through,” says 
Stahley-Zuniga. She reports 
that the chain stayed with 
basic school supplies and a 
few fashion-color items to 
spice up the section, so she 
only had to take limited 
fashion markdowns. 


Licensing strategies vary 


In licensed stationery 
product, Genovese targets 
key items, such as portfo- 
lios, lunch kits and back- 
packs. “Where the license 
drives the business, we defi- 
nitely do it,” she says. 

Chain drug buyers say 
they are cautious about li- 
censed B-T-S product be-

_STH ANNUAL CONSUMER BRAND PREFERENCE STUDY 


Brand loyal, 
value wise 


by Liz Parks 


hoppers are indeed conscious of the brand names drug 
chains carry, and, for the most part, they remain loyal to 
these brands, despite rampant price competition, the 
mushrooming of store-brand alternatives and the sluggish econ- 
omy. These are among the findings of the fifth annual Leo J. 
Shapiro & Associates study of the brand preferences and shop- 


ping habits of consumers. 
Continued on page 52 


Drug Store News, December 13,1993 49 


5TH ANNUAL CONSUMER BRAND PREFERENCE STUDY 


Consumers are brand loyal, value wise, says Shapiro study 


Continued from page 49 


In a recent telephone sur- 
vey of more than 1,000 con- 
sumers, Shapiro & Associ- 
ates found that consumers 
are extremely brand loyal 
when it comes to such cate- 
gories as toothpastes, bar 
soaps, aspirin and non-as- 
pirin pain relievers, sham- 
poos, batteries and film— 
where more than 90 percent 
of respondents said they 


have a brand preference. 
Eight out of 10 consumers 
surveyed prefer a particular 
brand of cough/cold medi- 
cines, moisturizing lotions 
and greeting cards, while 
more than 75 percent stated 
a preferred name in women’s 
fragrances and foundations 
base makeups. 


Drug sales inch up 


Despite competition, drug 


stores seem to be maintain- 
ing their share of consumer 
purchases in key HBA, cos- 
metics and OTC categories. 
For such products as 
shampoos, hand and body 
moisturizing lotions, suntan 
lotions/sunblocks and bat- 
teries, there has been little 
change over the past four 


years in the percentage of 


consumers who say they 
made their last purchase in 


a drug store. In the photo 
film and aspirin/non-aspirin 
pain relievers categories, in 
fact, drug stores showed 
slight gains. 


Big brands hold steady 


As any marketer knows, 
a brand name is not built in 
a day, and so it is not 
surprising that many of the 
most popular consumer 
brands have withstood the 
test of time. 

Suave, for example, was 
the most popular shampoo

Skin care 


Because this year the defi- 
nition of hand and body lo- 
tions was expanded to in- 
clude all moisturizing lotions, 
comparisons between what 
was popular in 1991 vs. today 
are not possible. For example, 
Oil of Olay, preferred by 8 
percent of consumers today, 
may not have ranked high in 
the past because it is consid- 
ered a face moisturizing prod- 
uct, not a hand and body 
product. 

There is some consisten- 
cy, though. The two brands 
named most often as pre- 
ferred brands, Vaseline In- 
tensive Care Lotion and 
Jergens, are used as hand 
and body lotions as well as 
all-over body lotions. 

It is also worth noting 
that for each year this study 
has been done, Avon skin 
care products have consis- 
tently ranked high in con- 
sumer popularity, coming in 
fourth, with 5 percent. This 
strength signals that chain 
drug stores need to be aware 
of this competitive presence. 

The growing clout of 
brands like Avon and Mary 
Kay are also persuading 
many retailers to develop 
their own marketing pro- 
grams, positioning their 
stores as the ideal setting for 
buying beauty care products. 


Sun care and bath soaps 


Coppertone continues to 
lead in popularity, but ap- 
parently, as more consumers 
come into the category, the 
increased activity is helping 
to boost sales of other lead- 
ing skin care brands. More 


consumers named Hawaiian 
Tropic, Bain de Soleil and 
Banana Boat as favorite 
brands in 1993 vs. 1991. 

Two direct-to-consumer 
brands, Avon and Mary Kay, 
are also making themselves 
more visible and accessible 
to consumers (preferred by 3 
percent and 1 percent of con- 
sumers, respectively), and 
private label brands are get- 
ting their share of consumer 
acceptance, earning the 
preference of 2 percent of 
consumers. Estée Lauder, 
with 1 percent, is the one de- 
partment store sun care 
brand to make the list, and 
it too has gained in populari- 
ty since 1991. 


The growing clout 
of brands like 
Avon and Mary 
Kay are persuad- 
ing retailers to 
develop their own 
marketing pro-

ing their stores as 
the ideal setting 
for buying beauty 


care products.

Fragrances/face makeups 


Then there are always

Chains: What they have—and need—to beat the competition 


hain drug stores like 

to cultivate certain 

departments as desti- 
nation stops for con- 
sumers—departments that 
drug store executives feel 
have the strongest chances 
of luring customers into 
their stores and away from 
competitors like mass mer- 
chandisers and food and 
drug combination stores. 

To get a fix on how con- 
sumers are currently shop- 
ping for some specific drug 
store department cate- 
gories—primarily toiletries, 
personal care products, cos- 
metics, pain relievers, greet- 
ing cards and film—Drug 
Store News commissioned 
Chicago-based Leo J. 
Shapiro & Associates to sur- 
vey consumers, both men 
and women, to find where 
they bought these items in 
the past month. 

Shapiro found that con- 
sumers were not faithful to 
any one type of store for 
these products and reported 
considerable cross shopping. 
While 60 percent of the re- 
spondents said they had 
made such purchases in food 
stores in the past month, 


5TH ANNUAL CONSUMER BRAND PREFERENCE STUDY 


five out of 10 respondents 
said they had purchased 
items in drug stores in the 
past month, and 40 percent 
said they had done so in a 
chain drug store. 

Specifically, four out of 10 
shoppers bought these items 
in a discount department 
store like Kmart, Wal-Mart 
or Target within the past 
month, and a surprisingly 
high number—13 percent— 
made such a purchase in a 
warehouse club. 


Clubs gain popularity 


The warehouse club in- 
dustry is the fastest grow- 
ing segment of mass retail- 
ing. Members of clubs can 
find almost any retail prod- 
uct they need, conveniently 
located under one roof and 
sold at cost-plus wholesale 
prices. 

Consumers tend to spend 
more on each purchase at 
outlets like warehouse clubs 
and discount stores, which 
are known for their low, 
everyday prices. Because 
most consumers stock up 
whenever they visit these 
stores, they don’t need to 
come back for repurchases

How this survey was compilet 


The 1993 Drug Store News Fifth 
Annual Consumer Top Brands Sur- 
vey was implemented by Chicago- 
based Leo J. Shapiro & Associates. 

The two-part study was based on tele- 
phone interviews conducted in August, 
with a national probability sample oj 
1,060 U.S. households. The sample was 
projectable to all households in the 
continental United States who are tele- 
phone subscribers, whether or not 
their numbers were listed in the tele- 
phone booh. 

Part One, based on interviews with 
a national sample of 605 house- 
holds, asks the “chief shopper” of 
each household about his or her 
past purchasing behavior, specifi- 
cally regarding brand preferences 
and brand loyalties for 14 product 
categories. 

Part Two, new this year, is based on 
a national probability sample of 455 
heads of households (half male, half 
female). It explores where consumers 
purchase their drug store merchan- 
dise and records their ratings of com- 
peting retail outlets that carry that 
merchandise. The margin of error is 


plus or minus five points.

‘5TH ANNUAL CONSUMER BRAND PREFERENCE STUDY 


Chains: What they have—and need 


Continued from page 60 
than discount department 
stores, deep discount drug 
stores or warehouse clubs. 
They are also quicker to en- 
ter into and exit from. Since 
about 20 percent of all mod- 
ern foced stores currently 
have full-line drug stores 
under the same roof, they 
are also exceptionally conve- 
nient to shop. 

The average number of 
items that consumers bought 
during a typical store visit 
seems strongly related to the 
pricing strategies of the dif- 
ferent retailers. 

Low-price warehouse 
stores and discount de- 
partment stores generated 
the highest number of pur- 
chases of drug store-type 
merchandise on their last 
visit: 6.4 and 5.4 respec- 
tively. 

Consumers bought an av- 
erage of 4.9 items in food 
stores, 4.6 items in discount 
drug stores and 4.2 in chain 
drug stores. 

When it came to de- 
termining where people 
would shop for these select 
drug store items in the fu- 
ture, warehouse clubs 
seemed to be positioned to 
achieve the greatest gains, 
while food and chain drug 
stores were in danger of suf- 
fering the heaviest losses. 

Almost half—45 _ per- 
cent—of all the respondents 
in the survey told Shapiro 
that they planned to shop 
more often at warehouse 
clubs in the coming year. 
Since warehouse clubs are a 
relatively new trade class— 
still in the process of enter- 
ing new markets—that find- 
ing was understandable. 

The findings also sug- 
gested that warehouse clubs’ 
sales gains would come most 
strongly from food stores and 
chain drug stores. Just 17 
percent of all respondents 
said they planned to shop 
food stores more often in the 
coming year, and only 20 
percent of all respondents 


said the same about chain 
drug stores. 

Consumers added that 
they would be looking for 
bargains more often in dis- 
count department stores 
and deep discount drug 
stores. Thirty-seven per- 
cent and 34 percent of all 
respondents told Shapiro 
they planned to shop dis- 
count department and dis- 
count drug stores, respec- 
tively, more often in the 
coming year. 

It’s clear that in a trou- 
bled economy, price is still a 
very powerful draw for re- 
tailers. 

The only weapon drug 
store retailers seem to have 
to offset the power of price is 
marketing. Consumers will 
stay with a store, marketing 
executives say, if the store 
offers enough services and 
pleasant attractions, along 
with reasonable prices, to se- 
cure their loyalty. 

For chain drug stores, 
that means building on the 
strengths they have, along 
with developing new 
strengths as a destination 
store. 


Competitive weapons 


However, the findings of 
the Shapiro study also sug- 
gested that drug stores need 
to develop a larger arsenal 
of weapons with which to 
fight the competition for 
their product categories. 

According to the re- 
spondents in the study, the 
presence of a pharmacist 
made drug stores seem su- 
perior to the competition. 
Almost half of the respon- 
dents—46 percent—said 
drug stores had “the best 
pharmacists.” 

When consumers were 
asked which type of store 
provided the best variety on 
the categories measured, 
drug stores still came in 
first, but narrowly edged 
out discount department 
stores in their performance 
measures. Food stores were 


not far behind. 

On other performance 
measures, however, drug 
stores came in second— 
sometimes a distant second. 

Chain drug stores and 
food stores were almost tied 
when it came to the ques- 
tion of which had the fastest 
checkouts. Thirty-two per- 
cent answered food stores, 
while 30 percent said chain 
drug stores. 

However, 29 percent of 
the respondents said the 
discount department stores 
gave the best value for their 
money, compared to 19 per- 
cent for chain drug stores. 

Thirty-nine percent 
thought food stores were 
more conveniently located, 
compared to 24 percent who 
said this was the case for 
chain drug stores. 

Thirty-eight percent said 
food stores were “the easiest 
to shop,” compared to 23 
percent for chain drug 
stores. 

Thirty-seven percent 
agreed that food stores had 
the best brands and private 
label items, compared to 22 
percent for chain drug 
stores. 

Thirty-three percent even 
said that food stores had 
better service, compared to 
27 percent for chain drug 
stores. 

Thirty-four percent 
thought food stores “most of- 
ten had the brands I want,” 
suggesting they are in stock 
more often than chain drug 
stores, at least in the minds 
of consumers; and 32 per- 
cent said food stores were 
the most interesting and en- 
joyable to shop. Just 18 per- 
cent said with this for chain 
drug stores. 

So clearly, while drug 
stores have won some of the 
battles for consumers’ share 
of mind, they have more 
challenges to address. How 
they meet these challenges 
will decide the fate of the 
drug store industry in the 
years to come.

Shopping preferences: 
“I buy skin care products at 
Kmart, Duane Reade and 
Cost Cutters deep discount 
store. I shop there because 
of the prices.

brands are Neutrogena 
and Curel.

when it has non-drying 
formulas that don't irri- 
tate my skin or have a 
heavy fragrance. 

“Ads, price and recom- 
mendations from friends 
will get me to try a brand. 

“Better sales help would 
make a drug store more 
fun to shop.”

and makeup in department stores.

ket or Sav-on next door. Occasionally I shop at Thrifty, but 
the Sav-on is more convenient to home. They have the 
same basic selection. If I just need shampoo, Ill go in Sav- 
on, but if I’m low Ill add it to my grocery list.” 

“My favorite hair care brands are Jhirmack hair spray,

selection of cards, better than my nearest Thrifty. Shoe- 


box is my favorite card line.”

ket and the Sav-on next door. Sometimes the lines are 
longer in one than in the other, or vice versa. I think it de- 
pends on how many checkout stands they bother to open 
when they get busy, or how quickly they respond.”

SECOND CLASS 


Thrifty plus PayLess: 


A look at_ recent 
developments at the two 
drug store chains sug- 
gests some ways Thrifty 
and PayLess’~ could 
strengthen each other or 
even divvy up their over- 
lapping markets. 

Streamlining: Thrifty’s 
20 percent reduction in 
store count already has 
reportedly helped boost 
same-store sales in the 
smaller number of up- 
graded stores, which are 
carrying sleeker invento- 
ry for better turns. Such 
a strategy could benefit 
PayLess, which expanded 
at a fast clip in the past 
three years and has had 
sluggish sales per square 
foot. In the first nine 
months of 1994, PayLess’ 
operating profit fell a re- 
ported 12.5 percent and 
same-store sales fell 4.6 
percent. 

Prototypes: Both Pay- 
Less and Thrifty intro- 
duced prototypes in the 
last 18 months: Thrifty’s 
was designed to trim in- 


A winning combination? 


ventory, upgrade its fad- 
ed image, improve cus- 
tomer service and reach a 
multi-ethnic market. 

Thrifty also played up 
its decades-long neigh- 
borhood tradition and up- 
dated its ice cream coun- 
ters. Thrifty’s ice cream 
is regarded as a prof- 
itable plus, noted ana- 
lysts, who expect the 
hand-dipped concept to 
be rolled out in the com- 
bined chain. 


News Analysis 


Taking a slightly differ- 


~ ent tack, PayLess is lean- 


ing toward suburbia with 
prototype concepts de- 
signed to attract depart- 
ment store shoppers who 
seek more upscale prod- 
ucts. Its latest prototype 
offers a bath-and-body 
boutique, serviced cos- 
metics, party and social

Thrifty/PayLess combination 


changing chain drug playing field 


by Allene Symons 


LOS ANGELES — 
The billion-dollar deal 
is expected to be final- 
ized by the end of the 
first quarter of the 
year: PayLess Drug 
Stores will combine 
with Thrifty Drug 
Stores to create a formi- 
dable drug store chain 
ranking second largest 
in the United States. 

The new 1,066-store 
entity, combining 494 
Thrifty sites and 572 
PayLess locations, will 
be headed by Tim 
McAlear, current chief 
executive officer of 
PayLess Drug—that is, 
if all legal hurdles are 
cleared for the defini- 
tive agreement struck in 
December between Thrifty’s 
parent company, Los Ange- 
les-based TCH Corp., and 
PayLess’ corporate parent, 
Kmart. 

Dan Seigel will remain as 
chief executive officer of 
Thrifty, while McAlear will 
keep his PayLess title until 
the transaction closes before 
the end of March, at which 
time McAlear will become 
chief executive of the com- 
bined chain. 

Seigel is expected to re- 
main with Thrifty in a top 
position, according to Jon 
Sokoloff, general partner 
with Leonard Green & Part- 
ners, the controlling stock- 
holders of TCH Corp. 

Since 1990, Seigel has 
been with Thrifty; he held 
the post of chief financial of- 
ficer and president before 
being named chief executive 
officer last spring. 

On other management 
changes, Sokoloff said: 
“We’re going to spend a lot 
of time to come up with the 


strongest management 
team for the combined com- 
panies.” 


“The name of the entity is 
TCH Corp.,” he said, adding 
that McAlear will be in 
charge of the Payless and 
Thrifty drug chains and Bi- 
Mart, a 41-store discount 
membership drug and gen- 
eral merchandise chain. Bi- 
Mart will be handled as a 
separate stand-alone busi- 
ness, he added. 

According to Sokoloff, no 


‘We're going to 
spend a lot of 
time to come up 
with the strongest 
management 
team for the 
companies.’ 


—Sokoloff

regarding store closings or 
headquarters location. 

Sales for the combined 
chain are projected to be 
$4.7 billion in calendar 
1994. This figure does not 
reflect store closings, ac- 
cording to Sokoloff, who ex- 
plained that an erroneous 
and overly-high 1998 esti- 
mate of $5.9 billion was pre- 
viously reported. 


Future downsizing? 


After the Thrifty/PayLess 
transaction is complete, a 
downsizing move is in- 
evitable, say some retail an- 
alysts, including John Gol- 
ish of Arthur Andersen in 
Los Angeles: “No question — 
whenever there is an 
acquisition of two compa- 
nies like this, the very at- 
tractive aspect is the ability 
to reduce overhead and con- 
solidate functional and or- 
ganizational activities to get 


The Thrifty/PayLess | combilabien will make the chain the second 
largest in the United States with a total of 1,066 stores.

The headquarters may 
not necessarily move to ei- 
ther Wilsonville, Ore. or Los 
Angeles, although many 
industry observers are bet- 
ting on Oregon. 

When asked about plans 
for TCH headquarters, 
Sokoloff would only say: 
“We are reviewing the best 
way to run the company in 
the most profitable fashion.” 

Golish of Arthur Ander-

can be handled remotely. 
For example, Price Club’s

Phar-Mor legal fees mounting 


YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — Companies trying to work 
their way out of Chapter 11 hai, cece can count on 
at least one certainty: steadily mounting legal and ac- 
counting costs. Such is the case with Phar-Mor, which 
in the first year of its Chapter 11 reorganization case 
racked up $04.8 million in fees and expenses, accord- 
Bip Nel ypmanson on court documents. 

t money has gone to more than a dozen legal and 
accounting firms, including the Cleveland office of De- 
loitte & Touche. The Big Eight firm, which became 
Phar-Mor’s chief outside accounting firm after the chain 
severed its relationship with Coopers & Lybrand; is a 
central component in Phar- ar-Mor’s reo ization efforts. 

Given the complexity of Phar-Mor’s case—which in- 
volves allegations of fraud exceeding $1 billion, ac- 
cording to estimates—legal fees are certain to go up. 


Elderly market potential surges 


WASHINGTON, D.C. — Chain drug retailers, al- 
ready poised to benefit from America’s aging popula- 
tion, now have more to get excited about. It seems peo- 
ple over 85 are going to account for a larger percentage 
of the total population than was originally thought. 

Revised Census Bureau estimates indicate in the year 
2020, there will be slightly fewer that seven million peo- 
ple 85 and older. By 2050, the number is projected to in- 
crease to almost 19 million. Previous estimations placed 
those numbers at 6.5 million in 2020 and 17.7 million in 
2050. Those over age 85 numbered about three million 
in 1990. Medical advances and lifestyle changes are 
credited for lengthening life expectancies. 


Eckerd stock a value? 


NEW YORK — Are shares of Eckerd Corp. a good 
buy? Apparently so, according to Morgan Stanley & 
Co., the latest brokerage house to issue a buy recom- 


mendation on Eckerd. 

Morgan Stanley analyst Debra Levin said, “We're ini- 
tiating coverage of Eckerd Corp. with a purchase rec- 
ommendation and have a 12-month target price of $24, 
a 37 percent upside from its current level.” Eckerd cur- 
rently trades at about $18 a share after gradually in- 
creasing in price since its early August 1993 initial 
public offering (IPO) price of $14 a share. 

Prior to the Morgan Stanley announcement, Ray- 
mond James & Associates issued its own research re- 
pas on Eckerd and recommended aggressive accumu- 

ation of the retailer’s stock. Both Morgan Stanley and 
Raymond James were involved in marketing Eckerd’s 
IPO, as was Bear, Stearns & Co, An investment opin- 
ion from Merrill Lynch & Co., the lead underwriter on 
the IPO, is expected in early 1994.

by Allene Symons 


2 Drug Store News, January 3, 1994 


NEW ORLEANS — Buyers from drug, 
combo and mass merchandise chains around 
the country made the third annual School 
and Home Office Products Association 
(SHOPA) trade show the largest yet. 

The event, held here Dec. 8-11, drew 483 
exhibitors, up from 473 last year, who 
treated buyers to new products and licensed 
lines and next season’s palette of fashion 
colors, ranging from hot tropicals to cool or 
textured black. Heading the list for new, 
high-visibility licensed product was Mead’s 
Nike “swoosh” logo on its Five-Star school 


products line. 


Ron Riviere, stationery buyer for Min- 
netonka, Minn.-based Snyder Drug Stores, 
told Drug Store News that he attended the 


show looking for promotional ideas as well 


as new items. “SHOPA has created an ad- 
vantage, since now manufacturers put to- 
gether programs earlier than they did five 
or six years ago, and it helps us prepare,” 


he said. 


Development of a strategic alliance be- 
tween retailers and suppliers is one of the 
three key issues the association plans to fo- 


Dan Mokaczerski of American Greetings (I) 
chats with Gary Wolf of | Got It At Gary’s. 


cus on, said association president Byron 
Rex Miller, along with the management of 
information and the globalization of the 
marketplace. SHOPA’s two-part study, in- 


cluding a strategic overview of the school 


and home office products industry and a 
distribution trends study, will be available 
in the first quarter of 1994. 


Revco a steadfast winner for 2nd atr. 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
Its once troubled past a 
quickly dimming memory, 
Revco D.S. scored solid 
sales and earnings gains in 
its second quarter ended 
Nov. 13. The strong perfor- 
mance provides further evi- 
dence that the company’s 
four-year hiatus in Chapter 
11 was time well spent in 
repositioning and rebuild- 
ing the company. 

Total second-quarter 
sales for the 1,200-store 
chain rose to $546.3 million, 
a 12.6 percent rise vs. the 
same period the previous 
year. Same-store sales 
jumped a strong 9.7 percent. 
Operating profit rose 31.2 
percent to $12.2 million. 

Net income for the period 
was $3.3 million, compared 
with a loss the previous 
year of $0.6 million. Exclud- 
ing the effect of a non-cash 
charge for amortization of 
goodwill, Revco generated 


net earnings of $7.4 million, 
compared with $3.5 million 
the previous year. 

“We are very pleased with 
our continuing strong 
growth in comparable store 
sales...along with continued 
controls on operating ex- 
penses,” said Revco presi- 
dent and chief executive D. 
Dwayne Hoven. “These re- 
sults are especially signifi- 
cant, given current econom- 
ic conditions affecting retail 
businesses and the relative- 
ly low inflation rate in our 
industry.” 

For the first half of the fis- 
cal year, Revco’s sales ad- 
vanced 11.4 percent to $1.07 
billion, with same-store re- 
sults up 8.5 percent. Operat- 
ing profit rose 51.3 percent 
to $15.4 million, with net in- 
come at $6.0 million vs. a 
first-half net loss of $2.1 
million in the prior year. 

Revco’s solid performance 
marks the fruition of a com- 


plete make-over of the chain 
under Chapter 11 protection 
in the late ’80s and early 
90s. It used that time to 
shed over 700 unwanted 
stores, restructure its fi- 
nances, cut costs dramati- 
cally, revamp its operating 
and distribution systems 
and automate virtually 
every facet of its business.

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


drug stores in some parts of the coun- 
try may have trouble finding any play- 
ing field at all! 

Indeed, the real decisions on retail 
pharmacy’s role under health reform— 
the ones that drug chains and inde- 
pendents will have to live with well 
into the next century—are being made 
right now at the state level. 

Perhaps the most immediate threat 
facing community pharmacy on this 
front is the danger that state Medicaid 
administrators will seek waivers from 


administrators 
and other state 
officials on the 
value of ensuring 
coverage for pharmacy services—not 
merely prescription drug benefits. 

Assuring community pharmacy a 
seat at the health reform table would 
be a hollow victory, however, if the 
drug pricing deck remains stacked 
against them. 

To guarantee drug stores a square 
deal in the health reform game, 
NACDS and NARD will spend much of 
the next six months urging state legis- 
latures to enact newly drafted model 
legislation to prevent price discrimina- 


6 Drug Store News, January 3, 1994 


States put obstacles on ‘level playing field’ 


tion. 

Under the model law supported by 
both chains and independents, phar- 
maceutical manufacturers will be 
strictly forbidden from offering any 
class of trade discounts to purchasers. 

All manufacturer drug price dis- 
counts, as well as all rebates, samples, 
deals or trade concessions on pharma- 
ceutical products, would have to be of- 
fered to all pharmacies on proportion- 
ally equal terms. 

Pharmaceutical manufacturers 
would be allowed to continue offering 
some discounts under the model legis- 
lation, including those reflecting 
prompt payment or volume buying 
practices that create economies or effi- 
ciencies for the manufacturer. 

Although drug manufacturers would 
also be allowed to offer discounts that 
reward the use of formularies or man- 
aged care-style programs to influence 
physician prescribing practices, such 
discounts would have to be proportion- 
al to the benefits realized by the man- 
ufacturer, and made available equally 
to pharmacies—including retail drug 
stores.

GENERAL MERCHANDISE / AUDIO TAPE & VIDEOTAPE 


Videotapes turn faster with added value 


rug chains alone sold $145.5 
million in blank videotape 
during the 12 months from 
October 1992 to October 19938, ac- 
cording to the A. C. Nielsen Compa- 
ny’s Scan Track multi-outlet report. 

Of the 32 different manufacturers 
tracked in Nielsen’s report (includ- 
ing a single category for private la- 
bel), Scotch led the drug channel 
pack with 19.1 percent of dollar 
sales, followed by private label, Po- 
laroid, Sony, Memorex and Kodak. 

The category is humming with 
value-added promotions ranging 
from on-pack premiums and point- 
of-purchase giveaways to cross-pro- 
motion coupons. 

That’s because manufacturers and 
retailers are battling for sales of the 
hotly competitive T-120 tapes, by far 
the most popular format. 

Since drug chains, supermarkets 
and discounters run frequent ads, 
consumers have easy picking. “T- 


Prerecorded video 
a hot draw 


Prerecorded video adds ex- 
citement and builds traffic for 
drug chains, even though it usu- 
ally has slim margins. 

In the fourth quarter of 1993, 
the hot sell-through video was 
Disney’s “Aladdin.” Says the 
marketing vice president of a 
major drug chain: “We did a lit- 


tle in advertising for “Aladdin,” 
but I think the video sold itself. 
We use prerecorded video as a 
draw, and we're always on top 
of the new feature videos. It’s 
very competitive and retailers 
often sell at cost as a traffic 
builder.” 

The Disney video also provid- 
ed a perfect drug chain fit with 
a Colgate tie-in supporting a $5 
rebate with purchase of the 
video and four Colgate oral care 
products. 

Wilsonville, Ore.-based Pay- 
Less Drug supported the “Al- 
addin” video and Colgate tie-in 
with dual displays and special 
signing. “It was very, very suc- 
cessful, and we promoted it at 
an extra hot price,” says mer- 
chandise vice president Andy 
Striefel. “It was probably the 
single largest video sell-through 
we have experienced.” 

PayLess carries a basic selec- 
tion in all stores year-round, 
usually in a three-way end and 
an additional 8 feet to 20 feet, 
depending on the size of the 
store. According to Striefel, chil- 
dren’s video is a strong catego- 
ry, along with hot theatrical re- 
leases. 

Don Vanecek of the Chain 
Drug Marketing Association re- 
ports that CD members who 
carry prerecorded video usually 
treat it seasonally, with the 
fourth quarter as the big oppor- 
tunity. “I think if a chain picks 
and chooses titles and does it 
carefully it can be a great item,” 
he says.

120—which is a very promotional

is,” notes Don Vanecek of the Chain

“Mark Holz of Longs Drug, based 
in Walnut Creek, Calif., notes that 
manufacturer prices continue to de- 
cline and intense downward price 
pressure remains. 

With prices falling, Vanecek ex- 
plains, most CDMA members work 
with name-brand product rather 
than promotional or secondary 
sources. “I think price points have 
come down to the extent that [busi- 
ness for the] secondary sources that 
were strong four to five years ago— 
when the customer looked strictly 
at the price advantage—has eroded 
and name brand is dominating.” 

As manufacturers cut prices, dol- 
lar totals are eroding, although the 
category remains a good traffic 
builder and an advertising hook for 
drug chain circulars. 


Margin builders 


Drug chains are looking for ways 
to gain margin and push more units 
of blank tape. Buyers point out that 
in this margin-hungry category, an 
advantage is gained when promot- 
ing off the shelf with value-added 
offers and at prices slightly higher 
than those in a fiercely price- 
slashed ad. 

Camcorder tape, with its higher 
rings and margins, helrs the cate- 
gory’s profitability, although this 
segment doesn’t reach the volume 
of standard VHS tape. Prices are 
starting to drop in this category too, 
report buyers. Both 8mm and VHS- 


‘C formats show growth, according 


to buyers’ reports. Kodak has just 
added the compact format VHS-C to 
its tape line 

More consumers are trading up to 
higher grade blark tape as manu- 
facturer prices drop on the higher 
grades and the gap between stan- 
dard and higher grade product nar- 
rows. Retailers benefit from these 
trade-up sales with heftier rings 
and better margins. 

Trade ups are also boosted by 
“sampling” when a consumer gets a 
higher grade tape in a multipack 
promotion—typically two standard 
and a high grade for the price of 
three standards. Although many 
drug chains reportedly sell more 
single tapes, the value-added multi- 
pack can entice a consumer to go for

Longs’ Holz reports that he is see- 
ing action in camcorder tape—8mm 
is very strong and VHS-C is start- 
ing to pick up in the Longs chain. 
When it comes to pack size, some 
buyers note that camcorder tape is 
generally a two-pack business. Holz 
agrees that there is a general shift 
toward high grade but explains that 
Longs’ sales ratio is three-to-one, 
standard over high grade. Longs 
has mainly emphasized singles in 
its videotape ads. This chain cur- 
rently carries a half dozen brands. 

Another major chain carries seven 
brands of videotape. Its buyer re- 
ports that units are up but dollars 
are flat. He agrees that success in 
this category is in branded product 
but adds, “There are so many quality 
brands that you just have to know 
your customer and be selective.” 

This chain is running more ads 
with both standard and high grade 
videotape in the same ad. “You can 
usually offer high grade at a higher 
margin and make a little more mon- 
ey,” he notes. 


Blank audio tapes in drug 
chains reached less than half the 
dollar total of blank video, or 
$64.4 million in sales from Octo- 
ber 1992 to October 1993, accord- 
ing to the Nielsen Scan Track 
multi-outlet report, which showed 
Maxell, followed by Sony and 
Memorex, leading the pack. 

But Towne-Oller’s October ’92 to 
October ’93 report shows sales of 
audio cassette tapes picking up 1 
percent in dollars and 4 percent in 
units, in contrast with flat dollar 
sales and a 1 percent unit decline 
for blank videotape sales in drug 
chains. 

The blank audio tape category 
enjoys a hardware-driven benefit: 
Compact disc players and audio 
cassette players coexist in many 
homes, a situation expected to 
continue for the foreseeable future 
because when a consumer buys a 
new CD, often he wants to dupli- 
cate the music on audio cassette to

use in another player. This con- 
tributes to modest growth—at 
least in units, if not in dollars—in 
the audio category. 

Compact discs’ quality stan- 
dards and longer playing time con- 
tinue to boost sales of high bias 
and longer length blank audio 


tape for recording, and have led to 
some product introductions. For 
example, TDK aims to get con- 
sumers to trade up with products 
like dual-layered SA-X audio tape 
for use with high-performance 
component systems. Fuji’s new 
high bias audio tape also offers a 
top-line niche opportunity. 

Still, one buyer says, there isn’t 
much excitement in audio tape. 
“Audio manufacturers aren’t turn- 
ing much attention to promoting 
audio cassettes. Manufacturers 
are driven by volume, and it’s in 
video, not audio,” this buyer adds. 

Audio tape sells well in two- 
packs, with most drug chains offer- 
ing some choice of multiple or brick 
packs. As one buyer notes, “When 
we run two-packs and lower price 
points on ads, then we drive more 
customers through our stores. On 
the other hand, the multi-pack dri- 
ves higher dollar sales. So each has 
its own use.” 


Name brands are duking it out 
for their share of the blank tape 
business. Value-added offers aim to 
divert shoppers from private label 
and low-cost brands. 

Branded promotions give lots of 
thrust in the blank tape category, 
since buyers agree that consumers 
prefer to buy quality-branded blank 
video and audio tape. Here is a 
sampling of the latest promotions, 
as well as other innovations. 


e BASF is extending its mail-in 
cash refund offer to new videocas- 
sette multi-packs. First introduced 
in June, the promotion is designed 
to provide incentive to consumers 
who purchase single tapes. The ad- 
ditional multi-pack promotion keeps 
the SRP under $10 for three tapes 
with rebate (four T-130EQ tapes for 
the price of three and a T-160 three- 
pack for the price of two). 


@ Fuji Tape promotes its brand 
image with sponsorships, including 
its highly promoted license as the of- 
ficial videotape and audio tape of 
the National Football League. Fuji 
is currently running an on-pack con- 
sumer. promotion backed by free- 
standing inserts, a Winning Play 
scratch-off prize game and Super 
Bowl commemorative T-shirt offer. 


® Kodak recently introduced its 
first longer videotape, High Stan- 
dard T-160, and entered the com- 
pact camcorder tape field with its 
TC-30 videotape. 

Kodak is also offering different 
year-round, off-the-shelf videotape 
promotions featuring $2 consumer 
rebates to tie in with other Kodak 
products. Retailers can choose be- 
tween programs with purchase of 
three Kodak videotapes: either a $2- 
off photofinishing coupon, $2-off 
movie rental promotion or a $2-off 
coupon toward purchase of a Kodak 
Fun Saver camera. 


@ Maxell’s “Max Award” frequent 
buyer blank tape program, estab- 
lished in 1991, has grown to 
400,000 participants. Prizes award- 
ed for accumulated points include 
posters and T-shirts, Maxell audio 
tape and videotape, sports bags and 
other items. In 1994, Maxell will 
continue to support the program 
with targeted consumer advertising 
and in-store POP. 

Product-wise, Maxell is offering a 
reformulated performance upgrade 
for its VHS and VHS-C lines of 
videotape. Both lines will feature 
updated graphics and on-package 
communications designed to be 
more user-friendly and to promote 
self-service. 


@ Memorex is repackaging its 
high-end audio tape in new black 
and gold packaging. New audio tape 
formats coming from Memorex in- 


clude CD2 and CDX2, new high-end 
formulations of Type II tape. 


@ Polaroid has two new cam- 
corder offers. One is an 8mm Vari- 
ety Pack with two 30-minute tapes 
and one 120-minute tape. This pro- 
motion is targeted to the consumer 
who already uses the efficient 
shorter tapes and provides value- 
added length variety for a home 
tape library. Polaroid is also run- 
ning a buy-two, get-one-free offer 
of a free 30-minute tape with the 
purchase of two 120-minute tapes, 
designed to introduce shorter 
length camcorder tape to 120- 
minute length users. 


© Scotch will mount a first-half 
1994 promotion with 7-Up to pro- 
mote its Performance High Grade 
videotape. The promotion offers a 
free liter of 7-Up at the time of pur- 
chase. The program can be cus- 
tomized to the drug retailer’s pref- 
erence for either three singles or a 
multi-pack, according to Lee

are going after the

GENERAL MERCHANDISE / GIFT WRAP 


Convenient si and poxes boost gift wrap sales 


by Allene Symons 


his shopper is in a 

hurry. She’s just left 

work and is head- 
ing for a friend’s birth- 
day dinner, but first she 
needs a way to gift wrap 
the potted plant she 
bought on her lunch 
hour. 

She finds the answer 
in her nearby chain drug 
store: A plastic gift bag 
large enough for her out- 
sized gift, and it comes 
with a decorative cord 
for the bow. She finishes 
her no-scissors, no-tape 
gift wrap by adding a gift 
card and the special 
touch of a bright tie-on 
satin heart. 


The gift wrap category is 
on the upswing, fueled by 
the demographics of busy 
working women who are 
switching to convenience 
wraps like gift bags and 
boxes. 

Convenience wraps are 
also drawing more men into 
the gift wrap department, 
buyers report, since now it’s 
easy for a guy who is all 
thumbs with tape and wrap- 
ping paper to sidestep both 
for a colorful bag or box. 

Buyer Penn Keller of 
Martinez, Calif.-based Valco 
Drug reports that his combi- 
nation greeting card and 
gift wrap department is up 
27 percent over last year. 
Keller says, “More and more 
of the business is with 
bags.” They are taking 
space from other depart- 
ments, he adds. Gift wrap at 
Valco is now 16 feet and ex- 
panding. 


Get a handle on it 


Diana Wolff of Med-X 
says, “Handle bags are hot.” 
So are stuffing tissue and 
other accessories. “That’s 
where the money is,” says 
Wolff. “We’re doing the vol- 
ume in accessories.” She has 
boxes in new sizes and 
shapes on order and says of 
the expanding novelty gift 
box business, “I think it will 
be interesting, and I think 
it’s great—if you have room 
to display them.” 

At a large national chain, 


aa 
Behe 


é es? ag 


Colorful gift boxes and bags are hot ‘ceiees and their pupulertly extends Pony accessories including 
printed ribbons, stuffer tissue and package decorations. 


Source: Message Factors Inc., Consumer Patterns Study 


the buyer notes that the 
new printed ribbons and tis- 
sues are good performers in 
the chain’s average 27-foot 
sections. A popular combi- 
nation, as selected by cus- 
tomers at this chain, is pro- 
motionally priced solid 
colored handle bags in the 
99-cent range with the pur- 
chase of the higher ticket 
filler tissue. Tie-ons or pack- 
age decorations—like a tiny 
baby rattle for a baby gift 
wrap—are also selling well. 

Several buyers, including 
Valco’s Keller, report that 
combo packs—flat wrap 
with a coordinated bow— 
are still selling. On the oth- 
er hand, many buyers would 
probably agree with one 
buyer who said that roll 
wrap is “probably losing 
some volume to the gift bag 
and colored boxes.” 

With an increasing num- 
ber of design choices and 
price points—new iridescent 
papers, printed ribbons and 
tissues, for example—a 
shopper can customize a gift 
with her own mix of decora- 
tive touches. Plus, she can 
economize on one item, such 
as a bag, then splurge on 
another item like tissue. 

Total gift cost is also a 
factor. In this tight economy, 
more consumers are discov- 
ering that they can cut back 
on gifts because a festively

buy all-occasion

wrapped gift conveys caring 
for a modest cost. A premi- 
um satin bow, especially for 
weddings or anniversaries, 
adds more perceived value 
to the gift than the extra 
cost of trading up from reg- 
ular ribbon. 


Display innovations 


Drug chain buyers also 
note that manufacturers 


are rallying to support the 
gift wrap surge by provid- 
ing innovation beyond prod- 
uct design. 

New compact fixtures 
from American Greetings, 
for example, display gift 
wrap and accessories in 
lifestyle or everyday occa- 
sion groupings instead of in 
categories (all bows together 
or all gift tags together). 
The manufacturer also of- 
fers new box sizes in a dis- 
play with a measuring rule 
to help shoppers choose the 
right size for different gifts. 

Ambassador and Hall- 
mark offer POS programs to 
reduce out-of-stocks while 
streamlining inventory, and 
both have beefed up their 
design offerings and li- 
censed gift wrap products. 

In addition, both Hall- 
mark and AG offer new sign- 
ing. Hallmark’s conveys the 
line’s value prices, while AG 
offers signing to call out its 
occasion-boutiqued products. 

In its new licensed pro- 
gram for 1994, Cleo offers 
14 new licensed designs, in- 
cluding Sesame Street, Tuff 
Mickey, Animaniacs, Min- 
nie!, The Lion King and The 
Flintstones. Also new for 
1994: 32 gift bag designs 
plus four new displays be- 
sides Cleo’s 3-foot perma- 
nent endcaps. Also offered 
are eight new printed tissue 


designs and licensed bag 
and accessory items includ- 
ing Mickey Mouse and other 
Disney favorites such as 
Goofy and Bambi, Michael 
Jordan and new this spring, 
Looney Tunes. 

Gibson introduces Gift 
Wrap To Go, a new conve- 
nience line of bag and box 
ensembles with tissue and 
gift tags. Other new gift 
bags include jumbo plastic 
sacks in different colors and 
designs for wrapping over- 
sized objects like an infant 
car seat. 


Lowering prices 


Hallmark is taking an ag- 
gressive stand in gift wrap 
with price reductions: 70 
percent of gift wrap prices 
are at or below 1991 prices; 
26 percent are below 1989 
prices. The manufacturer 
also offers bags in more 
sizes (SRPs range from $.79 
to $1.29), more licensed de- 
signs and a greater selec- 
tion of wedding and baby 
shower gift wrap. 

Hallmark’s design re- 
placement rate has in- 
creased from 30 percent to 
70 percent. Its gift-wrap dis- 
play has been expanded to a 
total of 54 feet, including 10 
feet of options. 

AG offers gift wrap super- 
trays, including Superman 
and Thomas the Tank En- 
gine, which can serve as fea- 
ture ends, endcaps or free- 
standing displayers. 

New gift wrap designs in- 
clude prismatics, package 
decorations with designs 
like puffy satin hearts. Gift 
Wrap Express offers a one- 
stop wrap display with re- 
volving pillars, including 
two stacked layers of roll 
wrap and 3-foot sections 
boutiqued by occasion to 
encourage impulse sales of 
accessories. 

Ambassador has intro- 
duced its new Choices pro- 
gram, a POS replenishment 
system providing automatic 
product reorder when sales 
reach a predetermined level. 

New Ambassador prod- 
ucts include video and CD 
gift boxes and padded en- 
velopes in colorful metallics 
with bubble-pack padding 
and Velcro closings in fus- 
cia, silver and gold.

Browett made vp 


TROY, Mich. — 
Kmart Corp. will take 
a $1.3 billion charge to 
close and relocate 800 
discount stores and ex- 
pand 700 others by late 
1996. Stores to be 
closed were first slated 
for renovation but were 
deemed too small to be 
competitive. Of the 800 
slated for closure, 650 
will be moved to a larg- 
er location. 

All new and relocat- 
ed stores will have 
pharmacies, said Orren 
Knauer, Kmart head of 
investor relations. 
Kmart has 1,644 phar- 
macies coast to coast. 

Separately, Kevin 
Browett, head of the 
drug store division, was 
made vice president of 
all hardlines merchan- 
dising, overseeing 
pharmacy, HBA, cos- 
metics, sporting goods, 
books a automotive. 


If Christmas 1993 is any 
indication, 1994 will be a 
pretty good year for the 
chain drug industry. 

Year-end sales for drug 
chains in almost every re- 
gion of the United States 
were convincingly better 
than in recent years, under- 
scoring the belief by most 
economists that the economy 
is truly gaining strength— 
and, equally important, that 
consumers are finally begin- 
ning to believe it. 

Among typical comments 
by drug chain executives 
was that of D. Dwayne Hov- 
en, president and chief exec- 
utive of Revco D.S. “We’re 
very pleased with the re- 
sults of our holiday sales, 
which met our aggressive 
sales plan,” he said. 

Added Eugene Apple- 
baum, chairman, president 
and chief executive of 
Michigan-based Arbor 
Drugs, “Our holiday sales 
broke all records. The com- 
pany was right on plan, 
which was aggressive... 
with all segments, including 
pharmacy and front end.” 


Sales were also strong at 
CVS. “People were buying 
that extra item or two at 
the checkout, and the sell- 
ing season was good in 
every market,” said CVS 
spokesman Fred McGrail. 
“Sales were strong across 
categories, with the pre- 
scription business particu- 
larly strong.” 

McGrail said the chain 
was aggressive in its buy- 
ing, and sales exceeded the 
chain’s plans. 

Even in California, which 
has been hit hard by layoffs 
and a slow recovery, Christ- 
mas was deemed a success. 
Said Chris Bement, execu- 
tive vice president of admin- 
istration for Thrifty Drug, 
“We did very well and were 
very pleased with our sales. 
For the month, we had in- 
creases in both sales and 
gross profit dollars.” 

This Christmas was par- 
ticularly satisfying for the 
chain drug industry, which, 
by and large, prided itself 
on anticipating correctly 
that consumer demand 
would pick ap at year-end.

icap Pharma-

named Steve 
Mullenix,

prescription volume.

85 percent of total prescription volume by the year 
2000,” said Johnson. Medicap is among the first pro- 
fessional pharmacy companies to focus on this new 
arena of managed care pharmacy services. 

In related news, Medicap has recorded annual 
same-store sales increases that are among the indus- 
try’s highest. Annual same-store sales growth for 
1992 shows an increase of 14.14 percent. 

Medicap has also named Rick Swalwell to the newly 
created position of director of communications.

Revco adds to base in Akron 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Beefing up its strength in 
the Akron, Ohio market near its home base, Revco 
D.S. has acquired a downtown Y-Mart Store and will 
convert the outlet to a Revco drug store. The company 
already operates a half-dozen stores in the city. 

“The acquisition of this store is part of our strategy 
for growth in Akron,” said Revco president and chief 
executive D. Dwayne Hoven.

Phar-Mor consolidates offices 


YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — Phar-Mor Inc. has 
merged its public relations department into its head- 
quarters here, after a decade in which the chain’s pub- 
lic and community relations activities were shared be- 
tween offices in Youngstown and Pittsburgh. 

The off-price chain’s association with Pittsburgh 
dates back to its inception, when executives of the 
Pittsburgh-based Giant Eagle supermarket chain, in- 
cluding former Phar-Mor president Mickey Monus, 
founded the deep discount chain. 

In a related personnel change, Carol Robinson, for- 
mer vice president of advertising and public relations 
for Phar-Mor, has resigned to become an independent 
consultant. 

The company’s new head of public relations is Di- 
ane Olenik, a Phar-Mor veteran who last served as 
head of Phar-Mor Productions, a broadcast produc- 
tion company.

Drug Store News, January 17, 1994 


by James Frederick 


YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — 
Fortified with new technolo- 
gy and shorn of excess, un- 
profitable stores and mar- 
kets, Phar-Mor appears to 
be off the critical list and 
well on its way to recovery 
as a smaller but better- 
managed retailer. 

The humbled off-price gi- 
ant—which navigated the 
tumultuous aftermath of 
one of Ohio’s largest finan- 
cial scandals by shedding 
close to half its stores, firing 
most of its top managers 
and declaring Chapter 11 
bankruptcy—has clearly 
made progress in its turn- 
around efforts. 

The chain has cut costs 
dramatically. It has re- 
vamped its merchandising 
and marketing strategy 
with new, technology-assist- 
ed buying systems, a re- 
newed focus on basic drug 
store merchandise and a 
new, more aggressive ad 
agency. It has vastly im- 
proved its financial over- 
sight and information sys- 
tems to avoid any repetition 
of the bookkeeping disaster 
of ’92, which led to $499 
million in charges against 
earnings and the company’s 
near-demise. 

What’s more, Phar-Mor 
has outpaced the sales and 
cash flow projections of its 
1993 business plan, accord- 
ing to chief executive Tony 
Alvarez. 

“We have been operating 
favorably against plan. 
We're $5 million to $7 mil- 
lion ahead of our EBITDA 
(earnings before interest, 
taxes, depreciation and 
amortization, or cash flow),” 
said Alvarez in an exclusive 
Nov. 30 interview with Drug 
Store News at Phar-Mor 
headquarters, which includ- 
ed president and chief oper- 
ating officer David Schwartz. 


What remains to 
be seen is what } 
kind of plan Phar- 
Mor will devise to 
pay its numerous 
creditors —includ- 
ing the many ven- 
dors left with un- 
paid bills when 
the chain filed for 
court protection in 
August 1992. 

The vast majori- 
ty of those vendors 
have renewed nor- 
mal or close-to-nor- 
mal credit terms 
with the chain, Al- 
varez said. But to 
emerge from bank- 


ruptcy, the compa- 
ny will need a 
workable payment 
plan and a demon- 
strated ability to 
generate earnings 
to support that plan. 
In addition, the company 
has yet to work out its com- 
plete operating strategy in 
the unforgiving, supercom- 
petitive era of ’90s retailing. 
Although Phar-Mor has 
shed unwanted and unprof- 
itable units, it remains sad- 
dled with some stores that 
are simply too large for its 
merchandise mix and con- 
sumer base. The company is 


Chief exec Tony Alvarez (I) and David 
Schwartz, president/chief operating offi- 
cer, are working toward a more financial- 
ly stable and better managed Phar-Mor.

retooling its competitive edge 


evaluating solutions— which 
could include subletting 
some space or relocating— 
on a store-by-store basis.

Emporium stores in the

franchises, opening its first

growth of the Cincinnati 
franchise, Drug Emporium 
became a joint venture part- 
ner with a substantial in- 
vestment several years ago. 

“We are pleased to as- 
sume full ownership and 
add this fine operation to 
our family of company- 
owned stores.” 


sluggish sales, capital projects

CAMP HILL, Pa. — Rite

net income dropped in the 
third quarter ended Nov. 
27, 1993. Sluggish sales 
growth and capital spending 
on new stores and automa- 
tion put a drag on earn-

company.

were $1.08 billion, a 6.8 

ercent increase over the 
$1.01 villion reported for

year. But Rite Aid’s net 
income declined to $23

for the same period last 
year. 

For the 39 weeks, rev- 
enues advanced 6.8 per- 
cent to $3.18 billion, com- 
pared to $2.98 billion for the 
comparable period last year. 
Total company earnings 
dipped to $80.7 million vs. 
$86.6 million reported last 
year.

“We are already begin-

stores are already strong.

tomer—who holds the key to the

Antitrust shield could come in handy 


the Maryland pharmacy groups “ex- 
horted their members not to partici- 
pate in the plan at the lower reim- 
bursement rate in order to coerce 
Prudential to increase the level of 
reimbursement under the plan.” 

The FTC cited evidence that MPhA 
and BMPA officials asked their mem- 
bers “to notify them if their pharmacies 
did not intend to participate in the 
plan” and “kept a list identifying those 
pharmacies that intended to stop 
participating and communicated this 
information to their members.” 

Whether or not these activities con- 
stitute proof of an illegal boycott is 
open to debate. Certainly the Mary- 
land pharmacists never admitted any 
illegal behavior (although they did set- 
tle the case by promising not to engage 
in future antitrust violations). 

But this much is clear: If Congress 
adopts the President’s plan allowing 
retail pharmacies to collectively nego- 
tiate payments with third-party insur- 
ers, there will be no reason for phar- 
macists to even consider boycotting a 
third-party prescription plan.

About these charts... 


New Product Watch is 
a Drug Store News 
reader service, an ongo- 
ing series of new prod- 
uct performance charts 
based on food and drug 
store sales information 
data supplied by Towne- 
Oller & Associates, a 
subsidiary of Informa- 
tion Resources Inc. 

To measure the suc- 
cess of new products 
launched into a catego- 
ry in a specific period, 
Towne-Oller developed 
a sales performance in- 
dex for each category 
segment. One index 
measures dollar sales 
by category, while the 
other measures unit 
movement. 

To eliminate  in- 
equities caused by the 
effect of varying levels 
of item distribution, 
Towne-Oller equalized 
sales by percent of na- 
tional distribution. 

All new items be- 
tween seven and 12 
months old within a 


sured if they had a national ef- 
fective distribution of at least 25 
percent in the Towne-Oller drug 
store sales tracking service. 

The base index is 100. Howev- 
er, it is calculated using only 
category items that have 
achieved an effective distribu- 
tion level of 25 percent or better. 

So, for example, if an item has 
an index of 295, as the Ponds 
Skin Smoothing Capsules, 21 
count, does in our dollar sales 
index performance chart for face 
moisturizers, its dollar sales 
rate is 195 percent greater than 
the dollar sales rate of the aver- 
age moisturizer item during the 
three-month period.

DRUG STORE NEWS SPECIAL REPORT | 


Retailers remain bullish on TV marketing 


Products that fit the bill move off the shelves 


by Allene Symons 


hen infomercials 
and TV-marketing 
segments hit the 


airwaves with just the right 
product, presentation and 
price point, sales increase, 
chain buyers report. 

While the 90s are more 
frugal than the ’80s and 
there are more infomercials 
battling for sales, still there 
is opportunity. 

Says Andy Striefel, vice 
president of merchandising 
for PayLess Drug Stores: 
“We are supporting a lot of 
infomercial items, but the 
rate of sale in no way com- 
pares to the first infomer- 
cial products.” 

TV-promoted products 
weren't as strong at Lewis 
Drug in 1993 as in recent 
years, reports general mer- 
chandise manager Douglas 
Gravning. But, “it was very, 
very strong in exercise and 
food dehydrators—we sold 
thousands of them last 
year.” 

According to buyers at 
seven large chains surveyed 
by Drug Store News;. the in- 
fomercial category is robust 
and varied, ranging from 
beauty items and OTC and 
exercise products to person- 
al care, gift, automotive and 
cookware products. 


An immediate impact 


When an infomercial 
runs, it can have a striking 


retail impact. One buyer re- 
ports, for example, that In- 
terplak was his No. 1 oral 
care appliance a year ago— 
until Braun Oral B ap- 
peared on infomercials. 
Sales at the chain quickly 
shifted to 60 percent/40 per- 
cent in favor of Braun. 

Lower prices also fuel re- 
tail sales. Lewis’ Gravning 
says when an 
infomercial 
product 
reaches re- 
tail—usually 
after an aver- 
age of two to 
three months 
from its first 
TV appear- 
ance—the 
consumer 
sees a 40- to 
50-percent 
Savings over 
the television 
price and rec- 
ognizes a good deal. Tops 
Tail, for example, was of- 
fered for $9.95 on television, 
but sold for $2.95 at retail. 
But, buyers warn, the dan- 
ger is that the retail price 
will keep dropping. “Now 
you see [Topsy Tail] selling 
for 50 to 75 cents,” says 
Harco Drug buyer Gene 
Bailey. 

Sometimes a product is 
too high-priced for drug 
chains. - Thrifty’s Gary 
Rocheleau, senior vice presi- 
dent of sales and merchan- 
dising, notes that many in- 
fomercials offer high-priced 


products that don’t fit 
Thrifty’s mix. 

The buyer for one regional 
chain cites one example: An 
all-purpose cleaner is being 
advertised on television for 
$19.95 for a 16.5-ounce tube. 
After the exclusive TV offer 
ends, the product will be of- 
fered to retail for between $5 
and $7.50. “So if I buy it for 
$7.50, I have 
to mark it up 
to $14.99 to 
make a good 
margin,” the 
buyer says. 
“But the retail 
price tag is too 
high for the 
consumer, so I 
have to knock 
it down to 
$9.99 for it to 
sell.” 

Who han- 
dles the buy- 
ing and how 
the TV-promoted product is 
displayed and positioned 
differ from chain to chain. 

At one major chain, TV- 
promoted products are or- 
dered by one buyer regard- 
less of category. At another, 
buying is done by individual 
buyers, a change of philoso- 
phy from the past when a 
single buyer was in charge 
of the entire infomercial cat- 
egory and usually ordered 
every item that came out. 


Endcap or in-line? 


Chains also adopt differ- 
ent display and positioning 


strategies. Chip Carter, 
president of manufacturers 
rep group Pacific Sales in 
Los Alamitos, Calif., which 
represents Direct to Retail, 
reports that many of his ac- 
counts use a combined TV- 
marketed-type product dis- 
play and, where warranted, 
a secondary display in indi- 
vidual category sections. 

I got it at Gary’s devotes a 
special endcap to the mer- 
chandise, which will usually 
contain the four or five 
hottest items. Signage flags 
the merchandise “As seen 
on TV.” 

That’s different from an- 
other chain, whose buyer 
explains: “We seldom use 
endcaps, and when we do, it 
depends on the season and 
what the product is going 
up against.” Most of these 
products are merchandised 
within the category or on 
adjacencies, he adds. 

But it isn’t just an endcap 
or category decision these 
days. Planograms add an- 
other decision. Alex Chaf- 
fetz, product manager for 
Regal Advantage, says, “We 
want to be in planograms. 
We are not interested in 
quick ins and outs. That im- 
pression of the business has 
changed.” Infomercial prod- 
ucts “are becoming even 
more difficult to merchan- 
dise because of plano- 
grams,” notes the buyer at a 
regional chain. 

At one major chain, the 

Continued on page 13 


What products keep consumers tuned in? 


What’s burning up the 
airwaves? 

Here’s a sampling: 

Thrifty’s Gary Rocheleau, 
senior vice president of 
sales and merchandising, 
says, “We do very well with 
‘As Seen on TV’ items like 
Chia Pet, Ginzu knives and 
Topsy Tail.” Another winner 
for Thrifty is Cybergenics, a 
diet aid program with a 
combination of supplements 
to suppress appetite. 

Successful infomercials 
attract copycat items, and 
although some can be suc- 
cessful, Rocheleau explains, 
“What we’re looking for is 
guaranteed sale items. If 
we're going to sell look- 
alikes, we want a guarantee 
because there is a risk in- 
volved.” 

At I got it at Gary’s, direc- 
tor of marketing and public 
relations Raymond Hoy be- 
lieves it is critical to be the 
first retailer in a market to 
offer the merchandise. This 
chain carries 10 to 15 hot 


items at any given time. 
Topsy Tail and Dental 
White did well at the chain 
in 1993, although Hoy says, 
“Nothing is screaming off 
the carts right now.” For a 
while, automotive merchan- 
dise was hot, then it was ex- 
ercise-related items. Now it 
seems that toiletries and 
OTC merchandise are sell- 
ing best, he adds. 

Douglas Gravning, gener- 
al merchandise manager at 
Lewis Drug, says timing is 
important: “We rely on job- 
bers to give us information 
on an item that takes off, 
and then we jump on it.” 

A trend like exercise 
equipment has legs, but 
fresh product keeps the cat- 
egory moving. This year’s 
twist is a Ski Slide priced at 
$29.95 that sold for $59.95 
on infomercials last year. 

At Lewis, there isn’t a hot 
infomercial item right now, 
says Gravning, but the 
chain is seeing some action 
on the Jet-Stream Oven 


10 Drug Store News, January 17, 1994 


cooking utensils priced at 
retail around $179 com- 
pared with $249 on televi- 
sion. 

PayLess is doing well 
with the Ginzu knife, Triple 
Edged Wiper Blades and 
Dental White, plus the 
chain is seeing action on the 
Magna Sound stereo receiv- 
er system, Micro Bead ear 
bug jogger radio and some 
familiar standbys like the 
Picker Upper lint remover 
and Pony Flips, one of sev- 
eral look-alike hair acces- 
sories. 

Harco buyer Gene Bailey 
notes that at any given time 
the chain will carry two to 
15 items. Lasting Kiss and 
Dental White are two items 
currently doing well. He 
aims for a 40 percent mar- 
gin on infomercial products 

ut says, “You can’t always 
do that.” 

At one major chain, the 
director of merchandise re- 
ports that this chain carries 
a few dozen items at any 


given time. In November, 
the chain carried 21 in- 
fomercial products. It only 
stocks two to five pieces of 
bulky items. 

“There’s not one category 
of merchandise that sells 
better than another—it’s 
newness and television that 
sell these items,” says the 
chain’s director of merchan- 
dising, who says he achieves 
a margin of 25 percent-plus 
on infomercial product. 

Like the race for TV rat- 
ings, infomercials compete 
for viewers. Even if in- 
fomercials have lost some of 
their luster recently, as one 
buyer says, “A good in- 
fomercial sells.” 

The convenience of drug 
chains captures a lot of that 
business just by spotlight- 
ing the TV cachet. “People 
who are going to buy the 
item buy it because they 
saw it on TV,” says Harco’s 
Bailey. “All you really need 
is signage that identifies the 
items.”

‘Off in '94 


hat products will be the up-and-comers in 
1994? Which established categories will spurt 
ahead in unexpectedly healthy growth? Which 
will catch consumers’ fancies and explode in 
triple-digit growth? 

Only the crystal ball knows for sure, but the 
editors of Drug Store News have taken some ed- 
ucated guesses and put their forecasts for 1994 out for all to 
read. Their predictions fill the following pages. 

Still, the only 20/20 vision is hindsight, and we looked to 
Towne-Oller & Associates to provide a sharply focused picture 
of last year’s performers. Our listing reveals the 25 categories 
that recorded the largest percentage gains in dollar sales in 
drug stores for the 12 months ended October 1993. The list is 
based on segments with annual sales of $12 million or greater 
for the 12-month period. 

According to Towne-Oller, herbal supplements climbed up 
from its No. 2 position last year to top the growth of women’s 
replaceable razors and blades and claim the No. 1 spot. Weigh- 
ing in with a 57 percent increase in dollar sales—totaling 
$53.1 million for the 12-month period—herbal supplements 
enjoyed vigorous growth, thanks to the vitality of such brands 
as Ginsana, Kwai and Kyolic. 

Other products benefited from consumers’ health con- 
sciousness. Just as consumers are buying herbal supplements 
for the health benefits they believe they can find in garlic and 
ginseng supplements, so are they stocking up on vitamin E 
and vitamin A/beta carotene supplements, which have also 
gotten some very positive press in recent months. Vitamin E 
supplements recorded a 40 percent jump in dollar volume, 
while vitamin A/beta carotene supplements followed along 
with a 29 percent jump. 

Thanks mainly to Gillette’s innovative launch of Lady Sen- 
sor For Women, womens replaceable razors and blades, last 
year’s star with a 200 percent climb in dollar volume, ranked 
No. 2 this year, turning in a 47 percent increase on sales of 
$21.1 million for this year’s 12-month period. Until Lady Sen- 
sor, the women’s replaceable category consisted mostly of 
products with handles, encouraging no real replacement blade 
business. 

Along with vitamin E and vitamin A/beta carotene sup- 
plements, other newcomers to Towne-Oller’s list of the fastest 
growing categories include: eye ointments, hot and cold thera- 
py products, foot care specialty inserts, chest rubs, women’s 
hair color, pregnancy test kits and asthmatic remedies. 

Will these be the top performers for 1994? Maybe, maybe 
not. Turn the page for more on Drug Store News’ predictions 
for the new year.
