Photo, greeting cards 
give chains an edge 
over the competition 


Among general merchan- 
dise categories the photo 
and greeting card depart- 
ments are expected to shine 
in ’94 according to chain 
drug buyers. 

Sales of phenomenally 
succesful single-use cam- 
eras were expected to reach 
26 million units for all trade 
channels in 1993, up from 
21 million the previous 
year, and growth should 
continue in 1994, according 
to the latest Wolfman Re- 
port. At Perry Drug, Steve 
Lund reports 1993 single- 
use camera sales increased 
30 percent over 1992. 

In other marketing ven- 
tures this year, manufactur- 
ers are expected to push 400 
ASA. if more consumers are 
persuaded of the film’s ad- 
vantages over 100 and 200 
ASA ratings, the trade-up 
will bring higher rings. 

Drug chains are expected 
to push photofinishing more 
than ever in 794. The drug 
store channel processed 26.2 
percent of all film rolls in the 
third quarter of 1993, ac- 
cording to just-released Pho- 
to Marketing Association fig- 
ures. This is up from 25.8 
percent compared with the 
same quarter of 1992. 

Eckerd recently opened 
its 400th Express Photo lab 
and plans to open an addi- 
tional 240 units by 1997. 

Thrifty Drug introduced 
its enhanced photofinishing 
service offering premium Ko- 


dalux processing in addition 
to regular processing. 
Thrifty’s director of photo 
imaging Sal Azzinaro ex- 
plains that the chain is giv- 
ing photofinishing more 
presence with new graphics 
and drop boxes promoting its 
new overnight program. 
Thrifty now has 30 one-hour 
labs and plans to add 20 in 
the first quarter 1994. 


Cards play well 


Greeting card sales will 
continue to rise in drug 
chains in 1994’s economic 
climate as consumers 
choose greeting cards as an 
affordable form of social 
expression. According to the 
Greeting Card Association, 
dollar sales reached $5.6 
billion in 1998, up 5.7 per- 
cent from $5.3 billion in 
1993 as consumers selected 
higher-priced cards. 

Buyer Penn Keller of Val- 
co Drug says that in the cur- 
rent economy, consumers are 
choosing an expensive card 
instead of a gift. 

Shoppers seeking the 
right greeting card now 
have a chance to create it 
themselves. The electronic 
kiosks from American 
Greetings and Hallmark/ 
Ambassador offer 30-per- 
cent margins, compared 
with the 50 percent average 
for greeting cards, but there 
is no inventory investment 
and rings are around twice 
as high as the average card. 


In 1994, the photo and 
greeting card categories 
are certain to continue to 
be strategic weapons in 
the drug chain battle 
against mass merchandis- 
ers and other re- 
tail formats, as 
they did in 1993.

Health-conscious consumers 


Drug chains have always 
cultivated a health care im- 
age. Now, that image is be- 
ing expanded as retailers 
target consumers’ healthier 
lifestyles and eating habits 
with nutritional foods and 
beverages. 

“We want to be at the 
forefront of this thing, so 
we're in it as we learn, and 
not wait for it to become a 
full-blown trend,” says Andy 
Streifel, vice president of 
merchandising for PayLess. 

PayLess has made good 
on that plan, opening full 
nutritional foods centers 
into all its drug stores in a 
rapid-fire rollout last year. 
The prototype featured nat- 
ural-oat cereals, granolas, 
natural-ingredient cookies, 
organic juices and a broad 
assortment of “healthy” 
snacks like Tiger Milk bars, 
rice cakes and organic corn 
chips. 


The reason for the rapid 
rollout was obvious, Streifel 
adds: “The category has 
very good margins and a lot 
of long-term potential. We 
see it as a very profitable 
category.” 

So too does Osco, which is 
adding large-scale nutrition 
centers to every new and re- 
modeled store under its Vi- 
sion store prototype rollout. 
“The whole country is mov- 
ing to this,” said David 
Gillis, vice president of Os- 
co’s Chicagoland region, in a 
store tour last year. “When 
you think of what we’ve 
done in the waters alone, 
it’s well worth the space and 
attention.” 

At Drug Emporium, 
“We’re picking our spots 
with health food,” says Joel 
Arnold, vice president of 
merchandising for the off- 
price drug chain. He says 
the chain is testing healthy,

HERE’S MORE SCRIPT 
PRICE LITIGATION 


A new legal challenge to 
discriminatory pricing by 
prescription manufactur- 
ers is being mounted in 
New York. 

A class action damage 
suit filed there “on behalf 
of all drug stores in the 
[United States]” by inde- 
pendent pharmacists at 
the Texas-based Pharma- 
cy Freedom Fund alleges 
that wholesaler “charge 
backs” foster price dis- 
crimination against retail 
pharmacies in favor of 
mail-order and hospital 
providers. Without unfair 
pricing differentials by 
prescription manufactur- 
ers, the suit claims that 
“the prices of brand name 
drugs to drug stores 
would have plummeted 
years ago.” 


LIABILITY REFORM 
MOVES IN CONGRESS 


Federal product liabili- 
ty reform legislation 
cleared the Senate Com- 
merce Committee, com- 
plete with a “government 
standards defense” that 
protects manufacturers 
and pharmacists from li- 
ability suits arising from 
injuries caused by FDA- 
approved drugs or other 
products that meet gov- 
ernment safety stan- 
dards.

Pharmacys third-party time bomb 


by Ken Rankin 


fter seeking safe 
A eessae through the 
third-party mine- 
field for more than a gen- 
eration, retail pharmacy fi- 
nally appears to have 
reached a clearing. To 
some pharmacy leaders, 
the profession is on the 
verge of turning the tables 
on its third-party tormen- 
tors and regaining control 
of its own destiny. But 
others see new dangers at 
the oasis ahead. 
Voracious health main- 
tenance organizations, 
cannibalistic mail-service 
pharmacy providers, pre- 
datory closed-panel pre- 
ferred provider organiza- 
tions and other managed 
care carnivores are ma- 
neuvering to bite off a 
larger share of pharmacy’s 
patient base. 


A race against the clock 


The reaction of third- 
party payors to these 
managed care providers 
has been predictably posi- 
tive. As a result, the num- 
ber of consumers being 
forced into restricted phar- 
macy networks and away 
from community pharma- 
cies is growing daily. What 
had been a marathon 
struggle to survive the eco- 
nomic pressures of a 
third-party domination of 
the marketplace is turning 
into a race against the 


clock. And with Congress, 
as well as state legisla- 
tures, being pressed to 
embrace the managed care 
approach to health reform, 
many community pharma- 
cists fear being squeezed 
out of their own markets. 
But others, however, see 
deliverance in the drive for 
health reform. Many are 
convinced that the Clinton 
Administration’s plan for 
health care reform offers 
hope for relieving many, if 
not most of pharmacy’s 
third-party headaches. 
Indeed, they point out 


that with one swing of the 
legislative bat, the Presi- 
dent’s new Health Security 
Act would extend outpa- 
tient prescription drug cov- 
erage nationwide as a ba- 
sic core benefit of the 
program; create a separate 
new Medicare outpatient 
drug program for the elder- 
ly complete with a relative- 
ly generous $5 per pre- 
scription dispensing fee 
indexed to adjust for infla- 
tion; “level the playing 
field’” for retail pharmacy 
by curbing drug manufac- 
turer price discrimination 


in favor of HMOs, hospitals 
and mail-order pharmacy 
services; eliminate the fed- 
eral antitrust exemption— 
which has given unfair 
leverage to third-party in- 
Surance companies in 
their negotiations with 
health care providers; cre- 
ate a new antitrust “safe 
harbor” to enable pharma- 
cists to collectively negoti- 
ate reimbursement rates 
and other terms of third- 
party participation; and 
outlaw abusive physician 
ownership of pharmacies. 


Association views 


“Never haye we had 
such a great opportunity 
to solve so many of our 
problems with one piece of 
legislation,” NARD execu- 
tive vice president Charles 
West told independent 
pharmacists at the associ- 
ation’s annual convention 
late last year. 

However, while NARD 
and NACDS are support- 
ing the Clinton health re- 
form legislation enthusias- 
tically, even the most 
ardent advocates of that 
plan acknowledge that it 
falls short of resolving all 
of pharmacy’s third-party 
prescription concerns. In 
addressing the inequities 
caused by the discrim- 
inatory pricing practices of 
some pharmaceutical 
manufacturers, for ex- 
ample, the White House 
proposal would curb so-

ing homes, HMOs and other “man- 
aged care” providers to buy drugs at 
prices far below those charged to re- 
tail pharmacies. 

But, even under the Clinton plan, 
HMOs, mail-order dispensaries and 
institutional pharmacies would still 
be able to demand price concessions 
from manufacturers in return for al- 
lowing their products on restrictive 
formularies or engaging in Medco- 
style “counter-detailing” activities 
against the products of competing 
pharmaceutical manufacturers. 

In spelling out the Administration’s 
proposed prescription pricing rules 
during a recent address to the Ameri- 
can Society of Consultant Pharma- 
cists, First Lady Hillary Rodham 
Clinton reassured nursing home 
pharmacists that the new restrictions 
on price discrimination would not 
hinder their “ability to use formula- 
ries and therapeutic substitution as 
a basis for negotiating discounts” 
from pharmaceutical manufacturers. 
Community pharmacies would be eli- 
gible for similar discounts, of 
course—but only if they are able to 
discover a way to implement hospi- 
tal-style formulary systems or ther- 
apeutic substitution schemes that 
produce documented “economic 
advantages” to manufacturers in re- 
turn for those discounts. 


Closed panel lockouts 


A separate and perhaps more trou- 
bling deficiency in the Clinton health 
reform plan is the failure to guar- 
antee patients freedom of choice of 
pharmacy provider, or to ensure that 
community pharmacy has equal ac- 
cess to participate in the system on 
the same basis as “managed care” 
providers. Without such protections, 
some pharmacy leaders fear that the 
Administration’s health reform sys- 
tem will be dominated by a series of 
closed-panel PPOs able to lock retail 
pharmacy out of their provider net- 
works altogether. 

The architects of the President's 
plan have already made it clear 
that these networks will be autho-

pharmacists allowed to participate, 
and may even designate “single-

products and services.” State 
“equal access” laws requiring third- 
parties to allow participation by 
“any willing provider” of pharmacy 
services may not prevent communi-

squeezed out of the health reform

For their part, officials at the

“seem to think that unless this bill 
solves every one of our problems, we 
should not support it,” West said. 
“That's a recipe for disaster.” 


Plan falls short

No matter what happens with the 
Clinton health plan in Washington, 
pharmacists and other health care 
providers will face significant 
changes this year as a result of re- 
forms already underway at the state 
level. 


State health reforms enacted 


A number of state legislatures have 
already enacted major new health re- 
forms in anticipation of federal ac- 
tion, and dozens more will be consid- 
ering significant changes affecting 
pharmacists over the next few 
months. According to state legisla- 
tive experts at NACDS, the greatest 
danger facing retail pharmacy on this 
front is the prospect of being locked 
out of the health delivery system in 
some states altogether. During a un- 
precedented summit conference on 
state issues facing pharmacy during 
the 1994 legislative session, repre-— 
sentatives of drug chains and inde- 
pendent pharmacists agreed to work 
together to help shape health legisla- 
tion across the nation.

brought the two camps together: 
Tennessee's newly approved "Tenn-

When third-party payors finally do 
begin to compensate pharmacists 
for cognitive services, it will happen 
because pharmacy has found a way 
to document the value of those ser- 
vices. That’s the philosophy behind 
the creation of an innovative new 
third-party Rx claim form developed 
by NARD and pharmacy manage- 
ment experts at the University of 
Tennessee College of Pharmacy. 

The newly introduced “Pharmacist 
Care Claim Form” is designed to be 
used by community pharmacists to 
record their patient care activities, 
document the cost-effective profes- 
sional services that they provide, 
and bill third-party insurers for the 
value of these services. The form, 
which has been field tested in a 
number of community pharmacies, 
includes a special section to record 
contraindications, adverse effects, 
product misuse, and other problems 
with the patient’s drug therapy not- 
ed by the pharmacist. 

Other sections of the form allow 
the pharmacist to record actions tak- 
en on behalf of the patient, recom- 
mendations concerning the therapy, 


ae

and the results of the pharmacist’s 
intervention. The form, which em- 
ploys an “easy-to-use coding system 
that allows data to be readily extract- 
ed and analyzed,” was patterned after 
similar forms used by physicians and 
dentists to document and charge for 
their patient care activities.

Pharmacy has found a 
way to document the val- 
ue of cognitive services. 


third-party form may be used in 
drug stores, NARD officials sug-

record that a prescribed drug du- 
plicated existing therapy from an- 
other physician, that the physician 
was contacted, and that the drug 
was not dispensed. In another pro-

complained of side effects with a

the prescription was changed to a 
different product.” 

These kinds of interventions by 
pharmacists “represent significant 
cost savings for health insurance 
plans, and the Pharmacist Care 
Claim Form will help gather the in- 
formation necessary to quantify 
these cost savings.” 

In unveiling the new claim form 
late last year, NARD executive vice 
president Charles West described it 
as “a critically important tool to as- 
sist pharmacists in documenting the 
cost-effectiveness of the professional 
services they provide.” The form 
“gives pharmacy an opportunity to 
demonstrate to government, to pri- 
vate third-party health insurers, and 
to the public that the services pro- 
vided by pharmacists save money 
and save lives,” he said. Interest in 
the new form has been high, with 
hundreds of orders outstanding.

be able to participate, crit-

CDMA mulls move to Chicago 


NEW YORK — Chain Drug Marketing Associates is 
looking to move its headquarters to Chicago in the 
next few months. No leases have been signed yet. 

“We need to be located near a national chain,” said 
CDMA president James Devine. “New York is not the 
draw it once was. We need to see the vice president of 
sales, not the New York sales rep.” 

Devine said CDMA had looked at Tampa, Troy, 
Mich. and Chicago as possible relocations. Chicago, 
wiiu its proximity to Walgreens, seems to have won. 


Thrifty-PayLess merger awaits FTC 


LOS ANGELES — As Drug Store News goes to 
press, Federal Trade Commission hearings are sched- 
uled to begin in early February in Washington, D.C. 
when the FTC will consider if the acquisition of Pay- 
Less Drug Stores by Thrifty Drug Store parent THC 
complies with federal antitrust legislation. 


Phar-Mor examiner clears Shapira 


YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — A court-appointed examin- 
er looking into the Phar-Mor fraud and embezzlement 
scheme has cleared board chairman and former chief 
executive David Shapira and other board members of 
wrongdoing in the scandal. The examiner’s report, 
made public late last year, concludes that Shapira and 
other directors were misled by former officers charged 
in the scheme, and “had no knowledge of the fraud.” 

The report confirms the conclusions of other agen- 
cies looking into the massive scandal, including the 
U.S. Attorney of the Northern District of Ohio and the 
FBI. According to its findings, financial reports were 
altered to conceal the fraud from Shapira and others, 
and “to avoid suspicion and...continue the charade 
that Phar-Mor was a profitable company.” 

The falsification of financial records destroyed the 
usefulness of Phar-Mor’s accounting system for man- 
agement purposes, the report concluded. 

Former chief financial officer Patrick Finn and a 
subordinate have already pleaded guilty to criminal 
charges in connection with the case. Former president 
Michael “Mickey” Monus is facing trial on criminal 
fraud charges. 


F&M adds more pharmacies 


WARREN, Mich. — The dust will be flying at F&M 
stores early this year as the Michigan-based deep dis- 
counter retrofits 17 of its units with pharmacies. The 
installation of the new pharmacies will give the chain 
prescription departments in 93 of its 121 stores. 

“The 28 stores that do not have pharmacies are be- 
ing investigated as to whether it is possible,” said 
Kevin Ball, F&M’s advertising director. “They were 
designed so that pharmacies could be put in, sc chat is 
being looked at, and we could potentially have phar- 
macies in all our stores.” 


Kmart tests health care call-in 


TROY, Mich. — Kmart Corp. has launched a test of 
a new service by which consumers can get free health 
care information through a toll-free phone service. 
The service, called Healthcare Line, offers prerecord- 
ed information from more than 30 pharmaceutical 
companies on nearly 125 topics. 

Initially, Healthcare Line directories will be avail- 
able at all Kmart pharmacies and delivered to most 
homes in three markets: Columbus, Ohio; Tampa-St. 
Petersburg, Fla.; and Indianapolis. By calling 1-800- 
77-HEALTH, consumers can learn more about cold 
remedies, allergies, diabetes, hypertension and other 
topics. The new program also invites callers to re- 
quest a printout of the information and coupons from 
brand sponsors.

respectively.

nancial firm that purchased Thrifty in 
mid-1992, has not yet revealed much 
information about its plans for combin- 
ing Thrifty and Payless, and many of 
the details are still being worked out.

may end up doing less volume than the

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


Last year, the number of new drugs 
approved by FDA actually dropped by 
more than 20 percent. 

While the FDA’s drug approval 
track record for 1993 is discouraging, 
the picture could get much worse. 

Suppose the drug industry scales 
back its research and development ac- 


president Ron 
Ziegler, aren’t 


buying the phar- 
maceutical indus- 
try’s doomsday 
predictions. For their part, however, 
pharmaceutical industry leaders say 
the downturn in drug R&D has al- 
ready started. 

According to the Pharmaceutical 
Manufacturers Association, the drug 
industry is no longer able to justify the 
more than 16 percent average annual 


4 Drug Store News, February 7, 1994 


vestment going forward with drug 
stores as its only business. And, ac- 
cording to Martin Grass, president 
and COO, the chain is not ruling out 
“selective” acquisitions in the drug 
store field in the future. 

In a conversation at Rite Aid’s head- 
quarters, Martin Grass told me that 
the chain hopes to shore up its drug 
stores by intensifying its efforts with 
pharmacy, which continues to grow 
versus front-of-store. To support phar- 
macy in a world that is rapidly becom- 
ing dominated by third-party insur- 
ance plans, Rite Aid is getting into the 
managed care business in a big way. 
In fact, Grass explained, Rite Aid just 
purchased two companies—PCI, a 
third-party administrator, and Intel- 
Rx, a drug utilization review firm— 
that will help Rite Aid compete more 
effectively in the managed care arena. 

In the midst of all this, the nation’s 
No.1 drug chain continues to thwart 
all challengers while racking up new 
sales and earnings records year after 
year after year. At its recent annual 
meeting, $8.3-billion Walgreens set 
forth a stepped-up expansion plan that 
calls for 175 additional units in fiscal 
1994, including major blitzes into new 
markets of Cleveland and Buffalo. 

American Drug Stores is the only 
company in the new top 5 that didn’t 
make news in the past month or so. 
But, the chain that recently earned a 
record three Rex Awards from Drug 
Store News isn’t known to rest on its 
laurels. I expect plenty of action and 
innovation from the parent of Osco 
and Sav-on this year, too. 

Remember that in nature the speed 
of the leader determines the rate of 
the pack. So, as the leading drug 
chains concentrate on their core busi- 
ness—which will surely lead to rapid 
and significant changes in 1994 and 
beyond—it’s time for everyone to pick 
up the pace. 


increases in R&D investment that 
took place between 1980 and 1992. 

Indeed, a new PMA member survey 
found that the industrywide R&D 
spending increase barely averaged 10 
percent last year, and that the growth 
in new drug research and development 
will drop to a single-digit pace in 1994. 

Pharmaceutical industry worries 
over heavy-handed price controls un- 
der the Clinton health reform plan are 
only one reason for the declining R&D 
growth, according to the PMA. 

Other factors depressing industry 
research include: efforts by “managed 
care programs” to reduce drug costs 
through “aggressive discount negotia- 
tions”; a “voluntary” commitment by 
PMA members to resist prescription 
price increases; and a sharp increase 
in the generic market share from 30 
percent in 1989 to an expected 50 
percent of all new scripts dispensed 
this year. 

For my part, I have no argument 
with the PMA’s statistics—only with 
the group’s conclusion. If anything, the 
growing pressure on pharmaceutical 
industry profitability should provide 
an incentive for more R&D of new drug 
products, not the other way around.

Managing hair care space a constant battle 


by Barbara White 


t’s an understatement to 

Say space management is 

a challenge in the com- 
modity hair care category. 

“There is such a variety of

and line extensions entering

based Chain Drug Market-

Calling space manage-

problems retailers face in 
this category,” Cincotta said 
drug chains need to make a 
careful analysis of their 
commodity hair care inven- 
tory. “Retailers could easily 
eliminate 20 percent of 
their inventory and their 
customers wouldn’t notice,” 
he said. 

Indeed, drug chains are 
looking at the department 
with a critical eye. Gregg 
Heller, buyer at Tulsa, Okla.- 
based May’s Drug Stores, 
has a firm policy: SKUs must 
have a unit movement of at 
least 300 pieces a year to 
stay in the chain’s mix. 


Slow movers nixed 


Tuscaloosa, Ala.-based 
Harco Drug is taking a sim- 
ilar tack. Buyer Charles 
Monk said the category is 
reviewed on a six-month ba- 
sis. The products that aren't 
moving are dropped. 

“Every time we review, 
we cut,” said Monk. “We 
only have 12 feet of space 
for the category, and that’s 
all we are going to get.” 

Manufacturers know that. 
Retailers said most vendors 
are partnering with chains to 
better manage their space. 
“Manufacturers realize that if 
they want to be in with a new 
item, they have to pull some- 
thing out,” said May’s Heller. 
“Even Procter & Gamble is 
starting to cooperate.” 

“There’s not much resis- 
tance to taking slow-moving 
products out of the mix to 
make room for innovative 
new items,” added Monk. 

Ann Carraher, director of 
marketing at Alberto-Cul-

About these charts: To measure 
the success of new products 
launched into a category in the 
most recent period, Towne-Oller 
and Associates has developed a 
sales performance index. To elimi- 
nate inequities caused by varying 
levels of item distribution, Towne- 
Oller equivalized sales by percent 
of national distribution. 

All new items between seven 
and 12 months old within a cate- 
gory were measured if they had a 
national effective distribution of at 
least 25 percent in the Towne- 
Oller drug store sales tracking 
service. 

The base index is 100. So, for 
example, if an item has an index of 
179, its dollar sales rate is 79 per- 
cent greater than the dollar sales 
rate of the average item during the 
three-month period.

agree with Carraher’s space 
management philosophy. 
According to Helene Curtis’ 
Power Brands, 20 percent of 
the brands produce 80 per- 


cent of the sales, so those 
brands should be given the 
lion’s share of shelf space. 
“Some peripheral brands 
are niche brands and have a 
strong following, such as 
Tegrin. We don’t suggest 
dropping those,” said Bob 
Shipley, retail area sales 
manager at Helene Curtis. 
“We suggest dropping those 
brands that are on a swift de- 
cline, brands that may once 
have had a following, but are 


shampoo with conditioners 
and styling aids so the brand 
makes a greater impact.” 

Other retailers use a more 
time-honored approach. “We 
don’t planogram our bottom 
shelf so that we can use it for 
overstocks when we run a 
promotion,” said Harco’s 
Monk. “I can’t give 10 facings 
to White Rain Extra-Body 
Formula every day, since it 
doesn’t sell as quickly when 
it’s not on promotion.”

HEALTH & BEAUTY AIDS/ COMMODITY HAIR CARE 


Intensive and leave-in conditioners bold new players 


Leave-in and intensive 
conditioners are showing 
signs of growth in the 
otherwise flat commodity 
shampoo and conditioner 
category. 

Drug store sales of inten- 
sive conditioners totaled 
$46.2 million, a 9 percent 
increase over the previous 
year. 

Sales of leave-in condi- 
tioners in drug stores to- 
taled $7 million last year, a 
42 percent increase over the 
previous year’s. sales, 
according to Towne-Oller 
and Associates’ estimates. 
That high percentage in- 
crease is attributed to the 
growth of a new category, 
but is impressive all the 
same. 


Quality, convenience 


Fueling leave-in con- 
ditioners’ popularity is 


their convenience and 
effectiveness. 

“There was a population 
of consumers who were very 
unhappy with the current 
choices and were not using 
conditioners,” said Michael 
Trese, director of public re- 
lations for L’Oréal’s hair 
care division. 

“So, the leave-in condi- 
tioner segment represents 
new sales, not cannibaliza- 
tion,” he said. 

L’Oréal’s research esti- 
mates that 80 percent of 
women aged 13 to 34 and 
45 percent of men use 
conditioners. 

L’Oréal added Light Step 
foam-in leave-in conditioner 
in four SKUs to its Studio 
Care line last summer; 
Trese said the products con- 
tinue to grow. “The products 
represent a new technology 
being brought to the 


marketplace,” he said. 

“Leave-ins are a very ef- 
fective short-term condi- 
tioner,” said Muggs Lerberg, 
a spokesperson for Red- 
mond. “They provide a de- 
tangler, shine enhancer, 
styling aid and conditioner 
all in one product.” 


Marketing a niche 


Manufacturers are now 
positioning leave-in and 
deep conditioners as sepa- 
rate steps in a consumer's 
hair care regimen, so that 
both become necessary 
purchases. 

“There is a potential for 
deep conditioners,” said a 
spokesperson from one 
leading hair care manufac- 
turer. “As people age, their 
hair changes, and it be- 
comes drier. Demographics 
point to big gains for these 
products.” 


More natural look the trend for ’94 


hat hair care trends 
will be important in 
1994? 


Drug Store News asked 
Tim Casey, creative director 
of the Pierre Michel Salon 
in New York’s Trump Tow- 
er, that question. Here’s 
what he said: 

@ Styling products will 
make hair modern for the 
‘90s. Hair styles will require 
more volume, and rather 
than setting or teasing hair 
into shape, women will use 
spray-on volumizers to 
achieve the desired effects. 

@ Spray gels and mousses 
will be lighter and serve a 
dual purpose; they'll provide 
volume and enhance shine. 

@ Leave-in conditioners 
will continue to grow in pop- 
ularity. “Leave-ins add shine 
and body and control frizz,” 


In-stock positions are 
crucial to this low-ticket, 
high-turn category, partic- 
ularly in the value seg- 
ment. High turns are all 
retailers can hope to 
achieve on such a price- 
competitive segment. 

“People are so price con- 
scious that no one is mak- 
ing money on the value seg- 
ment. These products are 
traffic-builders,” said John 
Cincotta, buyer at Manhat- 
tan-based Chain Drug Mar- 
keting Associates. 

“We’re giving the low- 
end stuff away,” said 
Gregg Heiler, HBA buyer 
at Tulsa-based May’s 
Drugs. “We have a lower 
than 5 percent margin in 
that area.” 

Retailers are depending 


said Casey. 

® Intensive conditioners 
will also become more impor- 
tant as consumers try to re- 
plenish moisture in the hair. 

@ Perms are out. Casey es- 
timates that salon perms are 
down 50 percent compared 
with five years ago. “People 
aren't subjecting their hair to 
damaging processes. Good, 
healthy hair in a simple cut 
is important,” he said. 

@ Color is in. People aren't 


just coloring to cover gray, 


but to enhance their own col- 
or and to create natural high- 
lights. Color conditioning, 
which deposits a bit of pig- 
ment on the hair shaft, and 
other methods of semi-per- 
manent color treatments are 
popular. “People are looking 
for more gentle, non-ammo- 
nia formulas,” said Casey. 


Managing margins in a competitive category 


on new, innovative items 
to make up the difference. 
Higher-priced products 
formulated for specific 
hair types have provided 
innovation and margin 
over the past few years, 
and retailers continue to 
give high marks to prod- 
ucts such as L’Oréal’s Per- 
mavive and Colorvive and 
Procter & Gamble’s ProV. 

But even those brands 
are moving toward a value 
image. P&G spokesperson 
Kimberly Stewart said 
value is the name of the 
game in hair care. 

L’Oréal has upsized its 
Studio line of styling aids 
and its Colorvive and Per- 
mavive shampoo and condi- 
tioners while lowering or 
keeping the price constant. 


e Sunscreens in hair care 
products will be more impor- 
tant. “Especially when they 
color their hair, women don't 
want to spend $100 on color, 
only to have it ruined by the 
sun,” said Casey. Gels and 
other styling products that 
contain SPFs will be show- 
ing up on retail shelves. 

@ Fragrance- and cruelty- 
free products are very impor- 
tant to Casey’s clients. 
“Women don’t want their 
hair care products competing 
with their perfume,” he said. 

@ Professional products 
will remain strong. “People 
want that ‘prescription’ from 
their salon. They want spe- 
cific products formulated for 
their specific hair types, and 
they will follow a regimen 
suggested by the person that 
cuts their hair,” said Casey. 


Forward-looking retail- 


“Our studies show us that 
people are shampooing 
more frequently, and that 
takes a toll on the hair,” 
said Ann Carraher, director 
of marketing for Alberto- 
Culver’s consumer toiletries 
division. 

Alberto-Culver recently 
introduced a line of inten- 
sive conditioners and inten- 
sive conditioning shampoos 
under the Alberto VO5 Hot 
Oil brand name. 

Redmond’s Australian 3 
Minute Miracle and Aussie 
Curing Muddy are specifi- 
cally aimed at the consumer 
seeking a deep conditioning 
treatment. 


Variety cherished 


Redmond’s Lerberg cited 
another reason for the seg- 
ment’s growth: “Women are 
cdoing more with their hair. 
I'd say that the jump in 


hair coloring is contributing 
in a large part to the 
growth in deep condition- 
ers.” A recent Gallup poll 
revealed that 50 percent of 


‘the women surveyed had 


perms; 40 percent colored 
their hair at home. 

Whatever the reasons, re- 
tailers have taken notice. 
“I’ve seen a big growth in 
conditioners,” said Gregg 
Heller, HBA buyer at Tulsa- 
based May’s Drugs. “Usual- 
ly, I expect a brand’s condi- 
tioners to generate about 
half the sales that the 
shampoo generates. In some 
cases, leave-ins and inten- 
sives are surpassing sham- 
poo sales.” 

Said a buyer at a deep 
discount chain: “People are 
starting to take better care 
of their hair. I am noticing 
a big growth in the deep 
conditioners.”

GENERAL MERCHANDISE / PET PRODUCTS 


Chains want sales to go to the dogs—and cats 


by Vicki Gerson 


here’s plenty of poten- 

tial in pet products— 

for the savvy mar- 
keter. “Your pet is eating 
more often than you’re 
shampooing your hair,” Rob 
Bevis, pet buyer, Hook Drug 
Division, pointed out. 

Some chains are capitaliz- 
ing on the opportunity. 
More need to do some work 
to compete, as the sales fig- 
ures indicate: Sales of pet 
food and pet supplies re- 
mained flat at chain drug 
stores in 1993. 

But the opportunity re- 
mains. A pet department 
can provide drug chains 
with greater profits and 
interesting traffic-building 
opportunities. 

According to a May 1992 
survey from the American 
Pet Products Manufacturers 
Association (APPMA), 53 
million dogs and 62 million 
cats live in U.S. homes, and 
thanks to a continued in- 
crease in the number of cats 
per cat-owning household, 
cats are extending their 
lead. The number of birds 
has reached 14.6 million, 
while the number of 
freshwater fish (89 million) 
and marine fish (5.6 mil- 
lion) has also increased. 

“Two hundred thousand 
households took part in this 
survey, said Claire DeNi- 
cola, director of public rela- 
tions for the association. 
“There are thousands of dif- 
ferent cat and dog products 
in the marketplace—no one 
store can sell them all. But, 
we find that pet owners are 
putting more emphasis on 
their animals.” 


The competition 


Grocery stores remain the 
leading outlet for dog food, 
treats and chew items, but 
since 1990, they have lost 
business to other channels. 
According to the APPMA, 
grocery stores account for 
62 percent of dog food pur- 
chases, while drug stores 
trail discount stores, feed 
stores, pet stores, veterinar- 
ians, pet food warehouses 
and warehouse clubs, with 
only 2 percent. Meanwhile, 
cat owners purchase 72 per- 
cent of their cat food in gro- 
cery stores and only 2 per- 
cent in drug stores. 

Chain drug store retailers 
fare a little better in other 
categories. For instance, 9 
percent of the total house- 
holds surveyed purchase 
flea/tick products at the 
drug store, while 6 percent 
purchase rawhide chew 
items. Chain drug store re- 
tailers sell 4 percent of the 
food treats and 7 percent of 
the toys.

Strategies regarding pet products vary widely among drug chains. The more successful stores 
have identified a niche and moved aggressively to fill it. 


Adding to the competi- 
tive nature of the pet food 
and pet supply market has 


pet food superstores. In the 
past 18 months, according 
to a Food Institute Report, 
about 500 pet product su- 
perstores have opened 
their doors to pet lacs 
who are spending more on 
their pets than ever before. 


been the rapid growth of 


A new competitor in the ring 


Their impact has been 
felt mostly by supermar- 
kets. Chicago-based Infor- 
mation Resources Inc. re- 

orted that in 1992, pet 
ood sales through super- 
markets declined 1.6 per- 
cent to $4.6 billion. For the 
12-week period ended 
Sept. 12, 1993, dry dog 
food sales declined 2.4 per- 
cent to $335.5 million, and 


canned cat food sales 
dropped 3.2 percent to 
$251.7 million. Canned dog 
food sales were down 3.7 
percent to $177.8 million. 
Supermarkets have 
found that they must now 
promote the once high- 
margin pet foods to stay 
competitive with super- 
stores, mass merchandis- 
ers and warehouse clubs. 


When examining cat 
households, percentages at 
drug stores don’t change 
greatly. Two percent of the 
households purchase cat lit- 
ter from drug stores; 9 per- 
cent purchase flea/tick prod- 
ucts; 8 percent, toys; and 4 
percent, treats. 


Solving the puzzle 


Drug chains take widely 
varying approaches to the 
market. Hyde Park Drug 
Inc., with nine stores in Ok- 
lahoma, is at one extreme. 
The retailer doesn’t empha- 
size its pet department. It 
carries a limited amount of 
pet food and other items 
from a rack jobber. “Each 
store can do what it wants 
to do,” says spokesperson 
Chris Surman. “Some have 
items for cats and dogs; oth- 
ers have items for birds or 
fish. It depends on sufficient 
sales.” 

The Rock Bottom Stores 
Inc. in New York takes a 
similar stance. Marvin 
Schor, pet buyer for the 34- 
store chain, said, “We’ve 
never had a large pet de- 
partment. We carry prod- 


Drug Store News, February 7, 1994 


ucts for birds and small ani- 
mals, and snacks for dogs 
and cats.” 


A few innovators 


Other retailers are taking 
a more aggressive stance. 

Because of the potential 
of the market, said Hook’s 
Bevis, “we need to look at 
this area and make it more 
attractive to the consumer. 
Right now, we're getting our 
customers to realize that we 
have a viable pet depart- 


ment. We advertise foods 
frequently and coupon 
accessories.” 


Bevis also sets up season- 
al displays, addresses the 
health of pets with senior 


‘Treats are a good 
high turnover item 


-and can mean 


repeat traffic.’ 
—Bevis, Hook 


brand foods and sells inter- 
active toys for cats. “A cat 
owner must play with their 
cat to make the toy work. 
This new type of toy allows 
cat owners to spend quality 
time with their pet,” he said. 

Right now, the only pet 
salespeople that really 
interest Bevis are those sell- 
ing dog and cat treats. This 
category is growing rapidly 
because today’s pet owners 
are interested in rewarding 
their pets with a special 
treat rather than with food 
or a toy. Therefore, Bevis 
adds new treats to his prod- 
uct mix when something ex- 
citing comes in. “A lot of 
new treat items are just 
bagged,” added Bevis. “It’s 
not an item that’s meant to 
last more than a week. 
Treats are a good high 
turnover item and can mean 
repeat traffic.” 

Hook Drug Division also 
does a steady business in 
bird, fish and small animal 
needs. These products are 
in stock but not emphasized 
by the company. 

Each summer Bevis does 
a planogram of his depart- 


ment. “Our space is limit- 
ed,” he said. “We cannot 
grow. Therefore, we have to 
make the most out of the 
space we have.” 

Bevis also pointed out 
that companies like Hartz 
Mountain plan to make 
their areas more attractive 
to consumers in ’94. Their 
space will have a boutique 
look, have point-of-purchase 
displays and be more trendy 
looking. 


Stock, convenience key 


Other chain drug retailers 
like Arbor Drugs Inc. look 
upon the pet department as 
an accommodation to its 
customers. “We believe the 
most important component 
of this department is to 
have items in stock,” said 
spokesperson Fred Marx. 
“Because all of our stores 
are highly profitable—and 
we're the market share 
leader in Detroit—each inch 
of the shelf is measured 
very carefully. With our 
computer technology, we are 
able to tell, store by store, 
the selling rate of pet items. 
Then, we stay in stock on 
these products per location.” 

Marx doesn’t believe a 
large assortment is the key 
to having a successful pet de- 
partment. He stressed what 
customers are looking for are 
items they want 365 days a 
year. “Our customers want 
convenience. They want to 
be able to run in and get the 
item quickly,” he said. 

In Vermont, City Drug 
Stores has taken a different 
approach to the pet busi- 
ness. “Most of our stores are 
next door to Grand Union 
supermarkets,” said John 
Mumley, buyer for pet prod- 
ucts. “We’ve found it a 
waste of time and space try- 
ing to sell what Grand 
Union sells. At one time, we 
had pet food departments— 
but not anymore. It makes 
no sense to have two stores, 
side by side, selling the 
same things. It doesn’t give 
us any profitability to do 
that.” | 

Thus, City Drug Stores 
has created a niche for it- 
self. It sells mainly bird 
products and deals only 
with Hartz Mountain. 

Over at Thrifty Drug 
Stores Inc., Lee Osborn, pet 
buyer, carries no pet foods. 
He carries pet accessories 
and Tidy Cat, which does 
well and is put on special 
occasionally. “At Christmas 
time, we notice our cus- 
tomers purchase their pets 
Christmas presents like 
toys and bones,” he said. 
“Our pet department is 
there for the convenience of 
our customers.” 

Osborn views the pet de- 
partment like the hardware 


and automotive sections of 
the stores. “We carry high 
impulse, high-gross margin 
items,” he explained. 

Rick Gonsalves, pet buyer 
for Douglas-Maxi Drug Inc., 
only carries Hartz Mountain 
products. However, he also 
shops the promotions from 
time to time. For the winter 
holidays, he brought in 
rawhide lollipops. A sum- 
mertime promotion featured 
a self-feeding food and wa- 
ter pet bowl. “We have no 
trendy items,” Gonsalves 


said. “We carry collars, fish _. SE 


food, bird and small animal 
food, chemicals for aquari- 
ums, litter pans, bowls, 
snack food and toys.” 

At Drug-Sav Company in 
east Texas, dry foods rather 
than accessories are selling. 
Plus, cat products are lead- 
ing all categories. “Right 
now, the department is

RX margins, distribution shift 
factors in HSI's first gtr. loss 


CINCINNATI — Hit with 
lower prescription margins 
and a costly shift in 
distribution and accounting 
practices, Hook-SupeRx Inc. 
posted a net loss of $6.9 mil- 
lion for the first quarter 
ended Nov. 30, 1993. 

The results include a 
change in tax accounting, 
and reflect a decline in 
pharmacy gross margins 
due to the growing impact of 
third-party plans. Margins 
were also hampered by “du- 
plicate warehouse and dis- 
tribution expenses incurred 
during the first quarter,” 
HSI noted in a report. The 
extra warehousing costs 
were due to the transition 
away from the chain’s out- 
side wholesaler, Peyton Inc., 
into its own enlarged Mid- 
western distribution center. 

The transition hit HSI 
with roughly $3 million in 
duplicate costs. Beginning 
early this year, the company 
is shipping everyday mer- 
chandise from its newly en- 
larged warehouse in Indi- 
anapolis, a practice that 
should yield cost benefits. 

Excluding the effects of 
the extra distribution ex- 
penses, HSI’s operating 
profit margin would have 


improved to 1.4 percent of 
sales. SG&A expenses de- 
clined from 24.3 percent to 
23.7 percent of sales, “pri- 
marily due to more strin- 
gent cost control measures, 
combined with the benefits 
derived from the company’s 
ongoing consolidation ef- 
forts” and the previous clos- 
ings of unprofitable stores. 

Sales for the first quarter 
grew 4.4 percent to $567.9 
million, with same-store re- 
sults up 4.5 percent. 


Bergen Brunswig reports 
net sales increase 


ORANGE, Calif. — Ber- 
gen Brunswig reported net 
sales of $1.8 billion for the 
first quarter ended Dec. 31, 
vs. $1.6 billion for the previ-

ST. PETERSBURG, 
Fla. — One-stop shopping 
for complete home health 
care needs will soon be a 
reality at the Eckerd

erd will enable customers 
to get blood drawn for lab

or visit with a nurse on 
staff at the new depart- 


ment. Convalescent aids 
such as wheelchairs, 
scooters, walkers, IV 
poles, oxygen, humid- 
ifiers, back supports and 
whirlpools are also avail- 
able, as are diabetes 
products. 

To accommodate the

mately 700 square feet of 
what used to be a district 
office in the rear of the 
store was converted. The 
center is adjacent to the 
pharmacy but is accessible 
through separate doors.

Reject Merck-Medco plan, 


by Ken Rankin 


WASHINGTON — NACDS president 
Ron Ziegler urged Congress to reject a con- 
troversial new Merck-Medco proposal that 
could give “managed care” mail-order drug 
dispensaries the inside track in filling 
Medicare prescriptions under the Clinton 
health reform plan. 

Testifying on behalf of the NACDS/NARD 
Community Retail Pharmacy Health Care 
Reform Coalition, Ziegler warned Rep. Hen- 
ry Waxman’s (D-Calif.) House Health Sub- 
committee that such an approach would im- 
pair “the right of the elderly to freely choose 
their pharmacy.” 

“This approach simply is not right for 
Medicare, it is not right for the elderly, and 
community retail pharmacy will firmly and 
actively oppose it,” he said. 

Ziegler’s concerns were fueled by reports 
that Merck, Genentech and other major 
pharmaceutical suppliers will soon actively 
lobby Congress to abandon President Clin- 
ton’s proposal for a Medicare outpatient 
drug benefit open to all pharmacies, in fa- 
vor of one built around “Pharmacy Benefits 
Management” (PBM) groups such as Medco. 

Testifying just moments before Ziegler, 
Merck chairman P. Roy Vagelos outlined 
his company’s plan to the subcommittee, 
describing it as a major improvement over 
“the antiquated and counterproductive ap- 
proaches to cost control” contained in the 
Clinton Administration’s Medicare outpa- 
tient drug plan. 


NACDS' Ziegler tells Congress 


NACDS president Ron Ziegler warns Congress 
that the Merck-Medco’s proposal will limit the 
elderly’s freedom of pharmacy choice. 


The savings that Medicare would realize 
by bidding out pharmacy services to Medco 
and other PBM groups would be substantial- 
ly greater than those generated by Clinton’s 
proposal to require 17 percent rebates from 
pharmaceutical makers, he maintained. 

Vagelos’ proposal sparked interest among 
several key Congressmen at the hearings, in- 
cluding Waxman, who characterized the Mer- 
ck-Medco alternative as an “intriguing idea.” 

Top Clinton Administration officials re- 
sponded more coolly to the Medicare drug pro-

Revco gains investment convert 


NEW YORK — Financial powerhouse Morgan Stan- 
ley & Co. has joined several other Wall Street firms in 
backing the purchase of Revco’s common stock as a 
sound long-term investment. 

“Based on its leading industry position, continued 
benefits stemming from management’s success in sub- 
stantially restructuring its operations, the company’s 
ability to drive sales through third-party prescription 
growth and an aggressive prescription file purchase 
program, and the ability-to-drive down operating ex- 
pense ratios offsetting margin pressure, we believe 
the company has excellent prospects,” noted Morgan 
Stanley research analyst Debra Levin in a report. 


Bashas begins pharmacy rollout 


CHANDLER, Ariz. — Southwestern supermarket op- 
erator Bashas Inc. has begun the gradual installation 
of pharmacy departments in its stores. The first phar- 
macy opened in November, and another is planned to 
open this spring, with a third slated for the fall. 

Bashas is based in the Phoenix area, where the ma- 
jority of its 61 stores are located. The chain faces blis- 
tering competition in its home market from six tough 
supermarket chain rivals, all of which already operate 
pharmacies. Among them are three major multi-state 
operators—Smith’s Food and Drug, Albertson’s and 
Safeway—as well as locally based ABCO Markets, 
Smitty’s Super Valu and Kroger Co.’s Fry’s Food 
Stores division. 


Trial of Phar-Mor’s Monus delayed 


CLEVELAND — The upcoming trial of Phar-Mor 
co-founder and former president Michael “Mickey” 
Monus has been postponed at the request of Monus’ 
lawyers. Guiginally set to begin Feb. 14 in federal 
court here, the trial is now expected to begin in late 
March or early April. 

Monus requested the delay shortly after the release 
of a massive report by a court-appointed examiner on 
the $500 million fraud and embezzlement scheme at 
Phar-Mor, which has already led to the conviction of 
two former financial officers at the company. 

In his motion for delay, Monus cited the need for 
more time to review records and the examiner’s report. 


AG adopts new pricing strategy 


CLEVELAND — American Greetings will launch a 
new tiered pricing program this June as part of its 
greeting card and gift wrap micromarketing strategy. 

The “Smart Pricing” program is designed to meet 
value preferences of different consumer market seg- 
ments with “value,” “core” and “premium” selections 
in cards and gift wrap. The value and premium selec- 
tions will be supported with POP signage and mer- 
chandising vehicles to help direct shoppers. 


FoxMeyer adds McKee, Estes 


DALLAS — FoxMeyer Corp. has named Peter B. Mc- 
Kee senior vice president and chief financial officer and 
William L. Estes senior vice president of operation :. 

McKee will be responsible for FoxMeyer's finance, 
treasury, Spreng Shes legal and public affairs 
functions. Estes will responsible for managing the 
pharmaceutical wholesaler’s distribution system, in- 
cluding 18 warehouses that serve customers nation- 
wide and in Puerto Rico. 

Commenting on the appointment of McKee and 
Estes, FoxMeyer president and chief operating officer 
Thomas Anderson said the addition of McKee would 
be key to strengthening financial management as the 
wholesaler surpasses $5 billion in sales. Estes, he 
said, will play an essential role in taking the company 
into the health care market of the 21st century. 


by Ken Rankin 


WASHINGTON — Total U.S. drug store 
sales reached $78 billion last year, but the 
industry’s sluggish 1.3-percent growth rate 
lagged well behind other segments of Amer- 
ican retailing in 1993, U.S. Commerce De- 
partment analysts reported. 

This year the nation’s drug chains and in- 
dependent pharmacies are on track for a 
stronger, 2.6-percent growth spurt which 
should boost industry dollar 
volume to the $80 billion 
mark, according to the 
Commerce Department’s 
newly released U.S. Indus- 
trial Outlook 1994. 

Over the longer term, 
drug store industry sales 
have increased 37 percent 
during the past five years, 
from $57 billion in 1988 to 
$78 billion last year, the government re- 
port noted. 


Growth peaked in ’89 


Significantly, however, the department’s 
figures indicate that almost all of that 
growth occurred during the 1988-90 period 
when industry sales rose 7 percent, 13.1 
percent and 10.1 percent respectively. Last 
year’s meager percentage gain was identi- 
cal to the 1.3 percent growth rate experi- 
enced by drug stores in 1992, the depart- 
ment reported. 

In contrast, sales of all U.S. retail stores 
rose 6.3 percent to $2,086 billion last year, 


OUTL eg gk 


Outlook hopeful after sluggish ‘93 


and for 94 the total should climb another 7 
percent to $2,232 billion, the report noted. 

The department’s anticipated growth 
rates for other retail segments in 1994 in- 
clude a 14.3 percent increase for “general 
merchandise” stores to $320 billion; a 3.7 
percent rise for apparel retailers to $112 
billion; and a 3.1 percent gain for food re- 
tailers to $399 billion. 


Market share steady | 


Despite “strong competition from super- 
markets and discount 
stores,” the drug store in- 
dustry’s overall market 
share has “remained rela- 
tively steady at about 6 per- 
cent,” the government ana- 
lysts noted. 

“Part of this stability,” 
the report said, “may be at- 
tributed to the strong sales 
position” of major discount 
drug chains like Drug Emporium. 

In contrast, “traditional and chain drug 
stores...have lost market position to super- 
markets and discount stores,” the analysts 
said. “In response to that competition,” 
these drug stores “have changed their mer- 
chandise mix to include many food and con- 
venience items, and downsized their hard- 
ware and related departments.” 

Additionally, some drug stores “have ex- 
panded their services to include free deliv- 
ery of medicines,” while “others have made 
shopping easier by relocating in strip malls 
and other easy in-and-out locations, rather 
than in large shopping malls.”

Drug chains bring relief after quake 


LOS ANGELES — The 
chain drug and wholesale 
community rallied to help 
customers, employees and 
needy strangers after the 
Jan. 17 Los Angeles earth- 
quake jolted thousands of 
lives into chaos. A few ex- 
amples: 

e@ In affected areas, Longs 
Drugs gave away all on- 
hand supplies of batteries 
and flashlights, along with 
thousands of gallons of wa- 
ter. After restocking, it sold 
water at or below cost. 
Longs also donated other 
emergency supplies, includ- 
ing disposable diapers and 


infant formula, and even 
handed out some free pre- 
scriptions. 

e Bergen Brunswig has 
provided help to employees 
who were displaced from 
their homes and is providing 
financial and other support 
to pharmacy customers who 
were impacted by the quake. 

e Thrifty Drug donated 
5,000 gallons of water after 
the earthquake, along with 
other items including soap, 
toothpaste and diapers. The 
chain also donated nearly 
7,000 cups of Thrifty ice 
cream to children, adults 
and relief workers. 


@ Barnes Wholesale, 
based in Inglewood, Calif., 
helped several pharmacies 
relocate to temporary trail- 
ers from their condemned 
buildings and assisted oth- 
ers in their move into new, 
permanent locations. 

@ McKesson Drug assisted 
pharmacies in relocation ef- 
forts. Its parent, McKesson 
Corp., contributed some 
100,000 bottles of Sparkletts 
water from its McKesson 
Water Products subsidiary.

$100,000 cash contribution 
to the Los Angeles earth-

There was a time not so long ago 
when retailers looked—in some cases 
“down”—upon a company called Wal- 
Mart and saw just another discount 
store. Numerous stores were out of 
business before they realized that 
Wal-Mart’s success has really come 
from advanced technologies and sys- 
tems, incredibly efficient distribution, 
a homogenized company culture, 
savvy real-estate planning, customer- 
focused service and forward-thinking 
merchandising, along with low prices.

proven that a lot of fat can be removed 
from the system, that consumers do ap-

ized data base giving pharmacists and 
doctors access to a patient’s file from 
anywhere in the country is an advan- 
tage—one that few traditional drug re-

WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


By its success, Wal-Mart caused 
consumers to question the prices and 
margin structures of other retailers, 
and suppliers and retailers alike had 
to change the way they did business. 

Similarly, today’s retailers of phar- 
maceutical products are finding that 
they must react to mail-order phar- 
macy. The success of these companies, 
who amassed some $5 billion in sales 
last year, has fueled the debate about 
the pricing and profit margins of phar- 
maceutical products. But, there may 


Earlier this month when the U.S. 
General Accounting Office released 
new figures showing vast differences 
in drug prices in the United Kingdom 
and the United States, pharmaceutical 
industry representatives dismissed 
the study as “flawed.” (See related sto- 


ry on page 32.) 

The GAO report “compares prices in 
the best health care system in the 
world with prices in one of the worst 
systems among major industrialized 
countries,” 


Pharmaceutical Manufac- 


combat manufac- 
turers’ discrimina- 
tory pricing— 
which favors 
hospitals and manaieed care providers, 
including mail-order—drug retailers 
are seeing that legislation, even if it 
does pass in its current form, is not the 
complete solution. Most of the industry 
now realizes that the battle must be 
fought in the marketplace as well. 

Due to the efforts of NACDS and 
NARD, community pharmacies will 
soon be able to join “networks” that 
will help them compete more effective- 
ly in the new world of managed care. 

The details are still being closely

According to Allnutt, socialistic poli-

The fact that

4 Drug Store News, February 21, 1994 


guarded by the two associations, but 
Drug Store News has learned that 
there will be two separate and some- 
what competitive networks that will be 
affiliated with NARD and NACDS. The 
networks will market the services of 
thousands of retail pharmacy locations 
to third-party insurers and large com- 
panies, competing directly with Medco, 

PCS and the other managed-care phar- 
macy companies. (For more details, see 
“NACDS, NARD: Negotiating Groups 
for Third Parties” on p. 1 of this issue.) 

Through these networks, retail 
pharmacists will presumably ‘be able 
to take advantage of significant vol- 
ume-related discounts, which will help 
them compete on price against mail- 
order companies. 

While these networks will help keep 
retail pharmacy “in the game,” they 
also, in a way, ensure that profit mar- 
gins in pharmaceuticals will never be 
the same again. Therefore, drug re- 
tailers large and small will be forced 
to find new ways to lessen their costs 
of doing business and to develop new 
profit opportunities. In a hurry. 

Through pricing, delivery, consulta- 
tive services and technology, mail-or- 
der has taught third-party payors and 
consumers some valuable lessons. 
Now retailers who want to stay the 
course will have to learn to do busi- 
ness differently —in almost all aspects. 

It might be helpful to remember this 
analogy: Just as Wal-Mart didn’t be- 
come a retailing powerhouse by low 
prices alone, Medco and companies 
like it are not transforming the phar- 
maceutical delivery system just be- 
cause the script is in the mail. 


lation before Rep. Henry Waxman’s (D- 
Calif.) House Health Subcommittee 
earlier this month. 

The answers from the drug company 
topkicks were not particularly enlight- 
ening. Merck-Medco chairman P. Roy 
Vagelos, M.D., for one, acknowledged 
that Americans are indeed forced to 
pay a disproportionate share of the 
cost of pharmaceutical R&D because 
manufacturers often sell their products 
at lower prices in other countries. 

But that’s just the way it is, P. Roy 
told Congress. The United States of- 
fers pharmaceutical manufacturers 
the biggest and richest market in the 
world, and they have to make their 
profits here. 

It never seemed to occur to the 
pharmaceutical fat cats at Waxman’s 
hearing that it is unfair, unwise and 
unreasonable to expect Americans to 
happily pay far more for medicine 
than people in other countries. 

But then, it never seems to occur to 
Merck-Medco and other pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturers that there’s any- 
thing wrong with charging discrimina- 
tory prices to pharmacies right here in 
the U.S.A. 

I think it’s time for Mr. Waxman 
and others in Congress set these drug 
industry people straight. It’s wrong to 
charge Americans 60 percent more 
than Britons for the same drugs. It’s 
wrong to charge retail pharmacies 90 
percent more than HMOs for the same 
drugs. And it’s time somebody ex- 
plained this to P. Roy and company.

Drug Store News, February 21, 1994 


Drug chains are combing 
photofinishing, like all cate- 
gories, for higher rings and 
better margins. 

Photo processing, free 
from shrink and breakage, 
is one of the most productive 
areas in the store. Gross 
profit is higher and net is 
much higher than many cat- 
egories. Gross profit per- 

photofinishing 
places it in the top three or 
four among all products for 
one major chain. 

For retailers who offer the 
option of premium overnight 
photofinishing, as do Gen- 
ovese and Thrifty, a premi- 
um option like Kodalux from 
Qualex or Genovese’s own 
premium line are trade- 
ups—higher gross profit per- 
centage and premium dollar 
rings. It’s a double benefit to 
the store, and the customer 
gets a better product. 

One-hour labs command 
higher prices than overnight 
with a similar margin poten- 
tial, but this depends on how 
efficiently a store structures 
its one-hour lab overhead, a 
highly variable factor. 


Faster film 


Film purchases increased 
4.6 percent in units through 
the first nine months of 
1993 for all trade channels, 
according to PMA estimates. 
Harrand said this growth 
was spurred by major pro- 
motional activity in the sec- 
ond and third quarters. 

Retailers and manufac- 
turers are aiming for higher 
rings and margins on film. 
Faster film like ASA 400 is 
a trade-up. But, in general, 
achieving higher rings isn’t 
easy because of the promo- 
tional price cutting on film, 
the consequent low margins 
and the growth of private 
label film. 

Chains have at least two 
defenses: trade customers 
up to faster and more ex- 
pensive film (from 200 
speed to 400 speed) and to 
offer differentiated qualities 
of film at tiered pricing. To 
address these niches, Kodak 
has just announced two new 
lines of film: the premium 
Royal Gold line and a new 
value line called Funtime, 
to be marketed only during 
spring and fall for one 
month each season.

well as sales of Polaroid’s 
Captiva. “If you come up 
with new features and bene- 
fits, then people will come

CONSUMABLES / BEVERAGES 


Consumers guzzle gallons of New Age drinks 


ccording to sales sta- 
A itssies in drug chains, 

candy is still king 
among consumables, ac- 
counting for some $1.5 bil- 
lion in sales in chain drug 
stores in the 52 weeks end- 
ing Sept. 12, 1993. But, the 
venerable category grew 
only at a 1.2-percent clip, 
according to Information 
Resources Inc. 

The impressive growth 
percentages, according to 
IRI, are being generated by 
beverages: Carbonated soft 
drinks grew by 8.95 percent 
in the drug channel; single 
serving juices, by 13.63 per- 
cent; and bottled waters, by 
13.16 percent. 

And, according to buyers 
and industry experts, the 
most explosive growth is in 
the smallest beverage seg- 
ment of all—ready-to-drink 
iced teas, with current total 
sales estimated to be worth 
some $950 million in whole- 
sale dollars, according to a 
just-released study by Bev- 
erage Marketing Corp. 

Obviously, the New Age 
movement, which includes 
bottled waters and flavored 
juices as well as ready-to- 
drink iced teas, has not yet 
reached mid-life crisis. 
That’s fine with buyers, who 
enjoy the consumer appeal 
and healthier margins these 
beverages generate. 


The grand dame of drinks 


Carbonated soft drinks 
are still the core draw in 
drug chains. But, today, it’s 
a category that lacks excite- 
ment. “There’s still some 
growth in the category, but 
it’s basically flat,” Frank 
Gable, vice president of dis- 
tribution, Harco Drug, said. 
“There’s really nothing new 
in the category.” Besides, he 
added, “we’re coming off a 
very high base of growth for 


carbonated soft drinks.” 

“In the total beverage 
market, soft drinks are No. 
2 (beer is No. 1),” said Hank 
Behar, editor, Beverage 
World magazine. “Both seg- 
ments are declining—in 
that they are not growing as 
fast as they used to.” 

Plus, added Raymond 
Hoy, director of marketing, 
I Got It At Gary’s, there’s 
little profit left in carbonat- 
ed soft drinks. The category 
is a traffic-builder. “We give 
it away,” Hoy said. 

Indeed, a sampling of ad- 
vertised prices across the 
country during the last week 
of November and first week 
of December showed prices 
ranging from 79 cents for a 
2-liter bottle of 7Up adver- 
tised by SupeRx in the 
Cincinnati Enquirer, to 88 
cents advertised for a 2-liter 
bottle of Pepsi at Drug 
World in the Columbus Dis- 
patch, to $1.99 advertised for 
a 12-can pack of 12-ounce 
Classic Coke at Phar-Mor in 
the Houston Chronicle. 

In-line pricing is extreme- 
ly competitive, with every- 
one competing against 
everyone else on razor-thin 
margins. Immediate con- 
sumption, however, is a dif- 
ferent story. “The cold sale 
is a different customer,” 
said Hoy. “If you’re thirsty 
and if the price is under a 
buck, you don’t care.” 

Depending on the retailer, 
immediate consumption 
beverages can generate 
margins from 25 percent to 
40 percent, according to 
Robert Baskin, director of 
public relations for Coca- 
Cola USA. 

In a market hungry for 
new product and better 
margins, Coca-Cola has in- 
troduced a 20-ounce plastic 
bottle single serving. The 
new product has evoked a 


The New Age 
movement—which 
includes bottled 
waters and 
flavored juices as 
well as ready-to- 
drink iced teas— 
has not yet 
reached mid-life 
crisis, and that’s 
fine with buyers. 


mixed reaction, however. 
Eckerd spokesperson 
Michael Polzin summed up 
the concerns: “We’re not 
sure that that’s what the 
customer is looking for. Is 
the customer who buys a 
caffeine-free diet drink go- 
ing to want to drink 20 
ounces all at once? We think 
our consumer is looking for 
a thirst quencher.” 

Plus the new size creates 
Space management chal- 
lenges. It’s several inches 
taller, therefore taking up 
more cubic space. That’s 
particularly a problem in 
crammed coolers where 
space is already tight. 


Cramming the cooler 


Contributing to the space 
management challenges is 
the burgeoning New Age 
beverage segment, which in- 
cludes ready-to-drink iced 
teas, bottled waters and sin- 
gle serving juices. 

“The growth is in the New 
Age beverages,” said Hoy. 

“New Age beverages are 
taking part of the carbonat- 


ed soft drink business,” 
added Gable. “These bever- 
ages are definitely a factor.” 

The ready-to-drink iced 
tea segment exploded in 
1993. According to the Bev- 
erage Marketing Corp., last 
year ready-to-drink iced 
teas grew 91.2 percent in 
wholesale dollars over 1992, 


partly because Lipton and 


Nestea went national with 
their products in 93, partly 
because the population was 
ready to drink iced tea; and 
partly because wide-mouth 
glass bottles solved the 
taste problem. 

Ready-to-drink iced tea’s 
growth is expected to re- 
main healthy for the next 
two years. Beverage Mar- 
keting, in its newly released 
study, the Ready-to-Drink 
Tea Report, estimates that 
ready-to-drink iced teas will 
grow 39.8 percent in 1994, 
reaching 465.1 million gal- 
lons and reach 570 million 
gallons by 1995. 

Gallons isn’t the only 
measure expected to grow in 
this segment, however. 
“Everybody and their broth- 
er will be trying to get into 
this market,” Hellen Berry, 
Beverage Marketing’s vice 
president of research, said. 
“I predict a minimum of 100 
brands by the end of 1994.” 

Still, Snapple dominates 
the market, and as one buy- 
er said, “As Snapple moves, 
my market moves.” Produc- 
tion and delivery problems 
have been plaguing the 
trend-setting supplier, how- 
ever, as it endures the grow- 
ing pains involved in evolv- 
ing from a regional company 
to a national powexnouse. 

“Demand (for Snapple) is 
certainly outstripping sup- 
ply,” said Andy Horn, Harco 
buyer. His strategy: He also 
stocks Nestea and Lipton. 
“They're not as popular,” he 


admitted, “but at least we 
have an iced tea in stock.” 


Waters doing well 
Bottled waters are also 


-spurting forward, and re- 


tailers are responding by al- 
lotting it and other New Age 
beverages more space. 

Drug Emporium said 
sales are excellent in any of 
its waters. The chain has 
expanded its set to between 
12 feet and 16 feet. 

Gary’s has expanded its 
beverage set as well. “We’re 
growing water by 10 per- 
cent,” said Hoy. “In general, 
we feel retailers didn’t allo- 
cate enough space to begin 
with. Carbonated soft drink 
Space will stay the same. 
Teas will be up 10 percent 
in space, and in the sum- 
mer, you'll see a lot more 
off-shelf activity.” 

“It’s a challenge to try to 
find room for all the new 
product,” said Eckerd’s 
Polzin. Harco, said Gable, 
has definitely increased its 
cooler space for iced teas— 
at the expense of soft drinks 
and beer. 

Adding to the challenge 
are regional bottlers of New 
Age beverages. “There are 
unique regional products. 
They may not be significant 
in terms of share, but they’re 
significant in terms of mar- 
gin dollars,” Hoy pointed out. 
One of the hottest sellers at 
Harco, Horn added, is a re- 
gional water. 

How does a buyer pick his 
way through the mass of 
suppliers? Finesse, said 
Hoy. “Product changes from 
region to region, and oppor- 
tunity can shift from a sin- 
gle store to a region.” 

But the effort is worth it 
as buyers tap into the New 
Age beverage segment that 
is growing at double-digit 
rates at many drug chains.

COLOR COSMETICS / EYE, LIP, NAIL & FACE 


or many chain drug store cos- 
Petes buyers, 1993 was a dis- 

appointing year in color cos- 
metics. Sales were either sluggish 
or down, with most of the declines 
reported in the face makeup and 
eye color segments. 

Sales of higher price-point brands 
were particularly soft in some chains, 
as value-conscious consumers traded 
down to lower priced lines. 

The strongest segments of color in 
1993, according to buyers, were lip 
and nail—the two segments that 
women bought most often on impulse 
and the two often most affordable. 

However, although most buyers 
said they sold more lip and nail col- 
or cosmetics than other types of 
cosmetics, the gains they reported 
were only moderate. And many buy- 
ers said they generated most of 
their sales when these products 
were on sale. 


Lip and nail the winners 


“My gut feeling is that lip was 
our hottest segment in 1993,” said 
Peggy Williams, who buys cosmet- 
ics for Snyder Drug in Minneapolis. 
“When we had-Revtor-hpstick 
sale, we sold a huge amount of 
pieces. But I can’t say that any seg- 
ment was outstanding in 1993. Af- 
ter lip, nail was probably our best 
performing segment.” 

At Perry Drug in Detroit, cosmet- 
ics buyer Mary Hoepfner also 
named lip and nail as her two best 
segments, but she noted: “It has not 
been a particularly strong year.” 

“Frustrating” was the word that 
the buyer for one major chain said 
best described the chain’s cosmetics 
year. “There were too many ‘me-too’ 
products and too much competition 
from other trade classes,” this 
source said. “The department stores 
seem to be getting stronger, and the 
competition from mass merchandis- 
ers is worse than ever.” 


Not enough innovation 


Some buyers pointed out that sales 
in many color segments have been 
soft because there haven’t been any 
major technological advances to drive 
sales as there have been, for exam- 
ple, in the nail accessory category. 

Eye lashes have sold better than 
eye shadows, Revco’s senior cosmet- 
ics buyer Judy Wray said, but they 
haven't been emerging as a strong 
growth category because the tech- 
nology hasn’t come through that 
would make it easier for women to 
apply and use false lashes. 

“Artificial nails have been grow- 
ing because technology keeps mak- 
ing it easier and easier for women 
to apply them, and they last 
longer,” said Wray “It’s the same 
with hair color. Technology has 
made it easier to apply, and so more 
women are using it. 

“But there’ve been no technological 
advances in lashes—nothing that 
makes them easier to apply. Manu- 
facturers are simply duplicating ex- 
isting lines, coming out with different 
size packs and other cosmetics modi- 
fications. So lashes remain a good 
category that everyone ought to have, 
but there are no dramatic increases.” 

Although 1993 was a soft year for

Growth still exists 


On the West Coast, PayLess’ cos- 
metics buyer Sheri Ralston reported 
that her cosmetics sales in 1993 were 
good—stronger than they were in 
1992—and she attributed that to the 
chain’s aggressive advertising for the 
department and to in-store cos- 
meticians whose presence gives Pay- 
Less a point of difference with con- 
sumers. She estimated that her 
strongest segments were lip and nail. 

In New York, Stephanie Hayter, 
who buys cosmetics for Genovese 
Drug, also reported that her color 
sales were up for the year. Hayter 
attributed the gains to a discount- 
ing program that the chain put into 
effect last March and to its new 
advertising for cosmetics. 

As an everyday pricing strategy, 
“we discounted Maybelline and Cov- 
er Girl by 20 percent and the other 
cosmetics lines by 10 percent,” she 
said. “We managed to have a good 
increase, plus our gross profit mar- 
gins were about the same.” 

She said profits were helped by 
the changes that Genovese made in 
its advertising. “Instead of advertis- 
ing all the color products in a line at 
25 percent off as we did before, we 
now feature a line and offer $1 off 
the everyday price of the lipsticks or 
the makeups,” she said. 

“We also discontinued our buy- 
one-get-one-free program. We did 
lose sales, but it evened out,” 
Hayter added. 


In addition, the chain enhanced 
the department’s profitability by us- 
ing its scanning data to weed out 
slow-turning SKUs and category 
segments, she said. “Sometimes,

Holiday trends 


At Christmas, some chains re- 
ported an increase in color cosmet-

uted it to advertising color and the

Sally Hansen Nail Color pre-packs 
did particularly well at some chains, 
and the color workshop kits from 
Markwins sold very well, especially 
in West Coast chains like PayLess. 

Some niche segments with a rela- 
tively small dollar base did well in 
1993. The best cosmetics segment, 
buyers absolutely agreed, was nail 
extensions and nail manicure prod- 
ucts—up over 10 percent in some 
instances. 

Sales of eye lash products were 
up moderately in some chains, as 
were sales of lipstick sealers, lip 
glosses, children’s cosmetics, facial 
masques and lip balms. 

Several buyers said their children’s 
cosmetics sales showed particularly 
strong gains at Christmas, but many 
buyers who carried Tinkerbell and 
the Bonne Bell Lip Smackers year- 
round reported good, consistent gains 
on their everyday business as well. 

In the ethnic cosmetics cate- 
gories, Black Radiance, with its val- 
ue position, did fabulously, and so 
did Artmatic’s Tropez budget line.

Pharmacy helps Eckerd 


over $4 billion mark 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — A 
14.5 percent increase in 
pharmacy sales and 6.3 per- 
cent comparable store sales 
growth pushed Eckerd Corp. 
over the $4 billion mark for 
the fiscal year ended Jan. 29, 
1994, according to prelimi- 
nary sales figures. 

Sales for the year in- 
creased 7.8 percent to $4.19 
billion from fiscal 1992 sales 
of $3.89 billion. Leading the 


way were pharmacy sales of —party-increases, categories _ 


$1.94 billion, accounting for 
46.3 percent of total sales, 
vs. last year’s 45.5 percent. 


Helping the year-end re- 
sults was a strong fourth 
quarter. Sales for the quar- 
ter totaled $1.18 billion, an 
8.2 percent increase from a 
year ago. Same store sales 
were also strong for the 
fourth quarter at 7.6 per- 
cent. Pharmacy sales surged 
18.1 percent during the 
quarter to total $535 million. 

Along with pharmacy 
sales growth, led by third- 


such as greeting cards, pho- 
to, OTCs and convenience 
foods contributed to growth. 


Revco to cut interest costs 
with new debt package 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
Revco D.S. has struck a re- 
vised bank credit agreement 
aimed at cutting its debt 
load and interest costs. The 
new, $262.5 million revolv- 
ing credit line, co-managed 
by Continental Bank N.A. 
and Banque Paribas, effec- 
tively cuts Revco’s interest 
rate on debt payments by 
nearly 2 percent, and is ex- 
pected to save the company

certainly raise interesting 
new antitrust questions.

COVER STORY 


Speeding up new drug approvals: 


TT 


Is Kessler running out of time? 


by Ken Rankin 


or more than a 
decade, Food and 
Drug Administration 


officials have been promis- 
ing to break the regulatory 
bottlenecks that have de- 
layed the availability of 
new lifesaving medicines 
to Americans. Each year 
top FDAers claim to be on 
the brink of a break- 
through that will eliminate 
the new drug application 
logjam and close the drug 
lag that has kept promis- 
ing new prescription prod- 
ucts off the shelves of U.S. 
pharmacies. But every 
year, it seems, the pay-off 
from the FDA’s efforts to 
streamline drug approvals 
turns out to be at least an- 
other year away. 

Now FDA commissioner 
David Kessler and his 
drug review staff may be 
running out of time, and 
out of excuses. The 
agency's performance dur- 
ing 1993—the first year 
under the new “User Fee’ 
law designed to finance 
massive improvements in 
the FDA’s drug review pro- 
gram—shows no sign of a 
breakthrough on NDA ap- 
provals. Indeed, a close 
analysis of the FDA’s track 
record last year suggests 
that Kessler and company 
may be falling even farther 
behind in the drive to 
streamline new drug ap- 
provals. 

Here’s how the new drug 
scorecard shapes up for 
1993: 

® The FDA approved 370 
new drug, generic drug 


FDA new drug approvals: 240 in 10 years

and biological product ap-

® Only 70 new drugs 
won FDA approval in

from the 91 approved dur-

® Generic drug ap-

up from 229 the year be-

® But the number of bio- 
logical products cleared 
for marketing last year fell 
to 51, from 67 approvals 
in 1992. 

Significantly, however, 
these totals do not reveal 
several disturbing trends 
in the FDA’s handling of 
applications for “New Mol- 
ecular Entities”—drugs 
that are distinctly different 
in structure from those al- 
ready on the market. 

Of the 70 NDAs ap- 
proved last year, 25 were 


for NMEs—a slight drop in 
the FDA's 1992 pace when 
the agency cleared a total 
of 26 NMEs. More impor- 
tantly, perhaps: Last year’s 
downswing marks the sec- 
ond straight annual drop 
in productivity for the FDA 
since the agency approved 
30 NMEs in 1991. 


Burning midnight oil 


Even more disturbing 
are the indications that 
Kessler may be encourag- 
ing FDA drug reviewers to 
rush their reviews of im- 
portant new drugs in order 
to pad the NME approval 
total each year. Indeed, of 
the 25 NMEs cleared by 
the FDA during calendar 
1993, nine were approved 
during the final four days 
of the year. 

So far, no one has sug- 
gested that Kessler or oth- 
er FDA officials cut any es- 
sential corners during this 


desperate year-end push 
to inflate the 1993 new 
drug approval count. But 
it is clear that without this 
late December frenzy of 
approval activity, the 
FDA's new drug approval 
track record would have 
appeared even worse. If 
1993 had ended on Dec. 
27, the FDA’s NME ap- 
proval total would have 
fallen to 16—the lowest 
level in more than a 
decade and a decline in 
productivity that would 
have almost certainly come 
to the attention of Kessler’s 
superiors within the Clin- 
ton Administration. 


Approvals take less time 


The good news in the 
FDA's performance last 
year is the small but mea- 
surable reduction in aver- 
age new drug approval 
time at the agency. The 
FDA spent an average of 
26.5 months to review 
NDAs for each of the 25 
NMEs approved during 
1993. That pace is better 
than three months faster 
than 1992’s average of 
29.9 months, and it rates 
as the shortest average 
NME review time in a 
decade. 

Despite this apparent 
progress, however, the 
FDA is not even close to 
approaching compliance 
with federal drug law 
which requires the agency 
to complete its new drug 
reviews within six 
months. Last year only 
one drug—BioDevelop- 
ment Corp.’s “orphan” 
narcotics addiction sup-
