hoff told DrSN For The 
Pharmacist. “There still is 
a very clear need to im- 
prove the efficiency of the 
Food and Drug Adminis- 
tration.” 

If there’s any reason for 
optimism about the future 
of the FDA’s ability to 
streamline the new drug 
approval process, it’s due 
to the expected impact of 
1992’s “User Fee” legisla- 
tion. 


User fees to the rescue 


Under that new law, the 
FDA is authorized to 
charge sponsors of new 
drugs stiff six-figure pro- 
cessing fees to underwrite 
the cost of the agency’s re- 
views to the tune of more 
than $320 million over the 
next five years. 

Although the pharma- 
ceutical industry had re- 
sisted such user fee pro- 
posals in the past, drug 
manufacturers endorsed 
the successful 1992 legis- 
lation because the bill re- 
quires the FDA to use the 
money to hire 600 new 
government drug review- 
ers—a move considered 
essential to breaking the 
NDA logjam and closing 
the drug lag. 

Although the User Fee 
Act failed to generate any 
measurable acceleration in 
the NDA approval rate 
during 1993, supporters of 
this approach say the new 
system was never sup- 
posed to have an impact 
until this year. The FDA's 
goal for 94 under the User 
Fee Act is to take final ac- 
tion 9n at least 55 percent 
of the “standard” NDAs 
submitted this year within 
12 months. In °95, the tar- 
get will be raised to 70 
percent, and in succeeding 


years the FDA will be ex- 


_pected to move on 80 per- 


cent and ultimately 90 
percent of all NDAs within 
12 months. 

Achieving those goals 
may be a tall order for 
Kessler’s crew, however. 
Not a single one of the 
standard NMEs approved 
by the FDA during 1993 
was Cleared in less than 
20 months, and for half of 
them the review time aver- 
aged nearly four years. 

The agency’s only hope 
is to use the User Fee 
funds to significantly ex- 
pand the current team of 
FDA drug reviewers—a 
strategy that was put in 
jeopardy last year when 
the Clinton Administration 
imposed a blanket hiring 
freeze throughout the U.S. 
Public Health Service. That 
freeze was lifted late last 
month, however, when top 
Health and Human Ser- 
vices officials exempted the 
FDA’s new drug review 
staff from the hiring mora- 
torium. 

PMA officials are now 
expressing optimism that 
the FDA will indeed be 
able to jump-start the 
sluggish new drug ap- 
proval process. Skeptics, 
however, aren’t convinced 
that more cooks in the 
FDA kitchen will solve all 
of the agency’s drug ap- 
proval problems. 

If they’re right—if more 
money and scientific man- 
power alone can’t cure the 
drug lag—then even more 
radical surgery may be 
needed. Indeed, Congress 
may have to redesign U.S. 
drug approval standards 
to strike a better balance 
between product safety 
and access to new lifesav- 
ing medicines. Pir

Continued from cover 


One study, “Diabetes in the United 
States: A Strategy for Prevention,” 
looked at the disease on a Sstate-by- 
State basis, analyzed the financial 
impact and revealed staggering an- 
nual human costs, such as 54,000 
lower-extremity amputations, 13,000 
cases of end-stage renal disease, be- 
tween 15,000 and 40,000 new cases 
of blindness and nearly three million 
hospitalizations. 

Another study from 1993 that will 
be referenced for years to come is 
the National Institutes of Health Di- 
abetes Control and Complications 
Trial. The 10-year study’s key con- 
clusion was that people who closely 
monitor their blood glucose levels 
through testing greatly reduce the 
chances of developing complications 
associated with the disease. When 
the results were released at the 
American Diabetes Association’s an- 
nual meeting last summer, it was 
predicted that sales of test strips 
would surge. Sure enough, testing 
picked up enough to cause nearly a 
30 percent increase in drug store 
Sales of test strips. 

As these findings are disseminated, 
more undiagnosed patients are sure 
to begin controlling their disease. 


Manufacturers battle it out 


Helping them in that regard are 
dozens of diabetes supply manufac- 
turers. Competition among these 
firms is giving patients more options 
than ever when selecting a meter, 
test strips and other supplies. This 
ongoing competition means patients 
can look forward to lower costs, 
innovations in meters that will make 
them easier and more convenient to 
use and lancets that barely punc- 
ture the skin and produce no more 
blood than needed. Eventually, no 
blood may be needed at all, pending 
further development of a non-inva- 
Sive blood glucose meter. 

Also benefiting patients and partic- 
ipating in the competition are drug 
store retailers eager for a share of 
the estimated $3,700 a diabetes pa-

One reason for all the interest is 
there still remains huge, untapped 
potential in the category. Estimates 
vary, but most sources place the 
number of people with diabetes 
somewhere between 13 million and 
14 million. And nearly half of those 
are undiagnosed. Roughly 90 per- 
cent have Type II diabetes; the re- 
mainder have Type I or insulin de- 
pendent diabetes. 

Expectations are that increasing 
numbers of people will recognize 
they have diabetes, the nation’s 
high-risk elderly population trend 
will swell the ranks of diabetes pa- 
tients, and those that already have 
the disease will test more frequently. 
They are also expected to turn to 
their pharmacists for answers. 

Two important ways pharmacists 
Can serve the needs of their diabetes 
customers is in helping them select 
and teaching them to use a blood glu- 
cose monitoring system.

F&M signs with ad agency 


DETROIT — Shifting away from its traditional re- 
liance on word-of-mouth advertising to carry its low- 
price message, F&M Distributors has awarded a mul- 
ti-regional advertising contract to W.B. Doner & Co., a 
major ad agency. 

The move marks something of a new marketing phi- 
losophy for 121-store F&M, which in the past has 
largely eschewed expensive advertising in order to 
hold down costs for its deep-discount operation. 

The contract with Doner followed a six-month re- 
view of ad agencies by the off-price chain. F&M presi- 
dent and chief executive Earl Weissert said the deci- 
sion to go with an ad agency came in the face of “rapid 
and dramatic changes” in retailing. Doner, he added, 
will be called on “to make a strong impact on the con- 
tinued growth of F&M.” 


Perry gears up for new openings 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Continuing a steady growth 
pace as it works simultaneously to improve profitabili- 
ty, Perry Drug Stores has signed three more leases for 
new stores in Michigan. 

Among them will be the chain’s 19th store in the 
city of Detroit, as well as its seventh unit in the 
Grand Rapids market and its 13th store in the Detroit 
suburb of Southgate. 

The openings, slated for July in Grand Rapids and 
for September in Detroit and Southgate, will bring 
Perry’s store count to 214. 


New dates set for Exclusively HBA 


CHICAGO — The 1994 Exclusively HBA show is 
set for March 23-25 at Chicago’s McCormick Place. 
The event, which brings together HBA suppliers with 
drug, discount, supermarket and specialty retailers, is 
being held in the first quarter for the first time since 
its inception five years ago. 

The new timing better serves the year-long promo- 
tional activities of the category, according to the 
show’s producer, Jay Spaulding. 


Drug Emporium inks lending pact 


COLUMBUS, Ohio — In a refinancing aimed in part 
at lowering the cost of its debt, Drug Emporium has ex- 
panded its secured credit agreement with its lenders, 
Bank One of Columbus and National City Bank. 

The new agreement consists of a revolving credit 
line of up to $30 million and $15 million in additional 
term loans. Initial funds borrowed under the new pact 
will be used to pay off borrowings under a previous 
line of credit, said Drug Emporium chairman and 
chief executive David Kriegel. 


Revco buys out Friendly Drug Stores 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco D.S. has acquired the 
30-year-old, five-store Friendly Drug Stores chain, 
boosting its home-market store count in northeast 
Ohio to 119 units. 

Three of the Friendly units serve Cleveland’s East 
Side, with additional stores in nearby Maple Heights 
and Monroe Falls. According to research from Drug 
Store News’ parent company, Lebhar-Friedman Inc., 
the Friendly stores average 5,000 square feet and 
generate roughly $400 in sales per square foot. An 
estimated 80 percent of those sales come from 
prescription at OTC medications, reports the 1993 
Directory of Drug Store and HBC Chains from 
Lebhar-Friedman’s Chain Store Guides division. 

Revco has added a total of 16 drug stores in the 
Cleveland/Akron/Canton area over the past 12 months. 
President and chief executive D. Dwayne Hoven called 
the latest acquisition “part of our strategy to 
strengthen our presence in northeast Ohio.”

NACDS conference focuses on 
distribution/logistics to cut costs 


by James Frederick 


ORLANDO, Fla. — For 
chain drug distribution and 
logistics people, automatic, 
just-in-time replenishment 
of inventory tied seamlessly 
to consumer demand re- 
mains the Holy Grail. 

In pursuit of that goal, 
several dozen of distribution 
execs gathered at Walt Dis- 
ney World here for three 
days in mid-February. The 
occasion: the fifth annual 
NACDS Distribution & Lo- 
gistics Conference. This 
year’s theme, appropriately 
enough, was “Navigating a 
Sea of Change.” 


Cutting edge of change 


The retailers came with 
the clear intent of getting or 
staying on the cutting edge 
of that change. They met 
face-to-face with nearly 200 
supplier representatives in 
pursuit of closer, more work- 
able partnerships aimed at 
smoothing out the product 
pipeline flow and cutting 
costs through EDI and more 
efficient distribution pat- 
terns. They huddled with 
vendors of software, truck- 
ing, pallet and racking sys- 
tems and anything else that 
might help move merchan- 
dise as efficiently as possi- 
ble. And they listened intent- 
ly in seminars to logistics 
experts and their own peers, 
seeking new techniques for 
cutting costs, speeding prod- 
uct flow and boosting turns. 

“If our business is going to 
save money and cut real 
costs at this point, it’s going 
to come through distribution 
and logistics,” said Garry 
Garrison, director of distri- 
bution for Pittsburgh-based 
Thrift Drug. “We know mer- 
chandising and distribution 
(functions) have to become 
closer partners; it’s highly 
critical to our industry.” 

With those goals in mind, 


Garrison told Drug Store 
News that Thrift is re-engi- 
neering the physical layout 
of its distribution center, 
“looking into EDI,” installing 
an automated A-frame pick- 
er in its warehouse and link- 
ing every aspect of buying, 
receiving and _ shipping 
through intelligent data sys- 
tems wherever possible. 

The goal, he said: paper- 
less management and lower 
inventory carrying costs. 
For Thrift and other chains, 
that means linking sales 
more closely with pro- 
duction, and getting orders 
to stores more quickly by 
cross-docking shipments at 
the warehouse door for 
rapid redistribution, rather 
than moving it through the 
warehouse, where handling 
costs quickly mount. 

“It requires the replace- 
ment of inventory, (ware- 
house) facilities and brute 
force with information,” not- 
ed James Andress, chief ex- 
ecutive of Information Re- 
sources Inc., in an address 
at the conference. 


What lies ahead 


Distribution managers 
came looking for ways to 
make that happen. Said 
Mike Winahradsky, vice 
president of distribution for 
Fay’s Inc., “The onus is on 
us...but NACDS has come a 
long way in terms of helping 
us. And our industry has fi- 
nally recognized the impor- 


tance of logistics. Some of 
the ‘blue sky’ stuff we were 
talking about five years ago 
is now the topic of serious 
discussion.” Added Fay’s di- 
rector of distribution Dick 
Lowery, “The world is chang- 
ing so fast. Unless you work 
at communicating (more di- 
rectly and efficiently) with 
your consumers, I don’t 
think you can keep up.” 

Nevertheless, even the 
most advanced drug chains 
still grapple with logistics is- 
sues. One reason: the lack of 
universal standards for 
warehouse management sys- 
tems, UPC coding and other 
facets of distribution; anoth- 
er reason: most retailers and 
suppliers are still sorting out 
EDI-based communications 
and information exchange 
with one another. “Every- 
body’s struggling with this,” 
acknowledged Randy Lewis, 
divisional vice president of 
logistics and planning for 
Walgreen Co. “No doubt in 
five to 10 years we'll all know 
it, but the execution is still a 
hurdle for most chains.” 

One big hurdle, Lewis 
said: major chains like Wal- 
Mart and Kmart—which lo- 
gistics people look to as low- 
cost models of distribution 
efficiency—are handling full 
case packs and massive vol- 
ume. “They can cross-dock 
that stuff,” said Lewis. “Drug 
chains deal in smaller quan- 
tities in split case, which 
[must] go through the DC.”

Corrections 


In the Feb. 7 issue of Drug Store News, L’Oréal’s 
hair care division’s director of public relations Michael 
Trese was incorrectly referred to with a male pronoun. 


Also, in a past issue, Drug Store News referred to the 
manufacturer of Physicans Formula Cosmetics and Klo- 
rane incorrectly. The Klorane brand is manufactured by 
Pierre Fabré, France, parent company, and Physicians 
Formula is manufactured by Pierre Fabré Inc., United 
States, a division of the French parent company.

McAlear: A man of vision, energy and impact 


McAlear is not afraid to be on the 
cutting edge of merchandising trends, 
and I think PayLess’ dedication to the 
“wellness” concept proves that he isn’t 
inclined to give up when a new idea 
doesn’t take hold immediately. 

Taking the wellness concept one 
step further, PayLess is modelling it- 
self on health food and nutrition spe- 
cialty stores and adding dedicated ser- 
vice staff to the OTC and wellness 
areas of the floor. This strategy raised 
eyebrows when I mentioned it to an- 
other retailer because of the high cost 
of adding staff. But McAlear contends 
that the investment in service will pay 
off “or we wouldn’t do it.” 

McAlear offered a couple of other 
opinions that might offer hints of di- 
rections to come: 

What’s in a name? McAlear noted 
that PayLess experimented with the 
name Key Drug for smaller-format 
stores, but all have since been convert- 
ed to the stronger PayLess name. His 
comment on the Thrifty Jr. moniker: 
“That’s saying to the customer walking 
in the door, ‘Lower your expectations.” 

Is everything up to date in 
Wilsonville? McAlear noted that one 
significant advantage PayLess offers 
Thrifty is its up-to-date technology and 
systems, including POS systems in all 
stores, an on-line PDX system for 
pharmacy, and a satellite system that 
links all stores with headquarters. 
Thrifty will be brought up to speed in 
time, said McAlear, noting that he 
doesn’t expect the transition to be easy. 

Of course, many key questions re- 
main, such as: What will the combined 
chain be called? Will all doors bear the 
same name? Where will headquarters 
be and who will still be working there 
when the merger is complete? 

Of all the words I could use to de- 
scribe Tim McAlear, laid back isn’t 
among them, so I think we'll know the 
answers very soon.

Act would double criminal penalties for 
health care fraud to 10 years in prison 
and would impose drug-lord style “as- 
set forfeiture” penalties for health 
providers, Warin told the group. 

But even without health care re- 
form, the third-party audit screws are 
tightening on the drug store industry. 

It is already becoming “quite com- 
mon” for third-party pharmacy audit 
recoveries to reach the $50,000 mark 
for single-store operators, and millions 
of dollars for chains, Pope said. 

State enforcers are also raising 
penalties against pharmacies charged 
with third-party claim violations. Ac- 
cording to Warin, however, the worst 
sanctions of all may well involve the 
practice of some third-party auditors 
to expand their audits to the sources 
and customers of pharmacies suspect- 
ed of filing violations. 

These hard-nosed enforcement activi- 
ties aren’t limited to government third- 
party programs. Increasingly, private 
insurers are adopting a harsher stance 
toward pharmacy claim irregularities.

PRIVATE LABEL SPECIAL REPORT 


Deep discounters finally see the light 


ammered by intense compe- 
Hite: and dwindling profit 

margins, the biggest deep 
discount drug store operators have 
finally come to terms with their 
own private label paradox. 

Stated simply, the paradox is 
this: Deep discounters need to buy 
inventory at low cost in order to 
pass on the savings that are the ba- 
sis of their appeal. They also need 
to sell at least a portion of their in- 
ventory at a decent gross margin to 
meet their profit objectives and stay 
in business. 

Private label can answer both 
those needs. But until recently, 
most off-price merchants felt store 
brands were pretty much off-limits. 

Their reasoning was simple 
enough. Off-price chains laid their 
retail foundations on a mix of well- 
known national brands bought on 
deal, at steep and sometimes not-so- 
steep discounts. Most rejected the 
high-margin lure of private label on 
the seemingly reasonable premise 
that store brands would dilute their 
core business as a low-priced alter- 
native to other, more traditional re- 
tail formats for the national brands 
found everywhere. 


Changing attitudes 


But times—and consumer atti- 
tudes about the quality and equiva- 
lency of store brands—have 
changed. In the past year or so, all 
three of the nation’s largest deep 


discount chains—Phar-Mor, Drug 
Emporium and F&M Distributors— 
have become private label converts. 
For them, the powerful low-price 
appeal, image-building potential, 
growing consumer acceptance and 
high margin opportunities have 
turned the tide. 


August to spearhead Phar-Mor’s 
fast-growing development of private 
label. The chain now fields roughly 
300 SKUs of store-brand HBAs, Gor- 
ley said, with another 50 SKUs in 
general merchandise. Snack and 
beverage items are being introduced.

NEW YORK — Packaging that 
closely resembles the leading 
brand is a common strategy 
among private label manufactur- 
ers and their retail partners. 
Such a strategy can and does 
spawn lawsuits, but packaging 
disputes can usually be resolved 
through communication, accord- 
ing to Mike Jandernoa, chairman 
and chief executive officer of pri- 
vate label manufacturing giant 
Perrigo. 

“Trade dress has been an issue 
in our industry for a number of 
years and we have been very in- 
volved in that aspect,” said Jan- 
dernoa, who recently addressed 
the issue at a marketing seminar 
in New York sponsored by the 
Nonprescription Drug Manufac- 
turers Association (NDMA). “The 
key...is to communicate the store 
brand quality and product identi- 
ty at the point of sale.” 

Jandernoa said the private la- 
bel supplier has been involved in 
discussions with the NDMA 
about how to resolve trade dress 
issues. “Our industry is willing 
to sit down and talk with 


Resolving trade dress disputes 


[branded manufacturers] if you 
have questions about the gray 
areas of packaging that are of 
concern,” Jandernoa said. “We 
have clearly found in the past 15 
years that the quickest and most 
efficient way to resolve trade 
dress issues is business person 
to business person. Typically 
those issues are resolved in a 
very short time and to both com- 
panies’ satisfaction.” 

Retailers are also an important 
player in trade dress issues, es- 
pecially considering private la- 
bel’s growth in recent years and 
retailer efforts to upgrade pack- 
age designs. 

“In Perrigo’s case, there are 
900 different products, 200 re- 
tail accounts and approximately 
23,000 SKUs,” said the execu- 
tive. “There is a tremendous 
amount of art work and regula- 
tory work that takes place with 
each individual product. There 
is follow-up work to be done on 
each package that involves our 
art and regulatory departments 
to assure the consistency in 
product labeling.” 


PRIVATE LABEL SPECIAL REPORT 


After 1993, can your brand survive? 


by Mike Troy 


EW YORK — Manufacturers 

N of brand-name products 

should cut prices if they wish 

to curtail further market share ero- 

sion at the hands of private label 

suppliers, urged Eckerd Corp. presi- 

dent and chief operating officer 
Frank Newman. 

“There is no escaping [that] the 
single biggest factor driving house 
brands is the price gap that exists 
between them and the national 
brands,” Newman said, addressing 
the recent Nonprescription Drug 


Manufacturers Association’s annual 
marketing seminar here. 

“We have a similar problem in 
our business,” Newman said. “At 
Eckerd we offer a convenient alter- 
native to stores like Wal-Mart and 
food and drug combos. Our more 
numerous and conveniently located 
stores give us an advantage over 
their ever-larger stores, but we are 
often unable to sell items profitably 
for the same price as Wal-Mart.” 

Thus, Eckerd’s task “is to make 
sure that what we charge the con- 
sumer for that greater convenience 
is within the consumer’s perception 
of the value of that convenience,” 

Newman said. “Brands 


Eckerd displays their private label to emphasize 
interchangeability and value. The chain has 1,153 
items covering all major categories. 


have a similar value 
equation with which to 
wrestle, only in their case 
it is to determine the val- 
ue of their tangible and 
intangible benefits, as 
perceived by the con- 
sumers, over the house 
brands.” 

Newman offered the re- 
tailer perspective to at- 
tendees at the seminar ti- 
tled “After 1993, Can 
Your Brand Survive?” 

As second-in-command 
at one of the chain drug 
industry’s most aggres- 
sive store-brand promot- 
ers, Newman is well-suit- 
ed to put that urgent 
question before branded 
OTC manufacturers. Eck- 
erd, he said, carries 1,153 
items covering all major 
categories of merchan- 
dise. Private labels gener- 
ate about 10 percent of 
Eckerd’s HBA sales and 
have profit margins 20 
percent to 70 percent 
higher than the national 
brands against which 


they compete. As a 


group, Newman 
said, “private labels 
sell faster, turn 


quicker and generate 
much better than av- 
erage gross margin 
dollars. 

“They are dis- 
played in a manner 
that... will help the 
customer easily make 
the choice between 
our brand and the 


business. They un- 
derstand customer 
service and manu- 
facturing and distrib- 
ution efficiencies. 
They are also often 
much more accommo- 
dating to their cus- 
tomer needs than are 
many of the branded 
manufacturers 
against which they 
compete.” 

Newman also cau- 
tioned branded man- 


national brand by 
suggesting  inter- 
changeability and ac- 
centuating value,” said Newman, 
who joined Eckerd last summer after 
seven years as the head of F&M Dis- 
tributors. 


Sophisticated manufacturers 


Newman reminded his audience 
that much of the success of private 
label is due to the growing sophisti- 
cation of its manufacturers. Their 
advances in production, packaging, 
distribution, marketing and EDI 
have taken the pain out of private la- 
bel and contributed to shifting mar- 
ket shares. Long lead times, mini- 
mum order quantities and limited 
product selection are not the impedi- 
ments to retailers they once were. 

“Recognize that your competition is 
not just knock-off artists,” Newman 
told roughly 300 product managers 
and brand executives at the meeting. 
“They are the largest sophisticated 
suppliers and manufacturers in the 


Newman 


ufacturers to think 
carefully about their 
promotional and pricing practices to 
avoid disrupting the market and 
adding to consumer skepticism. 
“Wildly erratic prices disturb the 
loyal consumer and make them un- 
sure just what the product is worth. 
Make sure promotions make sense,” 
he said. “They may create short- 
term excitement, but too frequently 
they result in long-term damage to 
the brand.” 

Newman added that “brands also 
have a responsibility to stay ahead 
of the competition by innovating 
and improving whenever their 
product attributes are no longer ex- 
clusive. 

“There is a huge requirement to 
make sure benefits are real and 
that points of differentiation are 
meaningful,” he said. “This is the 
hardest task of maintaining brand 
supremacy, but it is essential for 
long-term brand strength.”

by Barbara White 


Seacaucus, N.J.-based whole- 
saler Drug Guild, which was re- 
cently honored with a PLMA 
Salute to Excellence Award, has 
been offering private label prod- 
ucts in some form to its members 
since the company was founded 
nearly 40 years ago. 

In the early days, private label 
meant cough/cold products and 
analgesics. About 15 years ago, the 
wholesaler decided to expand into 
vitamins, a move that increased 
its private label program to 200 
SKUs. 

“One thing we always aimed for 
is value,” said Drug Guild vice 
president of marketing Mark Eng- 


lander. “We were never interested 
in making a cheap knock-off line. 
The Drug Guild brand name was 
designed to stand on its own.” 

Englander set packaging stan- 
dards that would often surpass the 
national brand products. Soon the 
wholesaler was offering its partici- 
pating independent pharmacies 
complete vitamin catalogs cus- 
tomized for their individual stores. 

With over 100 SKUs alone un- 
der the Drug Guild and Nature 
Guild vitamin brands, the whole- 
saler was well on its way to becom- 
ing a major private label force. 

The program expanded further 
in 1980 when Drug Guild 
branched into other categories. 
“We’re in dental floss, toothbrush- 
es, medicine dosage aids, foot

“Our marketing approach has 
been on maintaining an ethical 
image,” said Englander. “This is a 
private label line for pharmacies. 
Not supermarkets or convenience 
stores. Pharmacies.” 

Englander stays away from cat-

LT Meount a page from some of its 
counterparts in supermarket 
retailing, Shoppers Drug 
Mart, Willowdale, Ont., is mining a 
rich vein of incremental sales dol- 
lars by departing from the tradi- 
tional low-price allure of private la- 
bel with its own premium-priced, 
upscale brand of toiletries and other 
products. 

Shoppers launched its premium 
house brand, called Rialto, in the 
late 1980s. The launch gave Cana- 
da’s dominant drug chain a two-tier 
private label strategy, with its older 
Life brand appealing to budget- 
minded consumers and Rialto open- 
ing up new niche opportunities at 
the upper end of the market. 

Shoppers’ approach is similar to 
that of some U.S. and Canadian su- 
permarket chains like Loblaws and 
Jewel Food Stores, which have 
added upscale store brands like 
President’s Choice to their mix to 
capture both ends of the private la- 
bel spectrum. 


An instant hit 


Tha alto 


premium- pene pantyhose, cosmet- 
ic bags, gift items, beauty acces- 
sories and other products—was an 
almost immediate hit with Canadi- 
an consumers. So too was Rialto 
Naturals, a separate line of pricey, 
high-quality bath, body and skin 
care products, which the chain posi- 
tions as an alternative to even prici- 
er offerings from upscale specialty 
shops like The Body Shop and Crab- 
tree & Evelyn. 

“They're premium products, with 
price points slightly higher than 
Del’s Naturistics line,” said Roman 
Niemy, president of corporate 


a 
logo—n now found on 


Canadian consumers have reacted favorably to Rialto, Shoppers’ upscale line of private label. Rialto Naturals, the premium

brands for Shoppers. “But we’re 
priced somewhat below The Body

were every bit as good in quality.” 

Indeed, said Niemy, Shoppers 
had to search far and wide to find 
suppliers who could deliver the 
right mix of premium ingredients, 
packaging and manufacturing ca- 
pability the chain demanded for the

Nevertheless, the chain’s insis-

been very successful with it,” Niemy

there was absolutely no one in the 
chain drug industry doing anything 
quite like it. It’s caught on quite 
well, and there’s a lot of copycats 
now, a lot of new stuff creeping into 
the market.” 


Back to nature 


In the face of growing competition 
in the premium, “natural-ingredi- 
ent” bath and body segment, Shop- 
pers is now on the verge of restaging 
the Rialto Naturals line with new 
packaging, a wider selection of bath, 
body and skin creams, and an up- 
dated in-store presentation. Niemy 
is also looking to extend the line into 
more areas like aromatherapy, 
homeopathic and herbal remedies 
and other promising segments. 

“On the premise of the ‘natural’ 
presentation, there’s a lot more 


that can be done” in keeping with 
the growing demand for natural- 
ingredient health and personal 
care products, Niemy said. “Rialto 
offers a lot of line extension oppor- 
tunities.” 

With its two-tiered approach, 
Shoppers continues to wring solid 
sales and profits from its more than 
1,200 private label SKUs. Total 
store brand sales now account for 
nearly 8 percent of sales for the 
chain’s nearly 700 drug stores; fac- 
toring out prescription and tobacco 
sales, they account for 12 percent or 
more, said Niemy. 

Factoring in all promotional costs, 
private label products also average a 
38 percent gross margin for the com- 
pany, Niemy said. Taken separately, 
the Rialto brand does even better— 
gross Margins are averaging roughly 
45 percent, he said.

HEALTH & BEAUTY AIDS / ETHNIC PRODUCTS 


There’s hope for 1994. 

After 1993—a year in which eth- 
nic HBA sales, both overall and for 
the chain drug industry, remained 
soft—there are so many new 
launches under way this year that 
both chain drug ethnic product buy- 
ers and ethnic product distributors 
are encouraged, feeling that the 
segment will do better and possibly 
even grow in increments of middle 
to high single digits. 

According to Towne-Oller & Asso- 
ciates, a division of Information Re- 
sources Inc., total ethnic sales only 
increased 2 percent in units 
and dollars for the 12 months 
ending in November, 1993. 

Many chain drug buyers 
reported similar growth 
rates, or even a little less. A 
few chains, like Alabama- 
based Harco and New Or- 
leans-based K&B, reported 
stronger growth. Harco, for 
example, reported incremen- 
tal gains in the 5 percent to 
7 percent range. But part of 
that growth came from new 
store openings, and part was 
attributed to aggressive 
merchandising and advertis- 
ing for the department. 

At Walgreens, spokesper- 
son Michael Polzin reported 
that ethnic hair care prod- 
uct sales were down this 
year. Polzin attributed the 
decline to a decrease in 
product usage. 

“To kick off the category 
again, we're going to need 
some new hair styles,” he 
said. “The trend today, espe- 
cially with men, is for shorter hair 
and that means less use of mainte- 
nance products. Also, the braid look 
isn't really popular today, so we’re 
not getting sales of braid mainte- 
nance products.” 

The lack of exciting new styles 
has certainly depressed ethnic hair 
care sales, most buyers and distrib- 
utors agree, but some think that the 


category could be headed for a re- 
vival this year and in 1995, as the 
economy brightens and as manufac- 
turers put their energies into 
launching new products that are 
less “me-too” and more innovative. 


Drug chains go on the offensive 


Drug chains aren’t waiting. 
They’re gearing up to fight their 
competition for the African-Ameri- 
can, Hispanic and Asian consumer. 
Many chains are hoping that by re- 
fining their merchandise mix, ex- 
panding into new segments of eth- 


nic products and promoting more 
aggressively, they can capture a 
higher share of ethnic product sales. 
To that end, many chains are re- 
working their planograms to take 
more advantage of growth segments 
like relaxers, hair color, styling aids 

and children’s toiletries. 
At the same time, many are test-

focus groups sessions to show the

She added that many Hispanic 
women take cosmetics very seri-

face and an evening face. 

“At night, when they go out, 
they want to show themselves at 
their best. It’s almost competitive. 
They want to be the absolute best 
they can be,” Daggett said. 

To meet these different needs, 
scanning chains like Thrifty 
Drug, Walgreens, Eckerd, Revco 
and PayLess are now using the 
data they collect to customize 
their mix. Their goal is to have 
individual stores stock only what 
customers want to buy. 


Customers dictate ethnic 
merchandising trends 


T* drive sales in ethnic prod- 
ucts, many drug chains are 
now changing the way they 
merchandise these items, making 
ethnic cosmetics and toiletries eas- 
ier to find, easier to shop and more 
visible to greater numbers of con- 
sumers. 

Chains like Walgreens, Eckerd 
and Perry Drug have moved away 
from a segregated set for all ethnic 
products, choosing instead to mer- 
chandise ethnic segments like skin 
care, hair color and men’s shaving 
in the general market planogram 
where most customers would nor- 
mally expect to find them. 

Eckerd, for example, is testing an 
ethnic skin care section in its gener- 
al market planogram. The section, 
in test for over four months in sev- 
eral high-volume ethnic doors, con- 
sists of several 3-foot shelves of 
products formulated specifically for 
African-American skin. The pro- 
gram seems to be working well, a 
source said. 

Other drug chains are moving 
their ethnic cosmetics lines toward 
the front of the store where they 
will be the first selections women 
see as they come into the de- 
partment. 

To enhance their ethnic cosmetics 
presentations even further, many 
chains are moving their strongest 
ethnic lines to the wall, getting 
away from endcaps, spinner racks 
or floorstands. 

In the face of aggressive competi- 
tion from other trade classes, chains 
are also promoting ethnic products 
more, working closely with manu- 


facturers to create value oriented 
promotions like coupons, rebates, 
and buy-one-get-one-free offers that 
can spark sales. 

Still more chains are working 
alongside manufacturers to plan 
promotions eight to nine months in 
advance rather than five to six 
months in advance. The added time 
“gives us the chance to do better 
coordinated and stronger promo- 
tions,” said ethnic products buyer 
Charles Monk of Tuscaloosa, Ala.- 
based Harco Drugs. 


What works at Harco 


Harco Drug is one of the few 
chains that reported a sales in- 
crease in the ethnic category for last 
year; Monk estimated the chain’s 
ethnic HBA sales were up between 
5 percent and 7 percent in 93, and 
he’s hoping for a 10 percent in- 
crease this year. 

Aggressive promotions have cer- 
tainly helped drive sales, he said, 
but added that Harco has been re- 
viewing its merchandise mix in each 
door to ensure that such things as 
the mix, the size of the department, 
the placement of the products and 
the price points fit “the neighbor- 
hoods the stores are in.” 

Harco is hoping to develop new 
categories that it can use to bring 
new customers into its stores, and 
it’s searching for brands that will 
offer customers “something differ- 
ent, something that they can’t get 
anyplace else,” he said. 

“There’s no question the catego- 
ry’s gotten more competitive,” Monk

Drug chains court ethnic cosmetics shoppers 


hile statistics from market 
W researchers indicate that 
the ethnic cosmetics cat- 
egory is still growing—up 47 per- 
cent in units and 67 percent in dol- 
lars, according to Towne-Oller and 
Associates— many drug chain cos- 
metics buyers have reported the 
category has peaked for them, and 
sales have been flat or up only 
slightly, with most of the drug store 
industry’s current growth coming 
from increased sales of budget and 
mid-priced lines. 

Their problem, they said, has been 
both the depressed economy—which 
has softened sales of higher-end cos- 
metics like Revlon’s ColorStyles— 
and increased competition, which 
has made it hard to continue to build 
market share in ethnic cosmetics as 
well as ethnic toiletries. 

A handful of chains, like New Or- 
leans-based K&B, report seeing 
stronger growth in the category. 
The chain’s cosmetics buyer, Donna 
McManus, said her ethnic cosmetics 
sales are up in double-digit incre- 
ments, growth that she attributed 
partly to increased distribution of 
ethnic cosmetics in her chain, but 
also to K&B’s strong advertising for 
the category and enhanced mer- 
chandising presentations. 

Overall, buyers agree that the 
strongest lines right now are the 
value priced brands, particularly 
Pavion’s Black Radiance and Kiwi 
Product’s Tropez. Some segments of 
Maybelline’s Shades of You are also 
doing well, but according to most 
buyers, face makeup sales remain 
soft. 

On the West Coast, Claire 
Daggett, who buys cosmetics for Los 
Angeles-based Thrifty Drug, said 
her customers are buying more bud- 
get lines like Black Radiance and 
Tropez than ever before.

“We've gone from just a little em- 
phasis on ethnic cosmetics in 1991 
to a major presence,” said Mc- 
Manus. “We -now do print, radio and 
TV to support ethnic cosmetics, and 
it pays off. We also have ethnic cos- 
metics in more stores, and we hold 
training schools so our cosmeticans 
know enough about each line to rec- 
ommend specific purchases.” 

Stephanie Hayter, who buys cos- 
metics for Melville, N.Y.-based Gen- 
ovese Drug Stores, reported that 
while ethnic cosmetics remains “a 
good business in stores that have 
it,” her best sellers are the moder- 
ately priced Shades of You and val- 
ue priced Black Radiance. 

Hayter said that when she can of- 
fer consumers something extra on 
higher priced lines like ColorStyles, 
sales perk up. Revlon recently dis- 
tributed rebate coupons for Col- 
orStyles, and Hayter said that 
helped sales quite a bit. 

“People are looking for value, but 
a line like Black Radiance has more 
going for it than just price,” said 
Smith of Jack’s Service. “It’s also 
helped by its image and its packag- 
ing. They created a very classy look- 
ing package. It doesn’t seem cheap, 
but it does seem affordable.”

Customers, chains go on-line 


BETHESDA, Md. — Shoppers Express, which pro- 
vides home delivery services for supermarkets and 
drug store chains around the country, will add com- 
puterized shopping capability this spring. The move 
will allow customers to order by phone, fax or person- 
al computer and modem. 

Eckerd and Hook-SupeRx Inc. are among the first 
drug chains slated to offer the service, which can oper- 
ate through the current phone/fax systems at 40 su- 
permarket and drug chains. The electronic service is 
provided through Vienna, Va.-based America Online. 


Gary’s got another one 


EAGLEVILLE, Pa. — I Got It At Gary’s will open 
its sixth location in April. The newest Aston, Pa., loca- 
tion will be a 25,000-square-foot “super discount” 
store in a strip center. The chain, which posted sales 
of $43 million last year, opened its fifth unit last fall, 
and like that store, the Aston one will have strong 
seasonal merchandise, cosmetics, pharmacy and 
greeting card sections. The customer’service kiosk will 
offer one-hour photo developing, laminating, and fax 
and gift wrap services, among other features. 


Arbor promotes Gerhard to sr. VP 


TROY, Mich. — Arbor Drugs has 
promoted 1l-year company veteran 
Gilbert Gerhard to senior vice presi- 
dent of finance and administration. He 
last served as vice president in the 
same capacity. 

In his expanded role, Gerhard over- 
sees departments including accounting, 
administration, human resources, in- 
vestor relations, management information systems 
and treasury. He also directs all financial dealings for 
the 152-store regional powerhouse, including store ac- 
quisitions, and remains Arbor’s chief financial officer 
and treasurer.

Walgreen to settle civil suit 


WASHINGTON — Walgreen Co. has agreed to pay a 
$50,000 civil penalty to settle a federal claim stemming 
from the sale and export of a Chinese-made toy product 
deemed unsafe because it contained small parts. Wal- 
green voluntarily halted sale of the product nearly two 
years ago and denies that it knowingly violated any 
provisions of the Federal Hazardous Substances Act. 


Fruth realigns top management 


POINT PLEASANT, W.Va. — Fruth Pharmacy, 
which operates 17 stores in western West Virginia 
and southeastern Ohio, has shifted management du- 
ties to “ensure strong leadership and continuity of top 
management,” the company noted in a statement. 

Former president Jack Fruth has assumed the post 
of board chairman and chief executive. Named new 
president and chief operating officer is former executive 
vice president Don Pullin, a 24-year Fruth veteran. 

In another promotion, Paul Skinner was named as- 
sistant vice president of merchandising. He last served 
as coordinator of merchandising and warehousing. 


Kotynski fills new Revco post 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Revco D.S. has named Arbor 
Drugs veteran Richard Kotynski to the new post of di- 
rector of marketing systems. Kotynski will head up 
the development, implementation and management of 
all Revco information systems that support marketing 
operations, and will report to Edwin Gropp, senior 
vice president of information systems. 


Drug wholesalers seek profits 


from nonprescription goods 


by Mike Troy 


ORLANDO, Fla. — Squeezed by lower 
margins and a lack of price increases in 
pharmaceuticals, drug wholesalers hope to 
improve profits by focusing more on nonpre- 
scription product categories. 

“Wholesalers are finding suc- 
cess by encouraging more busi- 
ness, in all product categories, 
to be channeled through the 
wholesaler distribution system,” 
said Ron Streck, president and 
chief executive officer of the Na- 
tional Wholesale Druggists’ As- 
sociation, during a luncheon at 
the NWDA’s annual marketing 
conference here. 

Wholesalers are more than 
movers of product, Streck added. 
“They are a major marketing 
force that can influence product acceptance 
and market share as more prescription 
items are switched to OTC status.” 


Number of SKUs increasing 


For the past few years, wholesalers have 
gradually increased the number of OTC 
SKUs. “As a result of ongoing dialogue with 
our manufacturer trading partners and to 
help accommodate changing market forces, 
wholesalers have come to view over-the- 
counter medicines, health and beauty aids 
and home health care products in an entire- 
ly new light,” said John McNamara, chair- 
man, president and chief executive officer of 
Alco Health Services, speaking to the 
NWDA attendees. “We as an industry have 
opted to place greater emphasis than ever 
before on OTCs, home health care, diagnos- 
tics and consumer products in general. 

“Consequently,” he said, “it is no surprise 
that the latest NWDA survey shows the av- 
erage wholesaler stocking 3,000 more non- 


prescription items than in the mid-1980s.” 

OTCs have gained importance because of 
patient interest in self-medicating and be- 
cause of cost-containment pressure and po- 
litical intimidation that have suppressed 
price increases on prescription drugs, Mc- 
Namara said. Growth in the number of 
items that will be switched has also gained 
the attention of wholesalers. 

In a panel discussion called 
“Rx to OTC: What Wholesalers 
Need to Know,” Ray Modjeski, 
senior vice president of trade de- 
velopment with Schering-Plough 
HealthCare Products, said: 
“Switches just may be whole- 
salers’ biggest opportunity for in- 
cremental sales and profits, be- 
cause not one Rx-to-OTC product 


Alco’s John McNamara 


has failed in the marketplace. 
Wholesalers need to obtain all 
information as early as possible 
and get that information to customers and 
pharmacists. They need to ship at the ear- 
liest possible date, because retailers who get 
the product to the marketplace succeed.” 

There is also a burden on manufacturers 
to help wholesalers and retailers, agreed 
panelist Rudy Hauser, sales director with 
McNeil Consumer Products. “If there is one 
thing incumbent on manufacturers in a 
switch, it is to provide the right information 
and lead time to allow wholesalers and 
retailers to capitalize on it,” said Hauser. 

Retailers and wholesalers may also want 
to listen more closely to manufacturers’ ad- 
vice when it comes to switches. “Manufac- 
turers always want the full line in stores, 
but you have got to have a further trust 
with manufacturers when they say this is 
what you should stock,” said another panel 
member, Lou Schmidt, vice president of 
sales for Sandoz Consumer Pharmaceuti- 
cals. “You do have to stock more SKUs with 
a switch.”

Holding co. plans to buy out FoxMeyer 


DALLAS — National In- 
tergroup, the holding com- 
pany owning an 80.5 per- 
cent stake in FoxMeyer, has 
proposed a plan to purchase 
the remaining FoxMeyer 
shares held by the public, 
giving the holding company 
full control over the nation’s 
fourth-largest wholesaler. 

National Intergroup has 


proposed merging the 
wholesaler with a new sub- 
sidiary, allowing the compa- 
ny to purchase the public 
shares. 

Under terms of the pro- 
posal, FoxMeyer’s stock- 
holders would receive 
$14.75 principal amount in 
a new debt issue of 8.25 per- 
cent senior notes for each 


\ 


share of common stock not 
already held by National In- 
tergroup. To effect the deal, 
the new, proposed sub- 
sidiary, called FoxMeyer 
Holding, would issue a total 
of $81.3 million in new debt. 

FoxMeyer’s board has 
formed a special committee 
to consider the buyout pro- 
posal.

There's more to glasses than meets the eye 


Sometimes a golden opportunity can 
be as plain as the eyes on your face. 

Even though drug chains have sold 
sunglasses for years and have enjoyed 
success more recently with over-the- 
counter reading glasses, the optical 
category has a lot more to offer to the 
chain drug industry, especially to 
those drug stores ready to position 
themselves more firmly as destina- 
tions for health and wellness products. 

No matter what happens with the 
economy, the optical business is des- 


cal industry show, VisionExpo. 

The same consumer who has been 
driving your business in sunscreens 
and makeup with UV protection is 
ready to understand that UV light can 
be damaging to eyes as well. And even 
though regular sunglasses have be- 
come something of a commodity in 
drug stores, there is a whole new sub- 
category being born. 

At the recent optical show, I saw a 
surge of new products in the segment I 
would call “instant” sun wear, de- 
signed particular- 


.. | The optical category has a lot 

.| more to offer, especially to those 
}| Stores positioning themselves as 
health and wellness destinations

” < * 


ly for the con- 
sumer who is 
already wearing 
eyeglasses. This 
includes “wrap- 
around” sunglass- 
es that fit over 
prescription eye 
wear, as well as

underneath the 


WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


tined to grow throughout the 90s as 
the huge baby boomer population ex- 
periences presbyopia, the age-related 
visual condition that starts to affect 90 
percent of the population between the 
ages of 40 and 45. Statistically speak- 
ing, more than 95 percent of the over- 
65 population requires corrective eye 
wear. Seeing this demographic shift, 
manufacturers are paying a lot more 
attention to this category, which has 
resulted in a rush of more innovative 
and fashionable products. This trend 
was very apparent at the recent opti- 


eyeglasses. And, 
as manufacturers 
have successfully 
combined practi- 
cality and style, clip-on and flip-up 
sunglasses have resurged to become 
fast-moving items. In fact, one compa- 
ny, Midlantic Accessories, would like 
retailers to merchandise all the vari- 
ous sun wear options above under a 
banner called “Visual Healthwear.” 
There’s also a plethora of new items 
in the “cord” category, the variety of 
devices that keep people from losing 
their eye wear while engaging in active 
pursuits. Thanks to the popularity of 
lines like Croakies with the skiing and 
surfing sets, these products have be- 


come hot fashion items, and they are 
popular with retailers, too, because 
they offer fast turns and high margins. 
The latest trend is cords that float, and 
several companies introduced varia- 
tions of this theme at the recent show. 

There are a number of other seg- 
ments of the optical accessory business 
that could be appropriate in-line drug 
store items. Because they are shopped 
so much more frequently than optical 
outlets, drug stores are much more 
likely to capture impulse purchases by 
eyeglass wearers—if the category is 
merchandised correctly. 

Fashion has really energized the op- 
tical accessories business. Eyeglass 
cases come with more finishes, shapes 
and features than ever before, and 
eyeglass chains are available in a 
much wider variety of finishes, some 
with embellishments like beads, that 
give them greater fashion appeal. 

There have even been innovations in 
lens cleaning cloths. To care for lenses 
with delicate antireflective coatings—a 
growing portion of the lens business— 
lens cloths have been upgraded and 
improved, offering consumers a much- 
needed way to care for their expensive 
lenses and giving retailers higher 
price tickets and better margins. 

In today’s hyper-competitive, rapidly 
changing environment, it’s necessary 
to take a serious look at any likely av- 
enue for profit and competitive differ- 
entiation. Some products may be brand 
new, but many of the greatest opportu- 
nities can come from product cate- 
gories or services that have been over- 
looked or underdeveloped in the past. 
The optical category is just one of 
many such areas. 


Is retail pharmacy really ready to commit? 


Like the unattractive individual at 
the singles bar, President Clinton’s 
health reform plan figures to grow 
more appealing to retail pharmacy the 
nearer it gets to closing time. 

At least that’s what Washington rep- 
resentatives from NACDS and NARD 
are hoping for. So far, however, those 
hopes have not been fully realized. De- 
spite constant efforts by NACDS and 


openly worrying whether they could 
survive even one year under the Clin- 
ton health reform program. 

Among independents, concerns 
about the proposed plan are even more 
pronounced. At the NARD Multi-Loca- 
tions Conference last month, North 
Carolina pharmacist Bill Mast warned 
scores of independents that “the 
Hillary Bill” would doom community 
pharmacy. 


Despite the efforts of NACDS 
and NARD, many in the industry 
remain deeply skeptical of the 
Clinton health care reform plan 


But if NACDS 
and NARD are 
finding it difficult 
to sell health care 
reform to their 
members, they’re 
having even more 
trouble encourag- 
ing other groups 
to support the 
President’s plan. 


WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


NARD to portray the Administration’s 
Health Security Act as the best health 
reform deal retail pharmacy is going to 
be offered, many in the industry re- 
main deeply skeptical of the plan. 
NACDS president Ron Ziegler and 
senior vice president Rob Waspe both 
sought to resolve the health reform 
concerns of chain executives at the as- 
sociation’s recent Small Chain Confer- 
ence in California. But a number of 
NACDS members left the meeting 


8 Drug Store News, March 28, 1994 


Organizations 
such as the AMA 
and the AARP 
have carefully 
avoided giving the Clinton plan the 
kind of blanket endorsement that 
NARD and NACDS have. 

Similarly, the APhA and other na- 
tional pharmacy organizations have 
refused to openly embrace the Clinton 
proposal, “warts and all.” 

Moreover, a recent national survey 
of state pharmacy association execu- 
tives and pharmacy board officials by 
DrSN’s sister publication, Drug Store 
News For the Pharmacist, found a deep 


undercurrent of opposition to Clinton’s 
emphasis on managed care providers. 

And other retail industry segments 
that usually see eye-to-eye with drug 
chains on legislative issues are openly 
fighting the Clinton scheme. 

“Mandating employer-paid health 
benefits for part-time workers would 
impose enormous hardships on the su- 
permarket industry,” Food Marketing 
Institute government affairs chief Ty 
Kelley said. The typical supermarket 
would have to spend about $100,000 to 
insure its 50 part-timers, he said. 

Discount store industry lobbyists at 
the International Mass Retail Associ- 
ation are even more vocal in their op- 
position to the plan. 

Predicting “massive job losses” 
throughout retailing if the President’s 
bill is passed, the IMRA released a 
new study showing that one out of 
every five discount store industry jobs 
“will be eliminated or seriously threat- 
ened” by the Clinton plan. 

Drug stores, which also rely heavily 
on part-time workers, would likely 
face similar pressures. 

Are these problems minor warts on 
the face of a basically sound plan that 
advances the broader interests of re- 
tail pharmacy? 

Or are they fatal flaws that warrant 
a re-examination of the drug store in- 
dustry’s support for Clinton’s health 
reform? That’s a question that the in- 
dustry will have to answer soon. It’s 
almost closing time.

by Vicki Gerson 


here’s a lack of growth in the 
deodorant category at chain 
drug stores. 

Despite a flurry of new products, 
sales are down, and chains are find- 
ing that there is room for creativity 
in the deodorant department. Most 
need to do work on creating traffic- 
building opportunities. 

According to Information Re- 
sources Inc., for the 52-week period 
ending Jan. 2, 1994, dollar sales of 
personal deodorants in drug stores 
decreased 3.7 percent from the pre- 
vious year; unit sales dropped 4.2 
percent. 

On the other hand, mass mer- 
chandisers recorded 16.3 percent 
growth in dollar sales and 16.5 per- 
cent growth in unit sales for the 
same period, while food store sales 
dropped slightly. 

Mass merchandisers seem to be 
paying more attention to deodor- 
ant, drawing consumers into their 
stores with great prices and giving 
the category more space than drug 
stores give it. 

According to John Cincotta, se- 
nior category manager of HBA for 
Chain Drug Marketing Associates, 
manufacturers are attempting to re- 
vitalize this segment of the health 
and beauty business. “There are 
new trends and segments of the 
marketplace being specifically tar- 
geted,” he said. 


Is the answer clear? 


In 1992, Bristol-Myers Products, 
in an attempt to break new ground, 
introduced Ban Clear Solid Deodor- 
ant—the first clear solid deodorant. 
In April 1993, attempting to ad- 
dress the No. 1 female complaint 
against antiperspirants—the messy 
residue that white solid antiperspi- 
rants leave on skin and clothing— 
the company introduced Ban Clear 
A.P. to control odor and wetness. 

“We’re now seeing the copycat ef- 
fect of the clear products,” Cincotta 
said. “Manufacturers are putting 
out clear products because clear 
gives the appearance of purity. After 
all, detergent manufacturers are 
having success with this philosophy. 
Furthermore, since younger con- 
Sumers are in tune with the envi- 
ronment and recycled packaying, 
manufacturers believe clear prod- 
ucts’ [pure image] will succeed in 
the marketplace.” 

Carol Boyd, public relations man- 
ager of beauty care at Proctor & 
Gamble, disagrees with that philos- 
ophy. “The problem with clear prod- 
ucts as the technology exists today 
is that they don’t control wetness 
very well. We don’t think the con- 
sumer is going to be happy with 
these products, and we don’t have 
one on the market under our name. 
We think drug store buyers are go- 
ing to find that these products 
aren't going to be their best sellers. 
We see the numbers, and customers 
aren t making repeat purchases.” 

Likewise, Paul Carlson, beauty

with the clear products. “There’s

The customer has to make sure

Since Septemnber 1993, to combat 
the clear trend, Boyd said P&G 
been testing an “ultra dry” product

It vanishes once it’s rubbed into the

pected to average $2.50 for the 1.7-

Meanwhile, Snyder’s Carlson be- 
lieves that the retail price point for 
the best selling items is at the $1.99 
level. “Over that price level, the 
consumer has to perceive it as an 
added value product,” he said. 


Targeting teens 


According to Cincotta, about 70 
percent of the deodorant products 
are sold to the adult female market. 
Arrid and Gillette are trying to 
change these statistics with innova- 
tive products, creative planograms 
and new marketing styles. 

Because teenagers have quite a 
bit of discretionary money, Arrid’s 
six-SKU Teen Image line is_ being 
marketed aggressively to teenage 
girls. And since teens are attracted 
to color, the company has packaged 
its line of pastel antiperspirants in 
brightly colored containers. 

Yet, buyers like Steve Rubin of 
Keltsch Bros., a 15-store Indiana 
chain, are not really convinced that 
the teen segment is a viable mar- 
ket. “I don’t think it’s strong 
enough yet,” he said. 

P&G’s Boyd agrees. P&G has no

seem to be paying more 
attention to deodorant, 
luring consumers into 
their stores with great 
prices and giving the 
category more space 
than drug stores give it. 


plans to create a product for the 
teenage market segment. “We don’t 
want people to feel they grow out of 
our product. We want loyal con- 
sumers from 16 to 80,” Boyd said. 
“Making a product for just teens 
isn’t a viable business proposition. 
We would rather bring people into 
the franchise at an early age and 
make sure we can keep them there.” 


Marketing to men 


Meanwhile, Gillette thinks it 
knows how to change that 70 percent 
statistic. With the company’s new 
Wild Rain series, it’s asking drug 
stores to group all of its products to- 
gether. “Gillette wants to make a 
‘Gillette Story’ by grouping shaving 
cream with deodorants,” said Cincot- 
ta. “Consequently, what Gillette 
wants is a men’s grooming area.” 

Cincotta acknowledges that the 
CDMA has educated its drug store 
chains about this new strategy. 
“Most of the drug store chains are 
taking these Gillette products and 
placing them next to their shaving 
section. They are using this new 
marketing approach to increase 
sales in this category,” he said.

Drug Store News, March 28, 1994 


“The mass merchants rec- 
ognize that deodorants can 
draw in consumers,” Cincot- 
ta said. “Consequently, 
they’re aggressively trying 
to take more business away. 
That’s why mass merchants 
are devoting more space to 


these products and stocking 
more SKUs.” 


The space crunch 


Unfortunately, space is 
always one of the challenges 
at drug stores. Because 
solids and sticks are the 
best sellers, Cincotta recom- 
mends cutting back on 
aerosol sprays when space 
is tight. He also recom- 
mends conducting some 
management studies within 
a given space, studying the 
past history of each item, 
and being selective. “Work 
with key suppliers to get 
important industry data,” 
he said. 

New planograms are al- 
ways important to a basic 
department like deodorants. 
Because deodorants are a 
year-round seller, make 
your customer take a new 
look at this department, 
Cincotta advised. 

He strongly recommends 
that chains combat sluggish 
departments, like deodor- 
ants, by being aggressive 
and catering to travel size 
products. “Many drug stores 
have established a separate 
department for [high im- 
pulse] travel-size items. 
This is profitable to the 
drug store chain,” he ex- 
plained. 


Enter private label 


Carrying private label or 
control label products is an- 
other strategy being used by 
some drug store chains to 
increase profits. 

Consumers will not see 
private label deodorants as 
“cheap knock-offs anymore,” 
said Cincotta, “but as a 
good value for their money.” 
Some chains, like Big B 
Drugs, Kerr Drugs and 
Genovese already carry pri- 
vate label products. Cincot- 
ta said he believes that 
most private label or con- 
trol label deodorants sell for 
approximately 20 percent 
cheaper than brand-name 
products. 

“Since it’s so hard for the 
drug stores to make money 
on name-brand, highly com- 
petitive deodorant prod- 
ucts,” Cincotta said, “they 
are turning to private label 
products as an answer to 
their problems.”

HEALTH & BEAUTY AIDS / HAIR CARE 


The pros and cons of a pro/commodity mix 


by Barbara White 


ollowing the example of Wal- 
0 Mart, drug retailers have re- 
examined the wisdom of 
breaking out salon-inspired and 
professional hair care products in a 
separate section in hair care. Some 
have combined the sets; others op- 
pose consolidation and are leaving 
their sets separate. 
For those favoring consolidation, 


ae. 


Professional hair care may be going in-line in many drug stores, but some chains 
cite inconsistent supply and other factors for keeping pro in its own set. 


one motivation is the desire to buy 
product directly from manufactur- 
ers rather than from a distributor. 

Most quasi-professional, salon-in- 
spired lines once sold through dis- 
tributors are now direct. Redmond’s 
Aussie started the trend a few years 
ago, Alberto-Culver’s TRESémme 
was brought direct-to-retail over 
one year ago, and smaller lines are 
beginning to do the same. 

“Wal-Mart has never liked deal- 
ing with distributors,” said Ad- 
vanced Research Labs’ vice presi- 
dent of research and development 
Jim Parr. “If a retailer has to deal 
with a distributor, he knows he is 
not getting the best price.” 

There are other advantages. By 
selling directly to chains, Parr said, 
a manufacturer can offer the retail- 
er more services, such as the televi- 
sion and print advertising campaign 
Advanced Research Labs plans for 
this year. 

Said a spokesperson at Alberto- 
Culver: “One problem we faced was 
pricing of the TRESémme line that 
was all over the board. Distributors 
were also making between 5 and 30 
percent on lines. Now that we have 
that margin back, we can put that 
money into advertising the line.” 


Diverted goods scarce 


As more lines, such as Infusium 
and Focus, go directly to retailers, 
distributors are left with fewer lines 
to represent. Said Parr: “Out of the 
four main distributors, only one is 


really surviving. They don’t have 
enough product to sell.” 

As distributors fall out of the 
game, retailers have fewer reasons 
to keep a separate pro hair care set 
serviced by a distributor. 

It’s also more difficult today to se- 
cure diverted true salon goods. 
Technological advances in coding 
have increased the level of difficulty 
by allowing manufacturers to trace 
goods more easily. 

“True salon products, such as Se- 
bastian, Nexxus and Aveeda, are 
too hard to come by fer many retail- 
ers,” said one manufacturer of 
professional hair care products. 
“With their in-and-out availability, 
the merchandise often winds up 
harming the retailer rather than 
being an asset to the mix. Cus- 
tomers are often frustrated when 
they get to the drug store, only to 
find that merchandise they've previ- 
ously purchased there is no longer 


on the shelf.” 
Lack of consistency a factor 


Some retailers say that the diffi- 
culty in obtaining diverted goods is 


another strong argument to com- 
bine sections. Others strongly be- 
lieve just the opposite is true. 

One chain that has been affected 
is Eagleville, Pa.-based I Got It At 
Gary’s. “Better bar coding has defi- 
nitely put a crimp in the availabili- 
ty of lines,” said buyer Susan 
Swartz. 

She said it’s been difficult to 
maintain a consistent supply of true 
salon goods—and that’s one reason 
she is against bringing professional 
hair care goods into the commodity 
hair care planogram. “It’s difficult 
to maintain a consistent supply of 
any one product, and in a 
planogram, you can’t swap sizes 
based on availability,” she said. 

“It’s hard to planogram salon 
products in,” agreed Jerry Biarsky, 
buyer at Manhattan-based Pharm- 
house. “That’s why I keep a pro hair 
set. I'd rather have a hole on that 
shelf than in commodity.” 

Gary’s Swartz added that the de- 
partment is also too important to 
the chain’s corporate mission of pro- 
viding the greatest amount of choic-

Generics growing 


Retailers say they have had 
strong sales of generic pro hair care 
products from Russ Kalvin, Mr. 
Charles and European Mystique. 

“We originally filled a niche when 
retailers couldn’t get enough divert- 
ed goods,” said Russ Kalvin, presi- 
dent of the generic pro line that 
bears his name. “Now we are be- 
coming a brand name on our own.” 

Kalvin’s line is positioned against 
the top-selling salon brands at 30 to 
50 percent savings. And the retailer 
profits as well; margins on generic 
products run from 28 to 40 percent. 

Drug Emporium currently carries 
40 items and is expanding its set for 
Kalvin’s generics to 12 feet. F&M 
currently stocks 27 Kalvin SKUs. 

The success of the lines depends 
on their ability to knock off the 
most popular SKUs. 

“The market is driven by today’s 
products, and only five or six prod- 
ucts are really hot at one time,” said 
Charlie Kaye, president of Mr. 
Charles. “Shaper hair sprays and 
shine enhancers are very impor- 
tant. The customer knows the latest 
products.” 

Natural means success, according 
to Kaye. “Aveeda is the hottest 
thing in salons right now because 
it’s an all-natural product,” he said. 

Retailers say the success of gener- 
ics is dependent upon the retailers’ 


ability to stock the branded product 
as well. “Unless you have the 
branded products on the shelves 
convincing the customer to com- 
pare, generics don’t sell,” said Medic 
Discount’s Zlotnick. Added Pharm- 
house’s Biarsky: “We do a great job 
with generics, because customers 
can compare their prices with 
branded items. Of course, we do a 
better job with Sebastian products 
when we can get them.” 


All retailers agree on 
one thing: the 
profitability of the 
category. Hair products 
with a professional 
cachet are fetching solid 
35 to 40 percent margins 
at most chains. 


Gary’s Swartz said Aveeda, Paul 
Mitchell and Sebastian products 
continue to outsell generics by two 
to three times, although generics 
are strong at the chain. “There’s 
tremendous acceptance of generics 
in this market,” she said. The chain 
markets eight to 12 SKUs of private 
label pre hair products under the I 
Got It At Gary’s name. Swartz said 
those products are the strongest in 
the private label line.

— Al Kenney, Manager of Trade

dinator of category management ac-

$600 million 
feminine hy- 
giene manufac- 
turer, shared his 
views in an ex- 
clusive inter- 
view. “Manag- 
ing the category 
is a responsibil- 
ity” Kenney 
commented, 
“We do not strive for more shelf 
space than we deserve, we look at 
the data for the entire section and 
then make recommendations that 
benefit the entire category.” 

For category management pre- 
sentations, Tambrands_ uses 
Gladson & Associates, a Lisle, [IL 
based space management consult- 
ing firm. Kenney said, “We used 
to have contracts with two other 
companies, but our sales force 
chose Gladson unanimously. Our 
regional managers told us that they 
[Gladson] understood our business 
and were effective from day one.” 
Using a space management center 
gives the retailer an objective per- 
spective on the category. 

“We have chosen not to bring 
our space management in-house be- 
cause we do not want to lose our 
objectivity, Kenney added, 
“Gladson is like an extension of our 
company, we have access to a tre- 
mendous service without the huge 
capital investment.” 

By using a service center, 
Tambrands has been able to build 
planograms using sensitive retailer 
data that would not otherwise be 
available. “Retailers give their store 
specific data to Gladson on a con- 
fidential, nondisclosure basis which 
is then incorporated into the 
planogram analysis.” 

“Our relationship with Gladson 
& Associates has been a big chap- 
ter in our category management 
success story” concluded Kenney.

In 1993, drug stores’ dol- 
lar sales in hair color to- 
taled $341.8 million, accord-

Research, an increase of 8.5

Other channels cash in 


The bad news is that 
while drug stores held a 
lion’s share of the busi- 
ness—about 54.4 percent, 
according to Information 
Resources Inc.—other trade 
channels made inroads. 

In the mass class of trade, 
dollar sales for the category 
were up a hefty 21.2 percent 
to $176 million; units sales 
increased 13.8 percent to 
40.6 million. That channel 
holds a 28.4 percent market 
share of the category. 

Most surprising of all, in 
the food/drug combos, dollar 
sales were up 13.5 percent 
to $109.1 million and unit 
sales grew 12.3 percent to 
$21 million. Food/drug com- 
bos held a 17.2 percent of 
the market share. 

Drug stores aren’t doing 
anything wrong; it’s more a 
matter of other channels of 
trade doing more right. 

Mass and combo stores 
have expanded their section 
sizes and product mix to 
mimic drug stores. And 
mass merchants are selling 
at lower prices. 


Strategies for drug 


What can drug stores do 
to hold onto the business? 
“They can do a better job 
with their selections,” said 
Cincotta. “Drug stores can 
always carry more SKUs 
than other channels.”

Clairol’s director of trade 
marketing: “Drug stores 
should play up their point of 
difference with promotional 
formats that go beyond a 
sale price. Smart chains will 
leverage their hair color de- 
partment with their cosmet- 
ics section, offering a free 
gift with purchase and other 
promotions.”

Wanted: Standouts in crowded bath category 


‘Everybody thinks 
bath is expanding, 
which it is. But 
many of the mass 
lines don’t truly 
reach a niche...’ 


—Covault, Drug Emporium 


ath is due for a shakeout— 

even though the category had 

an 8 percent increase in 1993 
and sales totaled $88.5 million. 

Retailers say the category in- 
cludes too many small players with 
too many SKUs. 

Bath has become an established 
category and is no longer experienc- 
ing double-digit growth. As a result, 
drug chains are taking a closer look 
at the lines they currently carry. 
And they plan to analyze the cate- 
gory critically as they go forward— 
increasing the possibility of a 
shakeout. 

“This is not an endlessly growing 
category. There is definitely some- 
thing there, but people have to 
dampen their expectations,” said a 
vice president: of purchasing at one 
chain. 

The lines they will continue to 
carry, retailers say, are those that 
offer the best assistance with the 
category as a whole. 

“Manufacturers need to help re- 
tailers with merchandising and 
need to offer value to the customer 
at least once a quarter to spark tri- 
al, as well as repeat business,” said 
Kathy Covault, manager of cosmet- 
ics at Drug Emporium. 

Covault, like other retailers, is 
looking for lines that are backed 
with strong year-round merchandis- 
ing plans, have flexible display op- 
tions and are supported with adver- 
tising dollars. 

“Everybody thinks bath is ex- 
panding, which it is,” Covault 
added. “But many of the mass lines 
don’t truly reach a niche the way 
The Body Shop’s products do.” 

Many manufacturers, already 
gearing up for 

the anticipated 
i shakeout, are

Expecting a shakeout in bath, manufacturers are sticking close to retailers to 
work on merchandising strategies that weed out non-performing SKUs. 


“We are interested in line opti- 
mization,” said Dan Petchers, direc- 
tor of marketing at Yardley, which 
introduced Yardley Bath Shoppe last 
year. “We know we have to keep the 
line current and carefully examine 
SKU performance.” That’s why the 
company cut five SKUs from its line 
to replace them with new items. 

Benckiser is also sold on the idea 
of replacing rather than adding 
SKUs. Its new Calgon bath and 
shower foams, which began ship- 
ping this month, are replacing older 
Calgon products. 


Ad, promo budgets mean more 


The manufacturers that are back- 
ing their lines with ad and promo- 
tion dollars know that the support 
will keep them on retail shelves. 

“No one has been talking to the 
consumer about these lines,” said 
Karen Scheuermann, senior prod- 
uct manager at Chesebrough- 
Pond’s. “Unless a woman comes 
into the store, she doesn’t know op- 
tions exist beyond Vaseline Inten- 
sive Care or Calgon, and she 
doesn’t know what the benefits of 
specialty products are.” 


Drug Store News, March 28, 1994 


Retailers are now expecting man- 
ufacturers to tell their story. “We’re 
looking for some leadership in the 
category,” said Hope Stone, buyer at 
PayLess. “Going forward, we’re 
looking to carry the lines that can 
support the big retailers with mar- 
keting and promotion.” 

“If you want something to suc- 
ceed, you have to advertise it or it 
doesn’t do anything,” said Covault. 

“Let’s face it, the higher the noise 
level, the higher the interest,” said 
Jon Ruddin, vice president of mer- 
chandising at Happy Harry’s. 

And manufacturers know it. 
Those suppliers who have long sup- 
ported the category, such as 
Benckiser and Neutrogena, are be- 
ing joined by other manufacturers 
backing their new lines with the 
clout of consumer ads. 

Yardley and Chesebrough-Pond’s 
have harnessed the power of print 
advertising since the inception of 
their respective Bath Shoppe and 
Pears Personal Pleasures lines.

line geared to younger, active

concerned, said Yardley’s Petchers: 
“Promotion is important to a catego- 
ry that’s in the process of being de- 
veloped. Its success depends on re- 
peat business.”

trating. 

“We offered one retailer a promo- 
tional price of $2.20 on our Beautiful 
Bath products, which included a cus- 
tomer mail-in rebate of $2.20, “ said

in, so the retailer 
wasn’t selling at 
cost. We gave 
them the opportu-

product through the mail. It costs 
the retailer nothing.”

Multi-packs, off-shelf 
promos help regain 
slipping soap sales 


rug stores are quickly losing 
share to mass merchants in 
the bar soap category. 

What are discounters and clubs 
doing that drug stores are not? Two 
things, according to John Hooper, 
senior manager of national drug ac- 
counts for Lever Brothers. 


“Mass is putting more emphasis 


on display and selling more bundle 


packs,” said Hooper. “This really 


has given them an advantage.” 


Bar soap market share 


1990 1992 


on Drug ™ Mass

Source: Lever Brothers. 


Hooper said that mass mer- 
chants often use multiple packs as 
a draw. “The drug class of trade is 
the only channel that sells single 
bars. Mass is selling six- and eight- 
packs,” he said. 

Lever’s data supports the idea of 
selling larger packs. A full 67 per- 
cent of purchases of bar soap are 
packs of three or more bars. 

Dan Zarazan, senior vice presi- 
dent of Dial Corp.’s special market- 
ing sales division, agrees. “Multi- 
packs are the No. 1 area we'd like to 
see drug chains work on,” he said. 

Some chains have begun to offer 
more multi-packs. PayLess offers 
many brands in four-packs. 

Brooks has switched to multi- 
packs in three- and four-bar counts 
in many locations. “It’s not only a 
bigger sale, it’s the way the cus- 
tomer wants to buy it,” said a 
source at the chain. 


Displays aid impulse buys 


The bar soap category can also 
benefit from off-shelf displays and 
promotion. 

“Soap is such a highly impulsive 
sale that most households average 
at least three brands in the home at 
any given time,” said Lever’s Hoop- 
er. “An impulse category benefits 
from off-shelf display.” 

Drug chains need to be aggressive 
in this area to gain back their share 
from other channels, according to 
Dial’s Zarazan. 

“We see a lot of progress with 
chains doing promotion and ads

Lever holds that placing commodi- 
ty soaps in the skin care section 
rather than the household chemical 
set can be the first step in gaining 
back that share. 

Dial’s Zarazan agrees. “It makes 
sense to put it close to the skin care 
section, since many of those bars 
have skin care selling features,” he 
said. Dial’s Tone and Dial Plus, its 
new entry into the market that 
claims both anti-bacterial and mois- 
turizing features, are two examples. 

Brooks is pleased with the move 
and credits it in part with re- 
spectable increases in bar soap. 

Other retailers are considering 
the move as well. “We are thinking 
about moving bar soap,” said Hope 
Stone, buyer at PayLess. “We 
thought about trying it near the 


bath department. Bar soap is still a 
good category for us, so we feel if we 
can move the commodity soaps near 
the specialty soaps, we may get con- 
sumers to trade up.” 

One New Jersey-based retailer 
places soap in the skin care set or 
near feminine hygiene, depending 
on the size and layout of the store. 

“We do a tremendous job with 
bar soaps,” said the buyer at the 
chain. “We run them on the bottom 
of the shelf in the skin care set in 
cut case displays. Multi-packs sell 
very well.” 

Deep discount drug stores are 
making a strong statement with 
multi-pack soaps, displaying them 
in the center aisles or as part of the 
permanent set in cut case displays 
that signal value to the consumer.

Glycerin soaps may be more 
than a quick in-and-out promo- 
tion for drug stores. 


soaps’ moisturizing aspects, deco- 
rative look and pleasant smell, 
quickly become repeat customers. 

“One of the most frustrating 
things a retailer can do is run an 
in-and-out on glycerins,” said 
Stephen Hoffman, director of 
marketing at Shalom Interna- 
tional, which manufactures Hen- 
ri Bernard glycerin soaps. “The 
customer comes back looking for 
the items, then can’t find them.” 

Some retailers, such as Paw- 
tucket, R.I.-based Brooks Drug, 
have added the soaps to their 

ermanent sets. “We carry six 

avors in our planograms, and 
they do very well,” said a source 
at the chain. “We also bring in in- 
and-outs in floorstands.” 

The soaps round out the bath 
offerings and do best at chains 
which have a complete bath de- 
partment.

chains investing space

them until we grew bath. Now we 
carry them year-round.” 

PayLess promotes the soaps at 
$2.29 and retails them every day 
at $2.49. 

With several bath lines already 
including a glycerin soap SKU, 
it’s hard to convince retailers 
with little room to carry addition-

are pleased with the impulse 
sales and margins—about 20 per-

three-for-$5.

Some chains with smaller formats

strategies work. “I don’t object to the 
positioning of soap in the skin care 
department, but I just don’t have the 
room,” said Charles Monk, buyer at
