Other retailers aren’t so sure 
that the idea holds water. “That ar- 
gument has been going on for so 
long,” said Jon Ruddin, buyer at 
Newark, Del.-based Happy Harry’s. 
“The food channel isn’t about to 
move soap away from household 
chemical, so why should drug con- 
sider it? Procter & Gamble wants 
its Oil of Olay soap displayed in 
household chemical, so it just 
doesn’t make sense.” 

Some retailers feel that P&G ac- 
tually wanted two spots in the 
store: one in commodity soaps and 
another in specialty soaps in the 
skin care set. 

Carol Boyd, a spokesperson for 
P&G, said the company had no wish 
to position the Olay body bar in the 
specialty soap section. “We didn’t 
want Olay out of the mainstream in 
the specialty soap section,” she said. 
“The Olay bar is a body bar.” 

Asked why P&G wasn’t opting 
for moving soap entirely away 
from household chemical, Boyd 
said the answer had more to do 
with precedent than anything else. 
“We don’t want to confuse the con- 
sumer,” she said.

menu of display options next year.

Revco: Strong showing 


in sales and profits 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
Revco D.S. continued its 
steady record of improving 
results with strong gains in 
same-store sales and profits 
for the third quarter and first 
nine months of fiscal 1994. 

Same-store sales were up 
a healthy 9 percent for the 
quarter ended Feb. 5, in 
sharp contrast to meager 
Same-store gains recently 
recorded by some retailers. 
Total sales rose to $621.2 
million for the quarter, a 
12.5 percent gain over the 
same period a year earlier. 

Operating profits rose 28 
percent to $31.5 million, 
with net earnings for the 

eriod nearly tripling to 
$12.5 million. Excluding the 


impact of a non-cash charge 
for goodwill amortization, 
Revco generated net income 
of $16.6 million, vs. $8.4 
million the previous year. 

Year-to-date, sales rose 
11.8 percent to $1.69 billion, 
with same-store results up 
8.7 percent. Operating prof- 
its rose 37 percent to $54.8 
million, with net income 
growing to $18.5 million 
compared with $2.2 million 
for the first three quarters 
of fiscal 1993. 

Expressing pleasure with 
the results, chain president 
and chief executive officer D. 
Dwayne Hoven said the 
chain enjoyed “excellent sea- 
sonal sales” and “the benefit 
of a strong flu season.” 


Longs posts sales increase, 
net income dip, in tough year 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. 
— Longs Drug Stores posted 
a 1 percent sales increase 
but a 0.4 percent dip in net 
income for its fiscal year 
ended Jan. 27. Fourth-quar- 
ter results for the West 
Coast chain showed a late- 
year improvement in the 
picture, however, with a 3 
percent increase in net in- 
come and similar gains in 
sales.

total sales against the out- 
come of Longs stores in dif- 
ficult California and 
Hawaii markets. The chain 
also improved its gross 
margin last year to 25.5 
percent, up from 24.7 per- 
cent in the previous year. 

Sales for the fourth quar- 
ter totaled $684.7 million 
compared to $666.7 million 
for the same period last 
year. Net income for the pe-

PHARMACISTS CAN CUT 
MEDICARE COSTS $30B 
By encouraging commu- 
nity pharmacists to en- 
gage in “professional in- 
teraction” with elderly 
patients, the Clinton re- 
form plan could generate 
$30 billion in Medicare pro- 
gram savings over five 
years, according to a 
NARD/NACDS-funded 
study by Lewin-VH1. Ad- 
vanced pharmacy services 
(DUR, as well as voluntary 
formulary, generic substi- 
tution and prior authoriza- 
tion programs) will pro- 
duce $13.9 billion of the 
savings, the researchers 
said. Another $13.8 billion 
should result from more 
“appropriate use of phar- 
maceutical products” and 
$1.5 billion from using 
more cost-effective drugs.

Cash in on consumers sentiments 


he drug store own- 
er’s eternal pursuit 
of the perfect retail 


item that offers a high 
gross margin, quick turns, 
low labor costs and no 
warehousing continues. 
Such a perfect item does 
exist! It is greeting cards. 
Because of their nature, 
greeting cards are an inte- 
gral part of today’s typical 
drug store product mix. 
The card department size, 
selection and price range 
are determined by store 
demographics and the im- 
age desired. 

Where can you find in- 
formation to help you de- 
termine your mix? Card 
companies themselves are 
tremendous resources for 
the pharmacist regarding 
this department, and 
fierce competition between 
greeting card companies 
allows store owners to 
shop around. 

One thing you must re- 
member when dealing with 
card companies is that 
they have a tendency to 
try and take over a large 
area of the store with their 
products. Card companies 
want to stock what they 
“feel” is good for you (and 
them). You need to know 
your demographics and 
decide the mix on a store- 
by-store basis. 


Big profits 


Profitability is the 
biggest reason this depart- 
ment is a winner. There 
are very few items that 
you can carry in a drug 
store today and receive a 
90 percent gross profit. It’s 
the type of department 
that complements a drug 
store and the colorful and 
organized presentation of 
the products creates a fun

60532. (708) 810-0090. His bimonth- 
ly column on“Niche Departments” 
covers niche services and depart- 
ments that pharmacists may be in- 
terested in adapting to their stores.

area for shoppers. In most 
cases, the products that 
are sold in this depart- 
ment are for someone oth- 
er than the person making 
the purchase. This makes 
the purchaser feel good 
and creates a pleasurable 
shopping experience. 

Also pleasing to the re- 
tailer: Annual greeting 
card sales exceed $5.6 bil- 
lion, and drug stores con- 
trol 26 percent of this 
market. Cards have an im- 
pulse rate of 50 percent, 
and 85 percent to 90 per- 
cent are purchased by 
women. Selection and 
convenience are major fac- 
tors in selecting a place to 
shop for cards. 


The average person re- 
ceives 31 cards a year (in- 
cluding seven birthday 
cards), at an average retail 
price of $1.50. 

You. must have a recog-

ton or Hallmark. However, 
if you want to have out- 
standing sales, you must 
add alternative or contem- 
porary lines, such as Recy- 
cled Paper, Paper Moon 
and Renaissance. Alterna- 
tive cards account for 25 
percent of card sales, and 
are growing at an annual 
rate of 30 percent.

to Gladson and Associates.

Getting into 
gifts 


Getting into the gift 
business is a little more 
difficult than greeting 
cards. What traditionally 
happens is that at first, 
gift buyers purchase 
what they like and not 
what they should be buy- 
ing for the store. This is 
where the experience of a 
gift consultant, who can 
show you the items you 
should be carrying, is 
invaluable. In most cases, 
this department starts 
out small and expands as 
demand dictates. 

There is no other area 
within the store where 
the display fixtures have 
more impact on sales 
than the product itself. 
Specialty fixtures are a 
must. 

The combination of 
greeting cards and gifts 
has strong impulse and 
related impulse sales as- 
sociated with it. These 
two departments also en- 
hance jewelry, fragrance 
and candy sales if the 
store is merchandised 
correctly. 

The old philosophy in 
store design was to place 
the card and gift depart- 
ment back in a corner of 
the store to attract cus- 
tomers to that area. To 
be competitive, today’s 
drug store must sell so 
many products at little or 
no gross profit that the 
impulse departments 
need to be highlighted. 
For this reason, the best 
location for cards and 
gifts is in the front of the 
store, where it will re- 
ceive maximum visibility.

Montini takes Revco logistics post 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Chain drug merchandising 
veteran Tony Montini has taken the new position of 
divisional director of replenishment at Revco D.S. 
Montini took the post after serving briefly as vice 
president of merchandise administration for F&M 
Distributors. 


Pharmhouse to buy closeout chain 


NEW YORK — S.E. Nichols’ Pharmhouse chain of 
off-price drug stores has signed a letter of intent to ac- 
quire the All For A Dollar chain, which operates 168 re- 
tail closeout stores in the Northeast. 

The chain said the merger would allow the 15-store 
Pharmhouse to capitalize on economies of scale in gen- 
eral merchandise and to broaden the chain’s import, 
closeout seasonal and general merchandise offerings. 


Chains link with PCS mail order 


SCOTTSDALE, Ariz. — PCS has partnered with the 
American Association of Retired Persons (AARP), Wal- 
green Co. and Thrift Drug for the initial launch of its 
new mail-order operation, called Managed Mail Order. 

The AARP will serve as a “private label” supplier of 
pharmacy services as will Walgreens, which has an ex- 
tensive mail-order division called Healthcare Plus. 
Thrift Drug’s Express Pharmacy Services mail-order 
unit will also provide fulfillment services for PCS. 


Krelitz, Commons Bros. to merge 


MINNEAPOLIS — Wholesaler Krelitz Industries 
Inc.’s shareholders have approved an agreement to 
merge with New York-based Commons Bros. Inc. But 
Commons Bros., which has agreed to purchase Krelitz 
Industries for $5.1 million, has requested that the 
closing date be extended from April 30 to June 30. 

Meanwhile, Commons Bros.’ deal to acquire Secau- 
cus, N.J.-based wholesaler Drug Guild may be in jeop- 
ardy, said industry sources. 


Arbor promotes two to key posts 


TROY, Mich. — Arbor Drugs has promoted two vet- 
eran managers to new positions that reflect the com- 
pany’s growth as a regional powerhouse. 

Nineteen-year Arbor veteran Eric Bolokofsky has 
been promoted to senior vice president of merchandis- 
ing after serving as vice president in the same capaci- 
ty. Carol Bugdalski has been named vice president of 
pharmacy operations, and will oversee all pharmacy- 
related activities. 


F&M beefs up with appointments 


WARREN, Mich. — F&M Distributors is injectin 
new management muscle into its customer service an 
advertising programs with two new appointments. 

Diane Pattison, former director of field auditing and 
training for the off-price drug chain, has been promoted 
to assistant vice president of associate development. 
Kevin Ball has been promoted to director of advertising. 


Shoppers boosts Rx management 


TORONTO — Adding to its health services mar- 
keting strength, Shoppers Drug Mart has named 
Aubrey Browne vice president of pharmacy services 
and Martin Belitz vice president of pharmacy mar- 
keting and operations. ; 

Browne’s main role will be to maintain communica- 
tions with third-party os age Belitz will oversee and 


coordinate all aspects of pharmacy marketing.

F&M taking steps to put ‘tough year’ behind it 


by James Frederick 


WARREN, Mich. — Beset by a 
hard-to-shake string of disappoint- 
ing sales and earnings results, F&M 
Distributors is fighting back with a 
broad range of initiatives whose 
long-term effect will be to reinvent 
many aspects of its business. 

F&M reported significant declines 
in both sales and earnings for the 
fiscal year ended Jan. 29. Net in- 
come dropped to $5.8 million from 
$10.3 million the previous year, and 
sales dipped 6 percent. In the fourth 
quarter, earnings slid from $4.5 
million the prior year to $1.7 mil- 
lion, while sales were off 1.6 percent 
to $186.9 million. 

Same-store sales results were 
also disappointing, down 5 percent 
for both the fourth quarter and fis- 
cal year. Higher occupancy costs 
dragged down fourth-quarter gross 
margins—to 19.5 percent of sales 
vs. 20.2 percent the previous year— 
despite higher margins on merchan- 
dise sales. 


F&M president and chief execu- 
tive Earl Weissert warned that 
first-quarter results would also be 
down, with same-store sales expect- 
ed to decline further and an antici- 

ated loss of roughly $3 million to 
4 million. 

Other factors behind the expected 
loss include a further decline in 
margins due to lower levels of deal 
buying vs. everyday fill-in buying, 
higher occupancy costs for new 
stores and higher debt costs from 
the issue last year of high-interest, 
unsecured senior subordinated debt. 


A strong course 


“It’s a tough year,” Weissert ac- 
knowledged. But in an exclusive in- 
terview with Drug Store News, 
F&M’s chief executive said the com- 
pany has embarked on a strong 
course to restore sales and profit 
momentum and to position itself as 
a far more efficient and disciplined 
retailer. 

“Price is our hallmark and will re- 
main our hallmark, but we have to 
get better with our in-stocks, and 


we have to become more efficient,” 
said Weissert, who replaced former 
chief executive Frank Newman as 
head of the 121-store off-price drug 
chain last year when Newman left 
to join Eckerd Drug. “The key is to 
drive sales because as you drive 
sales, you lower your costs as a per- 
centage of sales.” 

F&M has taken several steps to 
stimulate customer traffic, Weissert 
said. One has been to focus more 
sharply on the health care end of 
the business in order to boost cus- 
tomer store visits and OTC sales 
and to enhance the chain’s health 
care image. To that end, the chain 
installed new pharmacy depart- 
ments in 17 stores early this year 
and is watching results as it con- 
templates a rollout in the 27 stores 
without pharmacies. 

“We believe very strongly in the 
health care part of the coin. We 
know it will help us from a sales 
standpoint, and we think it will also 
help from a margin standpoint,” 
Weissert told Drug Store News. 

F&M is also overhauling its mer- 


chandise mix, pulling away from 
some bulky GM items that do noth- 
ing to enhance its health and beau- 
ty care image—particularly cate- 
gories like pet supplies, infant foods 
and housewares, which are under 
competitive assault by other trade 
classes. Said Weissert, “We pulled 
some [GM] SKUs out. We’re being 
more careful and sophisticated 
about the mix. With items like pet 
foods and pet supplies, we know we 
can’t be a category-killer.” 


Smaller, with more services 


One result may be a downsizing 
of the prototype. “We think we can 
get smaller as we get more efficient” 
with merchandise and with invento- 
ry control, Weissert said. 

F&M is also trying to lure cus- 
tomers with additional services 
and more high-demand products. 
“The key is to get the customer to 
make that extra trip, so we’re look- 
ing at the categories that are more 
efficient for us to handle and that 
customers shop more often,” said 

Continued on page 144

Drug stores, 


Like the chess game we chose as 
the visual image on the cover, 1993 
was a year defined by the strategic 
moves taking place within the indus- 
try. But the real story for drug stores 
in 1993 wasn’t about winning and los- 
ing; it was, literally, about “how you 
play the game.” 

When you look at the results of 
1993, you might at first think it was a 
“quiet” year: A virtually flat—up 1.3 
percent—market. Only a handful of 
double-digit spikes or dips in the sales 


Its your move now 


drug channel slipped just 2 percent in 
front-end sales in 1993, from $41 bil- 
lion to $40 billion. But in critical HBA 
categories—core businesses for drug 
stores—mass merchants surged: up 21 
percent in cosmetics, up 24 percent in 
hand & body lotions, up 17 percent in 
shampoos, up 34 percent in suntan 
products, up 43 percent in vitamins, up 
30 percent in cough/cold/sinus, up 22 
percent in internal analgesics. All these 
gains convert to greater market share 
for mass merchants at the expense of 
drug stores.

compete head on with the likes of

The official party line at NACDS is 
that the new organization — Pharma-

board is likely to 
be dominated by

Among other things, the PDN board

The trend is accelerating in 1994 
with PayLess and Thrifty combining to 
form a dominant West Coast force, 
while a merger of Revco and HSI would 
create a 2,371-store powerhouse span- 
ning 25 Middle and Eastern states. 

@ Managed care is unquestionably 
changing the rules of the game, no 
matter how the national health care 
reform question is settled. In addition 
to taking on pharmaceutical manufac- 
turers in federal court for price dis- 
crimination—another volley in the 
war with mail-order firms—chains 
scrambled in 1993 to get themselves 
into the game of big third-party con- 
tracts, hoping volume will make up for 
the huge sacrifice in pharmaceutical 
profit margins. 

The managed care arena, again, fa- 
vors the large and lean players, and it 
intensely magnifies the pressure on 
independents and small to midsize 
chains. PDN, the Pharmacy Direct 
Network being unveiled at the NACDS 
Annual Meeting this week, may help 
balance the scales for smaller drug re- 
tailers, but at this point the new entity 


is yet another huge unknown in the. 


managed care world. 

There are a lot of unknowns, but we 
hope this Annual Report issue—which 
we have refined and redesigned this 
year—will give you some of the hard 
data you need as you formulate a 
game plan for 1994 and beyond. 

It’s a different game, but it’s got the 
same bottom line—win or lose. 

And it’s your move! 


Additionally, the directors of the 
network will be limited in their ability 
to share information concerning the 
terms and conditions of contracts with 
prescription drug insurers and payors. 

Similarly, the participating PDN 
pharmacies will be insulated from po- 
tential antitrust problems by the un- 
usual organizational structure of the 
new company — a “for-profit, non- 
stock corporation” with “no owners.” 

Antitrust considerations also 
prompted the framers of PDN to re- 
quire participating member pharma- 
cies to accept all contract terms nego- 
tiated by network staffers, sight 
unseen. 

Members of the network “cannot opt 
in and out of contracts and must ac- 
cept all contracts executed by PDN,” 
NACDS explained. “To remain com- 
petitive while avoiding antitrust con- 
cerns, PDN will not consult member 
pharmacies prior to preparing a re- 
sponse or executing a contract with a 

plan sponsor. 

NACDS legal experts believe these 
provisions will create an antitrust fire- 
wall that should insulate the associa- 
tion and participating pharmacies from 
charges of price fixing, bid-rigging or 
other anticompetitive behavior. 

But they may also render member- 
ship in PDN less attractive for drug 
chain executives and independent 
pharmacists accustomed to making 
business decisions with their eyes 
open.

A year of subtle, smart progress 


ike many other segments of 

the retail universe, the 

chain drug industry is greet- 

ing 1994 with the vast ma- 
jority of its power in the hands of a 
small universe of players. And with 
two major mergers already in the 
works this year, that power base is 
sure to become even more compact. 

Together, the 50 chains in Drug 

Store News’ annual ranking of the 
leading chain drug retailers rang up 
sales of $50 billion in 1993, repre- 
senting 91 percent of the $55-billion 
industry’s volume. Although the 
sales among 1992’s top 50 chains, at

$49 billion, totaled slightly less 
than 1993’s, the leading players in 
1992 actually commanded a larger 
share of the market—94 percent. 

Three names from last year’s list 
have disappeared in the continua- 
tion of acquisition/merger fever: Re- 
liable Stores, Standard Drug and 
Bill’s. And ALP/Freddy’s was liqui- 
dated after all efforts to sell off the 
bankrupt chain failed. 

After the Indianapolis-based re- 
tailer’s late-1992 bankruptcy filing, 
the Reliable name disappeared from 
the landscape as most of its 265 
units were sold off to American 
Drug, Rite Aid and other competi- 
tors. Standard Drug of Richmond, 
Va., was acquired by CVS, which 
also picked up nine-unit Austin 
Drug in Long Island, N.Y., and 10 
units from Fay’s Drug in southeast- 
ern Pennsylvania. Bill’s of Benecia, 
Calif., was acquired by neighboring 
Longs Drug in September. 


Only just begun to merge 


However, in retrospect, 1993 is 
starting to look like it was a stable 
year for chain drug stores. None of 
the top 20 players was involved in a 
major merger or acquisition, and 
not one cf the top 25 declared bank- 
ruptcy (although No. 10, Phar-Mor, 
remains under Chapter 11 protec- 
tion following its 1992 filing). 

The two major mergers that are 
already in the works in the first 
four months of 1994 eclipse all of 
1993’s activity put together. 

By the end of this month, TCH 
Corp. is expected to complete its ac- 


Drug Store News, April 25, 1994 


quisition of Wilsonville, Ore.-based 
PayLess from Kmart. TCH will 
merge Thrifty Corp., which it ac- 
quired in mid-1992, with PayLess to 
form a West Coast drug retailing 
powerhouse with more than 1,000 
stores and estimated combined 
sales of $4.7 billion for ’94. 

But the race for the No. 2 spot is 
looking like a dead heat. Earlier this 
month, Revco D.S. and HSI, the par- 
ent of Hook’s, SupeRx and Brooks, 
announced a merger agreement of 
their own. If that deal, which is siat- 
ed to be finalized this summer, goes 
through, the new chain will have 
2,371 stores in 25 states; combined 
sales for Revco D.S. and HSI for the 
most recent 12 months have also 
been estimated at $4.7 billion. 


Moves beneath the surface 


While 1993 might have appeared 
to be a “quiet” year in terms of ma- 
jor retailer news stories, the key 
drug chain retailers made signifi- 
cant progress on many fronts. 

Financially, for instance, several 
chains reported success in bringing 
down operating costs, a key issue in 
an environment where competitive 
“leanness” is becoming essential. 

At American Drug Stores, for ex- 
ample, operating and administra- 
tive expenses were 22.2 percent of 
sales in the last quarter of fiscal 
1993, compared with 22.6 percent of 
the same period a year earlier. At 
Longs Drug Stores, gross margins 
improved from 24.7 percent to 25.5 
percent in fiscal year 1994. At 
Revco, the restructuring that was 
initiated during the chain’s four- 
year bankruptcy enabled it to triple 
its net earnings to $12.5 million in 
the third quarter of fiscal 1994. 

For drug chains, which have 
tended to lag other retail channels 
in their adoption of automated re- 
tail technologies, installation of 


stores scanning. 

For HSI, the largest chain that is 
still not scanning, the proposed 
merger with Revco will provide a 
huge boost. While HSI had planned 
to start testing its first POS system 
in July, with full rollout by 1996, 
Revco chief executive D. Dwayne 
Hoven told DrSN that Revco plans 
a rapid rollout of its own POS sys- 
tem and pharmacy computer net- 
work into acquired stores. 

Drug chains also made efforts to 
capitalize on their convenient loca- 
tions by adding or expanding conve- 
nience-oriented services. A number 
of chains, including Snyder Drug, 
began offering package and mail 
services to customers. 

Other chains expanded one-hour 
photo concepts, also in a bid to be 
responsive to customers’ need for 
speed and convenience. For exam- 
ple, Eckerd, with more than 400 Ex- 
press Photo departments, plans to 
add another 60 units this year. 

Convenience is also the reason 
behind CVS’ expansion of its 24- 
hour stores—to a total of 57—ac- 
cording to CVS president and chief 
executive Thomas Ryan, who stat- 
ed: “The 24-hour stores really rein- 
force our corporate strategy, to be 
the best at providing convenience, 
value and service.” 

Drive-up pharmacy windows are 
yet another convenience that more 
drug chains are offering, from Med- 
icap Pharmacies, which includes 
the feature as a core aspect of its 
pharmacy-oriented franchise stores, 
to Revco, which has installed drive- 
through windows at six locations 
and plans to add more. 

If any one theme held true in 
1993, it was “stay true to your core 
business.” 

When there were acquisitions, 
they were drug chains buying drug 
stores—to fill in existing markets

@ Annual Report | RETAILER OVERVIEW 


oundaries that once distin- 
guished drug stores from 
discount stores and super- 


markets continued to disap- 
pear in 1993, as non-drug retailers 
expanded and nurtured their phar- 
macy and HBA businesses. 

While drug stores, for the most 
part, held their ground in key prod- 
uct categories, mass merchants saw 
the largest gains last year. 

In pharmacy sales, drug stores 

ained 5.5 percent, increasing from 
€36 billion to $38 billion, according 
to IMS America/DDD Division. 
However, mass merchants, includ- 
ing Wal-mart, Kmart and Target, 
increased their pharmacy sales 
from $5.0 billion to $5.8 billion, for 
a jump of 16 percent, and super- 
markets, with sales increasing from 
$5.0 billion to $5.7 billion, gained 
14 percent. 


-Non-drug stores with Rxs 


In terms of number of pharma- 
cies, mass merchandisers now place 
in two out of the top five slots. 

Wal-Mart overtook Kmart for the 
No. 1 spot among mass merchandis- 
ers in 1993. Wal-Mart operated 
1,776 pharmacies at the end of 
1993, a 17 percent increase over the 
1,520 it ran in 1992. Wal-Mart is 
now the third-largest operator of re- 
tail pharmacies in the nation after 
Rite Aid and Walgreen. 

Kmart, with 1,648 pharmacies, 
added 34 pharmacy units in 1993; 
Kmart is now the fifth-largest re- 
tail pharmacy operator in number 
of units, after Eckerd Drug, which 
is fourth. 

While growth in pharmacy units 
among supermarket/combo stores is 
less dramatic, several supermarket 
chains expanded considerably in 
1993. 

Cub Foods had the largest per- 
centage gain in terms of units with 
pharmacy, more than doubling its 
pharmacies from 41 to 86. Winn- 
Dixie added the greatest number of 
units, 64, going from 161 pharma- 
cies in 1992 to 225 last year. 


Other core drug categories 


As they expanded their pharma- 
cies, both mass merchants and su- 
permarket companies have also 
paid greater attention to the other 
components of the “drug store” 


within their stores, and they have 
continued to make inroads into 
HBA categories— often at the ex- 
pense of drug stores. 

For example, for the OTC/health 
care category, as tracked by Infor- 
mation Resources Inc. (IRI), mass 
merchants’ sales totalled $5.26 bil- 
lion in 1993, for an increase of 24 
percent over 1992’s $4.25 billion. 
For the same category, supermar- 
kets gained 4 percent, from $8.3 bil- 
lion to $8.6 billion. Drug stores, 
meanwhile, gained only 2 percent in 
a growing market. 

The news was even worse in cos- 
metics, where drug stores showed a 
6 percent decline in sales, while su- 
permarkets gained 2 percent in 
sales, and mass merchants in- 
creased by 21 percent, albeit on a 
smaller base. 

And competition will continue to 
heat up as operators within each 
distribution channel seek to make 
gains at the expense of those in 
other channels. For example, many 
supermarkets —including Vons, 
Jewel-Osco and Smiths Food & 
Drug—are gearing up to compete 
with warehouse clubs by creating 
club-like stores or departments of 
their own. 

Price competition between super- 
markets has also led to highly ad- 
vertised price wars; Lucky’s and 
Vons, for example, have been focus- 
ing the public on price as they have 
been slugging it out in Southern 
California. 


Wal-Mart sets pace 


Although competitive wars con- 
tinue to go on within and between 
channels, the largest single compet- 
itive force remains Wal-Mart. 

While Wal-Mart president and 
chief executive officer David Glass 
called 1993 a “difficult retailing 
year,” the nation’s No. 1 retailer’s 
sales increased 21 percent from 
$55.5 billion to $67.4 billion. Its 
store count of 2,021 included 68 Su- 
percenter stores and 419 Sam’s 
Clubs, including units acquired 
with the purchase of Pace Member- 
ship Warehouse from Kmart. 

This year, Wal-Mart plans to 
open 125 new stores in the United 
States, many of which, as per the 
chain’s current philosophy, will in- 
clude pharmacies.

Walgreens poised for health reform 


by James Frederick 


EERFIELD, Ill. — Wal- 
green Co.’s leaders think 
the industry’s premier drug 
chain is ready for whatever 
changes health care reform can 
throw at it. Said chairman and chief 
executive officer Charles R. Wal- 
green III early this year, “I believe 
Walgreens has the ability to take 
full advantage of health care re- 
form, in whatever shape it takes.” 

Making good on that prediction, 
Walgreens is strongly pursuing new 
pharmacy business by marketing its 
prescription-delivery capabilities 
aggressively to third-party man- 
aged care programs. The company 
has several advantages as it posi- 
tions itself for health care reform, 
Walgreen said. Among them: 

e A national, interconnected 
store presence with “a huge patient 
retail base.” 

@ Extensive regional store concen- 
trations in many major markets, 
“which is what those growing third- 
party plans often want for their con- 
stituents,” the chairman said. 

@ The most technologically ad- 
vanced systems in drug retailing, by 
all accounts. Those systems — includ- 
ing a powerful, interactive pharma- 
cy system, chainwide satellite com- 
munications and sophisticated 
inventory control capabilities— give 
the chain a powerful edge in third- 
party marketing and cost control. 

@ The company’s own, rapidly 
growing pharmacy mail-service 
business, called Walgreens Health- 
care Plus. The mail-order division 
more than doubled its sales in 1993 
to roughly $50 million, according to 
the company, and should double 
sales again this year, Walgreen not- 
ed. Among its recently signed pre- 
scription clients: B.F. Goodrich, 
Sara Lee, 3M and Motorola. 

To handle that growth, the com- 
pany will open a new, larger mail- 
order center in Tempe, Ariz. in Sep- 
tember. The Tempe site will be able 
to fill 7,500 scripts by mail a day, 
and will be expandable to 15,000 a 
day, according to the company. 

This is all to the good, according 
to company officials. Said Walgreen 
president and chief operating offi- 
cer Dan Jorndt in an interview 
with Drug Store News early this 
month, “I think managed care is 
coming, with or without govern- 
ment intervention.” 


Pharmacy still the lynchpin 


Walgreens’ efforts in managed 
care underscore its determined 
quest to avoid complacency. And 
thus far, at least, its deeply rooted 
pursuit of excellence at every level 
continues to yield an enviable 
track record. 

By any measure, Walgreens has 
become a force to be reckoned with 
among the nation’s top retail chains 
of any kind, and on Wall Street. Its 
$8.3 billion in 1993 sales make it 
the 17th largest retailer in the 
United States, according to Fortune 
as well as the undisputed heavy- 
weight champ of its own trade class. 
Inc'eed, Walgreens’ pharmacy busi- 


? 


ness alone—topping $3 billion last 
year— would earn it a place among 
the top-grossing drug chains. 

Strategically, said Walgreens’ 
leaders, pharmacy remains the 
lynchpin. Script sales were up 15.7 
percent in dollars last year, despite 
the slowdown in drug price inflation, 
and pharmacy now accounts for 
nearly 40 percent of total sales, said 
Walgreen. And so far, the chain’s 
new operating efficiencies, pharmacy 
marketing network, growing mail-or- 
der business and rising script vol- 
umes have allowed net profits to out- 
pace the tighter script margins. 

Walgreens has now notched 19 
consecutive years of record sales 
and earnings; its aggressive growth 
plan has made it the No. 1 or 2 drug 
chain in 34 of the nation’s 100 
biggest drug store markets. 

On paper, the chain’s formula for 
success seems simple enough. Wal- 
greens’ current success stems from 
two decades of disciplined adher- 
ence to tried-and-true principles of 
drug store retailing— mixed with a 
willingness to plow a big share of its 
profits back into the business, year 
after year. Add to that a corporate 
culture that encourages flexibility 
in adapting to shifting consumer de- 
mand and a determination to grow 
stores only in the most promising 
locations, and one has the makings 
for consistent leadership. 


Strategic goals 


Jorndt laid out Walgreens’ basic 
strategy at its annual shareholders’ 
meeting early this year. “No. 1, 
were staying very, very close to 
everyday business; we’re minding 
our stores. Second, we’re pouring 
profits right back into our company. 
Third, we’re testing, experimenting, 
taking risks— probably more than 
at any time since the early years of 
our company.” 

Walgreen executives make it 
sound simple enough. But in retail, 
of course, it’s the execution that 
separates winners from losers. 

“Customers are telling us this is 
the program they want: attractive, 
convenient, inviting and quick-to- 
shop stores,” said Walgreen. “[They] 
want quality merchandise— more 
quickly, more economically and more 


Walgreens at a glance 


Company name: Walgreen Co. 
Headquarters: Deerfield, Ill. 
Officers: Charles R. Walgreen III, 
chairman/ceo; L. Daniel Jorndt, 
president/coo; Charles Hunter, vice 
chairman/cfo; Vernon Brt.aner, ex- 
ecutive vp-marketing; Glenn Kraiss, 
executive vp-store operations. 
Sales: $8.3 billion (fiscal 1993, 
ended Aug. 31, 1993). 

Store count: 1,803. 

Average store size: 9,700 square 
feet (selling space). 

Markets: Coast to coast. 
Highlights: Net sales smash $8 
billion mark; 149 new stores 
added; 19th consecutive year of 
record sales and earnings; chain 
enters Indianapolis and prepares 
to enter Cleveland and Buffalo. 


conveniently—than they ever have 
before. They'll shop the retailers who 
deliver, and neglect the rest.” 

Walgreens is obviously deter- 
mined to deliver. Over the past five 
years, the chain has poured $840 
million into new and remodeled 
stores, new distribution centers and 
retail technology. It will spend an- 
other $300 million this year. 

“In addition to new stores and 
major technology improvements, 
this money will go toward the new 
pharmacy mail-service facility...and 
a new, $60 million distribution cen- 
ter near Sacramento, Calif., that 
will help supply our growing West- 
ern store base,” Walgreen said. 


Walgreens opened another 149 stores around the United States last year; in 
1994, it plans to open 175 more new stores and remodel an additional 100. 


Walgreens’ overall strategy re- 
mains the same, said Jorndt: to “in- 
crease coverage in existing and new 
markets, with the eventual goal of 
covering the entire U.S.” Along those 
lines, the chain opened another 149 
stores around the United States in 
’93—19 more than projected—and 
pushed store count to 1,836 drug 
stores and 14 RxPress pharmacy 
outlets in 30 states and Puerto Rico. 
Among those units: its first stores in 
Indianapolis and Spokane, Wash. 

Plans this year call for another 
175 new stores and 100 major re- 
models. New units will include 20 
rapid-fire openings in the Cleve- 
land/Akron area before Christmas — 
putting Walgreens into that region 
for the first time since the 1930s— 
as well as its first stores in Buffalo 
and the first units in Grand Rapids, 
Mich. and Green Bay, Wisc. 

Walgreens is also laying the 
groundwork to enter two more as 
yet unnamed major markets in the 
next year or two, Jorndt told DrSN. 

Quick fill-in growth is also 
planned for California’s Central Val- 
ley and Florida, as well as for inner- 
city neighborhoods nationwide. “By 
1996, one year ahead of schedule, 
Walgreens plans to be cutting rib- 
bons for 200 new stores a year,” said 
Walgreen. The goal remains 3,000 
units by the curn of the century. 

“We’re challenging ourselves with 
this expansion, really pushing our 
people to new productivity levels,” 
Jorndt added. “i'his much growth 
impacts our profits, too; it’s expen- 
sive. But we're hitting home runs 
with these stores—their sales are 
above projections.”

American Drug hones its edge 


by James Frederick 


ALT LAKE CITY — An ex- 

panding share in key West- 

ern and Southwestern mar- 

kets. An award-winning new 
store prototype in rapid rollout. A 
growing technological edge. An ag- 
gressive store remodeling cam- 
paign. Improving profitability. 

These are the milestones in 

American Drug Stores’ long-run- 
ning campaign to boost its sales and 
profit momentum and its strategic 
focus. And despite some bumps in 
the road along the way—shrinking 
pharmacy margins, a flattened-out 
growth curve in operating profits 
and modest, 2 percent same-store 
sales gains were the biggest of those 
hurdles last year—that campaign 
has worked remarkably well. 


American Drug won three Drug Store News REX (Retail EXcellence) awards 
last fall, including the Large Chain of the Year Award. 


American Drug is far leaner, more 
focused and more technologically ad- 
vanced than it was a few years ago, 
and the chain is in a strong position 
to run the gauntlet of 90s retailing. 
Among the reasons why: 

@ Parent company American 
Stores has restructured and low- 
ered its debt, allowing it to boost 
capital spending in its food and 
drug store networks for store ex- 
pansion and renovation and for re- 
tail technology. By the end of this 
fiscal year, the retail giant will have 
spent $2 billion over the past three 
years for those improvements. 

e The drug store division has 
been under stable management for 
more than four years under presi- 
dent and chief executive Dave Ma- 
her and a team of mostly veteran 
operations, merchandising, market- 
ing and logistics managers. 

@ American Drug is out of unprof- 
itable markets like Dallas/Ft. Worth, 
which were a drag on earnings and a 
distraction to management until 
1992. Instead, the company’s Osco 
and Sav-on divisions are growing 
market share in Southern Califor- 
nia, Arizona and Midwestern states 
like Indiana and Illinois. 

The growth is coming both from 
new-store development and from ac- 
quisitions. In the past two years, for 
instance, the company has added big 
blocks of stores to its roster through 


32 Drug Store News, April 25, 1994 


acquisition, including the takeover 
of 55 former Reliable drug stores 
last year in Kansas, Illinois, Mis- 
souri and Indiana. That purchase 
came on the heels of other major ac- 
quisitions the prior year when 
American added 63 former CVS 
stores to its roster in greater Los 
Angeles, as well as 21 former Rx- 
Plus units and nine former Thrifty 
stores in Nevada and Arizona. 

In all, the company opened or ac- 
quired 84 stores last year and 
closed or sold 38 older units, boost- 
ing combined store count for Osco 
and Sav-on to 787 units by the end 
of the fiscal year on Jan. 29, 1994. 
The company also remodeled anoth- 
er 137 drug stores. 

@ The rollout of the “Vision” store 
prototype has accelerated, with 
more than 150 new and remodeled 
stores now sporting the new, down- 
sized format, according to Steve 
Mannschreck, executive vice presi- 
dent and chief operating officer of 
Osco Drug. The stores feature grad- 
uated-height gondolas front-to-back 
for easier visibility of departments, 
as well as a roomier interior with 
wider aisles, easy-to-find perimeter 
departments set off by their own 
colors, full nutrition/health and con- 
venience foods centers, and strik- 
ing, more attractive graphics. Vi- 
sion store designers also enlarged 
the pharmacy area and gave it a 
more prominent location at the 
front of the store, often with a pa- 
tient waiting lounge. 

Vision stores also reflect the com- 
pany’s effort to refocus its merchan- 
dise mix. The stores feature a 
broader, denser mix of key core cat- 
egories like HBA, cosmetics/fra- 
grances, OTCs, photo supplies and 
convenience foods, and less empha- 
Sis on non-core and slower-turning 
items like automotive, electrical 
supplies, housewares or household 
chemicals. By shifting away from 
non-core merchandise, Vision’s 
planners were also able to boost 
turns in the new and remodeled 
units, with sales growii in newly 
remodeled stores showing double- 
digit gains in most markets, accord- 
ing to American Drug executives. 

e@ Automation and information 
systems have injected better infor- 
mation-based decision-making into 
many facets of the business. Func- 
tions like buying, billing, advertis- 
ing, planograming and distribution 
are becoming more closely aligned 
with real consumer demand as they 
are linked to POS scanning data 
through satellite communications. 

“Competitive forces continue to 
force gross margins downward, and 
this trend is expected to continue 
throughout the ’90s,” Maher told 
Drug Store News recently. “Addition- 
ally, our consumers’ values over the 
past years have changed. Today, our 
consumer seeks value and price.” 

For those reasons, he said, “Drug 
stores of the 90s must invest in the 
most updated and modern technolo- 
gy in order to achieve more efficien- 
cies and lower-cost operations.” 

American Drug has delivered on 
that mandate by upgrading its phar- 
macy and in-store computer systems

Eckerd trims debt, ups Rx sales 


by Mike Troy 


LEARWATER, Fla. — A 

stock ticker in the cafeteria 

at Eckerd Corp. headquar- 

ters continuously displays 
the retailer’s share price. It’s up 
over $20 these days, a 43 percent 
increase from the August initial 
public offering price of $14 and a 
visible indicator of the chain’s ac- 
complishments during 1993 and its 
bullish outlook for 1994. 

Sales topped the $4 billion mark 
for the first time during the fiscal 
year ended Jan. 29, 1994. Led by 
pharmacy sales growth of 14.5 per- 
cent and same-store sales growth of 
6.3 percent, Eckerd’s total sales in- 
creased 7.8 percent from the previ- 
ous year’s sales of nearly $3.9 billion. 

Along with a successful IPO, a 
massive $950 million debt restruc- 
turing package helped reduce annu- 
al interest expenses by about $40 
million and improved the company’s 
financial flexibility. Another $70 
million was saved as a result of an 
overhead reduction and restructur- 
ing program that began in the fall 
of 1992. Further savings were 
achieved later in the year when 
$200 million in bonds, priced at 9.25 
percent, were issued to redeem 
bonds at higher interest levels. 

“Eckerd is a company with a 
great future that is very well-posi- 
tioned in the industry, with a 
tremendous cadre of professionals 
able to take advantage of the con- 
solidation that is still likely to occur 
in the chain drug industry,” said 
Frank Newman, president and chief 
operating officer. 


Technological milestones 


Many of Eckerd’s most significant 
accomplishments during the previous 
year were of a financial nature, and 
they helped it get a grip on a debt 
burden that had been siphoning off 
profits since the retailer’s 1986 LBO. 
The coming year is shaping up to be 
one of technological advancement for 
the chain. A 10-year technology 
agreement, ranging from $320 mil- 
lion to $440 million, with IBM sub- 
sidiary Integrated Systems Solutions 
Corp., is helping Eckerd rapidly up- 
grade pharmacy systems and auto- 
mate stores with POS equipment 
that. will aid decision-making and po- 
sition it for the future. 

“We have some significant devel- 
opments technologically this year,” 
said Newman, who joined Eckerd in 
July after serving as president and 
chief executive officer at F&M Dis- 
tributors Inc. Two of the largest un- 
dertakings will include the installa- 
tion of POS equipment in 530 stores 
and a satellite network that allows 
pharmacies to communicate with 
one another and serve as a link for 
the transmission of POS data. Even- 
tually, all Eckerd stores will have 
scanning equipment and be connect- 
ed to each other via satellite. 

“No matter which Eckerd your 
pharmacy file is at, you will be able 
to go to another Eckerd and get 
your prescription refilled,” Newman 
said of the new system. 


As is the case industry-wide, phar- 
macy sales at the chain are increas- 
ingly accounting for a larger percent- 
age of total sales. For the recently 
ended fiscal year, 46.3 percent of 
Eckerd sales came from pharmacy, 
compared to 45.5 percent the previ- 
ous year. The trend toward a larger 
percentage of those sales coming 
from third party is also continuing. 

“Third party right now is around 
60 percent, and on its own, it would 
certainly get into the 75 percent 
range within the next relatively few 
years. With the added impetus of 
health care reform, it could eventu- 
ally be 95 percent,” Newman said. 

“Our best indication at this point 
is that health care reform will sim- 
ply accelerate the change in the per- 
centage of business that is done by 
managed care programs as opposed 
to cash, and it will increase overall 
the prescription volume by virtue of 
extending coverage to those who 
don’t have it,” he said. 

“I think advanced systems will be 
the standard, and we already have 
them, so it’s not an issue as far as 
were concerned, but it further im- 
pacts the independents who now 
have another technological obstacle 
to overcome in addition to all the 
other hurdles,” he continued. 

One of the hurdles for drug chains 
is the lower pharmacy margins of- 
fered by third-party payors. “We rec- 
ognize (lower pharmacy margins) 
are a fact of life, and as a company, 
we've taken the steps required to 
streamline our processes, and we be- 
lieve the investments we have made 
in technology will make us more effi- 
cient,” he added. “All of these things 
enable us to run the business on a 
more efficient basis and generate a 
healthy bottom line. Our margins 
are lower than they’ve ever been, but 
our profits continue to grow.” 

Another point Newman makes 
about Eckerd’s growing pharmacy 
business is that it does not bring 
the same growth in expenses as 
does growth in other areas. 

In addition to pharmacy, the HBA 
and OTC departments are shoulder- 
ing a greater burden for the chain’s 
bottom line.

Rite Aid focuses on pharmacy 


by Barbara White 


AMP HILL, Pa. — Eroding 

pharmacy margins, sluggish 

same store sales and in- 

creased competition made 
1993 a tough year for Rite Aid Cor- 
poration. 

By the end of its fiscal year, the 
chain announced the decision to 
close 200 under-performing stores, 
sell its non-drug store divisions and 
buy back several million shares of 
common stock. 

Rite Aid’s drug store division’s 
sales were $4.09 billion, an increase 
of 6.6 percent over year-earlier sales 
of $3.83 billion. 

The chain, the industry leader in 
units, continued its aggressive store 
expansion program. Rite Aid added 
81 stores, most as new store open- 
ings and 36 as part of its partial ac- 
quisition of the Reliable chain. 


The chain will 
direct energy 
on the managed 
care end of the 
pharmacy 
business 1n 1994 


At a shareholders meeting in July, 
Rite Aid chairman and chief execu- 
tive Alex Grass said the chain’s vast 
number of stores allowed the chain 
to achieve economies of scale and 
greater convenience than many of its 
competitors. 


Costs outpace sales 


The problem was that selling, 
general, and administrative expens- 
es increased faster than sales. 

By the end of the year, the chain 
had decided to close 200 “low vol- 
ume stores that were losing money,” 
according to Rite Aid’s senior vice 
president of finance Frank 
Bergonzi. 

Still, Rite Aid president and chief 
operating officer Martin Grass said 
the move was not an attempt to 
downsize the chain. Grass said Rite 
Aid planned to open 75 new units 
in 1994. 

Many of those will be 8,000 to 
9,000 square feet, an increase in 
space over Rite Aid’s prototype of 
7,700 square feet. The chain is also 
concentrating on opening free- 
standing stores. 


Rollout of POS, satellite system 


Rite Aid’s operating costs were af- 
fected by the cash the chain 
pumped into its operations—in ex- 
cess of $100 million. 

The rollout of its chainwide satel- 
lite system was completed by the 
end of 1993, but it was still too ear- 
ly for the chain to realize any signif- 


icant savings from the system for 
that fiscal year. 

The chain did, however, begin 
teleconferencing its monthly divi- 
sion managers meetings from its in- 
house studio. 

Rite Aid also aggressively contin- 
ued its rollout of POS scanning; 
over 2,300 stores have the system in 
place. The chain is also considering 
a test of a new space-saving system 
that will feature color and sound. 

“Rite Aid’s operating margins are 
higher than anyone’s in the indus- 
try, but they depend on static busi- 
ness conditions that can’t be count- 
ed on in the marketplace anymore,” 
said Gary Vineberg, an analyst for 
Merrill Lynch. “Pharmacy inflation, 
which was once 10 percent, is now 
only 4 percent. And they are com- 
peting against revitalized chains 
such as Revco and Kmart as well as 
strong chains, like Walgreens.” 

Vineberg noted that Rite Aid has 
not been known for a good in-stock 
position or aggressive pricing. 

As Rite Aid faces tougher compe- 
tition from all sides, the chain may 
have to re-examine its position on 
promotional pricing. The chain is al- 
ready considering promotional pric- 
ing when launching new stores. 


New look in cosmetics? 


Rite Aid did address competition 
by experimenting with some format 
changes. In a surprising twist, the 
chain began to bolster cosmetics. 

The test of a cosmetics prototype 
designed for select middle- to high- 
er-income neighborhoods grew from 
one store in fall of 1992 to several 
stores in the Northeast and Mid- 
west by spring of 1993. The proto- 
type set may reach as many as 200 
locations. 

Rite Aid also expanded into de- 
signer fragrances and created its 
first bath boutique, which empha- 
sized premium lines. 

The decision to beef up cosmetics 
was a surprise from a chain, which 
derives 52 percent of its sales from 
prescriptions and concentrates most 
of its marketing efforts on the de- 
partment. Cosmetics had tradition- 
ally been given only 49 feet in Rite 
Aid prototype stores. 

Still, a dalliance with cosmetics 
didn’t divert the chain from its fo-

CVS blankets markets, accents Rx 


by Barbara White 


OONSOCKET, R.I. — 

Acquisitions, the com- 

pletion of the installa- 

tion of chainwide scan- 
ning, a sales boost from the 
Peoples stores and increases in 
prescription and seasonal sales 
contributed to a year of outstand- 
ing earnings for CVS in 1993. 


CVS bought 10 Pennsylvania Fay’s stores in January of last year and all of the 
60 Standard units in October; and it acquired all nine Austin stores in May. 


The chain posted year-end sales 
of $3.95 billion, a 9 percent increase 
over the prior year’s sales of $3.63 
billion. 

CVS has its crew members in 
place for 1994. Thomas Ryan, who 
has been with CVS since 1975 
when he joined the company as a 
pharmacist, took command of the 
division in January 1994 as presi- 
dent and chief operating officer, 
and he was named chief executive 
officer in November. He replaced 
Harvey Rosenthal, who held the 
post for 10 years. Rosenthal has 
been named president and chief op- 
erating officer of CVS’ parent com- 
pany, Melville Corp. CVS also 
named Dan Nelson, a retailing vet- 
eran from the combo store industry, 
as its executive vice president of 
marketing last year. 

They, together with the rest of 
the CVS management team, will 
concentrate on building front-of- 
store sales and leveraging the 
chain’s strong pharmacy franchise. 

“Our goal is to make the front of 
the store a destination for shop- 
pers,” said Ryan. He said the 
chain’s strengths in private label, 
photofinishing and greeting cards, 
for example, will be even more im- 
portant to the chain going forward. 

CVS will also look to destination 
departments, such as professional 
hair care, upscale bath and one-hour 
photofinishing to offset declining 
margins in other parts of the store. 


Growing through acquisition 


CVS, which ended 1993 with 
1,284 stores, actively added new lo- 
cations by acquiring small to mid- 
size chains. 

In January 1993, CVS bought 10 
Fay’s stores in Pennsylvania; ac- 
quired the East Meadow, N.Y.-based

nine-unit Austin chain in May; and 
bought the 60-store, Richmond, Va.- 
based Standard chain in October. 
After closing some locations, CVS 
continues to operate 38 former Stan- 
dard stores under the CVS name. 

“We hold the No. 1 market share 
in 20 of the 29 markets in which we 
operate,” said Ryan. “The purchase 
of Standard, for example, solidified 
our market share in Richmond.” 

That acquisition, said Ryan, was 
seamless for both the chain and its

impact on sales and profits in 1994. 

CVS also announced that it will

about a change,” said Ryan. “From a 
promotional and private-label stand-

under one name chainwide.”

scanning will help the chain tailor

not only make micro-marketing eas- 
ier, it will [also] help us reduce 
markdowns, lower labor costs in our 
stores and warehouses and give us 
a better grasp on promotional activ- 
ity in each market,” said Ryan.

the number of stores which operate 
‘round the clock. At year-end, it op- 
erated 57 24-hour locations and 
hundreds more with extended 
hours. “The 24-hour stores really re- 
inforce our corporate strategy, to be 
the best at providing convenience, 
value and service,” said Ryan. 

“Our normal draw may be every- 
one within a one-mile radius and 
most people in a two-mile radius. At 
night, that draw is strengthened to 
include every customer in a two- 
mile radius and the pull extends to

Longs pursues competitive edge 


by Allene Symons 


ALNUT CREEK, Calif. 

— Longs Drug Stores 

blazed the Western ac- 

quisition trail in the 
third quarter of 1993—three 
months before the PayLess/Thrifty 
handshake—with its acquisition of 
the 20-unit Bill’s Drugs in a deal 
for $12 million in Longs common 
stock and the assumption of some 
liabilities. 

The acquisition of the Bill’s 
chain provided Longs with fill-in 
sites in affluent Northern Califor- 
nia suburbs. The two chains prac- 
ticed similar merchandising strate- 
gies, including prominent 
convenience and promotional foods 
selections. 

The deal marked the chain’s first 
major purchase, aside from some in- 
dependents and single chain loca- 
tions, in an assertive program to 
improve competitiveness and prof- 
itability along with greater third- 
party clout. 

The merger brought Longs to a to- 
tal of 305 stores, and it’s expected to 
enrich the chain with around $82.6 
million in additional sales, based on 
Bill’s previous year results. 


POS progress 


Among the 1993’s achievements 
for the chain, after a two-year roll- 
out, most Longs stores—91 per- 
cent—were on POS by the year- 
end. Early in 1994, some of Bill’s 
stores were integrated into the 
POS system, and eventually, all 
will be included. 

Product-movement information 
is gradually modifying Longs’ tra- 
ditional, decentralized system as 
departments like photo and elec- 
tronics, and cosmetics and bath 
are being reshaped. The chain in- 
tends to use its POS data to bene- 
fit from the product mix reflecting 
both the regional and local promo- 
tion opportunities. 

Store-specific marketing is still 
central to the Longs philosophy, as 
the expanded chain shifts gears to 
integrate turn and inventory level 
information from its scan data, 
while at the same time, empower- 
ing its store managers to take ad- 
vantage of local opportunities and 
respond quickly to competitive 
pricing. 

As part of its expanded informa- 
tion systems, Longs entered an on- 
going electronic data interchange 
(EDI) arrangement with McKesson 
and Bergen Brunswig. The paper- 
less communications strategy re- 
portedly works well with store au- 
tonomy as each store can set stock 
parameters and achieve quicker 
turnaround. 


Battling a difficult economy 


Despite inventory-decision advan- 
tages gained by the rollout of its 
POS system, Longs experienced a 
0.4 percent decline in net income 
compared to the previous year. This 
was largely due to continuing nega- 
tive economic conditions in Califor- 
nia and Hawaii, where the majority 
of the chain’s stores are located. 


In 1993 California continued to 
suffer from high unemployment, 
largely from the defense industry 
closures. 

Chainwide, gross margins im- 
proved from 24.7 percent to 25.5 in 
fiscal year 1994. Longs pharmacy 
sales rose from 27 percent of total 
sales to 29 percent with 63 percent 
in third party, up from 60 percent. 


A different design approach 


In another competitive strategy, 
Longs unveiled a new, state-of-the 
art store 30 miles north of Los An- 
geles in the affluent suburb of 
Thousand Oaks. 

Longs also opened an upscale 
one-of-a-kind store in the Fashion 
Island mall in Newport Beach, 
Calif., making its second mall-spe- 
cific store design (the other is in 
San Diego’s Horton Plaza). 

While the Thousand Oaks store 
features the most advanced design 
in the Longs Drug Stores chain, the 
retailer does not consider this a pro- 
totype. However, the design points 
toward a retail environment with a 
greater sense of decor and visual 
merchandising than is typical for 
the chain. 

The store also marks Longs’ first 
modified, 45-degree-angle store lay- 
out featuring diagonally positioned 
cosmetics and photo and electronics 
departments. 

Other features in the store in- 
clude a new bath set with custom- 
designed, island fixtures. Lower 
gondolas make the store appear 
more open than a typical Longs 
store. Wider aisles and the angled 
floor layout result in some loss of 
display space and slightly tighter 
inventory. 


New directions

der Longs, signs were changed, and 
the Bill’s chain began operating un- 
der the Long’s name. 

The Bill’s stores, which range 
from 6,000 to 28,000 square feet 
with an average of 15,000 square 
feet, are smaller than most Longs 
stores, which average 23,000 square 
feet (17,000 selling).

PayLess on brink of new era 


by Allene Symons 


ILSONVILLE, Ore. — 

PayLess Drug Stores 

ended 1993 poised at the 

edge of a probable whirl- 
wind in 1994. 

In December, parent company 
Kmart Corp. agreed to sell PayLess 
to privately held TCH Corp., led by 
investor group Leonard Green & 
Partners, whose holdings include 
Thrifty Corp. and the Thrifty Drug 
Stores chain. 

The drug chain industry and its 
suppliers await the inevitable con- 
solidation and certainty of store 
closings, as well as a decision on 
headquarters locale. 1993 ended 


a teen

PayLess faces a multitude of changes associated with its purchase by TCH 
Corp., including consolidation and a possible new headquarters location.

with many unknowns, such as how 
two different private label lines 
would be handled, and uncertain 
future business for vendors who 
have supplied one or the other of 
the two chains. (See page 48 for ac- 
quisition story.) 

For the year, PayLess posted an 
8.7 percent sales increase on total 
sales of $2.54 billion, but showed a 
4.2 percent decline in same-store 
sales. In the first quarter of 1994, 
before the sale was final, PayLess 
closed 35 underperforming stores. 
During the year it opened a net to- 
tal of 22 stores for 576 sites, up 
from 554 the previous year. 

Sales in private label reached 3 
percent of total sales and showed a 
21.6 percent increase for the year. 
PayLess mounted aggressive com- 
pare-and-save campaigns during 
the year to promote its private label 
line with strong endcap placement 
and repackaging. 

Pharmacy reached 28 percent of 
total sales, with 52 percent in third- 
party prescriptions. During 1993, 
PayLess Drug Stores absorbed its 
1992 acquisition of the 126-store 
Pay ’n Save drug chain, purchased 
from Thrifty Corp. and now slated 
to return under the umbrella of 
Thrifty ownership.

Annual Report 


HSI’s plans eclipsed by merger with Revco 


by James Frederick 


NDIANAPOLIS — Hook-Su- 

peRx Inc., which strove over 

the past year and a half to 

overhaul its business and re- 
turn to profitability, is likely to dis- 
appear as an independent company 
by mid-summer. That is when the 
parent company of Hook Drugs, Su- 
peRx Drug and Brooks Drug is 
scheduled to merge with Revco D.S. 
to create the nation’s second- 
largest drug chain. 

The planned change in owner- 
ship—announced early this 
month—will double Revco’s size, 
strengthen its position in overlap- 
ping markets and greatly extend its 
geographic reach, if Revco opts to 
keep all three divisions. It will also 
eclipse HSI’s own plans to meld the 
best aspects of each of its three divi- 
sions and to create a more stream- 
lined, integrated and technological- 
ly driven operating network. 

Indeed, the task of integration 
that has consumed HSI executives 
in Pawtucket, R.I., Cincinnati and 
Indianapolis for the past 18 months 
will be thrown into warp drive when 
Revco injects its own centralized, 
highly automated operating and 
merchandising systems throughout 
HSI’s 22-state operating network. 


Nevertheless, much of HSI’s most 
difficult work to integrate its three 
divisions has already been done, ac- 
cording to top managers. 

Lending urgency to the company’s 
streamlining efforts in 1993 was the 
need to reduce costs and boost effi- 
ciency and profits. HSI faced “a very 
challenging year” last year, accord- 
ing to chairman and chief executive 
Phil Beekman, as “lower pharmacy 
inflation, intense competitive activi- 
ties in major markets and continu- 
ing downward pressure on third- 
party gross margins all made the 
year extremely difficult.” 

Indeed, operating income for the 
company dropped 30.4 percent in 
fiscal 1993, to $47.5 million, exclud- 
ing the one-time effect of a restruc- 
turing charge of $19.7 million. 

Results from the first quarter of 
the new fiscal year also underscored 
HSI’s struggle with tough market 
conditions, dwindling prescription 
margins and high costs. Neverthe- 
less, HSI began to show improve- 
ment in some areas as more efficient 
distribution and reporting patterns 
started to take hold. Operating costs 
in the first quarter fell from 24.3 
percent of sales in the prior year to 
23.7 percent this year. Excluding 
one-time charges for accounting 
changes both years, net losses 
shrank to $6.9 million in the most 


recent quarter, compared with a loss 
of $20.6 million in the prior year. 

The company’s poor profit picture 
may have masked other structural 
improvements taking shape at the 
company. Among them: 

e@ A newly enlarged and automated 
distribution center is operating in 
Indianapolis, allowing HSI to finally 
cut its historic dependence on Kroger 
Co.’s Peyton warehouse subsidiary to 
supply its Midwestern stores. 

@ It began testing new store de- 
signs and departmental sets in line 
with efforts to develop its first com- 
prehensive, company-wide store pro- 
totype. Among ideas which were 
tried at a test store in Providence, 
R.1.: a full home health care/durable 
medical equipment center adjacent to 
the pharmacy and staffed by a nurse; 
a variety of open-air, highly accessi- 
ble pharmacy designs; an extensive 
book and magazine center with plen- 
ty of room for browsing; an expanded 
snack and convenience food section; a 
redesigned cosmetics/fragrance cen- 
ter staffed by a cosmetician; and a 
striking new greeting card boutique. 

e@ It expanded its one-hour 
photofinishing business rapidly in 
the past 12 months, with more than 
40 one-hour labs now installed. 

@ The field operating structure 
was simplified and integrated along 
geographic lines in a shift away 


from the old turf lines of Brooks, 
Hook and SupeRx. The positions of 
divisional president for each of the 
three logos were scrapped; in their 
place, vice president of store opera- 
tions Tom Stilgenbauer created five 
new regions. Some of them include 
stores from two of the three chains. 

@ New corporate-wide posts were 
created for marketing, purchasing 
and other functions. Named to head 
those departments last year: David 
Morocco, vice president-purchasing; 
Richard Morrissey, vice president- 
market research and merchandising; 
Bill Welsh Jr., vice president-market- 
ing and merchandising; and George 
Dozier, vice president-local buying 
and advertising, among others. 

Meanwhile, two key executives 
left the company last year: former 
vice president of marketing Mar- 
garet Urquhart, who had been in- 
strumental in forging some of the 
links in the integration effort, and 
senior vice president and chief oper- 
ating officer Michael Moore. 

HSI planned to start testing its 
first POS system in July, with full 
rollout by 1996. Under Revco, how- 
ever, that project will be scrapped 
as Revco installs its own POS sys- 
tem and PAL pharmacy computer 
networks— probably within six 
months of the takeover, said Revco 
chief executive D. Dwayne Hoven.

REVO 


Revco fights back to industry front ranks 


by James Frederick 


WINSBURG, Ohio — Revco 

D.S. early this month 

signed a definitive agree- 

ment to purchase 1,115- 
store Hook-SupeRx, Inc. in a deal 
that will double Revco’s store count 
and propel it to the No. 2 spot in 
chain drug dollar volume rankings. 
The move caps a stunning return to 
the front ranks of chain drug retail- 
ing for a company that was still in 
Chapter 11 two years ago. 

The chain has come a long way 
since the dark days of early 1992, 
when it was the bankrupt prize in a 
pitched takeover battle between 
Jack Eckerd and Rite Aid. At that 
time— when the company was still 
struggling to maintain its indepen- 
dence and convince hundreds of 
skeptical creditors that they would 
best be served if they let Revco sur- 
vive intact—few would have pre- 
dicted the chain would roar back to 
fiscal health so quickly. 

Revco virtually reinvented itself 
during its four years in Chapter 11. 
It shed unprofitable stores and mar- 
kets, overhauled the once-unwieldy 
merchandise mix, adopted new 
management at almost every level 
and directed its court-protected cash 
flow into top-grade retail technology 


and chainwide store renovations. 

Revco’s long climb out of bank- 
ruptcy and uncertainty ended in 
June 1992, when the chain won 
creditor and court approval for its 
business plan and emerged as an 
independent company with publicly 
traded stock. Since then, its operat- 
ing results have been on a steady 
climb, paying increasing dividends 
on the company’s massive invest- 
ment in its own future. 

Revco’s most recent fiscal period 
epitomized that winning streak. For 
the third quarter of fiscal 1994, end- 
ed Feb. 5, Revco doubled its net in- 
come, excluding the impact of non- 
cash charges, to $16.6 million. 
Actual net earnings nearly tripled to 
$12.5 million. Sales were up 12.5 
percent to $621.2 million. 

What’s more, same-store sales 
again showed some of the sharpest 
gains in the industry, increasing 9 
percent for the quarter and 8.7 per- 
cent year-to-date. 

“We continue to be a leader in 
comparable-store sales,” said D. 
Dwayne Hoven, Revco chief execu- 
tive since September 1993. “Our 
merchants were able to generate im- 
proved gross margins...despite con- 
tinued pharmacy margin pressure.” 

Hoven attributed much of the 
continuing improvement to “better 
purchasing, stronger vendor sup- 


port and improved inventory man- 
agement,” coupled with a disci- 
plined expense-control program. 

Hoven observed that Revco’s chief 
enemy now was “complacency and 
building more bureaucratic systems 
and losing the entrepreneurial 
sense of urgency that we have to get 
things done.” 

Thus far, at least, the 1,210-store 
drug chain appears to have retained 
its entrepreneurial spirit. Among re- 
cent developments: 

@ The company recently over- 
hauled its bank credit agreement, 
cutting interest costs and speeding 
up its debt-reduction plan. Revco 
lined up $262.5 million in revolving 
credit through its lending banks. 
The deal allowed the company to re- 
pay $112.5 million of old, higher-in- 
terest debt with $27.5 million in 
cash and $85 million borrowed un- 
der the new credit line. 

“This amendment of the credit fa- 
cilities confirms the significant im- 
provement in Revco’s financial 
strength... [and] provides the flexi- 
bility for Revco to carry out its busi- 
ness plan on an economically favor- 
able basis,” noted Greg Raven, 
executive vice president and chief 
financial officer. It should also save 
the company more than $1 million 
annually in interest costs, he added. 

@ Prior to the pending merger 


with HSI, Revco’s debt-to-equity ra- 
tio had nearly reversed itself since 
Revco emerged from bankruptcy in 
mid-1992. Said Raven, “Twenty 
months ago, the company had $433 
million of high-coupon debt and 
about $320 million of equity. Today, 
the debt level stands at $225 million 
and equity exceeds $460 million.” 

®@ Revco has now spent roughly 
$40 million to renovate its stores 
chainwide in nine states. It also con- 
tinues to refine the easy-to-shop, an- 
gled-aisle store format it first un- 
veiled at the beginning of the decade 
as it adjusts its mix and departmen- 
tal adjacencies based on its chain- 
wide POS information systems. 

@ Those systems—and a steadily 
lengthening history of product move- 
ment based on POS data—are also 
key to Revco’s ongoing efforts to cre- 
ate automatic reorder and perpetual 
inventory systems. So too are some 
additions to the management staff in 
recent months, including Edwin 
Gropp Jr. to senior vice president of 
information systems, David Lynn to 
vice president of distribution and 
Richard Kotynski to director of mar- 
keting systems, a new post. Kotyns- 
ki’s task: to tie information systems 
to marketing operations. 

® Revco installed drive-through 
pharmacy windows at six locations, 
with plans to add more.

tail powerhouse.

cers stunned the retail and

tions of massive bookkeep- 
ing irregularities and inter-

light that the company had 
been operating in the red 
for years. 


But Phar-Mor’s public 


troubles were in part only 


the messy end result of 
problems that had simmered 
for years at the company. 
Reeling from the effect of 
years of double-bookkeeping 
and inflated accounting of 
inventories, Phar-Mor was 
quickly forced into a series 
of Draconian steps of store 
closings, layoffs, and down-

then make recommendations that 
benefit the entire category.” 

For category management pre- 
sentations, Tambrands_ uses 
Gladson & Associates, a Lisle, IL 
based space management consult- 
ing firm. Kenney said, “We used 
to have contracts with two other 
companies, but our sales force 
chose Gladson unanimously. Our 
regional managers told us that they 
[Gladson] understood our business 
and were effective from day one.” 
Using a space management center 
gives the retailer an objective per- 
spective on the category. 

“We have chosen not to bring 
our space management in-house be- 
cause we do not want to lose our 
objectivity, Kenney added, 
“Gladson is like an extension of our 
company, we have access to a tre- 
mendous service without the huge 
capital investment.” 

By using a service center, 
Tambrands has been able to build 
planograms using sensitive retailer 
data that would not otherwise be 
available. “Retailers give their store 
specific data to Gladson on a con- 
fidential, nondisclosure basis which 
is then incorporated into the 
planogram analysis.” 

“Our relationship with Gladson 
& Associates has been a big chap- 
ter in our category management 
success story” concluded Kenney.

PRODUCT CATEGORY PERFORMANCE REVIEW 


How the chain drug industry 
fared in 1993 


Ithough new and exciting products weren't enough to 
blow away the persistent economic doldrums, drug 
stores weathered 1993 fairly well. Rather than growth, 
the emphasis was on improving merchandising, as well 
as attending to operational issues, cost cutting and strategic de- 
cision-making. 

In a $78-billion market that edged upward only 1 percent in 
1993, chain drug stores continued to outpace independents. 
Sales in drug chains increased 6 percent, from $52 billion to $55 
billion, while independents’ sales slipped 8 percent, going from 
$25 billion to $23 billion. 


Rx dominates chain sales 


Prescription drugs continued to top the list of product cate- 
gories sold within drug stores, with an average of 49 percent of 
total sales within all drug stores. Chains remained the dominant 
channel for prescription drugs, with $20 billion of the $38 billion 
drug store market, increasing 5 percent, while independents com- 
manded $18 billion at retail, for an increase of about 6 percent. 
But drug stores continued to wrestle with increased 
competition at retail for the prescription drug cus- 


tomer. In a growing market, ma*s merchandisers and 
supermarkets outpaced the growth of both chain drug 
stores and independent pharmacies in 1993.
