Annual Report CATEGORY OVERVIEVV 


How the industry fared in 1993 


Continued from page 49 

According to IMS America’s DDD 
Division, drug chains’ share of the 
prescription drug market at the 
warehouse level topped $15 billion 
in 1993, whereas independents paid 
$13 billion for prescription drugs. In 
a wholesale market that increased 
11 percent, or $6 billion, to $62 bil- 
lion, the largest gainers among re- 
tail channels in prescription drug 
sales (at retailers’ cost) were mass 
merchandisers, with 22 percent 
more sales in 1993, and supermar- 
kets, with a gain of 13 percent. 

With health care reform a hot 
topic under the Clinton Adminis- 
tration, drug chains continued to 
position themselves to participate 
more effectively in a managed care 
environment. 

While collectively supporting the 
Clinton plan for health care reform 
through the Community Retail 
Pharmacy Health Care Reform 
Coalition, formed by NACDS and 
NARD, several individual drug 
chains—including Walgreen, Rite 
Aid, CVS and Thrift Drug—in- 
creased their dedication to market- 
ing their chains to third-party 
providers and major employers, in- 
vesting in automated distribution 
centers, purchasing existing third- 
party companies and dedicating ex- 
ecutive-level positions to the man- 
aged care business. 


Front-end gap widens 


While pharmacy sales grew in 
both chain and independent drug 
stores, chains outperformed inde- 
pendents in the front end by a wide 
margin. Overall, front-end sales in 
drug stores slid 2 percent during 
1993, going from $41 billion to $40 
billion, but independents bore more 
than their share of the loss. 

In front-end categories, drug 
chains picked up $2 billion in sales, 
increasing from $33 billion to $35 
billion during 1993, for a gain of 6 
percent, while independents’ front- 
end sales decreased 37 percent, 
from $8 billion to $5 billion. 

Eighty-eight percent of front-end 
sales in 1993 came through chain 
drug stores, as compared to only 80 
percent in 1992. Independents’ 
sales, meanwhile, dropped to 12 
percent from 20 percent. 

Independents held onto more 
than one-fourth of OTC sales in 
1993, as well as 20 percent of cos- 
metics sales and 19 percent of toi- 
letries. Within the drug store chan- 
nel, chains clearly dominated the 
consumables and general merchan- 
dise businesses, with 96 percent 
and 95 percent of those categories, 
respectively. 

Some may say the story in many 
categories was the drug channel’s 
loss of market share in comparison 
to mass merchants. 

But even though market-share 
numbers seem to indicate that the 
drug channel lost ground in 1993, 
an industry statistician pointed out 
that much of the loss could be at- 
tributed to declining store count. 
rather than poor merchandising. 
Overall, the drug store industry lost 

1,030 units in 1993, for a loss of 2 
percent, while mass merchants 


were not only adding new stores but 
were also expanding the space they 

gave to such categories as toiletries, 
cosmetics and OTCs. 

“There is no defect in the chain 
drug industry,” said the source. 
“Rather than opening stores, drug 
chains have had a different focus— 
investing in technology, bringing 
down operating cost and saving 
money in other ways.” 


Capitalizing on convenience 


After prescription drugs, edible 
and non-edible groceries edged out 
general merchandise as the second- 
largest product category within 
drug stores. 

Continuing to capitalize on the 
convenience of their locations, drug 
stores are stocking up on candy and 
mints, chips and other snacks, and 
carbonated and New Age beverages. 

With 13 percent of all drug store 
sales, general merchandise cate- 
gories are the most diverse—and 
the most difficult to track. 

The largest single segment, greet- 
ing cards, racked up almost $1.5 bil- 
lion in sales in drug stores in 1993. 

Photofinishing, which more and 
more chains are expanding and 
moving to visible locations to create 
a destination department, repre- 
sented almost $1.3 billion to dru 
stores in 1993. Stationery, with $1.2 
billion in sales in drug stores, 
showed a gain of 9.6 percent, fueled 
by upscale school products and 
home office materials. 

In niche segments, drug store per- 
formance varied, with segments like 
humidifiers and weather protection 
benefiting from bad weather and flu 
conditions, while categories such as 
hair care appliances and batteries 
suffered from price competition. 


Core categories mixed 


In the core health and beauty care 
segments, drug stores’ performance 
in 1993 was uneven. The 
OTC/health care segment —fueled 
by growth in vitamins, first aid 
products and cough/cold/sinus reme- 
dies— gained 2 percent in sales in 
1993, growing from $9.5 billion to 


$9.7 billion. Cosmetics and fra- 
grances, by contrast, slid by 6 per- 
cent, declining from $2 billion to less 
than $1.9 billion. Toiletries shrank 
slightly, losing 1 percent, or $60 
million, on sales of $4.76 billion. 

In many segments—from eye/lens 
care to deodorants to nail polish to 
fragrances—drug stores saw sales 
decline and market share shift to- 
ward mass merchants. 

The outlook for 1994, however, is 
more positive. 

As consumers continue to take 
control through preventative health 
habits, products like vitamins and 
homeopathic and herbal medicines 
are expected to grow. The Rx-to- 
OTC switch phenomenon will also 
continue. This year, the analgesic 
business will be energized with the 
introduction of Aleve, a naproxen 
sodium product marketed by a Syn- 
tex/P&G joint venture. 

In cosmetics and fragrances, drug 
chains are taking their cue from de- 
partment stores, which have been 
able to recapture sales by improving 
service and merchandising panache. 
This year, along with introducing 
new products from a number of ma- 
jor players, drug chains will be 
striving to attract more customers 
with advertising that stresses fash- 
ion and value. 

In toiletries, drug stores are 
struggling as many categories, such 
as shampoo, are caught in an in- 
tense price war. To compensate, 
successful drug stores will be accen- 
tuating professional hair care prod- 
ucts and hot segments like hair col- 
or. Although the earlier meteoric 
growth in the bath segment has 
flattened out, retailers still see op- 
portunity in the area, and they are 
adjusting sets and assortments to 
find the most salable mix. 

Although mass merchants did en- 
croach on drug stores’ traditional 
territories in 1993, the drug chan- 
nel remains dominant in most core 
HBA categories—cosmetics, with a 
53 percent share; OTCs, with a 44 
percent share; hair care, with a 37 
percent share; and skin care, witha 
40 percent share. 


This year, Drug Store News 
has refined and improved its sta- 
tistical coverage of the drug store 
industry. 

Facts and figures about retail 
chains (which begin on p. 20) are 
the product of exclusive Drug 
Store News research. 

Category statistics (which be- 
gin with the coverage on p. 49) 
come from two sources: Most of 
the dollar volumes and percent 
share of market among trade 
classes were provided by Infor- 
mation Resources Inc., with ad- 
ditional figures in categories not 
tracked by IRI coming from Drug 
Store News exclusive industry 
research. 

This is a change from prior 
years—and a sign of the times. 


Where the numbers came from 


As more drug stores have in- 
stalled scanning systems, this 
hard point-of-sale data has be- 
come available. Using IRI num- 
bers, based on actual scanning 
data, we are able to provide a re- 
liable and comprehensive profile 
of the entire drug industry as 
well as chain drug’s role in that 
industry and analyses of the com- 
petitors— mass merchandisers 
and food/combo stores. 

IRI is a Chicago-based market 
research and software company. 
Its retail sales figures for the 52- 
week period ended Jan. 2, 1994 
are based on scanning data col- 
lected from a nationally repre- 
sentative sample of 2,700 super- 
markets, 500 drug stores and 250 
mass merchandisers.

Drug Store News, April 25,1994 53 


Annual Report PHARMACY 


Drug store Rx 


braces for 1994, 
evolving health 


care marketplace 


ncertainty about health re- 

form, concerns over phar- 

maceutical pricing prac- 

tices, increased friction in 
the third-party arena and the 
prospect of a severe pharmacy per- 
sonnel shortage are combining to 
cloud the outlook for retail pharma- 
cy operations in 1994. 

The biggest question mark for the 
drug store industry today involves 
the shape of health care reform and 
its impact on the prescription drug 
marketplace. 

The Clinton Administration’s for- 
mula for health care reform —uni- 
versal prescription coverage, a new 
Medicaid outpatient drug benefit, 
restrictions on multi-tier pharma- 
ceutical pricing and an antitrust 
safe harbor for retail pharmacy— 
has drawn unqualified support from 
both chain and independent drug 
store industry leaders. 

But the White House proposal is 
receiving much lower marks from 
the general public, and Congress is 
now actively debating a series of 
competing health reform bills that 
would have far different implica- 
tions for drug stores. 

State legislatures, meanwhile, 
are busily hammering out health re- 
form initiatives of their own, and 
many of those new laws have al- 
ready created serious new competi- 
tive problems for retail pharmacies 
(see story page 12). 

Adding to the uncertainty: efforts 
by several major pharmaceutical 
manufacturers to transform the 
proposed new Medicare outpatient 
drug program into a “managed 
care” plan administered by Pharma- 
cy Benefit Management (PBM) or- 
ganizations such as Medco’s PAID 
Prescriptions. 


Price discrimination 


Faced with stiffening competition 
from mail-order pharmacy 
providers, drug chains have stepped 
up efforts to outlaw the multi-tier 
pricing practices of pharmaceutical 

‘manufacturers under which man- 
aged care pharmacy providers are 
offered deep discounts not available 
to retail drug stores. 

Over the past year more than 40 
lawsuits have been filed by commu- 
nity pharmacists across the country 
challenging these discriminatory 
pricing practices as a violation of 
federal antitrust law. 

One of the most closely watched 
of these actions involves charges 


filed by Rite Aid, Revco, Thrifty and 
seven other drug chains against 
Medco and a number of leading 
pharmaceutical manufacturers al- 
leging a conspiracy to price-dis- 
criminate illegally against retail 
drug stores. 

A lawsuit filed earlier this year 
by Kroger, Albertson’s, Safeway and 
Vons alleges similar antitrust viola- 
tions against supermarket chain 
pharmacy operations. 

But just as brand-name pharma- 
ceutical manufacturers are fighting 
allegations of unlawful price discrim- 
ination, some major chains are de- 
fending themselves against charges 
of predatory pricing activities. 


Below-cost sales 


The most celebrated of these cas- 
es is being played out in Ben- 
tonville, Ark., where several inde- 


pendent pharmacies brought suit 
against industry giant Wal-Mart 
for allegedly violating the state’s 
Depression-era law against below- 
cost sales. 

To the surprise of many ob- 
servers, the trial court ruled in fa- 
vor of the independents, holding 
that Wal-Mart’s practice of selling 
prescription drugs and other prod- 
ucts below cost was indeed intended 
to eliminate competitors. 

Although that ruling is now un- 
der appeal, the decision against 
Wal-Mart quickly spawned a flurry 
of copycat price predation cases 
against other chains across the 
country. 

The latest of these was filed just 
last month by the California Phar- 
macists Association against Thrifty 
and Sav-on Drug Stores. In that 
suit, the CPhA is alleging that the 
two drug chains are engaged in ille- 
gal below-cost sales of prescription 
drug products to a pair of Califor- 
nia health maintenance organiza- 
tions (HMOs). 


Third-party warfare 


While feuding pharmacy factions 
slug it out in the courts, an even 
more bitter conflict is brewing in 
the third-party arena. 

During the past year, the two 
leading pharmacy benefit manage- 
ment firms—McKesson’s PCS and 
Medco’s PAID—both have come un- 
der heavy fire from drug store in- 
dustry leaders for establishing re- 
strictive networks. 

The most recent of these—PAID’s 
new deal with General Motors to 
provide pharmacy services to one

Total prescription drug sales 
rose by more than $6 billion dur- 
ing 1993, an increase of almost 
11 percent to $62 billion at the 
warehouse level.* Despite in- 
roads by mail-order providers of 
pharmacy services, retail phar- 
macies still managed to generate 
six out of every 10 dollars in U.S. 
prescription drug dollar sales last 
year, with chain drug stores cap- 
turing the largest slice. 

The cost of prescription prod- 
ucts sold by the nation’s more 
than 17,000 drug chain pharma- 
cies jumped 9.7 percent last year 
to $15.3 billion—a total gain of 
$1.3 billion over 1992’s level. 

On a per-store basis, the na- 
tion’s chain drug stores sold an 
average of almost $900,000 worth 
of prescription drugs last year — 
some $77,000 more than the pre- 
vious year.

sector of retail pharmacy, with 
prescription drug sales up nearly 
22 percent last year.

products sold in mass merchan- 
diser pharmacies climbed to $4.4 
billion in 1993, an average of al- 
most $968,000 per unit. 

Supermarket pharmacies also 
showed strong prescription sales 
gains as total volume rose 13.4 
percent to nearly $4.4 billion. On 
a per store basis, that works out 
to about $734,000.

Mail-order not letting up

Chain and independent pharmacies dispensed 60 precent of all prescription drug prod- 
ucts last year, valued at more than $37 billion wholesale. 


outlets). 

The dollar value of prescriptions 
dispensed by mail-order pharma- 
cies jumped by almost $900 million 
last year to nearly $4.7 billion. 

Although mail-order dispensaries 
still control a relatively small 7.5 
percent share of the total prescrip- 
tion market, the growth of these op- 
erations has been alarming to retail 
pharmacy segments. 

As recently as 1981, mail-order 
prescription dollar sales totaled less 
than $100 million. Since then the 
volume generated by these firms 
has exploded 40 fold. 

The strength of mail-order phar- 
macy is in maintenance drugs, and 
last year these providers captured 
14 percent of all maintenance drugs 
sold to the ambulatory pharmacy 
care market. 

Predicting that mail-order sales 


of maintenance prescription prod-

nual growth rate of better than 30 
percent, American Managed Care 
Pharmacy Association president 
Clifton Latiolais predicted recently 
that “our members will expand to at 
least $6.5 billion in sales by 1995— 
and this is a conservative estimate. 

The total number of prescriptions 
dispensed exceeded 2 billion last 
year, and although manufacturer 
prices are showing signs of stabiliz- 
ing, the cost of prescription drugs 
continues to rise. 

For 1992, NACDS estimates that 
the average prescription dispensed 
by retail drug stores cost consumers 
just over $26. Even assuming only a 
modest rate of pharmaceutical in- 
flation, average retail prescription 
prices are likely to approach the $28 
mark this year.

In addition to objections from re- 
tail pharmacy leaders, PAID’s GM 
network has also come under attack 
from the APhA— Medco’s “partner” 
in the development of a new Coordi- 
nated Care Network (CCN) de- 
signed to compensate participating 
retail pharmacists for patient coun- 
seling and other non-dispensing ser-

Although Medco officials claim 
that more than 46,000 pharmacies 
have joined that new network since 
the start of this year, the CCN and 
the APhA’s relationship with the gi-

sharp criticism from many commu- 
nity pharmacists. 

In sharp contrast to the APhA’s 
strategy of working with PBMs 
such as Medco/PAID, retail phar-

58 Drug Store News, April 25, 1994 


NACDS members are developing 
a separate Pharmacy Direct Net- 
work open to both chains and inde- 
pendents. 

Independent pharmacists at 
NARD are being urged to join a new 
network of their own—Rx Med— 
which may provide some with an al- 
ternative to the restrictive groups 
being formed by PAID and PCS. 


Pressure on profits 


Behind these initiatives: growing 
frustration among retail pharma- 
cists over the pressure being placed 
on operating margins by bottom- 
feeding third-party payors. 

In addition to squeezing the in- 
dustry’s profitability, this pressure 
is making it difficult for drug 
chains to devote the time and pro- 
fessional manpower needed to pro- 
vide extra value patient services. 
Too often, personal interaction be- 
tween the pharmacist and the pa- 
tient is sacrificed. 

Despite 15-month-old OBRA ’90 
requirements that pharmacists of- 
fer counseling and drug use review 
services to patients, regulators in 


many states acknowledge that most 
retail pharmacies are still not com- 
plying fully with that law. 

The pressure on profitability that 
many pharmacies are feeling today 
figures to get worse fast if pharma- 
cy educators continue their drive to 
establish the six-year Pharm.D. as 
the mandatory entry-level degree 
for all future pharmacists. 

A new study released earlier this 
year by American Stores found that 
the cost of mandating a six-year de- 
gree program for pharmacists could 
produce a severe new pharmacist 
shortage across the country. 

As a result of this shortage, the 
researchers concluded that the cost 
of employing pharmacists would 
rise by 10 percent—or an added 
$4,500 a year for every pharmacist 
on the payroll. 

These extra personnel costs, an 
estimated $500 billion annually, 
would ultimately have to be passed 
on to consumers through higher 
prescription prices or reduced ac- 
cess to pharmacy services, they 
warned. 

— Ken Rankin 


Annual Report : COSMETICS & FRAGRANCES 


Drug hangs on 


to lion’s share 


of cosmetic, 


fragrance sales 


has been another 
1 O QO tough year for 
drug store cosmet- 


ic and fragrance buyers. 

Drug stores still command the 
highest share of color cosmetic 
sales—53 percent for the 52 weeks 
ended Jan. 2, 1994. But mass mer- 
chandisers are coming on fast, hav- 
ing developed their portion of the 
business to the point that they now 
control 32 percent of all mass cos- 
metic dollar sales. 

According to IRI scanning data 
for the 12 months ended Jan. 2, 
1994, drug store sales of cosmetic 
products declined 6 percent to $1.3 
billion, a loss of $87 million in actu- 
al dollars over the previous year. 

Meanwhile for the same period, 
cosmetic sales in food and food/drug 
combination stores increased 2 per- 
cent to $392 million, for a gain of $6 
million in actual dollars, while sales 
in mass merchandisers went up 21 
percent. Mass merchandisers last 
year generated $804 million from 
the sales of cosmetic products. 


Competition breaks tradition 


Thanks to expanded and en- 
hanced cosmetic presentations, clos- 
er attention to product service and 
an expanded mix that often includes 
department store lines as well as 
franchised brands, mass merchan- 
disers like Kmart, Wal-Mart and 
Target are clearly now a force to 
reckon with when it comes to cos- 
metics and other key front-end cate- 
gory segments that were once tradi- 
tionally the province of drug stores. 

Perhaps no one feels the impact of 
this competitive assault quite as 
acutely as the chain drug store cate- 
gory buyers and division merchan- 
disers who are doing all they can to 
support the front-end categories, 
particularly core destination depart- 
ments like cosmetics and fragrances. 

Chains like Oregon-based Pay- 
Less Drug, New York-based Gen- 
ovese Drug and Louisiana-based 
K&B Drug report that they have 
been able to grow sales in the cos- 
metics department, but only with 
the help of a strong cosmetician ser- 
vice program; consistent, steady, 
aggressive advertising that stresses 


Drug chains’ piece 
of the cosmetics and 
fragrances pie 
Chains: $1,509M (80%) 
independents: $370M (20%) 


a combination of value and fashion; 
enhanced merchandising presenta- 
tions; and careful attention to 
growth brands, growth niches and 
growth items. 

On the West Coast, PayLess’ cos- 
metics buyer Sheri Ralston report- 
ed that her cosmetics sales in 1993 
were good, stronger than they were 
in 1992, and she attributed that to 
PayLess’ aggressive advertising for 
the department and to the in-store 
cosmeticians whose presence gives 
the chain a “point of difference 
with consumers.” 


Perhaps no 

one feels the 
impact of this 
competitive 
assault quite as 
acutely as the 
chain drug store. 


In New York, where Genovese 
Drug also registered gains in color 
cosmetic sales last year, buyer 
Stephanie Hayter attributed the 
growth to a discounting program 
that Genovese put into effect last 
March and to Genovese’s new ad- 
vertising for cosmetics. 

But the cosmetics buyers for 
many other drug chains said they 
were frustrated by the softness they 
are encountering in the category. 

“The department stores seem to 
be getting stronger, and the compe- 
tition from mass merchandisers is 
worse than ever,” said the buyer for 
one major regional drug chain. 

Several buyers pointed out that 
there are not many opportunities 
for drug stores to have “exclusives” 
on the new lines that are launch- 
ing, nor do they have exclusives on 
what they carry. Many mass mer- 
chandisers carry the major brands 
that drive mass cosmetics sales: 
Revlon, Cover Girl, Max Factor, 
L’Oréal and Maybelline. 

“All we can do,” said one buyer, 
“is to try harder to make our stores 
the destination shop for these kinds 
of purchases.” 

Most chain drug cosmetics buyers 


say they plan to do that in 1994 by 
manipulating the only variables 
they have under their control: 

® advertising; 

® product selection; 

® in-store service; 

® merchandising presentations; 

® prices; and 

® customized promotions. 

At Genovese, in addition to dis- 
counting cosmetics to build traffic, it 
plans to continue to advertise the 
category aggressively. There will be 
upgraded merchandising presenta- 
tions in select high-volume cosmetics 
doors and emphasis on the presence 
of trained in-store service cosmeti- 
cians. The chain will monitor the 
category's profitability by keeping an 
eye on turns and space allocations. 

At PayLess, the chain is going to 
continue to upgrade its cosmetic 
presentations, trying to attract 
women who favor buying cosmetics 
in department stores. 

The chain is also aggressively 
courting the everyday cosmetics 
shopper with advertising that 
stresses both fashion and value, and 
with in-store cosmeticians. 

At Snyder Drug in Minneapolis, 
the chain is investing more money 
and time in strengthening its cos- 
metician program. 

“We think the best way to grow 
sales is with in-store cosmetic con- 
sultants,” said Snyder Drug’s cos- 
metics buyer Peggy Williams. “We 
are encouraging them to try the 
products because we know that if 
our consultants like a product, they 
can sell it to our new customers.” 

“If we could get more women to 
shop us for cosmetics, we could 
broaden the pool of shoppers who 
visit our stores and all our depart- 
ments could benefit from the traffic,” 
said the buyer for one major chain. 

The buyer for this chain said 
there were two strategic questions 
to address this year: 

1. How to get more women to 
shop drug stores as their destina- 
tion store for cosmetics, and 

2. How to convert prescription 
shoppers into cosmetic shoppers. 

“If we could solve these two prob- 
lems,” this buyer said, “we could get 
the category back on track, and in 
the process make our stores more 
profitable and more appealing.”

Many buyers say there are two reasons why make- 
up sales showed overall gains in 1993. 

Manufacturers like Maybelline broadened their 
target market to focus on the underdeveloped 35- 
and-cliie? market, and manufacturers like May- 
belline, P&G and L’Oréal came out with innovative 
new formulas that gave women sheer, more sophisti- 
cated coverage with extra moisturizing and condi- 
tioning benefits. 

“Women over 35, and even younger women, are 
showing a strong interest in face makeups that are 
formulated with natural ingredients like vitamin E 
and aloe,” said the cosmetics buyer for one leading 
drug chain. 

hey are also looking for sun care protection in 
the form of SPFs to guard against premature aging 
and wrinkling, and they are opting for a lighter, 
sheerer coverage fortified with special emollients to 
moisturize the skin.” 

“In the past, whenever a new product was intro- 
duced, the cosmetics manufacturers always said it 
was ck, to women 18 to 34,” said one buyer. 

“People assumed women over 35 weren’t heavy 
users of makeup, but Revitalizing has shown that 
women over 35 probably just couldn’t find the right 
formulas in drug stores. Now we're getting sales 
from women who used to buy makeup in department 
stores, and we're starting to see this segment grow.” 


Convenience, value spark success 


Maybelline reported that from March 1993, when 
Revitalizing was introduced, through the end of the 
year. the line generated $14 million in sales. May- 

elline executives attributed the company’s 10.6 per- 
cent sales gain in 1993 to the success of Revitalizing. 

Part of the reason for Revitalizing’s success, buy- 
ers think, is that it is available to women at reason- 


New formulas, older consumers 


able prices in convenient locations. 

According to Maybelline’s market research, 57 per- 
cent of all women 35 and over purchase their makeup 
in either discount stores, food stores or drug stores. 

At suggested retail prices ranging from $5.25 to 
$5.95, the Revitalizing collection costs just a fraction 
of department store lines with similar ingredients. 

This year, many buyers think Revitalizing’s sales 
will continue to grow dramatically. In addition to 
spending $23 million on print and TV advertising to 
support Revitalizing, Maybelline is also introducing 
a slew of line extensions, including a Revitalizing 
skin care collection. 


Other fast-growing lines 


Along with Revitalizing, P&G’s Ultimate Finish 
emerged as one of the fastest growing new lines in 
the face makeup category in 1993. 

According to recent market research reports, Ulti- 
mate Finish was ranked as the fastest growing face 
makeup in unit sales in the combined trade classes 
of drug, mass and food. 

Ultimate Finish was one of the mass market’s first 
“advanced formula” makeups to deliver the benefits 
of a liquid and powder makeup in one form. After be- 
ing applied to the skin, Ultimate Finish transforms 
into a powder that creates a soft, natural finish. 

Cover Girl’s original Clean Makeup continues to 
maintain its dominant share of category sales. 
Launched 35 years ago, Cover Girl is the No. 1 foun- 
dation makeup in mass market stores. 

In 1993, “light diffusing” became a new marketing 
buzz word, and this year there are several new 
launches pending that have light-diffusing ingredi- 
ents to help diminish the appearance of under-eye 
circles, wrinkles and fine lines.

Many of the leading salon nail care manufacturers 


have introduced their best-selling salon SKUs to 


the retail market, and, in the process, they’ve 


invested in packaging and point-of-purchase 


displays that clearly explain what each product 


does and how it should be applied. 


working with chains to create the

drive sales in the segment.

many false nail manufacturers have 


had years of experience in develop-

take their best sellers from that 
market, repackage them and intro-

Women appreciate the conve- 
nience of being able to buy false 
nails and accessories in their local 
neighborhood drug store, especially 
at prices better than what most sa- 
lons charge, according to buyers. 
“Even salon technicians are coming 
into drug stores to buy the larger 
size packs of nail tips and the pow- 
ders and gels,” said one buyer.

past year has come from brands like 
Fing’rs, Nailene, PRO10, Five Sec-

lished retail brands, such as Del

the false nail category. 

They are bringing with them 
their years of experience as success- 
ful mass marketers and taking ad- 
vantage of the strength of their 
brand names to create lines, like 
Professionals by Sally Hansen, that 
are targeted to salon customers as 


well as salon technicians.

opened the door to growth in other 
segments of nail care, particularly 
treatment products, nail art and 
nail glue removers.

AGRANCES 


Displays, promotions aid fragrances 


Chain drug buyers would like the major fragrance manufacturers to spend more 
on promotions and advertising to support both the new and the ‘mature’ brands. 


hroughout 1993, chain drug 
cosmetics and fragrances buy- 
ers complained that fragrance 
sales were softening in their stores, 
often adding that they were frus- 
trated by the category’s lack of inno- 
vation and excitement. 

It appears that their frustration 
was justified. For the 12 months 
ended Jan. 2, 1994, IRI reported 
that fragrance sales fell 7 percent to 
$531 million in the drug store trade 
class, a loss of $41 million in retail 
dollar sales. 

The women’s fragrance segment, 
which accounted for the bulk of cat- 
egory sales (63 percent), dropped 10 
percent to $335 million, while the 
men’s segment fell 2 percent to 
$196 million. 

Meanwhile in food stores, the cat- 
egory grew 5 percent to $91 million, 
a gain of $4 million in dollar sales. 
The men’s category showed the 
strongest dollar gain in food stores, 
up 5 percent to $59 million, an in- 
crease of $3 million in retail sales. 
Women’s fragrances rose 3.2 per- 
cent to $32 million, an increase of 
$1 million in retail sales. 


Mass the big winner 


The category showed the largest 
growth surges, however, in mass 
merchandise stores, where women’s 
fragrances increased 9.6 percent to 
$287 million, a gain of $25 million 
in dollars, and men’s fragrances 
rose 20 percent to $217 million, a 
gain of $3 36 million. According to 
IRI, the entire category went up 14 
percent in mass to $504 million, a 
gain of $60 million. 

According to many chain drug 
store fragrance buyers, there were 
several reasons for the declines in 
drug and the gains in the other 
trade classes. 

The biggest factor: Mass mer- 
chandise stores, such as Kmart, 
Wal-Mart and Target, have been 
upgrading their fragrance presen- 
tations, creating fragrance boutique 
islands in many of their new proto- 
type and upscale market stores, 
adding diverted department store 
fragrances to their mix, putting 
trained service cosmeticians behind 


the counter, creating more value- 
added promotional programs with 
fragrance manufacturers, doing 
more in-store sampling of fra- 
grances and advertising them more 
frequently to enhance their image 
as a fashion merchandiser. 

Drug stores have used these tech- 
niques to build their fragrance 
sales, and their very effectiveness is 
now helping mass merchandise 
steal share from drug stores. 

Buyers said department stores 


Now, chain drug 
fragrance buyers are 
looking at the 
techniques the 
department stores 
used to resurrect their 
business, and they’re 
ready to fight back. 


contributed to their problems. For 
the past few years, department 
stores lost sales in the category, 
mostly because they were so pricey. 
Yet, last year, they went after the 
fragrance business ‘ike gang- 
busters. They promoted fragrances 
aggressively, reduced prices, offered 
several value-added promotions and 
introduced attractively priced 
miniature versions of popular 
scents to their mix. They wooed the 
customer back into their stores. 


Using department-store methods 


Now, chain drug fragrance buyers 
are looking at the techniques the 
department stores used to resurrect 
their business, and they’re ready to 
fight back. Many have visited the 
major fragrance players, saying 
they need more innovation and cus- 
tomized programs to drive fra- 
grance sales in chain drug stores. 

The fragrance buyer for one ma- 
jor chain told fragrance man- 
ufacturers that the drug store in- 


dustry today needs * ‘something spe- 
cial” for their stores. “Everybody 
wants to do a gift-with-purchase or 
a purchase-with-purchase,” he 
pointed out, “but even if you have 
cosmeticians in your stores to make 
that work, that alone is not enough 
to drive the category.” 

This buyer said he wants man- 
ufacturers to work with him to cre- 
ate “exclusive launches like you al- 
ways see in department stores.” 

Buyers say the major fragrance 
manufacturers must sperd more on 
advertising and promotions to sup- 
port the new fragrances they intro- 
duce, as well as their mature 
brands that have stabilized in the 
mass market. Nearly every buyer 
agreed that, except for Coty, which 
has had one winner after another in 
fragrance launches, none of the ma- 
jor companies spent enough on 
advertising and product support. 

Buyers realize the smaller volume 
fragrance manufacturers cannot al- 
ways afford to spend a lot on con- 
sumer advertising, but they should 
try to create more innovative dis- 
plays and packaging as well as cus- 
tomized promotions that will help 
their brands stand out in the store. 

In some chains, smaller brands, 
like Richard Barrie’s Moments and 
Dana’s Tabu, have done surprising- 
ly well, and buyers say it’s because 
of the flexible support these compa- 
nies give to individual chains. 


‘Alternative’ scents a plus 


Another bright spot in the cate- 
gory: alternative designer fra- 
grances. Buyers reported that while 
the category overall was flat last 
year, alternative designer brands 
like Lady in Red, Fragrance Im- 
pressions, Parfums de Coeur and 
Designer Quality Impressions did 
quite well. They said that was be- 
cause their manufacturers created 
a winning combination for their 
lines. While there was no massive 
investment in advertising, there 
was a lot of creativity and money 
invested in the packaging, displays 
and formulas. 

Among the major manufacturers, 
Quintessence continued to impress 
buyers with its innovative promo- 
tional programs that consistently 
kept its best-selling brands, like Jo- 
van Musk and Aspen, very visible. _| 
Last year, Coty’s launch of Vanilla | 
Fields was the best in its class. Buy- 
ers for every drug chain said it “blew 
out” their doors; it’s still selling well. 

Except for Vanilla Fields, chain 
drug fragrance buyers said there re- 
ally weren't any exciting new prod- 
ucts to drive sales in fragrances last 
year. But there’s much more new 
product activity planned for 1994,

COSMETICS & FRAGRANCES 


Chains rethink 
organizer segment 


he cosmetic organiz- 

er category in chain 

drug stores is going 

through a strategic 
identity crisis. 

Experts value the orga- 
nizer market—consisting 
primarily of the hard- and 
soft-sided plastic boxes and 

lastic carrying trays—at 
$80 million to €90 million at 
retail, with approximately 
70 percent of the business 
generated at mass and the 
rest in drug stores. 

While the category has 
been flat at retail this year, 
there has been a definite 
shifting of sales away from 
drug stores and into mass 
channels like Kmart, Wal- 
Mart and Target. 

As a result, most drug 
chains are looking for new 
ways to distinguish them- 
selves from the competition. 
Some have cut back their 
everyday planogramed sec- 
tions for organizers, putting 
more emphasis on an end- 
cap at peak seasonal periods 
or off-shelf displays at peak 
selling periods. 

Drug chains have also 
learned that their best sell- 
ers are usually the boxes 
and trays priced under $15, 
as well as those that come 
packaged with an added 
value, like a gift with pur- 
chase or bonus items. 


New end uses 


The leaders continue to be 
Caboodles, Cosmepak and 
Sassaby, which are all try- 
ing to drive sales by creating 
innovative new end uses for 
the box, by adding new fash- 
ion colors and textures to 
their palettes and by coming 
up with new forms or func- 
tions that will appeal to less 
traditional users—particu- 
larly mothers, college stu- 
dents and career women. 

This past year, Cosmepak 
did very well with its new 
Basket Case organizer, 
which expanded the func- 
tionality of the product type 
into bathrooms and dorms. 

Caboodles had a winner 
in its new granite-textured 
organizers, particularly 
when chains were able to 
get the price under $15, and 
Sassaby did well with its 
under-$10 smaller boxes. 

Paris Presents also con- 
tinued to strengthen its 
standing in the category by 
introducing new shades and

Hidden problem 


One manufacturer said

Too many drug chains want

and at the same time want 
to continue to make 60 per-

organizers, he said. 

“If we guarantee the sale, 
we have to include that in 
the acquisition price,” said a 
source at one leading manu- 
facturer. “Add in this extra 
cost and the fact that drug 
stores still want to make 60

have a situation where drug

with mass merchandisers 
head-to-head. It can and is 
hurting the category in drug

Drug chains 
remain No. 


for toiletries 


{ : he battle for toiletries sales 
was bitter in 1993, and there 
was good news and bad news 

for the chain drug industry. 

The good news? Drug stores re- 
main the dominant channel for toi- 
letries purchases. The bad news? 
They lost share to mass merchants 
in nearly every toiletries category 
in 1993. 

Drug store sales fell 1.4 percent 
in overall beauty care, ringing up 
sales of $4.7 billion compared to the 
previous year’s sales of $4.8 billion. 

Decreases in dollar sales showed 
up in many categories at drug 
chains. Those categories that 
weren't down showed flat growth. 

The food class of trade fared only 
slightly better. The channel had flat 
toiletries dollar sales of $4.8 billion, 
a mere 1.1 percent increase over last 
year’s dollar sales of $4.7 billion. 
Like drug stores, the food stores ex- 
perienced a slight dip in unit sales. 


Mass takes the cake 


The big winner for beauty care 
was the mass trade. Mass mer- 
chants posted double-digit increas- 
es—some as high as 30 percent—in 
virtually all beauty care segments. 

Overall, beauty care dollar sales 
for the year at mass merchants to- 
taled $3.9 billion, a hefty 20 percent 
increase compared with last year’s | 
dollar sales of $3.3 billion. Unit 
sales for the class of trade climbed 
17.7 percent to 1.2 billion. 

Mass merchants scored highest on 
hot, growing categories, such as fa- 
cial moisturizers and hair color. This 
class of trade is good at identifying 
trends and capitalizing on them. 

In hair care—a category that fared 
miserably at drug chains— mass 
merchants were making a major 


statement by displaying multi-faced 
top brands on the shelves and retail- 
ing them at rock-bottom prices. Drug 
stores just couldn’t compete. Mass 
merchants, who make their margins 
in other parts of the store, can afford 
to take a loss on toiletry items. 

But drug chains, beset by dimin- 
ishing margins in the pharmacy de- 
partment, had to at least break 


‘Drug chains can 
learn a lesson 
from mass mer- 
chants about 
how to create 
excitement in 
toiletries.’ 


even in toiletries. Drug retailers 
couldn’t fit one more 99-cent sham- 
poo into their mix if the item was 
only a loss leader. 

Mass merchants are also going af- 
ter sun care, a category that looks 
good in drug stores until you see the 
mass figures. 

In drug stores, the category grew 
7.9 percent in dollar sales and 4.8 
percent in unit sales. Not bad. 

Then the mass numbers have to 
be considered; over 34 percent unit 
and dollar sales growth. 


What are the mass merchants do- 
ing? For one, they are pricing about 
$1 below drug stores. Drug stores 
can get sharper on price without 
killing the category. 

Another thing the Kmarts and 
Wal-Marts of the world are doing, 
according to suppliers: they’re giv- 
ing the category better representa- 
tion. They’re using off-shelf displays 
to spark sales. And theyre making 
a statement with multiple facings. 


Still hope for drug stores 


While drug stores may reject the 
mass merchant style of shelf mer- 
chandising because of space limita- 
tions and the desire to offer variety, 
they can still learn a lesson from 
mass merchants about how to better 
create excitement in toiletries. 

In skin care, a category in which 
the drug trade had a percentage de- 
crease in unit sales, dollar sales did 
not drop. Instead, they grew at a 
minimal 1.9 percent. While that 
growth won’t set the world on fire, 
it also means that drug chains have 
stuck with the strategy to bring in 
new products and sell them at a 
profit, rather than give them away. 

And drug stores had the greatest 
dollar volume for the category of the 
three trade channels. Drug’s dollar 
sales were $1.2 billion for the year, 
while the mass trade’s dollar vol- 
ume was a little more than half 
that, at $675 million. 

Surprisingly, even supermarkets 
had an increase in dollar sales for 
the category, at nearly 6 percent. 
Dollar sales for the food trade, at 
$668 million, nearly caught up to 
the mass trade’s sales as supermar- 
kets introduced upscale products to 
their shelves as well. 

Of course, mass merchants are 
trying to close that gap; they had 
the greatest growth of the three 
channels—a 25 percent increase in 
dollar volume. 

Drug stores can continue to do 
the biggest skin care business by of- 
fering consumers the newest, most 
exciting products as soon as they 
can get them on the shelves. 

Those chains that don’t focus on 
bringing excitement to all toiletry 
categories will be forced to play a 
price-only game with mass mer- 
chants—a game drug stores can 
never win.

Chains seek better hair care margins 


ll in all, the hair care cate- 
gory suffered at drug stores 
this year. 

As drug stores struggled 
to keep the flat category profitable, 
they experimented with new meth- 
ods of allotting shelf space and de- 
bated whether or not to keep niche 
brands with slow turns on the 
shelves. 

Keeping the category profitable 
was a problem. Commodity hair 
care prices were so competitive that 
many chains were retailing top-sell- 
ing shampoos slightly above cost, of- 
ten at a retail price of 99 cents or 89 
cents, which represents a margin 
well below 10 percent. 

Even so, drug chains lost share to 
mass merchants, who drove the 
price on brands such as Suave and 
White Rain down to the bare mini- 
mum, often as low at 79 cents. 

Mass merchants posted 17 per- 
cent increases in both dollar and 
unit sales in shampoo. 

Drug store shampoo sales were 
down in both units and dollars. In 
unit sales, shampoo was down 7.1 
percent, according to Information 
Resources Inc. In dollars, the cate- 
gory dropped 4.7 percent to $451 
million, from $474 million the pre- 
vious year. 

The category was also down at 
food/drug combos, showing a de- 
crease of 3.2 percent in dollar sales 
and 2.4 percent in unit sales. 


Space management crucial 


Drug retailers struggled over how 
to best utilize their shelf space. One 
school of thought held that since 20 
percent of the brands on the market 
generate 80 percent of the business, 
retailers should give more facings to 
those “power brands,” making up in 
unit sales for what they were losing 
in dollar profits. 

Helene Curtis, one manufacturer 
proponent of the philosophy, recom- 
mended eliminating slow-moving 
peripheral brands from the shelves. 

Some retailers agree, claiming 
that it gives them an opportunity to 
make a greater shelf statement in 
commodity hair care. 

Said one retailer: “We are using 
the value brands as a lure to draw 
customers into the store in the 
hopes they will also pick up prod- 
ucts with higher margins. 

Retailers have indeed found that 
when they run a killer promotion on 
a major brand, it boosts the entire 
category. 


More space for fast turners 


To make room for multiple fac- 
ings of top-selling brands, retailers 
have trimmed the slow-moving 
brands from their commodity hair 
care departments. 

Scanning allows them to quickly 
determine which SKUs are moving 
and which won’t make the cut. 

One retailer, who reviewed the 
category every six months, said he 
pulled items from the department 
each time he reviewed it. 

And chain drug stores were get- 
ting tough when it came time to ac- 
commodate new products. 

Manufacturers were almost uni-

out of the planogram to introduce a 
new, innovative product. 

While retailers remain uniform in 
their objections to keeping slow- 
moving products on the shelves, 
they are not unanimous about what 
“slow-moving” means. 

Many retailers cling to the idea 
that drug stores should provide va- 
riety, and for them, that means 
keeping smaller, niche brands that 
may not have the unit movement of 
a Suave on the shelves ts keep cus- 
tomers loyal. 

“How many 99-cent shampoos can 
you carry and continue to make a 
profit?” asked one retailer. 


Niche brands mean profits 


Retailers say obscure niche 
brands give them the opportunity to 
earn back some of the margins that 
have all but disappeared in the bulk 
of the commodity hair care category. 

Indeed, research showed that the 
fastest-growing niche brands had the 
highest share of drug store sales. 

Since drug stores recognized 
these brands first and were willing 
to give them valuable shelf space, 
they benefited from the greate st 
market share for niche products, 
such as Wash ’N Curl and Frizz- 
Ease. And these are the products 
that carry the greatest margin. 

Higher-priced products formulat- 
ed for specific hair types have pro- 
vided the greatest excitement in 
the category. Hair care lines formu- 
lated for color-treated hair and 
those that added a dash of color 
also proved popular. 

CCA’s Wash ’N Curl and Wash ’N 
Tint, L’Oréal’s Permavive and Col- 
orvive and Pantene’s ProV contin- 
ued to hold their places as top-mov- 
ing brands. 

Clairol’s ColorHold System of 
shampoos, conditioners and color re- 
freshers designed especially for col- 
or-treated hair was a strong premi- 
um-priced addition to the category. 

The brand was the first to intro- 
duce a color refresher product, 
available previously only in salons, 
to the mass market. Redmond and 
Revlon followed with their own in- 


troductions. 

CCA’s Wash ’N Tint and Red- 
mond’s Aussie Intermissions gave 
women a wash-in color option and 
created some additional excitement 
in the hair color category. 


Pro hair gets mixed in 


Professional hair care sets were 
weeded out at some chains. Follow- 
ing the example of Wal-Mart, some 
chains decided to do away with pro 
hair care sets, which are dependent 
on distributor’s sets and merchan- 
dise, and order product directly 
from suppliers like Clairol, Ad- 
vanced Research Labs, Alberto-Cul- 
ver and Redmond. 

While retailers and manufactur- 
ers universally agreed that direct 
distribution was desirable, they had 
mixed opinions avout eliminating 
pro sets. 

Proponents of the move said pro 
hair care sets are too dependent on 
diverted salon goods that are diffi- 
cult to get on a regular basis. 

Those in favor of keeping the sets 
in place say that a lack of merchan- 
dise makes it all the more difficult 
to absorb the pro lines into a com- 
modity hair care planogram. 

These retailers and manufactur- 
ers felt that the separation of com- 
modity and pro hair care allowed 
pro hair care products to have a 
higher profile. 

Whatever their position on where 
to merchandise the products, retail- 
ers agreed that pro hair care was a 
profitable sub-segment. Margins 
were holding at 35 to 40 percent, 
and customers were not balking at 
paying as much as $8.99 for a spe- 
cialty products such as Frizz Ease. 

Retailers also did well with 
generic pro hair care product lines, 
such as Russ Kalvin, Mr. Charles 
and European Mystique. 


Color explodes 


Color in general was an explod- 
ing segment of the hair care catego- 
ry. As baby boomers aged and 
grayed, and improved technology 
brought superior products to the at- 
home market, hair color experi-

Conditioners gained 


Intensive and leave-in 
conditioners also grew as a 
segment. What had been a

perked up as new formula-

and effectiveness to the con- 
ditioner segment. 

Conditioner dollar sales

sales in the conditioner seg-

mass dollar sales of $223 
million. 

Food topped everyone in 
unit sales as well with 135 
million units, compared to 
drug at 107 million units 
and mass merchants at 122 
million.

however. Of the $274 mil- 
lion drug chains generated 
in conditioner sales, leave- 
in conditioners accounted 
for $7 million in 1993, a in- 
crease of 42 percent over the 
previous year. 

Intensive conditioners 
grew 9 percent to $46 mil- 
lion in sales in drug stores 
in 1993. The aging popula- 
tion boosted the popularity 
of intensive and deep condi- 
tioners, because as baby 
boomers age, their hair be- 
comes prone to dryness. 

Leave-ins, in liquid, 
mousse and cream formulas, 
offer a convenience factor 
previously unavailable to 
the market and satisfy 
needs that had been previ- 
ously unanswered. 

Best of all, both forms of 
conditioners represent added 
sales, not cannibalization of 
other conditioner products. |

thnic HBA sales in most 

chain drug stores remained 

soft through 1993. The 

problem was partly compe- 
tition, which forced many chains to 
discount ethnic hair care products, 
especially high-ticket products like 
relaxers, and partly the lack of 
new fashion styles, which are need- 
ed to drive sales in this category, 
buyers said. 

The strongest growth segments in 
hair care were styling aids, up 14 
percent in units and 13 percent in 
dollars; and hair coloring products, 
up 8 percent in units and 6 percent 
in dollars. These figures were sup- 
plied by Towne-Oller, the market 
research division of Information Re- 
sources Inc. that tracks ethnic prod- 
uct sales through distribution cen- 
ters and mass retail outlets like 
drug stores, discount stores and 
beauty and barber supply shops. 

For the 12 months through De- 
cember 1993, Towne-Oller reported 
that sales of ethnic products in all 
mass market retail trade classes re- 
mained essentially flat. 

No one is sure how much ethnic 
hair care business is done in mass 
merchandise stores and beauty/ 
barber supply shops vs. chain drug 
stores, but many chain drug ethnic 
product buyers say they are finding 
it hard to keep these two trade 
classes from stealing their business. 

“There’s no question the catego- 
rys gotten more competitive,” Har- 
co’s ethnic products buyer Charles 
Monk said. “The deep discounters 
are trying to steal our sales; dis- 
counting beauty and barber shops 
are turning up everywhere. We 
know we can’t compete by just drop- 
ping prices.” 

Monk said the strategy Tus- 
caloosa, Ala.-based Harco uses is to 
give its customers good value, as 
well as the selection and the variety 
they can’t get in other stores. 

“I have items my customers can’t 
get at Wal-Mart,” he said. “That’s 
how we try to compete.” 

At K&B in New Orleans, ethnic 
hair care buyer Chuck Gautreaux 
reported that in the face of intensi- 
fying competition, K&B now adver- 
tises ethnic products much more 
frequently. In addition to its two 
main promotions for Black History 
Month and Back To School, K&B 
also runs promotions in just about 
every circular. 

“We're doing more bonus packs,” 
said Gau‘~eaux, “because that’s 
what’s been driving the category. 
We're also doing more public service 
promotions.” 

Gautreaux said public service 
promotions give K&B a chance to 
reach out and build its visibility in 
the African-American community. 

Other drug chains say that in ad- 
dition to heavier competition for the 
ethnic consumer, sales are softening 
because product usage isn’t growing. 

At Chicago-based Walgreens, 
spokesperson Michael Polzin report- 
ed that ethnic hair care product 
sales were down this year, and 
Polzin attributed part of the decline 
to product usage being down. 

“To kick off the category again, 
we're going to need some new hair

As one of the largest segments 
of the ethnic hair care category, 
with almost a 20 percent share of 
all dollar sales, relaxers remain 
an important growth area for 
chain drug stores and ethnic 
product distributors. 

According to Towne-Oller, re- 
laxers were up 4 percent in units 
in 1993, but because of competi- 
tion that resulted in price dis- 
counting, they were flat in dollar 
sales. 

In some chain drug stores, 
however, relaxers were up mod- 
erately in dollars as well as 
units. In Detroit, for example, 
Perry Drug’s ethnic products 
buyer Michelle Jones reported 
that relaxers were one of her 
growth areas in 1993. 

“The increases are moderate, 
in single-digit increments,” she 
said, “but the segment is outper- 
forming the category.” 

“Relaxers have done very well 
for us,” said Rite Aid’s Beth 
Dugan, “It’s a very popular style 
right now, and there are a lot of 
new products coming out in that 
segment.” 

Hair color products have been 
one of the strongest segments in 
ethnic hair care, up 6 percent in 
dollars and 8 percent in units for 
1993, according to Towne-Oller. 

Now, with Soft Sheen launch- 
ing a new Optimum Care hair col- 
or line, many buyers think the 
category’s growth could be up in 
double-digit increments this year. 

In Oklahoma, Kent Hum- 
phreys, president of Jack’s Ser-

He said the packaging is “the 
most beautiful I’ve ever seen.” 

Styling products have been 
selling well in most ethnic stores. 
According to Towne-Oller, sales 
of ethnic hair styling products 
were up 13 percent in dollars and 
14 percent in units last year. 

At Rite Aid, Dugan said styling 
aids has been one of her strongest 
growth segments. Luster’s Pink 
Oil continues to remain very 
strong in Rite Aid stores. 

At Perry Drug, buyer Michelle 
Jones said the growth in hair 
styling aids “goes along with the 
increased use of relaxers.” 

The category did have one 
strong launch in the skin care 
segment, New York-based Bio- 
Cosmetic Research Labs’ Black 
Opal line has been doing very 
well in chains like Osco, Perry 
and K&B. 


Kids make their mark 


Children’s toiletries has been 
another strong performer in the 
ethnic segment, although there

since it’s not tracked as a sepa- 
rate segment.

ing report that some of their 
biggest increases have come 
from children’s kits like Pro 
Line’s Just For Me children’s re- 
laxer kit. Soft Sheen’s Baby 
Love children’s toiletries have 
also been a winner.

s baby boomers age, they 
are snapping up more up- 
scale facial skin care prod- 
ucts at drug stores. 

Facial skin moisturizers reached 
$645 million in dollar sales at drug 
stores in 1993, an increase of 1.7 
percent, according to Information 
Resources Inc. 

Consumers, convinced that they 
could buy products comparable to 
those offered at specialty and de- 
partment stores, were willing to 
move to the mass sector to fill their 
skin care needs. 

The new, upscale products that 
customers found on drug store 
shelves kept them interested in 
shopping the mass trade. 

Mass merchants benefited from 
the trend; their dollar sales for the 
segment reached $342 million, a 29 
percent increase over the previous 
year. And food/drug combos nearly 
caught up, with dollar sales of $341 
million, a 7 percent increase for 
that channel. 

The whole skin care category is 
up about 8 percent,” said Rosie Al- 
bright, executive vice president of 
Revlon’s Almay division. “Baby 
boomers are getting into skin care 
in a big way.” 

Facial moisturizers containing al- 
pha hydroxy acids (AHAs) led the 
market. With consumer press cov- 
erage contributing in a large part to 
the success of Neoteric’s Alpha Hy- 
drox line, L’Oréal’s Plénitude, Proc- 
ter & Gamble’s Oil of Olay and 
Chesebrough-Pond’s all introduced 
alpha hydroxy, hydroxy or other 
acid products to their lines. 

Said one buyer for a Canadian 
chain: “The 10 to 15 percent growth 
we had in skin was fueled by new 
entries by Olay, Plénitude and 
Pond’s into the category. The 
growth of anti-wrinkle facial mois- 
turizers points to the growth of this 
category at mass and away from the 
department stores.” 

Franchised cosmetics skin care 
lines also added their entries to the 
category. Maybelline expanded its 
Revitalizing facial skin care line, 
aimed at the 35-plus age group, 
with five SKUs of facial treatment 
products. Revlon added its answer 
to AHAs with Revlon Results, which 
uses a complex called alpha recap, 
and Almay’s Time-Off, formulated 
with a gentle glucose complex. 


AHAs and beyond 


“These represent the next genera- 
tion of products. Alpha hydroxy 
products are terrific at smoothing 
wrinkles, but they don’t really mois- 
turize. These products do both with- 
out irritating the skin, as many 
products do,” said a Revlon 
spokesperson. 
And buyers expect that the addi- 
tional ad dollars that cosmetic com- 
panies will put behind the products 
will further strengthen the category. 
“I think consumers need even 
more education,” said Marilyn 
Phelps, buyer at Indianapolis-based 
Keltsch Bros. “Lines like Results, 
with Revlon’s ad money behind it, 
will really add to the category.” 
Said a West Coast retailer: “These 
products are all doing well for new 


Technology drives skin care sales 


products, but they could 
use more advertising.” 

Phelps credits the prod- 
ucts with lifting the facial 
skin care category out of 
the doldrums. “Skin care 
was soft for a number of 
years. Now, it’s really mov- 
ing,” she said. 

Said Almay’s Albright: 
“Technology has been get- 
ting better and better. Not 
only are the products supe- 
rior, but consumers do per- | 
ceive a difference in the 
products available.” = 

A recent study sponsored 
by Almay and conducted 
through women’s maga- 
zines showed that a full 50 
percent of women surveyed 
understood how alpha hy- 
droxy products worked. 

More upscale high-tech 
products will follow and 
further inspire the catego- 
ry as suppliers chase after 
consumers over 30 who are 
determined to minimize 
wrinkles, hydrate dry skin 


and keep looking younger. 

AHAs found their way 
into toners and other skin 
care products. Neoteric’s 
expansion of its original fledgling 
two-SKU line to include, among oth- 
er products, a toner with AHAs, and 
Pond’s Self-Foaming Facial 
Cleanser with alpha nutrium, are 
just two examples. 

And technology paved the way for 
other breakthrough products aimed 
at other niche groups as well. 

For skin care for the youthful set, 
hydrogels have become the hottest 
new product segment. The oil-free, 
clear products offer consumers the 
benefit of moisturizing with a non- 
greasy water-base, rather than an 
oil-based formula, which can clog 
pores. Oil of Olay and Beiersdorf’s 
Visage products are just two prod- 
ucts filling that niche on the market. 


Relief for dry skin 


Therapeutic hand and body prod- 
ucts were also a driving force be- 
hind the skin care category. While 
dollar sales of the segment were 
down 1.2 percent at drug stores to 
$323 million, dollar sales were up 
24.1 percent at mass merchants to 
$2u8 million. Dollar sales were up 
3.2 percent at food/drug combos. 

Beiersdorf’s Eucerin and Chese- 
brough-Pond’s Dermasil were just 
two formulas for severely dry skin 
that found success in the market. 
These products, which carried the 
weight of the dermatologist’s ap- 
proval, answered the consumer 
need for high-performance OTC 
therapeutic skin care products. 

“Almost 14 percent of the 1,500 
women in a recent study considered 
their skin to be dry, but had found 
no effective product solution at the 
mass level,” said Alan Jope, mar- 
keting manager for Dermasil. 

The products also caused con- 
sumers to trade up to higher-priced 
products, a trend that pleased 
retailers. “Eucerin is doing very 
well for us. Without these new en- 
tries, hand and body would be a 


Facial moisturizers with alpha hydroxy acids and 
similar formulations led the way in skin care. 


very flat category segment,” said 
Keltsch Bros.’ Phelps. 

Technology played a big role in 
existing brands of hand and body lo- 
tions as well. Jergens continued its 
“Science You Can Touch” campaign, 
and Chesebrough-Pond’s began fea- 
turing the 800 number of its Pond’s 
Institute on new products. 


Marketing, research essential 


Research, as well as packaging 
and advertising, is selling product. 

Many drug chains ran more cir- 
cular ads on skin care items this 
year and devoted additional in-store 
promotion to the products. 

Manufacturers also provided more 
support in the form of promo packs 
and consumer offers. Couponing be- 
came more important to the catego- 
ry as new therapeutic brands fought 
existing brands, such as Keri, Curél 
and Lubriderm, and commodity and 
value lines jockeyed for position. 

“Historically, we didn’t do much 
couponing before,” said Stu Fine, 
vice president of marketing at St. 
Ives. “Now, the market is so 
competitive, we really have to. Hav- 
ing a low-price feature isn’t enough.” 

Fine said virtually every player is 
doing more in the way of rebates, 
following P&G’s and Pond’s exam- 
ples of offering “gift certificates” — 
coupons by any other name. 

St. Ives, like other brands, is 
searching for meaningful ways to 
bring value to customers through 
on-pack promotions. A recent promo 
included the offer of three free is- 
sues of Health magazine with the 
purchase of facial skin products. 
Fine said the promotion supported 
the product’s positioning as a 
healthy, natural product. 

Creative promotions will abound 
as more new skin care products 
crowd the shelves and consumers 
become even more savvy shoppers.

In bath, the shakeout 


he bath shakeout began this 

year. In drug stores, the 

segment dropped 11.9 per- 

cent in unit sales and 9.3 
percent in dollar sales to $432 mil- 
lion from $476 million the year be- 
fore, according to Information Re- 
sources Inc. 

Sales were down in the food chan- 
nel as well—2 percent in dollar 
sales and over 4 percent in unit 
sales. 

The only growth appeared in 
mass. There, dollar sales increased 
11 percent to $403 million, over last 
year’s $363 million. Unit sales grew 
18.1 percent. 

But double-digit increases are no 
longer the norm. As retailers start- 
ed overfilling a niche, bath prod- 
ucts moved much slower. Some 
chains were left with merchandise 
they found difficult to move. Now 
wiser, they are pruning the depart- 
ment of lines not sufficiently sup- 
ported by suppliers. 

“The category was overstated at 
some chains,” said Mark Kaplan, 
president of Sarah Michaels. “What 
started as a niche business became 
a free-for-all until the business be- 
came so diluted, it had little impact 
at many chains.” 

Some chains are trying to get rid 
of slow-moving lines but are finding 
themselves locked into agreements 
with suppliers who won’t take mer- 
chandise back. 

Chains that were slow to jump on 
the bath bandwagon are counting 
their blessings. “Our bath section is 
up because we’ve added a few 
items, not every new line that’s out 
there,” said one buyer at a Mid- 
western chain. 

Retailers who have considerably 
beefed up their departments over 
the past year are not interested in 
taking in any new lines. “Our sales 
were up last year, but I’m not 
adding anything else,” said Marsha 
Gaynor, buyer at Pharmhouse. 
“Slow-moving lines will be pulled. If 
the merchandise doesn’t move, it’s 
off the shelves.” 


Shower gels shine 


Gaynor, like many other retailers, 
is seeing the fastest growth in the 
shower gel segment of the category. 

The potential growth of that seg- 
ment has attracted new players. 
Upstart bath lines, such as the 
Generation X-targeted Zenue, are 
relying heavily on the draw of 
shower gels. 

Beiersdorf’s Nivea and Bencki- 
ser’s Calgon restaged their bath 
lines to make a greater shower 
statement. 

Jergens added an entry to the 
commodity segment with a body 
shampoo, which the company is 
merchandising in the personal wash 
section. 

“About 80 percent of German and 
60 percent of British consumers use 
a liquid shower gel instead of a bar 
soap,” said Richard Goheen, new 
products marketing manager for 
Jergens. “Ten years ago, only 1 per- 
cent of Japanese consumers used 
shower gels, but with the availabili- 
ty of new products, over one-third of 
consumers now use liquid body

drug chains are paring down their selection to include only the fastest movers. 


cleansers. We think that will hap- 
pen in the U.S. once women become 
aware of the products.” 

To make sure that women are 
aware of its new introduction, Jer- 
gens is spending $17 million in con- 
sumer advertising and sampling. 


Ad spending becomes key 


And other manufacturers— moti- 
vated by the desire to be the brands 
that retailers retain when other 
bath lines get the ax—are pumping 
more dollars into what had been an 
under-promoted category. 

Said one retailer: “Going forward, 
we're looking to carry the lines that 
can support the big retailers with 
marketing and promotion.” 

National print and television ad 
campaigns, couponing, sampling, 
trial sizes and on-pack promotions 
will become more important to the 
category in 1994. 

Benckiser, Yardley, Sarah 
Michaels and Zenue will all have 
stepped-up ad and promotion bud- 
gets this year. Some lines will use 
television ads for the first time. 


Price must be right 


Retailers are also carefully exam- 
ining lines based on pricing. 

“Freeman’s items do well in my 
market because they are value- 
priced but have great packaging. 
Anything over $5 is going to turn 
my customer off,” said one buyer. 

Items retailing at $9 and $10 are 
inappropriately priced for the mass 
consumer, many buyers said. Look- 
ing like a department store line is 
desirable, but retailing like a de- 


partment store line is another story. 


Said Paul Carlson, buyer for 
Standard Drugs: “We top off in the 
commodity bath at $3 to $4. When 
you talk about moving units, you 
can’t go above that.” 

Some retailers have turned to pri- 
vate label to offer consumers up- 
scale bath lines at reasonable 
prices. 

Said Carol Smith, director of 
marketing for the Cosmetic Group 
Inc., a manufacturer of branded 
and private label bath products: 
“The market is looking for value in 


bath. The consumer is still getting 
8 ounces for $8.” 

While more chains began to look 
favorably on private label products, 
most agreed that they would not 
put the chain name on the bottle. 
Said Hope Stone, buyer at PayLess: 
“Even though there’s not much 
brand recognition of the current 
lines, I would go for a control label.” 

When it comes to branded lines, 
retailers want it all. They wish for 
an upscale-looking line, but they 
want it to retail at a price point to 
which consumer can relate. 

And that’s not all they desire. 
They want help in merchandising 
their bath sections, but they don’t 
want large freestanding special fix- 
tures for every bath line they carry. 

While buyers will universally 
agree that a successful bath 
department depends on creating an 
ambiance around the merchandise, 
few have the space to devote to 
more than one special display. 
They want merchandise that can 
go in-line. 

They wish for manufacturers who 
offer them cardboard floorstands, 
sidekicks and shelf displays that 
can be used on a promotional basis. 
Tria! sizes and special offers also 
work well for retailers on floor- 
stands and counterstands, allowing 
the consumer to try the product. 


Help with sell-through 


Retailers also are searching for 
help from manufacturers in selling 
the merchandise once it’s on the 
shelves. Sinclair & Valentine, for 
example, is providing consumer ed- 
ucation on its Aromatherapaes line 
through packaging and consumer 
pamphlets. 

Signage is also important. Those 
suppliers who provide flexible sig- 
nage options for retailers received 
high marks. 

Suppliers who abandon the re- 
tailer are not being judged lightly. 
Lines with a poor reputation will be 
finding representation in fewer 
doors. “One supplier begged me to 
bring in a line of bath and skin care 
products, and once it was in the

Retailers are thankful 
that Gillette’s Series line 
has provided them with a 
higher margin and some ad- 
vertising dollars for the cat- 
egory. “That line does very 
well for us in terms of dol- 
lars,” said the buyer from 
the Midwest. 

The 14-SKU line of shav- 
ing preps, skin conditioners, 
deodorants and antiperspi- 
rants is being merchandised 
as one full line at most drug 
chains, much like Plénitude 
skin products are merchan- 
dised in the skin care set. 

A Gillette spokesperson 
said the positioning is the 
result of consumer research 
showing that men want to 
purchase all of their groom- 
ing products in one place. 

Gillette will make further 
inroads in the category with 
its introduction of a second 
scent in the Series line, 
Wild Rain. The company 
also plans to launch Sensor 
Excel, an even higher-ticket 
razor, sometime this year. 

Other brands, not content 
to let Gillette run away 
with business, advanced co- 
op funds and launched 
coupon drops and value 
packs last year. Some 
brought new products de- 
signed for consumers with 
sensitive skin to the mar- 
ket. Among them: Edge’s vi- 
tamin E and protective lu- 
bricant formulations and 
Mennen’s Razor Protectant 
and Advanced Lubricant 
shaving creams. 


Clear on deodorants 


Deodorant sales, which 
also showed double-digit dol- 
lar and unit increases at 
mass merchandisers, were 
slightly down at drug stores. 

The news in the category 
continues to be clear formu- 
lations, but at least one buy- 
er said that consumers are 
trying the products but not 
making repeat purchases. 

“The formulations haven’t 
been perfected yet. I think 
consumers react better to 
antiperspirants than they do 
to deodorants,” said another 
buyer. 

Higher price points may 
be standing in the way. Said 
Snyder’s Carlson: “I’m see- 
ing resistance to higher- 
priced clear products. My 
best selling deodorants re- 
tail at $1.99 or below.” 

— Barbara White

Annual Report 


Sun care needs right mix to maintain growth 


ncreased consumer con- 
cern about the harmful 
effects of the sun fueled 
the growth of sun blocks 
and sunless tanners in 
1993, making the sun care 
category one of the steadiest 
growth categories. But drug 
retailers, facing an over- 
SKU’ed category, are 
searching for the right mix 


of product. 

Dollar sales of sun care 
products climbed to $198 
million at drug stores, a 
7.89 percent increase over 
the previous year’s sales, ac- 
cording to Information Re- 
sources Inc. Unit sales in- 
creased 4.78 percent in the 
drug channel as well, to 34 
million compared to 32.5 


96 Drug Store News, April 25, 1994 


million the year before. 

Sunscreens and sun 
blocks will continue to gain 
momentum as consumers 
use sun products for protec- 
tive rather than cosmetic 
reasons. 

Schering-Plough’s success 
with Shade UVA Guard, 
which retails for $9.99 and 
protects against UVA and 


UVB rays, is high-ticket tes- 
timony to consumers’ con- 
cern about the damaging ef- 
fects of the sun. 

Schering’s Water Babies 
line has increased dramati- 
cally and Coppertone for 
Kids has also had a strong 
start after its introduction 
last year. 

Sport products, which stay 


on through perspiration and 
swimming, proved to be a 
hot segment, as did gel and 
spray-on formulations that 
are light and nongreasy. 

New water-in-oil emul- 
sion technology, which pro- 
duces lighter weight, less ir- 
ritating products that are 
water-resistant, will drive 
the category next year, ac- 
cording to Debbie Coles, 
marketing consultant for 
the new Sun Date’s line. 

Manufacturers also have 
begun combining sun blocks 
with bug repellents. Body 
Glove’s Bug and Sun Block 
formula is just one example 
of convenient, dual purpose 
entries in the market. 

The biggest gainers of all 
were the sunless tanners, a 
vast improvement over ear- 
ly sunless tanning products. 


Fighting for share 


But all the growth and 
niche products that come 
with it have led to an over- 
SKU’ed department. Drug 
stores are struggling to hit 
the right mix while keeping 
their share of the business. 

Mass merchants are pric- 
ing about $1 below drug 
stores. As a result, drug re- 
tailers will probably become 
more aggressive with pric- 
ing themselves. 

“We've always been very 
aggressive in our pricing,” 
said one buyer at a North- 
east chain. “We run a lot of 
promotions during the sum- 
mer. I think other chains in 
this market have been ad- 
justing their prices so they 
don't lose share.” 

The buyer said the chain 
also makes a statement 
with sun care, devoting 16 
to 20 feet to the merchan- 
dise and expanding facings. 

“When you do one or two 
facings, the department gets 
lost,” he said. 

Suppliers say that is in- 
deed the trick that has 
earned mass merchants a 
bigger share. 

“You can probably reach 
100 percent of the cus- 
tomers by stocking 100 
SKUs—88 SKUs of proven 
products and 12 new en- 
tries,” said Mike Jones, di- 
rector of trade marketing 
for Schering. “Stores don’t 
need to over-SKU, but they 
do need to give more than 
one facing to the category.” 

Off-shelf display is key to 
selling sun care, which is 
rarely a planned purchase. 


— Barbara White
