rug store sales of over-the- 
counter medicines in- 
creased a scant 1.87 per- 
cent last year, and in 
virtually every category drug retail- 
ers lost market share. 

There were strong sales gains in 
certain areas, most notably vita- 
mins. cough/cold and first aid, but 
drug stores still lost market share. 

Mass merchandisers, which had 
nearly across-the-board gains of 20 
percent to 30 percent in virtually 
every OTC category, grabbed mar- 
ket share from drug stores and su- 
permarkets. 

One of the year’s best OTC perfor- 
mances was turned in by the 
cough/cold category. Retailers na- 
tionwide reported that strong sales 
were driven by a harsh winter and 
a very severe flu season. 

Cough/cold racked up $3.38 bil- 
lion in total sales, for a 11.4 percent 
increase from the previous year’s 
tally of $3 billion, according to In- 
formation Resources Inc. - 

On its way to becoming a $2 bil- 
lion category is vitamins. Sales in- 
creased roughly 12 percent in drug 
stores, as the category in all trade 
classes grew from $1.42 billion to 
$1.67 billion. 

First aid rounded out the year’s 
biggest OTC gainers, increasing 13 
percent from $1.17 billion to $1.33 
billion. 

Laxatives, antacids, eye/lens care, 
foot care and feminine care recorded 
flat or declining drug store sales. 

Despite 1993’s lack of stronger 
sales gains in more OTC categories, 
the long-term outlook remains 
strong for a variety of reasons. 
Some of those most frequently cited 
by manufacturers, buyers and in- 
dustry trade groups include: 

@ Atop the list of why OTC sales 
will grow in the future is the fact 
that the elderly comprise the fastest 
growing population group. Senior 
citizens are also the heaviest users 
of OTC products. 

@ Right up there with the aging 
population is the Rx-to-OTC switch 
phenomenon. The success of prod- 
ucts previously available on a pre- 


OTC products defined 


“Misc. remedies” include anti-itch medica- 
tions, chest rubs, depilatories, anti-diarrheals, 
ear drops, hemorrhoid preps, wart removers, 
motion sickness remedies, ear care products, 
multi-purpose liquid and powder remedies. 

“Other” includes baby needs, misc. health 
treatments (epsom salts, hemorrhoid wipes, lice 
treatments, thumb-sucking remedies), external 
analgesic rubs, misc. remedy tablets (diarrhea 
tablets, diuretics, multi-purpose remedy 
tablets, motion sickness treatments), misc. 
health tablets (caffeine tablets, drinking water 
tablets, sleeping aids), moist towelettes and 
anti-smoking products. 


trong growth 
predicted for 
OTC category 


scription-only basis is well-docu- 
mented. Conventional wisdom holds 
that more of these seemingly sure- 
fire best-sellers are on the way. 

To take full advantage, manufac- 
turers recommend getting the prod- 
ucts in stores early, providing infor- 
mation, prominently merchandising 
the products and briefing store per- 
sonnel on the OTC availability of 
the new products. 

@ Consumers are increasingly be- 
coming better educated. They there- 
fore are more capable of self-med- 
icating with OTC products, 
according to the Nonprescription 
Drug Manufacturers Association, 
the trade group representing the in- 
terests of OTC manufacturers. 

e There is an untapped potential 
with OTCs. NDMA research indi- 
cates that many consumers still rely 
on home remedies and/or choose to 
tough out the condition. Sales 


growth is expected as more of these 
potential consumers are converted 
to OTC product users. 

e High margin private label ver- 
sions of leading brands are also im- 
proving profits. Today’s sophisticat- 
ed private label companies are 
manufacturing top-grade products 
that retailers promote aggressively 
with money-back guarantees. 

For the above reasons, many re- 
tailers and manufacturers expect 
that, longer-term, OTCs will com- 
prise a larger percentage of drug 
store profits. OTCs can deliver mar- 
gins in the 30 percent to 40 percent 
range, and the products’ small pack- 
age sizes also deliver better-than- 
average profit per square foot. 

OTC sales could also benefit from 
a reformed health care system that 
emphasizes self-treatment. 

“Switch brings lower health care 
costs through the saved costs and 
time of unneeded doctor’s visits,” 
said William Soller, senior vice presi- 
dent and director of science and 
technology with the NDMA. “It 
seems the FDA has concluded that 
switch is important as a means to... 


improve health care practice.” 
— Mike Troy 


Category overview 


Drug chains’ piece 
of the OTC pie 
Chains: $7,127M (73%) 
Independents: $2,600M (27%) 


Diabetes remains one of the 
strongest OTC categories for drug 
stores. 

“Probably the biggest increase I 
had in the OTC department was 
the diabetes section,” said K&B 
buyer Jude Eserman. 

“Last year we did phenomenally 
well with the diabetic category as 
we expanded our selection of me- 
ters to 10,” said PayLess Drug 
Stores buyer Joe Potts. 

Much of the growth has to do 
with drug retailers who have de- 
veloped creative merchandising 
strategies and displays. “There is 
certainly every indication that the 
drug class of trade is going to con- 
tinue growing the diabetes catego- 
ry,” said Ron Jackson, vice presi- 
dent of sales and marketing with 
Cascade Medical Inc., manufactur- 
er of the Checkmate Plus Blood 
Glucose Monitoring System. 

“Most of the growth came from 
those chains that are more aggres- 
sive in their merchandisizg ap- 
proach,” said Jackson. “The chains 
that are keeping the products be- 
hind the pharmacy counter where 
customers can’t see it, feel it and 
touch it are not maximizing their 
potential in the category.” 

Neil Luckianow, senior trade 
sales manager with LifeScan, 
agreed: “If [monitors] are going to 
be behind the counter, it is very im- 
portant they are clearly visible.” 

As retailers have begun to more 
openly merchandise the category, 
manufacturers have responded 
with new products and package 
designs that are best described as 


Diabetes care sweet for drug chains 


upscale and artistic. 

Boehringer Mannheim’s newest 
addition to the Accu-Chek family 
of products is the Advantage. Cas- 
cade Medical has introduced a new 
version of the Checkmate Plus 
Blood Glucose Monitoring System. 
Miles Diagnostics division will 
soon introduce a new monitor 
called Encore. In addition to being 
simpler to use with more features, 
the Advantage meter’s marbleized 
midnight and royal blue finish, 
Checkmate Plus’ purple and 
metallic copper color scheme and 
the peach and teal of Miles’ Encore 
make for eye-catching designs that 
shouldn’t be hidden from con- 
sumers. All three products will be- 
gin distribution this year. 

Demand in the category will con- 
tinue to be driven by the results of 
the Diabetes Control and Compli- 
cations Trial. The 10-year National 
Institutes of Health project illus- 
trated the health benefits of vigi- 
lant control of blood glucose levels. 

“As the effects of a healthy test- 
ing regimen demonstrated by the 
DCCT are communicated by doc- 
tors, certified diabetes educators, 
pharmacists and nurse educators, 
it will unleash the market poten- 
tial of patients who have been di- 
agnosed with diabetes but are not 
currently testing,” said Mark 
Stanton, Boehringer Mannheim’s 
retail marketing manager. 

Alternative test strips for use 
with all the major branded meters 
also present retailer opportunities 
that are not yet fully exploited.

Vitamins chalk up vigorous sales

More shelf space and better information on vitamin/mineral supplements’ health 
benefits helped the category’s sales increase 12.1 percent in drug chains last year. 


ith a 12.1 percent sales in- 

crease during 1993, the vit- 

amin category set the pace 
for chain drug retailers’ entire OTC 
department. 

The category totaled $880 million 
during the 52-week period ended 
Jan. 2, 1994, compared to $785 mil- 
lion for the same period the previ- 
ous year. 

Retailers and manufacturers at- 
tributed the growth to a variety of 
factors: additional shelf space, ongo- 
ing revelations about the benefits of 
nutritional supplementation and 
widespread publicity about the 
long-term health benefits of vitamin 
consumption. 

Although vitamin sales were 
healthy in drug stores, gains made 
by mass merchandisers and super- 
markets were even stronger. Mass 
merchandiser sales rose 43 percent 
to $335 million, up from $234 mil- 
lion. Supermarket sales increased 
slightly more than drug sales, regis- 
tering 12.4 percent growth to $454 
million, from $404 million. 

While still the dominant source 
for vitamins, drug stores lost mar- 
ket share in the category, slipping 
to 53 percent of sales in 1993, from 
55 percent of sales in 1992. 

Supermarkets also lost about one 
share point, from 1992’s 28 percent. 
Mass merchandisers were the big 
gainers, increasing their market 
share to 20 percent, from 16 percent. 

“More and more information is 
coming-eut about how vitamins pre- 
vent aging and how they promote 
wellness. It’s much cheaper to stay 
well than it is to get sick,” said John 
Higdon, director of marketing with 
Kyolic Ltd., manufacturer of Kyolic, 
an aged garlic extract; Be-sure, a 
food enzyme anti-flatulence prod- 
uct; and Kyo-Chrome, garlic with 
chromium and zinc. 

“Our research indicates that 37 
percent of adults take multi-vita- 
mins, so we feel like there is still op- 
portunity for category growth,” said 
Robert Sanders, a regional manager 
with Lederle Consumer Health. 
Lederle’s Centrum brand leads the 


category with a 19 percent market 
share. A new line of Centrum prod- 
ucts, Centrum singles in vitamins C 
and E, beta-carotene and calcium, 
began distribution in February. 

“We’re very excited that the 
brand is going to be a very big 
brand for us,” Sanders said. “We 
have been the innovators in the cat- 
egory, and we plan to support our 
brands with unprecedented levels of 
advertising during 1994.” 

An assortment of new products is 
also available from Nature’s Boun- 
ty. Because women are the biggest 
buyers of vitamins, a special line of 
six products has been created for 
women. Products include formula- 
tions for stress, menopause, iron 
support, bone density, premenstrual 
syndrome and hair, skin and nails. 


‘Sixteen feet is still our 
largest vitamin set right 
now, but we are looking 
at expanding it in the 
coming year. All the 
hype about vitamins that 
appeared in magazines 
and on television cer- 
tainly spearheaded the 
whole increase.’ 

—Musil, Snyder 


At Miles’ consumer health care 
products division, the continued 
success of Flintstones, the chil- 
dren’s segment leader, and the re- 
launch of the One-A-Day line were 
highlights. 

“The vitamin category did well 
because we got a lot of good publici- 
ty,” said Bill Turpin, Miles’ director 
of trade and consuiner relations. 
“One-A-Day needed a facelift, and 
we think there is still some upside 


potential with Flintstones. We are 
also looking at some marketing tie- 
ins with The Flintstones movie that 
is coming out soon.” 

The One-A-Day line also uses a 
new gravity-feed perpetual fullness 
display, Turpin said. 

Because of the success of the vita- 
min/supplement department, retail- 
ers expanded shelf space for the cat- 
egory or plan to do so in 1994. 

“Sixteen feet is still our largest 
vitamin set right now, but we are 
looking at expanding it in the com- 
ing year,” said Roger Musil, a buy- 
er with Snyder Drug Stores. “All 
the hype about vitamins that ap- 
peared in magazines and on televi- 
sion certainly spearheaded the 
whole increase.” 

At PayLess Drug Stores, buver 
Joe Potts said the category did well 
for the chain. “We got a lot of good 
press, and we are riding a wave 
right now with people realizing the 
benefits, both short- and long-term, 
of nutritional supplementation,” he 
said. “The category did so well that 
we expanded the mix and incorpo- 
rated them much more aggressively 
into the promotional cycle.” 

PayLess has a 20- to 24-foot vita- 
min set, 8 feet of sports nutritional 
products and 8 feet of herbal prod- 
ucts and natural toiletries. 


Homeopathics, herbals popular 


The herbal and homeopathic 
products are the hottest segment of 
the vitamin and nutritional catego- 
ry. These products continue to make 
the transition from health food and 
specialty stores to mainstream 
mass retail outlets. 

“The category did very well in 
1993, and I think 1994 is going to 
be our biggest year,” said Jeff 
Hilton, vice president of finance 
with Murdoch Healthcare, manu- 
facturer of the Nature’s Way line. 
“Herbal supplements are one of our 
hottest categories, and we now have 
a full herb line to offer and garlic 
and ginseng products that are new.” 

Murdoch has increased its offer- 
ing this year to 73 SKUs, up from 
25, and has developed new spinner 
racks and endcaps it calls the “nat- 
ural pharmacy.” 

Another player in the herbal sup- 
plement market is Nature’s Bounty, 
with its 14-SKU Herbal Harvest 
line introduced in early 1993. 

Also new in 1994 from Sunsource 
Health Products, manufacturer of 
Ginsana, Rejuvex and Garlique, is a 
new line called Sunsource Tradition- 
al Homeopathic Medicines. Products 
include allergy, sinus, insomnia, 
arthritis and cold/flu relief formulas. 
Sunsource promises to advertise the 
products heavily, and some retailers 
have already put the line in, hoping 
it will do as well as Ginsana, its 
market-leading ginseng product. 

Snyder’s Musil said, “We aren’t 
carrying those products yet, but we 
are seriously considering it because 
we feel there’s a need and a demand 
for herbal supplements.” He added 
that the category will be ap- 
proached conservatively at first. “I 
don’t see us putting in a 4-foot sec- 


tion right away.” 
— Mike Troy

“Annual Report 


Core OTC segments stay strong in ’93 


he cough/cold, analgesics 

and gastro-intestinal prod- 

uct categories are the heart 

of the OTC department. 
They account for combined sales of 
$7.7 billion, and the products com- 
prise some of the fastest turning, 
highest margin items carried by 
chain drug retailers. 

The largest of the three categories 
continues to be cough/cold, with 
sales that inched over the $3 billion 
mark during 1993. Fueled by one of 
the most severe cold and flu seasons 
in recent years, the cough/cold cate- 
gory proved to be a major traffic 
builder for chain drug stores. 

Sales for 1993 totaled $3.4 billion 
in all trade classes for a 11.4 percent 
increase from the previous year’s $3 
billion. “This was probably one of 
the best cough/cold seasons we have 
had in the last six or seven years,” 
said a buyer with a western chain. 

Chains throughout the country 
reported strong sales of the leading 
branded and private label 
cough/cold items. “Ciba [Consumer 
Pharmaceuticals’ new] Efidac/24 
did really well because it is a truly 
unique product with a new OROS 
delivery system. Tavist is still the 
best line, but Benadryl and Sudafed 
also did well,” said PayLess Drug 
Stores buyer Joe Potts. PayLess fur- 
ther increased sales by using three 
endcaps of cough/cold items. 

In Minneapolis, where the winter 
was particularly severe, Snyder 
Drug buyer Roger Musil agreed 
with Potts. “Efidac and Tavist 
would be two items that stood out 
for us,” Musil said. “The strong 
cough/cold season also enhanced 
analgesic sales.” 

At Big B, vice president of mer- 
chandising and advertising Vincent 
Bruno said, “We had an excellent 
cough/cold season, and that helped 
with our analgesic sales as well. We 
have a large, 24-foot department 
that is probably larger than some 
other chains, and we do push it 
quite heavily.” 

A buyer at a southern drug chain, 
who reported expanding the depart- 
ment last year, added, “Cough/cold 
did extremely well for me from last 
September through January, but it 
died out this spring.” 


Popular brands march on 


In addition to Tavist and Efidac, 
retailers said all of the top-selling 
products continued to do well. Men- 
tioned were Robitussin and 
Dimetapp by A.H. Robbins, Procter 
& Gamble’s NyQuil, Miles’ Alka- 
Seltzer Plus, McNeil’s Tylenol line 
and Burroughs Wellcome’s Su-dafed. 
Liquicaps were the year’s most popu- 
lar dosage form. Sales of liquicap 
products increased by 100 percent, 
according to manufacturers. 

OTC versions of Tavist-1 and 
Tavist-D have proven popular since 
their introduction over a year ago. 
These switch products were popular 
as prescription drugs, and their 
OTC availability has helped the al- 
lergy relief segment of the 
cough/cold category increase by 20 
percent, to more than $300 million, 
according to Kline & Co. OTC buy- 
ers continue to be happy with sales 


Sandoz has said exceeded ex- 
pectations. 

Ciba’s Efidac/24 cold tablets 
incorporate a controlled release 
technology that allows the prod- 
uct to remain effective for 24 
hours. The dosage form has 
proven popular with consumers, 
and Efidac/24 is the first in- 
troduction in a line of new OTC 
cough/cold/allergy products that 
Ciba says will use the new con- 
trolled release delivery system. 


No pain, big gain 


For the time being, the 
cough/cold category is larger 
than analgesics. However, that 
could change in 1994. Sales for 
1993 totaled $2.72 billion, for a 
6.2 percent increase from the 
previous year’s $2.56 billion. 

Buyers of the analgesics cate- 
gory said they are looking for- 
ward to an interesting year be- 
cause of the pending 
introduction of Aleve by the 
Syntex/P&G joint venture. The 
OTC version of naproxen sodi- 
um, approved by the FDA in 
early January, was originally said to 
be ready for shipment in the spring. 
However, the joint venture has been 
secretive about details of the prod- 
uct’s launch, which buyers now say 
may not be until later this year. 

Competing manufacturers said 
they expect it to have a marginal im- 
pact on the other major brands. Ac- 
cording to a spokesman with a major 
branded analgesic manufacturer, 
Aleve will convert prescription 
naproxen sodium customers to the 
OTC version, growing the entire cat- 
egory rather than taking sales away 
from acetaminophen, ibuprofen, as- 
pirin and combination products. 

Another branded manufacturer 
also said he thinks the product will 
grow the category. “Aleve’s big ad- 
vantage is its duration of effective- 
ness with two tablets that can last 
for almost 24 hours,” the manufac- 
turer said. “How successful the 
product is will really depend on 
what individual consumers are cur- 
rently using for their pain.” 

Naproxen products have been 
popular pharmacy items for more 
tha:. a decade. Naprosyn (naprox- 
en), available since 1976, had pre- 
scription sales last year of $503 mil- 
lion, for a 21.7 percent share of the 
$2.3 billion anti-arthritic market. 
Anaprox (naproxen sodium), avail- 
able since 1980, had sales last year 
of $190 million, for a 7.5 percent 
share of the $2.5 billion prescription 
analgesics market. 

Although generic versions of 
naproxen exist, P&G/Syntex 
switched Aleve’s ingredients via a 
new drug application. That gives 
the joint venture three years of 
marketing exclusivity to possibly 
build the drug into a multiple-line 
extension mega-brand. 


Gastro-intestinals mixed 


Not far behind cough/cold and 
analgesics are the gastro-intestinal 
categories of laxatives, antacids and 
anti-diarrheals. It was a disappoint- 
ing year for sales in two of the three 
major GI categories. Antacids had a

Sales of analgesics benefited from the cold, 
wet weather last year. 


slight decrease from $348 million to 
$346 million, and laxative sales had 
a barely perceptible increase from 
$404 million to $406 million. 

The big winner was anti-diarrheal 
sales, which have increased 15 per- 
cent for three consecutive years, and 
finished ’93 with sales of $89 million. 

Market leader Imodium A-D, 
from McNeil, started the category 
growing in 1987 when its active in- 
gredient loperamide hydrochloride 
was switched. Now, most other ma- 
jor digestive remedy companies 
have formulations with the switch 
ingredient, such as Upjohn’s 
Kaopectate II caplets, P&G’s Pepto 
Diarrhea Control and Rhone- 
Poulenc Rorer’s Maalox anti-diar- 
rheal. Retailers have also been 
quick to put in private label ver- 
sions of Imodium A-D. 

The antacids category continues 
to be watched closely because of 
growth potential that will be driven 
by Rx-to-OTC switches. Conversion 
of a popular prescription product 
could send sales skyrocketing. 

Among the most frequently men- 
tioned candidates are SmithKline 
Beecham’s Tagamet, Marion Mer- 
rell Dow’s Carafate, J&J/Merck’s 
Pepcid, Lilly/Whitehall’s Axid and 
Glaxo/Warner-Wellcome’s Zantac. 
When and if those products become 
available will be determined by the 
FDA and remains anyone’s guess at 
this point. Even without a hot-sell- 
ing prescription-heritage OTC, 
antacids have benefited in recent 
years from the introduction of new 
flavors. Cherry creme, cool mint, 
lemon-orange and lemon Swiss 
creme are among flavors offered. 

Laxatives are also being watched 
closely. The aging population is sin- 
gularly cited by manufacturers as 
the main reason sales can be expect- 
ed to flourish. Elderly women com- 
prise the majority of laxative con- 
sumers, and the elderly are also the 
largest users of prescription drugs, 
which can cause interactions and 


constipation problems. 
— Mike Troy

Feminine care sales remain solid 


he combination of improved 
fh technology, the fear of AIDS, 
Rx-to-OTC switches, shifting 

demographics and changing sexual 
attitudes continued to exert influ- 
ence on the family planning and 
feminine care categories in 1993. 

In the contraceptives (male and fe- 
male) segment of the family plan- 
ning category, sales during 1993 de- 
clined and drug stores lost market 
share as consumers sought other re- 
tail venues. Sales of all contracep- 
tives declined 3.36 percent during 
the 52-week period ended Jan. 2, 
1994, compared to the previous year. 

Sales for 1993 in all trade classes 
totaled $314 million, compared to 
$324 million the previous year. 
Drug store sales declined slightly 
more than 8 percent, and drug’s 
market share slid from 69 percent 
to 65.6 percent. Food store sales 
were flat, but mass merchandiser 
sales increased nearly 20 percent, 
and market share grew from 12.6 
percent to 15.6 percent. 


Condom sales rise 3 percent 


The decline in the contraceptives 
category is largely due to declining 
sales of female contraceptives. Drug 
store sales of condoms actually in- 
creased 3 percent to $180 million, 
from $175 million the previous year. 

“Just about every retail outlet in 
America has condoms out and 
available, which is the way it 
should be,” said Kerry Hoffman, 
vice president of national accounts 
with Ansell Consumer Products, 
manufacturer of the LifeStyles 
brand. “Drug stores need to look at 
the level of their gross margins if 
they want to keep customers com- 
ing back to their stores.” 

Other changes affecting the cate- 
gory are also taking place. Women 
now account for 35 percent of total 
condom sales of $280 million, influ- 
encing merchandising decisions 
and category adjacencies. The 12- 
count package is the most popular 
size, accounting for 55 percent of 
sales, followed by the three-pack, 
with 35 percent of the market. The 
36-count package makes up 10 per- 
cent of sales. 


Pregnancy test kits popular 


Growth of condom sales may have 
slowed, but more women than ever 
are using pregnancy test kits. Near- 
ly a third of women have used a 
pregnancy test kit in the past year, 
and usage has tripled since 1981, 
according to manufacturers. Preg- 
nancy test kit sales reached $92 
million in 1988 and are projected to 
surpass $200 million during 1994. 

“If you look at what you have to 
do to test today compared to the 
procedure used three years ago, it’s 
the ease of use that’s driving the 
category’s growth,” said Lou 
Marcinella, vice president and gen- 
eral manager with Becton-Dickin- 
son, manufacturer of the Precise 
home pregnancy test and the Q-test 
ovulation predictor. 

Manufacturers in the category 
continue to innovate and make 
products that are easier to use, give 
faster readings and produce reliable 
results as early as the first day af- 


ter a missed period. 

Johnson & Johnson’s Advanced 
Care Products division will have a 
new version of its Advance home 
pregnancy test available this sum- 
mer, according to vice president of 
sales Rick Ricca. 

“The birth rate is flat to declining, 
but we see growth coming from in- 
creased market penetration as more 
women realize the tests are easy to 
use,” Ricca added. 

Paralleling pregnancy kits’ 
growth in drug stores was ovulation 
kits. A smaller category, with sales 
of only $25 million, drug stores ac- 
count for about 85 percent of sales. 
Most kits rely on technology that de- 
tects a hormonal surge in a woman’s 
urine to determine the optimum 
window to achieve conception. 


Anti-fungals competitive 


Sales of vaginal anti-fungal prod- 
ucts have begun to level off after 
several years of explosive growth. 
And now a host of new competitors 
and line extensions of existing 
brands vie for shelf space that was 
once the exclusive domain of Moni- 
stat 7 and Gyne-Lotrimin. Many re- 
tailers now have a private label of- 
fering and stock mid-price value 
brands, such as Miles’ Mycelex-7, 
Lake Pharmaceutical’s Femizol-7 
and Schering-Plough’s FemCare. 


In the disposable 
applicators segment, 
dollar sales have risen 
about 75 percent last 
year and now account 
for 25 percent of the 
$300 million category. 


Miles’ Mycelex-7, introduced in 
July 1992, has been the most suc- 
cessful of the value brands. Its 1.5- 
ounce size cream and suppository 
products now trail only Monistat 
products. Although it has the third- 
and fifth-ranked SKUs in the cate- 
gory, Mycelex’s market share is 
about 14 percent, according to an 
independent source. Monistat has 
nearly 50 percent of the market, fol- 
lowed by Gyne-Lotrimin with 25 
percent. Private label’s share is ap- 
proaching 5 percent. 

One of the most significant trends 
in the category has been a shift to- 
ward disposable applicators. Accord- 
ing to manufacturers, consumers 
like the products because they are 
simpler and less messy to use. 

Dollar sales have risen about 75 
percent in the disposables segment 
last year and now account for 25 
percent of the $300 million category. 

Recent studies indicate that there 
is a growing consumer base that 
prefers disposables to traditional 
vaginal yeast infection remedy 
forms,” said Connie Ervin, Mycelex- 
7 product manager. “Our disposable 
product, which began distribution 
in February, contains the same ac- 


tive ingredient found in Gyne- 
Lotrimin and will give these women 
an equally efficacious but more cost- 
effective alternative.” 

Value-brand manufacturer Lake 
Pharmaceutical agreed about the 
importance of cost-effectiveness. “In 
the vaginal anti-fungal market, con- 
sumers are shopping price now be- 
cause they know the products all 
work, so they’re looking for value,” 
said a Lake spokesperson. “We still 
have a very large untapped market, 
because more than 33 percent of 
women are still not aware of the 
ability to self-treat infections with 
an OTC cure. It’s up to us and the 
retailers to make consumers aware 
that these products are available.” 


Moisturizers/lubricants sales up 


Another growing segment of the 
feminine hygiene category, al- 
though sales flattened this year, is 
the area of personal lubricants and 
vaginal moisturizers. 

Sales of moisturizers, such as 
Parke-Davis’ Replens, Schering- 
Plough’s Gyne-Moistrin and Lake 
Pharmaceutical’s Moist Again, ben- 
efit from increases in condom usage 
and the numbers of post-meno- 
pausal women—those most likely 
to suffer from vaginal dryness. 
Manufacturers contend that the 
category will experience further 
growth because an estimated 80 
percent of drug store shoppers are 
women, and 56 million women re- 
portedly experience vaginal dry- 
ness. Increased condom sales also 
help the personal lubricants catego- 
ry because about 50 percent of con- 
dom users also use a lubricant, ac- 
cording to one manufacturer. 

Drug store sales of personal lu- 
bricants totaled nearly $28 million 
last year, compared to $27.6 million 
in 1992 and $22.6 million in 1991. 


UTIs relieved by OTCs 


Another interesting development 
in the category is in the area of OTC 
treatments for urinary tract infec- 
tions. A yeast infection may be one of 
the most common ailments a woman 
encounters during her life, but uri- 
nary tract infections aren’t far be- 
hind. An estimated six million to 
eight million UTIs are experienced 
annually with approximately 70 per- 
cent of those experienced by women. 

Prescription products are the only 
way to effectively treat a UTI, but 
OTC products are available that 
provide symptomatic relief until a 
doctor can be seen. 

“We see a real opportunity here 
for pharmacists because they may 
not have a product available to 
treat urinary discomfort,” said Dr. 
Arthur Siciliano of PolyMedica, 
makers of AZO-Standard. 

If a woman does have a UTI, it 
takes 24 to 48 hours for prescription 
antibiotics to work, according to Si- 
ciliano. Therefore, an analgesic, like 
a phenazopyridine, can provide re- 
lief until the prescription kicks in. 
An OTC product will also help if it 
turns out. the woman doesn’t have a 
UTI—as is the case 30 to 40 percent 
of the time—and only needs tempo- 
rary urinary tract relief. 

— Mike Troy

Annual Report (SENERAL MERCHANDISE 


For 1993, the focus is on GM 


n the traditionally fragmented 
world of general merchandise, 
“focus” was the theme for ’93 in 
drug stores. 

For many key drug chain players, 
1993 was a year in which assort- 
ments were tightened, with ancil- 
lary segments jettisoned in favor of 
core categories. 

At Wilsonville, Ore.-based Pay- 
Less, for example, a wide array of 
apparel SKUs was eliminated in fa- 
vor of the chain’s wellness depart- 
ment, which, according to PayLess 
executives, is a category that better 
fits a drug store’s reputation for 
health care. 

Drug chains showed a great varia- 
tion in their dedication to GM cate- 
gories— percent of total sales in GM 
can range from 10 percent or less to 
30 percent among “typical” drug 
stores—and their performance in in- 
dividual segments also varied signifi- 
cantly. While pet supplies, for in- 
stance, shrank in space and dollar 
volume in most drug chains, one 
chain reported a 12.3 percent gain 
and almost $3 million in business in 


the category. That same retailer 
showed double-digit gains in small 
appliances, a category that tended to 
be flat in most drug chains 

In general, however, drug chairis 
continued their dedication to the 
dominant GM segments—greeting 
cards/party goods, photofinishing, 
film and cameras, and stationery/ 
Back to School. As chains adjusted 
their formats to create destination 
departments in recent years, greet- 


In 1993 assort- 
ments were tight- 
ened, with ancil- 
lary segments jet- 
tisoned in favor 
of core categories. 


ing cards and photofinishing were 
given more space and prominence 
in stores. Both of these categories 
proved to be traffic builders for 
chains, and interactive kiosks— 
American Greetings’ CreataCard, 
Ambassador/Hallmark’s Touch- 
Screen Greetings and Kodak’s Cre- 
ate-a-Print—helped attract con- 
sumer interest. 

Greeting card sales were up al- 
most 6 percent across all channels, 
and drug stores captured 26 percent 
of the market in 1993. While 
photofinishing revenues were flat 
for most chains in 1993, the Photo 
Marketing Association reported that 
drug stores gained a full point of 
market share in the third quarter. 

Inclement weather in 93 was ac- 
tually a boon for some GM seg- 
ments, such as humidifiers and um- 
brellas. An outbreak of the flu in 
the fall led to “tremendous” sales of 
humidifiers and vaporizers, and a 
series of storms in the latter part of 
the year pumped up sales of weath- 
er protection products by 10 percent 
or more in some chains. 


Drug chains sustain sales in blank tape 


ost drug chains would not 

want a playback of 1993’s 

lackluster blank video sales, 
although drug store convenience 
and value-added promotions did 
help to hold the line for a flat year 
in dollar sales. 

On the other hand, blank audio 
turned up the volume. Audio is a 
smaller segment of the blank tape 
business for drug chains, but indus- 
try research shows that the catego- 
ry rose a half-dozen points (in total 
dollars), thanks to higher rings and 
less competitive pricing than video. 

Videotape, the lion’s share of the 
blank-tape category, was hotly pro- 
moted year-round in all trade-chan- 
nels, as lower manufacturer prices 
kept a lid on the category. Drug 
chains lost sales to warehouse clubs 
and mass merchants, where rock- 
bottom prices persuaded customers 
to pantry load multipacks. 

All U.S. trade channels moved 
around $788 million in blank video- 
tape (factory value), and the tape 
industry expects a further dollar de- 
cline to $783 million for 1994, ac- 
cording to the Electronic Industries 
Associ.. ‘ion (EIA). 

The tune for blank audio tape 
was different: It reached 432 mil- 
lion units overall, with a factory 
value of $367 million in 1993, and 
EIA forecasts a slight rise in units 
and dollars in 1994. 

Tape manufacturers tried to 
prime the pump in 1993 with value- 
added multipacks by offering an ex- 
tra free tape or combining different 
bonus grades and lengths such as 
standard-plus high-grade in video or 
normal-bias plus high-bias tape in 
audio. The intention was to sample 
and trade up the customers to more 
premium product and higher rings. 

The audio cassette’s future as a 
viable format is tied to technology 
and affordability. In retail dollars, 
some drug chains experienced mod- 


est growth for high-bias blank au- 
dio cassettes, thanks to the rising 
popularity of prerecorded compact 
disks (CDs). 

High-quality CD sound reproduc- 
tion encourages consumers to trade 
up to high-bias audio cassette 
tapes, usually to copy a new CD 
onto an audio cassette for playback 
in existing cassette players. Sur- 
veys indicate that most cassettes 
are played in cars or portable play- 
ers—not at home. The tape trade- 
up sale means higher rings and bet- 
ter margins for the retailer. 


Good short term outlook 


Affordability is likely to keep the 
audio cassette format alive. In the 
short term, this could be good for 
drug chains. As some high-tech out- 
lets cut back on blank cassettes, 
drug chains could pick up pieces of 
this business, thanks to the drug- 
chain convenience factor, and it can 
pay off in decent margins, since au- 
dio isn’t as competitive as video. 

Although there are other new au- 
dio format options, the newest types 
in high-quality sound reproduction 
audio, like Sony’s mini disc (differ- 
ent than the micro disc) and the 
digital compact cassette (DCC) are 
not likely to become major factors in 
drug retail at any time soon. 

When changes do occur to impact 
audio tape sales, they’re expected to 
follow demographic lines. Whether 
the consumer demographics favor 
classical music (the fastest shift to 
CD of all music genre) or pop, rap or 
country (both of these prerecorded 
genre still sell well on prerecorded 
cassettes), sales of blank audio cas- 
sette tape should be sustained in 
drug chains for the forseeable future. 

Compared to audio, there’s more 
hot action in the blank video arena, 
where drug chains are battling to 
retain sales slipping over to big box 
retailers. As for audio tape, drug 


chain neighborhood convenience is 
a video selling point. Unlike audio, 
video demands cut-rate prices, espe- 
cially for the popular T-120 stan- 
dard tape touted in circulars. 


Video variety 


In 1993, camcorder tape formats 
VHS-C (compact) and 8mm made a 
good showing in percentage increas- 
es and helped sustain category to- 
tals. So far, 8mm dominates the 
camcorder category with 60 percent 
of sales, compared with 40 percent 
for VHS-C. Industry sources esti- 
mate VHS-C growth at about 25 per- 
cent on 14 million units sold in all 
channels, compared with an increase 
of around 14 percent on 21 million 
units sold for 8mm (a smaller per- 
centage of growth, since 8mm comes 
from a larger base than VHS-C). 

The big sales volume is still in 
VHS format tapes and still in stan- 
dard T-120. Consumers in this 
“couch potato” and family nesting 
decade continue to gobble up tapes 
on the VCR—from soap operas and 
classic films to sports events. 

1993 videotape sales also reflected 
convenience and technology. Longer 
length videos, including the increas- 
ingly popular T-160 and even longer 
tapes, like T-180, can record several 
hours of programming at an extend- 
ed recording speed. 


Sales in drug chains and all mass | 


market (as well as specialty) outlets 
are slowly and slightly shifting to 
higher grade videotape. This shift is 
prodded by technology, the intro- 
duction of more sophisticated VCRs 
and the anticipated arrival of high 
definition TV (HDTV). 

Retailers hope this will result in a 
stanching of the price drops in the 
blank video category. Promotions 
are expected to further aid the 
needed trade-up trend in blank 
videotape in the coming year. 

—-Allene Symons

Annual Report GENERAL MERCHANDISE 


Small appliances show mixed appeal 


Features like more wattage, Euro-designs and 
variable heat settings may draw more consumers 
to the hair dryer/curling iron department in ’94. 


esults were mixed in 1993 in 
the small appliance business 
at drug stores, with the hu- 
midifier and vaporizer seg- 
ment performing well and hair care 
appliances showing little growth. Al- 
though they're smaller segments, 
dental appliances and massagers 
also did well, retailers reported. 
Specifically, executives estimated 
that humidifiers and vaporizers 
rang up sales of nearly $80 million 
last year, about a 15 percent in- 
crease over 1992. “The past season 
was tremendous,” said Martin Co- 
hen, vice president of marketing for 
Kaz. “Inclement weather and out- 
breaks of flu in large numbers re- 
sult in increased retail activity.” 
“Our humidifier and vaporizer 
business was up by double digits, 
store for store,” confirmed Andy 


Striefel, vice president of 
merchandise purchasing 

| for Wilsonville, Ore.-based 
“a PayLess Drug Stores. “The 
cough and cold season 
started early. We were 
scrambling—everything 
we expected to sell by the 
end of December, we sold 
by mid-November.” 

Of the total category, ex- 
ecutives reported that the 
evaporative, or cool mist, 
segment grew the fastest 
at drug stores—by as much 
as 30 percent. They said 
this was largely because of 
the product’s relatively low 
price point—less than $50, 
as opposed to warm-mist 
humidifiers, which can re- 
tail for $129 or more. Said 
Tom Keyser, vice presi- 
dent of sales for Bionaire: 

“When it gets cold and you 
haven’t yet bought a hu- 
midifier, you’d sooner put down $40 
or $50 than over $100.” 

Vaporizers still accounted for 
about half of all unit sales in the hu- 
midifier and vaporizer category. 
Sales of warm-mist humidifiers were 
flat in units but slightly up in dollars. 

To make the most of their humidi- 
fier and vaporizer lineups last year, 
some retailers merchandised them 
in the cough and cold section. “We 
keep the items in the cough and cold 
set and take an endcap during cold 
and flu season,” said Irv Livon, vice 


president of merchandising with 
Melville, N.Y.-based Genovese. 


Hair appliance opportunities 


As far as the hair care segment 
went, manufacturers and retailers 
were less enthusiastic about last 
year’s figures. The $600 million cat- 


egory grew about 4 to 5 percent. Ad- 
ditionally, many of the category’s 
segments remained highly pro- 
motional, with dryers, for example, 
retailing as low as $9.99. 

“It’s a mature market with a high 
saturation level,” said Wayne Dick- 
son, vice president of marketing 
with Vidal Sassoon. 

“No new product or category was 
added,” said PayLess’ Striefel. 

Yet, executives said they’re hope- 
ful that consumers will respond to 
products with newer features—such 
as greater power and more sophisti- 
cated European designs— which will 
become more prevalent this year. 
The same goes for curling irons, 
where larger barrels and variable 
heat settings are expected to grow 
in popularity. 

Said Markus Ernst, executive 
vice president and chief operating 
officer of Detroit-based Arbor 
Drugs: “With features like 1800 
watts and European designs, the 
consumer is interested.” 

“The Eurostyle dryers, which 
have a sleeker, more upscale look, 
are really driving this category,” 
noted Chuck Gautreaux, a buyer at 
New Orleans-based K&B. “Dryers 
with higher wattage are also becom- 
ing more popular.” 

Manufacturers and retailers 
added that in contrast to hair care 
appliances, a few other personal 
care products did well in 1993. 
“Dental care products in excess of 
$60 with extra features are doing 
well,” said Arbor’s Ernst. 

“And massagers were a good cate- 
gory, particularly in drug stores,” 
added Frank Lindsey, vice presi- 
dent of marketing with Conair. 
“They grew in sales at a rate of 10 
to 15 percent.” 

— Barbara Solomon 


The sun shines on weather protection sales 


n improving economy, better 

retail merchandising and se- 

vere weather at the end of the 
year contributed to a strong show- 
ing by weather protection products 
in 1993, according to manufacturers 
and chain drug executives. 

They disagreed, however, on the 
extent to which more attractive 
products and better retail displays 
have made the category more suited 
to everyday purchasing. 

According to industry estimates, 
umbrellas rang up $250 million to 
$300 million in sales last year. 
About 20 percent of that, or $50 
million to $60 million, was estimat- 
ed to be drug store business. Manu- 
facturers and retail executives fur- 
ther estimated that dollar sales of 
umbrellas and related items at the 
drug store channel were up last 
year—at some stores by 10 percent 
or more. 

Said Barry Brinker, vice presi- 
dent of marketing and product de- 
velopment for J Jay Products Co., 
“The drug store channel is definite- 
ly gaining business.” 

Some executives attributed much 
of this increase to the general up- 
turn in the economy that began late 
last year. “As the economy picked 


up at the end of 93, we saw our sell- 
through pick up,” said John Catt, 
category director for rain products 
with Totes. 

“The economy impacts our take- 
away more than rain,” he added. 
“Only 30 percent of our take-away 
is due to rainstorms.” 

Other executives, however, ar- 
gued that weather was a critical 
factor in the year’s sales results. 
“Our cold-weather products did out- 
standing, and it was weather-relat- 
ed,” said Andy Striefel, vice presi- 
dent of merchandise purchasing for 
Wilsonville, Ore.-based PayLess 
Drug Stores. 

Added Bob Lackey, weather pro- 
tection buyer with PayLess, “We’re 
going with purely rainy-day sales, 
So we just keep the racks filled 
when it rains.” 


Improved merchandising needed 


What most agreed on, however, is 
that better retail merchandising 
also drives sales up at the drug 
channel. “Consumers are having the 
product put in front of them more 
effectively in the mass trade,” said J 
Jay’s Brinker. “If we or our competi- 
tors get rainwear displays in front 
of the public, sales will happen.” 


And Totes’ Catt contended that 
many drug chains improved their 
product mix, adding high-end, more 
fashionable products, which also 
helped sales. 

In terms of subcategories, retail- 
ers and manufacturers agreed that 
two umbrella categories continued 
to do notably well in 1993: golf (or 
sport) umbrellas and minicompacts. 
Markus Ernst, executive vice presi- 
dent and chief operating officer of 
Troy, Mich.-based Arbor Drugs, re- 
ported that promotional golf um- 
brellas were a key category in 1998, 
although others maintained that at 
a typical price point of $14.99, they 
were simply too expensive to be a 
big drug store business. 

Even more important to most 
drug stores is the minicompact seg- 
ment. “Styles like ultra-minis have 
broadened the market,” agreed Cyn- 
thia Stahley-Zuniga, merchandise 
manager for Melville, N.Y.-based 
Genovese. “Customers are willing to 
pay more for them.” 

While manufacturers offer a range 
of solid colors, and even prints, for 
the drug store channel, basic colors 
continued to maintain their strong- 
hold on the market last year. 

— Barbara Solomon

Chains see photo’ S opportunities 


rug chains are bullish 

about photofinishing and 

cameras—and with good 

reason. Consumers look to 
drug stores with professional trust, 
not only for pharmacy but also for 
film developing needs. 

And photo is growing. More con- 
sumers and households are sport- 
ing a wardrobe of cameras, ranging 
from high-tech equipment for Dad 
or daughter to point-and-shoot box- 
es for Mom (most are bought by 
women or for kids and teenagers, 
research shows) to single-use cam- 
eras that anyone any age can use 
anytime. 

Overall, noted Barry Harrand, re- 
search director of the Photo Market- 
ing Association, 1993 ended as a 
year of recovery with higher con- 
sumer confidence, especially in the 
second half of the year, as election 
uncertainty ended and people got 
back to the business of living. 

In 1993, film sales outpaced 
photofinishing in most trade class- 
es. Consumers scooped up multi- 
pack promotions but traveled less 
and developed fewer rolls, thanks to 
the sluggish economy that kept 
them at home. 

For all trade classes, the PMA’s 
preliminary figures showed a rise of 
6 percent in film rolls sold and a 2 
percent to 3 percent increase in 
rolls processed. 

The drug channel, however, didn’t 
do quite that well. 

In 19938, the average drug chain 
reported flat sales in the photo de- 
partment. An average chain drug 
store generates around 3 percent of 
total sales in the photo department, 
but some buyers say an aggressive 
and committed chain can grow this 
percentage as high as 5 percent or 6 
percent. In some of the more aggres- 
sive chains, photo department sales 
climbed around 2 percent over 
1992’s figures. 

According to IRI, drug stores sold 
$723 million of film and flash acces- 
sories in 1993, a drop of 1.5 percent 
compared to 1992. 

However, the drug chain channel 
made a fairly good showing in pho- 
tofinishing, helping to offset de- 
clining sales in film. 

So far, the PMA hasn’t tallied its 
final 1993 figures, but its third 
quarter 1993 photofinishing num- 
bers show that drug stores in- 
creased share by 1 percent, for a 
22.6 percent share vs. 21.6 percent 
in 1992—no small] feat in a time 
when mass merchants and discount 
clubs are gobbling up huge bites of 
many categories. 


Processing speaks 


Overnight labs and in-store labs 
helped sustain the photo category 
in 1993. The in-store lab is a grow- 
ing subcategory, with many chains 
choosing the microlab and others 
the larger, higher-roll volume 
minilab. 

One reason more drug chains are 
getting aggressive about 
photofinishing —like Thrifty Drug, 
which launched a major photofin- 
ishing campaign last fall—is that 
this subcategory can represent as 
much as 65 percent of photo depart- 


PRO Sra = 


er ~ 


Some chains use photofinishing to help promote an overall image of service 
and quality by adding one-hour labs and high-visibility promotions. 


The in-store lab 1s a growing 


subcategory, with many chains 


choosing the microlab and others the 


larger, higher-roll volume minilab. 


ment business in some chains. 

Photofinishing is profitable be- 
cause the chain pays its photofin- 
isher after it’s been paid by the con- 
sumer, so there is very little 
inventory cost. 

One reason drug chains do well in 
photofinishing, despite their big re- 
tail competition, is chains such as 
Perry, Genovese, Eckerd and others 
use photoprocessing to help promote 
a chain image of service and quality 
by adding one-hour labs (often with 
lab-coat clad operators) and high- 
visibility photoprocessing promo- 
tions. 

In-store or one-hour labs add that 
image of service and convenience, 
along with a higher ring per roll. In 
contrast, the overnight photofinish- 
ing business is hotly competitive. To 
really be in the game, a drug chain 
has to pump up promotion energy 
with free second sets of prints, free 
enlargements, free mini albums or 
other value-added promotions. 


Consumer interaction 


Interactive technology is proving 
to be one method of bringing the 
photo customer back into the store. 
The technology moved forward with 
Kodak’s Create-a-Print kiosk, which 
enables consumers to create en- 
largements and crop and manipu- 
late a film negative. Fuji’s staff-op- 
erated color print copier Pictrostat 
came on strong in 1993, moving the 
consumer further along toward 
quick gratification and paving the 
way for even more versions of staff- 
operated and consumer-operated 
imaging systems in 1994. 

“Interactivity is everywhere, from 


ATMs to online chat lines,” notes 
PMA’s Harrand. “The consumer 
wants to become involved.” Harrand 
likens the trend toward involve- 
ment to the days of the home dark- 
room. Only, he said, new imaging 
systems make a “light room” and 
are just as fascinating. The expan- 
sion of these photo options for the 
consumer is not expected to canni- 
balize, but rather to compliment dif- 
ferent subcategories. 

A Pictrostat print is an enlarge- 
ment that offers a convenience 
benefit for a more premium price 
per unit. The Kodak and Fuji sys- 
tems are already doing well in 
many drug chains. 

Some new technology in the 
works is not likely to hit the drug 
channel for years, but it wiil influ- 
ence the consumer from afar as the 
media spotlights the latest develop- 
ments in the ongoing image 
odyssey. One example is Apple’s 
just-announced digital camera, 
which uses no film and transmits 
directly to a computer. 


Single use has potential 


The percentage increase of single- 
use camera sales varied wildly 
among drug chains—with some 
chains doubling sales, and others 
reporting single digit increases in 
1993. It’s also important to remem- 
ber that single use represents 
around 4 percent of film sold and is 
growing from a small base. 

But it’s a category with 20 per- 
cent to 30 percent margins and 
plenty of growth potential. No won- 
der retailers are working with dif-

bring a camera; for a business op- 
portunity (when the realtor or 
insurance agent doesn’t want to car- 
ry acamera at all times); when it’s 
fun to experiment with different 
types of lenses (panoramic, telepho- 
to, portrait, waterproof); or when 
it’s a lively addition to social events, 
such as picnics and weddings. 

The use of single-use cameras is 
contagious. When a person sees 
someone else using it at a party or 
buying a store’s entire supply for 
wedding reception favors, the word 
gets out and converts discover the 
camera’s many applications. 

In 1993, Kodak brought out a new 
specialty lens, the portrait Fun- 
Saver. Even Polaroid joined the ros- 
ter of single-use camera manufac- 
turers mid-year with its Talking 
Sidekick. The camera features a 
sound chip that emits funny voices 
to make the subject smile. 

Small-business use of cameras 
was another trend pushing up this 
category in 1993. As more people 
see single-use cameras clicking 
away in both fun and workday set- 
tings and try this product them- 
selves, more photographers will en- 
ter the marketplace. That’s why 
retailers and manufacturers expect 
the word on single use (like a 

jumper cable for a mature category) 
to spread and energize the photo 
category—and sell as many as 34 
million single-use units by the end 
of this year. 


Conventional cameras still sell 


1993 was a good year for all cam- 
era sales in drug chains, largely be- 
cause point-and-shoot and lower 
priced, easy-to-operate cameras 
have been on the uptick. Some ag- 
gressive drug chains reported that 
camera sales were as high as 17 
percent to 20 percent over 1992. 

Kodak’s Cameo, with its sleek 
compact format in 110 and 35mm, 
helped boost camera sales in drug 
chains. In fact, some buyers report- 
ed that the 110 easy-load cartridge 
seems to have diehard adherents 
and is especially popular with teens 
and kids. For those who are discov- 
ering or rediscovering photography 
through single-use cameras, the 
user-friendly, pocket-sized camera 
is a good trade-up. Kodak’s Cameo 
offered the 110 fan a chance to up- 
date hardware in 1993. 

Many chain drug buyers reported 
positive customer response to a new 
camera at a higher price point. Po- 
laroid’s Captiva, introduced last 
year, offers the advanced feature of 


An aggressive and committed chain can grow the photo department to gener- 
ate as much as 5 percent or 6 percent of total store sales, some buyers say. 


allowing instant prints to remain in 
the camera rather than take the 
time to develop between each shot. 
This way the user can take several 
in succession. Its ad campaign fea- 
tured comic Sinbad and helped ex- 
tend the camera’s outreach to 
African-American consumers. In 
other micromarketing strategies in 
1993, Kodak helped retailers reach 
more Hispanic customers with 
bilingual signage for appropriate 
markets. 


Trading up 


It took years for consumers to 
trade up to 200 from 100 film. Now, 
the trade-up is to 400 ASA, which 
gives retailers better rings and mar- 
gins on the high-end of film’s 12 
percent to 20 percent average gross 
margin. 

The trade-up is being accom- 
plished partly through the 400 ASA 
film loaded in most single-use cam- 
eras. Most consumers will replace 
film with the type they last used, es- 
pecially if they bought the roll when 
they dropped off the exposed roll. 

The user-friendly trend in photo, 
with high-tech features more con- 
cealed and less intimidating in 
many models, meant that more film 
displays in 1993 told the consumer 
what to use a specific film or single- 
use camera for: bright daylight, in- 
door with flash, landscapes, people 
close-ups or sports. Konica even 
introduced a Baby Film in 1993, 
marketed as especially formulated 
to capture the tones of a baby’s skin. 

35mm film continued to grow, al- 
though 1993 saw an upsurge in 110 
and even some sales growth in 
black & white, thanks to the trend 
toward black & white images in 
advertising today. 

At Eckerd, 90 percent of the film 
sold is 35mm, and all single-use 
cameras use 35mm, which provides 
a high-quality negative suitable for 
enlargement. The growth of 35mm 
film has given rise to the enlarge- 
ment business. 

Film and camera manufacturers 
hit the airwaves and mounted print 
ad campaigns to push new products 
and promotions in 1993, increasing 
visibility for the entire category. 


Fuji started early to promote the 
1994 World Cup with the communi- 
ty-based “Kids in Gear” program to 
help local teams buy soccer equip- 
ment. The sport reaches an interna- 
tional audience and is a favorite 
sport for children in higher income 
families, a segment that indexes 
high for film consumption. 

Other promotions in 1993 includ- 
ed regional sports versions of Ko- 
dak’s single-use FunSaver camera, 
an example of reaching more specif- 
ic markets with custom packaging 
and technology. These editions were 
packaged for specific NFL teams, 
and the film included designs or 
borders to create a festive edge on 
prints taken at a football game or 
tailgate party. 

At retail, more drug chains found 
that cross merchandising film and 
single-use cameras on wing displays 
mounted in different departments 
prompts impulse sales. Retailers re- 
port success with almost every de- 
partment—from a summer barbe- 
cue display to a spring prom 
promotion in cosmetics, and from 
the infant department to toys and 
sporting goods. 1993 saw more wing 
displays for film and especially sin- 
gle-use cameras to remind con- 
sumers to capture more memories 
on film. 


Other angles 


Retailers also found they get 
hefty gross profits from an expand- 
ed photo department. Novelty items 
like blow-up posters, image T- 
shirts, photo greeting cards, mugs 
and all manner of customized image 
gift items can generate 40-percent- 
plus margins. 

So the wardrobe of cameras is ex- 
panding, along with photofinishing 
options and accessory sales. All are 
aimed to further satisfy photogra- 
phers and would-be photographers 
of all ages and degrees of interest 
in technology, from the rare cut- 
ting-edge customer to the female 
shopper who wants an easy-to-use 
camera for herself or her child— 
and she represents the greatest 
photo opportunity for drug chains 
today. 

—Allene Symons

Battery sales lose charge in chain drug stores 


ergers, promo- 
tions, rollouts 
and late-year 
product introduc- 
tions sparked interest in the 
battery category during 
1993—but when the tin- 
gling stopped, drug chains 
lost power for a drop of 2.8 
percent in dollar sales, ac- 
cording to research by Infor- 
mation Resources Inc. 

The drug chain decline in 
dollars came from sales lost 
to competing retailers, lower 
rings held down by every- 
day-low-price trends and hot 
off-price promotions for the 
most popular battery types. 

Consumer purchasing con- 
tinued its drift toward dis- 
counters and warehouse 
clubs, where stocking up on 
multi-packs meant fewer im- 
pulse purchases the next 
time at drug store checkouts. 


Alkalines top the list 


Alkalines continued to 
dominate the category in 
1993 with 68.5 percent of 
battery sales, according to 
Towne Oller research. 

Lithium and photo grew 
14 percent in drug stores, 
but it leaped 61 percent in 
food stores. This type now 
commands 11 percent of bat- 
tery sales in the drug store 
channel. Watch and hearing 
aid batteries grew 9 percent, 
to reach 10.8 percent of bat- 
teries sold in drug stores. 

In the $1.3 billion primary 
battery market, retail dollars 
grew faster than unit sales in 
all trade classes as con- 
sumers traded up from heavy 
duties to alkalines and lithi- 
ums. In 1993, heavy duties 
dropped 10 points (to 6.2 per- 
cent), and general purpose 
dropped 19 points (to 3.5 per- 
cent) in drug chains, accord- 
ing to Towne-Oller. This 
trade-up trend is expected to 
continue and will be boosted 
by the sale of hearing aid bat- 
teries as the population ages. 

Chains aggressively mer- 
chandised batteries this 
year with more outposts and 
wings to garner impulse 
sales in departments like 
toys, electronics and cosmet- 
ics. Manufacturers pushed 
self-service displays to help 
consumers choose among 
the many look-alike round- 
cell batteries for watch, cal- 
culator and especially hear- 
ing aid batteries, a prime 
product for the drug setting. 

Eveready/Energizer rolled 
out its lithium AA battery 
in 1993 (introduced previ- 


ously but not available na- 
tionally), offering a higher 
ring, long-life alternative to 
alkalines. Lithium is expect- 
ed to gradually mainstream. 
Changes in battery tech- 
nology and marketing also 
spurred corporate shifts in 
1993, when Eveready 
merged with rechargeable 
specialist Millennium and 


Sanyo merged with GE to 
form another new battery 
alliance with a major 
rechargeable market share. 

Rayovac’s September in- 
troduction of the Renewal 
battery system—a hybrid 
between alkaline and the 
traditional rechargeable sys- 
tem—caused a category stir 
in the fourth quarter. 


Rayovac’s introduction led 
to repositioning of recharge- 
able product by other manu- 
facturers—for example, 
Eveready updated the graph- 
ics on its rechargeables, and 
Panasonic launched a new 
three-hour charger. Manu- 
facturers geared up to edu- 
cate consumers. 

Disposables are a highly 


consumable habit and one 
not likely to give way to 
rechargeables in the near 
future, say many industry 
observers. But, others think 
there’s untapped potential 
for consumer interest by ed- 
ucating them and promoting 
the rechargeable’s environ- 
mental advantage. 

—Allene Symons

Street Smart Market Metrics analy- 
sis and Ambassador’s Prophet pro- 
gram, which focus on fine-tuning a 
store-specific mix. 


Alternative sales 


Alternative cards now account for 
around 25 percent of total card 
sales, with an estimated 50 percent 
of alternative card purchases im- 
pulse buys. In 1993, Gibson expand- 
ed its Life As We Know It line, 
added a blank card offering to this 
category and saw a leap in sales of 


| its Women to Women cards. 


Ambassador tripled its alterna- 
tive card offerings, including its My 
Thoughts Exactly and Cow Works, 
while Hallmark expanded its Shoe- 
box Greetings. Ambassador also 
launched its Alternative Card Shop 
with new configurations and modu- 
lar fixtures to draw attention to the 
selection. 

American Greetings’ 78th Street 
alternative card line added 25 per- 
cent more everyday designs and in- 
creased its Christmas alternative 
card offering sixfold. Also new from 
AG in 1993 was its Pet Shop line, in- 
troduced midyear and expanded be- 
fore year’s end to over 100 designs. 

In this growth category, manufac- 
turers are creating new organizing 
systems to guide shoppers toward 
making a selection. New sign con- 
cepts this year included new kinds 
of end-of-aisle direction cards to 
help shoppers find specific cards. 


Card kiosks 


Greeting card visibility increased 
in 1993 with the expansion of elec- 
tronic greeting card units with new 
and improved versions: CreataCard 
from American Greetings (DOS 
based), Touch-Screen Greetings from 
Ambassador/Hallmark (Apple-based) 
and the new Gibson Card Writer. 
These custom-card kiosks added ex- 
citement, service and incremental 
sales, but they are not expected to 
reach the volume or in any way re- 
place preprinted greeting cards. 

Hallmark/Ambassador launched 
Touch-Screen Greetings midyear 
while American Greetings reduced 
its CreataCard from four to three 
feet (it offers 1,100 designs) and 
Gibson launched its Card Writer in 
the fall. With the introductions,

Ethnic up 


The importance of micro-market- 
ing in drug chains is evident in eth- 
nic greeting card expansion. Am-

Hispanic line and its Mahogany 
African-American line in 1993,

It’s a wrap 


In some chains and food/drug 
combos, party departments were 
created in 1993 to offer a boutique 


setting for cards, wrap, party, gifts 
and even flowers and balloons. In 
other expanded card departments, 
new fixtures and displays, expand- 
ed ethnic cards and coordinated 
party/wrap products garnered addi- 
tional sales. 

Gift wrap and party goods got a 
boost in 1993, especially in the 
wrap category with convenience 
concepts like gift boxes and bags in 
a wide range of sizes, new pear!l- 
ized materials and innovative 
graphics. 

Ambassador launched its Choic- 
es gift wrap program in 1993. 
American Greetings expanded gift 
bags and boxes and offered self- 
serve signing to help consumers 
choose the right box for different 
gifts. 

Other hot items in gift wrap were 
trade-up accessories like premium 
bows and gift tie-ons or decorations, 
miniature objects for occasions like 
baby or bridal showers that add 
perceived value to a gift. 

Juvenile party goods drove the 
party goods subcategory. A big 
slice of party goods for kids is li- 
censed patterns. Big winners in 
1993 included Disney favorites, 
like Aladdin and the Little Mer- 
maid, and Barney and Thomas the 
Tank Engine. 

At Gibson, over 80 percent of its 
juvenile party goods are licensed. 
The company also launched a Par- 
ty Shop in 1993 to help retailers 
compete with the increasing num- 
ber of party shops or superstores 
that are springing up across the 
country.

Women seeking fashion 


In 1993 there were more 
than 54 million women in 
the work force compared 
with 39 million women 15 
years ago, according to the 
federal Bureau of Labor 
Statistics. 

With women representing 
more than half of today’s 


Stationery on the move in drug chains 


business professionals, more 
office products are being de- 
signed and packaged: fash- 
ion elements for portfolio 
covers; shades and textures 
for paper (such as Stuart 
Hall’s expanded Executive 
Suite); and pale clear tones 
for desk sets and organizers. 
In 1993, colors and textures 
with marbleized and granite 
or clear finishes blended in- 
terest in the environment 
with fashion image. 

Social stationery also 
showed signs of growth, re- 
ported some retailers and 
manufacturers, although 
compared to school and 
home office, this is coming 
from a smaller base. 

The growth of these high- 
quality products— which 
could signal a nostalgic 
trend for hand-written let- 
ters as an offshoot of a 
more home-centered era— 
is seen in the movement of 
boxed stationery, colored 
bulk stationery and en- 
velopes in clear dispensers, 
and special gift-boxed sta- 
tionery year-round but es- 
pecially for Christmas and 
Mother’s Day. 


B-T-S basics 


This strong seasonal cate- 
gory enjoyed the spice of 
fashion colors and licensed 
images, but in 1993 many 
drug chains were cautious 
and stuck mainly to basics 
while going light on trendy 
licensed lines. As a result, 
back-to-school sales were 
strong in most regions, re- 
ported many drug chains. 

Buyers noted that large 
floor space is needed for a 
major licensed presentation 
of related products. But 
most drug chains success- 
fully made room in 19983 for 
sure-fire licenses like Bar- 
ney, Thomas the Tank En- 
gine and popular Disney 
characters like those from 
Little Mermaid and AIl- 
addin, plus perennial fa- 
vorites Lisa Frank and 
Sesame Street. 

A 1993 trend in the big 
box vs. drug chain saga—as 
drug chains work to rede- 
fine their competitive 
niche—is strong last-minute 
back-to-school shopping at 
some drug chains around 
the country, where the flur- 
ry of activity occurs just be- 
fore and after school starts. 

Another benefit for drug 
chains was reported by some 
chains as a side effect of of- 
fice warehouse clubs: The 
demise of more stationery 
stores means many cus- 
tomers pick up home office 
supplies at drug stores. 
Making stationery a reliably 
in-stock and easy to shop 
destination is key to keeping 
this business, said buyers.

Annual Report | GENERAL MERCHANDISE 


Socks and tights run away with hosiery category 


hile sheer 

hosiery sales in 

1993 were wide- 

ly described as 
flat at best, manufacturers, 
analysts and chain drug re- 
tailers were enthusiastic 
about their sales of women’s 
socks and tights. 

The alternative legwear 
products, they said, had a 
strong showing in 1993, 
gaining more than 10 per- 
cent in dollar sales over 92 
across all classes of trade— 
and scoring even higher 
numbers in drug stores. 

“Sheer hosiery is off, but 
alternative legwear is up,” 
said Bill Koslowe, director 
of market information for 
Kayser-Roth, manufacturer 
of the No Nonsense brand. 

According to the National 
Hosiery Manufacturers As- 
sociation (NHMA), total re- 
tail unit sales of women’s 
sheer hosiery for 1993 stood 
at 1.5 billion pairs, up 3.7 
percent from the year before, 
while dollar sales were $2.9 
billion, up 5.6 percent. Ex- 
plained NHMA president 
Sid Smith: “What this tells 
you is that unit sales were 
flat, but retailers increased 
their prices ever so slightly.” 

Some industry experts es- 
timated that drug stores 
took an even bigger hit than 
the industry at large last 
year, declining in dollar and 
unit sales of sheer hosiery 
by as much as 15 percent. 
Total hosiery sales, accord- 
ing to Information Re- 
sources Inc., dropped 16 

ercent in drug stores, to 
415 million. 

Manufacturers attributed 
last year s figures largely to 
women’s increasingly casual 
lifestyle. “Look how many 
businesses have one day a 
month or week that’s a casu- 
al day,” said Nancy Young, 
director of corporate affairs 
for Leggs. “That’s the 
biggest reason. And there 
are other factors, like women 
hitting the glass ceiling, so 
they may go out and start 
their own business from 
home, where they don’t need 
sheer hosiery. This isn’t hap- 
pening in overwhelming 
numbers, but it is a trend.”

Annual Report } | | CONSLMABLES 


Consumables command 


‘New Age’ drinks 
saturate the segment 


he fastest growing category in drug chains last 

year—ready-to-drink teas—rang up more than 

$1 billion in sales in 1993. Much of this phe- 

nomenon for alternative, or “New Age,” bever- 
ages, has been spurred by an increased desire among 
consumers for products they perceive as healthier to 
drink. Consumers are drinking more bottled water, 
ready-to-drink teas and juices and juice drinks—three 
of the hottest categories at retail last year. 

Although significantly smaller than the $48-billion 
soft drink market, ready-to-drink teas, along with New 
Age beverages, are garnering more interest among 
drug chain retailers than any other segment. These 
beverages, which include clear and sparkling bottled 
spring waters, juice-based carbonated beverages, fla- 
vored iced teas, fruit-flavored waters and other prod- 
ucts, generated about $6 billion in sales last year. 

“Bar none, ready-to-drink teas were the fastest grow- 
ing category last year,” said Hellen Berry, vice president 
of marketing research for Beverage Marketing Corp. 

With the entrance of major cola companies, such as 
Coca-Cola, with its Nestea partnership, and Pepsi-Cola, 
with its Lipton alliance, to the category, retailers have 
high hopes that the increased marketing and advertis- 
ing muscle of those companies, as well as leading sup- 
plier Snapple, will help propel these ready-to-drink 
teas even further in 1994. 

“Soda has been steady, but there’s more excitement 
in teas,” said Robin Koon, chain merchandise manager 
for Horton and Converse Pharmacies. “It’s an alternate 
taste to cola. Without teas, we probably would not have 
had much growth at all. We’ve seen a huge increase in 
Snapple, which has been the big star this year.” 

“Snapple, Snapple, Snapple” is what’s selling, said a 
buyer at a Northwest drug chain. However, the buyer 
noted that the product is so popular he has trouble 
keeping it in stock. “We’re hoping Lipton and Nestea 
will come along and fill that gap,” he said. 


Teas’ popularity increases 


Industry experts note that ready-to-drink teas have 
doubled and tripled in sales in the past three years 
and are expected to increase at the same pace again 
this year. 

“Ready-to-drink teas were a major focus in 1993,” 
said Ken Traenkle, national sales administrator for 
Snapple Beverage Corp., who added that there are al- 
ready “350 new tea products on the horizon” this year. 

“Ready-to-drink teas bring convenience, flavor vari- 
ety, single serving and affordability,” said JoAnn 
Miller, director of marketing and marketing services 
North America for Coca-Cola Nestlé Refreshments Co. 

Raymond Hoy, director of marketing for I Got It At 
Gary’s, described the New Age market as “exciting, 
unique and different. Every six to seven months a new 
product takes the category to a new level. First it was 
Evian, then Clearly Canadian and now Snapple. We 
are waiting for the next thing.” 

While retailers anticipate the introduction of new 
products, flavors and va- 


riety in the ready-to- er 
drink tea market, many Drug chains’ piece 
say those new additions of the consumables

finding adequate shelf Pp

Continued on page 134 


14 percent in 1993 


Consumers lap up 
liquor by the liter 


luggish sales in the alcoholic beverage category 
have prompted some drug store retailers and 
manufacturers to use more sophisticated tools, 
such as category management and scanning, to 
maximize their shelf space and improve profits. 

Consumption of beer was flat in 1993, while sales of 
wine and hard liquor dropped again, as they have for a 
few years, said John C. Maxwell, analyst for Wheat 
First Securities. 

For Bernie Guerrero, buyer for San Francisco-based 
Drug Barn Inc., “Alcohol sales are pretty consistent,” he 
said. “I haven’t seen any big increases in beer or wine.” 

With sales sluggish, competition has been heating up 
among trade channels, particularly in the beer category. 

“Beer is a very competitive item in drug stores, and 
they are seeing stronger competition from supermar- 
kets and mass merchandisers for the beer consumer,” 
said Mike Hennick, public relations manager for allied 
brands for Miller Brewing Co. “Yet, beer continues to 
be a draw [for] drug stores.” 

Jack Mannix, senior account executive for the drug 
trade channel for Coors Brewing Co., noted, “Many 
drug store retailers use beer ads as a traffic builder and 
as a strategic weapon against grocery stores. They tar- 
get the in-between grocery store shopper and use beer 
to generate traffic and cash.” 


Convenience, displays move beer 


To combat increased competition, Hennick noted that 
drug outlets are putting more emphasis on conve- 
nience, like selling cold beer, and doing a better job of 
displaying the products. 

Drug stores are also placing more emphasis on prof- 
itability. “They are more interested in doing a better 
job of managing the space they have and employ cate- 
gory management,” he added. 

This January, Coors formed a category management 
team focused on the drug channel to help retailers rec- 
ognize opportunities that could grow their business. 

“Our drug customers realize the contribution beer 
has made to their overall business, and we’re happy to 
see many increase their space,” said John Hanichak, 
vice president of national retail sales for Anheuser- 
Busch Inc. 

The beer market, with estimated sales of $49 billion, 
has been growing at a slow pace in recent years. “There 
has been a lot of trading down since the recession, but 
there’s been growth in the above-premium brands and 
super-premium products, such as importers Heineken 
and Guinness and specialty brewers like Samuel 
Adams,” added Benj Steinman, president of Beer Mar- 
keter’s Insights newsletter. 

In addition to super-premium and specialty brews, 
two of the fastest growing categories in 1993 were light 
and non-alcoholic beers. 

Hanichak estimated that the non-alcoholic beverage 
category, which represents between 2 and 3 percent of 
the industry’s total sales, increased 15 percent in 1993. 

Manufacturers also reported that the new “ice beer” 
products have been selling well. “There has been a flur- 
ry of activity [in ice beer] for a segment that is relatively 
unproven,” Steinman said. “All of the manufacturers are 
rushing to market with brands.” 

Hennick said Miller expects the ice beer category to 
capture the attention of the U.S. consumer in the same 
way it did the Canadian consumer during the past year 
and a half. Today, ice beer represents 10 percent of the 
Canadian beer market. 

However, retailers are unsure about its future. “Ice 
beer has sold pretty well, but I think it may be a ‘flash in 
the pan,’ ” said one chain drug buyer. “Consumers tend 
to try new brands, but they seldom stick with them.” 

—Lisa Casey Weiss

Consumer behavior 


Efforts by the cola compa- 
nies to expand into new 
markets may be fueled by 
sluggish cola sales. Accord- 
ing to Mark Preisinger, 
public relations manager 
for Coca-Cola, the category 
has slowed as consumer be- 
havior patterns have 
changed. Consumers are re- 
defining refreshment —they 
are recognizing that carbon- 
ation is no longer necessary 
in beverages. 

Those behavior patterns 
are driving changes in the 
nonalcoholic beverage mar- 
ket. Said Preisinger, there 
are less daily drinkers of 
soft drinks, consumers are 
drinking smaller ounces 
per occasion, and they’re 
becoming lighter users of 
soft drinks. 

That trend is likely to 
continue. Preisinger noted 
that as consumers age, soft 
drink consumption de- 
clines. According to statis- 
tics provided by Coca-Cola, 
by the year 2000, 51 per- 
cent of the population will 
be 35 years or older.
