Drug Store News, April 25,1994 137 


Annual Report PRIVATE LABEL 


Private label’s success rings true 


rug chains took their store- 

brand business to record 

levels in 1993, doing their 

best to capitalize on the 
post-recession private label phe- 
nomenon. 

Chain drug private label sales 

ew nearly 4.5 percent to almost 

2 billion last year, according to re- 
search from Information Resources 
Inc. and the Private Label Manufac- 
turers Association. That’s a far cry 
from the roughly $30 billion in store 
brands supermarkets are doing, but 
it shows that drug chains are play- 
ing successfully to the times. And 
the times, as economists and brand- 
ed manufacturers have come to re- 
alize, have changed fundamentally. 

“There’s been a fundamental 
shift of consumer buying habits to 
value; there can be no argument 
abet that,” said Jeff Needham, 
vice president of marketing for Per- 
rigo Co., the largest private label 
manufacturer. 

“The store-brand phenomenon is 
real,” added Gabe Lowie, industry 
analyst for Oppenheimer & Co., at 
the last PLMA annual convention. 
“This isn’t a recession-type thing.” 


Price is key 


Understanding the increasing al- 
lure of private label isn’t rocket sci- 
ence: Lacking the high marketing 
and development costs of national 
brands, they’re relatively cheap for 
both retailers and their customers. 

In a talk early this year on the im- 
pact of store brands, Eckerd Drug 
president and chief operating officer 
Frank Newman put it succinctly. 

“There is no escaping,” said New- 
man, “(that) the single biggest fac- 
tor driving house brands is the price 
gap that exists between them and 
the national brands.” 

What’s more, the comparable 
quality of house brands is no longer 
much of an issue. A slew of deter- 
mined drug, supermarket and dis- 
count store retailers have carefully 
nurtured the image of their store 
brands by sourcing and testing 
products carefully, by upgrading 
packaging and by hammering con- 
stantly on the quality and integrity 
of their own offerings in ads and 
product guarantees. 

“In many cases, we’re now selling 
not the price but the quality and 
image of our own label,” said a 
spokesman for Troy, Mich.-based 
Arbor Drugs. “The fact tha* Arbor is 
well-identified with health care is a 
big advantage in that respect.” 


Branded miscalculation 


Also working in favor of contin- 
ued demand has been a fundamen- 
tal miscalculation by manufactur- 
ers of branded goods. By and large, 
the packaged goods giants assumed 
chat private label was largely a 
temporary phenomenon, whose 
fortunes were tied to a whirligig 
economy. 

In the past, said retail consuitant 
Willard Bishop, the response of 
branded manufacturers has been to 
maintain the big price gap between 
national and private brands with 
steady price increases, relying on ad- 


vertising and promotion 
and the traditional 
strength of their brands in 
response to growing pres- 
sure from low-priced alter- 
natives. 

But as the economy re- 
mained stalled in the ear- 
ly 1990s, consumers, wor- 
ried about jobs and 
money, gave store-brand 
OTCs, toiletries, paper 
products, household 
cleaners and consumables 
another, longer look. In 
many cases, they made 
permanent changes in the 
way they buy those items. 

Drug chains have been 
only toc happy to oblige. 
Successful store-brand 
programs can mean good 
turns, solid margins and 
image-enhancement to 
chains willing to commit 
the attention of top man- 
agement and the promo- 
tional dollars to make 
them work. 

“In our type of busi- 
ness,” said Scott Gorley, 
head of Phar-Mor’s fast- 
growing store brand pro- 
eram, “private label can 
have a dramatic effect on margins.” 

“You can price them 10 to 20 per- 
cent lower than national brands 
and still make a healthy profit,” 
added Bill Harris, a retail consul- 
tant and former vice president of 
nonfoods merchandising for Ran- 
dall’s Food and Drug in Texas. “The 
best approach is to place them next 
to the national brand... and pro- 
mote the (price) comparison.” 

There’s also a hidden benefit to 
establishing a solid private label 
program, according to Harris. 
“When you establish that you can 
be a threat with private label, you 
have an advantage you can lever- 
age when you negotiate ads (with 
branded suppliers).” 


“Se ae 


Chain success stories 


One standout performer in pri- 
vate label has been Eckerd, which 
now carries 1,153 items covering all 
major categories of merchandise. 
Private labels generate about 10 | 
percent of Eckerd’s HBA sales and 
have profit margins 20 percent to 
70 percent higher than the national 
brands against which they compete, 
said Newman. 

Canada’s dominant drug chain, 
Shoppers Drug Mart, has also rung 
big sales gains and profits from its 
more than 1,200 private label 
SKUs. According to Roman Niemy, 
director of corporate brands, Shop- 
pers’ Life and Rialto brands now ac- 
count for nearly 8 percent of sales, 
or 12 to 12.5 percent when prescrip- 
tions and tobacco are factored out. 
They also generate average gross 
margins of 38 percent. 

“It’s an amazing category,” added 
Irwin Livon, vice president and di- 
rector of merchandising for Gen- 
ovese Drug Stores. “We’ve had more 
than 30 percent private label growth 
for the second year in a row.” 

Like many other chains, Gen-

Private label accounted for nearly $2 billion in 
sales in drug stores in 93, thanks to careful nur- 
turing from retailers and the sluggish economy. 


ovese has pushed store branding 
into new areas of the store recently, 
adding hand lotions, skin creams, 
tissues, cotton balls and other 
items. 

Deep discount giants Drug Empo- 
rium and Phar-Mor have also 
branched out in recent months. 
Drug Emporium has added a new 
private label bath and body set, 
while Phar-Mor has launched with 
much fanfare QV, a new line of soft 
drinks. 


Is the honeymoon over? 


Just how much of the drug store 
business the private label industry 
can devour remains a guess, but 
even the most vocal industry propo- 
nents caution that the industry’s 
easiest days are behind it. Said 
Michael Jandernoa, chief executive 
of Perrigo, “It’s a new world out 
there. The national brands have 
woken up and made some dramatic 
cost cuts and changed the way they 
do business. 

“The bar is going to be raised,” he 
added. “We as an industry are going 
to have to tighten up our relation- 
ships, emphasize strategic alliances 
and... improve turnaround time.” 

Added David Brubaker, chair- 
man, founder and managing part- 
ner of Leiner Health Products, 
“Everybody on the retail side is 
looking at how they can take days 
out of the (order) cycle. The manu- 
facturers who position themselves 
to meet and facilitate the retailer’s 
need for more efficiencies... will be 
the ones to survive.” 

What’s more, both retailers and 
manufacturers seem to agree that 
brand names are still the engine dri- 
ving the business. “There can be a 
killing of the brand if your pro- 
gram’s out of balance,” admitted one 
supplier. “Both sides need support.” _ 

—James Frederick

Eckerd plans secondary public offering; 
Merrill Lynch, Eckerd maintain control 


by Mike Troy 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
Merrill Lynch and 10 other 
major institutional in- 
vestors in Eckerd Corp. will 
reduce their ownership in- 
terest in the 1,713-store 
drug chain with the com- 
pletion of a secondary stock 
offering. 

A registration statement 
for five million shares and 
an over-allotment of 750,000 
shares was filed with the Se- 
curities and Exchange Com- 
mission on March 31. At 
press time, brokers reported 
the shares would begin trad- 
ing on April 25. 

Eckerd management is 
not selling any shares, but 
Merrill Lynch will reduce 
its stake in the company 
from 46.4 percent to 37.5 
percent by selling 2.82 mil- 
lion shares. Of the 31.6 mil- 
lion Eckerd shares out- 
standing, Merrill Lynch 
currently owns 14.6 million. 

The 10 other investors in- 
volved in the offering will 
sell 2.17 million shares and 
reduce their ownership from 
27.2 percent to 20.4 percent. 
Merrill Lynch and the other 
investors will participate on 
a proportional basis if there 
is demand for the over-al- 
lotment of 750,000 shares. 

Even with Merrill Lynch’s 
reduced ownership, the bro- 


kerage house—along with 
Eckerd managers, who to- 
gether own 6.3 percent of the 
outstanding shares—will 
maintain control of Eckerd. 

“If the Merrill Lynch in- 
vestors and the manage- 
ment investors were to vote 
together, they would likely 
continue to be in a position 
to elect the board of direc- 
tors...and to effectively con- 
trol the affairs and policies 
of the company,” a registra- 
tion statement noted. 

Three of Eckerd’s nine 
board members are also on 
the board of Merrill Lynch 
Capital Partners, according 
to the registration statement. 


A roller coaster market 


The new stock offering 
will enter a volatile market. 
Uncertainty over interest 
rates, inflation concerns and 
the threat of a bear market 
have sent the Dow Jones av- 
erage on a roller coaster 
ride in recent months. Eck- 
erd has not been immune to 
price fluctuations, but its 
share price has trended up- 
ward since last August’s 
IPO price of $14. The chain 
has also made big strides to 
improve its competitive po- 
sition (see story page 33). 

During the fiscal year 
ended Jan. 29, sales rose to 
$4.1 billion from $3.8 billion 
the previous year. Further 
gains are expected as new 


Treasury Drug acquisition 


hoosts Big B's bottom line 


BIRMINGHAM, Ala. — 
An 18.5 percent sales in- 
crease and a 27.7 percent 
earnings increase at Big B 
were highlights of a record- 
setting fiscal year that end- 
ed Jan. 29, 1994. 

Sales increased to $595 
million from $503 million 
the previous year, and earn- 
ings grew to $11.7 million 
from $9.2 million during the 
same period. 

Big B chairman Anthony 
Bruno attributed the strong 
results to the acquisition 
early last year of 45 Trea- 
sury Drug stores from Thrift 
Drug and to a robust 8 per- 
cent same-store sales in- 


crease. He added that the 
addition of the Treasury 
stores in the Atlanta market 
provided economies in ad- 
vertising and distribution. 

In addition to the Trea- 
Ssury acquisition, Big B 
opened 10 new stores to fin- 
ish the year with 354 units. 
An estimated 15 to 20 new 
stores will be opened this 
year. Alabama remains the 
chain’s largest market with 
153 stores, but neighboring 
Georgia (152 stores) is now 
equally important in terms 
of Big B’s growth plans. 

Big B also has 22 units in 
Florida, 19 in Tennessee 
and eight in Mississippi.

Debt still worrysome 


One of the biggest con- 
cerns for the retailer contin- 
ues to be its large debt bur- 
den. Eckerd has long-term 
debt of $954 million, but an- 
nual interest expenses have 
been declining due primari- 
ly to last year’s $950 million 
refinancing of high-interest 
debt and the use of a por- 
tion of $65.8 million in IPO 
proceeds to pay down debt. 

Interest expenses in the 
last fiscal year totaled $113 
million. Analysts project 
that amount will drop to $95 
million during the current 
fiscal year that ends Janu- 
ary 1995, enabling Eckerd to 
record for the first time in 
several years a net profit. 
Interest expenses will de- 
cline further to a projected 
$90 million during the fiscal 
year ending January 1996. 

While still sizable, Eck- 
erd’s new interest charges 
mark a substantial decrease 
from the more than $140 
million in annual interest it 
paid during the previous 
three years. Those interest 
payments helped drag it into 
the red, where it accumulat- 
ed net operating loss carry- 
forwards of $332 million as 
of Jan. 29. The carryforward 
amount is being used to off- 
set future taxable income. 


Walgreens on track for 
another record year 


DEERFIELD, Iil. — Ex- 
tending its 19-year win- 
ning streak, Walgreen Co. 
reported sharply higher 
sata and earnings for the 
second quarter and first 
half of fiscal 1994. 

Net earnings for the 
quarter ended Feb. 28 
jumped 16.8 percent to 
$97.6 million, reflecting a 
strong Christmas season, 
healthy flu season sales and 
sharp cost controls. Sales 
for the period were up 10.7 
percent to $2.5 billion. 

For the first half, net 
earnings rose 15.1 percent 
to $141.8 million, with 
sales up 10.6 percent to 
$4.62 billion. 


The pharmacy depart- 
ment again led the charge, 
with prescription sales up 
18.9 percent for the first 
six months. Same-store 
pharmacy sales rose 12.3 
percent. 

Walgreens’ operated 
1,901 stores in 30 states 
and Puerto Rico at the end 
of the second quarter and 
was on track to open 175 
total new stores this fiscal 
year, said chairman and 
chief executive Charles R. 
Walgreen III. “We’ll enter 
two new markets—Cleve- 
land with at least 15 full- 
service drug stores and 
Buffalo with five—in the 
fall.” 


Wheels keep Fay’s rolling 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — The strength of its core drug store 
business helped Fay’s Inc. post record net earnings for its 
final quarter ended Jan. 29. Net earnings increased 11.9 
percent to a record $5.9 million compared to the $5.2 mil- 
lion reported for the same quarter one year earlier. 

Included in operating results for the quarter: a gain of 
$328,000, which resulted from the termination of leases for 
two of the nine Paper Cutter stores Fay’s closed during the 
first quarter. 

Revenues for the quarter were $255.1 million, an in- 
crease of 6.1 percent over the $258 million reported in the 
previous year’s fourth quarter. Same-store sales for the 
quarter increased 4.9 percent. Prescription sales rose 12.3 
percent. 

President and chief operating officer David Panasci said 
the quarter’s sales had been strong despite harsh weather be- 
cause, unlike many other businesses, the Wheels auto parts 
division thrives in harsh weather. 

Net earnings for the year rose 7.3 percent to $12.0 million 
vs. the $11.2 million reported one year earlier. Revenues for 
the year reached $919.7 million, an increase of 3.5 percent 
over last year’s revenues of $902.6 million. Same-store sales 
for the year rose 3.5 percent. 


Investors sought for troubled combo chain 


TAMPA, Fla. — West Florida supermar- 
ket and combo store operator Kash n’ Kar- 
ry’s advertising promises additional check- 
out lanes will be opened if customers are 
more than three deep. And, if all the lanes 
are full, “we'll just open another store,” the 


TV ad boasts. 


It’s an image far from reality. What is real 
is this: Kash n’ Karry’s weak financial posi- 
tion has put it in an uphill battle in a very 
competitive and growing market. 

Constrained by the financial 
a 1988 leveraged buyout and a $354 million 
debt burden, Kash n’ Karry and the chain’s 
majority stockholder, Leonard Green & 
Partners—which is also majority owner of 
Los Angeles-based Thrifty Corp—are look- 


ing for additional investors. 


An infusion of cash is needed since nu- 
merous cost-trimming efforts have already 
been tried. More than a dozen stores were 
closed last year, paring store count to 103 
units, including 50 with pharmacies. Capi- 
tal spending was curtailed in December. 
Forward buying and inventory levels were 
reduced, and employee and officer wages 
and salaries frozen or cut. A recapitaliza- 
tion plan that would have restructured the 
chain’s high-interest debt and improved 
cash flow was unsuccessful last August. 

Nevertheless, said a Kash n’ Karry 
spokesman, “To say we are trying to sell the 
company is an overstatement. We hope very 


soon that we will be in a position to live up 
to [the new store opening statement we 
make in our advertising].” 

One possibility: Leonard Green itself may 
invest more capital in Kash n’ Karry, said 
Robin lori, a spokesperson for the invest- 
ment firm. 

Leonard Green became involved with 
the supermarket operator in 1988, when 
Kash n’ Karry was formed through the 
combined buyout of Lucky Stores Inc.’s 
Florida supermarket division for $386 mil- 
lion and Kroger Co.’s Florida supermarket 
and liquor stores for $64 million. The in- 
vestment company sank another $30 mil- 
lion into the retailer in 1991 to become the 
largest shareholder. 

The chain’s financial condition has 
caused its bond rating to sink to B- on se- 
nior unsecured debt and CCC+ on subordi- 
nated debt. “The major issue is Kash n’ 
Karry’s financial structure doesn’t support 
the business,” said Ned Komar, a bond ana- 
lyst with Standard & Poor’s. “They built a 
couple of stores last year, but because they 
weren't able to complete the refinancing, 
they had to pay for the stores out of work- 
ing capital—and you just can’t run a busi- 
ness like that. 

“In a growing market such as west cen- 
tral Florida they have got to continue to 
build new stores if they are going to stay 
competitive,” Komar said.

Access, ease of use 
transform category 


here is a scene in the 1971 
motion picture “Summer of 
"42” when teenage actor 
Gary Grimes musters up 
enough courage to go into a drug 
store to buy a condom. It’s an awk- 
ward situation for young Grimes be- 
cause during the early 1940s con- 
doms were kept behind the counter. 

All that has changed, and to a star- 
tling degree. Condoms of various col- 
ors, textures and even sizes now per- 
vade the marketplace. Pharmacists 
don’t get asked for condoms much 
any more, as consumers can freely 
select from among dozens of choices. 

“Just about every retail outlet in 
America has condoms out and avail- 
able, which is the way it should be,” 
said Kerry Hoffman, vice president 
of national accounts with Ansell 
Consumer Products, manufacturer 
of the LifeStyles brand. 

There have been other changes as 
well. Women now account for 35 
percent of sales in the $280 million 
category, and the 12-count package

FOR THE PHARMACIST/FAMILY PLANNING 


somes ANNUAL REPORT 


Pharmacys high-stakes ride 


by Ken Rankin 


or the past year, 
) ee pharma- 

cists have been 
strapped to a health care 
reform roller coaster for a 
high-stakes thrill ride that 
will almost certainly deter- 
mine pharmacy’s fate well 
into the 21st century. 

The end-point of that 
ride is still in question, 
but the picture should 
snap into clearer focus 
this summer when Con- 
gress and the Clinton Ad- 
ministration try to ham- 
mer out details of a 
compromise health pro- 
gram that will seal phar- 
macy’s future one way or 
the other. But no matter 
what happens in Washing- 
ton over the next few 
months, the events of the 
past year have already re- 
shaped retail pharmacy 
priorities and redirected 
the profession's course. 

Nowhere is that more 
apparent than in Wash- 
ington, where the prospect 
of far-reaching health re- 
form legislation prompted 
NARD and NACDS to 
put aside past differ- 
ences and forge a new 
“Community Retail 
Pharmacy Health 
Care Reform Coali- 
tion” to represent the 
interests of both drug 
chains and indepen- 
dent pharmacists. 


By joining forces on the 
health reform front and by 
moving quickly and deci- 
sively to support the Clin- 
ton Administration's 
initiatives, the new NARD/ 
NACDS coalition was able 
to influence the shape of 
the White House plan. The

Other coming attractions 


Although health reform 
has dominated the agenda 
for retail pharmacy over 
the last year, it is far from 
the only critical concern of 
practitioners in 1994. 

Here’s what’s been cook- 
ing on some of the other 
burners: 

Education: The ques- 
tion of a_ universal 
Pharm.D. is heating up 
again, thanks to a new 
study from Abt Associates 
which predicts that a six- 
year degree could add 
nearly $1 billion a year to 
the cost of educating and 
employing pharmacists in 
the United States. 

On Capitol Hill, mean- 
while, Sen. Orrin Hatch 
(R-Utah) is voicing strong 
concerns about the eco- 
nomic impact of the 
ACPE’s plans to mandate 
the Pharm.D. Those con- 
cerns haven’t dampened 
the enthusiasm of acade- 
mics for lengthier edu- 
cational requirements. 

FDA: Commissioner 
David Kessler has toned 
down the agency’s rhetoric 
about restricting pharma- 
cy’s historic right to com- 
pound prescriptions, but 
some pharmacy leaders 
suspect the FDA is likely 
to continue meddling in 
this area. One scheme def- 


initely in the planning 
stages: born-again patient 
package insert regulations, 
under which the agency 
hopes to require pharma- 
cists to dispense written 
“patient labeling” along 
with prescription drugs. 
Third party: Relations 
between retail pharmacy 
leaders and third-party in- 
termediaries reached an 
all-time low during the 
past year, and they appear 
to be sinking even further. 
Leaders of both NARD and 
NACDS have expressed 
particular concern over the 
continued emergence of re- 
strictive networks that se- 
verely limit participation 
by community pharmacy. 
in response, chain drug 
store industry leaders are 
about to unveil a new 
“Pharmacy Direct Network” 
that will enable retail drug 
stores to negotiate directly 
with third-party payors. A 
separate community phar- 
macy network, Rx Med, is 
being organized with the 
support of NARD. 
Pharmacy unity: Forget 
it! Notwithstanding the un- 
precedented alliance be- 
tween drug chains and 
independents, health care 
reform appears to have dri- 
ven a wedge between retail 
pharmacy groups and oth- 


er segments of the profes- 
sion. Relations between the 
APhA and the NARD/ 
NACDS alliance are run- 
ning particularly rough in 
the wake of the APhA’s ef- 
forts to promote Medco’s 
controversial Coordinated 
Care Network. 

Antitrust: The continu- 
ing anti-pharmacy posture 
of antitrust enforcers at the 
Federal Trade Commission 
underscores the signifi- 
cance of provisions of the 
Clinton health reform bill 
offering limited antitrust 
immunity for retail phar- 
macy third-party negotia- 
tions. Despite information 
submitted from community 
pharmacy leaders and oth- 
ers concerning the anti- 
competitive nature of the 
Merck/Medco merger, The 
FTC rubber-stamped the 
deal without a single public 
hearing. 

Since then, the FTC has 
attacked the Maryland 
Pharmaceutical Associa- 
tion for discouraging par- 
ticipation in the prescrip- 
tion plan for Baltimore city 
workers, and it has given a 
green light to non-profit 
hospitals to resell drugs 
purchased at “non-profit” 
discounts to nursing 


homes currently supplied 


by community pharmacies.

And now the good news 


On a positive note,

present drug stores with 
the opportunity to regain 
lost market share. 

Seen as positive factors 
influencing OTCs: Rx-to-

usage; the untapped po-

choose to tough out condi-

the possibility that OTCs 
will become more popular 
with government officials 
anxious to lower costs.

and they are so basic there 
is little likelihood that these 
principles will be lost from 
policy considerations of the 
future,” said William Soller,

ural fit for switch products.

health care costs through 
the saved costs and time of 
unneeded doctor's visits. It

(Above) Food stores gained 522 units in ’93, followed by mass mer- 
chants who added 358 pharmacies. Chains fared better than inde- 
pendents, with a net gain of 42 units vs. a loss of 1,134 independent 
stores. In spite of the loss in head count, indys, and indeed all phar- 
macies, increased purchases through wholesalers and warehouses 
over those in 1992 as follows: mass merchandisers (+12.1%), chains 
(+9.4%), independents (+9.0%) and food (+3.5%). 

(Above right) Chain pharmacies broke a four-year downward spiral 
in 1993 by claiming a 24.6% market share in pharmacy, up from 
24.5% in 1992, but down from 26% in 1989. Other winners: mail or- 
der (+0.8%), mass merchandisers (+0.5%) and food store pharma- 
cies (+0.5%). Independents reached a six-year low of 20.9%. (In 
1988, they enjoyed a 28.8% share.)

Rite Aid to buy LaVerdiere's 


by Barbara White 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — 
Accelerating the rapid 
consolidation of the chain 
drug industry’s mid-sized 
players, Rite Aid Corp. has 
signed an agreement to buy 
67-unit LaVerdiere’s Super 
Drug Stores, headquartered 
in Winslow, Me. No pur- 
chase price was disclosed. 

LaVerdiere’s operates 
stores in Maine, New Hamp- 
shire and Vermont. Rite Aid 
currently operates in all 
three states, with 29 units in 
Maine, 23 in New Hamp- 
shire and 9 in Vermont. 

The chain was attractive 
to Rite Aid because of its 
strong pharmacy focus and 
its similarly managed front- 
end business, said Suzanne 
Mead, Rite Aid’s vice presi- 
dent of advertising and cor- 
porate communications. 

“The purchase made sense 
because the chain comple- 
ments our business. We are 
looking to enhance our third- 
party plans, particularly in 
Maine,” said Mead. 

All LaVerdiere’s stores 
will operate under the Rite 
Aid name beginning as early 
as next month, pending fed- 
eral approval of the merger. 
Although the stores are simi- 
lar in focus and size to Rite 


Aid units—LaVerdiere’s 
stores average 7,500 square 
feet, while Rite Aid stores 
range from 7,700 to 8,000 
square feet—there are some 
differences in merchandise. 
LaVerdiere’s carries more 
general merchandise and 


For more on Alex Grass’ 


role at Rite Aid see pg. 2. 


seasonal sundries than a 
typical Rite Aid. 

“The stores do carry some 
nontraditional drug store 
merchandise, but we are 
planning to run the stores 
with the merchandise in 
place,” said Mead. The move 
may be an effort by Rite Aid 
to experiment a bit more 


“The purchase 
made sense be- 
cause the chain 
complements our 
business. We are 
looking to enhance 
our third-party 
plans, particularly 
in Maine’ 

—Mead, Rite Aid 


with its merchandise mix. 
The purchase did not in- 
clude LaVerdiere’s ware- 
house or headquarters. The 
New England stores will be 
serviced from Rite Aid’s 
warehouse in Rome, N.Y. 


Doing business difficult 


LaVerdiere’s president 
Stephen LaVerdiere said 
the 72-year-old, family- 
owned chain decided to seek 
a buyer as business became 
more difficult for a small 
chain in New England. 

Five years ago, he said, 
Maine blue laws were re- 
pealed, allowing stores other 
than small businesses to 
open for business on Sunday. 
“We found ourselves compet- 
ing seven days a week rather 
than six,” LaVerdiere told 
Drug Store News. 

The blue law repeal also 
made the state more attrac- 
tive to large chains. In the

Sears: Private label cosmetics 


CHICAGO — In a bold joint venture with former 
Lancéme president Pierre Rogers, Sears is preparing 
the major launch of its own line of cosmetics in the fall 
of 1995. 

The partnership with Rogers could herald the roll- 
out of several beauty care lines, according to a Sears 
spokesperson. Cosmetic and fragrance products will 
combine quality and affordability, she said. 

The launch is in line with Sears’ expansion of its new 
in-store beauty boutiques, and it could have a major 
impact on chain drug cosmetic business. A complete re- 
port will appear in the next issue of Drug Store News. 


Southern Drug builds membership 


GAINESVILLE, Fla. — Southern Drug, a loose-knit 
but well-established coalition of chain drug retailers, 
recently added five new members to its ranks, further 
extending its national reach beyond its regional begin- 
nings. New members include Walnut Creek, Calif.- 
based Longs Drug Stores; Raleigh, N.C.-based Kerr 
Drug Stores; Eagleville, Pa.-based I Got It At Gary’s; 
Chariton, Iowa’-based Drugtown Drugstores chain; 
and Point Pleasant, West Va.-based Fruth Pharmacy. 

This year’s meeting will be held Sept. 28 in Oak- 
land, Calif., hosted by Bill Eames, who served as 
chairman and chief executive officer of Bill’s Drugs 
prior to the chain’s acquisition by Longs. 

Founded in the 1930s, Southern Drug’s 21 chain 
and 40 supplier members meet once a year to discuss 
common problems and ways to deal effectively with 
them. Since most participants aren’t direct competi- 
tors, discussions are usually candid.

by Allene Symons 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. 
— Longs Drug Stores, 
known for its decentralized 
style of store-manager au- 
tonomy, has named Sharon 
Findley as its first category 
manager, according to pres- 
ident Steve Roath. 

Roath told Drug Store 
News in a recent interview 
that as manager for a sub- 
category of OTC, Findley 
will help the chain define 
the category manager con- 
cept. Initially, Findley will 
concentrate on laxatives 
and antacids. 


Changing tides 


Since rolling out its POS 
system two years ago, Longs 
has realized new opportuni- 
ties based on electronic 
sales data. “It is a process— 
it has chased us through a 
lot of questions about our- 
selves,” said Roath. 

One outcome so far has 
been inventory reduction, al- 
though that was not an in- 
tended goal. Planograms 
will be one of the next steps, 


marking a sea change for 
the big West Coast chain: 
Until recently, Longs did not 
centrally lay out schematics,

has been allocated for some 
planogrammed or standard 
sets like cameras.

an opportunity to implement 
their own merchandising 
and override the planogram 
if they can improve on 
planogram performance 


standards, noted Roath.

learn,” he said. He added 
that it is unclear how many 
category managers Longs 
will have or need, and it is 
likely that the 305-store 
chain will not have a catego- 
ry manager for every de- 
partment. “Category man- 
agement means different 
things to different people. 
We will create our own defi- 
nition,” said Roath.

WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


A native of Jackson, Ala., Dwayne 
Hoven has a relaxed, friendly manner, 
but he doesn’t take a laid-back posi- 
tion when it comes to business. 

Hoven made it clear that changes 
will be implemented very quickly at 
HSI after the anticipated close of the 
deal in July. 

“Immediately,” he revealed, Revco 
will begin installing its POS and phar- 


front end of the 
HSI stores. “We 
will be able to 
improve’ their 
front-end business pretty dramatical- 
ly and pretty quickly by adding mer- 
chandise and utilizing our pricing, 
which is more competitive, and our 
advertising, which is more aggres- 
sive,” he said. 

Hoven had heard the rumors that 
all or part of HSI’s Brooks division 
might be sold. His comment: “All the 
pro forma work includes them, and 


we're prepared to run them.” 

Like McAlear, Hoven has the chal- 
lenge of overseeing a merger that will 
double the size of his chain. This is a 
huge undertaking, but Hoven has 
earned his spurs with another daunt- 
ing challenge. 

Hoven, 52, has been president of 
Revco since shortly after it exited a 
four-year-long bankruptcy, and he 
weathered the bankruptcy as a mem- 
ber of Revco’s executive committee. 

His presidential years have been 
years of significant success for Revco, 
largely because of the investments in 
technology and store renovations 
made during the bankruptcy. 

Not a self promoter, Hoven has 
clearly proven his worth at Revco. He 
joined in December 1987 as senior 
vice president of distribution, and he 
held two executive vice president ti- 
tles before being given the post of 
president and chief operating officer 
in July 1992—after a fairly lengthy 
search that included outside people. 
He was named chief executive officer 
in September 1993. 

Hoven is pragmatic about his new- 
found status in the chain drug indus- 
try. With a smile, he noted that among 
the suppliers who are eager to applaud 
him now are those who, as creditors 
during Revco’s bankruptcy, tried to get 
the executive committee replaced. He 
said he jokes with those individuals 
about the situation now. 

Hoven doesn’t take himself too seri- 
ously. But his serious approach to 
business is the secret of his success.

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


Despite a full-court press from the 
NACDS/NARD Retail Community 
Pharmacy Coalition for Health Care 
Reform, the White House failed to at- 
tract enough Congressional support to 
ensure passage in either the House or 
the Senate. 

House Energy and Commerce Com- 
mittee chairman John Dingell (D- 
Mich.) all but threw in the towel last 
month when he introduced his own 


4 Drug Store News, May 16, 1994 


president Ron 
Ziegler abstain- 
ing, the NRF 
board voted earli- 
er this month to endorse “incremental” 
health reform legislation sponsored by 
Reps. Roy Rowland (D-Ga.) and Mike 
Bilirakis (R-Fla.). 

That plan, which avoids employer 
mandates but would require Medicaid 
to seek care from “community health 
centers,” represents a “practical way 
to solve the real problems in our 
health care system without risking the 
economic viability of America’s retail- 


ers,” federation officials said. 

To be sure, it is way too early to 
write an obituary for the President’s 
health reform initiative. But it is clear 
that the White House Health Security 
Act simply won’t pass Congress as cur- 
rently written. 


President to nix two issues 


Even top Clinton Administration of- 
ficials acknowledge that much. Ira 
Magaziner, the chief White House 
health reformer, has already conceded 
that the Administration is prepared to 
scrap two key parts of the original bill 
that have drawn heavy fire from the 
pharmaceutical industry: 

@ Creation of a new advisory counsel 
on “breakthrough” drugs responsible 
for determining whether the prices of 
these products are “fair”; and 

@ Fresh authority for federal 
Medicare officials to withhold pay- 
ments for certain drugs considered to 
be overpriced. 

Meanwhile, other Administration of- 
ficials are hinting at a possible compro- 
mise on the employer mandate issue. 
Concessions on these points shouldn’t 
affect the drug store industry’s support 
for the President’s plan—if anything, 
they should make the White House re- 
form proposal more attractive. 

But if the Administration makes 
other compromises—such as backing 
down from its commitments to stamp 
out discriminatory pricing practices by 
drug manufacturers—then even the 
strongest drug store industry support- 
ers of the President’s plan could sour 
on health reform.

| EXECUTIVE 


Lessons from north of the border 


Continued from page 1 

have kept sales growth on track despite the coun- 
try’s still-sluggish economy; some, like Coutu and 
Shoppers, are also recording modest gains or at least 
holding to prior-year levels in operating earnings. 
They do it by keeping a lid on costs, staying in touch 
with local consumer demand, pumping private label 
and making the most of their tight shelf space. 

Shoppers, for instance, managed to push up oper- 
ating earnings 5 percent to a record $100 million 
(Canadian) on sales of $3.2 billion in fiscal 1993, 
thanks to higher sales, tight cost controls and grow- 
ing support for its higher-margin private label busi- 
ness, which now accounts for 10 percent of sales. 

Nevertheless, Shoppers chairman and chief execu- 
tive David Bloom acknowledged in the report, “It was 
not a year in which earnings growth came easily. 

“Throughout 1993, prescription margins were un- 
der pressure as governments, employers and indi- 
viduals looked for ways to save on health care 
costs,” Bloom noted. “Moreover, very competitive 
retail conditions affected gross margins in virtually 
every other product category.” 

' What’s more, Shoppers’ tobacco sales plummeted 
21 percent, Bloom said, as millions of Canadians 
turned off by high federal and provincial cigarette 
taxes “turned to the contraband market.” Recently, 
federal and provincial governments moved to cor- 
rect the problem of contraband and cross-border 
cigarette traffic by a huge rollback in taxes. 

In Coutu’s case, meanwhile, the Longeueil, Que- 
bec-based chain drug power forsook short-term 
earnings gains for long-term gains in market share 
and still maintained earnings on a par with last 
year. Noted chairman and chief executive Jean 
Coutu in a statement early this year, “In spite of an 
economic context that continues to be characterized 
by low consumer spending and keen competition, 
The Jean Coutu Group held onto and increased its 
market share thanks to the implementation of a 
highly dynamic marketing strategy.” 


Swimming upstream 


Nevertheless, Coutu and others are still swim- 
ming upstream in this sprawling, sparsely populat- 
ed nation. One big reason: an economy still mired 
in recession, job layoffs, relatively high taxes and 
cross-border spending. 

Chain drug executives across Canada agree that 
the recession has bitten deep into the prescription 
drug business, as cash-strapped provincial govern- 
ments attack health care reimbursement levels. 
“All the provinces are under tremendous economic 
duress...and we’re seeing lower (pharmacy) remu- 
neration from third-party and government plans,” 
said Bloom in an interview. “The dispensing fee in 
Ontario is now $5.86; it used to be $6.47.” 

Added Rochelle Stenzler, president and general 
manager of 146-store Pharma Plus Drugmarts, 
“Where recessionary impacts hit employers... there’s 
a lot of pressure to roll back drug dispensing fees.” 


Not all of Canada’s provinces are hurting as bad- 
ly as Quebec and Ontario, according to some. In 
British Columbia, investment by Pacific Rim na- 
tions never completely dried up, said Mark Nuss- 
baum, executive vice president and chief operating 
officer at Richmond, B.C.-based London Drugs. 

Nevertheless, Nussbaum agreed that retail 
pharmacy was yielding razor-thin profit margins. 
“The prescription business is strictly convenience- 
based, since price is virtually the same every- 
where. The only money to be made in pharmacy in 
Canada is the dispensing fee.” 

Nussbaum, who is American, added a warning to 
his U.S. counterparts: “Retailers had better learn to 
live with that, because that’s all you’re going to get.” 

Canada’s chain drug retailers are also concerned 
with the looming invasion of Wal-Mart. The retail 
megalith gained an immediate and powerful na- 
tional entree into Canada with its purchase in 
March of 122 Woolco stores. 


Up in smoke 


In Ontario, meanwhile, drug retailers face anoth- 
er major challenge: the almost certain passage this 
year of the so-called Tobacco Control Act, or Bill 
119. One of the bill’s effects will be to will outlaw 
tobacco sales in all pharmacy outlets. The measure 
is expected to be law by the end of the year, forcing 
drug chains in the province to shed one key pillar of 
their business on the grounds that tobacco and 
health care don’t mix. 

Chains like Shoppers and Pharma Plus have lob- 
bied hard but unsuccessfully to overturn the pro- 
posed ban, which is making its way through the 
provincial legislature. “It’s falling on deaf ears; it’s 
now an emotive issue,” said Stenzler. “In the view of 
the Ontario government, retail pharmacy is a 500- 
to 800-square-foot dispensary. They're refusing to 
acknowledge that a drug store has become a mass 
retailer, competing with all other mass merchants.” 

Nevertheless, said Rhondda Snary, a spokesper- 
son for the Ontario Ministry of Health, “The legisla- 
tion is quite clear: there can be no tobacco sales in 
any retail outlet which contains a pharmacy.” 

Added Bloom, “The food/drug combos and Wal- 
Mart will have to choose between selling prescrip- 
tions and selling tobacco.” 

That leveling of the playing field may take some 
of the sting out of the sales ban for some drug retail- 
ers. But supermarkets and discount stores may 
have a loophole if their stores are big enough or so 
situated as to allow for a new, separate pharmacy 
configuration. “If the pharmacy is separate, with a 
completely separate entrance, then it is fine to sell 
cigarettes in the other part of the store,” said Snary. 

Canada’s efforts to restrict tobacco sales and use 
are already receiving interest from some U.S. states, 
Snary said. “There have been contacts between On- 
tario and California for some time,” she told Drug 
Store News. Ohio, she said, has also sent a team to 
Toronto to study the anti-smoking initiatives.

he condom category’s run of 

strong sales growth a few 

years back has flattened. 

Drug stores’ sales remained 
at $178 million during the 12 
months through February 1994 as 
the influence of factors that led to 
explosive growth in the 1980s 
seems to matter no longer. 

Magic Johnson is old news, and it 
has been eight years since former 
surgeon general C. Everett Koop 
first told us that condoms helped 
prevent the spread of AIDS. The 
death toll from AIDS in the United 
States stands at 220,000 people, 
but newspaper headlines lately 
have been more preoccupied with 
health care reform, Whitewater 
and Bosnia. 

While sales in the category may 
currently be sluggish, this high- 
margin profit center is again ex-

pected to grow, according to manu- 
facturers. Among the factors cited: 
innovative new products, a series of 
government-sponsored public ser- 
vice announcements and the in- 
evitable publicity the category will 
receive with future AIDS deaths of 
high profile individuals. 

“What is disappointing to us is 
the category is not growing as much 
as it should. So much of our target 
audience is young people who either 
don’t think they are going to get 
AIDS, or by the time they do get it, 
think there will be a cure for it,” 
said Kim Leffler, product manager 
of Aladan Corp.’s Safetex division, 
manufacturer of the Saxon Gold 
line of condoms. 

“Everybody has a responsibility 
to get the word out to people that 
this product will save lives and pre- 
vent a lot of unhappiness,” she 
said. “The Centers for Disease Con- 
trol is doing its part with public 
service announcements, manufac- 
turers are doing their part by mak- 
ing the best possible products, and 
retailers are doing their part by ful- 
filling their responsibility to make 
the products available. If we all do 
our part, we will see growth in the 
category as well as doing a great 
human service.” 


Promos, merchandising 


Lately, retailers have become 
more aggressive with promotions. 
Manufacturers report that they are 
seeing increased circular advertise- 
ments featuring special prices on 
condoms. Manufacturers see the cir- 
cular ads, combined with the public- 
ity from the CDC’s public service 
announcements that are currently 
airing, as a wise strategy to boost 
category sales. 

Another factor that will con- 
tribute to growth is more innovative 
merchandising strategies on the 
part of retailers, according to manu- 
facturers. Typically, the category is 
placed near the pharmacy adjacent 
to feminine hygiene. Retailers have 
been reluctant to experiment with 
cross-merchandising strategies so 
prevalent with categories such as 
film, batteries and cosmetics. Since 
women are accounting for a larger 
portion of sales, one manufacturer 
questioned, why not place a clip 
strip next to the lipstick or a 
counter display near the cosmetics 
register? The same holds true for 
men’s toiletries. Why not a clip strip 
near the men’s shaving section? 

“Retailers have historically posi- 
tioned condoms near the pharmacy, 
but that is not necessarily the best 
spot,” said one manufacturer. “That 
makes it hard sometimes for people 
who don’t know where to look for 
them. I would position them in as 
many different places as your target 
customer would be looking for them.” 


Struggling for market share 


The condom category continues to 
be dominated by Carter-Wallace, 
which is easily the most significant 
player with more than 60 percent 
market share in both unit and dol- 
lar volume in drug and food stores. 

Carter officials declined to com- 
ment for this article, but invest- 
ment analysts that follow the com- 


pany project that Carter and its 
flagship Trojan line will maintain 
more than a 60 percent share of the 
market through 1998. 

“The condom industry has high 
barriers to entry because name 
recognition plays such a vital role in 
the consumer’s purchase decision,” 
said Patricia Lee with Vector Secu- 
rities Internat:onal. “Brand identifi- 
cation is more important than shelf 
space. Advertising constraints also 
tend to preserve the status quo be- 
cause it is difficult for new entrants 
to buy share.” 

Products in the Trojan line com- 
prise 12 of the 15 highest dollar vol- 
ume condoms and nine of 15 top 
unit volume items. 

“Revenue growth has slowed in 
recent years as fear of AIDS, which 
sparked exceptional unit demand in 
the late 1980s, has abated,” Lee 
said. “The Surgeon General’s new 
campaign to encourage condom us- 
age among teenagers to prevent 
pregnancy and sexually transmitted 
diseases should revitalize industry 
growth and enable Carter-Wallace 
to report a 13 percent increase in 
condom profits in fiscal ’95.” 

While Carter’s share has held

WHITE PLAINS, NEW YORK 
— Al Kenney, Manager of Trade 
Marketing, Tambrands, Inc. coor- 
dinator of category management ac- 
tivity for the 
$600 million 
feminine hy- 
giene manufac- 
turer, shared his 
views in an ex- 
clusive inter- 
view. “Manag- 
ing the category 
is a responsibil- 
ity” Kenney 
commented, 
“We do not strive for more shelf 
space than we deserve, we look at 
the data for the entire section and 
then make recommendations that 
benefit the entire category.” 

For category management pre- 
sentations, Tambrands_ uses 
Gladson & Associates, a Lisle, IL 
based space management consult- 
ing firm. Kenney said, “We used 
to have contracts with two other 
companies, but our sales force 
chose Gladson unanimously. Our 
regional managers told us that they 
[Gladson] understood our business 
and were effective from day one.” 
Using a space management center 
gives the retailer an objective per- 
spective on the category. 

“We have chosen not to bring 
our space management in-house be- 
cause we do not want to lose our 
objectivity, Kenney added, 
‘““Gladson is like an extension of our 
company, we have access to a tre- 
mendous service without the huge 
capital investment.” 

By using a service center, 
Tambrands has been able to build 
planograms using sensitive retailer 
data that would not otherwise be 
available. “Retailers give their store 
specific data to Gladson on a con- 
fidential, nondisclosure basis which 
is then incorporated into the 
planogram analysis.” 

“Our relationship with Gladson 
& Associates has been a big chap- 
ter in our category management 
success story” concluded Kenney.

Enter the female condom 


Even as traditional con- 
doms gain popularity among 
women, distribution of Wis- 
consin Pharmacal’s Reality 
female condom will begin in 
a few months, following the 
Food and Drug Administra- 
tion approval of a manufac- 
turing plant in London. The 
product is expected to retail 
for about $2.50 each. 

Reality, the first product 
of its kind, was originally 
approved by the FDA in 
May 1993 and has been 
manufactured at the compa- 
ny’s Jackson, Wisc. plant. 
However, mass distribution 
of the condom was delayed 
until the FDA approved the 
company’s’ high-volume 
manufacturing facility lo- 
cated in London. 

The female condom is a 
polyurethane sheath with 
two flexible rings on each 
end. It covers the cervix, 
lines the vaginal canal and 
partially extends over the 
labia. Women who have use 
the condom report it feels 
better than a male condom 
and can be inserted several 
hours before intercourse. 
However, its widespread ap- 
peal may hinge on whether 
consumers accept the prod- 
uct’s appearance since it 
protrudes from the vagina 
when inserted.

Fresh attention paid to mail order 


Or over a decade 
now, mail-order 
pharmacy services 


(MOPS) have been cutting 
in on community phar- 
macy’s customer base, 
winning over cost-con- 
scious third-party 
prescription payors and 
posting huge, double-digit 
sales gains. Now there are 
indications that the mar- 
ket for mail-order pre- 
scription drugs may be 
shifting into higher gear. 

In part, the brightening 
outlook for mail-service 
pharmacy is a by-product 
of the debate over health 
reform. The current em- 
phasis on “managed care” 
solutions to the problems 
afflicting the nation’s 
health delivery system is 
focusing fresh attention on 
mail-order drugs by gov- 
ernment and private third- 
party payors. 


At the same time, new 
technological develop- 
ments are beginning to 
overcome obstacles to pa- 
tient acceptance of mail- 
order drugs. The latest: 
the PharmaPhone—a new 
interactive video-phone 
pharmacy kiosk being 
road-tested today by a 
Canadian mail-service 
pharmacy, which may well 
be the harbinger of a new 
generation in mail-order 
drug service (see page 11). 

If that innovative Phar- 
maPHONE system pans 
out, this new technology 
may undermine retail 
pharmacy’s key argument 
against mail-order dis- 
pensing—the absence of 
personal, face-to-face in- 
teraction between the 
pharmacist and patient. 
Even without  break- 
through technological ad- 
vances, mail-order phar- 


macy operators are likely 
to continue as the fastest 
growing segment of the 
prescription drug market. 


Healthy sales growth 


During 1993, mail-order 
prescription sales climbed 
by 23 percent to approach 
$5 billion—a 50-fold in- 
crease since 1981 when 
the entire MOPS segment 
generated only $100 mil- 
lion in sales. The Ameri- 
can Managed Care Phar- 
macy Association—a trade 
group representing most of 
the major U.S. MOPS— 
predicts that sales by its 
members will top $6.5 bil- 
lion in 1995. If anything, 
that estimate appears to 
be conservative. 

Others are projecting an 
even deeper market pene- 
tration for the mail-order 
segment over the next few 
years. A study by the Vista 


Who’s who in mail-order pharmacy services 


Information Group pre- | 
dicts continued growth for 
MOPS by more than 30 
percent a year, and a total 
market for mail-order 
drugs in excess of $14 bil- 
lion by 1996. 

According to researchers 
at IMS America, mail-or- 
der pharmacies now ac- 
count for 7 percent of all 
U.S. prescription drug 
sales, and for mainte- 
nance drugs—the bread- 
and-butter of mail-order 
prescription providers — 
MOPS now controls an 
even larger market share. 
The AMCPA contends that 
its members now dispense 
over 14 percent of all 
maintenance drugs for the 
ambulatory pharmacy care 
market, and indications 
are that this share will rise 
rapidly in the current 
managed care climate. -

than $4 billion in prescrip- 
tion sales for mail-order 
pharmacy providers by 
1996, the study estimates. 

Behind the rosy growth 
projections for MOPS: 
growing pressure from 
third-party payors to chan- 
nel patients into mail-order 
plans. Over the past five 
years, scores of major em- 
ployers have added mail- 
order coverage “options” 
that financially penalize 
beneficiaries who continue 
to fill prescriptions at com- 
munity pharmacies. 

In response to this prod- 
ding from third-party pay- 
ors, McKesson’s PCS has 
forged a new alliance with 
the AARP to provide a na- 
tionwide mail-order pre- 
scription option. PAID pre- 


14 


wide” pharmacy network 
and buying group being 
formed by independent 
pharmacists (see page 38, 
FTP March ‘94 )—will offer 
mail-order prescription op- 
tions to third-party ad- 
ministrators who request 
them./Similarly, the Phar- 
macy’ Direct Network 
(PDN), developed by 
NACDS (see page 8), will 
also include a mail-order 
component. 


But what are we saving? 


But while PBMs eye 
mail-order dispensaries as 
a cost-cutting alternative to 
retail pharmacy, there are 
indications that the actual 
savings may be an illusion. 

One recent study con- 
ducted for the Health Care 


Financing Administration 
estimated the savings from 
mail-order prescriptions at 
barely 2 cents per day, 
while a comparison-shop- 
ping survey published in 
Changing Times magazine 
concluded that mail-order 
dispensaries are frequently 
more expensive than com- 
munity pharmacies. After 
c-omparing prices for a 
dozen drugs between sev- 
eral MOPS and “a typical 
drug store,” the magazine 
reported the average com- 
munity pharmacy price for 
10 of the 12 was lower 
than at least two of the 
mail order firms surveyed. 
Add in postage and han- 
dling and MOPS prescrip- 
tion prices were higher over 
44 percent of the time. 


Hidden costs 


Still other researchers 
have concluded that the 
hiddei costs associated 
with MOPS may all but 
eliminate any economic 
edge over community phar- 
macy practitioners. A pair 
of PCS-sponsored studies 
found that the large, 90- 
day or longer supplies typi- 
cally dispensed by mail-or- 
der providers often result in 
wasted medication. After 
interviewing patients of 
mail-order and community 
pharmacies, they conclud- 
ed that the number of 
tablets wasted per person 
was twice as great in the 
MOPS group. Similarly, two 
separate actuarial studies 
conducted by Sieben & 
Associates found that the 
“excess waste from mail-or- 
der prescriptions more than 
offset the savings.” 

The upshot, according to 
chain drug industry offi- 
cials, is that there is little 
hard evidence to support 
the cost-effectiveness 


claims of mail-order 
providers. “I haven’t seen 
any studies that show 
mail order to be any less 
expensive than a well- 
managed community retail 
pharmacy,” said Kurt 
Proctor, NACDS vice presi- 
dent for policy and pro- 
gram administration. 
Another factor working 
in community pharmacy’s 
favor is the apparent re- 
luctance of many con-

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, May 9, 1994 


ee EE IE 


Drug stores’ share of eye care fades 


by Mike Troy 


ales growth in the eye and 
S lens care category slowed to a 

virtual standstill during 1993 
after years of steady growth. 

Drug stores were hit the hardest, 
recording a 7 percent decline. Sales 
in drug stores decreased to $574 mil- 
lion in 1993 from $5621 million the 
previous year. In all trade classes, 
sales in the category totaled $1.24 
billion during 1993, a slight 1.1 per- 
cent increase from sales of $1.23 bil- 
lion during 1992. 

Drug stores’ losses came at the 
hands of supermarkets and mass 
merchandisers, who continue to 
nibble away at drug’s dominant 
market share position (see accompa- 
nying chart). Mass merchandisers 
increased sales 18 percent to $338 
million. Supermarkets also gained 
ground on drug stores by increasing 
sales 2.4 percent to $328 million. 

Even with last year’s loss of mar- 
ket share and declining sales, 
eye/lens care is still a major OTC 
category for drug stores. Only anal- 
gesics, cough/cold, vitamins and 
first aid surpass its sales. Although 
the category isn’t growing overall, 
internal shifts among product seg- 
ments are taking place. 

“Disinfectants is what is really 
growing, and that is where the future 
of the category is going to continue to 
be,” said a spokesperson for a major 
manufacturer. 

Disinfectants, including products 
such as Alcon’s Opti-Fres, Allergan’s 
UltraCare and Bausch & Lomb’s 
ReNu, allow lens wearers to clean, 
disinfect and rinse their lenses with 
the same solution. These multi-pur- 
pose products and other soft lens 
care items account for more than 80 
percent of sales in the category. 


Growth has been 
fueled by a mi- 
gration of hard 
lens wearers to 
soft lenses, An 
estimated 50 per- 
cent of today’s 
soft lens wearers 
previously wore 
hard lenses. 
Unlike other 
categories that 
are expected to 


Total sales: 
$1.24 billion 


Source: Information Resources Inc. 


Total sales: 
$1.23 billion 


benefit from 
America’s aging population, the 
eye/lens care category could actual- 
ly suffer. The majority of contact 
lens wearers today are under 40. As 
people age, eyesight worsens, and 
many shift to bifocal lenses. Manu- 
facturers contend development of an 
easy-wear, easy-care bifocal contact 
lens would explode solution sales by 


converting wearers of glasses back 
to contacts. 

Until then, retailers are turning to 
other profit generating opportunities. 
One program, being used by Revco, 
Eckerd, Walgreen and Kmart, allows 
lens wearers to get their contact lens 
prescriptions refilled within two days 
through retail pharmacies. FTP

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, May 9, 1994 


Bergen reports solid 
rise in sales, revenues 


ORANGE, Calif. — 
Bergen Brunswig reported 
net sales of $1.85 billion for 
the quarter ended March 31, 
compared to the $1.7 billion 
for the second quarter of last 
year ended Feb. 28, 1993. 

Net earnings for the peri- 
od were $14.5 million, after a 
charge of $800,000 for earth- 
quake-related losses, com- 
pared to $12.8 million for the 
same quarter last year. Last 
year’s figure included an af- 
ter-tax charge of $2.6 million 
for early debt payments. 

The company changed its 
fiscal year in 1993 but ad- 
justed reporting periods 
(September was a stand- 


alone month), so that quar- 
ters are comparable, a 
spokesperson said. 

For the six months ended 
March 31, revenues rose 
11.4 percent vs. the prior- 
year period, to $3.68 billion. 
Net earnings were relative- 
ly flat at $24.9 million com- 
pared to $24.7 million for 
the first half of last year. 

Bergen recently bought 
Fayetteville, N.C.-based 
Southeastern Hospital Sup- 
ply. The acquisition extends 
the Durr Medical division, 
allowing the company to 
supply product to more hos- 
pitals and alternate-site 
health care providers. 


McKesson posts gains 


SAN FRANCISCO — 
McKesson Corp., parent of 
McKesson Drug Co. and 
PCS Health Systems, post- 
ed an 8 percent rise in rev- 
enues to $3.18 billion for the 
fourth quarter ending 
March 31 and showed a 7 
percent increase for the 
year to $12.43 billion. 

McKesson operates 
McKesson Health Services 
(McKesson Drug and PCS), 
Armor All Products and 
McKesson Water Products. 
Health Services accounts for 
97 percent of McKesson’s 
revenues and 76 percent of 
operating profits. 

Total yearly sales for 
McKesson Drug rose 9 per- 
cent to $9.74 billion. Oper- 
ating profit was down 
slightly for the quarter and 
year, although the Health 
Care Services segment, 
which includes PCS, posted 
a 7 percent revenue rise to 
$12 billion, with a 7.4 per- 
cent increase in operating 
profit to $239.2 million. 

PCS’ revenues mush- 
roomed 56 percent in both 
the quarter and the year to 
$52.4 million and $177 mil- 
lion respectively, with oper- 
ating profit rising at a simi- 
lar pace, according to the

SECOND CLASS 


Sears’ cosmetics line debuts in the fall of '95 and will be 
merchandised as a boutique in the cosmetic department. 


Sears prototype a success; 
cosmetics line in the works 


by Liz Parks 


CHICAGO — Sears, 
the retail conglomerate 
that wants to make its 
stores more attractive to 
women shoppers, has de- 
cided that cosmetics is 
the perfect lure. 

The giant retailer is 
rolling out an upscale cos- 
metics department proto- 
type that’s only been in 
test for six months. The 
test put Sears back into 
the cosmetics business for 
the first time in a decade. 

The chain is also pre- 
paring to launch its own 
cosmetics line, fragrances 
and skin treatments by 
forming a joint venture 
with cosmetics maven 
Pierre Rogers, who was 
president of Lancéme, 
USA for three years. 


High quality, low price 


According to Sears, the 
underlying logic for the 
line will be “high quality 
products at affordable 
prices.” The store-brand 
cosmetics, when they ap- 
pear in the fall of 1995, 
will be merchandised as a 
boutique within the Sears 
cosmetics department and 
supported with strong 
print and TV advertising. 


At maturity Sears be- 
lieves the line could gen- 
erate up to 25 percent of 
its total cosmetics rev- 
enues. That could make it 
a big business: Cosmetics 
sales for Sears have been 
increasing in dramatic 
double-digit increments 
since the chain launched 
its new cosmetics proto- 
type last November. 

Company executives 
say the strategy behind 
the rollout is simple. “We 
want Sears to be a more 
compelling place for 
women to shop by offering 
good value for their dol- 
lars, fashion, fun, shop- 
ping convenience and 
pleasant surroundings,” 
said Arthur Martinez, 
chairman and chief execu- 
tive officer of the Sears 
Merchandise Group. 

Sears hopes to have the 
new prototype, as well as 
its new private label cos- 
metics line, in 500 stores 
by the end of 1996 and in 
800 by the end of 1998. 

Sears will not say how 
much its cosmetics bou- 
tique sales are averaging 
per store or how fast they 
are going up, but cosmet- 
ics and fragrance vendors 
who sell to Sears say the 
prototype has been “wild- 
ly” successful. 


Longs focuses on technology 


by Allene Symons 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. 
— Longs Drug Stores is be- 
ginning to harness point-of- 
sale data in its bid to marry 
central buying systems with 
its traditional flair for 
store-level autonomy and 
merchandising creativity, 
chain executives said at the 
annual shareholders meet- 
ing here. 

Longs’ thrust now, said 
its leaders, is to apply 
greater efficiency through 
retail technology as it moves 
to category management 
and a more centralized mer- 
chandising and buying 
strategy. At the same time, 
Longs is working to retain 
the store-specific flavor of 
its unique, entrepreneurial 
store manager culture. 

Longs president Steve 
Roath noted that with 290 
stores now using POS scan- 
ning, Longs is already see- 
ing benefits from sales 
tracking, inventory reduc- 
tion and stock transfers be- 
tween stores. 

Roath told shareholders 
that the company’s strategic 
plan “focuses on actions 


and community health i image 


that will attract 
more customers, 
grow sales and in- 
crease our earn- 
ings.” Central to 
that strategy, in 
addition to the 
growing use of 
technology, is an 
expanded cam- 
paign promoting 
Longs as a health 
resource, with the slogan 
“Longs for a healthy com- 
munity.” 

One example: the Longs 
diabetes center, launched in 
recent months and now in 
each store. The center offers 
a full array of products, in- 
cluding a glass case to hold 
the more expensive items. 
The chain also intends to 
arrange more alliances with 
associations such as the 
American Diabetes Associa- 
tion (ADA), the Arthritis 
Foundation and the Ameri- 
can Heart Association 
(AHA) in the form of in- 
store and community out- 
reach programs. Using its 
own video production stu-

Reports cite McKesson/Glaxo talks 


SAN FRANCISCO — Britain’s Glaxo Holdings PLC 
and McKesson Corp. are reportedly negotiating to 
form a strategic alliance with McKesson’s PCS Health 
Systems unit, the largest drug-benefits manager in 
the United States. Talks between the two sides were 
reported in The Wall Street Journal and the Los Ange- 
les Times. The latter referred to a report in London’s 
Sunday Times. At presstime a spokesperson for 
McKesson Corp. declined to comment. 


Eckerd details improved finances 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — An easing debt burden and 
a much improved financial position at Eckerd Corp. 
were highlights at the retailer’s annual meeting, its 
first since returning to public ownership last August. 

Chairman and chief executive officer Stewart Tur- 
ley, addressing 60 attendees, said he expects action 
this year in the health care reform area, which may 
yield benefits for chain drug retailers. In addition to 
that potential new prescription volume, Eckerd plans 
to increase sales by opening about 50 new stores and 
remodeling 400 other locations. 

The chain also plans to open 50 to 60 more Express 
Photo departments, Turley said. 


Fay’s to double auto parts business 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — Rite Aid may be abandoning 
non-core businesses, but Fay’s Inc. is expanding at 
least one non-drug division. It plans to buy the assets 
of 26 National Auto Supply stores and four Whitlock 
Auto Supply stores. The stores will join Fay’s 35-unit 
Wheels auto supply division, nearly doubling its size. 


Perry names HSI veteran sr. buyer 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Richard Spotts, a veteran of 
Hook-SupeRx, Inc. with 21 years of chain drug experi- 
ence in merchandising, buying, advertising and store 
operations, has joined Perry Drug Stores as senior 
buyer. Spotts will oversee purchasing of all seasonal 
and promotional general merchandise, photofinishing, 
film, frames, albums and greeting cards. 

Spotts last served as a merchandise manager for 
household chemicals, photo, school supplies and other 
categories at HSI, which will shortly merge with 
Revco D.S. He has also served with Gray Drug Co.

CLEVELAND — Former Revco

Boake Sells has been named

retailer of used video games and equipment that has 
grown to 53 outlets in 10 states since its launch here 
in 1990. 

Sells, 56, was instrumental in guiding Revco 
through four years of bankruptcy and back to fiscal 
health. He abruptly left the chain within days of its 
emergence from Chapter 11 in a dispute with Revco’s 
new board of directors.

Walgreen to roll out EAS system in 150 stores 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Wal- 
green Co. plans to test 
Checkpoint Systems’ elec- 
tronic article surveillance 
(EAS) systems in 150 of its 
stores. 

“We're going to do an ad- 
vanced test in 150 stores in 
our eastern region that are 
served by our Lehigh Valley 
warehouse,” said Tom Mam- 
moser, Walgreens vice pres- 
ident of communications. 
He said the expanded roll- 
out “is based on a test we 
did in 40 of our stores where 
we felt the systems served 
as an effective deterrent.” 


He indicated that it was 
too early to say whether 
Walgreens would go chain- 
wide with EAS. But its ex- 
pansion of the Checkpoint 
test will likely add new pres- 
sure to ongoing efforts by the 
chain drug industry to adopt 
a technology standard for 
EAS and involve manufac- 
turers in source labeling. 

NACDS’ Loss Prevention 
Committee has overseen an 
effort over the past two 
years to identify the most 
effective and efficient EAS 
technology applicable for 
chain drug retailing. Sup- 


port for that effort was reaf- 
firmed by the NACDS board 
at the recent annual meet- 
ing in Palm Beach, Fla. 

Source tagging of inven- 
tory by manufacturers is a 
top objective of the commit- 
tee. NACDS has employed 
an outside firm, Battelle 
Laboratories, to develop a 
test of existing EAS technolo- 
gies, “and to assess whether 
other technologies currently 
under development are vi- 
able,” according to NACDS 
spokesman Phil Schneider. A 
test of available systems is 
set for this summer.

by Barbara White 


LONG ISLAND CITY, yg 
N.Y. — Duane Reade is ex- 
panding on its successful for- 
mula with aggressive growth 
plans and some fine-tuning 
in its mix and mission. 

The high-volume New 
York chain is gearing for a 
record number of new open- 
ings this year. It is also de- 
voting more space and atten- 
tion to new departments, is 
experimenting with in-store 
bath shops and is planning 
to focus more heavily on 
pharmacy. 

“We’re not trying to change the Duane 
Reade concept,” said Gary Charboneau, the 
chain’s senior vice president of sales and 
marketing. “The Cohens [the company’s 
founding family] have made the format 
very successful.” Under ownership of 
Boston-based investment firm Bain Capital 
since 1992, the company is now poised for 
growth. 

Charboneau said the 42-unit chain plans 
to open nine new stores by the end of the 
year and up to 14 new sites within the next 
18 months. Among those new units will be 
Duane Reade’s first stores in residential up- 
per Manhattan, with one store on the Upper 
West Side and three on the Upper East Side. 

In residential locations, housewares, baby 
products and stationery have been expanded. 

“We’re targeting families in those neigh- 
borhoods,” said Charboneau. “We'll expand 
diapers and bring them up to the first floor 
for easier access. We’ve also added baby ac- 
cessories in these locations.” 

A full 24 linear feet of housewares and a 
magazine section have been added to the 
chain’s newest location on 14th Street. Sta- 
tionery has been expanded to 120 feet.

'NSULTATION ———__ 


Duane Reade, which does below-industry-average script busi- 
ness, has targeted its pharmacy for growth. 


The chain’s prescription business, which 
currently falls below the industry average, 
is targeted for growth as well. “We'll do bet- 
ter with prescription business in residential 
areas (of Manhattan),” said Charboneau. 
“Our objective is to optimize our prescrip- 
tion business.” That includes looking into 
delivery in those neighborhoods, he said. 

As the chain moves to more residential 
turf, its traditional work-day hours must be 
modified as well. Residential stores are open 
longer to accommodate their customer base. 

Duane Reade is also experimenting with a 
24-hour store in its newest location. “Phar- 
macy is very important to a 24-hour store,” 
said Charboneau. “This one has only been 
open a few weeks. We'll see how it does and 
then possibly consider other locations.”

@ Experimentation with an in-store Na- 
ture’s Elements bath section in two loca- 
tions. The departments, which include nat-

cover about 200 square feet and will be 
staffed by a trained salesperson.

op ad program around its Midtown stores.

Gaddis and Pohlit buy Joel & Jerry's 


terized the acquisition as a leveraged deal 
that involved many months of negotiations. 

“We remain committed to the founding 
principles of the business,” he added, 
“which include offering products that our 
customers need at deep-discount prices 
every day and meeting [their] service level 
expectations.” 

The chain was founded in 1983 by Joel 
Fisher and Jerry Finland in the highly com- 
petitive Tampa Bay region, and was sold by 
former owner and outgoing president and

square feet and carry more than 25,000

Tampa/St. Petersburg and Clearwater area.

new president, is no stranger to deep dis- 
count drug retailing. He was part of the 
owner/manager investment team that pur- 
chased and briefly ran dot Drugs, a small 
chain of off-price stores founded and later 
spun off by Wal-Mart Stores. Gaddis served 
as chairman of the enterprise until dot’s liq- 
uidation at the end of 1991. 

Gaddis also lent his name to the former 
deep-discount drug division of Dominick’s 
Finer Foods in Chicago, and served with 
Gray Drug Fair and other chains. 

Pohlit, who will be chairman, built his ca-

Drug benefits 
termed at risk 


WASHINGTON — Con- 
gress is closing in on a fi- 
nal health care reform 
package that could leave 
retail pharmacy’s favorite 
provisions on the cutting 
room floor, Congressional 


and Administration offi- 


cials warned industry 
leaders attending a NARD 
conference here. 

At highest risk: the 
President’s plan for a $68 
billion Medicare outpatient 
drug benefit and a provi- 
sion to forbid drug manu- 
facturers from engaging in 
discriminatory pricing 
against retail pharmacy. 

In an address to NARD’s 
National Legislative Con- 
ference, Senate Finance 
Committee member Jay 
Rockefeller (D-W.Va.) told 
independent pharmacy 
leaders that there is no 
hope that the Clinton bill 
will survive intact. 


Key provisions dropped 


Several key provisions in 
the President’s original pro- 
posal—including plans for 
a Breakthrough Drug Com- 
mittee to discourage exces- 
sive pricing for new phar- 
maceuticals—have already 
been dropped, and Con- 
gress is actively seeking to 
trim other provisions. 

Noting that prescription 
drug benefits for the elder- 
ly are in danger of being 
dropped, Rockefeller said 
the President’s Medicare 
drug proposal currently 
ranks at the top of the leg- 
islative “endangered 
species list.” 

Even White House rep- 
resentatives at the meet- 
ing admitted that the 
President’s plan is in seri- 
ous trouble in Congress 
and will require legislative 
surgery to survive. 

“It’s sink or swim” for 
the President’s bill, said 
White House senior health 
care policy advisor Chris 
Jennings . 

“We think it’s going to be 
‘swim,” Jennings said, but 
he acknowledged that the 
Administration will have 
to make compromises in 
order to maneuver any 
health plan through Con- 
gress this year. 


Compromises in store 


NACDS president Ron 
Ziegler said that preserving 
plans for Medicare outpa- 
tient drug benefits is “ex- 
tremely important” for re- 


that compromises will be 
made in coming weeks, but 
he urged pharmacists to 
lobby their congressmen to 
include Medicare drug cov- 
erage in final legislation. 


IMRA goes to 
bat for Wal-Mart 


Lawyers for the Interna- 
tional Mass Retail Associ- 
ation, representing the na- 
tion’s discount chains, 
have urged the Arkansas 
Supreme Court to over- 
turn last year’s surprise 
lower court ruling that 
Wal-Mart engaged in ille- 
gal predatory pricing 
against independent phar- 
macists in the state. 

That decision, now on 
appeal to Arkansas’ high- 
est court, is an “aberra- 
tional” ruling that con- 
demns “ordinary, effective 
and pro-consumer market- 
ing practices” by discount 
chains, IMRA said. 

In concluding that Wal- 
Mart violated Arkansas’ 
Depression-era Unfair 
Practices Act, the lower 
court had cited the use of 
loss leaders as evidence of 
below-cost selling intended 
to injure competition. 

But attorneys for IMRA 
told the high court that the 
use of “promotional pricing 
on a handful of items can- 
not drive other competitors 
out of business.” 

In a freshly filed “friend 
of the court” brief urging a 
reversal in the Wal-Mart 
case, IMRA argued that 
the state law should be in- 
terpreted to prohibit “only 
true predatory pricing con- 
duct”—not “everyday pro- 
motional pricing on select- 
ed items.” 


Wal-Mart not alone 


Indeed, the discount 
chain group said, promo- 
tional pricing is so wide- 
spread that at least two of 
the three independent 
pharmacy defendants in 
the Wal-Mart suit promot- 
ed loss leaders themselves. 

IMRA also criticized the 
trial court for inferring an 
anti-competitive intent by 
Wal-Mart because the 
chain priced products low- 
er at stores near indepen- 
dent pharmacies and other 
retail competitors. 

The “practice of pricing 
products lower in areas of 
greater competition is ex- 
actly what should be ex- 
pected in a competitive 


tail pharmacy. marketplace,” IMRA said.

Every retailer knows— intellectual- 
ly, at least—that it’s easier and cheap- 
er to keep an existing customer than 
to find a new one. As a chain drug re- 
tailer, the prescription drug shopper is 
presumably your “best” customer. 

Right now, you're paying a lot of at- 
tention to prescription customers, 
working hard to maintain access to 
these people through managed care. 

But what are you doing to get that 
prescription shopper—for whom 
you've fought so hard and willingly 
sacrificed your profit margins—to 
spend more money in the front end of 
your stores?

reveals that if you want to convert the

Concentrate on OTCs, film and greet- 
ing cards. Fifty-four percent of chain 
drug prescription shoppers buy their

buy film or process photos there, and

WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


To help you develop strategies to 
keep these customers and serve them 
better, Drug Store News commissioned 
The Gallup Organization to conduct 
an exclusive survey of consumers who 
have purchased prescription drugs 
within the past year. (See our Gallup 
report, starting on page 8.) 

Our 500 consumer respondents (all 


and toiletries, two 
categories where 
drug stores are 
much less likely to 
convert the prescription customer’s dol- 
lars. For those 21 percent of script shop- 
pers who also bought cosmetics in a 
chain drug store, “low, everyday prices” 
and convenience were equally impor- 
tant. For the 16 percent of prescription 
shoppers buying toiletries, price was the 
No. 1 reason for making that purchase 
in a chain drug store. 


Entice the Rx shopper to the front-end 


Now, if you want to shore up your 
vulnerable areas, consider this find- 
ing: The chain drug store prescription 
shopper is actually more likely to buy 
cosmetics in a department store than a 
chain drug store, while supermarkets 
and mass merchant/discounters pick 
up more toiletries sales from chain 
drug store prescription shoppers than 
chain drug stores do. 

As you look toward the future, this 
study reads as a cautionary tale. 

We developed a “Store Attraction In- 
dex” (see page 14) to find out how well 
each distribution channel is doing to 
convert the prescription customer into 
a buyer of front-end products. That’s 
where you see chain drug stores get- 
ting below-average scores across the 
board (discount stores scored above 
average in all categories except 
film/photoprocessing). 

Meanwhile, in all categories but toi- 
letries— where supermarkets scored 
highest— general merchandise/discount 
stores outscored the other channels. 

And, although they were the phar- 
macy of choice for only 11 percent of 
our female respondents, supermarkets 
scored highly in our Store Attraction 
Index in every category but cosmetics. 

The message is clear: Where other 
types of stores have captured the pre- 
scription shopper, they are doing a 
better job in converting her into a 
front-end shopper. 

In the era of managed health care, 
you've got to fight to protect your fran- 
chise in pharmacy. Just remember 
that your front-end business is still 
under siege, too.
