WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


A good portion of the President’s 
ian health reform proposal has al- 
ready been sliced away—due in part to 
intense lobbying by pharmaceutical 
manufacturers opposed to new federal 
controls over their pricing practices. 

Now Moynihan’s panel and other 
congressional committees responsible 
for health reform legislation are under 
pressure to scale back or eliminate the 
Administration’s plan for a Medicare 
outpatient drug benefit structured 


4 Drug Store News, May 30, 1994 


ever, dropping 
Medicare outpa- 
tient drug cover- 
age from the final 
reform legislation may be the path of 
least resistance. 

On one hand, they would be able to 
“reduce” the price of health reform leg- 
islation by the $68-billion, 5-year cost 
of the Medicare drug benefit (a claim 
disputed by NARD and NACDS). 

On the other, they may at least tem- 
porarily placate the carnivorous phar- 
maceutical industry lobbyists who 
have been hoping to scuttle the equal 
access provisions. 


In a briefing to independent pharma- 
cy leaders at NARD’s National Legisla- 
tive Conference in Washington, Chris 
Jennings, White House senior health 
care advisor, said the “equal access” 
provisions are at the top of the phar- 
maceutical industry’s “must kill list.” 

Drug manufacturers aren’t the only 
ones lobbying to preserve the current 
pricing system that discriminates 
against retail drug stores. A new 
group calling itself the “Coalition of 
Health Care Providers Concerned 
About Rising Drug Costs” is trying to 
add legitimacy to the efforts of some 
drug manufacturers to scuttle Clin- 
ton’s equal access plan. 

“On its face, requiring manufactur- 
ers to offer the same discounts to 
every purchaser on the same terms 
may sound like a reasonable idea,” the 
coalition said in newspaper ad dis- 
guised as an open letter to members of 
Congress. But the coalition believes 
that drug manufacturers are likely to 
respond to such legislation “by limit- 
ing discounts to all purchasers.” 

“Consumers of retail pharmacies will 
not benefit in any way from this provi- 
sion, and the majority of consumers 
who currently benefit from discount 
pricing will be harmed,” the ad said. 

The “letter”—signed by the Ameri- 
can Hospital Association, a parade of 
leading HMOs and APhA’s health re- 
form coalition partner, the American 
Society of Consultant Pharmacists— 
did not explain which consumers 
would benefit from continued drug 
price discrimination.

Category 


by Liz Parks 


harmacy is chain drug’s 

greatest strength. It is the 

fastest growing major cate- 

gory in chain drug stores, 
and in most drug chains it is the 
dominant category. Pharmacy ac- 
counted for 49 percent of all chain 
drug retail sales in 1993. 

But for many chains, the strength 
of their pharmacy centers does not 
spill over into the rest of their stores. 

While pharmacy sales grew 6 per- 
cent last year, toiletry sales de- 
clined 1 percent, over-the-counter 
remedial sales only grew by 2 per- 
cent, and cosmetics and fragrance 
sales slipped by 6 percent. 

To help drug chains discover why 
they are not growing their front-end 
business at a rate at least equal to 
their growth in pharmacy, Drug 
Store News commissioned the 
Princeton, N.J.-based Gallup Orga- 
nization to study where women who 
get prescriptions filled go most of- 
ten to buy products like shampoo, 
film, greeting cards, over-the- 
counter remedials, and cosmetics 
and fragrances. 

Why do prescription buyers shop 
other trade classes? How often? 
And, on average, how many were 
converted into chain drug store 
front-end shoppers? These ques- 


~ tions, and others, are the subject of 


this special report. 
The shoppers are there 


Chain drug stores are doing a 
good job attracting women to their 
prescription departments. 

One third of all women who 
bought a prescription in the last 
year had it filled “most frequently” 
in a chain drug store. . 

But chain drug stores are not do- 
ing as good a job persuading their 
prescription shoppers to buy other 
types of products once they are in 
the store. 

According to the Gallup prescrip- 
tion shopper survey sponsored by 
Drug Store News, six out of every 10 
women who needed a prescription 
last year went to a drug store most 
often to have it filled. 

Twenty-nine percent most often 


Conversion rate Category 


independent drug stores 


% of all women who bought Rx in 
independent drug stores: 24% 


Conversion rate 


went to a chain drug store, 24 per- 
cent most often went to an indepen- 
dent drug store, and 8 percent most 
often went to a discount drug store. 

Only 13 percent had their pre- 
scriptions filled most often in a gen- 
eral merchandise or discount depart- 
ment store like Wal-Mart or Kmart, 
11 percent took their prescriptions 
most of the time to a pharmacy in a 
food store, 7 percent had their pre- 
scriptions filled most often at a hos- 
pital pharmacy, and 4 percent used a 
mail-order prescription service. 

On the surface, it would seem 
that with 60 percent of women 
shopping drug stores ‘nost often for 
prescriptions, it should be fairly 
easy for drug stores to stimulate 
companion sales of other products 
like cosmetics, greeting cards, 
shampoo, aspirin and film. 

But it turns out that most chain, 
discount and independent drug 
stores are not that successful in 
converting their prescription shop- 
pers into front-end shoppers. 

Only 21 percent of all women who 
most often buy a prescription in a 
chain drug store, for example, say 
they also most often buy cosmetics 
or fragrances there. 

Only 29 percent of chain drug 
stores’ prescription shoppers say 
they also buy greeting cards there 
most often. 

Only 32 percent say they buy film 
or process photos most of the time 


in chain drug stores, and only 16 
percent say they buy toiletries there 
most often. 

Chain drug stores have the great- 
est success cross-selling over-the- 
counter products. Fifty-four percent 
of prescription shoppers do buy 
their OTC products in chain drug 
stores most of the time. 


Perceived price a factor 


The consumers’ perception that 
chain drug stores don’t always have 
the lowest prices is one reason why 
many prescription shoppers aren’t 
also buying front-end products in 
chain drug outlets. Convenience is 
another factor. Some consumers say 
they find it more convenient to shop 
supermarkets or discount depart- 
ment stores rather than drug stores. 

Analyzing where chain drug pre- 
scription shoppers go to buy front- 
end products can be very revealing. 

Discount department stores, for 
example, are two and a half times 
more likely than drug stores to con- 
vert a prescription shopper into a 
cosmetic shopper. 

Twenty percent of women who 
most often buy a prescription in a 
chain drug store say they most often 
buy their cosmetics and fragrances 
in a discount department store. 

Twenty-six percent of chain drug 
prescription shoppers say they 
most often buy their cosmetics in

cent say they buy their cosmetics 
most often from door-to-door sales

When it comes to greeting cards, 
29 percent of all chain drug pre- 
scription shoppers prefer to buy 
their cards most often in specialty 
card shops. Another 15 percent buy 
them most often in supermarkets, 
while 13 percent buy them most of- 
ten in discount drug stores. 

With film or processed photos, 21 
percent of chain drug prescription 
shoppers go into discount stores 
most often for their photo needs, 15 
percent use supermarkets most of- 
ten, and 5 percent go to discount 
drug stores. 

Another 7 percent most often go 
to specialty film stores. 

With toiletries, 24 percent of 
chain drug prescription shoppers go 
into discount stores most often to 
get items like shampoo, skin lotions 
and bath products. Twenty-nine 
percent shop supermarkets, while 9 
percent shop discount drug stores 
most often. 


Facing the challenge 


Many chain drug executives are 
trying to figure out how they can 
convert more prescription shoppers 
into front-end shoppers. Their chal- 
lenge is to figure out why it is not 
happening now and what to do to 
improve the situation. 

If drug stores could just get 25 
percent of unconverted front-end 
shoppers to buy their supplies in a 
drug store while they’re getting 
their prescriptions filled, the indus- 
try could show a dramatic increase 
in growth. 

Survey respondents have given 
them a hint. When asked what 
would make drug stores a better 
place to shop, nearly a quarter of all 
respondents (24 percent) said com- 
petitive pricing/value. Fifteen per- 
cent asked for more brand variety, 
and seven percent pointed to more 
convenient locations. 

Many chain drug retailers also 
think the answer lies in how cre- 
ative they are in merchandising 
their stores. 

One chain drug executive said it 
isn’t enough for chain drug stores 
just to carry broad selections of 
front-end products nor is it enough 
to lowball prices. He said merchan- 
dising has to be “exciting, attrac- 
tive, alluring. You have to make it 
almost impossible for that pharma- 
cy shopper to get out the door with- 
out wanting to buy something else.” 

“Low prices are important,” said a 
merchandiser for one large regional 
drug chain. “But shoppers don’t just 
go to a store because it’s got the 
sae sk prices. 

“Shoppers want ambiance. They 
want value. They want a complete 
shopping experience. In some cate- 
gories, like cosmetics, they want 
service, and in others, like greeting 
cards, they want a broad selection. 

“You have to take all these factors 
into account when you try to per- 
suade people to come to your stores 
rather than go somewhere else, and 
you have to be sure you make your 


12 Drug Store News, May 30, 1994 


stores fun to shop if you’re going to 
get women to cross-shop different 
categories.” 

Deep discount drug chains do of- 
fer their shoppers great prices, but 
that has not helped them convert 
prescription shoppers into front-end 
shoppers. 


Flaunting fashion 


A buyer for one leading discount 
drug chain said she tries to mer- 
chandise the cosmetics department 
as a fashion center because she be- 
lieves women look for a fashion im- 
age when they shop for cosmetics. 

“That’s why Wal-Mart and Kmart 
put their cosmetics department 
right next to women’s apparel,” she 
said. “The two departments comple- 
ment one another. Their presence in 
the store reinforces the perception 
that the store is a fashion center.” 

Fashion is probably what lures 
the 20 percent of discount drug 
stores’ prescription shoppers who 


most often buy their cosmetics in a 
department store. 

But not all women are swayed by 
fashion considerations. Many women 
are very time-conscious and they will 
often buy beauty and health care 
products in the stores where it is 
most convenient for them. 

Convenience, for example, prob- 
ably accounts for the 17 percent of 
the discount drug store prescription 
shoppers who prefer to buy cards 
and film in supermarkets most of- 
ten, and probably comes into play 
for the 28 percent of discount drug 
store prescription shoppers who 
buy their OTC drugs most often in 
supermarkets. 

Discount drug stores lose very 
few front-end sales to conventional 
or traditional drug chains. 

Only 10 percent of discount drug 
stores’ prescription shoppers go to a 
chain drug store most often to buy 
cosmetics, and just 17 percent go to

One buyer said she doesn’t think 
chain and discount drug stores nec- 
essarily have to have the lowest 
prices in town to lure shoppers away 
from places like Kmart, Wal-Mart 
and Target, but she does think “we 
have to be more competitive; more of 
a value than what we now are. 


“If we can offer customers conve- 
nience, a pleasant atmosphere to 
shop in and value, we ought to be 
able to persuade more of them to 
shop our stores for front-end prod- 
ucts. Especially when we already 
have them in the stores buying pre- 
scriptions.”

hile chain drug stores 
proved to be a strong 
destination draw for the 
prescription shopper 


(three out of 10 women who bought 
a prescription last year bought it 
most often in a chain drug store), 
the industry’s strength did not spill 
over into cosmetics and fragrances. 

Only 12 percent of all the women 
who bought both a prescription and 
a cosmetic or fragrance last year 
bought their cosmetic products 
“most often” in a chain drug store, 
and only 9 percent went to discount 
drug stores most often for cosmetics. 

Instead, many women seemed to 
prefer to buy their beauty care prod- 
ucts in stores with a higher fashion 
image. Twenty-three percent of the 
women surveyed bought their cos- 
metics and fragrances “most often” 
in department stores, while 26 per- 
cent bought them “most often” in 
discount department stores like 
Wal-Mart, Kmart and Target. 

Twenty-seven percent of de- 
partment-store cosmetic shoppers 
said they liked these stores because 
they had “the products I want.” 
Nineteen percent reported they 
liked the wide selection of product 
in these stores. 

While four out of every 10 women 
said price was one of the major rea- 
sons they shopped a store for cos- 
metics and fragrances, just 8 per- 
cent who bought cosmetics in 
department stores gave this as one 
of the reasons they shopped there. 

Clearly, the ambience of the de- 
partment store, its ability to project 
a sense of high fashion, its service 
and the exclusivity it maintains 
with select brands mattered sub- 
stantially to some women. 


Discount drug stores push price 


Still, nine out of 10 women who 
bought cosmetics in a discount drug 
store said they shopped there be- 
cause of low prices, and 68 percent 
of discount-department-store shop- 
pers said that low prices were why 
they bought their cosmetics and fra- 
grances most often in these stores. 

Unlike department stores, most 
drug stores don’t have exclusives on 
the brands they carry, nor do they 
have the lowest, everyday prices. 

However, drug stores offer conve- 
nience, and one-third of all women 
shopped chain drug stores because 
of convenience. Drug stores also 
have a nice selection of product, and 
one-third of all cosmetic shoppers 
recognized this. 

It appears that chain drug stores 
might have an opportunity to in- 
duce more frequent visits as well as 
attract more women to their stores 
if they take a trick from the depart- 
ment stores’ book and put more em- 
phasis on their cosmetic depart- 
ments as fashion centers. 

Getting new products into the 
store and on the wall as soon as 
possible helps; so does a merchan- 
dising presentation that stresses 
color, cleanliness, ease of shopping 
and high-quality products at top- 
value prices. Making the products 
accessible, easy to find oat easy to 
touch also helps by stimulating im- 
pulse sales and creating an aura of 
a department that’s fun to shop.

44 Drug Store News, May 30, 1994 


EXCLUSIVE DRUG STORE NEWS CONSUMER SURVEY 


Greeting card shoppers prize variety, not price 


To enhance their 


attraction asa 


destination shop 


for cards, some 


chain drug stores 


have added party 


centers to their 


mix, where women 


can buy paper 


tablecloths, party 


hats, paper 


napkins, gift wrap, 


ribbons and all the 


essentials for 


festive occasions. 


46 


nly 14 percent of all women 

who bought prescriptions 

last year also bought greet- 

ing cards “most often” in a 
chain drug store. And only one 
woman in 10 reported shopping dis- 
count drug stores “most often” for 
cards. 

Half of the women who bought 
cards never shopped drug stores or 
else shopped them very infre- 
quently for cards. Twenty percent 
told Gallup they “never” bought a 
card in a chain or discount drug 
store, and 24 percent said they only 
shopped there once or twice a year. 

Still, 20 percent shopped chain or 
discount dr ig stores at least once a 
month, and 9 percent shopped there 
more than once a month. 

Gallup found that nearly half of 
all women preferred to buy their 
cards either in specialty card shops 
or discount department and general 
merchandise stores. Many younger 
women between ages 18 and 29 
were particularly fond of shopping 
card shops, where they could often 
find stuffed animals, gift items, nov- 
elty candies and other appealing 
products to sample. 

Because of the traffic they can 
generate, food stores also got a fair 
share of greeting card sales. Gallup 
found that 17 percent of all women 
said they bought their greeting 
cards “most often” in a food store. 


Price not a factor 


Since cards aren’t a high-ticket 
item, and perhaps because they are 
bought for sentimental reasons, 
price wasn’t a driving factor in this 
category. Only 24 percent of all 
women said low everyday prices 
were a major reason why they often 
shopped a specific store for cards. 
Thirty-four percent said conve- 
nience was a major reason, and 29 
percent attributed it to selection. 

Convenience was a motivating fac- 
tors for most women who bought 
their cards in a chain drug store. 
Fifty-eight percent of all chain drug 
store greeting card shoppers said 
getting to the store easily was a ma- 
jor reason for shopping there. 

Sixty-eight percent of food store 
card buyers agreed that conve- 
nience was a major reason for their 
purchases, while 57 percent of dis- 
count-department-store card buyers 
and 50 percent of discount-drug- 
store card buyers said it was be- 
cause of low, everyday prices. 

But selection and mix were clear- 
ly strengths for the specialty card 
store. Seventy percent of women 
who bought cards in specialty 
stores said the selection was a ma- 
jor incentive. 

To enhance their attraction as a 
destination shop for cards, some 
chain drug stores have added party 
centers to their mix, where women 
can buy paper tablecloths, party 
hats, paper napkins, gift wrap, rib- 
bons and all the essentials for fes- 
tive occasions. 

One source for a chain with a par- 
ty center in selected test stores said 
the concept has been proving to be 
very viable as a traffic generator. 
The only problem with expanding it, 
she moe bas been finding the space 
as stores are remodeled.

EXCLUSIVE DRUG STORE NEWS CONSUMER SURVEY 


Convenience, price lure younger film shoppers 


Because the costs 


could rapidly add 


up when a 


customer IS a 


frequent 


photographer, four 


out of 10 women 


said that low prices 


were very 


important to them. 


oday, more younger women 
than older women are buy- 
ing film, and they’ve been 


buying it most often in 
stores where they could get conve- 
nience and low, everyday prices. 

Gallup found that young women 
between 18 and 44 bought film more 
often than women 45 and older. 

That makes sense. Younger 
women tend to have young children 
at home, and they have many more 
occasions for preserving memories: 
birthday parties, vacations, holi- 
days, graduations, dance recitals, 
team sports and more. 

Because the costs could rapidly 
add up when a customer is a fre- 
quent photographer, four out of 10 
women said low prices were very 
important to them. 

But convenience mattered too. 
Women naturally wanted to shop 
stores that were nearby, both to re- 
stock their film supply and to have 
easy, fast access to the photos they 
sent in for processing. 


Discount department stores lst 


Thirty percent of all women said 
they bought their film “most often” 
in discount department stores, while 
18 percent said they preferred to 
shop chain drug stores most often, 
and 14 percent said supermarkets. 

The attraction for the discount 
department store shopper was 
price. Nearly seven out of 10—66 
percent—of the women who bought 
film in a discount department store 
said that price was one of the main 
reasons they shopped there. 

Only one in four discount depart- 
ment store shoppers said they 
bought film there most often be- 
cause of convenience. 

For chain drug store film shop- 
pers, however, convenience was a 
major attraction. Forty-seven per- 
cent of all women who bought film 
in a chain drug store in the last year 
said the ability to get to the store 
easily was very important to them. 

Only 25 percent of those surveyed 
said that low, everyday prices were 
a major reason for shopping chain 
drug stores. 

In food stores, convenience was 
even more of a factor. Seventy-three 
percent of all consumers who 
bought film most often in food 
stores said that convenience was a 
big reason they shopped there. 


Core destination 


Most chain drug stores consider 
their photo department one of their 
most important core destination de- 
partments, and many depend on 
their photo department to create 
traffic that the rest of the store’s 
front end can live off. 

Most drug stores already do a 
great job building up their photo de- 
partments by offering consumers 
added value such as a free set of 
— free enlargements and 24- 

our processing. 

But since price is so important to 
so many consumers, it may be possi- 
ble to attract even more shoppers to 
the chain drug film department by 
promoting the category more, dis- 
counting prices on selected items 
and advertising the department 
more in print and on television.

48 Drug Store News, May 30, 1994 


Winter storms put chill 
in Hook-SupeRx's earnings 


CINCINNATI — Beset by 
severe winter storms and 
lower gross margins, Hook- 
SupeRx Inc. reported a de- 
cline in net income for the 
second quarter. 

Net earnings for the peri- 
od ended Feb. 28 declined 
40 percent to $8.9 million 
vs. the second quarter of 
last year, when the compa- 
ny benefited from the addi- 
tion of $4.7 million in tax- 
loss carryforwards. Sales for 
the most recent quarter— 
likely to be one of the last 
fiscal reporting periods for 
HSI prior to its expected ac- 
quisition this summer by 
Revco D.S.—were up a mea- 
ger 1.4 percent over the pri- 
or-year second quarter, with 
same-store sales up a mod- 
est 2.1 percent. 

HSI blamed “the large 
number and severity of win- 
ter storms in many of the 
states where the company 
operates” for the anemic 
sales increases. Same-store 
sales gains outpaced overall 


gains because HSI ended 
the quarter with 48 fewer 
drug stores than it had a 
year earlier. 

Behind the lower earnings 
was a decline in operating 
margin to 3.6 percent from 4 
percent the previous year. 
Duplicate warehouse and 
distribution costs related to 
the transition of the SupeRx 
stores from an outside dis- 
tributor, Peyton, to HSI’s 
own enlarged Midwestern 
DC led to the decline, and 
offset improvements in cost 
controls along with “the ben- 
efits derived from the com- 
pany’s ongoing consolidation 
efforts,” HSI reported. 

Script sales for the period 
rose 5.6 percent to $309.9 
million, which pushed phar- 
macy’s contribution to 50.5 
percent of total HSI sales, 
compared with 48.5 percent 
a year earlier. Third-party 
prescription sales were up 
13.4 percent, to 51.1 percent 
of total script sales vs. 47.6 
percent the prior year. 


Medicine Shoppe profits 
from healthy script sales 


ST. LOUIS — Extending 
its winning streak, Medi- 
cine Shoppe International 
pushed net earnings ahead 
14 percent for the second 
quarter and first half of fis- 
cal 1994, to $3.6 million and 
$7.2 million, respectively. 
Solid same-store results and 
strong script sales account- 
ed for the gains. 

Operating earnings for 
the quarter ended March 31 
increased 20 percent to $5.5 
million, with corporate 
(franchise) revenues up 16 
percent to $12.5 million. For 
the first half of fiscal 1994, 
operating income was up 19 
percent to $10.8 million, 
with revenues up 12 percent 
to $24.8 million. 

Total store sales for the 


first six months of fiscal 94 
grew 11 percent to $415.8 
million, driven by strong 
same-store sales gains of 9 
percent. 

Medicine Shoppe opened 
27 stores and closed 11 in 
the most recent quarter, 
ending the period with 
1,014 retail pharmacies, in- 
cluding 59 units in Canada, 
Taiwan and Malaysia. The 
fast-growing franchiser is 
also preparing for an entry 
into Thailand. 

“We continue to position 
the system to take advan- 
tage of future growth oppor- 
tunities,” said president 
David Abrahamson. 

Medicine Shoppe derives 
over 90 percent of its retail 
sales from prescriptions.

to the pharmaceutical industry’s pric-

taken law enforcement action to chal- 
lenge the pricing practices of drug 
manufacturers “cannot and should not 
be taken as a clean bill of Robinson- 
Patman health for the entire pharma- 
ceutical industry,” he said. 

McNeely’s letter to Rite Aid rein- 
forces earlier statements by Federal 
antitrusters to Sen. David Pryor (D- 
Ark.), who revealed that the FTC re- 
mains concerned about the antitrust 
implications of pharmaceutical indus- 
try pricing practices. 

Rather than closing the books on the 
discriminatory pricing issue, the an- 
titrusters told Pryor that “we have an 
ongoing investigation in this area.” 

For their part, officials at NACDS 
said these admissions by the FTC rep- 
resent “a smoking gun in the Rite Aid 
discriminatory pricing suit.” 

That may be a bit strong—but they 
do appear to throw water on the am- 
munition being used by manufacturers 
to defend their controversial pricing 
practices.

IMER SHOPPING 


hy do shoppers buy 
what they do? Why 
do they shop where 


they do? 

Who knows? Sometimes, 
not even consumers do. 

But what they buy—and 
where they buy them—is 
tangible—and measurable. 
And that data can be gath- 
ered, inputted, statistically 
analyzed and cross tabbed. 
By studying the results, re- 
tailers and manufacturers 
can learn a great deal about 
their businesses and how to 
improve them. 

That’s why, in the follow- 
ing pages, you will find a 
ream of information. The 
charts are based on informa- 
tion provided by Nielsen 
Marketing Research’s Na- 
tional Electronic Household 
Panel. This panel provides 
consumer purchase behavior 
information with data from 
40,000 nationally representa- 
tive households across the 
United States. 

Panelists in the household 
panel use Nielsen’s patented 
hand-held scanner to record 
their purchases from drug 
stores, grocery stores, mass 
merchandisers, warehouse 
clubs, convenience stores, 
specialty stores and more. 
Every household member 
scans all barcoded purchases 
made in every store shopped. 

Household panel data mea- 
sures the ongoing purchase 
habits and practices of house- 
holds. 

The data in this study rep- 
resents 52 weeks of purchase 
information, for the period 
from December 1992 to De- 
cember 1993. 


Basic definitions 


There are four sections of 
information presented for 
each category segment, each 
revealing a different aspect 
about the category: The com- 
ponents of sales, the power of 
the deal, consumer shopping 
habits by trade class and de- 
mographics of buyers. 

The components of sales 
are four: 

1. Penetration, the percent 
of households who have pur- 
chased the product at least 
once during the time period 
(in the case of this study, a 
one-year time period). For ex- 
ample, 21.6 percent of house- 
holds purchased the face 
cream category at least once 
during 1993. 

2. Percent of volume share 
reveals each segment’s share 
of total category volume. 

3. Volume per purchase oc- 
casion is obtained by dividing 
the average volume pur- 


What the study reveals 
about consumers 


chased during the time peri- 
od by the average purchase 
occasions per buyer. 

4. Annual purchase occa- 
sions per buyer is the average 
number of occasions in which 
a category, segment, brand or 
package size is purchased. For 
example, on average, house- 
holds made 1.9 shopping trips 
during 1993 to purchase the 
face cream category. 

The components of sales, 
however, add up to far more 
than their individual parts. 
Each is a variable in the 
equation. Change one, and 
the solution to the equation 
changes. Studying the rela- 
tionships will provide insight 
into factors affecting a cate- 
gory’s sales performance re- 
garding how many con- 
sumers purchase the product, 
how much they purchase and 
how often. 

Certain precautions should 
be taken when interpreting 
the data presented in the fol- 
lowing charts. As a rule, none 
of the base household facts 
are additive. For example, 
penetration for bar soap plus 
penetration for liquid soaps 
does not equal penetration 
for the total soap category 
since some households may 
have purchased both and 
would thus be counted twice. 

Buying rate, purchase fre- 
quency and purchase size 
represent average behavior. 


The power of the deal 


The power of the deal looks 
at six elements. Four of 
them—percent of volume 
bought on deal, percent of vol- 
ume bought with manufactur- 
er/store coupon; percent of 
units bought on deal and per- 
cent of units bought with 
manufacturer/store coupon 
refer to consumer-perceived 
deals. Percent of volume pur- 
chased in conjunction with a 
consumer-perceived deal can 
represent manufacturer 
coupons, store coupons, store 
deals or other deals. 

Purchase cycle refers to the 
average number of days 
elapsed between purchase oc- 
casions or repeat buys of an 
item. 

Careful study of these ele- 
ments can provide insights 
into price sensitivity and per- 
ceived response to deals.

Demographics 
of heavy buyers. 


This chart contains a 
wealth of information for 
those willing to mine it. 
You'll notice the first column 
of numbers are the same in 
each category. That’s be- 
cause those numbers tell 
what percent of the panel 
falls into the varous demo- 
graphic characteristics. 

The second two columns 
are volume indices. These 
volume indices identify ar- 
eas of volume development 
by comparing the distribu- 
tion of the product category 
volume to the distribution of 
all households. For example, 
a huge volume index tells us 
which demographic seg- 
ments represent a greater 
than expected proportion of 
volume relative to their inci- 
dence in the population. 

There are two indices: one 
represents the total panel. 
The other represents heavy 
purchasers. Heavy buyers, 
defined in this study are the 
top one-third category 
spenders. 

Here’s some basic defini- 
tions for understanding the 
“Demographics of buyers”: 

Household lifestage de- 
finitions: 

Young singles—house- 
holds with one member un- 
der 35 years old 

Childless younger cou- 
ples—1+ member house- 
holds under 35 years old 
with no children under 18. 

New families—house- 
holds with children under 6 
years old only. 

Maturing families — 
households with children 
aged 6-17 years old. 

Established families — 
households with children 
aged 13-17 years old only. 

Middle-aged singles— 
households with one mem- 
ber aged between 35 and 54 
years old. 

Middle-aged childless cou- 
ples—1+ member house- 
holds, aged between 35 and 
54 years old, with no chil- 
dren under 18. 

Empty nesters—1+ mem- 
ber households, aged be- 
tween 55 and 64, with no 
children under 18. 

Older singles-—house- 
holds with one member over 
55 years old. 

Per capita income defi- 
nitions: 

Poor households are de- 
fined by:

With the introduction of the Coordinated Care Network on 
January 1, 1994, the design of managed prescription plans was 
changed forever. Since April 1, the momentum continues — 
with new features that increase the pharmacist’s role in providing 
patient management and counseling. 


Now, the Coordinated Care Network rewards pharmacists for 
improving patient health in three important ways: 


@ Prescription Drug Screening 
* Disease Management Counseling 
e Drug Regimen Review 


These innovations in third-party compensation can only come 
from a network program that supports the pharmacist’s professional 
role in the changing managed care environment.

he data show that wo- 
men are not buying 
specialized creams as 
often as they are buying all- 
purpose creams. Women 
don’t seem to want several 
specialized creams as part of 
their beauty regimens and are 
relying on an all-purpose fa- 
cial cream for all their mois- 
turizing needs. 

Specialized eye gels and 
night creams may be crowa- 
ing retail shelves at the ex- 
pense of more new all-pur- 
pose products. Retailers 
whose scanning data show 
slow movement on special- 
ized line extensions may opt 
not to add those products to 
a line.

Drug chains search for new ways 
to stem cosmetics sales erosion 


t happened to toothpaste. It 

happened to shampoos, and 

now chain drug stores are try- 

ing to keep it from happening to 
cosmetics. 

It is the erosion of saies share that 
chain drug stores experience when- 
ever a category like toothpaste or 
shampoo becomes so easily available 
in all types of mass outlet stores 
that, to consumers, it becomes a 
commodity, to be picked up on their 
next shopping trip as if it were a 
quart of milk or a loaf of bread. 

Chain drug stores have good rea- 
sons to want to prevent that from 
happening to cosmetics. 

According to Nielsen North Ameri- 
ca, color cosmetics is currently the 
fourth highest dollar-volume HBA 
category in the drug store trade class. 

It is also one of the last traditional 
drug store categories where the in- 
dustry still retains the dominant 
share of sales.

Drug stores vs. mass merchandisers: Cosmetics 


cosmetics dollars in mass merchan- 
dise stores. In comparison, heavy 
cosmetics users only spent 37.6 per- 
cent of their cosmetics dollars in 
drug stores. 

However, drug stores were still 
able to generate a higher cosmetics 
ticket. Heavy cosmetics buyers spent 
an average $16.40 on cosmetics an- 
nually in drug stores compared to 
$15.55 in mass merchandise stores 
and $9.88 in food/drug combos. 

The findings, once again, rein- 
force how very important the cos- 
metics shopper is to drug stores and 
how much drug stores have to lose 
if mass merchandisers continue to 
make in-roads with this consumer. 

Based on the household panel 
data, Nielsen discovered that the 
consumer who buys cosmetics in a 
drug store is more “loyal” to drug 
stores than consumers who buy OTC 
products in drug stores or consumers 
who buy toiletries in drug stores. 

According to Nielsen, women in 
households that are “most loyal” to 
drug stores spend 63 percent of all 


Consumer data shows how 
important the cosmetics 
shopper is to drug stores 
and how much they can 
lose if mass merchandis- 
ers continue to make in- 


roads with this consumer.

their cosmetics dollars in drug stores. 

In comparison, women in house- 
holds that are loyal to drug stores 
spend only 45 percent of their OTC 
dollars in drug stores and just 38 
percent of their toiletry dollars in 
drug stores. 

Buyers of cosmetics tend to 
spend more money during their av- 
erage shopping trip than buyers of 
some other HBA/OTC categories. 

Nielsen household panel data 
shows that while a cough/cold buyer 
spends an average $13.03 ona 
shopping trip to a drug store, a color 
cosmetics buyer will spend $13.44 
on an average trip. 

In the last few years, chain drug 
stores have tried to make the cos- 
metics category more profitable in 
their stores by trimming slow-turn- 
ing SKUs from their inventory at 
store level. 

While this strategy has helped 
many drug chains improve their 
gross margin return on investment, 
it may have also 
made it easier for 
mass merchandisers

Drug Store News, June 27, 1994 


products in 1993 than they did in 
1992. 

That resulted in a 10 percent de- 
cline in unit sales for 1993, as well 
as a parallel drop in the number of 
SKUs handled by cashiers at the 
front end of drug stores. 

According to Nielsen scanning 
data, drug stores handled, on aver- 
age, 911 SKUs at the front end in 
1993, a drop of 7 percent vs. the pri- 
or year. 

At the same time, mass merchan- 
dise stores increased the number of 
cosmetics SKUs handled through 
their front ends by 7 percent to 
1,026. 

Increasing the variety of items no 
doubt contributed to the 11 percent 
gain mass merchandisers registered 
in unit sales in 19938 vs. 1992. 

In essence, that means that - 
women can now find a broader as- 
sortment of product in mass mer- 
chandise cosmetics departments 
than they can find in drug stores. 

Clearly, chain drug stores do not 
want to carry “deadwood” in their 
cosmetics inventory. If a store can’t 
turn an item at least once every six 
months, it surely can’t afford to con- 
tinue to carry that item. But when 
chains pare back deadwood, they 
should be on the lookout for some- 
thing new and exciting to put in its 
place. 

Specialty cosmetics stores have 
done an excellent job ferreting out 
interesting niche items that women 
can't seem to resist. 

Some of the better sellers seem to 
be in the aromatherapy family, like 
scented candles, scented massage oils 
and sachets. Natura! bristle brushes, 
makeup applicators, natural ingredi- 
ent soaps, bath oils and skin lotions 
are also great impulse items. 

The challenge for buyers is to find 
the right items to add to the cosmet- 
ics mix without risking that stores 
will be over-inventoried.

Retailers speed into “fast” finishing 


o lease or buy a minilab? 
That is the question. But 
the answer’s not black and 
white. Drug chains are shifting 
strategies these days, from in- 
house to outsourcing and some- 
times back again in the quest to 
improve profitability while trim- 
ming operating costs. 

What factors impact the deci- 
sion to own, lease or contract 
with a lessor/concessionaire 
whose program provides every- 
thing from supplies to the depart- 
ment’s image to promotional 
strategies? 

The answer depends on a drug 
chain’s goals, as retailers and 
manufacturers discuss below. 
But all agree that even though 
on-site processing accounts for a 
small but growing part of the 
photofinishing business, an on- 
site lab boosts the entire depart- 
ment and not just the “fast” fin- 
ishing business. 

Call it same-day, one-hour or 
30-minute, the message is “fast” 
photofinishing. That’s why 
chains like Eckerd and wholesale 
finisher Qualex use the name 
“express” in their programs, to 
tell the shopper they can get 
their film when they want it, ei- 


ther fast (for a premium ring, of Drug chains are gaining ground with increasing 
trade-channel share of on-site photoprocessing. 


course) or overnight. 

However the retailer markets 
its fastOphotofinishing, the drug 
store image as a convenience desti- 
nation gets a big boost with an on- 
site lab. 


Focus on profit 


As the photo buyer for a regional 
chain observed, photoprocessing is 
one of the most productive areas in 
the store. It is free from shrink and 
breakage, so gross profit is higher 
and net is much higher than many 
categories. “Gross profit percentage 
from photofinishing places it in the 
top three or four in all products 
handled by the chain,” he observed. 

In gross profit, photoprocessing 
ranges from around 27 percent to 
35 percent and even higher for 
overnight

On-site processing is growing in 
drug stores as chains maximize this 
core department’s benefits— profit, 
traffic and professional image—in 
the drug retail setting. Neighborhood 
convenience has its rewards, and one 
is the ease of returning to pick up 
same-day processing. 

Drug is also garnering an increas- 
ing trade-channel share of on-site 
processing, most of which is coming 
from camera stores and freestanding 
minilabs. Discount stores are gaining 
share even faster, but drug chains 
are outpacing supermarkets, accord- 
ing to the latest figures from the Pho- 
to Marketing Association (PMA). 

Drug store market share of on-site 
photofinishing increased from 11.9 
percent in 1992 to around 12.6 per- 
cent in 1993, according to prelimi- 
nary estimates from the PMA.

Overnight boost 


On-site labs don’t 
generate most of the 
photoprocessing 
business, but a photo 
department outfitted 
with an on-site lab 
shines brighter in 
margins, traffic- 
building and profes- 
sional image than 
one without a lab. 

Since drug chains 
are struggling for dif- 
ferentiation from 
other mass trade 
channels—and see- 
ing prescription mar- 
gins decline—the in- 
store lab can bolster 
the pharmacy’s pro- 
fessional image for a 
stronger store con- 
cept plus bring the 
benefit of a high 
gross margin subcategory. 

The total fast photoprocessing 
market for all channels reached 21.1 
percent of all photoprocessing con- 
sumer sales in 1993, according to the 
PMA’s U.S. Consumer Photo Buying 
Report, to be published next month. 
(These figures will be adjusted later 
this year to reflect additional indus- 
try data.) 

It isn’t likely we’ll see in-store 
labs in all drug chain locations in 
the near future, since demograph- 
ics, floor space and overnight pro- 
cessing volume determine whether 
a location is a good in-store lab 
candidate for reaching break-even 
and better. 

But with 20-plus percent of rolls 
being developed in a one-hour or 
same-day processing service, and as 
consumers see minilabs in more 
mass market outlets, the average 
consumer expectation about having 
a “fast” option is almost certain to 
increase in the future.

Rechargeables bring higher rings, 
but pose marketing challenge 


echargeable battery 

sales are beginning to 

rev up. They doubled 
(99.5 percent) in food 
chains, jumped up 25 per- 
cent in mass merchandisers 
and edged up 10 percent in 
drug chains in unit sales in 
the year ending May 1994, 
according to Nielsen N.A. 

Manufacturers say better 
merchandising would move 
even more high-ring re- 
chargeable batteries and 
chargers, and they want to 
educate the consumer, in- 
crease awareness about us- 
ing rechargeables and enlist 
the retailers’ help in the 
conversion process. 

The position of most drug 
retailers is typified by Wal- 
greens, where spokesperson 
Michael Polzin noted that 
rechargeable batteries are 
still a small part of the 
chain’s battery business, 
but “it is growing slowly.”

unit increase

Some drug retailers resist 
rechargeables, objecting to 
the price point of the three- 
hour, six-hour or overnight 
charger units that hold dif- 
ferent numbers of batteries 
(round cells) and range from 
$9.95 retail up to $30 or 
more. They think customers 
will get sticker shock even 
though it’s a one-time ex- 
pense. 

What’s more, consumers 
have to change their think- 
ing at checkout’ since 
rechargeable batteries ini- 
tially cost two or more times 
the price of disposable bat- 
teries (typically around $6 
for a two-pack of AA 
rechargeables) although they 
last much longer. 


Drug destination 


In some ways, however, 
drug chains are a natural 
for rechargeable batteries. 

Drug stores are an estab- 
lished destination for batter-

ies of any kind, including 
new formats or new technolo- 
gies. Hearing aid batteries, 
for example, once were only 
purchased in professional of- 
fices but are now found on 
drug stores’ pharmacy coun- 
ters or in photo/electronics 
departments. 

Drug chains are also 
among the leaders in com- 
munity outreach for a “well” 
community, and often that 
means recycling efforts. 


Consumers must 
change their 
thinking at 
checkout since 
rechargeables cost 
twice as much as 
disposable 
batteries, but last 
much longer. 


Rechargeables fit the trend 
toward recycling. 

Even if rechargeables are 
more trouble than popping 
in a one-time-use battery, 
more people are getting ac- 
customed to separating

This change of routine 
bodes well for rechargeable 
batteries in the future. 
(There are still environmen- 
tal issues surrounding stan- 
dard nickel-cadmium [Ni- 
Cad] rechargeable batteries 
because, when exhausted 
after much use, they should 
be sent back to the manu- 
facturer or otherwise dis- 
posed of safely.) 

Rechargeable technology 
is not new, but the category 
became more visible in the 
third quarter of 1993 when 
Rayovac launched its alka- 
line “renewable” recharge- 
able called Renewal Power 
System. 

Other battery manufactur- 
ers responded. Eveready ac- 
quired the rechargeable 
manufacturer Millenium 
and created Energizer Power 
Systems. In its announce- 
ment release, the supplier 
stated: “Rechargeables are a 
growing segment of the bat- 
tery category...” The merger 
brought Eveready into a 
very strong position in 
rechargeable battery sales. 

Another rechargeable con- 
tender was created from the 
merger of GE and Sanyo.

tery giant Duracell an-

ripe for more rechargeable

say manufacturers. Drug 
chains with strong photo 
and electronics departments

many consumers are em-

Manufacturers are betting 
that education and promo- 
tion could persuade more 
consumers to try recharge- 
ables since the concept fits 
today’s trend away from 
avoidable waste. 

As a step in this direction, 
Panasonic promotes use of 
rechargeable batteries with 
its consumer Power Club 
and a free family-oriented 
Club newsletter. (Details 
are enclosed in its prod-

Rayovac offers two Re- 
newal information bro- 
chures covering how it 
works, how to use it, ad- 
vantages, what to expect 
and environmental issues. 
A brochure holder is built 
into displays. 

The future could be bright 
for rechargeables as more 
consumers get used to 
charging the built-in batter- 
ies in their portable comput- 
ers or other devices like per- 
sonal digital assistants 
(PDAs). Many of these de- 
vices are also moving toward 
popular-sized batteries like 
AAs. As these personal de- 
vices become more common, 
the drug store as a conve- 
nience retailer could become 
a destination for recharge- 
able batteries.

The OTC consumer’s perspective 


by Mike Troy 


ho we are and how oth- 

ers view us are often 

quite different. The 

Same principle applies 
to the drug store industry. 

Most retailers regard their stores 
as convenient places to shop and be- 
lieve that customers like the ability 
to get in and out of the store quickly. 
That assumption drives merchandis- 
ing strategies and multimillion dollar 
store location decisions. 

But do OTC consumers regard it as 
a valid benefit? Yes, but apparently 
it's no more of a benefit for drug 
stores than for supermarkets or 
mass merchandisers, according to 
exclusive research conducted by the 
Gallup Organization. 

For the survey, Drug Store News 
and Drug Store News For The Phar- 
macist commissioned the Gallup Or- 
ganization to poll the drug store’s 
most valuable customer: female pre-

drug stores, pharmacists and OTCs. 
Some of the study’s key findings: 

® The highest percentage of pre- 
scription shoppers purchased OTCs 
from chain drug stores, independent 
drug stores or discount stores. Dis- 
count stores captured 26 percent of 
the business. (See chart 1 below.) 

® Discount stores with pharmacies 
did the best job of converting the 
prescription shopper into an OTC 
buyer. Of those who have prescrip- 
tions filled most frequently in dis- 
count stores, 66 percent also bought 
OTCs there most frequently. (See 
chart 2.) 

® Convenience and low prices were 
the two most powerful motivating 
factors in determining where survey 
respondents shopped for OTCs. (See 
chart 3.) However, respondents did 
not perceive drug stores to be more 
convenient than discount stores or 
supermarkets.

® Nonwhite prescription drug

consumers lean more toward dis-

in chain and independent drug

than 12 percent of the industry’s to- 
tal sales of $78 billion.

source, according to the prescription

Gallup surveys 
OTC attitudes 


Drug Store News commissioned the 
Gallup Organization of Princeton, 
N.J., to conduct a telephone survey 
exploring the cross-shopping behavior 
of women who have prescription med- 
ications filled and who shop for vari- 
ous over-the-counter products. The 
study included a nationally represen- 
tative sample of 500 women, 18 years 
of age and older, who have had a pre- 
scription medication filled, either for 
themselves or for another household 
member, in the past year. The survey 
was conducted between March 28 
and April 12, 1994. 

The results of the survey were 
weighted to reflect the current Cen- 
sus Bureau population estimates. In 
addition, to avoid what is known as 
“listing bias,” or the exclusion of un- 
listed and recently issued but not yet 
listed numbers, Gallup used a ran- 
dom digit procedure designed to pro- 
duce an accurate representation of all 
working telephone numbers. 


deep discounters at 12 percent and 
independents with 7.6 percent. 

Supermarkets and discount stores 
were relatively as popular as chain 
drug stores, according to survey re- 
sults. Discount stores were identi- 
fied by 26 percent of respondents 
and supermarkets by 21 percent of 
respondents as the location where 
they most often buy OTCs. 

Interesting preferences were re- 
vealed among different age groups. 
The 55 and older group favored 
chain drug stores for their OTC pur- 
chases, with 29 percent shopping 
there most often for OTCs. For the 
35-to-44 age group, about 30 per- 
cent said discount stores are their 
favorite place for OTCs. Supermar- 
kets scored highest with the 18- to 
29-year-olds,

cent said they also buy OTCs most 
often there. Discount drug stores 
and independents didn't fare as 
well, converting 32 percent and 25 
percent, respectively.

well as mass merchandisers with

and recommending over-the-counter

According to the survey, roughly 
half of the respondents who had a 
prescription filled in the past year 
also asked the pharmacist for advice

The 30-to-34 age group ask for 
more advice than the average, as 72 
percent said they asked questions of 
their pharmacist. The 35-to-44 age 
group was also a curious lot. Sixty- 
six percent said they sought advice 
during the past year. 

Surprisingly, those over So, the 
largest consumers of prescription 
drugs and OTCs, asked the fewest 
questions. Only about 30 percent of 
those over 55 said they sought a 
pharmacist’s advice about an OTC 
product during the past year. Retail- 
ers interested in improving pharma- 
cist access for this group could turn 
this into an opportunity. 

But increasing pharmacist advice 
to seniors will not necessarily trans- 
late into proportionately increased 
OTC sales. The study revealed that 
those over 55 who do ask for OTC 
advice were also the ones most likely 
to disregard the advice given. Twen- 
ty-six percent said they hardly ever 
or never followed the advice given.

OTCs a drug store draw 


Eighteen percent of 
those who had a pre-

the past year said they 
go to the drug store once

About 30 percent shop 


OTC products in drug stores only

also indicate an untapped potential 
for drug retailers as 22 percent of 
respondents said they never buy 
OTCs at drug stores. 

To get people to shop more at drug 
stores, survey results indicate that 
lower prices and product variety are 
two main areas where drug stores 
could improve. When asked what 
chain and discount drug stores 
could do to make themselves a better 
place to shop, 24 percent said lower 
prices and better value, and 15 per- 
cent cited greater product selection. 

Low prices were most important 
to the 35-to-44 age group. Thirty- 
six percent said drug stores could 
make themselves a better place to 
shop by lowering prices. Price selec- 
tion and variety were most impor- 
tant to the 18- to 29-year-olds. And 
slightly more than 18 percent said 
expanded product offerings would 
make drug stores better places to 
shop for OTCs.

OTC behaviors vary among ethnic groups 


hites are more likely than 
nonwhite consumers to 
seek the advice of a phar- 


macist about an OTC product. But, 
nonwhites are more loyal drug store 
shoppers and, when they sought the 
pharmacist’s advice, they were more 
likely to follow it. 

Those were just a few of the find- 
ings relating to race revealed in the 
exclusive study “Shopping Behav- 
iors of Prescription Purchasers.” 

Of those female prescription shop- 
pers surveyed, 54 percent of whites 
said they had sought'the advice or 
recommendation of a pharmacist in 
the past 12 months on an OTC prod- 
uct. Nearly 60 percent of the time the 
advice was followed. About thirty 
percent of the respondents said some 
of the time the advice was followed, 
and slightly more than 10 percent of 
those who sought advice said they 
hardly ever followed it. 

Conversely, nonwhites tended to 
seek advice less often. Only 32 per- 
cent of nonwhite female prescription 
shoppers said they queried their 
pharmacist about OTCs. Although 
nonwhites asked fewer questions of 
their pharmacist, when advice was 
given, 44 percent followed it most of

Labels a ‘must read’ for most 


recently released study by 
Prevention magazine and 
the Council on Family 
Health supports the Non- 
prescription Drug Manufacturers 
Association's position that Ameri- 
cans are able to use OTC medicines 
responsibly. 

The study, conducted by Prince- 
ton Survey Research Associates, 
found that 88 percent of people who 
use OTCs and 92 percent of those 
who use prescription drugs read the 
labels before using the products. 
Women were slightly more likely 
than men to read labels. 

The study also revealed that: 


® Twice aS many men as women, 
22 percent vs. 11 percent, said they 
use OTCs often. 

® About 62 percent of people who 
use medicines read the label each 
time they purchase them, and 50 
percent read the label each time the 
product is used. 

® When people read labels, they 
look for different things. Forty-seven 
percent said they look for interac- 
tion warnings, 39 percent look for 
general directions, and 30 percent 
look for dosage information. 

Study results are based on inter- 
views with 1,250 adults conducted 
during November 1993. 


Behavior varies among ethnic groups 


Continued from page S9 

clearly identified chain drug stores as 
the location where OTC products are 
most frequently purchased. Almost 
34 percent said chain drug stores are 
where they buy OTCs. About 20 per- 
cent said discount stores and 16 per- 
cent said supermarkets. 

Chain drug stores are a much less 
popular location to purchase OTCs 
for whites, according to survey re- 
sults. Only 23 percent said that’s 
where they buy OTCs most often. At 
28 percent, discount stores are the 
most popular OTC venue for whites. 
Supermarkets, discount drug stores 
and independent drug stores were 
identified by whites more frequently 
than nonwhites. 

As far as factors motivating their 
shopping trips for OTCs, there 
wasn't much difference. Both whites 
and nonwhites identified conve- 
nience and everyday low prices as 
the two most significant reasons in 
determining where they shop. One 
notable difference was nonwhites in- 
dicated a greater preference for pur- 
chasing OTCs at stores out of habit 
because they always shop there. 

What do drug stores need to do to 
improve? Lower prices/better value, 
21 percent, and greater selection, 10 
percent, were identified by whites. For 


$18 


nonwhites, a broader product selec- 
tion was more important, identified 
by 25 percent of respondents. Lower 
prices and better service each scored 
about 10 percent of those surveyed.

Sales of core OTCs remain strong 


Continued from page S13 


At Walgreens, the emphasis is on 
heavy coupon newspaper advertising. 
On special occasions, the chain will 
send out coupon books. 

Meanwhile, Snyder never uses 
newspapers to advertise. Instead the 
chain relies on “marriage mail,” a 
packet of ads bundled in a wrapper. 
“We do this 26 times a year, and 
every time, we cover these four cate- 
gories,” said Perkins. 

Arbor pays particular attention to 
the assortment plan and the stock. 


It uses off-shelf displays for new 


products. Applebaum added: “End- 
cap displays are based on perfor- 
mance and seasonality. They are 
not used for closeouts. Meanwhile, 
our radio and TV ads concentrate 
on theme advertising. For example, 
we may promote our large selection 
of vitamins.” 

Fred’s relies on full-color ads in 
local newspapers to promote these 


categories. In addition, a few times a 
year the chain will mail coupon 
books to its customers. 

Genovese uses many methods to 
promote these core product cate- 
gories, including item and price pro- 
motions, off-shelf displays, circulars 
and coupons. 

Big V also uses various techniques 
to promote its core OTCs. In the past 
few months, it has started using au- 
tomatic coupon dispensing machines 
for national brands. “Instant redemp- 
tion is a great way to get a product 
off the shelf,” said Goyeau. “In addi- 
tion, we use flyer inserts in newspa- 
pers and send out coupon books 
three times a year on national as well 
as our private label products.” 

Thrifty/PayLess uses point-of-sale 
signage, in-store couponing, health 
and beauty books mailed twice a 
year, weekly newspaper flyers and 
automatic coupon dispensing ma- 
chines to promote its core OTCs.

Fay's snaps up Peterson Drug 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — Fay's Inc. has purchased 12- 
unit Peterson Drug Co. of Western New York for an 
undisclosed amount. 

Peterson, a member company of NACDS with stores 
scattered throughout western New York State, is the 
latest in a long line of small- to medium-sized drug 
chains being snapped up in the rush by many drug 
chains to strengthen their prescription provider base 
and thus better position themselves for the era of man- 
aged health care. The chain is also a market-building 
plum for Fay's, which operates 261 drug stores in New 
York, Pennsylvania, Vermont and New Hampshire. 

Fay's chairman and chief executive Henry Panasci 
Jr. said the purchase will enable Fay's to more deeply 
penetrate the New York market and “will bring to Fay's 
a solid base of loyal prescription customers." 

Gerald Rosenberg, retiring president and chief execu- 
tive of Peterson Drug, said the company will continue to 
operate six freestanding card and gift shops. The deal 
for Peterson, which has been in business since 1926, 
was expected to close in late July. 

Fay's also recently completed the purchase of 26 Na- 
tional Auto Supply stores and four Whitlock Auto 
Stores. The stores will join Fay's 35-unit Wheels Dis- 
count Auto Supply division. 


Eckerd creates new logistics post 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — Eckerd Corp. has named 
chain drug veteran Curt Neel senior vice president of 
logistics, a new position. The move reflects Eckerd's 
growing commitment to using automation and data to 
control costs and streamline its distribution and store 
reorder systems. 

Neel, who has logged more than 20 years with Eck- 
erd, previously served as vice president of distribution. 

In his new position he will be responsible for distrib- 
ution operations and inventory trafficking, as well as 
managing the total flow of data and products from 
manufacturers to 1,709 Eckerd drug stores. 

Neel is active with NACDS and is an original mem- 
ber of the committee that initiated the annual NACDS 
Distribution and Logistics conference. 


Cuff named to Thrift board 


PITTSBURGH — Thrift Drug 
has named Dennis Cuff, a 24-year 
company veteran, to its 10-member 
board of directors. 

Cuff joined the 512-store chain 
in 1970 as assistant store manag- 
er, and rose through the ranks to 
regional vice president before be- 
ing promoted to senior vice presi- 
dent of administration last year. 
He is also a member of Thrift’s 
Management Committee and Man- 
agement Council. 

Cuff, a 1966 graduate of Duquesne University with 
a degree in pharmacy, is also involved in numerous 
business and community activities.

FoxMeyer inks major supply pact 


DALLAS — In a deal that represents a bonanza in 
expected sales over the next three years, FoxMeyer 
Corp. has signed a multi-year, primary distribution 
agreement with University Hospital Consortium, the 
nation's biggest alliance of academic medical centers. 
The deal could generate $4 billion to $5 billion in pre-

life of the agreement, the company said.

ters in California, Arizona, Utah, Washington, Penn- 
ft msg and Tennessee to supply UHC member hos- 
pitals.

MALVERN, Pa. — In line with its efforts 


Bergen builds on-ramp to 
information superhighway 


ORANGE, Calif. — Bergen Brunswig 
has unveiled an on-line, multimedia phar- 
macy inventory and information system 
that links retailers, suppliers and the na- 
tion’s second-largest drug wholesaler 
through a sophisticated interactive net- 
work. The new system, called AccuSource 
and available as of July 15, is the first 
computer link offered to drug retailers 
that features the combined technologies of 
high-density video and color graphics with 
sound, text information and E-mail net- 
work communications. 

AccuSource’s various programs allow re- 
tailers to compile orders based on informa- 
tion such as real-time inventory levels in 
the wholesaler’s warehouse system. Using 
options such as the “Competitive Edge” 
menu, retail buyers can make decisions re- 
garding on-deal offers by reviewing prod- 
uct sales history or return-on-investment 
charts. 

Orders are entered either through a Tel- 
zon unit or through the keyboard by call- 
ing up items by any of several selection 
choices. Information from suppliers, which 
appears in full color and either in flat 
graphics or full video, will be updated 
twice monthly on CD-ROM. For Bergen

Revco finishes fourth with a flourish 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
Revco D.S. finished its sec- 
ond full year out of bank- 
ruptcy with a solid fourth- 
quarter profit performance 
and industry-leading same- 
store sales gains. 

Comp-store sales rose 8 
percent for the final quarter 
of fiscal 94, with total sales 
advancing 1).5 percent to 
$815.5 million. Operating 
earnings were up 26.9 per- 
cent to $45.7 million, which 
Revco president and chief 
executive D. Dwayne Hoven 
called “particularly satisfy- 
ing, given the strength of 
our operating results in last 
year’s fourth quarter.” 

The strong sales perfor- 
mance and improving cost 
controls led to a dramatic 
rise in net earnings, which 
rose more than 68 percent 
over prior-year levels to 
$20.2 million in the final 
quarter ended May 28. 


For the full year, Revco’s 
sales were up 11.7 percent to 
$2.5 billion, with same-store 
results up 8.5 percent. Oper- 
ating profit jumped 32.2 per- 
cent to $100.5 million, with 
net profits up sharply to 
$38.7 million vs. $14.2 mil- 
lion the previous year. 

“For the fiscal year, we 
continued to improve all 
segments of the business,” 
said Hoven. “Comparable- 
store sales increases led the 
industry, gross margins im- 
proved despite continued 
pharmacy margin pressure, 
and expense ratios declined 
for the fifth consecutive 
year.” 


Chapter 11 helped 


Revco owes its strong per- 
formance to a host of fac- 
tors. Many of them —includ- 
ing advanced information 
and distribution systems, a 
powerful pharmacy comput- 


er system and a lower oper- 
ating cost structure— were 
put in place while the 
1,248-store chain was still 
under Chapter 11 protec- 
tion. Other factors behind 
the chain’s continuing 
growth momentum include 
careful cost controls, disci- 
plined management and an 
ongoing program of store 
upgrades and renovations. 
Wall Street reacted favor- 
ably to Revco’s performance, 
pushing up the company’s 
stock price the day of the 
announcement. Said David 
Magee, a retail analyst with 
Robinson-Humphrey Com- 
pany, “I’m very positive 
about them. They came in 
at the very high end of the 
range of analysts’ estimates, 
and in my opinion they have 
the best operating momen- 
tum of any publicly held 
company in the drug store 


group.”

your continuing battle for market 
share—and, perhaps, survival. 

When it comes to facts, figures and 
other statistics, in fact, we want to go 
beyond the “scorecard” approach to in- 
dustry data. We are looking for your 
ideas about research projects—like our 
recent Gallup survey of the front-end 
shopping habits of consumers of pre- 
scription drugs—that will give you in- 
formation you can put to use to increase 
your sales, your market share, your cus- 
tomer appeal and your efficiency. 

What questions would you like us to 
ask in our next consumer study? 
Which merchandising techniques 
would you like us to poll other drug 
chains about? If you have ideas for 
studies that you'd like to conduct but 
haven’t got the budget, we’d like to 
hear about them. 

Please write to me, Marie Griffin, at 
Drug Store News, 425 Park Ave., New 
York, N.Y. 10022 with your ideas for 
research projects. We might be able to 
create some “good news” together. 


Value vs. volume: Debating Rx price discounts 


Securing legislation to outlaw dis- 
criminatory pricing practices has been 
a top priority for drug chains and inde- 
pendent pharmacists throughout the 
debate over health care reform. 

The original Clinton Health Securi- 
ty Act called for eliminating anticom- 
petitive pricing practices, and that 
provision remains in the various re- 
form bills that have been approved by 
House and Senate committees. 


tices—say they share retail pharma- 
cy’s dislike for pharmaceutical dis- 
counts available to some classes of 
trade but not others. 

Indeed, the long-held position of the 
American Society of Consultant Phar- 
macists is that “it is unfair for any 
pharmaceutical purchaser to be denied 
access to negotiated prices simply on 
the basis of business environment or 
class of trade.” 

Moreover, “The 


The ASCP does not be- 
lieve that volume of a 
pharmacy’s drug purchases 
should determine the 
price charged by the 
manufacturer. 


ASCP supports 
laws and govern- 
ment policies that 
enable all phar- 
macies, irrespec- 
tive of class of 
trade, to have equal 
access to negotiated 
prices,” discounts or 
rebates from drug 
manufacturers. 


WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


Now, it seems that community phar- 
macy isn’t alone in supporting the 
principle that all pharmacy providers 
should have equal access to the best 
prices offered by the pharmaceutical 
industry. 

The nation’s consultant pharma- 
cists—a group of practitioners whose 
nursing home clients have long bene- 
fited from discriminatory pricing prac- 


4 Drug Store News, July 25, 1994 


Does this mean 
that pharmacists 
are united in 
their support for 
abolition of pharmaceutical price dis- 
crimination? Don’t bet on it. The fine 
print in the ASCP’s new Policy State- 
ment on Drug Pricing suggests that 
retail pharmacists and their cousins 
who service HMOs or nursing homes 
are still poles apart on this question. 

Unlike community pharmacy, the 
ASCP does not believe that volume of 
a pharmacy’s drug purchases should 


determine the price charged by the 
manufacturer. 

Rather, the consultant pharmacists 
contend that the prices charged for 
pharmaceuticals should be based 
largely on the pharmacy’s ability to 
“influence appropriate prescribing 
and utilization/consumption pat- 
terns” which achieve cost-effective 
outcomes. 

Translated back into semi-English, 
that means that drug manufacturers 
should be allowed to offer lower prices 
to pharmacists who employ strategies 
that produce changes in the way 
drugs are prescribed and purchased. 

What kind of “strategies” should 
serve as the basis for discounts from 
manufacturers? According to the 
ASCP, they include the use of formu- 
laries, preferred therapy guidelines, 
therapeutic substitution, prescriber 
education initiatives and other activ- 
ities that shift market share to the 
advantage of a deep-pockets pharma- 
ceutical manufacturer. 

Some would argue that the offer of 
rewards to enhance one manufactur- 
er’s market share at the expense of 
another’s may create an inherent con- 
flict of interest for pharmacists. 

I don’t know if that’s so. But a sys- 
tem that allows a supplier to set dif- 
ferent prices for different purchasers 
based on the customer’s perceived val- 
ue to the manufacturer is one that is 
vulnerable to abuse.

Foot care sales step up the pace 


by Mike Troy 


ctive lifestyles, an aging 

America and people’s desire 

to take care of their own 
health problems are driving foot 
care sales, according to manufactur- 
ers. Those trends combined to pro- 
duce a 9 percent sales increase dur- 
ing the 12 months ended May 1994, 
according to Towne-Oller. Sales for 
the period totaled $223.9 million, 
compared to $206 million the previ- 
ous year. 

From a consumer standpoint, to- 
day’s product offerings have come a 
long way. Product innovation, de- 
sign and new materials and ingredi- 
ents have made foot care products 
more effective. Also boosting sales, 
say buyers, are packaging changes 
and product directions that make it 
easier for people to self-diagnose 
their condition and select an appro- 
priate product. 

Today, foot care products are 
higher in quality as manufacturers 
have introduced upscale, premium- 
priced products. And, as suppliers 
attempt to squeeze every ounce of 
profit out of the category, no niche 
has gone unfilled, giving consumers 
greater selection than ever before. 


The retail perspective 


Foot care may not be the most 
glamorous category for chain drug 
buyers, but its current sales in- 
creases, above-average margins and 
long-term growth prospects are 
earning it increased attention. 

“Foot care is a category that is of- 
ten neglected because it is not that 
attractive or exciting of a category 
to work in, but people are starting 
to pay a lot more attention to it as 
sales keep going up,” said John 
Cincotta, senior category manager 
with the Chain Drug Marketing As- 
sociation. 

For most chain drug retailers, an 
8- to 12-foot set is fairly typical. 
However, “that could increase in 
size as people expand their private 
label offerings,” Cincotta said. “Dr. 
Scholl’s has become pricey on some 
items, and that opens the door for 
value-priced items.” 

The door may be open, but other 
retailers are finding that customers 
don’t mind paying the $7 to $8 for a 
quality insole customized for a spe- 
cific purpose. 

“We carry Dr. Scholl’s full line, 
and it still sells the best, but once 
in a while we'll put in some of the 
lower-priced insoles,” said buyer 
Sherry Horowitz with south Flori- 
da-based Corner Drug. “The people 
I’ve found like the quality of Dr. 
Scholl’s, and most would rather pay 
the difference.” 

Corner carries an 8-foot set, with 
other foot care items such as anti- 
fungals merchandised on the lower 
shelves. “The Lotrimins are proba- 
bly No. 1 right now, followed by Tin- 
actin, and overall profitability is 
good in the category because it is 
not as competitive as other OTC 
categories,” Horowitz said. 

Another retailer looking forward 
to good Lotrimin sales is K&B. “The 
big thing this year was the four new 
Lotrimin items that came out. It is 


really too early to tell, but it looks 
like they are going to do pretty 
well,” said Jude Eserman, OTC buy- 
er for the chain. 

Eserman said K&B recently re- 
vised its foot care planogram, which 
ranges from 8 to 12 feet, to include 
the new Lotrimin SKUs, six private 
label insoles and three premium in- 
sole products from Spenco, a Kim- 
berly Clark subsidiary. 

“Foot care is a money-making cat- 
egory, and I promote it about four 
times a year with ads for 1/3 off Dr. 
Scholl’s. It is a steady category, but 
there is nothing very exciting about 
it,” Eserman said. 

At Snyder Drug Stores, buyer 
Roger Musil echoed Eserman’s com- 
ments. “Foot care is a pretty steady 
and strong category, but it is not 
something I’m getting too excited 
about at this time,” Musil said. “The 
new Lotrimin items are starting to 
show some signs of accelerating.” 

The Lotrimin line extensions 
seem to be on everyone’s mind. “We 
are doing real well with the Lotri- 
min products,” said Pat McCafferty, 
senior vice president of purchasing, 
Super D Drugs. “[In foot care] we 
are getting increases in both dollar 
and unit sales. But the increases 
don’t warrant a reallocation of 
space.” 

Similar to other retailers, Super D 
has an 8-foot set and is developing a 
private label line that will consist of 
insoles, cushions and pads. 


Who’s who 


Schering-Plough’s Dr. Scholl’s 
complete line of foot care products 
remains king of the hill, and the 
manufacturer has been aggressive 
in the past 18 months with re- 
launches and product introductions. 

“We've spent several years and 
millions of dollars in research and 
development of high-tech, superior 
performance products that very 
specifically meet the foot health 
needs of today’s more active con- 
sumer,” said Steve LaMonte, vice 
president of foot care marketing 
with Schering-Plough HealthCare 
Products. Earlier this year 22 new 
Dr. Scholl’s products across all cate- 
gory segments were shipped to re- 
tailers, and last year the Dr. 
Scholl’s line underwent a makeover 
as package designs and products 
were changed and upgraded. 

“Today consumers want to be 
comfortable in all kinds of shoes, 
and these products provide that 
comfort,” added LaMonte. “They’re 
value-added, high-performance and 
premium priced. We estimate that 
the retailer will see as much as a 25 
percent return on initial investment 
with these new products.” 

While Dr. Scholl’s remains the 
categorys dominant player, has one 
of the oldest and most recognizable 
trademarks in the packaged goods 
industry, dominates shelf space in 
the category and has a majority of 
market share in every segment but 
soaks, other manufacturers are 
emerging to provide retailers and 
consumers with an alternative. 

“There has been a big change, 
and the we is ongoing in drug 
stores,” said Steve Corsun, presi- 
dent of Premier Brands of America. 


“For a long time, it was just Dr. 
Scholl’s, but now othe brands and 
private label are emerging.” 
According to Corsun, several fac- 
tors are driving sales. “It used to be 
that when people had foot problems, 
they just lived with it. Increasingly, 
they realize there are products 
available to help them,” he said.

at retail,” Feldman said. “What we 
want to do is give people exciting 
products that tie into the two trends 
driving sales in this category.” 

Feldman believes more chain 
drug stores should be pursuing foot 
care customers. “The foot care cus- 
tomer is a pretty loyal customer 
who will keep coming back to your 
store if you have the right selection 
of products,” Feldman said. “I can’t

Corn, callous growing

were up in drug stores a

Insoles/inserts heat up

$17.2 million.
