GENERAL MERCHANDISE / BOOKS AND MAGAZINES 


Cross merchandising boosts book, magazine sales 


by Allene Symons 


\ Ithough overall magazine 
sales are not a growth catego- 
, there is still a lot of action 
for drug chains. 

Chicago-based distributor Chas. 
Levy Circulating Co. reported that, 
in its Walgreens and Osco accounts, 
comic books sales are experiencing 
double-digit growth. Both chains 
utilize 20-pocket wing units as their 
primary display vehicle. Osco also 
has two separate laneblocker fix- 
tures with African American and 
Hispanic magazines. 

Last year, PayLess Drug Stores 
buyer Pat Pemberton reported, “We 
have begun to develop comics in a 
big way.” It was a good decision, as 
she reported this year that comic 
books are selling well. 

Book sales have also increased, 
said Pemberton, boosted in part by 
increased book advertising—with 
help from the volume generated by 
legal-thriller, bestseller-author 
John Grisham. The chain also does 
well with children’s book titles—es- 
pecially coloring and activity books. 

In addition, PayLess now has a 
chainwide health and fitness paper- 
back book program in the pharmacy 
department. The chain tested the 
concept with a few stores and 3- to 
4-foot endcaps of health-related 
books located across from the phar- 
macy before rolling the pharmacy 
endcap program out chainwide in 
either endcap or spinner rack. Ac- 
cording to Pemberton, the program 
“is doing great.” 

One tip for chains selling paper- 
back health books located in or near 
the pharmacy: Buyers report that 
these titles sell by subject rather 
than by title or author. Subjects in- 
clude managing stress and control- 
ling high blood pressure and fat. 


Beauty moves magazines 


Cross merchandising and catching 
extra sales of special issues are oth- 
er proven strategies to increase 
magazine sales in drug chains. 

Publisher Conde Nast encourages 
cross merchandising with The Beau- 
ty Corner, a display for eight to 10 
beauty magazines with alternating 
display space for cosmetics products. 

The Beauty Center is now in Drug 
Emporium and several other drug 
chains as well as some supermarket 
combos, reported Conde Nast na- 
tional sales manager Jim Maki. 

A field merchandising unit (FMU) 
is another successful approach, 
used by chains like Osco Drug. An 
FMU is a disposable freestanding 
unit with a life-span of a week or 
two. This allows extra capacity to 
maximize sales for special issues 
like the September issue of Vogue. 
Sales of a title can increase by 30 
percent to 50 percent or more in a 
store, according to Maki. 


Magazine source 


Customers expect to find maga- 
zines in drug stores. In their minds, 
drug chains are the neighborhood 
magazine stand—in most regions of 
the country. Even in cities where 
newsstands still thrive, drug chain 
customers expect to find an easy-to- 


browse magazine section (and often 
a bestselling paperback book de- 
partment), plus a fresh display 
every week when the local distribu- 
tor delivers new titles. 

“Customers look to drug stores for 
magazines. It’s an area just like 
greeting cards and HBA. A cus- 
tomer knows there will be a maga- 
zine assortment,” said a spokesman 
for Arbor Drug. 

For the retailer, magazines trans- 
late into impulse sales at around 20 
percent margins, slightly more for 
paperback books and up to 50 per- 
cent for hardcovers, although most 
chains discount bestsellers by 10 
percent to be competitive. 

There are other advantages. In- 
ventory dollars aren’t tied up in 
magazine stock since the retailer 
only pays for what sells (the rest is 
returned for credit). Periodicals also 
help the bottom line by requiring 
minimal labor since they are dis- 
tributor-serviced. Most books are 
also distributor-serviced in drug 
chains. 

In 1993, drug stores accounted for 
13 percent, or around $481 million, 
of the $3.7-billion retail magazine 
business; book sales brought in 
around an additional $100 million 
to drug chains, according to the 
New York-based Council for Period- 
ical Distributors Associations 
(CPDA). 

These figures represent—or don’t 
represent—a growth in magazine 
sales, depending on whose statistics 
are considered. According to the 
CPDA, magazine sales increased 5 
percent and books 4 percent. But, 
the Audit Bureau of Circulation 
(ABC) reported a decline in maga- 
zine sales. The difference, according 
to the CPDA, is the small sampling 
of 500 major magazine titles 
tracked by the ABC, whereas much 
of the magazine growth is in newer 


and more specialized titles not 
tracked by the ABC. 


Face forward 


Among other advantages, maga- 
zines offer a good opportunity for 
micromarketing. Chains can work 
with a store’s local independent dis- 
tributor to customize the mix slight- 
ly differently by store. 

And, there’s plenty of options for 
customization. It’s not just a major 
magazine business any more. Spe- 
cialty magazines are a growing seg- 
ment, appealing to every consumer 
group from teens and Generation X 
to babyboomer sports trainers, eth- 
nic consumers and retirees interest- 
ed in gardening or hobbies and 
crafts. 

Arbor Drug emphasizes assort- 
ment and works with local distribu- 
tors to customize the mix at its 153 
stores, said an Arbor spokesperson. 
An example of micromarketing, he 
noted, is that stores that serve a 
business clientele will sell more 
Forbes magazines or Wall Street 
Journals, while other stores will in- 
clude a dozen specialty sport titles 
covering subjects like rollerblading. 

Finding space for books and mag- 
azines, however, is becoming in- 
creasingly difficult. Distributor 
Chas. Levy, for example, said in- 
line space for books and magazines 


Chains like PayLess and Bartell are gaining sales by cross merchandising beau- 
ty books near cosmetics and health-related books near the pharmacy. 


is being reduced as drug chains ex- 
pand the space allotted to non-tra- 
ditional categories like food and 
shift space to other areas, like larg- 
er pharmacy waiting rooms. 

Still, merchandised correctly, as 
more chains define destination de- 
partments including cosmetics, pho- 
to and greeting cards, the magazine 
and book department offers more 7% 
than just SKUs. It provides another 
opportunity to create a more excit- 
ing and highly visual shopping ex- 8% 
perience for the consumer. 

Fixtures are changing at many 
chains to reflect this. New Orleans- 
based K&B, for example, recently 
moved to attractive angled fixtures 
in its new stores. And PayLess 
changed its magazine and book de- 
partment fixturing a year or two 
ago, getting rid of standard wire 
shelves in favor of wood and mylar 
set at an angle. The results are up- 
scale and appealing for browsers 
and boosted sales. 

“Our book sales increased dra- 
matically by store when we did a 
fixture change,” said Pemberton.

Winning customers in the 90s 


Continued from page 1 


among a multitude of shopping lo- 
cations—who is forcing the scram- 
ble by retailers to market more ef- 
fectively. 

The initial power shift, to the re- 
tailer from the manufacturer, oc- 
curred in the late 1980s, said MCA 
partner Anil Jagtiani, who prepared 
the survey. “But the second quan- 
tum shift, now taking place, is to 
the consumer,” he said. “The real 
reason is because the consumer has 
so many alternatives about where 
to shop. That has put more pressure 
on both the manufacturer and re- 
tailer to better serve...the needs of 
the new power consumer.” 


Harnessing information 


Retailers have clearly seized the 
initiative. Of the more than 100 
chains surveyed by MCA, more 
than half—including 60 percent of 
the drug chains—claimed that con- 
sumer marketing and value-added 
services were even more important 
strategically than quick-response 
capabilities and efficient consumer 
response (ECR). 

Seventy percent of all retailers 
said they were analyzing scanner 
movement data to manage their 
business better, and nearly that 
many are studying consumer demo- 
graphics and conducting consumer 
focus groups. 

Drug chains lag in some of these 
target marketing efforts, but not by 
much. More than half of the drug 
chains surveyed are analyzing scan- 
ner data in at least a rudimentary 
way, and they’re now basing their 
promotion decisions at least as 
much on consumer sell-through as 
on the old lure of vendor promotion- 
al money. 

What’s more, a majority of chain 
drug respondents said they were 
planning for more aggressive mar- 
keting efforts via direct-mail, fre- 
quent shopper programs and image 
advertising. 

“Retailers are in the vanguard,” 
said Jagtiani, and are gaining pow- 
er because of their front-line prox- 
imity to consumers and their grow- 
ing ability to gather and harness 
information. 


A call for help 


But retailers polled by MCA also 
want more help from thir suppli- 
ers. As it now stands, MCA reports, 
manufacturers only get a “B-” when 
it comes to providing value-added 
services to the chains. 

Drug chain executives want man- 
ufacturers to understand their busi- 
ness better. They want more catego- 
ry expertise and more coordinated 
planning, with both sides sitting 
down and planning the sales year 
together, from scratch. And retail- 
ers want more specific market intel- 
ligence and consumer research from 
their vendors to help them in their 
own growing efforts to implement 
category management throughout 
the store. 

That cuts against the grain of 
what many manufacturers still re- 
gard as their chief objectives. The 
survey indicates that many suppli- 
ers are still focused primarily on

space management and 
planograms—instead of on 
programs that will put them 
and their retail partners in 
closer touch with con- 
sumers. 

What’s needed, said Jag- 
tiani, is more store-level re- 
search into consumer be- 
havior and motivation, and 
more effective ways of tai- 
loring marketing programs 
between retailers and man- 
ufacturers to reach those 
consumers. 

“The real key to winning 
in the 90s is understanding 
the ‘why’ of consumer be- 
havior,” said Jagtiani. By 
the same token, he said, 
“Not all retailers recognize 
that (‘why’) answers are not 
to be found in information 
systems—which tell you 
what is going on—but only 
through direct dialogue 
with consumers.” 

Indeed, POS automation 
and demographic data are 
helping many chains draw a 
bead on exactly what prod- 
ucts move through the reg- 
isters and a pretty clear 
sense of who buys them. 
But only 36 percent of all 
chains surveyed said they 
can monitor the price/pro- 
motion sensitivity of their 
customers, and fewer than 
three in 10 know why con- 
sumers in a particular mar-

buy the products they do. 

For manufacturers, that 
can mean an “incredible op- 
portunity to help the retail- 
er understand the ‘why’ of 
consumer behavior” and 
help drug chains stand out 
from the competition, thus 
boosting their own role in 
product marketing, said 
Jagtiani. Those suppliers 
who do learn to truly forge 
strategic alliances with re- 
tailers through the applica- 
tion of their resources stand 
to gain in sales and market 
share, the study indicates. 

“Drug chains have to fo- 
cus on efficiency to play in 
the retail game, but in order 
to win, they'll need to 
strengthen their differentia- 
tion in the minds of shop- 
pers,” said Jagtiani. “That 
means going back to under- 
standing the ‘why’ of con- 
sumer behavior, developing 
who their target is and go- 
ing after them.” 

Manufacturers have a key 
role to play in those efforts, 
he added. “All of the manu- 
facturers’ market research 
is focused on consumer atti- 
tudes and usage,” Jagtiani 
said, “but all this wealth of 
consumer insight resides in 
an ivory tower. Manufactur- 
ers lack the organizational 
priorities to apply that in- 
sight to retailer-specific sit- 
uations. 

“For both sides,” he con- 
tinued, “the real break- 
through idea is going to be 
to merge these two sources 
of consumer information” in 
pursuit of more creative 
marketing strategies and 
closer ties with consumers.

Ni to take FoxMeyer 


private in stock swap 


DALLAS — FoxMeyer 
Corp., the nation’s third- 
largest drug wholesaler, has 
agreed to be acquired by its 
principal shareholder, hold- 
ing company National Inter- 
group. 

Under terms of the deal, 
FoxMeyer will become a 
wholly owned subsidiary of 
NI, which already owns 80.5 
percent of the wholesaler. 
Current shareholders of 
FoxMeyer, whose shares are 
still traded on the New York 
Stock Exchange, will receive 
nine-tenths of a share of NI 
common stock for each 
share of FoxMeyer common 


in a tax-free reorganization 
transaction. 

In line with the agree- 
ment, NI’s board of direc- 
tors is expected to change 
that company’s name at its 
upcoming annual meeting 
to better reflect NI’s ex- 
panding focus on the grow- 
ing health care industry. 
The annua! shareholder 
meetings for both compa- 
nies, however, have been 
postponed until after joint 
proxy statements have been 
issued to shareholders. 

FoxMeyer’s sales reached 
$5.1 billion for the fiscal 
year ended March 31. 


Kash n Karry delays 
bond interest payments 


TAMPA, Fla. — Interest 
payments due to bondhold- 
ers of Kash n’ Karry Food 
Stores Inc. will not be made 
in August, as the troubled 
combo operator continues to 
negotiate a proposed recapi- 
talization plan. 

The company announced 
that its lending banks have 
granted an_ extension 
through Sept. 30 of previ- 
ously granted waivers of fi- 
nancial covenants under its 
bank credit agreement. 
That extension eases pres- 
sure somewhat on the 
company as it seeks to 
work its way out of a fi- 
nancial crisis brought on 
in part by a too-heavy debt 
burden.

ization plan, first proposed 
in May, would deleverage

eS GENERICS STUDY 


Generic drugs are primed 


to fill four out of every 10 
prescriptions written,” 
Ferm told a Global Gener- 
ics Conference in New 
York last month. “By the 
year 2000, seven out of 
every 10 prescriptions 
written will be filled by 
generics.” 

Despite the rosy scenar- 
ios being painted for the 
U.S. generic drug market, 
there are more than a few 
nightmares keeping gener- 
ic manufacturers awake at 
night. 

Although the generic 
scandals that almost de- 
stroyed the industry in the 
late 1980s are now only a 
painful, fading memory, 
other threats to the viabili- 
ty of generics are surfacing 
in Washington, on Wall 
Street, and even in the 
European Community. 


First the good news... 


The good news for the 
makers of generic pharma- 
ceuticals is that both gov- 
ernment and _ private 
health care decision-mak- 
ers are increasingly recog- 
nizing the potential of 
generics to hold down pre- 
scription drug costs. 

In the private sector, the 
growing emphasis on 
managed care cost con- 
tainment strategies has 
spawned a sharp upsurge 
in the use of generic for- 
mularies and incentives 
for generic dispensing. 
Pharmacy Benefits Man- 
agement (PBM) organiza- 
tions like McKesson’s PCS, 
Merck-Medco’s PAID Pre- 
scriptions and the new

‘Blockbusters’ coming 


Even without health 
care reform legislation, 
however, the generic drug 
market figures to experi- 
ence explosive growth as a 
result of the large number 
of big-money brand name 
drugs scheduled to come 
off patent over the next 
few years. A study re- 
leased earlier this year by 
Frost & Sullivan concludes 
that “in 1995, 40 of the 50 
top-selling patented drugs 
will be available from 
generic manufacturers.” 

This year, for example, 
“blockbusters” such as 
Tagamet, Seldane, and- 
Vanceril will all lose their 
patent exclusivity, and 
generic producers appear 
on the verge of capturing 
billions of dollars in sales 
from the brand-name sec- 
tor based on the 1994 
crop alone. Indeed, a new 
study by market re- 
searcher David Saks at 
Gruntal & Co. estimates 
that the total annual dol- 
lar sales of brand-name 
drugs set to go off patent 
this year will top $6 bil- 
lion. 

Other top-selling phar- 
maceuticals such as Zovi- 
rax (1993 sales of $410 
million), Toradol ($263 
million), and Mevacor 
($782 million), figure to 
add even more punch as 
they come off patent with- 
in the next five years. Ac-

If you can’t beat ’em, 
join ’em 


So promising are the 
prospects for the generic 
industry that the nation’s 
brand name manufactur- 
ers are themselves scram- 
bling to cash in on the im- 
minent generic boom. 

Leading research-based 
pharmaceutical giants like 
Hoechst, Miles and Mari- 
on Merrell Dow have mus- 
cled in directly by acquir- 
ing existing generic 
companies (i.e., Copley, 
Schein, Rugby). Others 
(e.g., Syntex/Hamilton 
and Merck/West Point 
Pharma) are joining the 
party with their own cap- 
tive generic production 
and distribution firms. 

Still other branded drug 
makers from Allergan to 
Zeneca have hammered 
out innovative new 
“strategic alliances” with 
generic firms—arrange- 
ments that frequently give 
the “partnering” generic 
house a critical head-start 
in marketing generic ver- 
sions of brand name prod- 
ucts before patents expire. 

Meanwhile, some brand- 
ed companies have en- 
tered the action more sub- 
tly by “genericizing” their 
own products—a strategy 
designed to give the “pio- 
neer” manufacturer a sol- 
id foothold in the generic 
market. 

The next step, according 
to industry consultant 
Ferm, will be for research- 
based pharmaceutical 
companies to form special 
new alliances with other 
brand name manufactur- 


emcees, 11. ..1/ ees 


ers who are marketing 
generic products—a devel- 
opment he expects to see 
within the next two years. 
Although imitation may 
be the sincerest form of 
flattery, many indepen- 
dent generic manufactur- 
ers are becoming more 
than a little nervous over 
the efforts of their brand- 
name competitors to meld 
into the generic pharma- 
ceutical market. Industry 
experts say the generic ex- 
ecs may have good reason 
for their concerns. Citing 
the rash of recent acquisi- 
tions, Ferm predicts that 
“before the end of this 
decade, independent 
generic manufacturers will 
be few in number and in- 
significant in volume.” 


Is Walgreens next? 


International pharma- 
ceutical industry consul- 
tant Nicholas Hall con- 
tends that once the 
current feeding frenzy on 
generic companies is over, 
branded manufacturers 
may look toward other, 
even more controversial 
types of acquisitions. 

“How long will it take 
before major manufactur- 
ers want to become drug 
wholesalers or even retail- 
ers?” Hall asked during 
the Global Generic Confer- 
ence co-sponsored by his 
consulting firm last 
month. “How long before 
Walgreens or Eckerd be- 
come takeover targets for 
brand-name pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturers?” 

Concerns over recent in- 
dustry mergers are also 
surfacing in Washington, 
where government an- 
titrusters are starting to 
take a closer look at acqui-

Pregnancy Category X. See CONTRAINDICATIONS and WARNINGS

11. NURSING MOTHERS 

Small amounts of oral contraceptive steroids have been identified in the milk 
of nursing mothers and a few adverse effects on the child have been 
reported, including jaundice and breast enlargement. In addition, oral 
contraceptives given in the postpartum period may interfere with lactation 
by decreasing the quantity and quality of breast milk. If possible, the nursing 
mother should be advised not to use oral contraceptives but to use other 
forms of contraception until she has completely weaned her child 


12. INFORMATION FOR THE PATIENT 
See PATIENT LABELING 


ADVERSE REACTIONS 


An increased risk of the following serious adverse reactions has been asso- 
ciated with the use of oral contraceptives (see WARNINGS section) 


¢ Thrombophlebitis 

¢ Arterial thromboembolism 

¢ Pulmonary embolism 

¢ Myocardial infarction 

* Cerebral hemorrhage 

¢ Cerebral thrombosis 

¢ Hypertension 

* Gallbladder disease 

¢ Hepatic adenomas, carcinomas or benign liver tumors 


There is evidence of an association between the following conditions and the 
use of oral contraceptives, although additional confirmatory studies are 
needed: 


¢ Mesenteric thrombosis 
¢ Retinal thrombosis 


The following adverse reactions have been reported in patients receiving oral 
contraceptives and are believed to be drug-related 


¢ Nausea 

¢ Vomiting 

¢ Gastrointestinal symptoms (such as abdominal cramps and bloating) 
* Breakthrough bleeding 

* Spotting 

* Change in menstrual flow 

¢ Amenorrhea 

¢ Temporary infertility after discontinuation of treatment 
« Edema 

¢ Melasma which may persist 

¢ Breast changes: tenderness, enlargement, secretion 

¢ Change in weight (increase or decrease) 

¢ Change in cervical erosion and secretion 

* Diminuiion in lactation when given immediately postpartum 
¢ Cholestatic jaundice 

¢ Migraine 

¢ Rash (allergic) 

¢ Mental depression 

¢ Reduced tolerance to carbohydrates 

¢ Vaginal candidiasis 

¢ Change in corneal curvature (steepening) 

* Intolerance to contact lenses 


The following adverse reactions have been reported in users of oral contra- 
ceptives and the association has been neither confirmed nor refuted 


¢ Pre-menstrual syndrome 
¢ Cataracts 

¢ Changes in appetite 

* Cystitis-like syndrome 

* Headache 

¢ Nervousness 

* Dizziness 

* Hirsutism 

* Loss of scalp hair 

¢ Erythema multiforme 

¢ Erythema nodosum 

* Hemorrhagic eruption 

* Vaginitis 

¢ Porphyria 

¢ Impaired renal function 
¢ Hemolytic uremic syndrome 
* Budd-Chiari syndrome 

* Acne 

¢ Changes in libido 

¢ Colitis 


NON-CONTRACEPTIVE HEALTH BENEFITS 
In addition to preventing pregnancy, use of oral contraceptives may provide 
certain non-contraceptive health benefits 
* Menstrual cycles may become more regular 


* Blood flow during menstruation may be lighter and less iron may be lost 
Therefore, anemia due to iron deficiency is less likely to occur 


¢ Pain or other symptoms during menstruation may be encountered 
less frequently 


* Ectopic (tubal) pregnancy may occur jess frequently 
* Non-cancerous cysts or lumps in the breast may occur less frequently 
* Acute pelvic inflammatory disease may occur less frequently 


* Oral contraceptive use may provide some protection against developing 
two forms of cancer: cancer of the ovaries and cancer of the lining of the 
uterus

tainly improved.

become important in store

My customers are not

@ Profit and inventory — 
Generics can increase pharmacy 
profit since they presently deliver 
higher profit margins. Stocking and 
dispensing generics helps reduce 
inventory expense. In this day of 
shrinking gross margins, generics 
help keep the pharmacy depart- 
ment as profitable as possible. 

®@ Third-party — Most third-party 
plans have discovered the financial 
benefits of lower cost generic 
drugs, too. Many will only reim- 
burse the pharmacy for the generic 
when available. Others require a 
higher co-pay—often 2-3 times 
higher—for the brand name when a 
generic is available. Some insur- 
ance companies even offer the 
pharmacy incentives such as high- 
er dispensing fees for generics. 

@ Patient compliance — The pa- 
tient also benefits from the proper 
use of generic drugs. The obvious 
benefit is the immediate cost sav- 


macy today.” 


quality products with an 
“A” rating and a continu- 
ity of manufacturing ensuring con- 
sistent size, shape and color of 
product. Price is also a considera- 
tion, but the competitive pricing of 
the generic companies leaves this 
as just one more factor in the over- 
all generic equation. 

Of course, patients on medica- 
tion with a narrow therapeutic 
range or those whose blood levels 
must be monitored closely should 
stay with the same manufacturer 
to ensure consistent performance 
from their medication. 

I view generic drugs as an ethical 
and professional way to increase 
the pharmacy department's profits. 
Generic drug use will also reduce 
the patient’s health care costs and 
improve medication compliance. 
Pharmacists should promote the 
use of generics, and patients 
should take advantage of the bene- 
fits generic drugs provide.

Just last month the Feder-

The European menace 


Assuming generic manu- 
facturers survive the acqui- 
sition frenzy, the industry 
may still face potentially 
crippling bulk chemical 
supply shortages due to 
controversial new patent 
rules adopted in the Euro- 
pean Community. 

The result of these rules, 
according to the NAPM, 
will be to delay the intro- 
duction of generic versions 
of many drugs by years, 
and drive up U.S. health 
costs by tens of billions of 
dollars (see story page 30). 

Worse yet, NAPM Presi- 
dent Robert Milanese sees 
little hope of reversing the 
new European patent 
rules. He told FTP, “our 
emphasis now is on pre- 
venting the spread of such 
patent provisions to other 
supplier countries.” 

Even health care re- 
form—the basis for much 
of the optimism within the

generic drug industry dur- 
ing the past year—is fast 
becoming a source of con- 
cern for the producers of 
generics. The most press- 
ing potential problem: a 
proposal supported by 
brand name pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturers that 
would require generic 
companies to offer rebates 
in return for the right to 
supply Federally funded 
drug programs. 


Generic rebates 


The Clinton Plan would 
require such rebates only 
from branded makers—an 
approach supported by 
both GPIA and NAPM. But 
under pressure to reduce 
the cost of health reform, 
Congress is giving serious 
consideration to applying 
similar rebate require- 
ments to generics—an ap- 
proach that industry offi- 
cials say could backfire by 
reducing the availability of 
cost-saving generic drugs 
(see story on page 30). Still 
other Congressional 
schemes would pose even 
greater problems for the 
generic drug industry. 

Proposals to promote 
pharmaceutical research 
and development by 
lengthening patent protec- 
tion for brand name drugs 
are drawing particularly 
strong objections from 
generic lobbyists. In let- 
ters to Congressional lead- 
ers, officials at NAPM 
warned if “U.S. patent pro- 
tection for brand name 
drugs is extended beyond 
current parameters, low 
cost generics will be un- 
available for an extended 
period of time and con- 
sumers will inevitably pay 
billions of dollars more for 
pharmaceuticals.”

Industry optimistic 


Despite these concerns, 
there’s a strong feeling of 
optimism within the 
generic drug community. 
Regardless of how the 
health care reform saga 
plays out in Washington 
this summer, industry 
leaders are confident that 
public policy makers will 
recognize the importance 
of maintaining a viable 
generic drug market. And 
as for the incursions by 
research-based pharma- 
ceutical companies, some 
generic execs say this 
strategy could backfire on 
brand-name companies. 


“In the long run, brand- 
ed companies may not 
prosper or even survive in 
the generic market be- 
cause of their lack of prop- 
er perspective for the 
generic business,” Martec 
Pharmaceutical chief exec- 
utive Richard Spears said. 
The inability of these 
brand-name drug manu- 
facturers “to meet contin- 
uous generic price erosion 
and their entrenched high- 
er overhead costs” will 
make it even tougher for 
these companies to keep 
pace with their lean and 
mean generic cousins, he 
added.

a GENERICS STUDY 


Generic industry wresties with 
evolving health care reform 


epresentatives of 

two rival generic 

manufacturer orga- 
nizations, the National As- 
sociation of Pharmaceuti- 
cal Manufacturers and the 
Generic Pharmaceutical 
Industry Association, are 
urging Congressional 
health reformers to in- 
clude strong incentives for 
generic dispensing in any 
final reform legislation 
sent to the President. 

Testifying before Rep. 
Henry Waxman’s (D-Cailif.) 
House Health Subcommit- 
tee earlier this year, GPIA 
president Lewis Engman 
praised key provisions of 
the Clinton Administra- 
tion’s bill under which 
prescription reimburse- 
ment would be based on 
the “competitively derived 
open market generic price” 
for each multi-source 
drug. This provision, cou- 
pled with the President’s 
commitment to include 
prescription drug coverage 
as a core benefit under his 
program, will help to 
maintain a “vitally compet- 
itive generic drug indus- 
try,” Engman told the sub- 
committee. 

For his part, NAPM Pres- 
ident Robert S. Milanese 
struck a similar chord in a 
recent letter to Congres- 
sional leaders arguing that 
“any national health plan 
should mandate the use of 
generic drugs to ensure 
cost containment.” In out- 
lining a series of basic 
principles of health reform 
supported by generic drug 
manufacturers, the NAPM 
told Congress that “health 
care, including cost-effec- 


tive pharmaceuticals. 
should be made readily 
available to all Americans 
including expanding 
Medicare to encompass 
outpatient prescription 
drugs.” Additionally, Mi- 
lanese maintained that the 
finai health reform legisla- 
tion should include provi- 
sions prohibiting states 
from taxing generic drug 
usage or establishing for- 
mularies that conflict with 
the principles of the na- 
tional health plan. 

At the same time, both 
NAPM and GPIA are prod- 
ding Congress to resist 
pressure from brand-name 
manufacturers to adopt 


provisions that could dis- 
courage the use of lower- 
cost generic pharmaceuti- 
cals. One of these 
proposals would require 
generic drug makers to 
pay rebates to the govern- 
ment in return for cover- 
age of their products un- 
der federal programs such 
as Medicaid and Medicare. 
“Ironically, rebate laws 
have the effect of reducing 
generic competition by in- 
hibiting further price cut- 
ting among existing prod- 
ucts and discouraging new 
manufacturers from enter- 
ing the market,” Engman 
said. NAPM officials agree, 
noting that “since the 


generic industry is in- 
tensely cost-competitive, it 
should not be burdened 
with rebates or user fees 
which would inevitably in- 
crease the cost to the con- 
sumer.” 

Milanese and other 
NAPM representatives are 
also warning against pro- 
posals for adding addition- 
al patent life to brand- 
name pharmaceuticals. 
Rule changes “making it 
more difficult or lengthen- 
ing the period it takes for 
a generic to achieve mar- 
ket entry” will drive up 
health care costs by bil- 
lions of dollars, the NAPM 
warned Congress.

Brief Summary: 

Contraindications: Patients who have had allergic reactions to NAPROSYN.® 
ANAPROX® or ANAPROX® DS or in whom aspirin or other NSAIDs induce the syn- 
drome of asthma, rhinitis, and nasal polyps. Because anaphylactic reactions usu- 
ally occur in patients with a history of such reactions, question patients for 
asthma, nasal polyps, urticaria, and hypotension associated with NSAIDs before 
starting therapy. If such symptoms occur, discontinue the drug. 

Warnings: Serious Gi toxicity such as bleeding, ulceration, and perforation, can 
occur at any time, with or without warning symptoms, in patients treated chroni- 
cally with NSAIDs. Remain alert for ulceration and bleeding even in the absence 
of previous GI tract symptoms. In clinical trials, symptomatic upper Gi ulcers, 
gross bleeding or perforation occur in about 1% of patients treated for 3-6 
months, and in about 2-4% of patients treated for one year. Inform patients of 
signs and/or symptoms of serious Gl toxicity and what steps to take if they occur. 
Studies have not identified any subset of patients not at risk of developing peptic 
ulceration and bleeding. Except for a prior history of serious Gl events and other 
risk factors associated with peptic ulcer disease, such as alcoholism, smoking, 
etc., no risk factors (e.g., age, sex) have been associated with increased risk. 
Elderly or debilitated patients seem to tolerate ulceration or bleeding less well 


and most spontaneous reports of fata! GI events are in this population. In consid- 


ering the use of relatively large doses (within the recommended dosage range), 
operon benefit should be anticipated to offset the potential increased risk of 
toxicity. 
Precautions: DO NOT GIVE NAPROSYN® (NAPROXEN) CONCOMITANTLY WITH 
ANAPROX® OR ANAPROX® DS (NAPROXEN SODIUM) SINCE THEY CIRCULATE IN 
PLASMA AS THE NAPROXEN ANION. Acute interstitial nephritis with hematuria, 
proteinuria, and nephrotic syndrome has been reported. Patients with impaired 
renal function, heart failure, liver dysfunction, patients taking diuretics, and the 


elderly are at greater risk of overt renal decompensation. If this occurs, discon- 


tinue the drug. Use with caution and monitor serum creatinine and/or creatinine 
clearance in patients with significantly impaired renal function. Use caution in 


patients with baseline creatinine clearance less than 20 mi/minute. Use the low- 


est effective dose in the elderly or in patients with chronic alcoholic liver disease 
or cirrhosis. Borderline elevations of liver tests may occur in up to 15% of 
patients. Elevations of SGPT or SGOT occurred in controlled trials in less than 1% 
of patients. Severe hepatic reactions, including jaundice and fata! hepatitis, have 
been reported rarely. If liver disease develops or if systemic manifestations occur 
(e.g., eosinophilia or rash), discontinue therapy. If steroid dosage is reduced or 
eliminated during therapy, do so slowly and observe patients closely for adverse 
effects, including adrenal insufficiency and exacerbation of arthritis symptoms. 
Determine hemoglobin values periodically for patients with initia! values of 10 
grams or less who receive long-term therapy. Peripheral edema has been 


reported. For patients with restricted sodium intake, note that each tablet con- 


tains approximately 25 or 50 mg(1 or 2 mEq) sodium. Use with caution in patients 
with fluid retention, hypertension or heart failure. The drug may reduce fever and 
inflammation, diminishing their diagnostic value. Conduct ophthalmic studies if 
any change or disturbance in vision occurs. Information for Patients: Side 
effects can cause discomfort and, rarely, more serious side effects, such as GI 
bleeding, may result in hospitalization and even fatal outcomes. Physicians may 
wish to discuss with patients potential risks and benefits of NSAIDs, particularly 
when they are used for less serious conditions where treatment without NSAIDs 
may be acceptable. Patients should use caution for activities requiring alertness 
if they experience drowsiness, dizziness, vertigo or depression during therapy. 
Laboratory Tests: Because serious Gi tract ulceration and bleeding can occur 
without warning symptoms, follow chronically treated patients and inform them 
of the importance of the follow-up. Drug Interactions: Use caution when giving 
concomitantly with coumarin-type anticoagulants; a hydantoin, sulfonamide or 
sulfonylurea; furosemide; lithium; beta-blockers; probenecid; or methotrexate. 
Drug/Laboratory Test Interactions: May decrease platelet aggregation and 


prolong bleeding time or increase urinary values for 17-ketogenic steroids. Tempo- 


rarily stop therapy for 72 hours before adrenal function tests. May interfere with 


urinary assays of SHIAA. Carcinogenesis: A 2-year rat study showed no evi- 


dence of carcinogenicity. Pregnancy: Category B. Do not use during pregnancy 
unless clearly needed. Avoid use during late pregnancy. Nursing Mothers: Avoid 
use. Pediatric Use: Single doses of 2.5-5 mg/kg (as naproxen suspension), with 
9 daily dose not exceeding 15 mg/kg/day, are safe in children over 2 years 
of age. 

Adverse Reactions: In a study, Gl reactions were more frequent and severe in 
rheumatoid arthritis patients on 1650 mg/day naproxen sodium than in those on 
825 mg/day. In children with juvenile arthritis, rash and prolonged bleeding 


times were more frequent, GI and CNS reactions about the same, and Uiher reac-

ES GENERICS STUDY 


Alliances prompt FIC scrut 


he rash of recent ac- 

quisitions of generic 

drug manufacturers 
by competing brand name 
pharmaceutical companies 
is beginning to raise eye- 
brows among antitrust en- 
forcers at the Federal 
Trade Commission. 

In testimony before Sen. 
David Pryor’s (D-Ark.) 
Special Committee on Ag- 
ing late last year, FTC 
Competition Bureau 
deputy director Mark 
Whitener warned that cor- 
porate takeovers of gener- 
ic houses by brand name 
manufacturers may well 
create anti-competitive 
problems. 

More recently, during 
last month’s Washington 
meeting of the National 
Association of Pharmaceu- 
tical Manufacturers, 
Whitener confirmed that 
the FTC’s concerns on this 
front have intensified, and 
that during the last six 
months the agency “has 
opened over a dozen new 
investigations” into sus- 
pected anti-competitive 
practices in the pharma- 
ceutical marketplace. 


MMD challenged 


The first federal enforce- 
ment action to result from 
those investigations was 
announced late last month 
as FTC antitrusters for- 
mally challenged Marion 
Merrell Dow’s October 
1993 acquisition of the 
Rugby-Darby Group. 

Because MMD and Rug- 
by are the only two FDA- 
approved producers of di- 
cyclomine in the U.S., the 
FTC concluded that the ac- 
quisition not only eliminat- 
ed direct competition be- 
tween the two companies, 


iny 


During last month’s meeting of the 


NAPM, (FTC deputy director Mark! 
Whitener confirmed that the FTC’s con- 
cerns on this front have intensified. 


but also “created a monop- 
oly in the manufacture 
and sale” of these drugs. 

That complaint was set- 
tled quickly under a con- 
sent agreement requiring 
MMD to license a its dicy- 
clomine formulations and 
production technology to 
a third-party acceptable to 
the Commission. Until the 
new licensee obtains FDA 
approval to manufacture 
the product, MMD will be 
required to supply that 
firm with dicyclomine at 
no more than 48 percent 
of the Average Wholesale 
Price charged by Rugby 
for the drug on July 3, 
1993. 

The MMD-Rugby order 
and the complaint that 
sparked it could set a pat- 
tern for additional federal 
antitrust challenges of 
pharmaceutical industry 
mergers. Without specifi- 
cally mentioning Ciba 
Geigy’s takeover of Gene- 
va, AHP’s purchase of 
Elkins Sinn or other high- 
profile acquisitions of 
generic pharmaceutical 
firms by brand-name 
competitors, Whitener told 
the NAPM that these de- 
velopments are attracting 
“considerable attention” 
among federal = an- 
titrusters. 

Significantly, however, 
he stressed that the com- 
mission’s concern is not 


limited to cases such as 
the MMD-Rugby acquisi- 
tion involving direct com- 
petitors. “Even if a brand- 
name firm acquires a 
generic company that is 
not a direct competitor for 
a particular drug, the ac- 
quisition may raise an- 
titrust concerns if... the 
generic manufacturer ap- 
pears to be well-positioned 
to enter the market in 
competition with a drug 
produced by the brand- 
name manufacturer,” 
Whitener said. 


Genericizing themselves 


Additionally, the FTC is 
examining the anticompet- 
itive potential of marketing 
alliances between brand- 
name and generic com- 
petitors, as well as recent 
efforts by some pioneer 
manufacturers to “generi- 
cize” their own drugs prior 
to patent expirations. 

“In some cases, the pro- 
duction of new generic 
products prior to patent 
expiration may well be 
pro-competitive,” Whitener 
told the NAPM meeting. 

But before giving these 
practices a clean bill of an- 
titrust health, he said the 
FTC would have to “care- 
fully analyze any evidence 
of exclusionary or predato- 
ry conduct that may im- 
pede entry by generic 
firms.”

ES GENERICS STUDY 


Generics gain share of cimetidine sales 


he jury is still out as 

hard sales figures 

are unavailable, but 

it appears generic cimeti- 

dine sales are rapidly 

gaining market share from 

SmithKline Beecham's 
Tagamet®. 

The popular Ho» blocker 
lost its patent protection 
on May 17, 1994, and re- 
tailers pounced on the op- 
portunity to gain higher 
margin sales on the less 
expensive generic alterna- 
tives. Promotions encour- 
aging Tagamet users to in- 
quire about’ generic 
cimetidine were common 
in the marketplace just 
days after the patent ex- 
piry. And according to sev- 


eral major pharmacy 
chains, early sales are en- 
couraging. 


“The stores are reorder- 
ing generic cimetidine, so 
that is an indication it is 
selling well,” a spokesman 
for one chain said. A 
generic supplier who de- 
clined to be identified also 
confirmed cimetidine is 
selling well and said, “we 
are very pleased with the 
product.” 

Currently, three generic 
houses manufacture cime- 
tidine: Novopharm, Endo 
Labs and Mylan. They 
gained approval on May 
17, according to an FDA 
spokesman. A fourth com- 
pany, Lemmon, will re- 
portedly get its Abbreviat- 
ed New Drug Application 
approved by the FDA this 
fall. Cimetidine is also dis- 
tributed by a number of 
other sources such as 
Rugby, Goldline, Geneva 
and Schein. 

SmithKline Beecham has 
also gotten involved in the 
generic side of the busi- 


The next evolution of Tagamet may be 
its conversion to OTC status. 


ness through supply 
arrangements for generic 
cimetidine with various 
managed care organiza- 
tions and with Lederle for 
retail distribution, accord- 
ing to company spokes- 
man Rick Koenig. 


Mitigating losses 


To mitigate anticipated 
market share losses upon 
patent expiration, 
SmithKline Beecham es- 
calated its rebate program 
on the product. Rebates of 
$20 kicked in on May 17. 
Prior to then, a $10 rebate 
had been offered since No- 
vember 1993. The $20 of- 
fer is effective through 
year-end and makes Taga- 
met less expensive than 
its chief H9 rivals: Lilly’s 
Axid®, Merck’s Pepcid® 
and Glaxo’s Zantac®, on a 
dose-per-dose basis. Pep- 
cid and Axid have patent 
protection until the year 
2000; Zantac until 2002. 

Even with the rebates, 
Tagamet is considerably 
more expensive than it 
was in 1986 when the 
AWP on a 100-count pre- 
scripticn was about $80, 
according to Medi-Span’s 
new PRICE-CHEK PC ser- 
vice. As of April 1, 1994, 
AWP on the same quantity 
was almost $150, accord- 
ing to Medi-Span. 

Competition for Taga- 
met’s slice of the Ho pie will 
likely intensify as generic 
firms scramble for their 
share of the product’s 1993 


U.S. sales of nearly $650 
million and 8.2 million pre- 
scriptions. Competition for 
market share among the 
generic houses is expected 
to drive the cost down, ac- 
cording to one supplier. 
The product’s pricing 
could eventually parallel 
Syntex’s Naprosyn®. That 
product lost market share 
when its patent expired 
Dec. 21, 1993 and generic 
manufacturers severely 
undercut the price. Today, 
naproxen sells at a 90 per- 
cent discount to branded 
Naprosyn, a Syntex 
spokesman confirmed. 
Generic cimetidine is cur- 
rently priced at about a 15 
percent discount to Taga- 
met, but could head lower, 
according to one generic 
manufacturer. 


Is OTC next? 


The next evolution of 
Tagamet may be its con- 
version to OTC status, 
which would help Smith- 
Kline Beecham shore up 
lost prescription sales. 
Both Tagamet and Pepcid 
are on the agenda for an 
upcoming joint meeting of 
the FDA’s Nonprescription 
Drugs Advisory Committee 
and Gastrointestinal 
Drugs Advisory Committee 
on July 29, according to a 
source familiar with the 
proceedings. A New Drug 
Application for OTC cime- 
tidine submitted in De- 
cember 1991 suffered a 
setback last fall when the 


16-member OTC advisory 
committee unanimously 
voted against Tagamet’s 
efficacy for the treatment 
of heartburn. 

There is speculation that 
by changing the product’s 
indication to “prevention 
of heartburn,” Tagamet 
could improve its chances 
of gaining approval, since 
there hasn’t been enough 
time since the last meeting 
to perform the clinical ftri- 
als necessary to substanti- 
ate the relief of heartburn 
claim. 

Pepcid has not previous- 
ly been discussed by the 
OTC committee, although 
the drug is frequently 
mentioned as a viable OTC 
candidate.

‘Survey shows sharp rise in dispensing of generic drugs 


generic dispensing is a re- 
flection of the fact that a 
rising proportion of scripts 
are being written generi- 
cally. Four years ago the 
pharmacists responding to 
our survey reported that, 
on average, 19 percent of 
the scripts they received 
were written generically— 
up from 18 percent in 
1989. In the June 1994 
study, this had jumped to 
25 percent. Perhaps more 
significantly, this year’s 
survey found a sharp de- 
cline in the percentage of 
“dispense as written” pre- 
scriptions. In 1990 phar- 
macists reported that pre- 
scribers prohibited generic 
substitution on 22 percent 
of the prescriptions for 
multi-source drugs that 
they received. In this 
year’s survey, the propor- 
tion of DAW prescriptions 
had dropped to 9 percent. 


‘Substitutable’ scripts up 


At the same time, the 
nation’s community phar- 
macists are receiving more 
prescriptions for which 
they may exercise their 
product selection authori- 
ty. Four years ago, less 
than one-third of the 
scripts dispensed by our 
respondents (29 percent) 
were written by brand 
name but allowed to be 
filled by a generic. In this 
year’s survey, the propor- 
tion of “substitutable” pre- 
scriptions jumped to 42

Store-level automatic replenishment

year.

when Walgreens finish-

the end of this decade, 
the chain hopes to have reduced its

Arbor revs up in Motor City 


TROY, Mich. — Showing an increasing interest in 
the potential of urban marketing, Arbor Drugs opened 
its seventh store in Detroit Aug. 1. The move is the 
latest in a growing battle for control of Detroit’s urban 
neighborhoods between Arbor and rival Perry Drug 
Stores, which already has a commanding 15 stores in 
the city, with three more under construction. 

Arbor will also open two new stores in the greater 
Detroit region over the next month, including its third 
store in Mt. Clemens and its first in Brownstown 
Township. 


Publix denies N.C. rumors 


LAKELAND, Fla. — A spokesman for Publix Super 
Markets has denied reports that the combo operator is 
looking for store sites in Charlotte, N.C., damping 
speculation that Publix was planning a rapid move 
northward after establishing a strong base in Atlanta. 

The company source was responding to a recent re- 
port in a Tampa, Fla., business newspaper. According 
to that report, real estate brokers said they were in- 
formed by Publix that the chain is putting on hold its 
North Carolina expansion. The brokers, who were 
unidentified in the article, said they had been working 
on locating sites for more than a year. 

Publix, which has grown rapidly in Georgia with 15 
stores now open in Atlanta, is the dominant grocery 
store chain in most Florida markets. The chain has 
about 450 stores, including more than 100 with phar- 
macies, but didn’t open units outside of Florida until 
1992. A 3 million-square-foot warehouse is under con- 
struction near Atlanta.

Eckerd’s star rising on Wall Street 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — Robinson-Humphrey Co. 
investment analyst David Magee recently initiated 
coverage of Eckerd nae. with a strong “buy” recom- 
mendation on the drug chain’s stock. 

Magee said the 1,700-store chain has significant up- 
side potential as it benefits from technology invest- 
ments, potential expansion into new markets and its 
strong name recognition. Investment negatives cited 
by Magee tachi 3 Eckerd’s high level of variable in- 
terest rate debt and its lack of involvement in the 
growing prescription mail-order business. 

Other investment houses that have issued “buy” 
ratings on Eckerd include Bear Stearns, Morgan 
Stanley, and Raymond James & Associates.

Drug store products have star power, too 


Infomercials—those now ubiquitous 
program-length TV commercials—have 
proven that products have star power. 
Through demonstration, association 
with “stars,” and other techniques, in- 
fomercials breathed life into long-faded 
product categories and launched brand 
new ones. Better yet, as retailers quick- 
ly discovered, the majority of sales of 
products featured on TV actually occur 
in stores. 

This fall, you—and millions of other 
people across the nation—will be able 
to see a program/commercial hybrid 


mornings. Hosted by actress/model 
Nancy Stafford, formerly of “Matlock” 
and “St. Elsewhere”, Main Floor is 
billed as a “fashion, beauty, and good 
advice” program. 

People at Alton Entertainment evoke 
“Entertainment Tonight” to describe 
the pace and feeling of Main Floor. The 
pilot mixed personality interviews, 
how-to’s, fashion trend pieces and in- 
terviews with consumer magazine edi- 
tors. 

Michael Young, president of Alton, 
emphasizes that Main Floor is a broad- 
cast television pro- 


ei Main Floor, a new TV 
show, will feature products 
that have mass appeal and 
drug store distribution. 


gram, just like the 
nationally syndi- 
cated Oprah Win- 
frey show. But it 
is unique, he says, 
because of the 
“marketing oppor- 
tunities” offered to 
“a select group of 
companies and 
products.” 


WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


that is designed to marry television and 
shopping in a new way. And the good 
news is that the only way viewers will 
be able to buy the products featured on 
this show will be at retail. 

Called “Main Floor” and produced by 
a Miami Beach, Fla., company called 
Alton Entertainment, the program is 
scheduled to appear on ABC, NBC, 
CBS and Fox affiliates and indepen- 
dent stations in more than 100 mar- 
kets starting on Sept. 4. In most mar- 
kets, it will appear weekly on Sunday 


What makes 
Main Floor differ- 
ent are the three- 
minute manufac- 
turer-sponsored “advertorials,” not 
quite commercials but not quite tradi- 
tional stories either. 

According to Young, the advertorials 
are collaborative efforts. “Alton Enter- 
tainment is responsible for content and 
production of the programs,” he says, 
but “no one knows” the manufacturer’s 
message better than the people at the 
company. 

In the pilot I saw, Paloma Picasso’s 
men’s fragrance was featured via an in- 
terview with Picasso and her husband, 


said to be the man behind the artist and 
her new fragrance. For Lancome, a 
Bloomingdale’s store was the setting for 
the makeover of a fashion model by a 
Lancome cosmetician; the theme was us- 
ing makeup to achieve a “natural” look. 

Main Floor viewers will find out 
which segments are sponsored only at 
the end of the 30-minute program, 
when a list of manufacturers scrolls 
across the screen. 

To buy products featured on the pro- 
gram, viewers have to call a toll-free 
number and ask for a newsletter, which 
will give “more information” on prod- 
ucts and services, including contacts at 
the sponsoring manufacturers. 

Retailers can get involved by buying 
advertising from the local stations that 
air the program. Carson Pirie Scott, the 
Chicago department store, is said to be 
one such sponsor. 

But because it will appear on broad- 
cast TV, Main Floor won't be geared ex- 
clusively to the department store shop- 
per. According to Alton executives, 
many of the featured products will 
have mass appeal and drug store distri- 
bution. In fact, sources assure me that 
some manufacturers who supply drug 
stores are already involved. 

Will Main Floor really drive retail 
sales, which is one of its key objec- 
tives? If so, to what extent? I think it’s 
too early to tell. But, I think there’s a 
message in the fact that people outside 
the retail business recognize that the 
products drug stores carry really do 
have star power. Imagine how exciting 
early apothecaries must have seemed 
to their customers. That’s entertain- 
ment, and I think drug stores need to 
get that excitement back. 


Eliminating the pharmaceutical in- 
dustry’s discriminatory pricing prac- 
tices should do more than level the 
playing field for drug chains and inde- 
pendent pharmacies. It also should 
help to bring down the overall cost of 
prescriptions to consumers. 

That's the theory behind the Federal 
Robinson-Patman anti-price discrimi- 
nation law and of Maine’s new “Im- 
proved Access to Pharmaceuticals Act.”

that a proposal similar to the Maine law 
is being proposed for the national health 
care reform legislation, which may serve 
to extend the type of action taking place 
in Maine to a national level,” he warned. 

Like the rest of us, pharmaceutical 
manufacturers have a right to express 
their opinions on any subject. They also 
have a right to raise prices in response 
to legislation. 

But no industry has a right to agree 
collectively to raise prices for any rea- 
son. Some Maine pharmacists who sup- 
ported the state’s anti-price discrimina- 
tion law sus that it’s no coincidence 
that over a dozen leading manufacturers 
responded by eliminating discounts. 

e state attorney general has been

asked to a an alleged price fix- 
ing conspiracy. There’s talk of a civil an- 
titrust suit by pharmacists and con- 
sumers in Maine. And superlawyer Joe 
Alioto is developing a sudden craving 
for lobster. 

The Maine price discrimination battle 
may be just beginning.

Category management still in experimental stages 


by James Frederick 


C onversion to category manage- 
ment remains a high priority 
for the nation’s drug chains, 
according to a major survey of top 
chain drug executives by Marketing 
Corp. of America. 

MCA surveyed more than 260 re- 
tailers and manufacturers in 1993 
to gauge current business prac- 
tices, priorities and vendor-retailer 
relationships. More than half the 
chain drug executives included in 
the survey said their companies 
had already shifted to a category 
management approach in their 
buying, merchandising and mar- 
keting practices, but they differ on 
ways to measure their performance 
by category. 

Among the benchmarks drug 
chains currently employ to track 
category performance: sales, gross 
margin return on investment (GM- 
ROD), return on inventory invest- 
ment (ROI) and share of total mar- 
ket sales. 

What’s more, the chain drug re- 
tailers polled by MCA clearly un- 
derstood that they have a long way 
to go to fully understand and ex- 
ploit the dynamics of each catego- 
ry. The chain drug industry wants 
more help than it is currently get- 
ting from its suppliers to fully im- 
plement category management; as 
it now stands, MCA reports, manu- 
facturers only get a “B-” from chain 
drug retailers when it comes to un- 
derstanding their business and 
providing the kinds of consumer in- 
formation and category expertise 
drug chains need to shift their own 
paradigm. 


Understanding consumers 


The 25 chain drug execs polled by 
MCA displayed a clear sense of 
what they need to better manage 
categories from purchase to promo- 
tion to sell-through. Two-thirds of 
them said understanding category 
and consumer dynamics was crucial 
to successful category management. 
Also high on the list of needs was 
better information with which to 
manage shelf space, benchmark 
profitability standards and analyze 
on- and off-promotion pricing 
strategies. 

The study showed clearly that 
drug chains are also serious about 
cutting costs wherever possible. 
Chain drug retailers think their 
biggest chunk of cost savings will 
come from demand-based reorder- 
ing and more efficient distribution, 
which is a big element of the much- 
vaunted strategy of ECR, or effi- 
cient consumer response. 

According to the MCA report, ef- 
forts among all trade channels to 
cut excess inventories have already 
cut backup inventories in the distri- 
bution pipeline dramatically, from 
six to four weeks. 

Chain drug retailers polled by 
MCA also have high hopes for the 
cost-saving potential of better 
shrink-control methods, EDI, the 
elimination of unprofitable stores, 
and efforts by manufacturers to cut 
down on the number of SKUs clog- 
ging store shelves.

Among the survey’s other find- 
ings: 

e SKU rationalization is gaining 
ground among manufacturers, as 
well. Among those polled by MCA, 
38 percent reported they had al- 
ready cut the number of SKUs they 
bring to market, by an average of 14 
percent. Another 24 percent said 
they were pianning on cutbacks. 
The trend marks a 180-degree turn 
from the strategy of most packaged 
goods makers in the ’80s, when line 
extensions and me-too products ex- 
ploded in an all-out battle among 
suppliers for shelf space. 

@ EDLP has made significant in- 
roads in retailer acceptance and 
use, but most drug chains have 
broadened and softened the original 
formula and are calling it “value 
pricing.” Traditional high-low pric- 
ing is still the norm for 79 percent 
of drug chains surveyed, but three 
of four respondents said they were 
moving toward a “modified” EDLP, 
and another 9 percent had plans to 
convert to “pure” EDLP. 

The implication: price promotions 
will continue to diminish in impor- 
tance as chains de-emphasize for- 
ward buying and cyclical deals in 
favor of tighter inventories and 
faster turns.

Ethnic skin, hair care growth 
fueled by new products 


ales of toiletry products for-

African-American consumers 
remain soft in retail stores.

strong growth segments, particular-

ments of hair care. 

According to Towne-Oller, which 
tracks ethnic product sales through 
mass market stores and through 
ethnic product distributors, dollar 
sales of ethnic products for the 
twelve months ended May 1994 
were only up 2 percent while unit 
sales were up just 1 percent. 

While about 70 percent of the 
chain drug store ethnic product 
buyers interviewed by Drug Store

were still seeing some growth in the 
category, it was primarily because 
of new store openings or expanded 
distribution of the category into ad- 
ditional stores.

growth or new products 
to initiate demand.

Managed care: 


Dealing into a high stakes game 


The traditional issues of cost, quality and access meet the latest 


players, alliances and outcomes. The ante: covered “lives.” At 
stake: community pharmacy’ ability to serve these “lives.” 


Special report: 


13 


Critical issues for the geriatric patient 


Rising prescription prices and lack of prescription coverage may put 
drugs, the most effective tools of health care, out of reach of your most 
important customer; an arthritis epidemic is predicted; there are new 
guidelines for prostate problems; and service is a critical 


element for HHC success. 


center 


Continuing education for two credits: 
Suicide: Your elderly patients may be at risk 


One person commits suicide in the U.S. every 20 minutes. The elderly 
are particularly vulnerable, with a 50 percent higher suicide rate than 
younger people. Pharmacists are in a unique position to help 


identify those at increased risk, given their accessibility, high 


trust scores and drug profiles.

COVER STORY 


Managed care pharmacy: 
Dealing into a high stakes game 


by Allene Symons 


e managed care 
game is shifting fast 
as the high stakes ac- 


tion has players scrambling 
to partner for their share of 
the pot. Today, cost, quality 
and access are three cards 
in the winning hand. And 
July’s big news of the PCS 
sale by wholesaler Mc- 
Kesson to drug maker Eli 
Lilly may make alliances 
the ace in the hole for man- 
aged care. Indeed, both 
large and small companies 
who serve the growing 
managed health care mar- 
ket are merging or partner- 
ing for greater clout. 
Alliances—some unlike- 
ly, many anticipated—are 
accelerating change, too, 
as super pharmacy benefit 
management firms (PBMs) 
are forged with the 
strongest materials in the 
industry—PCS by Lilly, 
Medco by Merck, DPS by 
SmithKline Beecham, and 
others like Pfizer’s joint 
venture with Value Health 
Managed Care (See chart). 
This trend is sure to im- 
pact community pharma- 
cy’s access to third-party 
contracts. It will influence 
distribution through mail 
order, retail, hospital and 
HMO channels. It will 
even impact the nature 
and credibility of outcomes 
studies, which are vital for 
securing retail pharmacy’s 
place as a cognitive ser- 
vices player in the man- 
aged health care game. 


Hot words 


Rules are changing so 
fast that even the lan- 


guage of pharmacy man- 
aged care is a moving tar- 
get. Today’s wordsmiths 
are buzzing around “out- 
comes” (some have called 
it “outcomes mania”), “in- 
tegrated health care sys- 
tems” and “infomatics,” 
meaning the futuristic 
electronics to deliver such 
integration. 

In recent months, the 
rash of acquisitions, merg- 
ers and alliances has shift- 
ed power in the pharmacy 


Leading PBMs

subsidiary of PMSI. 


managed care arena. The 
result is new and expanded 
pharmacy provider net- 
works on the one hand and 
even more powerful PBMs 
on the other. Four of the 
top 10 PBMs are now 
owned (or acquisition is 
pending) by pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturers. 

On the network side, 
providers are banding to- 
gether for clout. The trend 
is to be your own drug bro- 
ker by owning or forming a 
PBM. 

The largest new con- 
tender is the combination 
PBM/provider network 


Pharmacy Direct Network 
(PDN), an entity spear- 
headed by, but separate 
from, the National Associ- 
ation of Chain Drug Stores 
(NACDS) and open to both 
chain and independent 
community pharmacies. 


What is a PBM? 


The merging and meld- 
ing gets confusing. “No 
one knows what a PBM 
is—everybody is using 
that terminology. What is 


a PBM? A TPA (third-party 
administrator)? A mail-or- 
der pharmacy? Who is do- 
ing managed care, or is 
everyone?” asks Del Kon- 
nor, executive vice presi- 
dent of the Alexandria, 
Va.-based American Man- 
aged Care Pharmacy Asso- 
ciation (AMCPA). 

In today’s functional defi- 
nition, PBMs provide ser- 
vices including drug benefit 
design, claims processing, 
drug utilization review and 
formulary management, 
and distribution through 
retail networks and mail or- 
der. These services are con- 


oe 


tracted by third-party pay- 
ors such as insurance com- 
panies, government agen- 
cies, large employers or 
other third-party adminis- 
trators. 

It is estimated that 
plans managed by PBMs 
cover around one-third of 
the U.S. population—re- 
ferred to as “lives” in PBM- 
speak. PCS alone claims to 
manage plans covering 50 
million lives. 

But the way lives are 


tallied is tricky because 
the definition of PBM is 
fluid. Some PBMs provide 
the full range of services 
while others provide niche 
services like claims pro- 
cessing and subcontract to 
other PBMs, so lives can 
get counted more than 
once. Also, a PBM can 
evolve from a claims 
processor to a full PBM, as 
did PCS. 

“It’s one of the big ques- 
tions because if you add 
up lives, it totals half of 
the population of the U.S., 
which is too high. The

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, August 15, 1994 


13 


eS 


COVER STORY 


eee 


Managed care: A high stakes game 


Continued from page 13 
pharmacy industry is try- 
ing to grapple with [just] 
how many lives are cov- 
ered,” says Bob Shew- 
brooks, manager of health 
care services for Scott- 
Levin & Associates, a 
health care information 
firm. 


Getting a deal 


Regardless of how many 
lives are covered today, 
new pharmacy provider 
networks are emerging — 
and merging—around the 
country in an attempt to 
get more lives. Besides 
banding together to form 
larger combines with more 
doors and volume advan- 
tages, another selling 
point these networks take 
to the third-party bargain- 
ing table is quality. 

Quality—as in quality 
pharmaceutical care—is a 
marketable feature, per- 
ception mixed with reality. 
It's where you go after 
cost, and it is difficult to 
quantify. 

Daniel Jadosh, manager 
of third-party marketing 
for Kmart, notes that 
“price has become so com- 
petitive in the third-party 
contracting arena that 
we've reached the bottom 
as to what any pharmacy 
can do and stay in busi- 
ness.” He adds that price 
cannot vary much from 
one chain to another be- 
cause of the competitive 
nature of the business, so 
“service and location has 
become much more of a 
focal point than it ever 
was before.” 

Chains use the quality 
argument at the bargain- 
ing table, too. Kmart, for 
example, underlines its 
quality care claim by 


pointing out that its phar- 
macists are kept current 
via the Kmart satellite in- 
formation system, which 
covers CE and provides 
other information specifi- 
cally regarding third-party 
program changes. 

Quality is a defense 
against various oppo- 
nents—independents 
against chains and vice 
versa—and it is the argu- 


partner in prescription 
distribution. It appears 
that some combination of

Outcomes rush 


Outcomes support this

drug history in relation to 
diagnosis and treaiment, 
have become a buzzword

need. We all agree it’s

the one thing we all agree 
on.”

knowledges “the frustra-

without outcomes stud- 
ies—the problem we face 
with pharmacy is how to 
figure out if a drug does 
what it is supposed to do.”

the amount spent on ac-

that do to their research

Tomorrow's breakthroughs 


Will the elderly be able to afford new therapeutics? 


by Ken Rankin 


ver the past 20 years, 

pharmaceutical research- 

ers have developed scores 

of important new medi- 
cines to treat diabetes, Alzheimer’s 
Disease, incontinence and other 
conditions that afflict the elderly. 
Today the new drug pipeline is brim- 
ming with even more exciting phar- 
maceutical breakthroughs that 
promise to add years to our lives, 
and life to the years of millions of 
older Americans. 

But will senior citizens be able to 
afford the important new pharma- 
ceuticals that will be coming on the 
market over the next five to ten 
years? Maybe not. Although in- 
creased use of lower-priced generic 
versions have helped to hold down 
the cost of older prescription drugs, 
the price of new breakthrough 
pharmaceuticals is rising steeply. 
And with the cost of pharmaceuti- 
cal research and development 
climbing at a double-digit clip, it’s 
likely that the next generation of 
new geriatric medicines will be even 
less affordable. Indeed, advocates 
for the elderly warn that many old-

er Americans are already being 
priced out of the market for neces- 
sary, even potentially life-saving 
prescription drugs. 


Older Americans are vulnerable 


The elderly are particularly vulner- 
able to rising prescription drug costs 
because their need for pharmaceuti- 
cal care increases at the same time 
that their incomes tend to decline. 

About 85 percent of the approxi- 
mately 30 million Americans age 65 
or older will use at least one pre- 
scription drug during the year, and 
many regard spending for pharma- 
ceuticals as their number one 
health-related expense. According to 
the Health Care Financing Adminis- 
tration’s National Health Accounts, 
senior citizens account for between 
one-third and 40 percent of the total 
U.S. spending for prescription drugs. 
Of the $36 billion spent on drugs 
during 1991, for example, the elderly 
accounted for between $12.7 billion 
and $14.3 billion. On a per capita 
basis, that calculates out to between 
$425 and $475 annually, and among 
Medicare recipients average Rx costs 
are even higher. 

If anything, these averages may 
understate the financial impact of 
prescription drug costs for millions 
of older Americans. One recent 
study found that more than one-in- 
ten seniors (11 percent) incur pre- 
scription drug costs in excess of 
$1,200 a year. In 1991, prescription 
drug spending for these 3 million- 
plus eiderly Americans averaged 
$150 per month. 


Seniors lack Rx coverage 


Underscoring this dilemma is the 
fact that a large proportion of the 
nation’s senior citizens lack any in- 
surance coverage for outpatient pre- 
scription drugs. “Nearly half of older 
Americans had no prescription drug

is contributing to the overall rise in 
health care expenditures. Noting 
that most older Americans have ei- 
ther no drug coverage or inadequate 
benefits, AARP board member Esther 
“Tess” Canja said that “the elderly 
who cannot afford to pay for their 
medicines out of their own pockets 
frequently receive unnecessary and 
more expensive care.”

Rx options for the 
elderly 


The AARP/RAND report pre- 
sents four separate options for 
enhancing Rx insurance cover- 
age for 30 million U.S. seniors. 

1. Require Prescription 
Drug Coverage for “Qualified 
Medicare Beneficiaries.” But 
$600 million in drug benefits for 
1.3 million of the neediest elder- 
ly Americans “would not con- 
tribute to prescription drug cost 
containment in any fashion.” 

2. Encourage State Pharma- 
ceutical Assistance Programs. 
Nine states offer such programs 
but"...program coverage would 
substitute for private coverage, 
but with no increment to the 
total number of elderly covered 
for Rx drug costs.” 

3. Require All Medigap Poli- 
cies to Cover Prescription 
Drugs. This would provide no 
assistance to the one-in-nine 
elderly Americans with no sup- 
plementary insurance and 
could drive the cost of Medigap 
premiums beyond the reach of 
many low-income seniors. 

4. Extend Medicare Bene- 
fits to Include Prescription 
Drugs. This would provide cov- 
erage for the 13.8 million se- 
niors currently uninsured for 
Rx drug costs. Objections to 
this option are likely to be 
raised by those philosophically 
opposed to substituting “public 
financing, and hence, control 
over decisions for private.”

he indicators that make home 
“| Preattn care (HHC) a golden 

opportunity for pharmacy are

leased from hospitals sooner and 
sicker. 

The average length of stay at 
short-term acute care community 
hospitals declined to 7.1 days in 
1992 from 7.6 days roughly a 
decade earlier, according to the 
American Hospital Association. The 
U.S. Department of Health and Hu-

even lower. 

The decline has been fueled in 
part by a change in Medicare reim- 
bursement rules that means hospi- 
tals get paid a flat rate for certain

the patient stays. “That caused hos- 
pitals and physicians to pay much 
more attention to length of stays,” 
according to an AHA spokesman. 


Trends in aging 


As people spend less time in hos- 
pitals they are also living longer. The 
projected average life expectancy in 
the year 2000 for men is 73.2 years 
and 80.2 years for women. Com- 


pared to 1970, that’s an increase of 


6.7 years for men and 5.6 years for 
women. 

If those trends weren't enough to 
make retailers seriously eye home 
health care, there is the frequently 
cited aging segment of the popula- 
tion known as baby boomers. In 
1990, 27 percent of the population 
was over the age of 50. 

Faced with these trends, pharma- 
cies have a golden opportunity. The 
question for many then, whether a 
chain or independent, is how to best 
take advantage of these trends, not 
only to perform a valuable service 


but to operate a profitable F

Independents and chains 
get involved 


Regardless of reimbursement po- 
tential, home health care is often 
seen as one of the most valuable 
niches for an independent pharmacy 
to pursue. “This is really an emerg- 
ing business and as independents 
seek ways to differentiate them- 
selves in the marketplace this is a 
way for them to do that,” said Jim 
Grigg, FoxMeyer’s director of Rx 
purchasing. “If they are looking at a 
way to combat mass merchandisers 
and other retailers, this is a way to 
get closer to the end consumer and 
it gives them an opportunity to show 
their expertise as pharmacists.” In- 
deed, many independents have gone 
this route because the strategy has 
proven successful. 

“The real differentiation is you will

store’s back room and put in a com- 
plete home health care department 
staffed by a registered nurse with an 
extensive product offering. The store 
serves as a hub for 14 other nearby 
Eckerd stores. Perhaps as a testa- 
ment to its success, a second hub 
store is slated to open in mid-Au- 
gust in nearby Clearwater. 


Product vs. services 


When it comes to home health 
care, the biggest difference lies in 


whether merely product needs are 
going to be met or whether addition- 
al services are to be provided. “Satis- 
fying product needs is something 
they can do as part of their normal 
business, but if they want to go be- 
yond that with additional services, it 
requires more professional people 
the farther up the ladder you go,” 
Grigg said. Whichever route a drug 
store takes, “there are a lot of re- 
sources available for pharmacists if 
they want to get more involved, and 
a good place to start is with their 
wholesalers,” Grigg said. 

“What always scares people about 
getting more involved with home 
health care is the inventory com- 
mitment and the personnel com- 
mitment,” said Paul Higgs, vice 
president of sales and marketing 
with Carex, recently acquired by 
Rubbermaid. “To really get serious 
about it you need to work with 
trained technicians and expand the 
store’s presence. Many stores are 
content with the profits and turns 
as they exist, and others are going 
to pursue it as a niche and get 
more out of it. You are only going 
to be able to get out of it what you 
put into it,” Higgs said.

range of motion to lift small items. (604)538-1401. 

Bath Board by Frohock-Stewart. Marketed as the first portable 
bath board, it fits in a suitcase and extends and locks into position to 
fit any standard size bathtub and is capable of supporting 300 


Multi-purpose Tennis Elbow Support by Accu-Back. A new spin 
on a familiar device, the Accu-Back, machine-washable model con- 
tains a re-usable hot/cold gel pack to further help reduce pain. 


Wrist Blood Pressure Meter from Omron. An ideal and compact 
meter for virtually everyone. Finger meters can be hampered by poor 
circulation while arm meters may not have large enough cuffs. Inflates 
in seconds and gives reading quickly. (708)680-6200.

and available through McKesson. Features Pacifier and Pacifier Plus 
newborn thermometers. (800)634-1164.

Fla. — The Chain Drug 
Marketing Association will 
unveil a packed event 
schedule and a growing list 
of new services for retailers 
at its sellout 94 Fall Con- 
ference & Expo here, includ- 
ing new private label and 
import programs. 

The show—which sold out 
faster than any in the organi- 
zation’s history, according to 
CDMA president Jim 
Devine—is set for Sept. 8-11 
at Walt Disney World’s Dol- 
phin Hotel. On hand will be 
242 exhibitor booths, execu- 
tives and buyers of some 60 
drug chains and total atten- 
dance of roughly 800. Non- 
member companies on the 
guest list include Eckerd 
Corp., Thrifty PayLess, H.E. 
Butt, Ames Department 
Stores, Snyder Drug Stores, 
Duane Reade and Wegman’s. 


Retailers and suppliers 
are being drawn by a resur- 
gent buying organization 
that’s becoming increasingly 
adept at harnessing the 
combined clout of its mem- 
ber chains to set up diverse 
service programs and part- 
ner with suppliers. Said 
Devine in an interview ear- 
lier this month at the orga- 
nization’s new headquarters 
in Deerfield, Ill., “We think 
we have something people 
can really use. It’s a new 
CDMA.” 

Chief among the new ser- 
vices to be formally an- 
nounced at the fall show 
will be the CDMA’s first pri- 
vate label/controlled label 
program for its members, 
called QC, or Quality 
Choice. The program, to 
kick off in January, will pro- 
vide chains with the ability

YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — 
Opting to focus its resources 
on a few less battlefronts, 
Phar-Mor said it will shut 
down operations in Chicago, 
Houston and Michigan and 
close 25 of its 168 stores. 
But the off-price chain pre- 
dicted the new round of 
shutdowns would be the last 
related to its top-to-bottom 
restructuring, and said it 
would add new stores in 
core markets when it 
emerges from Chapter 11 
bankruptcy protection. 

Phar-Mor said it will close 
its 12 units in Chicago— 
which it first opened in 
1987—as well as its seven- 
store presence in Houston, 
where it has been active 
since 1988. Also closing are 
three units in the greater 
Detroit region, which the 
chain haltingly invaded in 
1990. 

In addition, one store 
each will close in Toledo, 


Ohio, and in Tampa and 
Hallandale, Fla. 


“We decided to exit these 
areas after an extensive 
evaluation of where our best 
long-term growth prospects 
lie,” explained Phar-Mor 
president and chief operat- 
ing officer David Schwartz. 

The shutdowns— expected 
to begin with going-out-of- 
business sales after U.S. 
Bankruptcy Court ap- 
proval—will leave the chain 
with a core group of 143 
profitable stores in 21 
states, the company said. 
The bulk of its network will 


Phar-Mor 


be concentrated in the east- 
ern and southeastern U.S., 
but scattered units will re- 
main in outlying states like 
South Dakota, Nevada and 
Colorado. 

If the shutdowns are in- 
deed the final round of clos- 
ings, they will conclude a 
two-year retrenchment that 
will cut the chain’s opera- 
tions to less than half its 
peak store count of 310 units 
in mid-1992, when revela- 
tions of massive fraud led to 
$1 billion in charges against 
earnings, the firing of top 
managers and a retreat into 
bankruptcy protection. 

When the chain may 
emerge from Chapter 11 re- 
mains a murky issue, how- 
ever. A day after announc- 
ing its latest store closing 
plan, the company said it 
had asked the bankruptcy 
court to extend until Jan. 
15, 1995, the period during 
which it has exclusive right 
to seek acceptance from 
creditors of its own reorga- 
nization plan, which it filed 
in late July.
