Eckerd pharmacist wants O.T. pay 


WILLS POINT, Texas — Eckerd Corp. pharmacist 
Steve Schifani is taking his employer to court in a 
payroll dispute that could have wider industry ramifi- 
cations. 

Schifani, a 12-year Eckerd pharmacist, has filed 
suit in U.S. District Court in Tyler, Texas seeking un- 
specified back pay for overtime worked since 1991. 
The lawsuit alleges that Eckerd is in violation of the 
Fair Labor Standards. Act because in 1991 the chain 
stopped paying pharmacists time-and-a-half for hours 
worked in excess of 40. 

Eckerd spokesman Gerry Hoeppner said the retailer 
“will review the case and respond vapioriagon pil 

Schifani’s law firm has hired public relations spe- 
cialist Halcyon Associates to publicize the case, and is 
planning ads in trade publications to solicit additional 
plaintiffs. 


Arbor to acquire Maple units 


TROY, Mich. — Indicative of the rapid consolida- 
tion of the chain drug industry in the managed care 
and health reform sweepstakes, Arbor Drugs has 
agreed to acquire three drug stores from seven-store 
Maple Drug in the greater Detroit metro area. 

The three units sold to Arbor are in Ypsilanti, 
Farmington and Lincoln Park, Mich. Two of the units 
will be integrated into existing Arbor units. 

Arbor is also set to open new stores in Mt. Clemens 
and Brownstown Township by early September. 

Maple is headed by Alvin Wander, the former exec- 
utive vice president and chief financial officer of Perry 
Drug Stores, who bought a controlling interest in the 
small chain in the late 1980s and overhauled its store 
base, market image and ad strategy. 


Thrift adds managed care posts 


PITTSBURGH — Continuing to build a management 
and sales team for its new managed care subsidiary, 
Thrift Drug has named two managers to new posts. 

Bill Jardine has been hired as national sales man- 
ager for TDI Managed Care Services, overseeing the 
new company’s national sales team. Karla Tirimacco, 
with Arbor since 1990, is now manager of marketing 
services for the subsidiary, in charge of pharmaceuti- 
cal and market analysis and support services. 

Thrift formed TDI Managed Care Services earlier 
this summer to tap the growing market for prescrip- 
tion benefits management (see “Thrift Drug expands 
effort in managed care arena,” Drug Store News, July 
11, 1994, page 1, for more information). The company 
will integrate a national pharmacy network, POS 
claims processing, a drug formulary and drug utiliza- 
tion review into a comprehensive package. 


Bellini appointed Revco director 


TWINSBURG, Ohio — Carl Bellini, 
who as head of operations has been a 
key architect in the success of Revco 
D.S. since his return to the company in 
1992, has been named to Revco’s board 
of directors. He replaces resigning 
board member Stuart Sloan. 

Bellini served at Revco under former 
chief executive Boake Sells from 1987 
through 1989, leaving to become presi- 
dent of Erol’s Inc., a > ee of video rental outlets. He 
returned to Revco two years ago as executive vice 
president of marketing and operations under presi- 
dent D. Dwayne Hoven, and last fall was promoted to 
the additional post of chief operating officer. 

He joins two other inside directors at the 2,400-store 
chain, including Hoven and Greg Raven, executive vice 
president of finance and chief operating officer.

SALT LAKE CITY — 
American Stores Co. is exit- 
ing the New England retail 
arena by selling its 33-unit 
Star Market chain of gro- 
cery and combo stores to In- 
vestcorp, an international 
investment bank. The 
transaction—valued at $285 
million in cash and assumed 
debt—is expected to close 
next month. 


Focus on strong markets 


The sale of Cambridge, 
Mass.-based Star Market 
will enable American to fo- 
cus on “operations where we 
have significant market po- 
sitions,” said president and 
chief operating officer Vic 
Lund. Among those markets 
are retail drug strongholds 
in Chicago, Boston, South- 
ern California, Kansas City, 
Phoenix and Indianapolis. 

Investcorp has holdings in 
Saks Fifth Avenue, Camelot 
Music Inc., Color Tile, 
Tiffany & Co. and Peebles 
Department Stores. 

Operating 1,686 grocery 
and drug stores in 27 states, 
American Stores acquired 
Star Market in 1984. Its 
American Drug division in- 
cludes 538 Osco Drug stores 
in 20 states and 249 Sav-on 
Drug stores in two states. It 
now operates 871 food 
stores, including Lucky

and Acme Market.

Horida's Joel n' Jerry's readies 


aggressive growth strategy 


by Mike Troy 


ST. PETERSBURG, Fila. — The already 
stiff competition in Florida’s Tampa Bay 
market is being turned up another notch 
following the recent acquisition of the Joel 
n’ Jerry’s deep discount chain by veteran 
retailers Steve Pohlit and Jerry Gaddis. 

The 10-year-old, eight-store chain has 
been a viable player in the market, achiev- 
ing $56.6 million in sales 


we are, and that is a discount drug store,” 
Pohlit said. “We like that business, and we 
don’t want to change that.” 


What will be changing, he said, are the 


ways customers are treated, merchandise is 
presented and stores are operated. 


“When you look at the difference between 


people who have been successful in retailing 
and those who haven’t, the people who have 
been successful have been able to execute on 
a handful of basic retailing fundamentals,”

Pohlit added that Joel n’ Jerry’s would

build a track record and validate our as-

are more aggressive: Within 24 months,

“The sales growth will be achieved by im-

from the front end. Pharmacy currently ac-

Gaddis would like to see that number drop 
to about 25 percent as front-end sales accel- 
erate faster than pharmacy growth. 

The two new owners also say they will 
base the chain’s future prosperity on what 
they refer to as the fundamentals of re- 
tailing.

Bankrupt Kash n’ Karry 
works out refinancing 


TAMPA, Fla. — A recently announced fi- 
nancial restructure at Kash n’ Karry Food 
Stores Inc. will allow the chain to continue 
operating under a prearranged Chapter 11 
bankruptcy filing. Bondholders of the chain 
will also swap their debt for stock. 

The arrangement is expected to reduce by 
a third the chain’s burdensome, $350 mil- 
lion debt load, leftover from a 1988 lever- 
aged buyout. It will also free up capital for 
new store growth and inventory while the 
chain is in bankruptcy protection, company 
officials said. 

In a related move, Ron Floto, chairman 
and chief executive officer for the past nine 
years, has resigned. He is replaced by Tony 
Petrillo, who served as a consultant to the 
chain while it worked out its financial prob- 
lems. Petrillo will serve as a transitional 
chief executive office and is expected to 
eventually name a replacement. 

In addition, 43 administrative positions 
have been eliminated. Twenty-two people 
were laid off, 17 were reassigned, and four 
resigned, according to a spokesman. 

Kash n’ Karry operates 100 food stores, 
half of which contain pharmacies. Annual 
sales exceed $1 billion.

Pepsi-Cola, Starbucks debut line 


SOMERS, N.Y. — Pepsi-Cola Co. is tapping into the 
$75 million ready-to-drink, coffee-based beverage in- 
dustry through a joint venture with Starbucks Coffee 
Co., the fast-growing chain of gourmet coffee outlets. 

Under the newly hatched agreement, the firms will de- 
velop ready-to-drink, coffee-based beverages. A 
spokesman for Pepsi-Cola said manufacturing of the 
product has begun. However, no decision has been made 
about when and where the drink will be test marketed, 
nor when it will be available for broader distribution. 

The new product, which has not yet been named, will 
have independent marketing and distribution teams 
from both Pepsi-Cola and Starbucks. The distribution 
channels will include drug stores, supermarkets and 
convenience stores, the spokesman said. 

In January 1992, Pepsi-Cola signed a joint agree- 
ment with Thomas J. Lipton to produce tea-based bev- 
erages under the Lipton Original and Lipton Brisk la- 
bels. In addition, the company has another joint 
agreement with Ocean Spray Cranberries Inc. for fruit 
juices and drinks. 

Seattle-based Starbucks is a leading roaster of 
gourmet coffees and operates more than 400 retail out- 
lets throughout the United States. 


Rumored Neutrogena takeover 


LOS ANGELES — Neutrogena Corp., whose name 
has become synonymous with skin, bath and hair care, 
is raising a different kind of lather with rampant 


_ takeover speculation. The company is said to be in 


talks about being purchased by a larger company, ei- 
ther home-based or overseas. 

A Neutrogena spokeswoman said that acquisition of 
the 40-year-old company is “mere speculation,” adding, 
“There have been a number of companies who’ve been 
said to be in negotiations to buy the company.” 

Speculation it may be, but this time around there are 
increasing indications that at least three prospective 
buyers are in negotiations with Neutrogena executives. 
Unconfirmed reports link such firms as Procter & Gam- 
ble, Colgate-Palmolive Co. and Anglo-Dutch Unilever to 
takeover speculation; Unilever has previously proposed 
an offer for the company. 

Commenting on the prospective sale of Neutrogena, 
a Paine Webber analyst said: “The time is right for the 
simple reason that you strike when the iron is hot. 
Business conditions aren’t getting any easier and 
growth has slowed. [Neutrogena] has had steady sales, 
and it’s time to pass the baton on to someone with 
deeper pockets.” 


AHP to take over Cyanamid 


WAYNE, N.J. — American Cyanamid Co.’s agree- 
ment to a takeover by American Home Products will 
position both companies for looming changes in health 
care and set up a new pharmaceutical powerhouse with 
combined sales of more than $12 billion. 

The merger agreement, announced Aug. 17, is the 
latest in a growing list of consolidations among major 
drug companies. American Home will pay richly for its 
new prize—$9.7 billion in cash. 

For its money, American Home will get Cyanamid’s 
$4 billion-plus product line, including Centrum vita- 
mins. Cynamid is also the parent of Lederle Laborato- 
ries and Lederle Consumer Health, and owns a majori- 
ty interest in Immunex Corp. 


Alleghany buys Lustrasilk 


Lustrasilk Co. has been purchased by Alleghany 
Pharmacal Corp. from The Gillette Co., effective Aug. 
2. Tessa Brown has been appointed president and 
Kevin Maxberry director of sales of the newly acquired 
division. Lustrasilk, a manufacturer of ethnic hair care 
products, joins Hask Toiletries and The Vigorol Corp., 
previous Alleghany Pharmacal purchases, as part of 
the manufacturer’s stated strategy to become a major 
factor in the hair care industry.

WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


Lots of generalizations can be made 
about the various retail channels, but 
the fact is that there are excellent re- 
tailers in “doomed” channels and fail- 
ures in “stellar” ones. In the long run, 
success in retail has almost nothing 
to do with the type of store you run or 
the categories of merchandise you 
carry. 

This is clearly shown in Chain Store 
Age Executive’s “Exec 100,” a list of the 
big winners in the ever-more-challeng- 


permarket chain, 
Safeway, is in the 
eighth spot. 

The ninth and 
newest member of the top 10 is 
Price/Costo, created when the two ma- 
jor warehouse clubs merged last Octo- 
ber. May Department Stores was 
ranked 10th, but the chain to be creat- 
ed in the merger of Federated Depart- 
ment Stores and Macy’s is now larger. 

The Exec 100 is a diverse group— 
with more than 30 supermarkets, 10 
drug chains, and multiple home cen- 
ters, catalogs, catalog showrooms, con- 
venience stores, and specialty stores 


from The Gap to Blockbuster Enter- 
tainment—but all the successful re- 
tailers in the Exec 100 share one es- 
sential characteristic: the ability to 
adapt. 

Veteran chains like Sears and 
Woolworth have had to make some 
painful decisions; Sears shut its “big 
book” catalog, and Woolworth was 
forced to close or convert many of its 
general merchandise stores. Compa- 
nies like Kmart and Rite Aid, mean- 
while, have sold off non-core busi- 
nesses. Several retailers on the list 
have survived bankruptcies, includ- 
ing Revco, which, like Federated, is 
now seizing a leadership role through 
aquisition. 

The bottom line: No one can afford a 
myopic view in today’s retailing cli- 
mate. There are many successful re- 
tailers out there, and most of them are 
not drug chains. To succeed and pros- 
per as a drug chain, you've got to pick 
up ideas and strategies from outside 
the industry as well as inside. 

On a final note, ’m happy to admit 
a big mistake in my July 25 column. 

Wal-Mart has not overtaken Wal- 
greens as the largest retailer of pre- 
scription drugs. The figure I gave for 
Wal-Mart’s prescription sales actually 
includes OTC drugs. 

And, as Walgreens’ Tom Mammoser 
pointed out, the comparison I made, 
based on fiscal years, was not “apples 
to apples.” If you look at Walgreens’ 
12-month sales ending on Jan. 31, 
1994, when Wal-Mart’s fiscal year 
ended, Walgreens’ prescription sales 
jump to $3.457 billion, higher than 
Wal-Mart’s prescription and OTC 
sales put together.

Does home health care offer level playing field? 


have already been brought against one

Additionally, new legislation set to 
take effect at the end of this year will 
specifically outlaw Medicare payments 
for “referrals” by physicians to home 
infusion companies in which they have 
a financial interest. 

But according to Cohen, much more 
needs to be done to curb these practices. 
As the ranking Republican member of 
the Senate’s Special Committee on Ag- 
ing, Cohen has introduced new legisla- 
tion aimed at rooting out fraud and 
abuse in home infusion therapy and 
other corners of the health care system. 

In addition to expanding the present 
federal anti-kickback statute to cover 
private third-party payers as well as 
Medicare and Medicaid, Cohen’s plan 
would toughen current criminal and 
civil laws against health care fraud. 

Some provisions of the bill are cer- 
tain to raise concerns among pharma- 
cy practitioners. Example: Cohen envi- 
sions a “national health care fraud 
data base” fingering pharmacists and 
other health providers who have been 
disciplined for abusive or fraudulent 
practices. 

Both other parts of the legislation— 
clearer guidelines to help providers 
avoid illegal activities, and a simpli- 
fied reimbursement claim form—are 
steps that pharmacists themselves 
have proposed.

Tearless Liquid Soap for children 
from Minnetonka Brands.

phistication of the licensing indus- 
try and the ever-more-aggressive 
partnering efforts between manu- 
facturers and licensing firms as 
they seek new tie-in opportunities. 


Once burned, twice shy

approach their licensed merchan- 
dise by erring on the side of caution, 
after having been burned once or 
twice by themes that worked fine in 
the entertainment world but fizzled 
on store shelves. The list of disap- 
pointments includes licenses based 
on movies like “Dick Tracy,” “Annie” 
and the sequel to “Batman,” none of 
which made a successful transition 
to retail.

about is being buried in 
product. The key [with hot 
new licensed themes] is to 
go in, sell it fast, make your 
profit and get out.” 

The payoff for both retail- 
ers and manufacturers in 
chasing product tie-ins can 
be a lucrative new source of 
revenue. The danger is that 
both sides of the industry 
can be left holding a very ex- 
pensive bag. 

“A hot license can blow in 
in January and be dead by 
October, before the Christ- 
mas season even begins,” 
said an experienced toy buy- 
er for a major Southern drug 
chain. “I remember when 
Michael Jackson products 
were one of the hottest 
things going. We ended up 
putting half-price on 8,000 
pieces we couldn’t get rid of.” 


Empathy from suppliers 


Suppliers come to product 
licensing from a different 
perspective but with the 
Same goal: to leverage the 
explosive popularity of en- 
tertainment and sports fran- 
chises as a way of nourish- 
ing core category sales and 
catching incremental busi- 
ness. And they empathize 
with chain drug merchants 
who are leery of flash-in-the- 
pan product trends. 

“The last thing retailers 
want is to be at the end of a 
cycle, over the top of the 
curve, with a lot of product 
in their stores,” said Jim 
McDowell, brand marketing 
director for Hallmark’s Am- 
bassador Cards division. 
“The retailers want [li- 
censed themes] that will be 
around a long time, but the 
‘Barbies’ of the world are 
few and far between. 

“With the media explosion 
and the micromarketing of 
TV and entertainment in 
general, it’s made it difficult 
for properties to survite a 
long period of time,” he said. 

For that reason, many 
chain drug vendors—like 
their retail counterparts— 
tend to avoid some of the 
risk in hot new properties. 
According to Maynard New- 
man, product manager for 
American Greetings, char- 
acters like Superman, the 
Muppets and Rocky and 
Bullwinkle do well on gift 
wrap, party goods and cards 
year-in and year-out. 

“In general, we try to go 
with the evergreen proper- 
ties rather than trying to 
beat the odds with some of 
the trends,” added Newman. 
“That works out to both our 
benefit and the retailers’ 
benefit in the long run.”

by Mike Troy 


ealth conscious Americans 
continue to gobble vita- 
mins, driving up chain 
drug sales and creating 
store traffic. In drug stores, sales 
are up 11 percent to $912.8 million 
from $822.3 million for the 52-week 
period ended June 19, according to 
Information Resources Inc. The 
drug trade continues to dominate 
the category with a 51.7 percent 
market share, although alternative 
distribution channels and other 
mass retail outlets have whittled 
drug’s share down from almost 54 
percent during the previous year. 

Vitamins have been riding high 
for several years now. During 1993, 
surging vitamin sales were attrib- 
uted to enormous amounts of press 
coverage about health benefits of vi- 
tamin consumption. The category 
has maintained its momentum this 
year, even though two highly pvbli- 
cized studies were critical of the dis- 
ease-fighting properties of vitamins. 

The most recent of the two, a 
study conducted at Dartmouth Med- 
ical Schooi and published in the 
July 21 issue of the New England 
Journal of Medicine, focused on 
beta carotene and vitamins C and 
E. Researchers wanted to learn 
whether a daily antioxidant vitamin 
regimen would prevent the develop- 
ment of polyps which lead to the on- 
set of colorectal cancer. The study’s 
results, which were widely reported, 
concluded that “the lack of efficacy 
of these vitamins argues against the 
use of supplemental beta carotene 
and vitamins C and E to prevent 
colorectal cancer.” 

A study conducted earlier in the 
year and published in the April 14 
issue of the New England Journal of 
Medicine also showed no statistical 
benefit from vita- 


the studies. “The thing that is most 
important is that a string of nega- 
tive reports doesn’t continue to 
come out. I don’t think they will, 
and I don’t think people in the busi- 
ness anticipate they will either,” 
said Marc Sterger, a national mer- 
chandise manager with McKesson, 
responsible for private labels and 
vitamins. 

“I’m concerned right now because 
in the vitamin world there always 
seems to be trends. We haven't felt 
any impact, but we are concerned 
about the possibility,” said Patrick 
Dewane, senior director of OTC/ 
HBA/GM at FoxMeyer. 

At Nature’s Bounty, vice presi- 
dent of marketing and advertising, 
Jim Flaherty, said the negative con- 
sumer press caused sales to drop off 
a bit, but the decline was so small 
that it could have been a modest de- 
cline in consumer take-away or a 
slower than normal week for orders. 
Flaherty felt in the future positive 
news about the benefits of vitamins 
will easily outweigh the negative. 

In the Southeast, a spokesman at 
a major Southern drug chain said, 
“There has been some trailing off of 
sales, but it could be due to the two 
negative studies, or it could be the 
two continuous years of great 
erowth cycling. Other retailers are 
also continuing to expand their 
business in vitamins, so it could be 
more a spreading of the pie.” 

The long-term prognosis for vita- 
mins appears to be good as con- 
sumers continue to cling to the per- 
ception that vitamins can help them 
stay healthy and ward off illness. 

“There are an awful lot of people 
concerned about wellness, and as 
long as the concept is taught and 
preached to the elderly and middle- 
aged, there is a very bright future 
for the vitamin business,” said De- 
wane.

In addition to a flurry of new 
product activity, manufacturers are 
focusing on product quality. United 
States Pharmacopoeia (USP) Volun- 
tary Standards for vitamins, while 
in existence for many years, just 
went into effect in 1992. “Your Life 
is the first brand to ship USP-quali- 
ty products in terms of potency, pu- 
rity, quality and dissolution,” said 
Leiner’s marketing director Aruna 
Dorin. “We have spent about $50 
million, $40 million on new manu- 
facturing equipment and another 
$10 million to put all the systems in 
place to comply with the voluntary 
USP standards.” 

Pharmavite, however, contends 
that it has been complying with 
USP standards for the past 20 
years. The Nature Made brand as 
well as private label products, meet 
all USP guidelines including those 
for disintegration and dissolution, 
which assure that vitamins and 
minerals will properly release so 
that they can be available for ab- 
sorption by the body, according to 
the company. 

Compliance with USP guidelines 
may have retail implications. Com- 
pliance is being undertaken by many 
manufacturers and may eventually 
be reflected in the cost of products, 
according to Eugene Damon, presi- 
dent of the consumer products and 
chemical specialties division of the 
Herbert V. Shuster Consumer Prod- 
ucts Research Company. 

“We test vitamins to make sure 
they have what they say they have,” 
Damon said. “Our customers are 
having us test their products more 
thoroughly than ever before, and we 
have seen a significant improve- 
ment in the products that come 
through our laboratories.” 

The bottom line: Damon esti- 
mates that manufacturer compli- 
ance with USP standards will add 
an estimated 12 percent to 15 per- 
cent to production costs. 


Herbs spice up vitamin category 


broader “wellness” category de- 

fined more by user demographics 
than narrower product definitions, 
then herbal and homeopathic prod- 
ucts would be its close cousins. 
Many chain drug retailers have 
tested or are considering plano- 
gramming these categories because 
of growing consumer demand and a 
push by manufacturers to go main- 
stream through mass distribution 
channels. 

The herbal supplements segment 
appears to be earning its wings 
quickly as it has been one of the 
hottest front-end categories in re- 
cent years. Total sales increased 23 
percent in 1993 to reach $666.7 mil- 
lion, according to David Weiss, pres- 
ident of Packaged Facts. It marked 
the fifth year of double-digit sales 
gains, Weiss said. 

Drug stores have been grabbing a 
bigger slice of the herbal pie as sales 
increased 39 percent to $63.8 mil- 
lion from $45.8 million during the 
12 months ended May 1994, accord- 


[: vitamins are included ina 


Drug Store News, August 29, 1994 


ing to Towne-Oller. 

“Herbs are the hottest opportuni- 
ty in the market right now,” said 
Marc Sterger, a national merchan- 
dise manager with McKesson re- 
sponsible for private label and vita- 
mins. “Pharmavite is coming out 
with a herbal program that we are 
going to support strongly and rec- 
ommend to our customers.” 

At McKesson’s annual trade show, 
held recently in San Diego, herbal 
product vendors reported receiving 
orders beyond their expectations. 

At Longs, OTC products category 
manager Sharon Findley said, “We 
have taken a little longer to jump 
headlong into the herbal category 
because we are concerned about the 
quality of products we are offering 
our customers. Longs is closely look- 
ing at label claims before putting 
them into our stores. Pharmavite 
has a line of herbal supplements 
that we are interestea in.” 

A spokesman for a major South- 
ern drug chain said he is also inter- 
ested in tapping the herbal market, 


adding that “vitamins are definitely 
something [the chain] promotes 
heavily, and herbs and homeopathy, 
which are coming things, will also 
be promoted heavily.”

with the response to herbs from the

Eckerd sees strong sales 
gains as debt costs shrink 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — A 
strong 8.6 percent same- 
store sales gain was the 
highlight of second-quarter 
financial results for Eckerd 
Corp. 

Total revenues increased 
9.7 percent to $1.06 billion 
for the second quarter end- 
ed July 30, 1994. For the 
first six months of the fiscal 
year, sales were up 9 per- 
cent to $2.19 billion, and 
same-store sales were up 
7.9 percent. 

Second-quarter earnings 
were unavailable at press 
time. 

On another financial 
front, the chain shaved $7 
million from its annual in- 
terest costs with the recent 
completion of an amend- 
ment that lowers a floating 


interest rate spread on an 
$850 million bank credit 
agreement. The amendment 
doesn’t provide any addi- 
tional proceeds to the com- 
pany, but it does provide in- 
creased operating flexibility 
with respect to acquisitions, 
capital expenditures and 
lease payments. 

“Obviously we are pleased 
to achieve lower borrowing 
rates, and this latest trans- 
action is another positive de- 
velopment in our objective of 
enhancing the company’s 
capital structure while pur- 
Suing potential growth op- 
portunities,” said Stewart 
Turley, Eckerd chairman 
and chief executive. 

Eckerd operates 1,714 
drug stores, 460 of which 
contain Express Photo labs. 


Competition and California 
erode results at Smith's 


SALT LAKE CITY — A 
stubborn recession in Cali- 
fornia, price-cutting at 
home and an increasingly 
crowded retail field took a 
toll on sales and earnings at 
Smith’s Food & Drug Cen- 
ters in the second quarter of 
fiscal 1994. 

Sales for the period ended 
July 2 rose 6 percent over 
the same period last year, to 
$748 million. But compara- 
ble-store revenues declined 
3.1 percent vs. the previous 
year, or 1.9 percent after 
factoring out last year’s 
Easter sales, which oc- 
curred in the second period 
vs. the first quarter of this 
year. 

Net income also suffered, 
dropping 15 percent in the 
most recent period to $11.9 
million. 

For the first half of fiscal 
94, sales were up 8 percent 
to $1.5 billion, with same- 
store results down 1.8 per- 
cent. Net income slid 24 
percent to $21.2 million. 

The combo store power- 
house attributed the net in- 
come decline primarily to 


“continuing pressure from 
opening new stores in the 
recession-plagued Califor- 
nia market,” as well as a 
“very aggressive pricing 
program in the Utah mar- 
ket and the effect of new 
store openings by competi- 
tors.” Smith’s operates 31 
large-scale food/drug com- 
bos in California. 


Expansion continues 


Despite the recent tough 
sledding, the chain contin- 
ues to expand in anticipa- 
tion of economic upturns in 
the Golden State and else- 
where. Smith’s opened five 
combos in California in the 
first half, bringing its store 
total to 134 units. 

The chain plans to open 
between 10 and 12 new 
stores a year, but has cut 
their total square footage to 
54,000 to 66,000 square feet 
from the earlier average of 
75,000 square feet. Accord- 
ing to Smith’s, the new, 
smaller units will have a 
lower break-even point and 
a better return on the in- 
vestment.

Chain pharmacy execs 
assail six-year mandate 


by Ken Rankin 


ORLANDO, Fla. — Chain 
drug industry frustration 
over the mandatory 
Pharm.D controversy 
sparked a sharp-edged con- 
frontation with representa- 
tives of the American Coun- 
cil on Pharmacy Education 
at the NACDS Pharmacy 
Conference here late last 
month. 

The sparks started fly- 
ing during a special 
ACPE hearing at the on- 
set of the meeting, when a 
parade of chain pharmacy 
execs challenged the 
Council’s determination 
to withhold accreditation 
to pharmacy schools that 
fail to switch to the 
Pharm.D as their sole en- 
try-level degree program. 

Shifting from the cur- 
rent five-year B.S. degree 
to a six-year Pharm.D re- 
quirement would hike the 
cost of pharmacy services by 
nearly $1 billion a year, 
American Stores executive 
vice president and chief 
counsel Donald Holbrook 
told a stone-faced panel of 
ACPE representatives. 


Vowing to fight the Coun- 
cil’s Pharm.D mandate in 
Congress, state legislatures 
and the courts, Holbrook 
told the panel, “We won’t 
back off.” If necessary, he 
warned, American Stores 
and other critics of the uni- 
versal Pharm.D plan will 
lobby to strip the ACPE of 
its authority to accredit col- 
leges of pharmacy. 


‘No evidence exists to 
suggest that pharmacists 
with an education of five 
years or less are unable 
to practice... ina 


competent manner.’ 


— Janice Meikle, 
Thrift Drug 


Janice Meikle, Thrift 
Drug’s vice president for 
professional and public af- 
fairs, challenged the need 
for a six-year entry-level 
doctorate program. 

“No evidence exists to 
suggest that pharmacists 
with an education of five 


years or less are unable to 
practice today and well into 
the future in a competent 
manner,” she said. 

NACDS academic affairs 
vice president Kenneth Kirk 
struck a similar note, call- 
ing ACPE’s five-year-long 
campaign to eliminate the 
pharmacy B.S. degree “irra- 
tional and inconsistent with 
what is best for society. 

“We also believe it is 
highly inappropriate for 
this movement to be mar- 
shaled along by the 
agency responsible for ac- 
crediting educational pro- 
grams in pharmacy,” Kirk 
said. 

Kirk also accused 
ACPE leaders of attempt- 
ing to stampede pharmacy 
colleges into dropping 
their B.S. degree programs 
by suggesting that they 
would lose accreditation if 
they failed to convert to an 

all-Pharm.D system by the 
end of this decade. 

“Clearly, the impression is 
being given that the year 
2000 is when B.S. programs 
will cease to be accredited, 
and we think it would be in- 
structive for ACPE to pub-

Perry snaps up indys on home turf 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Matching a steady upturn in 
fiscal performance with a moderately aggressive ex- 
pansion pace, Perry Drug Stores said it has acquired 
12 independent drug stores in metro Detroit and other 
Michigan locations. 

Eight of the acquired stores—some of which will be 
closed and merged with existing Perry units—are in 
suburban Detroit communities like Alien Park, Dear- 
born Heights and Farmington Hills. Another is locat- 
ed within the city limits; three others are in the outly- 
ing Michigan towns of Petoskey, St. Johns and 
Houghton Lake. 

Perry has also opened seven new drug stores and 
begun construction on seven others since the start of 
the year. A spokesman said the 216-store chain will 
open or acquire 45 new units in the next three years. 


J&J wins in bid for Neutrogena 


NEW BRUNSWICK, N.J. - Johnson & Johnson has 
os the Neutrogena Corp. for about $906 mil- 
ion, ending rumors that began earlier this month 
about the skin, bath and hair company being on the 
selling block. 

Lloyd Costen, Neutrogena's chairman and chief ex- 
ecutive officer, said the takeover by J&J would en- 
hance his company's image and growth goals. 

An executive at J&J said it's too early to predict the 
direction the parent company will take with Neutro- 
gena. He did say, however, that he doesn't anticipate 
any changes within the channels of distribution at the 
drug store level. 


SuperValu caps buyout ot Biggs 


MINNEAPOLIS — SuperValu has completed a 
takeover of Hyper Shoppes, operator of five Bigg's hy- 
permarkets with pharmacies and two Bigg's food stores 
in Ohio, Colorado, Indiana and Kentucky. Terms of the 
deal were not disclosed.

Drug stores lift American's results 


SALT LAKE CITY — The 
drug store division of Amer- 
ican Stores turned in a solid 
sales and earnings perfor- 
mance in the second quarter 
of fiscal 1994, pushing up 
overall results for the giant 
food and drug retailer. 

The Osco and Sav-on com- 
ponents of American Drug 
Stores combined to produce 
a healthy 4.7 percent gain 
in same-store sales in the 
quarter ended July 30, with 
total drug store revenues up 
6.7 percent over the same 
period last year to $1.11 bil- 
lion. Second-quarter operat- 
ing earnings grew 10.6 per- 
cent to $59.1 million. 


That was enough to give 
American Stores a fraction- 
al gain in overall same-store 
sales, despite anemic same- 
store gains in its Eastern 
food stores and a continuing 
decline in Western super- 
market sales. The drug 
stores also helped produce a 
10.5 percent increase in op- 
erating profits company- 
wide, to $169.8 million. Net 
earnings grew 17.9 percent 
to $69 million, with total 
sales down fractionally to 
$4.7 billion. 

“This marks the first time 
in nine quarters that com- 
parable store sales ventured 
into positive figures,” noted 


American Stores president 
and chief executive Vic 
Lund. “The increase [in op- 
erating profits] was pow- 
ered by solid results in the 
Eastern food operations and 
the drug store operations.” 
Lund said drug store re- 
sults were boosted by in- 
creased sales of high-mar- 
gin generic drugs and “a 
more favorable mix of gen- 
eral merchandise products” 
as American Drug used 
POS data and computer-as- 
sisted buying systems to 
hone its merchandise mix. 
American operates 1,679 
supermarkets, combo stores 
and drug stores in 27 states. 


Eckerd disputes pharmacist's lawsuit 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
Firing its first return salvo 
in a dispute over compensa- 
tion practices, Eckerd Corp. 
said its pharmacists are 
paid in accordance with fed- 
eral and state laws, and said 
it would vigorously defend 
its payroll practices against 
a recently filed lawsuit. 

Eckerd pharmacist Steve 
Schifani filed suit against 
his employer for overtime 
pay, according to court 
records. An Eckerd pharma- 
cist for 12 years, Schifani is 
seeking unspecified back 
pay for overtime worked 
since 1991. The lawsuit al- 
leges that Eckerd is in vio- 


lation of the Fair Labor 
Standards Act because in 
1991 the chain stopped pay- 
ing pharmacists time-and- 
a-half for hours worked in 
excess of 40. 

“As highly educated pro- 
fessionals and members of 
Eckerd management, our 
pharmacists are paid in ac- 
cordance with the same 
standards used to pay other 
Eckerd professionals and 
members of management,” 
Kckerd said in a prepared 
statement. “We regret not 
being given the opportunity 
to address the plaintiff's 
concerns internally before 
the plaintiff decided to file 


and publicize the lawsuit.” 

The Dallas law firm han- 
dling the case, Lynn, 
Stodghill & Melsheimer, is 
seeking other plaintiffs and 
has hired the public rela- 
tions firm of Halcyon Asso- 
ciates to publicize its efforts. 
It also faxed lawsuit docu- 
ments to the media before 
Eckerd was served with the 
papers. 

Eckerd called the law 
firm’s actions peculiar and 
disturbing, adding, “These 
tabloid journalism tactics do 
little other than perpetuate 
the public’s negative image 
of lawyers and the Ameri- 
can legal system.”

American VP leads battle vs. Pharm.D 


It’s not over ’til the fat lady sings, 
and there may be a slim chance that 
Pharm.D won’t become a prerequisite 
for entering pharmacy practice at the 
dawn of the next century. 

That’s the view of David Maher, se- 
nior executive vice president and chief 
operating officer-Drug for American 
Stores Co. and this year’s vice chair- 
man of the board of NACDS. 

The debate about whether a six-year 
Pharm.D degree should become the 
entry-level requirement for pharma- 
cists has been going on for several 


publicly that no firm deadline has 
been set for the schools. Nonetheless, 
anticipating that the change will be 
required within the next five to six 
years, schools of pharmacy are gradu- 
ally moving forward to implement all- 
Pharm.D programs. 

That is the trend that Maher is try- 
ing to halt. He notes that while the 
ACPE conducts hearings and prolongs 
the decision-making process, the argu- 
ment is becoming moot because schools 
of pharmacy are making the conver- 
sions anyway. 

“However, with

argument is becoming moot.

way it is and with 
all the discussions 
about health care

there was an op-

at the situation 
again,” he said.

WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


| 


years, with the chain drug industry 
protesting the elimination of the Bach- 
elor of Science option. Although the 
ACPE (the American Council on Phar- 
maceutical Education), the only ac- 
crediting body for pharmacy schools, 
has been holding a series of “open 
hearings” on the entry-level Pharm.D, 
the word circulating throughout the 
industry has been that Pharm.D is a 
“done deal” and that all schools will 
have to convert to all-Pharm.D pro- 
grams by the year 2000 in order to 
maintain their accreditation. 
Confronted on the issue at the hear- 
ing held in conjunction with the recent 
NACDS Pharmacy Conference, Hal 
Godwin, president of the ACPE, stated 


first moves was to 
commission Abt 
Associates, a poli- 
cy research and 
consulting firm, to review literature on 
pharmacy education and practice pat- 
terns, survey pharmacy school deans 
and drug chain managers, and analyze 
other data. 

Abt Associates concluded, in the 
words of Donald Holbrook, American 
Stores’ executive vice president and 
chief legal officer: “...there is no show- 
ing of the need for an extra year of for- 
mal education, the costs would be 
enormous—approaching $1 billion a 
year—the waste of time and earning 
power for students would be excruciat- 
ing, and there is a more cost effective 
and practical way to achieve and 
maintain quality in the practice of 
pharmacy” through continuing educa- 


tion or other similar programs. 

If they act now, Maher believes a 
coalition of several interested groups 
will be able to make a difference. 

Maher has already put together a 
delegation that includes representa- 
tives of Kroger, the country’s largest 
supermarket chain; the Food Market- 
ing Institute; and NACDS, as well as 
American Stores. The group met with 
ACPE officials in late May to personal- 
ly present the Abt study results. 

He now hopes to enlist other phar- 
macy-oriented associations and major 
retailers in his campaign. 

Because the ACPE hasn’t publicly 
indicated how practicing B.S. pharma- 
cists would secure a Pharm.D—lead- 
ing to concerns that these pharmacists 
might have to return to the classroom 
for up to a year—associations like the 
NABP and NARD are reportedly tak- 
ing a second look at their positions on 
the Pharm.D proposal. 

Among the most important groups 
Maher is approaching are the state 
boards of pharmacy, which, with re- 
sponsibility for the licensing of phar- 
macists, can have a powerful impact. 
Maher is also making some inroads 
with figures in government, including 
Utah’s Senator Orrin Hatch. 

If none of these moves leads to what 
they consider a fair hearing of its posi- 
tion, the chains could pursue lawsuits 
against the ACPE or form a new ac- 
crediting body that would either com- 
pete with or replace the ACPE. 

If there’s a chance to stop the trend 
toward an ali-Pharm.D profession, 
“the next few months will be a critical 
time,” Maher maintains. And he em- 
phasizes that while he disagrees with 
going to a mandatory six-year course 
of education, any alternative plan 
must prepare pharmacists to provide 
the best possible level of care for their 
patients in the year 2000 and beyond.

WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken Rankin 


Even if Congress does manage to re- 
vive some form of health care legisla- 
tion over the next few weeks, the final 
version will likely be a pale shadow of 
the comprehensive proposal that Pres- 
ident Clinton unveiled just a year ago 
this month. 

Under even the rosiest legislative 
scenario for health reform in ‘94, 


mail order phar- 
macy providers. 

The only health 
reform legislation 
that appears to stand even a remote 
chance of enactment this session is a 
bare-bones package of insurance in- 
dustry reforms offering little, if any- 
thing to retail pharmacy. 

But is this really the end of the trail 
for “meaningful” health care reform? 
Two months ago, the conventional wis- 
dom here in Washington would have 


8 Drug Store News, September 12, 1994 


answered affirmatively. The consensus 
then held that if comprehensive health 
reform failed in ‘94, the window of op- 
portunity would close, and it may take 
another decade before Congress and 
the White House muster the political 
stamina to grapple with this issue 
once again. 

Now, however, a new consensus 
seems to be embracing the hope that 
the campaign for health care reform 
won't be allowed to end with a whimper. 

There’s a growing belief that the 
next Congress can and will revisit 
health care reform in 1995. A number 
of states are already neck-deep in 
their own legislative programs to re- 
form the health delivery system, and 
Congress won’t dare sit on the side- 
lines while the health reform steam- 
roller sweeps through still other states 
next year. 

The drug store industry has a right 
to be disappointed over the outcome of 
the 1994 health reform debate. But 
there’s no need to be disheartened. 
This is the beginning of the process, 
not the end. 

Health care reform will squirm back 
to life as top priority legislative issue 
in the new Congress, and community 
pharmacy better be prepared for it.

Searchin 


that work for drug chains 


by Liz Parks 


ith only a few excep- 
tions, chain drug stores 
have reported flat sales 
in the fragrance category 
for the 12 months ended last June. 

Eight out of 10 drug chains con- 
tacted by Drug Store News reported 
flat or declining sales for the catego- 
ry. Growth has come primarily from 
new brands, promotional items and 
value-priced alternative designer 
brands. 

According to chain drug store re- 
tailers, there are several reasons 
why fragrance sales are declining in 
most chain drug stores. 

Some retailers, like Gordon 
O’Reilly, vice president and mer- 
chandising manager for The Bartell 
Drug Co. in Seattle, think the cate- 
gory is flat because usage is flat. 

Others think that their sales may 
be flat because “the percent of our 
shoppers who use fragrances might 
not be very high,” as a buyer for a 
regional chain doing almost 50 per- 
cent of its business in pharmacy 
sales put it. 

Two buyers told Drug Store News 
that while their stores had high 
traffic counts for their pharmacy de- 
partments, the chains weren’t doing 
enough to encourage these cus- 
tomers to browse through the cos- 
metics and fragrances department 
before leaving the store. 

One buyer said her chain was 
looking for ways to cross-promote 
pharmacy with fragrances} perhaps 
by putting coupons for fragrances 
on or in the bags that the pharma- 
cists use for the prescriptions they 
dispense. 


Manufacturer efforts needed 

More than half of the buyers in- 
terviewed for this report felt that 
mass fragrance manufacturers are 
partly to blame for the category’s

destination? 12

store. 26 


softness, primarily 
because, with the ex- 
ception of Coty, mass 
fragrance manufac- 
turers are not doing 
anything “exciting” 
to promote the cate- 
gory. 

Margie DeLong, 
who buys cosmetics 
for Perry Drug in 
Detroit, said that for 
the most part, mass 
fragrance manufac- 
turers are not taking 
“that extra step to 
build the category.” 

“You don’t see as 
many launches, and 
there is very little 
exciting promotional 
activity,” she said. 

The buyer for one 
of the industry’s 
biggest chains said 
that except for Coty, 
none of the mass 
market manufactur- 
ers are spending 
enough advertising dollars to create 
a demand for their products. 


Older brands ignored 


The buyer for a Midwest-based 
regional chain said mass fragrance 
manufacturers were also neglecting 
their more established brands. 
“When they do spend money,” she 
said, “it’s on their current launch. 
But if you don’t advertise the older, 
more established lines, people stop 
buying them. In this category, peo- 
ple tend to buy what they see ad- 
vertised.” 

“Our fragrance sales are flat,” 
said Bartell’s cosmetics and fra- 
grances buyer Lisa Scott, “and it 
may be because there isn’t enough 
advertising to support the older 
brands. 

“New items do okay when they 
first come out, but then when the 
advertising stops, they slow down. 
This category needs year-round sup- 
port. We support it year-round, We 
don’t just promote it seasonally.” 

Some buyers also believe that 
mass manufacturers have hurt the 
category by creating too many low- 
price promotions that create im- 
pulse sales at the expense of basic 
business. 

Penny Wade, cosmetics and fra- 
grances buyer for Harco Drug in 
Tuscaloosa, Ala., said too many 
mass fragrance manufacturers are 
taking their best selling sizes, the 
1.7-ounce and the 0.5-ounce; pack- 
ing them in a box with a value 
statement, a premium or a bonus 
size; and shipping them to stores in 


for strategies 


f Lf a 


pre-packs for counter display. 

“And because many manufactur- 
ers repeat value-added promotions 
on these same sizes every 90 days, 
she [the customer] never has to buy 
the basic stock item. 

“I'd rather see manufacturers 
think of other types of promotions. 
That way I would get better turns on 
my basic stock, and they could still 
do promotions that might bring new 
users to their brand,” Wade said.

that for her chain, fragrances are

ing it just seasonally is not even an 
issue.” 

Swartz said Gary’s can make a 
strong commitment to the fragrance 


category because the chain has the 
two basic building blocks that any 
drug store must have to make the 
category work. 

“We give it the space it needs to 
make a statement, and we support 
it with dedicated in-store salespeo- 
ple, our cosmeticians. The reality is 
that you have to have trained cos- 
meticians in your stores. If you 
don’t have that as a sales tool, you 
can’t make your stores destination 
centers,” said Swartz. 

Arbor Drug in Detroit was one of 
the few chains to report growth in 
the fragrance category, and 
spokesperson Fred Marx said the 
chain’s success with fragrances is a 
direct result of treating it as a desti- 
nation category and supporting it 
with service and high-impact mer- 
chandising presentations. 

“One of Arbor’s strengths,” he 
said, “is that we are consistent. Em- 
ployees and customers have an un- 
derstanding of what Arbor is. Fra- 
grance for us is a destination 
department. 

“Most people come to our stores 
knowing what they want. We do a 
strong replenishment business in 
fragrances. People buy fragrances 
in our stores for themselves and, of 
course, they also buy it as gifts. But 
we know they buy it for themselves 
because they shop us for fragrances 
52 weeks out of the year, not just at 
Christmas or other holidays.”

Support for prestige fragrances 


In past years, one of the strongest 
growth segments, and really the 
only bright spot according to several 
buyers, were the prestige fra- 
grances, the department store 
brands that most mass chains ac- 
quire primarily through diverters. 

But while drug chains were able 
to get a limited number of prestige 
brands, they could never get much 
marketing support from manufac- 
turers who tried to protect the ex- 
clusive distribution agreements 
that they negotiated with depart- 
ment and specialty store chains. 

Some drug store buyers say that 
by favoring the class trade, the 
prestige manufacturers are partly 
to blame for the flatness in mass 
market fragrance sales. 

To enhance the upscale images of 
their brands, prestige manufactur- 
ers offer department store and spe- 
cialty chains value-added market- 
ing support programs like point- 
of-purchase selling aids and testers, 
along with promotional incentives 
like gifts-with-purchase and pur- 
chase-with-purchase that they do 
not offer to the mass market retail 
trade. They also offer department 
and specialty stores promotional 
monies that help subsidize and pay 
the salaries of cosmeticians, the 
“line people,” this source said, “who 
service department store customers 
and who are ostensibly working for 
those retailers.” 


So even though some drug chains 
generate as much as 50 percent to 
75 percent of their fragrance dollar 
sales from prestige brands, acquired 
through diverters, this buyer point- 
ed out, the preferential treatment 
that prestige brand manufacturers 
give department stores makes it 
even harder for chain drug stores to 
become destination shops for fra- 
grances. 

“T think it’s unfair,” she said, “and 
I hope somebody some day starts a 
class action suit to oppose it.” 

Lately, however, there have been 
some signs that at least some pres- 
tige manufacturers are coming to 
terms with the persistent presence 
of some of their brands in mass 
stores—these days even Kmart and 
Wal-Mart have some prestige fra- 
grances in their stores, locked up in 
glass-enclosed fragrance islands. 

That fact of life, two buyers told 
Drug Store News, has motivated at 
least some of the prestige manufac- 
turers to work out exclusive distrib- 
ution arrangements with some of 
the industry’s leading diverters. 

Both buyers said the arrangement 
will give the manufacturers more 
control over how their fragrances 
are distributed in mass channels, 
but it will also give diverters the op- 
portunity to give the mass trade 
more marketing support for the 
brands they carry, including testers, 
point-of-purchase selling aids and 
even advertising and co-op dollars to 
be used by retailers to help them 
build their prestige business. 

That, according to DeLong, could 
be a “real plus for the drug trade.” 


EXCLUSIVE DRUG STORE NEWS CONSUMER SURVEY 


A coast-to-coast analysis 


Where prescription shoppers 


ere do prescription cus- 
tomers buy their front- 
end merchandise—and 
why? 
___And how are they affected by 
where they live? 

Do Easterners patronize the same 
channels as their brethren on the 
West Coast? 

Do the hardy folk in the Midwest 
shop more often at discount stores, 
where this channel is strongest? 

How does the chain drug channel 
measure up, region to region? 

The prescription shopper is the 
strength of the chain drug channel. 
According to Drug Store News’ An- 
nual Report of the Chain Drug In- 
dustry, pharmacy accounts for some 
49 percent of chain drug annual 
sales. And every prescription shop- 
per is a potential front-end cus- 
tomer. 

Earlier this year, Drug Store 
News published the first findings of 
an exclusive survey conducted by 
the Gallup Organization (see Drug 
_Store News, May 30, 1994, p. 8). It 
focused on how well drug stores are 
converting their prescription shop- 
pers into cosmetics and fragrance 
customers, greeting card customers, 
film/film developing customers, OTC 
customers and toiletries customers. 

The score card was mixed. Drug 
stores’ best conversion rate, 54 per- 
cent for OTC shoppers, while solid, 
‘was bested by GM/discount stores’ 
66 percent. And the overall perfor- 
mance award had to go to mass, 
with close to a 50 percent conver- 
sion rate for all categories studied. 

The study also showed that 29 
percent of respondents (women who 
had a prescription filled in the past 
year) shopped most often for pre- 
scriptions at chain drug Stores; 24 
percent went to independent drug 
stores, and 8 percent shopped dis- 
count drug stores. Discount store 
pharmacies were shopped most of- 
ten for prescriptions by 13 percent. 

But only 12 percent of prescrip- 
tion shoppers purchase cosmetics 
and fragrances from drug chains; 18 
percent buy film/developing; 25 per- 
cent buy OTCs; and just 9 percent 
buy toiletries most often from drug 
chains. 


Regional variations 


How do these percentages hold 
up, region to region? 

In the East, when compared to 
the national average, independent 
drug stores gain sharply as a source 
most often shopped for prescrip- 
tions, whereas discount store phar- 
macies fall a bit below the national 
average. Eastern women also cite 
discount stores less often as the 

lace most often shopped for all 
ront-end categories surveyed, espe- 
cially toiletries. Supermarkets 
seemingly pick up the slack in toi- 
letries, being cited by some 40 per- 
cent of Eastern women as the place 


they most often shop for that front- 
end category. Drug chains should 
take note of a conversion opportuni- 
ty being missed: Eastern women 
name specialty stores more fre- 
quently than the national norm as 
the place they most often shop for 
photo/film developing. 

In the West, supermarkets are the 
big gainers, picking

Western women don’t appear as 
price-sensitive as the national aver- 
ages, either, with price being cited 
fewer times in regard to film, OTCs 
and toiletries, in particular. Conve- 
nience, however, was mentioned 
more often than the national norm 
for purchases of film and toiletries.

Sluggish home-state economy 
hampers growth for Longs 


WALNUT CREEK, Calif. 
— Longs Drug Stores re- 
ported sales of $626.3 mil- 
lion for the second quarter 
ended July 28, up from 
$609.3 at ae for the same 
period last year. 

Net income was $12 mil- 
lion for the quarter, down 
from $13 million in last 
year’s second quarter. Year 
to date, the chain’s sales 
were flat at $1.2 billion. 

Continuing weakness in 
the economies of California 
and Hawaii were behind the 
flat sales picture, said 
William Combs, vice presi- 


dent of administration and 
corporate relations. “While 
this creates operational dif- 
ficulties, it also presents ex- 
cellent expansion opportuni- 
ties,” Combs said. “We have 
been taking advantage of 
this opportunity by adding 
33 stores during the past 
year and will continue to ag- 
gressively seek additional 
opportunities.” 

Along with the sluggish 
West Coast economy, the 
rapid growth in new units 
also put a damper on earn- 
ings and expense ratios, 


Combs added. 


Genovese again in record territory 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — Gen- 
ovese Drug Stores, Inc. re- 
ported record sales and in- 
come for the seventh 
consecutive quarter. 

Sales for the first quarter 
ended May 20 jumped 11.8 
percent over the same peri- 
od last year, to $159.5 mil- 
lion. Net income grew a 
healthy 14.6 percent to $1.7 
million. 

Chairman and chief exec- 
utive Leonard Genovese 
said the chain is “benefit- 


ting from the improved eco- 
nomic climate in our phar- 
macy trading area.” He also 
said that enhanced systems 
and efficiencies have helped 
the chain make gains. 

“The most satisfying first 
quarter result is the im- 
provement in same-store 
sales,” Genovese said. “Last 
fiscal year, same-store sales 
increased 2.6 percent. In the 
first quarter this year, 
same-store sales increased 
7.4 percent.”

HHS WARNS AGAINST Rx 
COUNTER DETAILING 
Pharmacists engaged in 

counter detailing activities 

on behalf of pharmaceuti- 
cal manufacturers risk 
criminal prosecution un- 
der federal anti-kickback 
laws if their activities in- 
volve drugs paid for by 

Medicaid, the HHS Inspec- 

tor General warned. In a 

“special fraud alert” solic- 

iting reports of such activ- 

ities by pharmacists, the 

IG served notice that fed- 

eral investigators are on 

the lookout for offers of 

“cash or other benefits to 

pharmacists...in ex- 

change for performing 
marketing tasks in the 
course of pharmacy prac- 
tice related to Medicare or 
Medicaid.”

Dealing with diversion: 
The nations other war on drugs 


Pharmacists are the last line of defense in the war on drug diversion. 
Instead of using guns, today’s enemy pens phony prescriptions, dupes 
doctors and, occasionally, comes from within pharmacys own ranks. 
Despite ongoing efforts by conscientious pharmacists and 49 


CONTENTS 


aggressive enforcement by the Drug Enforcement Agency (DEA), 
the problem persists. 


Special report: 
Caring for kids 


When pharmacists fill prescriptions or offer OTC advice for the 
treatment of children, they have a good opportunity to help their 
business grow. Read about the latest advances in using topical 
analgesics for injections, about how to recognize and treat colic, and 
about how the overuse of antibiotics is creating highly resistant 
“superbugs.” Also included in this special report is this 
month’s CE lesson, which explores the treatment of coughs 
and colds in pediatric patients. 


center 


Bonus CE sponsored by Lilly: 
Patient compliance 


In addition to the CE lesson contained in the pediatrics special report, this 
months issue offers a free lesson on non-compliant patients. Pharmacists 
can take steps to detect and prevent non-compliance, which is 
estimated to cause 2.5 million medical emergencies a year and 
may also cause half of all therapeutic failures.

SMITHFIELD, R.I. — 
Maxi Drug, Inc., the U.S. re- 
tail arm of Quebec chain 
drug powerhouse Jean 
Coutu Group, has agreed to 
buy Brooks stores in six New 
England states from Revco 
D.S. for $147.5 million. 

The deal, expected to be fi- 
nalized in late October pend- 
ing FTC approval, will mark 
only the second major U.S. 
incursion by a Canadian 
company into U.S. drug re- 
tailing in modern times. 
(Shoppers Drug Mart parent 
Imasco Corp. bought Peoples 
Drug Stores in the mid- 
1980s, but later sold the 
chain to CVS.) More impor- 
tant, the Brooks purchase 
could herald additional cross- 


border drives by the Quebec 
retailer in coming years. 

“We bought Brooks to es- 
tablish ourselves in New 
England. On a smaller 
scale, we will look for other 
acquisitions in the next two 
or three years,” said Michel 
Coutu, president and chief 
executive officer of Maxi 
Drug. 

“We will look for expan- 
sion within these six states 
[Brooks currently operates 
in], but there is no reason to 
be in only six states. I see 
an opportunity to operate 
400 stores [in the U.S.] in 
the next three to four 
years,” he added. 


Revco plans cn track 


The buyout agreement 
came only eight weeks after 
Revco completed the land- 


mark purchase of Brooks’ for- 
mer parent company, 1,157- 
store Hook-SupeRx Inc. 

The sale of Brooks is a ma- 
jor element in 
Revco’s’” rapid 
consolidation of 
HSI’s_ former 
store network as 
it moves to con- 
vert the core 
Hook and Supe- 
Rx chains it is 
keeping. Revco 
announced its in- 
tent to divest 272 
of the former HSI 
units in 12 
states, including 
the company’s 221-unit 
Brooks division in New Eng- 
land, just four days after 
completing the takeover of 
HSI in July: 

“Revco has a very clear 


Coutu 


formula as to what they are 
looking for in market share,” 
said one industry insider. 
“When they bought HSI... 
their basic per- 
spective was, 
‘It'll take six to 
10 years to get 
these stores run- 
ning to the effi- 
clencies we want 
in advertising 
and distribution,’ 
and they didn’t 
want to wait that 
long.” 

By its own 
analysis, Revco 
found it would 
have to add as many as 300 
stores to achieve market 
leadership in New England, 
according to president and 
chief executive D. Dwayne 
Hoven. 


Coutu targets New England with deal to buy Brooks 


For Maxi Drug’s corporate 
parent, however, Brooks is a 
powerful entree to vast new

Jean Coutu a strong pres-

Rhode Island, Vermont, 
New Hampshire and Maine. 
It also puts Coutu, through 
its U.S. subsidiary, in direct 
competition with power- 
house drug chains operating

and Rite Aid.

Rite Aid converts LaVerdiere’s 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — Given a green light by the Fed- 
eral Trade Commission (FTC), Rite Aid Corp. has 
capped its takeover of 72 former LaVerdiere’s Super 
Drug stores in Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont. 

The FTC approved the deal earlier this month, on 
the condition that Rite Aid divest three drug stores in 
scattered markets to satisfy federal antitrust guide- 
lines. The chain will sell or close one unit each in 
Bucksport and Lincoln, Maine, and in Berlin, N.H. 

“Whether [the stores to be closed] will be Rite Aid 
stores or LaVerdiere stores, we don’t know yet,” said a 
Rite Aid spokeswoman. 

The remaining LaVerdiere units are being rapidly 
converted to Rite Aid’s logo and store format, she 
added. In addition, the company said in a statement 
that it “plans to keep many of the specialty items that 
LaVerdiere’s is known for, such as sporting goods and 
outdoor equipment, while expanding the product mix 
to include a wider assortment of health and beauty 
aids, convenience foods and more than 1,200 private 
label products.” 


Hallsey returns to Smith’s 


SALT LAKE CITY — Jim Hallsey 
will leave McKesson Drug Co. and re- 
turn to Smith’s Food and Drug Centers 
in a new marketing capacity, according 
to industry sources. 

Hallsey, a well-known industry fig- 
ure, retired from Smith’s last October 
after a 32-year career, in which he last 
held the position of senior vice presi- 
dent of drug operations and director of non-foods. 

He joined McKesson as senior vice president last 
March and since then has had broad purchasing, mar- 
keting and merchandising responsibilities. 

Hallsey was also in charge of McKesson’s Valu-Rite 
division, which provides coordinated purchasing, mar- 
keting and operations services for independent and 
small-chain drug stores.

Kroger taps Kobach for Rx post 


CINCINNATI — The Kroger Co. has 
promoted James Kobach to the new po- 
sition of vice president of corporate 
pharmacy, era combo giant’s 
growing concern with the shift in retail 
pharmacy to managed care. 

In his new role, Kobach will coordi- 
nate and oversee the activities of more 
than 800 in-store pharmacies in 24 
states, and will report to Terry Cox, Kroger vice presi- 
dent of drug, general merchandise, pharmacy and the 
Peyton’s warehouse subsidiary. He will also be re- 
sponsible for third-party business and pharmacy pro- 
curement. 

Kobach is a 34-year veteran of Denver-based combo 
operator King Sig aS a unit of Kroger subsidiary 
Dillon Companies. He last served as director of phar- 
macy for the division.

ORLANDO, Fla. — In its 
first convention since the re- 
location of its headquarters 
to Deerfield, Ill., the Chain 
Drug Marketing Association 
(CDMA) unveiled a host of 
new programs and intro- 
duced a largely new staff. 

The sold-out trade show 
featured 245 exhibit booths; 
42 of the 60 CDMA member 
chains were in attendance, 
as well as guests from 20 
non-CDMA member chains. 

One of the highlights of 
the five-day event was the 
unveiling of the CDMA’s QC 
(Quality Choice) controlled- 
label program, which is be- 
ing put together by Shurfine 
International. 

By Jan. 1, the CDMA 
plans to be shipping 400 QC 
items, ranging from OTCs 
to cleaning products to pa- 
per goods. Another 200 
items will be available April 
1, according to Jim Devine, 
the group’s president. 

The products are designed 
to look like a single line with 
a distinctive logo and pack- 
aging that features a blue- 
and-white grid pattern. 

“We’re trying to support 
the products all the way to 
sell-through,” Devine said. 
That includes point-of-pur- 
chase displays, ad slicks, 
printed inserts and a train-

In the rain forest, the tall, strong 
trees have a virtual monopoly on sun- 
light, and their canopy greatly limits 
the growth of other plant life below. 
However, each time a tree falls, a 
stream of sunlight hits the earth, and 
seeds burst into life and start growing 
toward the sky. For the seedlings, the 
opportunity is clear: Beat out all the 
other little seedlings for that place in 
the sun, or die trying. 

With all the mergers and acquisi- 
tions in the chain drug industry, along 
with the increasing encroachment of 


stantly monitoring consumers, com- 
petitors and suppliers—and they must 
find ways to remain competitive, in 
every area from technology, pricing 
and service to store locations, renova- 
tions and operations. 

A good study in responding to the 
new competitive environment can be 
found at the Chain Drug Marketing 
Association (CDMA), which has made 
great strides under the direction of 
Jim Devine, president for the past 
four years.

really responded

WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


LL a NT LL a ae ITE SMT SIRS NI Te RR IR AA 


huge mass merchants and combo 
stores into the business, the drug store 
retailing environment is starting to re- 
semble a rain forest—with huge enti- 
ties blocking off growth, and even sur- 
vival, opportunities for smaller 
individuals: 

And yet, each consolidation in the 
chain drug field—like the single 
falling tree in the rain forest—creates 
an opening for a small chain to take 
advantage of a niche that’s no longer 
being effectively served. 

To be able to seize that opportunity, 
smaller players must be vigilant—con- 


of the CDMA. 

As far as this 
group goes, Gen- 
Ovese is a large 
chain, with 110 stores and sales that 
have just surpassed the $500 million 
mark. But for a company like four- 
store Ark Drugs, 14-unit Concord 
Drugs, 18-store Med-X Corp. or 18- 
unit Keltsch Bros., this member- 
owned organization plays a much 
more vital role. 

Since moving the CDMA’s head- 
quarters from New York City to Deer- 
field, Ill., “Jim has put together an ex- 
tremely exciting new staff, made up of 
talented and experienced people,” ex- 
plained Patrick. “It’s a whole new or- 
ganization.” 


Don't let the tall trees get you down 


In more ways than ever, CDMA is 
leveraging its greatest asset—the col- 
lective buying power of 60 drug 
chains—to secure for its members the 
prices, support programs and exclu- 
Sive products that are usually re- 
served for the “big guys.” 

A great example is the Quality 
Choice (QC) program, a controlled-la- 
bel line of hundreds of items available 
only to CDMA members. 

The reaction of Rick Keltsch of 
Keltsch Bros. was typical of the com- 
ments I heard at the show. “We have 
to take on things like the QC pro- 
gram,” he said. “It is imperative that 
we find ways to differentiate ourselves 
from all the competition.” 

Jim Devine noted that the alliance 
between the CDMA and Shurfine In- 
ternational, which is handling QC, 
could also enhance the CDMA’s buy- 
ing clout with manufacturers of name- 
brand goods. “With block buys, CDMA 
members, like the big chains, would 
be able to offer exclusive bonus packs, 
special sizes and so forth,” said 
Devine. 

Another way members can compete 
with the big guys in the race to offer 
exclusive items and value-oriented 
products is through the CDMA’s ex- 
panded direct-import program for sea- 
sonal products. 

And, to help smaller chains compete 
in the core pharmacy department in 
an era of managed care and shrinking 
product margins, the CDMA has also 
launched a generic pharmaceuticals 
buying program. 

Small chains and independents: As 
the big chains keep getting bigger, 
keep on the lookout for those “shafts of 
light.” They are critical to your growth 
and survival in the retail rain forest. 


New regulatory impositions in the pipeline 


If you’re discouraged by the outcome 
of this year’s legislative debate over 
health reform, wait until you hear 
what else is coming down here in 
Washington. 

The Clinton Administration is mov- 
ing on a series of new regulatory ini- 
tiatives certain to raise costs, reduce 
jobs, add paperwork and impose new 
compliance burdens on the drug store 
industry.

@ An end to Targeted Jobs Tax Cred- 
its (TJTC)...at least if administration

4 Drug Store News, September 26, 1994 
\ 


get their way. 

Although many drug chains employ 
economically disadvantaged individu- 
als in order to claim these tax credits 
(up to $2,400 per worker), the depart- 
ment’s inspector general claims that 
most of those employees would have 
been hired anyway without federal 
subsidies. Upshot: Congress is under 
pressure to allow TJTC to expire per- 
manently at the end of this year. 

e A crackdown by the federal De- 
partment of Health and Human Ser- 
vices inspector general against phar- 
maceutical “product conversion” 
programs. The inspector general’s 
concerns are focused on drug manu- 
facturers who pay pharmacists for 
coaxing doctors to switch Medicaid pa- 
tients from competing brands to their 
products. 

But drug stores participating in 
Medco-style “counter-detailing” pro- 
grams could also find themselves tar- 
geted for investigation under the fed- 
eral “anti-kickback” laws. 

e A controversial new enforcement 
strategy from Labor Secretary Robert 
Reich to subject retailers to penalties 
under the federal wage and hour laws 
for selling apparel produced by manu- 
facturers who use “sweatshop” subcon- 
tractors. Reich’s idea is to “encourage” 
chains to police their own garment 
suppliers or risk federal charges of dis- 
tributing “hot” goods.

GENERAL MERCHANDISE / PHOTO : 


Single-use cameras eererging 
into hottest photography sellers 


by Allene Symons 


The single-use or disposable cam- 
era is hot. 

“This is the fastest growing cate- 
gory in the photo business for us,’ 
said K&B buyer Chris Michel. 

That’s a typical response for a 
drug chain where film and photo- 
processing are almost always major 
front-end contributors. 

Adding to the heat in the last few 
months has been the new 15-expo- 
sure “trial size,” priced at around 
$4.99 to $5.99, half the price of 
standard 24- or 24-plus exposure 
versions. 

To date, more than 20 million 
households have tried one-time-use 
cameras, according to the Photo 
Marketing Association (PMA). And, 
according to Konica marketing ser- 
vices manager Dennis Puccio, stud- 
ies show single-use is about 75 per- 
cent impulse purchase. 

Most chain drug buyers are opti- 
mistic and enthusiastic that usage 
figures will go even higher, thanks 
in good part to the new trial size 
cameras, introduced first by Kodak 
last spring, then Fuji. 

Accompanying the smaller sizes, 
from both manufacturers, are limit- 
ed time offers with bounce-back 
coupons offering discounts on pur- 


chases of standard size versions. 

Coupons and rebates are strate- 
gies other manufacturers are em- 
ploying as well, which is good news 
for retailers who want to maintain 
single use’s profitability. That prof- 
itability averages 20 to 30 percent, 
while film averages 12 to 15 percent. 

Starting in September, for exam- 
ple, Konica is offering a $1 rebate 
on its single-use cameras to encour- 
age more users. 

“The rebate price is unbeatable,” 
Puccio said. “The slashing of prices 
in the long run isn’t going to be 
good for manufacturer or retailer— 
it’s better to market it better.” 


Two good years for sales 


Although figures have not yet 
been finalized, unit sales of single- 
use cameras in 1993 reached an es- 
timated 32 million units in the 
U.S., according to PMA research di- 
rector Barry Harrand. 

Those figures are expected to get a 
big boost, and even be skewed, this 
year because of the trial size. 

According to Harrand, sales of 
one-time-use cameras grew an esti- 
mated 47 percent in the first quar- 
ter of 1994, compared to the same 
time last year. 

“That’s very strong double-digit 
growth continuing this year,” he 
said. 

“The category continues 


dollars a challenge

there’s no significant slow- 
down,” agreed Rod King, direc- 
tor of marketing for Fuji.

only about 25 percent of house- 
holds have actually tried one-

Sales cannibalized? 


Not all chain retailers feel 
that way, however. Bartell 
Drug buyer Paul Lofgren, for 
one, voiced some concern that 
the trial size might cannibalize 
standard unit sales if it became 
permanent. 

King agreed there can be a 
risk of cannibalizing the regu-

children and sports enthusiasts. Af-

e sun care category is changing 
to better suit end users and their 
varied lifestyles, according to drug 
store and manufacturing executives. 

“This is really becoming a spe- 
cialty business,” said Ken Meeker, 
vice president of sales for Banana 
Boat, a division of Playtex. “We 
have special purpose products for a 
special purpose audience—sports 
products, baby products and kids’ 
products. That’s come from the fact 
that people have come off the basic 
15 (SPF) to something else.” 


New highs 


“Higher SPFs are growing really 
fast,” said L.A. Tan’s Dennis Geb- 
hart, vice president of sales and 
marketing, noting that “The lower 
SPFs have no growth or are on a 
slow decline.” 

The biggest wave of introductions 
during the resort season, beginning 
in November, consists of sun care 
lotions with SPF reaching up to 50, 
including Banana Boat’s Sport 50 
and Kid 50, and Hawaiian Tropic’s 
Sport 45 in a lighter, more ab- 
sorbent lotion than its predecessor. 

L.A. Tan has taken protection 
even further with Ozone Block lo- 
tion, said to block “all environmen- 
tally hazardous” elements. It’s 
keeping company with Procter & 
Gamble’s UVA Guard and Schering- 
Plough’s Shade UVA. 

The trio may well be on the mark 
with such protection. The Environ- 
mental Protection Agency sent out a 
warning earlier this year: “As ozone 
levels increase, measured levels of 
ultraviolet radiation are increasing 
and can be expected to increase for 
at least 15 to 20 more years.”

Manufacturers are also expanding 
their children’s lines. 

L.A. Tan’s Gebhart said: “Kids 
are demanding. They want their 
own product. Parents need to have

facturers are busily expanding the

Medicus, makers of the Original

Middle-aged women 


The study shows that

the least likely are adults 
with no children in the 
household. 


Red ink masks Perry's 
third quarter improvement 


PONTIAC, Mich. — Two 
extraordinary charges 
against earnings pulled Per- 
ry Drug Stores’ results into 
the red for the third quarter 
ended July 31, but sales and 
operating earnings showed 
continued gains. 

Perry took a one-time, af- 
ter-tax charge of $1.1 mil- 
lion in the quarter to settle 
litigation stemming from a 
class-action lawsuit by 
shareholders, who had 
charged the company with 
violations of federal securi- 
ties laws related to the com- 
pany’s stock price. While 
not admitting guilt, Perry 
and its insurance carrier 
agreed to settle out of court 
with a combined $2.2 mil- 
lion payment. 

“We strongly believe the 
company did not violate any 
securities laws,” said Perry 
senior vice president and 
general counsel Bob Berlow, 
adding that the company 
agreed to the payment to 
avoid the time and expense 
of a protracted court case. 

Perry also took a $1.3 mil- 
lion charge against earnings 
related to the early retire- 
ment of its former, higher- 
interest bank debt and 10 
percent senior notes. 


Both were replaced in late 
July with a lower-interest, 
$65 million revolving credit 
agreement which “reduces 
the cost of borrowing and 
provides greater flexibility 
in continuing [Perry’s] ex- 
pansion program” the chain 
noted in a statement. 

The combined $2.4 mil- 
lion in charges dropped Per- 
ry to a $1.1 million net loss 
in the third quarter. Exclud- 
ing their effects, net earn- 
ings would have reached 
$1.3 million for the period, 
compared with a third-quar- 
ter 1993 net income of $1.2 
million. For the first nine 
months of fiscal 1994, net 
earnings reached $3.6 mil- 
lion, vs. a loss of $2 million 
last year. 

Sales for the third quarter 
rose 5.6 percent over the 
same period last year, to 
$183.2 million, with same- 
store results up 3.6 percent. 
Nine-month sales for the 
215-store drug _ chain 
reached $552.5 million, a 
gain of 5.8 percent over pri- 
or-year levels. Perry’s phar- 
macy sales rose 9.2 percent 
for the quarter and 9.1 per- 
cent for the nine months, to 
$98.9 million and $295.8 
million, respectively. 


Margin squeeze flattens 
Fay’s second quarter growth 


LIVERPOOL, N.Y. — A 
Squeeze on gross margins 
flattened the earnings 
growth curve at Fay’s Inc. 
in the second quarter ended 
July 30, despite a sales gain 
of nearly 13.7 percent over 
the same period last year, to 
$252.4 million. 

On a comparative store 
basis, sales increased al- 
most 5 percent. 

Net earnings in the sec- 
ond quarter dropped to $2.6 
million, down 13 percent 
compared to $3.1 million in 
the same period a year ago. 
Last year’s results were bol- 
stered by a one-time gain of 
$481,000 stemming from the 
termination of lease obliga- 
tions for two discontinued 
Paper Cutter stores; even so, 
earnings for the most recert 
period were hampered by 
tighter margins in a compet- 
itive market. 


“Despite strong gains in 
prescription sales and im- 
provement in expense ra- 
tios, earnings fell short of 
our expectations due pri- 
marily to downward pres- 
Sure on gross margins in 
both our drug store and Pa- 
per Cutter operations,” said 
Fay’s chairman and chief 
executive Henry Panasci Jr. 
“While sales of prescription 
drugs during the quarter in- 
creased 19.7 percent in total 
and 9.7 percent from compa- 
rable stores, these increases 
were largely from lower- 
margined third-party pre- 
scription plans.” 

Sales in the first half of 
the year jumped 12 percent 
to $491 million from $438 
million during the same pe- 
riod a year ago, with same- 
store sales up 5 percent. 
First-half net income rose 
4.6 percent to $4.5 million.
