TWINSBURG, Ohio — 
In a convincing show of 
continued strength, Revco 
D.S. doubled its net earn- 
ings and pushed same- 
store sales up sharply in 
the first quarter of fiscal 
1995 ended Aug. 20. 

Net income before an 
extraordinary after-tax 
charge reached $5.8 mil- 
lion, vs. $2.7 million for 
the same period a year 
earlier. Quarterly operat- 
ing profits rose 69.3 per- 
cent to $18.8 million. 


Revco’s fiscal muscle shows 


Lured by a strong ad- 
vertising program, a 
sharply defined merchan- 
dise mix and an attrac- 
tively remodeled store 
base, consumers pushed 
Revco’s same-store sales 
up 9.2 percent in the first 
quarter. Total sales rose 
33.3 percent to $694.4 mil- 
lion, due both to the 
strong same-store gains 
and to the partial inclu- 
sion of operating results 
from 800 former Hook-Su- 
peRx Inc. drug stores, 35 


home health care centers 
and a mail-order operation 
acquired from HSI July 
15. The HSI operations 
added $101.9 million to 
Revco’s quarterly sales in- 
crease during the final 
three weeks of the ac- 
counting period. 

Revco took a one-time 
charge of $2.9 million to 
write off the costs of replac- 
ing its former bank credit 
line with a new financing 
package used to complete 
its purchase of HSI. 


Walgreen will open store 2,000 


CLEVELAND — Walgreen Co. will celebrate the 
grand opening of its 2,000th drug store here Nov. 4, 
marking the occasion with a special breakfast event at 
the city’s new ballpark and a big turnout by the com- 
pany’s top brass. 

The store is located in the Kamm’s Corners shop- 
ping center on Cleveland’s West Side. Among those 
expected at the ribbon-cutting ceremony are former 
chairman and chief executive Charles R. Walgreen 
Jr., chairman and chief executive Charles R. Wal- 
green III, president and chief operating officer L. 
Daniel Jorndt, executive vice president Vern Brunner 
and Cleveland Mayor Michael White. 

The grand opening will also mark Walgreen’s offi- 
cial entry into the Cleveland market, with 15 stores 
expected to be open in the metropolitan area by the 
date of the ribbon-cutting. 


Eckerd hits the in-store airwaves 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — Utilizing its existing VSAT 
satellite system, Eckerd Corp. has launched a new in- 
store radio network. The Eckerd Radio music network 
is set up to broadcast music and messages into all 1,716 
of the chain’s stores 24 hours a day, seven days a week. 

For customers, the network offers music, entertain- 
ment and information. For Eckerd and its suppliers, it 
offers a wide variety of marketing opportunities. 
Broadcast selections can include advertising messages 
customized for specific neighborhoods, geographic lo- 
cations, seasonal promotions and community events. 

Already installed in Eckerd’s two largest markets, 
Florida and Texas, the network will reach the remain- 
ing 11 southeastern states in which the chain oper- 
ates by year-end. Manufacturers interested in partici- 
pating in the program can call RJ Media Marketing at 
813-393-2307. 


Court grants Phar-Mor time 


YOUNGSTOWN, Ohio — U.S. Bankruptcy Court 
Judge William Bodoh gave Phar-Mor Inc. some 
breathing room last month in its efforts to come up 
with an acceptable way to pay off its creditors and 
come out of Chapter 11. 

The court on Sept. 21 granted Phar-Mor’s motion to 
extend, until Jan. 15, 1995, the period during which 
the off-price chain has the exclusive right to solicit ac- 
ceptances of its own plan of reorganization. The motion 
was supported by the unsecured creditors committee, 
but was opposed by the company’s secured creditors, 
who failed to win court approval for permission to file 
their own reorganization plan prior to that time. 

A Phar-Mor spokesman said Judge Bodoh’s decision 
will give the chain more time “to negotiate with its 
creditors and work toward a consensual plan of reor- 
ganization.” 

Upon completion of a recently announced store clos- 
ing program, the chain will operate 143 deep discount 
drug stores in 21 states. Phar-Mor filed for bankrupt- 
cy Aug. 17, 1992. 


Eckerd names two to new posts 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — Eckerd Corp. has named 
Robert Lewis vice president and general counsel and 
Chuck Sajeski to the new position of director of in- 
bound logistics. 

In his new role, 21-year company veteran Sajeski 
will direct and manage the inbound flow of merchan- 
dise and data from suppliers to Eckerd’s distribution 
centers “in the most cost efficient and timely manner 
possible,” according to the company. He last worked 
as director of transportation. 

Lewis is new to Eckerd, and last worked as a part- 
ner in the Tampa law firm of Shackleford, Farrior, 
Stallings & Evans.

GAINESVILLE, Fla. — 
Gresham Drugs, already 
well established in a niche 
as this city’s leading health 
care provider, is entering 
another niche, this time as 
a discount merchandiser. 

To stock the new format, 
expected to open this fall, 
Gresham Drugs president 
Steve Gresham wants to 
buy closeout merchandise 
from trade show exhibitors 
and vendors. 

Gresham plans to use the 
store—to be called Bob’s 
Discount City—to help sell 
through slow-moving mer- 
chandise from the six Gre- 
sham Drug stores in 
Gainesville. But he expects 
the main source of products 
to be leftover products from 
manufacturers’ trade show 
displays. 

One example was the re- 
cent Chain Drug Marketing 
Association (CDMA) show 
in Orlando, a two-hour drive 
south of Gainesville. The 
show proved to be a good 
source of products for the 
chain and its upcoming de- 
but of Bob’s Discount City.

this store is create the im- 
pression that you don’t 
know what you are going to 
find but when you find it, it 
will be the best price you’ve 
ever seen,” Gresham told 
Drug Store News. 

That means being able to 
hold acquisition costs down, 
something Gresham believes 
he will be able to achieve by 
working closely with trade 
show-site hotels and conven- 
tion centers in the Orlando 
area. Trade show exhibitors, 
many of whom give away 
their merchandise to show 
attendees or local charities, 
now have an additional op- 
tion with Gresham.

at the CDMA event offered 
Gresham a good deal on 
grills.

WARREN, Mich. — F&M 
fell more deeply into the red 
in its second quarter with a 
significant operating loss, 
but the chain took steps to 
halt the slide and launch a 
turnaround. 

The nation’s pioneering 
deep discount chain report- 
ed a loss of $8.4 million for 
the quarter ended July 30, 
compared with a net income 
gain of $1.3 million for the 
same period last year. Year- 
to-date, the latest results 
set net losses at $12.1 mil- 
lion in the first half of fiscal 
1995, compared with net in- 
come of $2.7 million the pre- 
vious year. 

Net sales rose 5 percent 
in the quarter to $187.5 mil- 
lion for F&M, which oper- 
ates 124 off-price drug 
stores in 11 states. Same- 
store sales declined another 
1 percent, but the drop 
marked an improvement 
over first-quarter comp- 


store sales declines of 3 per- 
cent. For the first half, sales 
rose a meager 3 percent to 
$364.2 million. 

F&M president and chief 
executive Dale Ward said 
the latest earnings disap- 
pointment was due to a re- 
duction in gross margin, and 
to a lesser extent, a decline 
in comparable-store sales. 
But he said the chain is close 
to reversing its slide, which 
was brought on by a combi- 
nation of factors including a 
tight New England economy, 
a buildup of debt related to 
its rapid expansion in past 
years and high inventory 
and operating costs. 

“This is a transition year 
for F&M,” Ward said. “The 
company has two primary 
objectives in the current 
year. First is to restore sales 
trends and second to gener- 
ate positive cash flow 
through a reduction in in- 
ventory.” 


Eckerd to sell Insta-Care 
in stategic move to cut debt 


CLEARWATER, Fla. — 
Eckerd Corp. will exit the 
institutional pharmacy 
business in a strategic bid 
to cut debt and focus on its 
core drug store business. 

Eckerd spokesman Gerry 
Hoeppner said the chain 
has agreed to sell its Insta- 
Care Pharmacy Services 
subsidiary to Pharmacy 
Corp. of America, a sub- 
sidiary of Beverly Enter- 
prises, for $112 million. 
The deal, which is subject 
to regulatory approval, will 
take a sizeable bite out of 
Eckerd’s $960 million debt 
and eliminate the manage- 
ment distraction of running 
a separate business, offi- 
cials said. 

“This transaction allows 
our company to focus on our 
core business of drug retail- 
ing,” said chairman and 
chief executive Stewart Tur- 
ley. “We intend to maintain 
our direction of strategic ex- 
pansion in existing markets, 
and we’re just as deter- 
mined to pursue any new 


opportunities relevant to 
our business and industry.” 

Insta-Care provides phar- 
maceutical services includ- 
ing prescription drugs, 
record keeping and consult- 
ing to 65,000 patients in in- 
stitutional settings like 
nursing homes and correc- 
tional facilities. Pharmacy 
Corporation of America 
(PCA) is the nation’s largest 
provider of institutional 
pharmacy services. The ad- 
dition of Insta-Care, the fifth 
largest institutional pro- 
vider, is expected to push 
PCA’s annual revenues over 
the $400 million mark. 

“This [acquisition] in- 
creases our purchasing pow- 
er and also expands our 
ability to build operating ef- 
ficiencies,” said David 
Banks, chairman and chief 
executive officer of Beverly 
Enterprises. “It positions 
PCA to be the low-cost 
provider of institutional 
pharmacy services and to 
compete effectively for man- 
aged care contracts.”

Consolidation claims another victim 
as Kay Wholesale calls it quits 


by James Frederick 


WILKES-BARRE, Pa. — 
Staggered by ever-larger 
competitors, shrinking pre- 
scription margins and other 
factors, Kay Wholesale 
Drug Co. ceased operations 
Sept. 26 after 54 years in 
business. The company, 
which filed for Chapter 11 
bankruptcy protection Aug. 
15, has begun liquidating 
its remaining inventory af- 
ter failing to secure the 
long-term financing needed 
to allow it to reorganize and 
remain in business. 

“We did $400 million in 
sales last year, and this 
year we're out of business,” 
said one embittered employ- 
ee of the firm. 

Kay controller and chief 
financial officer Jim Nocera 
said the venerable drug 
wholesaler was done in by 


“a combination of a lot of 
things,” including the ex- 
tended recession of the ear- 
ly 1990s in its trading area, 
the slowdown of drug price 
inflation and even the 
weather. Severe winter 
storms early this year halt- 
ed shipments from the 
wholesaler’s single distrib- 
ution center in Wilkes- 
Barre for 11 days and cut 
deeply into cash flow, No- 
cera said. 


Inventory woes 


In combination with oth- 
er factors, that was enough 
to prompt vendors to freeze 
shipments to the company 
beginning last spring, No- 
cera told Drug Store News. 
Since then, Kay has been 
supplying its customers— 
most of which are indepen- 
dent drug stores operating 
in the Northeast and mid- 
Atlantic states—by deplet- 


ing its existing inventory 
stocks. 

“We had $42 million 
worth of inventory, and we 
were down to about $8 mil- 
lion worth when we shut 
down,” he said. That inven- 
tory and other assets are be- 
ing liquidated at the behest 
of major creditors in a plan 
approved by U.S. Bankrupt- 
cy Court Judge John 
Thomas. 

According to Nocera, the 
firm owes about $40 million 
to lending banks and trade 
creditors, and has roughly 
$12 million to $15 million in 
total assets. 

At its peak, Kay employed 
roughly 600 people, and still 
had 330 workers on the pay- 
roll early this year. The 
wholesaler served indepen- 
dents and small chains in 
eastern Pennsylvania, New 
Jersey, New York State, 
Delaware and Maryland.

Philly prepares for major chain reaction 


drug stores take the place of such

the Philadelphia paper, all the 
chains will do fine, perhaps even 
better than before, because in- 
creased competition will cause all 
the chains to market and promote 
more aggressively and to find more 
ways to get consumers to shop drug 
stores. 

To answer Francesca’s original 
question, I’m not sure Philadelphia 
will end up with too many more 
drug stores in the long run. But 
I’m willing to bet that there will be 
different names on the doors of 
those drug stores.

Source: Market Segment Research Inc. 


Extremely strong Hispanic cultural identification: 
These Hispanics are almost exclusively Spanish-language speak- 
ing, live in areas more densely Hispanic, consume the most 
Spanish-language media and are lower on all social-economic in- 
dices. Their ties to their countries of origin remain strong. 

Moderately strong ties to native culture: These Hispanics 
live in areas of moderate Hispanic density, have moderately 
strong ties to their native culture, consume moderate amounts of 
Spanish-language media and have average incomes. 

Less strong ties to Hispanic culture: These Hispanics are 
almost exclusively English speaking, live in areas less densely 
Hispanic, have less strong ties to the Hispanic culture, consume 
the least amount of Spanish-language media and earn the high- 
est incomes.

about most shopping issues. African-Americans are 
a bit more likely to agree that they like to have a lot 
of information before buying a product and that 
shopping is fun even if they don’t buy anything. They 
also agree a bit more often that they'll pay more for 
items if shopping is made faster and easier.

African-Americans 


frican-Americans, 
the second largest 
population group 


in the United States, are 
about to slip to No. 3. By 
2020, projections esti- 
mate, there will be 42 
million African-Ameri- 
cans in the country, but 
there will be 51 million 
Hispanics. 

Still, growth estimates 
for African-Americans 
show this group growing 
to 62 million by 2050. 

From 1980 to 1992, the 
number of African-Amer- 
ican households in- 
creased faster than the 
white population, grow- 
ing by 29 percent to 11.1 
million households. At 
the same time, the aver- 
age size of the household 
declined, to 2.83 persons 
compared to 3.02 in 1980. 
Five in 10 African-Ameri- 
can households are con- 
sidered small, and about 
14 percent considered 
large (with five or more 
persons). 

African-Americans use 
coupons less often than 
the general market (43 
percent of African-Ameri- 
cans vs. 63 percent of the 
general market). But, 
their sources of coupons 
virtually mirror the gen- 
eral population’s: 85 per- 
cent are from newspa- 
pers; 33 percent in the 
mail; and 7 percent in the 
store. But, in contrast 
with Hispanics and 
Asians, who use coupons 
from the shelf signifi- 
cantly more often than 
the general market, 
African-Americans use 
none from the shelf.

Drug Store News, October 10, 1994 41 


Past month product purchases 


ow do product pur- 
chases by Asians, 
African-Americans 


and Hispanics compare 
to the total market? 

Hispanics are much 
heavier users of OTCs, 
purchasing in particu- 
lar more analgesics/ 
headache remedies and 
stomach remedies than 
the general market. 
African-American purchases 
are mixed, showing heavier pur- 
chases of cough syrup and lax- 
atives, in particular. Asian 
purchases usually lagged 
behind the general mar- 
ket trends, especially in 
antacids and stomach 
remedies. 

Asians are again the 
lighter purchasers of toi- 
letries, exceeding general 
market purchases only in 
facial soap and mousse. His- 
panics tended to be heavier pur- 
chasers in virtually all toiletry 
_ categories, whereas African- 
Americans showed a more 
mixed pattern. 

In cosmetics, Asians 
came close to the gener- 
al market percentages 
in past month purchas- 
es of lipstick, but were 
below the general mar- 
ket. elsewhere. African- 
Americans also showed 
fewer purchases, except for 
nail polish. Hispanics like to buy 
cosmetics, showing percentages 
above the general market for 
all categories. 

Women’s feminine hy- 
giene purchases vary 
dramatically by ethnic 
background. While all 
groups purchased more 
sanitary napkins than 
tampons, less than 20 
percent of Hispanic 
women reported purchas- 
ing tampons in the last 
month—the smallest percentage. 

In consumables purchases, 
Asians, African-Americans and 
Hispanics all made more pur- 
chases of bottled water than the 
general market. Hispanics ex- 
ceeded the general market in 
regular carbonated soft drink 
purchases; whereas African- 
Americans and Hispanics exceed- 
ed the general market percent- 
age for fruit juice drink 
purchases and ready-to-drink 
iced teas.

Drug Store News, October 10,1994 43 


CAMP HILL, Pa. — Fu- 
eled by strong gains in both 
prescription and front-end 
sales, Rite Aid’s sales and 
earnings continued to re- 
bound in the second quarter 
ended Aug. 27. 

The chain pushed net in- 
come 15 percent ahead of 
last year’s second-quarter 
levels, to $27.1 million. For 
the first half of the fiscal 
year, net earnings rose 5.8 
percent to $61.1 million. 

Sales in the second period 
increased 6.4 percent over 
prior-year levels, to $1.03 
billion. For the first half, 
sales rose 5.8 percent to 
$2.09 billion. Same-store 
revenues were up a healthy 
6.8 percent for the quarter 
and 5.8 percent for the first 
half of the fiscal year—com- 
pared to same-store gains of 
2.5 percent and 3.2 percent, 
respectively, for the compa- 
rable periods last year. 

Commenting on the 
strong sales results, senior 
vice president of finance 
Frank Bergonzi said, “Phar- 


Strong gains fuel 
Rite Aid momentum 


The shuttering of 
200 under- 
performing stores 
contributed to the 
healthy bottom line. 


macy continues to be very 
strong. We’ve also seen good 
increases in the front end of 
the store, which in the last 
fiscal year were very weak.” 

Also sparking sales at the 
front end, he said, was a 20 
percent cut in cigarette 
prices, which Rite Aid imple- 
mented in August of 1993. 

Contributing to the 
healthy bottom line was the 
shuttering of the 200 under- 
performing stores, a move 
which Bergonzi described as 
being “a strong factor for 
the quarter.” 

Thus far this year, Rite 
Aid has opened or acquired 
30 stores and brought its to- 
tal to 2,520 drug stores. 


Genovese sees growth 


In profits, store count 


MELVILLE, N.Y. — 
Spurred by an improving lo- 
cal economy, Genovese Drug 
Stores continued its strong 
momentum with record re- 
sults for the second quarter. 

Revenues climbed 12.5 
percent over the same period 
a year earlier, to $125.4 mil- 
lion. Net profits for the quar- 
ter ended Aug. 12 increased 
4 percent vs. the year-ago 
level, to $1.4 million. 

“Net income for the sec- 
ond quarter did not meet 
our projection,” said chair- 
man, president and chief ex- 
ecutive Leonard Genovese. 
“This was the result of our 
accelerated new-store open- 
ing program.” 

For the first half of the 
year, Genovese’s sales in-

creased 12 percent to $284.8 
million, with net income up 
9.5 percent to $3.1 million. 

Genovese’s growth was 
fueled both by a strong gain 
of more than 7 percent in 
same-store sales, and by the 
company’s continuing ex- 
pansion. Nine stores were 
opened in the greater New 
York area in the past 10 
months, and another six are 
slated for opening by year’s 
end, according to Genovese. 
He added that drug store 
growth will continue vigor- 
ously into next year, with 10 
to 12 new units due. 

As of the beginning of Au- 
gust, Genovese became fully 
automated, a move that 
should help the retailer curb 
its inventory and further en- 
hance profits as the chain 
actively solicits third-party 
business. Fueled by increas- 
es in cash customers joining 
third-party plans, Gen- 
ovese’s prescription sales 
soared nearly 20 percent in 
the first half of the year.

NACDS URGES FTC TO 

SCUTTLE PCS PLAN 

Federal antitrusters should 
shoot down Lilly’s proposed 
acquisition of McKesson’s 
PCS as a threat to free com- 
petition, NACDS president 
Ron Ziegler said in a petition 
to the FTC. Ziegler voiced 
special concern about Lilly’s 
agreement to “designate 
McKesson wholesalers as 
the sole source of Lilly prod- 
ucts” and as the sole phar- 
maceutical supplier for phar- 
macies filling prescriptions 
for PCS clients. The petition 
also urged the FTC to re-ex- 
amine the anticompetitive ef- 
fects of Merck’s Medco 
takeover and SmithKline 
Beecham’s merger with Di- 
versified Pharmaceutical 
Services.

he market for home diagnostic 
[res kits continues to outpace 
most other health and beauty 
categories in drug and food stores. 
Coming off of 12 percent sales 
growth in 1992 and 21 percent sales 
growth in 1993, the test kit category 
is well on its way to another year of 
double-digit sales gains in 1994. 
Through the first six months of 
this year, drug store and food store 
sales were up 18 percent to $342 
million, on track to easily surpass- 
ing last year’s total sales of $608 
million, according to Towne-Oller & 
Associates. Roughly half (53.7 per- 
cent) of the total volume is done in 
blood glucose meters and test strips. 
Continued strong growth is project- 
ed for that segment of the category, 
but other new segments and some 
familiar ones are creating excite- 
ment as well.

genuinely innovative new products 
are the biggest news in the category.

Technology has improved 


Trends influencing growth of this 
segment continue to be ease of use 
and improved technology. The

of the total category, accounting for 
only 3.5 percent of sales.

DRUG STORE NEWS FOR THE PHARMACIST, October 17, 1994 


FEMININE FOCUS 


Changing therapy for change of life 


by Allene Symons 


umbers speak when it 
comes to hormone re- 
placement therapy 
(HRT). In the United 
States, approximately 43 
million women are over 
the age of 45, and the 
Bureau of the Census 
projects that 20 million more 
women will reach 45 by the year 
2000. 

For the past two years, a female 
hormone product, Premarin—conju- 
gated estrogens tablets manufac- 
tured by Wyeth-Ayerst Labs and 
with no generic equivalent—has 
been the most prescribed mail-order 
drug in the U.S. 

The growth of female hormone 
products mirrors the aging of the 
baby boomer population, as more 
women born in the early years of 
the baby boom (1946-1964) reach 
their later 40s and start to experi- 
ence the primary symptoms of 
menopause: irregular periods, 
painful sex due to vaginal dryness, 
hot flashes and night sweats. 

HRT is an evolving therapy with 
new drugs on the market or in the 
FDA pipeline to address the chal- 
lenges of HRT, which are to: 

®Reduce or eliminate uncomfort- 
able menopause symptoms; 

®Protect the patient from disfigur- 
ing osteoporosis; and 

®Provide the minimum effective 
dosage to minimize side effects. 


Risk management 


HRT is not without controversy 
over risks vs. benefits. The popular 
medical belief is that, except for pa- 
tients who are contraindicated 
such as those with active liver dis- 
ease, a history of pulmonary emboli 
or thrombophlebitis, the benefits 
far outweigh the risks. And some 
studies suggest that breast cancer 
patients may actually benefit from 


FEMININE FOCUS 


estrogen 
(ERT). 

FDA guidelines recommend pre- 
scribing the lowest effective dosage 
for benefits and protection from loss 
of bone mass. 

In March, Bristol Myers Squibb 
released a new, low-dosage (0.5 mg) 
form of its plant-derived estrogen 
product, Estrin, which also comes in 
2.0 mg. and 1.0 mg doses, and ina 
vaginal cream. 

The new low dosage has been 
shown in clinical studies to be effec- 
tive for the prevention of osteoporo- 
sis, according to the manufacturer. 
Premarin’s similarly low dosage of 
0.625 is also at the reported mini- 
mum, according to another set of 
studies, for osteoporosis benefits. 


replacement therapy

market growth

ERT users (age 45-64) | 5.8million | 7.4 million

Source: Wyeth-Ayerst based on Bureau of Census 
data. 


HRT is driving the product 
pipeline in other ways. Close to the 
top of the most-prescribed list is Up- 
john’s’ progesterone’ product, 
Provera, which has generic equiva- 
lents, including Wyeth’s Cycrin. 

Progesterone is frequently pre- 
scribed for use in cycle with Pre- 
marin to offset possible negative 
side effects to the uterus. 

The cyclic therapy was designed 
in response to studies that showed 
estrogen in high doses is associated 
with possible excessive cell growth 
(hyperplasia) in the lining of the 
uterus (endometrium). 

Lower doses of estrogen cycled with 
progestin have been shown to reduce 
buildup. But now, Wyeth-Ayerst has 
a new combination product in the 
FDA pipeline—a therapeutic combi- 
nation of estrogen and progestin. 

Studies show that the first five 


years of menopause are the critical 
time of bone mass loss. Penny Wise 
Budoff, M.D., assistant professor of 
OBGYN/family medicine, Cornell 
University in Ithaca, N.Y., notes that 
a high percentage of women only 
stay on HRT for a short time. Her 
patients usually stay on HRT from 
one to five years, or even as long as 
10 or more because they under- 
stand the personal benefits and feel 
well with the therapy. 

With many questions, new prod- 
ucts and risk/benefits issues, it is 
likely that pharmacists will face 
more questions about menopause 
and HRT in the next few years. It’s 
not a woman’s secret anymore—and 
the osteoporosis issue is one reason. 


Treatment fits lifestyles 


The benefits of symptom relief 
and bone-mass preservation fit the 
lifestyle of today’s middle-aged 
women, who often work outside the 
home, are concerned with fitness 
and maintaining a youthful 
physique, and who, in short, don’t 
want limitations on any facets of 
their conjugal, career or family life. 

Most women who are under HRT 
treatment are in close contact with 
their gynecologist, but a significant 
number of physicians do not ap- 
proach HRT as a therapy which re- 
quires fine-tuning. 

The pharmacist can at least help 
the patient raise questions that 
could lead to a discussion with her 
physician and eventually to more 
satisfactory HRT treatment. 

“I think almost all side effects [of 
HRT] can be done away with ifa 
doctor will work with a woman and 
with different estrogen treatments,” 
says Budoff. 

This new generation of HRT users 
demands consumer choices. This 
generation also wants the facts to 
help them make the best decisions 
about their health, and this is 
where the pharmacist can help 
make a difference. FTP

Female self-diagnosis becomes OTC issue 


hen people get 
sick, it’s some- 
times pretty sim- 


ple to figure out what is 
wrong without going to a 
doctor. Everyone knows 
when they have a 
headache, diarrhea or 
acne. This ability to self-di- 
agnose, along with other 
issues, must be considered 
before the Food and Drug 
Administration (FDA) will 
allow the over-the-counter 
sale of a product. 


More self-diagnosis 


In 1991 when the active 
ingredients in today’s top- 
selling vaginal anti-fungal 
products were switched, 
the FDA broke new ground 
and extended the self-di- 
agnosis boundaries. It 
found, with a lot of en- 
couragement and support- 
ing documentation from 
manufacturers, that once 
a women has been to a 
doctor and been diagnosed 
with a yeast infecticn, she 
is able to self-diagnose 
subsequent yeast infec- 
tions. Manufacturers con- 
tend that three out of four 
women experience a yeast 
infection at some point 
during their lives. 

“Yes, women can self-di- 
agnose yeast infections,” 
said a spokesperson for 
Schering-Plough, manufac- 
turer of Gyne-Lotrimin. 

A spokesman for John- 
son&Johnson Advanced 
Care Products division, 
manufacturer of market 
leader Monistat-7, said 
once a woman has been di- 
agnosed by a doctor, she is 
able to self-diagnose future 
infections. 

Women are so success- 
ful at self-diagnosing that 
they have created a boom- 
ing market for OTC vagi- 


nal anti-fungal products 
(see chart on this page). 
Dollar volume continues to 
grow even though branded 
product prices have come 
down considerably and 
value brands are available 
for less than $10. 

Another explanation for 
this growth, since the inci- 
dence of yeast infections 
doesn’t vary considerably 
from year to year, is that 
while many women self-di- 
agnose correctly, there are 
many others who are mis- 
diagnosing their condition 
and inappropriately using 
heavily advertised OTC 
anti-fungals. 

Some health profession- 
als believe women are us- 
ing anti-fungals to treat 
conditions that may or 
may not be yeast infec- 
tions and they are not go- 
ing to see doctors even if it 
is their first experience 
with a yeast infection. 
That was the viewpoint ex- 
pressed by Sharon Hillier, 
Ph.D., at the University of 
Washington School of 
Medicine during a recent 
meeting of the Association 
of Reproductive Health 
Professionals. 

According to Hillier, 
studies by herself and oth- 
ers show that two out of 
three women may be self- 
diagnosing incorrectly. 
Symptoms of other vaginal 
conditions such as bacter- 
ial vaginosis, urinary tract 
infections and sexually 
transmitted diseases are 
in some cases confused 
with a yeast infection. 


Inappropriate uses 


“There is probably a lot 
of inappropriate use going 
on, and the research I 
have seen suggests there 
is also a lot of misdiagno-

Walgreens vaccinates the nation 


DEERFIELD, Ill. — Walgreen Co. is making flu 
vaccinations available this month at its nearly 2,000 
stores nationwide in time for the winter flu season. No 
appointment is necessary for the vaccinations, which 
are being administered by home health agencies ASB 
Medi-Test and Nurses PRN in virtually every Wal- 
greens store. 

Flu shots cost roughly $10, and are being especially 
encouraged for older Americans and those with cer- 
tain chronic diseases. The chain unveiled a toll-free 
number, 1-800-FLU-9950, to dispense information on 
vaccination times at individual stores.

Cadbury, Hershey ink drink pact 


STAMFORD, Conn. — The Hershey Grocery divi- 
sion of Hershey Foods Corp. is joining with Cadbury 
Beverages North America to produce Hershey’s 
Chocolate Drink, a new beverage to be distributed in 
bottles and cans. The product, dubbed 99 percent fat 
free, will begin national rollout in early 1995. 

The addition of a chocolate drink will strengthen 
the “New Age” beverage lineup for Cadbury, which 
markets Canada Dry, Schweppes, A&W, Crush, 
Sunkist and other brands, according to John Brock, 
president of Cadbury Beverages North America. For 
Hershey, the new venture extends what Hershey Gro- 
cery general manager Dennis Eshleman called a “very 
positive” relationship with the beverage supplier. 

That relationship dates back to 1988, when Hershey 
i a licensing agreement with Cadbury 
Schweppes to produce and market Cadbury’s U.S. 
confectionery brands including Peter Paul Mounds 
and York Peppermint Pattie. 


Mahoney to head new McK unit 


SAN FRANCISCO — David L. Mahoney has been 
named oe am in charge of McKesson Corp.’s new 
Health Care Delivery Systems (HDS) division. 

Mahoney, formerly vice president of strategic plan- 
ning for McKesson, will head up the company’s newest 
unit, which was formed earlier this year to create and 
manage cost-effective delivery systems for biotechnolo- 
gy drugs and other health care products for patients 
who require specialized therapies. HDS manages the 
delivery system for Betaseron, a drug for the treat- 
ment of multiple sclerosis from Berlex Laboratories. 

The formation of HDS was announced in May by 
PCS Health Systems. Subsequently, McKesson an- 
nounced its plans to sell PCS to Eli Lilly & Co., while 
retaining HDS. 

In another appointment, Kevin Ferrell was named 
vice president and chief financial officer of McKesson 
Corp. Ferrell was formerly executive vice president of 
global investment management for Bank of America. 


Fla. indys gain access to contracts 


MIAMI — Chain drug stores in Florida are seeing 
increased competition from independent drug stores 
due to a new pero: benefits management group 
formed by Gulf Distribution Co. 

Independent Pharmacy Access (IPA), with 450 Flori- 
da in ——— as members, was created by the 
wholesaler about a year ago. Recently it wrote new con- 
tracts with managed care providers including TDI 
Managed Care, Caremark, C.H.A.M.P.U.S. and Feisco, 
the largest workers’ comp insurance writer in Florida. 

“Unlike the chains, we are not looking for exclusivi- 
ty. All we want is access,” said IPA marketing director 
Lazaro Amores. “We are not looking for any special 
treatment... we just don’t want to be lotheod out. 

Exclusion from third-party contracts—even when 
reimbursement rates are low—is a sore spot for many 
independents. “In forming this group we hope to turn 
that around,” Amores said. “We would like the patient 
to be able to choose, even if it means the drug store 
bites the bullet and accepts average wholesale price 
minus 18 or 19 percent.”

whose outlines are still com- 
ing into focus, the first an- 
nual Store Specific Market-

more like a full-course meal

lisher of Drug Store News, 
Discount Store News and 
Chain Store Executive, was 
packed with information 
and well-articulated strate- 
gic insights, served up by 
some of the best and bright- 
est in chain drug retailing. 

That was enough to draw 
a total of 110 drug, dis- 
count, supermarket and 
other chain retailers and 
drug/HBA distributors and 
52 exhibiting companies to 
the Chicago Hilton and 
Towers in early October. 

The conference theme: to 


maximize store performance 
through micromarketing, 
through a better understand- 
ing of changing consumer de- 
mographics and behavior, 
and through marketing and 
merchandising strategies 
that more effectively target 
today’s consumers where 
they live and shop. An “A- 
list” of high-caliber retailer 
and supplier executives 
turned out to take up that 
challenge, explore possible 
solutions and cross-pollinate 
the industry with new ideas. 
“We can no longer just fo- 
cus on what the promotion 
is going to be next month,” 
said one retail panelist, cap- 
turing the challenge of mod- 
ern retailing in an era of 
POS data capture, informa- 
tion-driven buying and dis- 
tribution, EDI, category 
management and efficient

AMCPA sees pharmacy’s future in the mail 


by Ken Rankin 


McLEAN, Va. — Mail-order 
pharmacy providers are continuing 
to slice into the drug store indus- 
try’s prescription drug market with 
double-digit sales gains, according 
to new industry figures released 
during the American Managed 
Care Pharmacy Association’s an- 
nual meeting earlier this month. 

The latest statistics, presented 
by IMS America at the conference, 
show mail-order pharmacy dollar 
volume rising 18.2 percent to $5 
billion for the 12 months ending 
June 1994. 

At that pace, the mail-order seg- 
ment is on track to approach the 
$6.5 billion mark during 1995— 
with most of that growth expected 
to come at the expense of prescrip- 
tion sales by independent phar- 
macies. 

Other speakers at the AMCPA 
meeting predicted that the-mail or- 
der pharmacy boom will continue 
well into the next century. “Futur- 
ist” Marvin Cetron, for one, told 
the managed care group that by 
the year 2000 “the great bulk of 
our pharmaceuticals will be bought 
by mail service—including mail 
service advertising on television.” 

In a keynote address to the con- 
ference, Cetron also predicted that 


Americans. 


the vertical integration that is 
changing the face of the health 
care system will result in im- 
proved pharmaceutical care for

ed distribution from the manufac- 
turer to the people who are going 
to use (pharmaceutical products)

OPINION 


Excellence. 

When facing the everyday tasks of 
running a retail operation or supply- 
ing retailers with products, there’s not 
a lot of time to ponder the concept of 
excellence. And yet, the achievement 
of excellence—if it is to be reached at 
all—comes only as a result of making 
the right decisions and operating in 
the correct manner during the course 
of everyday life. 

Excellence is not a one-shot deal. 


Excellence is a long-term commitment 


been recognized by their counterparts 
(suppliers selected retailers; retailers 
selected suppliers) for having the qual- 
ities of excellence—reliability, creativi- 
ty, flexibility, good communication 
skills, willingness to be partners—as 
well as excellent performance in their 
respective fields. 
Who’s on this All-Star Team? 
Walgreen, the nation’s No. 1 drug 
store chain, won the Large Chain 
award hands down. Genovese, the 
suburban New 


Epitomizing excellence 
. | from the vantage point of 
» a 10-year period: there is a 
true achievement. 


York City chain 
that surpassed 
the 100-store 
count and $500- 
million-sales 
landmarks in the 
past year, earned 
the nod as Re- 
gional Chain of 
the Decade. The 
term Comeback 


WHAT'S IN STORE by Marie Griffin 


And epitomizing “excellence” from 
the vantage point of a 10-year period: 
There is a true achievement! 

Because this is the 10th year of our 
REX (which stands for Retail EXcel- 
lence) Awards, we asked the industry 
to select the “best of the best” over the 
span of 10 years, and in this special is- 
sue, we applaud half a dozen retailers, 
a wholesaler, and 34 suppliers who 
have earned Drug Siore News’s REX 
Awards of the Decade. This outstand- 
ing group of companies—and the indi- 
viduals who comprise them—have 


Chain of the 
Decade epito- 
mizes winner 


Revco. Only three 
years out of bankruptcy, Revco is not 
only a darling of the chain drug indus- 
try but also of Wall Street. From the 
edge of oblivion, the chain has become 
a true powerhouse with its acquisition 
of HSI. 

No longer second-class citizens, 
many combo stores see themselves as 
drug chains that just happen to be lo- 
cated inside supermarkets. And it is 
commitment to being in the drug store 
business that earned Smith’s Food & 
Drug of Salt Lake City the REX 
plaque for Combo of the Decade. Rec- 


ognizing the importance of whole- 
salers to the strength and survival of 
both chains and independent drug re- 
tailers, McKesson was recognized as 
Wholesaler of the Decade. And for de- 
signing a prototype with a distinctive 
“vision” of the drug store as a health 
care center, American Drug Stores 
picked up the award for Design/For- 
mat of the Decade. 

Only one REX award was given to 
an individual rather than a company, 
and that individual was none other 
than Vern Brunner, executive vice 
president of marketing for Walgreen 
Co., who received the honor of being 
named Marketer of the Decade. 

The special section that begins on 
page 39 delves into the success stories 
of these retail winners, and the Sup- 
plier of the Decade Awards are an- 
nounced beginning on page 79. 

The retailers have weathered a time 
of phenomenal change—a period that 
has seen a host of well-regarded 
names tumble or disappear—and come 
out stronger than ever before. The 
suppliers, meanwhile, have managed 
to create newness and excitement in 
the face of me-too opportunists, to sup- 
port their drug store accounts in the 
face of economic doldrums and con- 
sumer lethargy, and—hardest of all— 
to find new ways of doing business in 
the face of new technologies and new 
competitive challenges. 

Each of these winners has earned 
their accolades in the real world of 
everyday business, and each of their 
stories is worth reading, for ideas, for 
inspiration, for proof that your efforts 
to achieve excellence can pay off too. 


The leaders of mail-order pharmacy 
took a look at the future and they 
liked what they saw. 

Earlier this month during the Ameri- 
can Managed Care Pharmacy Associa- 
tion’s fourth annual membership meet- 
ing, a parade of industry experts 
predicted continued success for the mail 
service segment—and continuing prob- 
lems for retail pharmacists who are un- 
willing to “change with the times.” 


Santo told the meeting. 

Santo—an independent pharmacist- 
turned chain drug exec-turned mail 
order pharmacy apostle—is the presi- 
dent of the AMCPA. And he’s a man 
with a vision of how managed care and 
pharmaceutical care can fit together. 

“We need to manage both the drug 
benefit and its interaction with other 
health care benefits,” he said. “We 
have to help manage disease.” 

That’s a tall or- 


market share. 


Pharmacists engaged in 
‘managed care’ are too often 
being rewarded for helping 
drug manufacturers shift 


der for any seg- 
ment of pharma- 
cy, especially the 
supposedly im- 
personal mail-or- 
der providers. 
But Santo says 
AMCPA members 
can and must be- 
gin to “interact 
with other health 


Moreover, mail-order pharmacy will 
itself continue to evolve, AMCPA lead- 
ers said. 

“We are no longer just a prescription 
dispensing service,” and “we cannot 
simply be managers of the prescription 
drug benefit alone,” Thrift Drug Phar- 
macy Services vice president Dennis 


WASHINGTON PERSPECTIVE by Ken tan 


care providers 
from a clinical 
point of view. 

“We have valu- 
able information we need to share 
with physicians: information about the 
drugs the patient is taking, their ef- 
fects, and possible interactions,” he 
maintains. “Only when all this infor- 
mation is shared will we achieve cohe- 
Sive disease state management.” 

However, this vision of the future of 


Which is the real future of managed care? 


managed care pharmacy doesn’t mesh 
with today’s realities. 

Instead of being encouraged to better 
manage disease, pharmacists engaged 
in “managed care” are too often being 
rewarded for helping pharmaceutical 
manufacturers shift market share. 

The Inspector General of the Depart- 
ment of Health and Human Services 
(HHS) has already raised concerns 
that these kinds of counter-detailing 
activities could leave pharmacists open 
to criminal prosecution under the fed- 
eral anti-kickback laws. 

They could also erode public confi- 
dence in the nation’s most trusted pro- 
fession. 

Traditionally, “pharmacists have 
been trusted to provide treatments 
and recommend products in the best 
interest of the patient,” the IG said. 
But in the current “era of aggressive 
drug marketing,” patients may be un- 
aware that their pharmacists are be- 
ing “compensated for the selection of a 
specific product.” 

There’s a clear warning in this to 
practitioners on both sides of the man- 
aged care fence: Pharmacists who 
make patient care decisions based on 
payoffs from pharmaceutical manufac- 
turers or third-party administrators 
risk more than federal prosecution. 
They risk endangering the soul of the 
profession.

provider” laws banning 
closed networks also drew 
fire from the AMCPA presi- 
dent. 

These “benignly mis- 
named” proposals could 
more appropriately be 
called “any willing free rid- 
er” laws, Santo said. “These 
laws would not only hurt 
us—they’d hurt consumers.” 


Mail-order gains 


Despite concerns over 
these issues, AMCPA lead- 
ers appeared bullish about 
the prospects for the contin- 
ued success of mail-order 
pharmacy services. 

Although mail order ac- 
counts for only 7.4 percent 
of total U.S. prescription 
drug dollar sales, it is one 
of the fastest growing seg- 
ments of the market, ac- 
cording to the new IMS 
figures. 

In contrast, pharmaceuti- 
cal sales in chain drug 
stores increased 11.1 per- 
cent during that same peri- 
od, while the gain for inde- 
pendent pharmacy was only 
3.9 percent, said Douglas 
Long, vice president of field 
services for IMS America. 


Retail No. 1 source 


Despite losing market 
share to mail-order pro- 
viders, however, retail phar- 
macy continues to dominate 
as the primary source of 
prescription drugs for most 
Americans. 

For the year ending June 
1994, sales of pharmaceuti- 
cal products in community 
pharmacies topped $29 bil- 
lion—more than 44 percent 
of the total $66.9 billion 
U.S. pharmaceutical mar- 
ket, according to IMS. 

Chain drug stores gener- 
ated $16.4 billion in phar- 
maceutical sales (24.6 per- 
cent), while independents 
rang up $13.2 billion (19.7 
percent). Pharmacies in 
mass merchandise stores 
such as Wal-Mart and 
Kmart added another $5 bil- 
lion (7.4 percent) while 
pharmaceutical sales by su- 
permarket pharmacies 
reached $4.7 billion (7 per- 
cent). 

In contrast, hospitals ac- 
counted for 21.9 percent of 
the market ($14.6 billion), 
clinics produced 4.2 percent 
($2.8 billion), home health 
providers represented 1 per- 
cent ($800 million), while 
HMOs and nursing homes 
each achieved a 2.5 percent 
market share ($1.7 billion).
